profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:40:08.216+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Hanlin Academician, Court Gentleman for Scattered Service, Right Admonisher, Drafter of Edicts, Concurrent Lecturer, Co-Supervisor of the Wànshòu Temple, Concurrent Judge of the Jíxián Academy, Upper Protector of the Army, Marquis of the Hénèi Commandery with a Fief of One Thousand Three Hundred Households, Granted the Purple Goldfish Bag, Your Subject
by Imperial Order Compiles
Later Student Tiāntāi
When Xiàng Yǔ divided the empire,
enfeoffing the various generals as kings,
he enfeoffed the Lord of Pèi in Bā, Shǔ, and Hànzhōng,
calling him the King of Hàn.
The King was angry,
and wished to attack Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiāo Hé remonstrated, saying:
"There is a saying, 'Celestial Hàn,'
its designation is most auspicious."
Thereupon he proceeded to his state.
After destroying Xiàng Yǔ,
and possessing the empire,
he then followed the name of his initial enfeoffed state and called it Hàn.
【Chapter note:
"From 'Xiàng Yǔ arrived' to 'called Hàn,'"
the eleven-line edition lacks these fifty-nine characters.
Emperor Gāo, the Great Ancestor, First Part, Upper Section
His surname was Liú,
his personal name was Bāng,
his courtesy name was Jì;
he was a man of Zhōngyáng Village, Fēng Township, Pèi County.
Zhāng Yàn said: The posthumous naming system has no 'Gāo';
because the Emperor's achievements were the highest and he was the Great Ancestor of the dynasty,
this name was specially created for him.
【Chapter: In the eleven-line edition,
after "man"
there is
"In the first year of Qín Èrshì,
Chén Shè rose in Qí;
the elders of Pèi established Jì as the Lord of Pèi;
in the second year,
Xiàng Yǔ further established him as the King of Hàn;
the next year, the first year of Hàn was proclaimed;
in the fifth year he ascended the imperial throne."
thirty-seven characters.
It lacks
"Zhāng Yàn"
to
"name for him"
twenty-five characters.
1 Winter,
tenth month,
In ancient times, there were three zhēng: Zǐ was the celestial zhēng,
used by the Zhōu,
taking the eleventh month as the start of the year;
Chǒu was the terrestrial zhēng,
used by the Yīn,
taking the twelfth month as the start of the year;
Yín was the human zhēng,
used by the Xià,
taking the thirteenth month as the start of the year.
The Qín,
with the virtue of Water,
said that in the month of Jiànhài, Water attains its position,
therefore they took the tenth month as the start of the year.
Emperor Gāozǔ arrived at Bàshàng in the tenth month,
and thus did not change it.
By the first year of the Tàichū era of Emperor Wǔ,
the calendar was fixed,
and they changed to use the Xià zhēng,
beginning to take Yín as the start of the year;
up to the present day, this is followed.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Records of the Grand Historian, the Book of Hàn, and Xún Yuè's Annals of Hàn,
all say
"In this month, the five planets gathered at Dōngjǐng."

According to the Book of Later Wèi by Wèi Shōu, in the biography of Gāo Yǔn: Cuī Hào gathered various astronomers to examine and compare solar and lunar eclipses and the movements of the five planets since the beginning of the Hàn era,
and also criticized the errors of previous histories,
separately creating a Wèi calendar,
which he showed to Yǔn.
Yǔn said:
"Those who speak well of distant matters must first verify with the near.
Moreover, in the winter tenth month of the first year of Hàn, the five planets gathered at Dōngjǐng,
this is a shallow matter of calendrical technique.
Now you criticize Hàn histories but do not perceive this error,
I fear that later critics of the present will be just like the present critics of the past."
Hào said:
"What is the error you speak of?"
Yǔn said:
"According to the Star Tradition: The two planets Venus and Mercury always follow the sun in their movement.
In the winter tenth month,
at dawn the sun is at Wěi and Jī,
and sets in the south of Shēn,
while Dōngjǐng is just rising in the north of Yín.
How could these two planets move opposite to the sun!
This is the historians wishing to deify the event,
not further reasoning it out."
Hào said:
"If one wishes to create an anomaly,
what is not possible!
You alone do not doubt the gathering of three planets,
yet find the coming of two planets strange."
Yǔn said:
"This cannot be disputed with empty words,
it should be re-examined."
Those present at the time all thought it strange.
Yóu Yǎ, Junior Tutor of the Eastern Palace, said:
"Lord Gāo is skilled in calendrics,
he surely does not speak idly."
Over a year later,
Hào said to Yǔn:
"Regarding what we discussed earlier,
I originally did not pay it much mind;
but upon further investigation,
it indeed was as you said.
They gathered at Dōngjǐng in the previous third month,
not the tenth month."
Now we follow this,
and do not say the five planets gathered in the tenth month.
With a silk cord tied around his neck,
sealing the imperial seal, tally, and scepter,
he surrendered by the side of the Zhǐdào road.
Yìng Shào says: Zǐyīng did not dare to assume the imperial title,
but only called himself king.
Plain carriage, white horse,
the attire of a mourner.
The cord,
is the sash of the Son of Heaven.
Tying it around the neck,
indicates the wish to commit suicide.
Master Yán says: This cord,
refers to the ribbon,
used to carry the seal.
Cord,
is pronounced zǒng wǔ fān,
it is the present-day multicolored ribbon.
Yìng Shào says: The seal,
is a token of trust;
in ancient times, high and low alike used it.
The Zuǒzhuàn: When Duke Xiāng was in Chǔ,
Jì Wǔzǐ sent Gōngyě to inquire about the sealed letter,
pursued and gave it to him.
In Qín and Hàn, the esteemed considered it a token of trust,
those below avoided it.
The Hàn Official Ceremonial says: Zǐyīng presented the First Emperor's seal,
and it was thus used;
passed down generation after generation,
it was called
"the Hàn Hereditary Imperial Seal."
Shěn Yuē says: When Gāozǔ entered the passes,
he obtained the First Emperor of Qín's Lántián jade seal,
with a chīhǔ knob,
the inscription said
"Having received Heaven's Mandate,
the Emperor's longevity and prosperity."
Later generations named it the Hereditary Imperial Seal.
The Correct Meanings of the Records of the Grand Historian says: The Son of Heaven has six seals: the Emperor's Travel Seal,
the Emperor's Seal,
the Emperor's Trust Seal,
the Son of Heaven's Travel Seal,
the Son of Heaven's Seal,
the Son of Heaven's Trust Seal,
used for all matters,
the seal orders are implemented.
The Son of Heaven's Trust Seal,
is used for promotions, appointments, and enfeoffing feudal lords,
for mobilizing troops,
all sealed with Wǔdū purple clay.
Yú Xǐ's Zhìlín says: The Hereditary Imperial Seal is naturally outside the six seals;
the Son of Heaven has seven seals in total.
Tally,
the Shuōwén says: a token of trust.
Wéi Zhāo says: The tally,
is the troop mobilization tally.
Master Yán says: The tally,
is what is matched to form a contract.
The Zhōulǐ,
under the Earth Officials section, has the Keeper of the Scepter.
Zhèng Xuán comments: The scepter,
is like a token of trust,
the token carried by the envoy.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng says: The scepter is one foot two inches long;
from Qín and Hàn onward, it was changed to the shape of a banner [AS-FBEF] square [AS-FBED]([AS-FEF4] [AS-FBEC] child)[AS-FBF0].
Wéi Zhāo says: The scepter,
is what the envoy holds.
The Shìmíng says: It is the scepter for issuing commands, rewards, and punishments.
Master Yán says: The scepter is made of fur,
layered top and bottom,
modeled after bamboo joints,
the messenger holds it as a token of trust.
Xú Guǎng says: Zhǐdào,
is in Bàlíng.
Sū Lín says: It is the name of a station,
located thirteen lǐ east of Cháng'ān.
The Hàn Palaces and Halls Commentary says: Zhǐdào station is four lǐ east of the Bàchéng observatory,
the observatory is a hundred paces east of the Bà River.
The Expanded Geography: Zhǐ,
pronounced zhǐ.
Zhǐdào is located sixteen lǐ northeast of Wànnián County in Yōng Prefecture, within the park.
The Lord of Pèi said:
"When King Huái first sent me,
it was certainly because I could be tolerant.
The event is seen in the second year of the Second Emperor of Qín in the previous scroll.
Killing him would be inauspicious."
He then handed him over to the officials.
Hand over,
means to entrust.
Handing over to the officials means,
entrusting him to the officials,
to have them guard him.
Hand over,
is pronounced zhī yù fān.
Jiǎ Yì's Discourse says: Qín, with its small territory, attained the power of ten thousand chariots,
summoned the eight provinces and made the other feudal lords pay court,
for over a hundred years,
and then made the six directions its home,
the six directions being
heaven, earth, east, west, south, north.
One man raised trouble and the seven temples collapsed,
he died by the hands of others,
becoming the laughingstock of the world.
Why?
Because benevolence and righteousness were not applied, and the circumstances of attack and defense were different.
2 The Lord of Pei entered Xiányáng from the west.
The various generals all rushed to the treasuries containing gold, silk, and valuables to divide them;
only Xiāo Hé went in first to collect the maps and registers from the Qin chancellor's office and stored them away.
Because of this, the Lord of Pei was able to fully understand the strategic passes and barriers of the empire,
the number of households, and the locations of strength and weakness.
The Lord of Pei saw the Qin palaces, curtains and canopies, dogs and horses, precious treasures, and women, numbering in the thousands,
and intended to stay and reside there.
Fán Kuài remonstrated, saying:
"Does the Lord of Pei wish to possess the empire,
or does he wish to become a wealthy householder?
All these extravagant and luxurious things
are precisely what caused Qin's downfall.
What use are they to the Lord of Pei!
I urge you to quickly return to Bàshàng,
and not remain in the palaces!"
Fán Kuài rose from being a dog butcher,
yet his insight was such.
I say that among Kuài's merits, his remonstrance against staying in the Qin palaces should be considered foremost.
His reproach of Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén comes second.
The Surname Genealogy states: King Xuān of Zhōu enfeoffed Zhòng Shānfǔ at Fán,
and later they took this as their surname.
Zhāng Liáng said:
"Because Qin was without the Way,
therefore the Lord of Pei was able to come here.
Now, to rid the empire of its cruel oppressors,
one should use plain white silk as one's capital.
Plain white silk
is the clothing of mourning;
it means to console the people.
'For' (wèi)
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
'Plain white silk' (gǎo)
is pronounced gōng lǎo fān.
If you immediately settle into its pleasures,
this is what is called 'aiding Jié in his tyranny.'
Moreover, loyal words grate on the ears but benefit conduct;
strong medicine is bitter to the mouth but benefits illness.
I hope the Lord of Pei will heed Fán Kuài's words!"
The Lord of Pei then led his army back to Bàshàng.
In the eleventh month,
the Lord of Pei summoned all the elders and prominent men of the various counties,
and said to them:
"Elders, you have long suffered under the harsh laws of Qin!
I made a pact with the other feudal lords:
whoever enters the passes first shall be king there;
I am to be king within the passes.
I make a pact with you elders:
the laws shall be only three articles: he who kills shall die;
he who wounds or steals shall be punished according to the crime.
Fú Qián said: Laws are made according to the severity [of the offense].
Lǐ Qí said: In wounding, there is right and wrong;
in theft, the booty may be more or less;
the charges cannot be predetermined.
Generally speaking of 'punishment according to the crime,'
one does not know what crime it matches.
Master Yán said: 'Dǐ'
means 'to reach,'
'to match.'
The explanations of both Fú and Lǐ are correct.
'Dǐ'
is pronounced dīng lǐ fān.
All officials and people shall remain in their places as before.
'Àn'
means order;
'dǔ'
means a wall: it means not to move or relocate.
'Qù'
is pronounced qiāng lǚ fān.
I have come to rid you elders of harm,
not to commit any violence or encroachment;
do not fear!
Moreover, the reason I have led the army back to Bàshàng
is to wait for the other feudal lords to arrive and settle the agreements."
He then sent men to travel with Qin officials through the counties, townships, and settlements,
to announce and instruct them.
According to the Qin system: A county was generally about a hundred *li* square,
with one亭 (tíng) every ten *li*,
and ten亭 (tíng) made one乡 (xiāng),
which were the enfeoffed food estates.
'Wèi'
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
'Xíng'
is pronounced xià mèng fān.
[The people] vied to bring oxen, sheep, wine, and food to offer to the soldiers.
The Lord of Pei again declined and would not accept,
saying:
"The granary grain is plentiful,
we are not lacking,
and I do not wish to burden the people."
The people were even more pleased,
fearing only that the Lord of Pei would not become the King of Qin.
Xiàng Yǔ, having pacified Héběi,
led the armies of the feudal lords, intending to enter the passes from the west.
Previously,
when officers, soldiers, conscript laborers, and garrison troops of the feudal lords passed through Qínzhōng,
the officials and soldiers of Qínzhōng often treated them very badly.
This means they showed no good conduct.
'Xiān'
is pronounced xī jiàn fān.
'Yáo'
is read as 'yáo' (conscript labor).
The officers and soldiers of the feudal lords, riding on their victory, often treated them as slaves and captives,
lightly insulting and humiliating the Qin officers and soldiers.
The Qin officers and soldiers harbored much resentment,
and whispered among themselves:
"General Zhāng and others deceived us into surrendering to the feudal lords.
If we can now enter the passes and defeat Qin,
that is excellent;
but if we cannot,
the feudal lords will take us captive eastward,
and Qin will in turn execute all our parents, wives, and children.
What then shall we do?"
The generals heard hints of their plan,
and reported it to Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ summoned Qíng Bù and General Pú to discuss, saying:
"The Qin officers and soldiers are still numerous,
and their hearts are not submissive.
If they do not obey upon reaching the passes,
the situation will certainly be dangerous.
It would be better to attack and kill them,
and enter Qin only with Zhāng Hán, Chief Clerk Sīmǎ Xīn, and Commandant Dǒng Yì."
Thereupon, the Chǔ army attacked at night and buried alive more than two hundred thousand Qin soldiers south of Xīn'ān city.
According to the Treatise of Bān Gù,
[Xīn'ān] county belonged to the Hóngnóng commandery.
Master Yán said: It is present-day Gǔzhōu county.
The *Kuòdìzhì* states: The old city of Xīn'ān
was twelve *li* east of Miǎnchí county in Luòzhōu.
3 Someone advised the Lord of Pei, saying:
"Qin's wealth is ten times that of the empire,
and its terrain is strong.
I have heard that Xiàng Yǔ has titled Zhāng Hán as the King of Yōng,
to be king within the passes.
Now if he comes,
I fear the Lord of Pei will not be able to possess this.
You should quickly send troops to guard Hángǔ Pass,
and not allow the armies of the feudal lords to enter;
gradually conscript soldiers from within the passes to increase your own strength,
and resist them."
The Lord of Pei agreed with this plan,
and followed it.
Soon after, Xiàng Yǔ reached the pass,
and the pass gate was closed.
Hearing that the Lord of Pei had already secured the area within the passes,
he was greatly enraged,
and sent Qíng Bù and others to attack and break through Hángǔ Pass.
In the twelfth month,
Xiàng Yǔ advanced to Xì.
The Lord of Pei's Left Marshal Cáo Wúshāng sent someone to tell Xiàng Yǔ:
"The Lord of Pei wishes to be king within the passes,
to make Zǐ Yīng his chancellor,
and to possess all the precious treasures."
He wished to seek enfeoffment [by reporting this].
Xiàng Yǔ was greatly enraged,
feasted his soldiers,
and planned to attack the Lord of Pei's army the next morning.
At this time,
Xiàng Yǔ had four hundred thousand troops,
号称 (hàochēng) one million,
stationed at Hóngmén in Xīnfēng;
Xīnfēng county was originally the Qin settlement of Líyì,
established only in the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ's reign;
the historian uses the later county name to record it.
Yìng Shào said: The Grand Supreme Emperor longed to return east,
so then Emperor Gāozǔ rebuilt the city's streets and wards to resemble Fēng,
moved people from Fēng to populate it,
hence it was called Xīnfēng (New Fēng).
Mèng Kāng said: Hóngmén is seventeen *li* east of Xīnfēng,
the name of the old main road descending a slope.
Yáo Chá said: It is east of the old Xīnfēng city,
before reaching the Xì River.
South of the road is a broken plateau,
with a cave opening running north-south, that is the place.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* notes: East of the present old Xīnfēng city there is a slope,
over two *li* long,
a channel cut through the plateau forming a passage,
open north and south,
like a wide gate opening,
called Hóngmén.
Mèng Kāng said it was seventeen *li* east of Xīnfēng,
but that is not so;
he probably referred to the county seat,
not the city.
From the old Xīnfēng city west to Bàchéng is fifty *li*,
ten *li* west of Bàchéng is the Bà River,
and another twenty *li* west is Cháng'ān city.
[The Lord of Pei]号称 (hàochēng) two hundred thousand troops,
stationed at Bàshàng.
Fàn Zēng advised Xiàng Yǔ, saying:
"When the Lord of Pèi resided east of the mountains,
he was greedy for wealth
and fond of women.
Now that he has entered the passes,
he takes no goods or property,
and shows no favor to women.
This shows his ambitions are not small.
I had someone observe his aura,
and it was all dragons and tigers,
forming five colors.
This is the aura of the Son of Heaven.
The Zhōu Rituals state: The Shìjìn official was in charge of the ten methods of atmospheric phenomena,
to observe omens of calamity and auspiciousness,
and distinguish good and bad fortune.
These are what later generations called 'aura observers.'
The Astronomical Treatise of the Jìn History states: The aura of the Son of Heaven
is red inside and yellow outside.
Wherever it emanates from the four directions, there should be a king.
If the Son of Heaven wishes to travel to a place,
that place will also first emit this aura,
sometimes like a city gate faintly visible in the misty aura,
sometimes the aura resembling a person in black clothes without hands,
to the west of the sun,
sometimes like a dragon horse,
sometimes multicolored and densely soaring to the sky—
all are the aura of an emperor.
The Left Assistant of Chǔ, Xiàng Bó—
the Chǔ government had Left Assistant and Right Assistant.
had always been on good terms with Zhāng Liáng.
So he galloped by night to the Lord of Pèi's army,
privately met with Zhāng Liáng,
and fully informed him of the matter,
wanting to call him to leave together,
saying:
'Do not die together!'
Zhāng Liáng said:
'I am here on behalf of the King of Hán to escort the Lord of Pèi.
Now that the Lord of Pèi is in danger,
to flee and leave
would be unrighteous.
I must inform him.'
Liáng then entered
and fully informed the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi was greatly alarmed.
Liáng said:
'Do you estimate your soldiers are sufficient to withstand Xiàng Yǔ?'
The Lord of Pèi remained silent and said:
'Certainly not.
So what should be done about it?'
Zhāng Liáng said:
'I request to go and speak to Xiàng Bó,
saying that the Lord of Pèi does not dare to rebel.'
The Lord of Pèi said:
'How are you, sir, acquainted with Xiàng Bó?'
Zhāng Liáng said:
'During the Qín era, he traveled with me.
He once killed a man,
and I saved his life.
Now that there is urgent business,
he fortunately came to inform me.'
The Lord of Pèi said:
'Who is older, you or him?'
Liáng said:
'He is older than I.'
The Lord of Pèi said:
'Please call him in for me,
I will treat him as an elder brother.'
Zhāng Liáng went out
and firmly invited Xiàng Bó;
Xiàng Bó then entered to see the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi offered a cup of wine to toast his longevity,
and they pledged to become relatives by marriage,
saying:
'When I entered the passes,
I dared not take the slightest thing,
Wén Yǐng said: 'Háo'
means that in autumn it becomes fine,
speaking of its abundance.
Master Yán Gǔ said: When the háo forms,
its tip is extremely fine,
precisely suitable to illustrate smallness,
not speaking of its abundance.
'Jìn'
is pronounced 'qí jìn.'
I sealed the treasuries and storehouses to await the general.
The reason I sent generals to guard the passes
was to guard against other bandits entering and exiting and unexpected events.
Day and night I have hoped for the general's arrival.
How would I dare to rebel!
I hope you, elder brother, will fully explain that I dare not betray virtue.'
Xiàng Bó agreed,
and said to the Lord of Pèi:
'Tomorrow morning you must come early to apologize.'
The Lord of Pèi said:
'Yes.'
Thereupon Xiàng Bó again left at night,
reached the army camp,
and fully reported the Lord of Pèi's words to Xiàng Yǔ;
then he said:
'If the Lord of Pèi had not first broken through Guānzhōng,
would you, sir, dare to enter?
Now when a man has great merit and you attack him,
it is unrighteous.
It would be better to treat him well because of this.'
Xiàng Yǔ agreed.
The next morning, the Lord of Pèi came with over a hundred horsemen to see Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén,
and apologized, saying:
'You, general, and I joined forces to attack Qín.
You, general, fought north of the Yellow River,
and I fought south of the Yellow River.
I did not expect that I would be able to first enter the passes and defeat Qín,
and meet you again here.
Now there are the words of petty men
causing you, general, and me to have a rift.'
Xiàng Yǔ said:
'This was said by the Lord of Pèi's Left Marshal Cáo Wúshāng.
Otherwise,
why would Jí have come to this!'
Xiàng Yǔ then kept the Lord of Pèi to drink with him.
Fàn Zēng several times glanced at Xiàng Yǔ,
and three times raised the jade jué he wore to show him.
A jué is like a ring but with a gap.
Zēng raised it to show Yǔ,
probably wanting him to resolve to kill the Lord of Pèi.
Fàn Zēng stood up,
went out,
summoned Xiàng Zhuāng,
and said to him:
'Our king is too kind-hearted.
You go in and offer a toast,
'ruò'
means 'you.'
Master Yán Gǔ said: Whenever one speaks of 'offering a toast,'
it means presenting a cup to a superior and wishing him boundless longevity.
Request to perform a sword dance,
and take the opportunity to strike the Lord of Pèi in his seat,
and kill him.
If not,
you and your kind will all be captured!'
Zhuāng then entered to offer a toast.
After the toast,
he said:
'In the army there is nothing for entertainment.
I request to perform a sword dance.'
Xiàng Yǔ said:
'Yes.'
Xiàng Zhuāng drew his sword and began to dance.
Xiàng Bó also drew his sword and began to dance,
often using his body to shield the Lord of Pèi like wings,
so Zhuāng could not strike.
Then Zhāng Liáng went to the army gate to see Fán Kuài.
Kuài asked:
"How are things today?"
Liáng said:
"Now Xiàng Zhuāng has drawn his sword and is dancing;
his intention is always on Pèi Gōng."
Kuài said:
"This is urgent;
I beg to go in,
and share his fate!"
Kuài then took his sword and shield and entered.
Shield,
is used to protect the body.
Shield,
Shí Yǐn fān.
Fán Kuài tilted his shield and charged,
the guards fell to the ground.
Then he entered,
parted the curtains and stood,
at the side it is called curtains.
Shìmíng says: Curtains,
are for surrounding,
to enclose oneself.
His hair stood on end,
his eyes were wide with anger.
Xiàng Yǔ pressed his sword and knelt, saying:
"Who is this guest?"
Zhāng Liáng said:
"He is Pèi Gōng's chariot guard, Fán Kuài."
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"A brave man!
Give him a goblet of wine!"
Then he was given a large goblet of wine.
Kuài bowed in thanks,
rose,
stood and drank it.
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"Give him a pig's shoulder!"
Then he was given a raw pig's shoulder.
Fán Kuài placed his shield on the ground,
put the pig's shoulder on it,
drew his sword, cut it, and ate it.
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"Can the brave man drink more?"
Fán Kuài said:

7. Earlier,
Hán Xìn of Huáiyīn,
whose family was poor,
had no reputation for conduct.
(Treatise of Bān Gù: In the sixth year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Wǔ,
Línhuái Commandery was established,
and Huáiyīn County was placed under it.
The Correct Meaning of the Records of the Grand Historian states: It is present-day Chǔzhōu County.)
"No reputation for conduct"
means he had no good conduct that could be recommended for selection.
(Conduct: read xiàng, with the falling-rising tone.)
Furthermore, he could not make a living by trade;
(traveling to sell is called shāng,
sitting and dealing is called gǔ.)
(Make: read zhí, with the rising tone.)
Many people disliked him.
Xìn was fishing beneath the city wall
when an old washerwoman, seeing Xìn hungry,
gave him food.
Xìn was pleased and said to the washerwoman,
"I will surely repay you generously someday."
The woman angrily replied,
"A great man cannot feed himself;
I pitied you, a noble scion, and gave you food—
how could I expect repayment!"
A young man from the Huáiyīn butcher's market who insulted Xìn said,
"Though you are tall and big,
fond of wearing sword and dagger,
inwardly you are a coward."
Then, humiliating him before the crowd, he said,
"If you dare to die,
stab me;
if you dare not die,
crawl between my legs!"
(Xú Guǎng said:
"Legs,"
one version reads
"thighs";
thigh means the leg.
The Book of Hàn writes it as
"straddle,"
meaning the same.
Master Yán notes: Straddle means between the two legs.
Suǒyǐn says: Thigh, read kūhuà.
However, examining this text, it is written as
"legs";
if read according to the character,
why would it not make sense!
"Between the legs" means between the thighs—
why must it be "between the thighs"!)
Xìn bent down and crawled between his legs,
prostrating himself.
Everyone in the market laughed at Xìn,
considering him a coward.
When Xiàng Liáng crossed the Huái River,
Xìn, grasping his sword, followed him;
serving under his command,
he remained unknown.
After Xiàng Liáng's defeat,
he joined Xiàng Yǔ,
who appointed him as a Gentleman of the Palace;
he repeatedly offered strategies to Yǔ,
but Yǔ did not employ them.
When the King of Hàn entered Shǔ,
Xìn fled from Chǔ and joined Hàn,
still unknown.
He served as Lián'áo,
and was sentenced to execution for a crime;
(according to the tables in the Records of the Grand Historian,
Xìn served as Lián'áo,
in charge of guests;
the tables in the Book of Hàn write it as
"Piào Kè,"
which Suǒyǐn considers an error.
Xú Guǎng, in the tables for Zhōu Zào,
equates Lián'áo with the official in charge of guests,
likely based on Xìn's table.
Lǐ Qí says: It is a Chǔ official title.
Rú Chún says: Lián'áo is a Chǔ official.
In the Zuǒzhuàn,
Chǔ had the titles Lián Yǐn and Mò'áo;
later they were combined into one official title.)
When it was Xìn's turn,
Xìn looked up
and happened to see Lord Téng,
saying:
(Lord Téng was Xiàhóu Yīng;
he initially followed Gāozǔ as the Magistrate of Téng,
hence called Lord Téng.)
"Does His Majesty not wish to conquer the world?
Why execute a strong warrior?"
Lord Téng, struck by his words
and impressed by his appearance,
released him without execution;
he spoke with him
and was greatly pleased,
then reported to the King.
The King appointed him as Commandant of Grain Supply.
(Tables of Bān Gù: The Chamberlain for the National Treasury was a Qín office,
in charge of grain and goods;
the Commandant was likely a subordinate.
By the Hàn dynasty,
the Chamberlain was changed to Grand Minister of Agriculture.)
Hán Xìn had spoken with Xiāo Hé several times,
and Hé found him extraordinary.
When the King of Hàn arrived at Nánzhèng,
his generals and soldiers all sang songs expressing their longing to return east,
and many deserted along the way.
Xìn reckoned that Hé and others had already recommended him to the king several times,
but the king did not employ him,
so he fled.
When Hé heard that Xìn had fled,
he did not have time to report it,
but personally pursued him.
Someone told
the king, saying:
"Chéngxiàng Hé has fled."
The king was greatly angered,
as if he had lost his right and left hands.
After a day or two,
Hé came to see the king.
The king was both angry and pleased,
and scolded Hé, saying:
"You fled,
why?"
Hé said:
"I did not dare to flee,
I was merely pursuing a deserter."
The king said:
"Whom did you pursue?"
Hé said:
"Hán Xìn."
The king scolded again, saying:
"The generals who have fled number in the tens,
yet you pursued none of them;
to pursue Xìn,
is deceitful!"
Hé said:
"Generals are easily found;
but as for one like Xìn,
he is a state scholar without equal.
Shī Gǔ said: meaning an extraordinary scholar for the state.
I say Hé meant that among the scholars of the Hàn state, only Xìn was such a man,
with none to compare.
If you have no use for Xìn;
but if you truly desire to contend for the world,
then without Xìn there is no one with whom to plan affairs.
It only depends on what strategy Your Majesty decides upon!"
The king said:
"I too wish to go east,
how can I remain depressed here for long!"
Hé said:
"If your plan is indeed to go east,
and you can employ Xìn,
then Xìn will stay;
if you cannot employ Xìn,
he will eventually flee."
The king said:
"For your sake, I shall make him a general."
Hé said:
"Even as a general,
Xìn will not stay."
The king said:
"Make him a great general."
Hé said:
"Excellent!"
Thereupon the king wished to summon Xìn and appoint him.
Hé said:
"Your Majesty is usually careless and disrespectful;
now to appoint a great general
as if calling a child,
this is precisely why Xìn left.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to appoint him,
select an auspicious day,
fast and purify yourself,
set up an altar and ceremonial ground,
and prepare the rituals,
only then may it be done."
The king agreed.
The generals were all pleased,
each thinking himself to have obtained the position of great general.
When it came to appointing the great general,
it was Hán Xìn,
and the entire army was astonished.
When Xìn's appointment ceremony was completed,
he took the seat of honor.
The king said:
"The chéngxiàng has spoken of you, General, several times;
what strategies do you have to teach me?"
Xìn modestly declined,
then asked the king, saying:
"Now, to contend for power over the world facing east,
is it not against King Xiàng?"
The King of Hàn said:
"Yes."
Xìn said:
"Your Majesty, consider for yourself,
in bravery, fierceness, benevolence, and strength, how do you compare with King Xiàng?"
The King of Hàn remained silent for a long while,
then said:
"I am not his equal."
Xìn bowed again and congratulated him, saying:
"Only Xìn also believes that Your Majesty is not his equal.
"Wéi",
the Shǐ Jì writes
"wéi",
the Hàn Shū writes
"wéi".
Shī Gǔ said: wéi,
pronounced yì guǐ fān,
is a particle of response.
Zhòng Féng said:
"wéi"
should belong to the following sentence,
read with its original meaning.
I say if following the Hàn Shū text,
then it should be as Shī Gǔ says;
if following the Shǐ Jì text,
then it should be as Zhòng Féng says.
"Hè yuē",
ends the sentence.
Allow me to speak of King Xiàng's character: King Xiàng roars and shouts,
and a thousand men are all rendered useless,
Jìn Zhuó said: fèi,
means not gathered.
This is merely the courage of a common man.
When King Xiàng meets people,
he is respectful, courteous, kind, and loving,
his speech gentle,
when someone is ill,
he weeps and shares his food and drink;
but when it comes to appointing men,
those with merit deserving of enfeoffment,
he wears the seals smooth and old,
grudging and unable to give them;
Sū Lín said: fondling the corners until worn,
unable to bear granting them.
I say "jiǎo é" [corner-worn]
is the meaning of wán;
bì,
means old and worn.
Shī Gǔ said: wán,
pronounced wǔ wán fān,
Sū Lín tài guān fān,
also pronounced zhuān.
Though King Xiàng dominates the world and makes the feudal lords his vassals,
he does not dwell in Guānzhōng but makes Péngchéng his capital;
he violates the covenant of Yì Dì,
and enfeoffs his close favorites as kings,
which is unjust;
he expels the former lords and makes their generals and ministers kings,
and further moves and expels Yì Dì to Jiāngnán,
wherever he passes, nothing is left undestroyed;
the people do not feel close or attached to him,
they are merely coerced by his might and strength.
Though in name he is a hegemon,
in reality he has lost the hearts of the world,
thus his strength can easily be weakened.
Now if Your Majesty can truly act contrary to his ways,
employ the brave and martial of the world,
who will you not destroy;
enfeoff meritorious ministers with the cities and towns of the world,
who will not submit;
lead righteous troops with soldiers who long to return east,
what enemy will not scatter!
Sàn,
means to scatter and achieve merit.
Liú Shì said: using east-returning troops to strike eastern enemies,
such enemies will all be defeated and scattered.
Gòngfù said: "hé bù sàn zhě",
means righteous troops are invincible,
the troops of the feudal lords will all disperse and be defeated.
Referring to the three: Zhāng Hán, Sīmǎ Xīn, Dǒng Yì.
Those killed and lost are beyond counting;
moreover, he deceived his masses,
surrendered to the feudal lords,
reaching Xīn'ān,
King Xiàng deceitfully buried over two hundred thousand surrendered Qín soldiers alive,
only Hán, Xīn, and Yì escaped.
The elders and brothers of Qín resent these three men,
their hatred piercing to the marrow.
Now Chǔ, by force, has made these three kings,
and the people of Qín do not love them.
When Your Majesty entered Wǔguān,
not the slightest harm was done;
you abolished the harsh laws of Qín,
and made a three-article covenant with the people of Qín;
the people of Qín all desire to have Your Majesty as their king.
According to the covenant among the feudal lords,
Your Majesty should be king of Guānzhōng,
the people of Guānzhōng all know this;
Your Majesty, deprived of your rightful position, entered Hànzhōng,
and the people of Qín all feel regret.
Now if Your Majesty raises troops and marches east,
the three Qín regions can be settled by proclamation alone."
Thereupon the King of Hàn was greatly pleased,
feeling he had obtained Xìn too late,
and so heeded Xìn's plans,
deploying the generals to their respective attacks;
Shī Gǔ said: assigning and appointing them.
Supplying the army with provisions.
In the eighth month,
the King of Hàn led his troops out from Gùdào,
and launched a surprise attack on Yōng.
The Spring and Autumn Annals Explanatory Examples states: "To strike when the enemy is unprepared is called a 'surprise attack'."
According to the Treatise of Bān Gù,
Gùdào County belonged to Wǔdū Commandery.
The Expanded Geographical Records states: Gùdào
is present-day Liǎngdāng County in Fèng Prefecture.
Dù Yòu's Comprehensive Compendium states: Gùdào
comprised the lands of Liángquán and Liǎngdāng counties in Fèng Prefecture.
The Yōng troops were defeated,
and fled back;
they halted,
fought at Hǎozhì,
and were again defeated.
According to the Treatise of Bān Gù,
Chéncāng County belonged to Fúfēng;
it corresponds to the Táng dynasty's Bǎojī County in Qí Prefecture.
Dù Yòu states: The old city was twenty *lǐ* east of the county seat.
According to the Treatise of Bān Gù,
Hǎozhì County belonged to Fúfēng.
Mèng Kāng states: Zhì,
pronounced *zhǐ*,
is where the spirits and deities dwell.
Master Yán states: It is present-day Hǎozhì County in Yōng Prefecture.
Sòng Bái states: The old Hàn dynasty Hǎozhì County
was located forty-three *lǐ* southeast of the present county, at the site of the old Hǎozhì city within the boundaries of Fèngtiān County.
Lǐ Wénzǐ states: It was within the boundaries of Tiānxīng County in Fèngxiáng during the Hàn.
The King of Hàn thus secured the territory of Yōng,
and advanced east to Xiányáng;
he led his troops to besiege the King of Yōng at Fèiqiū,
and dispatched his generals to seize territory.
The King of Sài, Sīmǎ Xīn, and the King of Zhái, Dǒng Yì, both surrendered,
and their lands were made into Wèinán, Héshàng, and Shàngjùn commanderies.
Wèinán
was later called Jīngzhào;
Héshàng,
was later called Féngyì.
He used Wáng Líng's troops to welcome his father, the Tàigōng, and Empress Lǚ.
When King Xiàng heard of this,
he dispatched troops to block them at Yángxià,
preventing them from advancing.
Wáng Líng
was a man of Pèi.
He had previously gathered a band of several thousand men,
and resided in Nányáng.
It was at this time that he first placed his troops under Hàn's command.
King Xiàng took Wáng Líng's mother and placed her in his army camp.
When Wáng Líng's envoy arrived,
he would seat Wáng Líng's mother facing east,
intending to summon Wáng Líng.
In ancient times, the east-facing position was considered honorable.
When the Lord of Pèi met Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén,
Xiàng Yǔ sat facing east;
Hán Xìn seated Lǐ Zuòjū facing east and treated him as a teacher;
these are examples.
Xiàng,
is read as *xiàng*.
She wept and said:
"I beg you to tell Líng for this old woman: Serve the King of Hàn well.
The King of Hàn is a magnanimous man,
he will ultimately gain the empire;
do not, on account of this old woman, harbor divided loyalties.
I shall send off the envoy with my death!"
She then fell upon her sword and died.
King Xiàng was enraged,
and had Wáng Líng's mother boiled alive.
8 King Xiàng appointed Zhèng Chāng, the former magistrate of Wú, as King of Hán,
to block Hàn.
According to the Treatise of Bān Gù,
Wú County belonged to Kuàijī Commandery.
9 Zhāng Liáng sent a letter to King Xiàng, saying:
"The King of Hàn has been deprived of his rightful position,
and wishes to obtain Guānzhōng;
if the covenant is fulfilled, he will stop,
and will not dare to advance east."
He also sent King Xiàng letters from Qí and Liáng stating their rebellion:
"Qí wishes to join with Zhào to destroy Chǔ together."
For this reason, King Xiàng had no intention of heading west,
and instead attacked Qí to the north.
10 The King of Yān, Hán Guǎng, refused to go to Liáodōng;
Zāng Tú attacked and killed him,
and annexed his territory.
11 That year,
he appointed Zhōu Kē, the Nèishǐ of Pèi, as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
According to Bān Biǎo: The Yùshǐ Dàfū,
was a Qín office,
ranking as Senior Minister,
in charge of assisting the Chancellor.
Yīng Shào states: He was the head of the Attending Secretaries,
hence called Dàfū.
12 King Xiàng sent messengers urging Emperor Yì to depart,
and his close ministers and attendants gradually began to betray him.
1 In winter,
the tenth month,
King Xiàng secretly ordered the Kings of Jiǔjiāng, Héngshān, and Línjiāng to attack Emperor Yì,
and killed him in the river.
The King of Jiǔjiāng
was Qíng Bù;
the King of Héngshān,
was Wú Ruì;
the King of Línjiāng,
was Gòng Áo.
2 Chén Yú mobilized all the troops from three counties,
and together with Qí troops launched a surprise attack on Chángshān.
The King of Chángshān, Zhāng Ěr, was defeated,
fled to Hàn,
and paid his respects to the King of Hàn at Fèiqiū;
the King of Hàn treated him generously.
Chén Yú welcomed the King of Zhào back from Dài,
and he was restored as King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào, grateful to Chén Yú,
established him as King of Dài.
Chén Yú considered the King of Zhào weak,
and the state newly stabilized,
so he did not go to his kingdom,
but remained to assist the King of Zhào;
and sent Xià Yuè to guard Dài as Chancellor.
3 Zhāng Liáng returned to Hàn from Hán, traveling in secret:
the King of Hàn appointed him as Marquis of Chéngxìn.
Liáng was often ill,
and never held independent command;
"independent command"
means he never led troops alone.
Jiàng,
is pronounced *jiàng*.
He often accompanied the King of Hàn.
4 The King of Hàn went to Shǎn,
to pacify and reassure the elders outside the passes.
5 The King of Hénán, Shēn Yáng, surrendered,
and Hénán Commandery was established.
6 The King of Hàn appointed Xìn, a grandson of King Xiāng of Hán, as Grand Commandant of Hán,
and sent him with troops to seize Hán territory.
Xìn urgently attacked the King of Hán, Chāng, at Yángchéng,
and Chāng surrendered.
In the eleventh month,
Xìn was established as King of Hán;
he often led Hán troops to follow the King of Hàn.
7 The King of Hàn returned and established his capital at Yuèyáng.
8 The various generals captured Lǒngxī.
9 In spring,
the first month,
King Xiàng went north to Chéngyáng.
The King of Qí, Tián Róng, led his troops to join battle,
was defeated,
fled to Píngyuán,
and the people of Píngyuán killed him.
King Xiàng again established Tián Jiǎ as King of Qí.
He then proceeded north to Běihǎi,
burning and leveling city walls, dwellings, and houses,
burying alive the surrendered soldiers of Tián Róng,
capturing and enslaving the old, weak, women, and children,
and wherever he passed, he wrought great destruction.
The people of Qí banded together and rebelled against him.
10 The Hàn generals captured Běidì,
and captured the younger brother of the King of Yōng, Píng.
This was Zhāng Píng.
Yōng,
is pronounced *yōng*.
11 In the third month,
the King of Hàn crossed the river from Línjìn.
Línjìn,
see the annotation in the fifth year of King Nǎn, third scroll.
Master Yán states: Its location was on the western bank of the river,
facing the territory of Jìn to the east,
which is present-day Zhāoyì in Tóng Prefecture.
The *Shǐjì* Correct Meaning states: Línjìn was the Pújīn Pass.
He led his troops to follow;
descended upon Hénèi,
captured the King of Yīn, Sīmǎ Áng,
and established Hénèi Commandery.
12. Initially,
Chén Píng of Yángwǔ,
whose family was poor,
was fond of reading.
During the village community sacrifice,
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: According to the Sacrificial Code: Officials below the rank of dàfū who form groups may establish a shè, called an established shè.
The commentary states: A dàfū may not independently establish a shè;
living among the people,
if there are over a hundred households, they may jointly establish one shè,
which is the present-day village shè.
As Zhèng [Xuán] says here,
then according to the laws and institutions of the Zhōu,
those with over a hundred households could establish a shè;
from the Qín and Hàn dynasties onward,
even if not a dàfū,
if the people numbered over twenty-five households, they could establish a shè,
hence it is called the present-day village shè.
Furthermore, the Zhèng Zhì states: The Yuèlìng
"orders the people to perform the shè sacrifice"
refers to the Qín shè.
From Qín onward,
the people began to be allowed to establish shè.
Shī Gǔ said: Zǎi,
means presiding over the cutting of meat.
The village elders said:
"Excellent,
how well young Chén acts as the zǎi!"
Chén Píng said:
"Alas,
if I, Píng, could govern the world,
it would be just like this meat!"
When the feudal lords rebelled against Qín,
Chén Píng served King Jiù of Wèi in Línjì,
as Grand Coachman.
According to the Bān Biǎo: Grand Coachman,
a Qín official position,
in charge of carriages and horses.
Yìng Shào said: Established by King Mù of Zhōu,
likely the chief of the many coachmen.
Jì,
read zǐ lǐ fān.
[King Jiù] did not heed [his advice].
Someone slandered him,
and Chén Píng fled.
Later, he served Xiàng Yǔ,
who bestowed upon him the rank of a qīng.
Zhāng Yàn said: His ceremonial rank was like that of a qīng,
but he did not handle affairs.
Xiàng Yǔ sent Chén Píng to attack and subdue [the King of Wèi];
upon returning,
he was appointed Commandant,
and was granted twenty yì of gold.
Not long after,
Shī Gǔ said: Meaning not much time had passed.
King Xiàng grew angry,
and intended to execute the generals and officials who had pacified Yīn.
Chén Píng, fearing for his life,
sealed up the gold and his seal,
and sent a messenger to return them to King Xiàng;
then, straightening his body, he traveled in secret,
carrying his sword, he fled,
crossed the Yellow River,
and went to Xiūwǔ to join the King of Hàn,
requesting an audience through Wèi Wúzhī.
The King of Hàn summoned him in,
bestowed food upon him,
and then sent him away to his quarters.
Chén Píng said:
"I have come on business,
and what I have to say cannot wait beyond today."
Thereupon, the King of Hàn spoke with him and was pleased,
asking:
"What office did you hold in Chǔ?"
He replied:
"I was a Commandant."
That very day,
the King of Hàn appointed Chén Píng as Commandant,
made him his carriage companion,
and put him in charge of supervising the army.
He had Chén Píng take charge of supervising the army and overseeing the generals.
"Your Majesty, upon obtaining a deserter from Chǔ in a single day,
without knowing his worth,
immediately shares his carriage with him,
and even has him oversee us elders!"
The King of Hàn, hearing this,
favored Chén Píng even more.
13. The King of Hàn crossed the Píngyīn Ford southward,
reaching Xīnchéng in Luòyáng.
According to the Bān Zhì,
Píngyīn County belonged to Hénán Commandery.
The Shuǐ Jīng states: The Yellow River passes north of Píngyīn County.
Emperor Wén of Wèi changed Píngyīn to Héyīn.
Luòyáng County belonged to Hénán Commandery;
Xīnchéng was then within the county's boundaries,
and Emperor Huì established Xīnchéng County in his fourth year.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Yīquè County of Luò Prefecture,
located seventy lǐ south of the prefecture,
was originally Hàn's Xīnchéng;
Emperor Wén of Suí changed Xīnchéng to Yīquè,
taking the name from Mount Yīquè.
for the name.
According to the Bān Biǎo: Every ten lǐ there is a tíng,
with a tíng chief;
every ten tíng make a xiāng,
and a xiāng has three elders,
in charge of education and moral guidance;
this was the Qín system.
Blocking the road to speak for oneself is called zhē.
Shuō,
read shì ruì fān.
"Your servant has heard that 'those who follow virtue prosper,
those who oppose virtue perish';
'military action without just cause,
attacking those who are guilty gives military action just cause.
Therefore it is said: 'Make clear that he is a traitor,
and then the enemy can be subdued.'
Xiàng Yǔ acts without principle,
having exiled and murdered his sovereign.
Exiled,
refers to moving the Righteous Emperor to Chēn;
murdered,
refers to killing him in the river.
Shā,
read as shì.
Benevolence does not rely on bravery,
righteousness does not rely on force."
Wén Yǐng said: Yǐ,
means to use;
if one possesses benevolence oneself,
the world will submit to him,
and he can subdue the world without using bravery;
if one possesses righteousness oneself,
the world will support him,
and he can stabilize the world without using force.
Proclaiming this to the feudal lords and attacking him,
then within the four seas, none will fail to look up to your virtue.
This is the action of the Three Kings."
Thereupon, the King of Hàn held a funeral for the Righteous Emperor,
bared his shoulders and wailed loudly,
mourning for three days.
Rú Chún said: Baring the shoulders,
is also like the ritual of baring the shoulders and leaping [in grief].
Shī Gǔ said: Baring the shoulders,
means to remove the sleeves of one's garment.
Tǎn,
read tǔ hàn fān.
The collective wailing is called lín,
read lì jìn fān.
"The world jointly established the Righteous Emperor,
and we faced north to serve him.
Now Xiàng Yǔ has exiled and murdered the Righteous Emperor south of the Yangtze,
a great act of treason and unprincipled conduct!
I, the humble one, will mobilize all the troops from within the passes,
gather the men of the Three Hé regions,
Wéi Zhāo said: Hénán, Hédōng, and Hénèi.
and wish to follow the feudal lords and kings to attack the one in Chǔ who murdered the Righteous Emperor!"
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: Gathering the men of the Three Hé regions in the south,
mobilizing troops from within the passes,
entering Hànzhōng from Yōng Prefecture via the Zǐwǔ Road,
proceeding down the Hàn River,
and marching east to Xúzhōu to attack Chǔ.
I say the explanation of the Zhèngyì is circuitous!
The Three Hé regions are north of Péngchéng,
so one can hardly speak of gathering the men of the Three Hé regions in the south.

"Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr, riding the momentum of victory, have left their own state to fight far away,
meaning they are relying on the victorious momentum from conquering Dài.
Advised,
shuì, read as shuì.
Your servant has heard, 'When provisions are transported a thousand miles,
the soldiers will have hungry faces;
gathering firewood and grass before cooking,
qiáo,
means gathering firewood;
sū,
means gathering grass.
Now, the path through Jǐngxíng,
does not allow chariots to run side by side,
fāng guǐ,
means chariots running parallel.
Traveling several hundred lǐ,
the situation dictates that their food supplies must be trailing behind.
Zhèng Kāngchéng said: Provisions for the road are called liáng,
meaning dried grain;
food for staying in place is called shí,
meaning rice.
Take a hidden path to cut off their baggage train;
Shī Gǔ said: Jiàn lù,
means a small, concealed path.
Jiàn,
read as jiàn.
Shī Gǔ said: Zī,
refers to a carriage for clothes;
zhòng,
refers to a carriage for heavy loads;
thus all supplies for those on the march,
are collectively called zīzhòng.
The Shìmíng says: Zī,
means mixed,
because the clothes and other items carried are mixed within it.
Zhòng,
read as zhòng.
Then they will be unable to fight forward,
unable to retreat and return,
with nothing to plunder in the wilds,
within ten days,
the heads of their two generals can be delivered before your banner;
otherwise, we will surely be captured by those two men."
Chéng'ān Jūn had always claimed his army was one of righteous soldiers,
and would not use deceitful strategies or clever plans.
He said:
"Hán Xìn's army is few and weary,
if we avoid battle like this,
then the various lords will say we are cowardly and will lightly come to attack us."
Hán Xìn sent men to secretly observe,
and learning that he did not adopt Guǎngwǔ Jūn's strategy,
was greatly pleased,
and only then dared to lead his troops and proceed down.
Thirty lǐ from the mouth of Jǐngxíng,
he halted and made camp.
Meaning he halted the army and rested.
Shè,
read as shè.
Chuán fā,
he selected two thousand light cavalry.
Chuán fā,
means transmitting an order through the army to dispatch troops.
The Hàn banners and flags were all red.
Zhì,
read as zhì.
He instructed them, saying:
"When Zhào sees us flee,
they will certainly empty their fortifications to pursue us;
you must swiftly enter the Zhào fortifications,
ruò,
means you.
Jí,
means swiftly.
and erect the Hàn red flags."
He ordered his subordinate generals to distribute rations,
saying:
Fú Qiān said: Lì,
means to halt.
Chuán cān,
means to eat.
Rú Chún said: A small meal is called cān.
Meaning they would eat their fill only after defeating Zhào.
Cān,
read as cān.
"Today, after defeating Zhào, we will feast together!"
The various generals all did not believe it,
but pretended to assent, saying
"Yes."
Xìn said:
"Zhào has already occupied advantageous ground and made their fortifications;
moreover, they have not yet seen my commander's banners and drums,
and will not be willing to attack our vanguard,
fearing I will retreat upon reaching difficult terrain."
Xìn likely meant that Zhào had gathered troops to block the mouth of Jǐngxíng,
wanting to wait for Xìn to emerge from the dangerous pass before attacking him;
if they saw the vanguard and immediately unleashed their troops to engage,
then Xìn would certainly retreat upon reaching the difficult terrain.
Huán,
read as xuán,
or also as huán.
He then emerged,
and deployed his troops with their backs to the river;
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: The Miánmàn Shuǐ flows north from Bīngzhōu into the boundaries of Jǐngxíng County,
which is where Xìn deployed his troops with their backs to the water.
Bèi,
read as bèi.
Chén,
read as zhèn.
At dawn,
Xìn raised his commander's banners and drums,
and marched out of the Jǐngxíng pass with drums beating;
Zhào opened their fortifications and attacked him,
and a great battle ensued for a long time.
Thereupon, Xìn and Zhāng Ěr pretended to abandon their drums and banners,
and fled towards the army by the water;
the army by the water opened ranks to let them in,
and then fought fiercely again.
Zhào indeed emptied their fortifications to contend for the Hàn banners and drums,
pursuing Xìn and Ěr.
Xìn and Ěr had already entered the army by the water,
and the troops all fought with desperate resolve,
Shī Gǔ said: Shū,
means extreme;
meaning determined to fight to the death.
The two thousand cavalry of Xìn's surprise force, waiting together for Zhào to empty their fortifications in pursuit of gain,
then galloped into the Zhào fortifications,
pulled out all the Zhào flags,
and erected two thousand Hàn red flags.
The Zhào army, now unable to capture Xìn and the others,
wanted to return to their fortifications;
but the fortifications were all Hàn red flags,
seeing this, they were greatly alarmed,
thinking that Hàn had already captured the King of Zhào's generals,
the troops then fell into chaos,
fled in disorder,
even though the Zhào generals beheaded some,
they could not stop them.
Thereupon, the Hàn troops attacked from both sides,
greatly defeating the Zhào army,
and beheaded Chéng'ān Jūn by the Chíshuǐ River.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù says: The Chíshuǐ is the mountain stream of Jǐngxíng,
commonly called Lùquán Shuǐ,
flowing northeast,
it bends past Chén Yú's fortifications,
and then flows east into the Miánmàn Shuǐ.
Shī Gǔ said: Chí,
read as zhī,
also as dīng jì,
also as dīng lǐ.
The various generals presented the heads and captives,
and after all congratulations,
they asked Xìn, saying:
"The Art of War says: 'Have hills and mountains to the right,
and water and marshes to the front and left.'
Yet today, General, you ordered us instead to deploy with our backs to the water,
saying 'After defeating Zhào we will feast together',
we were not convinced,
yet in the end we were victorious.
What strategy was this?"
Xìn said:
"This is in the Art of War,
it's just that you gentlemen did not notice it!
Does not the Art of War say: 'Place them in a deadly situation and they will then survive,'
Sūnzǐ's Nine Terrains: Where fighting fiercely leads to survival, and not fighting leads to destruction, is called 'deadly ground'.
Cáo Cāo's commentary says: Where there are high mountains in front,
and great waters behind,
one cannot advance,
and retreat is obstructed.
Moreover, I could not have trained and familiarized these officers and men beforehand,
this is what is called 'driving market folk into battle',
Shī Gǔ said: Meaning it is like suddenly entering a marketplace,
driving its people off to battle,
men not ordinarily trained and drilled.
I had to make each man fight for himself;
if I had given them ground where they could survive,
they would all have fled,
so how could I have possibly used them then!"
Yǔ,
read as yǔ;
same below.
The various generals were all convinced,
saying:
"Excellent!
This is beyond what we could have achieved."
Hán Xìn offered a thousand catties of gold for anyone who could capture Guǎngwǔ Jūn alive.
When someone brought him bound to the camp,
Hán Xìn untied his bonds,
seated him facing east,
and treated him as a teacher.
He asked:
"I wish to campaign north against Yān,
and east against Qí.
What must I do to achieve success?"
"What must I do"
means the same as "how should I proceed."
Guǎngwǔ Jūn said,
"I am a captive from a defeated and ruined army,

"To weigh"
refers to using a scale to measure objects,
to assess their lightness or heaviness.
Zuǒchē (Guǎngwǔ Jūn) meant that military affairs are matters of grave importance for the state,
and someone like himself, a remnant of defeat and ruin,
is not fit to carefully judge their relative weight.
Hán Xìn said, "I have heard: Bǎilǐ Xī dwelled in Yú and Yú perished;
he went to Qín and Qín became hegemon.
Bǎilǐ Xī
was a senior minister of Yú.
The Lord of Yú could not employ him properly, and Yú was lost;
Duke Mù of Qín trusted and employed him,
and thus became hegemon over the Western Róng.
It is a matter of being employed or not employed,
of being heeded or not heeded.
If indeed Chéng'ān Jūn had followed your strategies,
someone like me would already have been captured;
because he did not employ you,
I have the fortune to be in your presence now."
This means he has the fortune to be by his side to seek instruction.
"I beg you not to decline!"

captured the King of Wèi,
and took Xià Yuè prisoner;
marched east and descended Jǐngxíng,

and executed Chéng'ān Jūn;
your name is known throughout the land,
your might shakes the world.

dressing finely and eating sweet foods,
listening intently, awaiting your commands.
These are the strengths of you, General.

and in reality, they are difficult to employ.
Now if you, General, wish to raise these tired and depleted troops and station them beneath Yān's fortified walls,
you will wish to fight but be unable,
you will attack but not take them,
your true situation will be exposed and your momentum exhausted;
warfare
is the way of deception,
it relies on exploiting momentum for its effectiveness.
"Exposed"
means revealed.
"Exhausted"
means used up.
If our true situation is exposed, the enemy knows how to prepare;
if our momentum is exhausted, the enemy can exploit our weakness.
"Exposed"
is pronounced xiàn.
"Exhausted"
is pronounced jué.
Your provisions will be depleted and exhausted.
"Depleted"
is the same as "exhausted,"
meaning used up.
Qí will certainly fortify its borders to strengthen itself.
If you and Yān are locked in stalemate with no resolution,

These are the weaknesses of you, General.
One who excels at employing troops
does not use weakness to strike at strength, but uses strength to strike at weakness."
Hán Xìn asked:
"Then what course should I follow?"
"Follow"
means to proceed,

Guǎngwǔ Jūn said, "For the present, planning for you, General,

Within a hundred *lǐ*,
oxen and wine will arrive daily,
to feast your officers and gentlemen.
Point your vanguard toward the road to Yān,
and afterward dispatch a persuasive envoy bearing a letter of but a foot or so,
Yán Shīgǔ said: Eight inches is called a *zhǐ*.
"A foot or so"
means the bamboo slips may be a *zhǐ* long,
or a foot long,
signifying something light and easy.
"To display"
means to manifest,
to show,
to reveal.
Once Yān has submitted, then advance east to face Qí.

If you proceed thus,
then all affairs under heaven can be plotted."
"In warfare, there is indeed the principle of first demonstrating one's reputation and then following with substance;
this is what it means."
Hán Xìn said:
"Excellent!"
He followed this strategy,
and sent an envoy to Yān.
Yān submitted like grass bending before the wind.
He sent an envoy to report to Hàn,

Chǔ several times sent surprise troops across the river to attack Zhào.

dispatching troops to join Hàn.

and Hàn
weak.

If I am granted an audience,
and what I say is correct,

The Grand Steward then spoke of this to the King.
The king saw him.
Suí Hé said:

The King of Jiǔjiāng said:

he personally carried the wall boards and rammers,

Lǐ Qí says: Bǎn,
are wall boards;
zhù,
are rammers.

acting as Chǔ's vanguard;

'Idly watched' means
to let one's robes hang and fold one's hands.

Your Majesty clings to an empty title in leaning towards Chǔ, hoping to secure a firm reliance for yourself.

Jiào
means to patrol.

It is probably because men are sent to patrol the borders,
and
inspect

Using jiào to encircle the frontier,

Jiào,
is pronounced jí diào fān.
Chéng,
means to ascend;

The men of Chǔ have penetrated eight or nine hundred lǐ into enemy territory.

Hàn holds firm and does not move.
When Chǔ advances, it cannot attack;
when it retreats, it cannot extricate itself.

If Chǔ were to defeat Hàn,

the strength of Chǔ

Thus, Chǔ is not equal to Hàn,

Now, Your Majesty does not align with the perfectly secure Hàn but relies on the endangered and doomed Chǔ.
I am privately perplexed for Your Majesty!

King Xiàng is sure to remain;
if he remains for several months,
Hàn's conquest of the world can be perfectly secured.
I request to accompany Your Majesty, sword in hand, in submitting to Hàn.
The King of Hàn is sure to apportion land and enfeoff Your Majesty;
moreover, Jiǔjiāng will certainly remain in Your Majesty's possession."
The King of Jiǔjiāng said:
"I beg to receive your command."
He secretly agreed to rebel against Chǔ and join Hàn,
but did not dare reveal it.
A Chǔ envoy was in Jiǔjiāng,
staying at a relay station.
A relay station
is a guesthouse;
when former guests leave their lodgings,
later guests again come to lodge there,
they are received in succession,

Zhuàn,
is pronounced zhí liàn fān.
Suí Hé went straight in,
sat above the Chǔ envoy,
and said:

How can Chǔ dispatch troops?"
Bù was stunned.
The Chǔ envoy rose.
Hé thereupon advised Bù, saying,
"The matter is already settled.
Shī Gǔ says: Gòu,
means to conclude;
meaning the matter of betraying Chǔ is already concluded.
Do not let him return,

Bù said:

Chǔ sent Xiàng Shēng and Lóng Jū to attack Jiǔjiāng.
After several months,
Lóng Jū defeated the Jiǔjiāng army.
Bù wished to lead his troops and flee to Hàn,

In the twelfth month,
the King of Jiǔjiāng arrived in Hàn.
The King of Hàn was just then sitting sprawled on his bed washing his feet,

Bù was greatly angered,
regretted coming,

Bù was again overjoyed beyond expectation.

to make Bù submit;
afterwards, he made the tent curtains beautiful,
the food and drink lavish,
and the attendants numerous,

This was a stratagem of expediency.
Zhàng,
is like present-day tent furnishings;
yù,
refers to clothing and equipment.
Cóng,
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
Chǔ had already sent Xiàng Bó to gather the Jiǔjiāng troops,

Hàn increased the King of Jiǔjiāng's troops,

Chǔ repeatedly attacked and seized Hàn's supply routes,

The King of Hàn plotted with Lì Yìjī to weaken Chǔ's power.

Your Majesty, facing south, will proclaim hegemony,

Rèn,
is the lapel of a garment.
Xiàng,
is read as xiàng.
Cháo,
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
"Excellent!
Hasten to carve the seals,

This means he intended to send Yìjī on a mission to the Six States,

Cù,

the same below.
Before Shíyì had set out,

To measure whether one can control the life and death of others;

The King of Hàn stopped eating,
spat out his food,

means you.

is a term of respect.

"this lord,"

is pronounced jū yī fān.

second is momentum,

Form
refers to the general numbers of gains and losses;
momentum
