the opportunity for advance or retreat;
sentiment
refers to the reality of whether the heart and will are willing or not.
Therefore, when strategies are the same and affairs equal, yet achievements differ,
it is because these three methods are different.
Initially,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú advised Chén Shè to restore the six states,
to establish their own factions;
this matter is seen in the seventh volume, the first year of Qín Èrshì.
The reason why the advice was the same but the gains and losses differed is that
when Chén Shè rose,
the world all wished to destroy Qín;
but the division between Chǔ and Hàn was not yet settled,
now the world may not necessarily wish to destroy Xiàng.
Therefore, establishing the six states,
for Chén Shè,
was called increasing one's own faction and adding to Qín's enemies;
moreover, Chén Shè could not exclusively possess the land of the world,
which is called taking what is not one's own to give to others,
performing empty favors and gaining real fortune.
Establishing the six states,
for the King of Hàn,
is called cutting off what one has to aid the enemy,
setting up empty names and receiving real disaster.
This is the same affair but with different forms.
As for Sòng Yì waiting for Qín and Zhào to perish,
this matter is seen in the eighth volume, the third year of Qín Èrshì.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ stabbing the tiger.
The stable boy stopped him, saying:
"Two tigers are just eating an ox,
the ox is sweet, they will certainly fight,
then the larger will be injured,
the smaller will die;
follow the injured one and stab it,
with one move you will certainly gain both."
Zhuāngzǐ agreed,
and indeed obtained two tigers.
When neighboring states attack each other,
if there is no immediate urgency,
then it is acceptable.
The establishment of the Warring States,
its time was long,
the victory or defeat of one battle,
did not necessarily determine survival or destruction;
the momentum was not such that it urgently needed to destroy the enemy state,
advance to take advantage of benefits,
retreat to preserve oneself,
therefore accumulate strength and await the time,
take advantage of
the enemy's perishing,
the momentum was like this.
Now the rise of Chǔ and Zhào,
their situation with Qín is such that they cannot coexist,
the critical moment of safety and danger,
changes with every breath,
advance then establishes merit,
retreat then brings disaster.
This is the same affair but with different momentum.
In the campaign to attack Zhào,
Hán Xìn stationed his army on the banks of the Zhī River, and Zhào was unable to defeat him.
This event is recorded in the third year of the previous volume.
The King of Hàn fought on the banks of the Suī River,
where his soldiers all plunged into the Suī River, and the Chǔ army achieved a great victory.
This event is recorded in the second year of the previous volume.
Nán,
pronounced as nàn.
The Zhào troops marched out of their state to engage in battle,
advancing when they saw an opportunity,
retreating when they knew it was difficult,
harboring concerns for their homeland,
with no resolve to fight to the death;
Hán Xìn’s army, isolated on the riverbank,
had soldiers determined to die,
with no second thoughts,
which is why Xìn was victorious.
The King of Hàn, deep in enemy territory,
held banquets and grand feasts,
his soldiers grew complacent and at ease,
their will to fight was not firm;
Chǔ, with its formidable might, had lost its capital,
and its soldiers were filled with indignation and fervor,
rushing to rescue their defeat and avert destruction,
staking their lives on a single day’s battle,
which is why Hàn was defeated.
Moreover, Hán Xìn selected elite troops for defense,
while Zhào attacked with soldiers concerned for their homeland;
Xiàng Yǔ selected elite troops for attack,
while Hàn responded with lazy and negligent troops.
These are situations that appear similar but differ in essence.
Therefore, it is said: Strategy cannot be predetermined,
changes cannot be anticipated in advance;
moving with the times,
adapting to circumstances,
this is the essence of planning.
5 The King of Hàn said to Chén Píng:
“The world is in turmoil,
when will it be settled?”
Chén Píng said:
“Among King Xiàng’s loyal and upright ministers,
such as Yàfù, Zhōnglí Mò, Lóng Jū, and Zhōu Yīn,
Zhōnglí,
descendants of the ancient Zhōnglízi,
took their state as their surname.
The surname Lóng originated from the Lóngbó clan;
it is also said,
to have originated from Lóng, the advisor to Shùn.
Shī Gǔ said: Mò,
pronounced mò,
its character is derived from the ‘mò’ meaning end.
Jū,
pronounced zǐyú.
If Your Majesty can indeed sacrifice tens of thousands of catties of gold,
to carry out counterintelligence,
sow discord among his ministers,
and make him suspicious:
King Xiàng, by nature,
is suspicious and believes slander,
and will surely turn against his own internally.
Hàn can then raise an army and attack him,
and defeating Chǔ is certain.”
The King of Hàn said:
“Excellent!”
He then gave forty thousand catties of gold to Píng,
allowing him to act freely,
without questioning his expenditures.
Píng used much of the gold to spread counterintelligence in the Chǔ army,
proclaiming:
“Generals like Zhōnglí Mò and others have served King Xiàng,
with many achievements,
yet they have never been granted lands to become kings.
They wish to join Hàn,
to destroy the Xiàng clan and divide its lands to become kings.”
Xiàng Yǔ indeed became suspicious and distrusted Zhōnglí Mò and others.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Chǔ besieged the King of Hàn in Xíngyáng,
and the situation was critical;
the King of Hàn requested peace,
offering to cede the lands west of Xíngyáng to Hàn.
Yàfù urged Yǔ to urgently attack Xíngyáng;
the King of Hàn was troubled by this.
Xiàng Yǔ sent an envoy to Hàn,
and Chén Píng had a grand feast prepared.
When it was presented,
upon seeing the Chǔ envoy,
he feigned surprise and said:
“I thought it was Yàfù’s envoy,
but it is King Xiàng’s envoy!”
He then took it away,
and replaced it with coarse and simple food for the Chǔ envoy.
Fú Qiān said: The meat dishes were removed,
and replaced with coarse and simple fare.
Coarse,
meaning rough;
simple,
meaning hastily prepared.
The envoy reported this to King Xiàng;
King Xiàng indeed became highly suspicious of Yàfù.
Yàfù wanted to urgently capture Xíngyáng city,
but King Xiàng did not trust him,
and refused to listen.
Yàfù, hearing that King Xiàng suspected him,
angrily said:
“The affairs of the world are largely settled,
Your Majesty may handle them yourself.
I beg to be granted
my retirement!”
On his way back,
before reaching Péngchéng,
he died of a carbuncle on his back.
In the fifth month,
General Jì Xìn said to the King of Hàn:
“The situation is critical!
I request to deceive Chǔ,
so that Your Majesty may escape in secret.”
Jiàn,
pronounced gǔxiàn.
Chǔ then attacked from all sides.
Jì Xìn then rode in the king’s carriage,
with a yellow canopy,
and a left banner,
Lǐ Fěi said: The Son of Heaven’s carriage uses yellow silk as the inner lining of the canopy.
The banner,
is made of feather tassels,
mounted on the left side of the carriage crossbar.
Cài Yōng said: It is made of yak tail hair,
as large as a dou,
sometimes placed on the horse’s head,
sometimes on the crossbar.
Yìng Shào said: It is made of pheasant tail feathers,
placed on the left horse,
above the bit.
Shī Gǔ said: Yìng’s explanation is incorrect.
Ěryǎ Yì: The yak,
is a long-haired ox from the southwestern barbarians,
resembling an ox,
with red hair over a foot long on its four joints, belly, and elbows,
and its tail is especially fine,
as large as a dou.
The Son of Heaven’s carriage has a left banner,
made from this yak tail hair,
tied to the yoke of the left horse.
Generally, the middle horse is called the center horse,
the outer ones are called side horses,
side horses,
are the flanking horses;
it is placed on the head of the outermost horse,
to confuse its vision,
preventing it from seeing clearly.
Dào,
pronounced túdào,
also pronounced dú.
“With provisions exhausted,
the King of Hàn surrenders.”
The Chǔ soldiers all shouted “Long live,”
and gathered east of the city to watch.
Thus, the King of Hàn was able to escape through the west gate with several dozen cavalry,
ordering King Hán Xìn, Zhōu Kē, Wèi Bào, and Cōng Gōng to defend Xíngyáng.
Yǔ saw Jì Xìn,
and asked:
“Where is the King of Hàn?”
He replied:
“He has already left.”
Yǔ burned and killed Xìn.
Zhōu Kē and Cōng Gōng said to each other:
“A king who has rebelled,
is difficult to trust in defending the city!”
They then killed Wèi Bào.
The King of Hàn left Xíngyáng,
reached Chénggāo,
entered the Pass,
and gathered troops intending to advance east again.
Yuán Shēng advised the King of Hàn:
Yuán,
is a surname.
The Genealogy of Surnames states: Descendants of Yuán Táotú, a senior official of Chén.
Examining its origin,
it is also connected with the two surnames Yuán and Yuán.
"Hàn and Chǔ have been confronting each other at Xíngyáng for several years,
and Hàn has often been hard-pressed.
I hope Your Majesty will march out through the Wǔguān Pass.
King Xiàng will certainly lead his troops southward.
Your Majesty should fortify your defenses deeply and do not give battle.
Let the area between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo have a chance to rest and recuperate.
Enable Hán Xìn and others to pacify and consolidate the Zhào territory north of the Yellow River,
and link up with Yān and Qí.
Shī Gǔ comments: Jí,
is the same as jí (集),
meaning to harmonize and unite.
The Preface to the Book of Songs says:
"To comfort, to settle, to pacify and to gather them";
the Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuǒzhuàn says:
"Your ministers are harmonious and united."
Other instances are all similar to this.
If this is done,
then Chǔ will have many fronts to defend against,
and its strength will be divided;
Hàn will gain rest and recuperation,
and then fight them again.
Defeating them will be certain!"
The King of Hàn followed his plan,
and led his army out between Wǎn and Yè.
According to Bān Zhì,
these two counties belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Wǎn,
is a county in Dèng Prefecture.
Yè,
is a county in Rǔ Prefecture.
Wǎn,
is pronounced yuán.
Yè,
is pronounced shè.
Xiàng Yǔ heard that the King of Hàn was at Wǎn,
and indeed led his troops south;
the King of Hàn fortified his defenses and did not engage in battle.
When the King of Hàn was defeated at Péngchéng,
and retreated westward,
Péng Yuè lost all the cities he had previously captured,
and alone led his troops north to station by the Yellow River.
He constantly moved about, acting as Hàn's roving troops to attack Chǔ,
cutting off their rear supply lines.
In this month,
Péng Yuè crossed the Suī River,
and fought Xiàng Shēng and Lord Xuē at Xiàpī,
defeated them,
and killed Lord Xuē.
Xiàng Yǔ then had Zhōng Gōng guard Chénggāo.
Zhōng,
is a surname.
The Genealogy of Surnames says: Descendants of Lù Zhōng.
The King of Hàn led his troops north,
attacked and defeated Zhōng Gōng,
and again stationed his army at Chénggāo.
In the sixth month,
Xiàng Yǔ, having already defeated and driven away Péng Yuè,
heard that Hàn had again stationed its army at Chénggāo,
so he led his troops west, captured Xíngyáng city,
and captured Zhōu Kē alive.
Xiàng Yǔ said to Kē:
"Serve me,
and I will appoint you as Supreme General,
and enfeoff you with thirty thousand households."
Zhōu Kē cursed:
"If you do not hasten to surrender to Hàn,
you will soon be a captive;
you are no match for the King of Hàn!"
Xiàng Yǔ boiled Zhōu Kē alive,
and also killed Lord Cōng and captured Hán Wáng Xìn,
then besieged Chénggāo.
The King of Hàn fled,
alone sharing a carriage with Téng Gōng, exiting Chénggāo through the Yùmén Gate.
Zhāng Yàn says: Yùmén,
is the north gate of Chénggāo.
They lodged at the postal station at Xiǎo Xiūwǔ.
Jìn Zhuó says: It is east of Dà Xiūwǔ city.
Claiming to be an envoy of Hàn,
he galloped into the Zhào encampment.
Zhāng Ěr and Hán Xìn had not yet risen,
so he entered their sleeping quarters,
seized their seals and tallies to summon the various generals by waving them,
and reassigned their positions.
When Xìn and Ěr arose,
they then realized the King of Hàn had come,
and were greatly astonished.
After the King of Hàn had taken command of the two men's armies,
he immediately ordered Zhāng Ěr to patrol
and inspect,
and prepare the defenses of the Zhào territory.
He appointed Hán Xìn as Chancellor of State,
and gathered the Zhào troops that had not yet been mobilized to attack Qí.
The various generals gradually managed to get out of Chénggāo and follow the King of Hàn.
Chǔ then captured Chénggāo,
and intended to advance west;
Hàn sent troops to block them at Gǒng.
According to Bān Zhì,
Gǒng County belonged to Hénán Commandery,
which was where the Lord of Eastern Zhōu resided.
The Rǔ Luò Map states: Gǒng,
means solid.
Gǒng County lies between the Luò River,
meaning it is surrounded by mountains on all sides,
making it solid and secure.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
a comet appeared at Dàjiǎo.
The Suí Tiānwén Zhì states: A bó,
is a type of comet;
one pointing to the side is called a huì,
one with rays of energy radiating in all four directions is called a bó.
A bó,
appears suddenly and brightly,
born from an exceptionally evil qi.
If there is not great internal disorder,
there will certainly be major military conflict.
The world conspires together,
dark and obscured, unclear,
causing harm and injury.
Yànzǐ said:
"If you, my lord, do not reform,
a bó star will appear.
What is there to fear from a huì!"
From this it can be said,
the calamity is greater than that of a huì.
Bó,
is pronounced pèi,
also pronounced pò.
Bān Zhì: The cluster of stars south of the Room constellation is called the Cavalry Officials,
the left horn is the Judge,
the right horn is the General.
Dàjiǎo,
is the court of the Heavenly King's Imperial Seat.
7 Línjiāng Wáng Áo passed away,
and his son Wèi succeeded him.
8 The King of Hàn, having obtained Hán Xìn's army,
again greatly revived his spirits.
In the eighth month,
he led his troops to the Yellow River,
facing south,
and stationed his army at Xiǎo Xiūwǔ,
intending to fight Chǔ again.
Gentleman of the Palace Zhèng Zhōng advised and stopped the King of Hàn.
The Hàn system: Consultant Gentlemen and Palace Gentlemen,
rank equivalent to six hundred shi;
Attendant Gentlemen,
equivalent to four hundred shi;
Gentlemen of the Palace,
equivalent to three hundred shi;
all belonged to the Superintendent of the Palace Gentlemen.
Shui,
is pronounced shuì.
The King of Hàn heeded his plan,
and sent Generals Liú Jiǎ and Lú Wǎn to lead twenty thousand infantry,
several hundred cavalry,
cross at the Báimǎ Ford,
enter Chǔ territory,
assist Péng Yuè,
burn Chǔ's accumulated stores,
to ruin their livelihood.
Shī Gǔ comments: Accumulated stores,
refers to stored military provisions, fodder, and such.
Jī,
is pronounced zī.
Jù,
is pronounced jù.
Chǔ troops attacked Liú Jiǎ,
but Jiǎ consistently fortified his defenses and refused to engage in battle,
instead maintaining mutual support with Péng Yuè.
9 Peng Yuè attacked and overran the region of Liáng,
capturing seventeen cities including Suīyáng and Wàihuáng.
Suīyáng,
a county of Qín,
belonged to Dàng Commandery,
under Hàn it belonged to the Kingdom of Liáng,
the former state where Wēizǐ was enfeoffed;
in Táng it was Sòngchéng County of Sòng Prefecture.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Hàn Wàihuáng,
was east of Yōngqiū County in Chénliú Commandery,
the place mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals
"Duke Huán of Qí met with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū",
was this.
King Xiàng said to Grand Marshal Cáo Jiù:
"Guard Chénggāo carefully!
Even if the King of Hàn wishes to provoke battle,
be cautious and do not engage him in combat,
just do not let him advance eastward.
I will certainly pacify the region of Liáng within fifteen days,
and then rejoin you, General."
Yǔ led his troops eastward,
attacking cities such as Chénliú, Wàihuáng, and Suīyáng,
and captured them all.
The King of Hàn wanted to abandon the area east of Chénggāo,
stationing troops at Gǒng and Luò to resist Chǔ.
Lìshēng said:
"I have heard that 'he who understands the heaven of heaven,
can accomplish the king's affairs';
a king regards the people as his heaven,
and the people regard food as their heaven.
The Dàdài Lǐ says: Those who eat grain are wise and skillful.
Gǔshǐ Kǎo says: In ancient times, people ate hair and drank blood,
Suìrénshì drilled for fire,
and people began to wrap meat and roast it, calling it páo.
In the time of Shénnóng,
people began to eat grain,
placing rice on heated stones to eat it.
By the time of Huángdì,
there were cauldrons and steamers,
and the way of cooked food was established.
The empire has been transporting grain for a long time,
I have heard that below there are stored grains in great abundance.
The men of Chǔ captured Xíngyáng,
but did not firmly hold Áocāng,
instead leading their troops eastward,
ordering conscripted soldiers to separately guard Chénggāo,
this is what heaven uses to aid Hàn.
Now Chǔ is easy to take but Hàn instead retreats,
forfeiting its own advantage,
I privately consider this a mistake!
Moreover, two heroes cannot stand together,
Chǔ and Hàn have long been locked in a stalemate,
the land within the seas is in turmoil,
farmers have laid down their plows,
lěi,
a curved wooden tool for hand plowing.
The hearts of the empire are not yet settled.
I hope Your Majesty will quickly advance the troops again,
recapture Xíngyáng,
seize the grain of Áocāng,
block the strategic pass of Chénggāo,
cut off the road of Tàiháng,
and hold the pass of Fēihú,
Rú Chún said: This is Húguān in Shàngdǎng.
Chén Zàn said: Fēihú Pass is in Dài Commandery.
Shī Gǔ said: Zàn is correct,
Húguān does not have the name Fēihú.
Dìdào Jì: Héng Mountain is 140 lǐ northwest of Shàngqūyáng County,
going north 450 lǐ,
one reaches the Héng Mountain ridge,
called Fēihú Pass,
to the north is Dài Commandery.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Dài Commandery has Fēihú Pass 40 lǐ to the south.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: According to this, Yù Prefecture's Fēihú County has the old Qín and Hán Dài Commandery city 150 lǐ to the north,
to the southwest there is a mountain,
commonly called Fēihú Pass.
Sāi,
read as xīzé.
Xíng,
read as hùgāng.
To show the feudal lords the strategic advantage of controlling the terrain,
meaning to rely on the terrain to control the enemy.
The King followed this advice,
and again planned to capture Áocāng.
Shíqì also persuaded the King, saying:
"Now Yān and Zhào are already pacified,
only Qí has not yet submitted.
The various Tián clans are powerful and strong,
backed by the sea and Dài,
protected by the Hé and Jì rivers,
Qí's territory reaches the sea to the east,
and Tàishān to the south,
hence 'backed by the sea and Dài',
protected by the clear Jì to the west,
and the muddy Hé to the north,
hence 'protected by the Hé and Jì rivers'.
Jì,
read as zǐlǐ.
The people are many and crafty;
even if Your Majesty sends tens of thousands of troops,
they cannot be defeated within a year or month.
I request to receive your clear edict to persuade the King of Qí,
to make him become an eastern vassal for Hàn."
Kǎoyì says: Shǐjì and Hànshū both combine Shíqì's advice to capture Áocāng and his request to persuade Qí into one event,
only Liú Xiàng's Xīnxù separates them into two;
I believe separating them into two is correct.
"Good!"
Then he sent Lìshēng to persuade the King of Qí, saying:
"Does the King know to whom the empire will submit?"
The King said:
"I do not know.
To whom will the empire submit?"
Lìshēng said:
"To Hàn!"
He said:
"How does the Master say this?"
He said:
"The King of Hàn first entered Xiányáng;
King Xiàng broke his promise,
making him king in Hànzhōng.
King Xiàng moved and killed Yìdì;
the King of Hàn heard of this,
raised troops from Shǔ and Hàn to attack Sān Qín,
marched out of the pass to demand an account for Yìdì's whereabouts.
He gathered the weapons of the empire,
established the descendants of the feudal lords;
when a city surrendered, he enfeoffed its general as a marquis,
when spoils were obtained, he distributed them among his soldiers;
he shared benefits with the empire,
heroes, elites, and talented men all gladly served him.
King Xiàng has the reputation of breaking promises,
and the guilt of killing Yìdì;
Máo Huǎng said: Betraying kindness and forgetting virtue is called fù.
Bèi,
is the same as bèi,
read as púmèi.
He never forgets anyone's faults;
those who win battles do not receive rewards,
those who capture cities do not receive fiefs,
none but the Xiàng clan can hold power;
the empire rebels against him,
talented men resent him,
and none are willing to serve him.
Therefore, the affairs of the empire will submit to the King of Hàn,
this can be predicted while sitting still!
The King of Hàn raised troops from Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified Sān Qín;
crossed the Xīhé,
defeated Northern Wèi;
The Hé River from Dǐzhù upwards and Lóngmén downwards is called Xīhé.
Suǒyǐn says: Northern Wèi,
refers to King Bào of Wèi,
because Bào's state was north of the river.
Also called Western Wèi,
because Dàliáng and Ānyì were considered east.
He executed Chéng'ān Jūn;
this was not due to human strength,
but the blessing of heaven!
Now he already holds the grain of Áocāng,
blocks the strategic pass of Chénggāo,
guards the ford of Báimǎ,
cuts off the slopes of Tàiháng,
and holds the pass of Fēihú;
those in the empire who submit later will perish first.
Lìshēng's persuasion,
is the argument of controlling terrain and restricting momentum.
For by holding Áocāng,
blocking Chénggāo,
then Xiàng Yǔ cannot go west;
guarding Báimǎ,
cutting off Tàiháng,
holding Fēihú,
then the lands of Héběi, Yān, and Zhào will all belong to Hàn,
where will Qí and Chǔ go then!
Báimǎ Ford was in Táng's Huá Prefecture.
Tàiháng slopes were within the boundaries of Táng's Zé Prefecture.
Dù Yòu said: Yù Prefecture's Fēihú County,
was the location of Hàn's Guǎngchāng County;
Fēihú Pass is north of the county,
which was Hàn's Fēihú Road,
connecting to Guīchuān Commandery's Huáiróng County.
Then the state of Qí can be preserved;
if not,
peril and destruction can be expected immediately!"
Previously,
Qí heard that Hán Xìn was about to lead troops east,
and sent Huà Wúshāng and Tián Jiě to station heavy troops at Lìxià,
to
resist Hàn.
After accepting Lìshēng's words,
they sent an envoy to make peace with Hàn,
and then removed the defensive preparations at Lìxià,
indulging in drinking and pleasure with Lìshēng daily.
Hán Xìn led his troops eastward,
but before crossing the Píngyuán region,
he heard that Lì Yìjī had already persuaded Qí to surrender,
and he wanted to halt.
The rhetorician Kuǎi Chè advised Xìn, saying:
"The general received an imperial edict to attack Qí,
yet Hàn alone dispatched a secret envoy to subdue Qí.
Is there any edict ordering the general to stop?
How can you not proceed?
Moreover, Lì Shēng
is but a single scholar,
who, leaning on the chariot rail, wagged his three-inch tongue.
The rail
is the horizontal bar in front of the chariot,
upon which people lean.
'Wag'
is pronounced 'diào',
meaning to shake.
The general, with tens of thousands of troops,
took over a year to capture more than fifty cities of Zhào.
Having been a general for several years,
how can you be inferior to the achievements of a mere pedantic scholar!"
Thereupon, Xìn agreed with him,
and thus crossed the river.
1 In winter,
the tenth month,
Xìn launched a surprise attack and defeated the Qí army at Lìxià,
then advanced to Línzī.
The King of Qí, believing that Lì Shēng had betrayed him,
had him boiled alive;
then led his troops eastward, fleeing to Gāomì.
Gāomì County was located in Jiāoxī.
In the first year of the Běnshǐ era of Emperor Xuān, it became the Kingdom of Gāomì.
Sòng Bái said: Gāomì
was the fief of Yàn Píngzhòng during the Spring and Autumn period.
Tián Héng fled to Bóyáng.
This is according to the Records of the Grand Historian.
The Book of Hàn records
"Héng fled to Bó."
Bóyáng was near the Bó Pass in Qīnghé,
which was precisely the route Hán Xìn took to advance his troops from Zhào.
After Línzī was captured,
the ruler and his ministers all fled.
Later, after Hán Xìn captured Tián Guǎng at the Wéi River,
Guàn Yīng again defeated Tián Héng at Yíngxià.
Yíng County also belonged to Tàishān Commandery.
The Expanded Geographical Records: The old Yíng City was located a hundred lǐ northeast of Bóchéng County in Yǎnzhōu.
Táng's Bóchéng
was Hàn's Bó County in Tàishān;
this Bóyáng
refers to the southern side of Bóchéng.
General Tián Jì stationed his army in Jiāodōng.
The Expanded Geographical Records: The old Jímò City was located sixty lǐ south of Jiāoshuǐ County in Láizhōu,
in the ancient territory of Qí.
In Hàn times, it was the Kingdom of Jiāodōng,
named so because its location was east of the Jiāo River.
2 The Chǔ Grand Marshal Jiū defended Chénggāo.
Hán repeatedly challenged them to battle,
but the Chǔ army did not emerge.
They sent men to insult them,
and after several days,
Jiū grew angry,
and led his troops across the Sì River.
Zhāng Yàn said: The Sì River is within the boundaries of Jìyīn.
Rú Chún said: Sì
is pronounced 'sì'.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The border is at Sì in the territory of Zhèng."
Chén Zàn said: When Gāozǔ attacked Cáo Jiū at Chénggāo,
Jiū crossed the Sì River to fight.
This is the Sì River east of present-day Chénggāo City.
Master Yán said: Zàn's explanation is correct;
this river is not in Jìyīn.
"The border is at Sì in the territory of Zhèng,"
the commentator says it is in Xiāngchéng,
so this is also not that Sì River.
The old reading was 'fán',
but now the local people pronounce it 'sì'.
Suǒ Yǐn said: This river is now called the Sì River,
pronounced 'sì';
Chén Zàn is correct.
Zhāng Yàn said: It being in Jìyīn is not entirely wrong.
According to this, the ancient Jì River at this point cut across the Huáng Hé and flowed south,
then eastward, overflowing to form the Xíngzé Marsh.
'South of the water' is called 'yīn',
so this is also south of the Jì River,
not that Jìyīn Commandery.
The Expanded Geographical Records: The source of the Sì River is at Fāng Mountain, thirty-two lǐ southeast of Sìshuǐ County in Luòzhōu.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas: From Fúxì Mountain,
the Sì River emerges.
Hàn attacked them,
greatly defeating the Chǔ army,
and capturing all of Chǔ's gold, jade, and valuables.
Jiū and Simǎ Xīn both cut their own throats on the Sì River.
The King of Hàn led his troops across the river,
recaptured Chénggāo,
and stationed his army at Guǎngwǔ.
Mèng Kāng said: At Xíngyáng, two cities were built facing each other, called Guǎngwǔ,
located on Sānhuáng Mountain west of Áo Granary.
The Expanded Geographical Records: East Guǎngwǔ and West Guǎngwǔ are twenty lǐ west of Xíngyáng County in Zhèngzhōu.
Dài Yánzhī's Record of a Western Campaign states: On Sānhuáng Mountain there are two cities;
the eastern one is called East Guǎngwǔ,
the western one is called West Guǎngwǔ,
each on a separate mountain peak,
a hundred paces apart.
The Biàn River flows southeast from the wide ravine between them,
but now it is dry and waterless.
Each city has three sides,
and they are west of Áo Granary.
Guō Yuánshēng's Record of a Military Expedition states: A ravine cuts horizontally across,
named Guǎngwǔ,
with opposing cities and moats built on each side,
hence named East and West Guǎngwǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ captured over ten cities in the Liáng region.
Hearing that Chénggāo had fallen,
he led his troops back.
The Hàn army was just besieging Zhōnglí Mò east of Xíngyáng.
Hearing that Yǔ had arrived,
they all fled to rugged terrain.
Yǔ also stationed his army at Guǎngwǔ,
facing off against Hàn.
After several months,
the Chǔ army's food supplies dwindled.
King Xiàng was troubled by this,
so he prepared a chopping block,
placed Tàigōng upon it,
and told the King of Hàn:
"If you do not surrender immediately,
I will boil Tàigōng alive!"
The King of Hàn said:
"You and I both received our mandates from King Huái facing north,
and swore to be brothers.
My father is thus your father;
if you insist on boiling your father,
I hope you will share a cup of the broth with me!"
Rú Chún said: The chopping block
is a high table.
Lǐ Qí said: In the army, a watchtower is called a chopping block.
Master Yán said: The chopping block
is used to present meat,
so to show the intent to boil him,
he was placed upon it;
Rú's explanation is correct.
Chopping block
is pronounced 'zǔ'.
The Dialects: In Zhōu, Jìn, Qín, and Lǒng, 'father' is called 'wēng'.
'Ruò'
means 'you';
'ér'
also means 'you'.
In ancient times, a cup was used to hold broth,
like today's cups which have two handles on the sides.
Yǔ wanted to kill him.
Xiàng Bó said:
"The outcome of the empire is still uncertain;
moreover, those who contend for the empire do not care for their families.
Even if you kill him, it will be of no benefit,
and will only increase misfortune!"
King Xiàng heeded him.
King Xiàng said to the King of Hàn:
"The reason the empire has been in turmoil for several years
is solely because of the two of us.
I wish to challenge the King of Hàn to single combat,
to decide who is superior,
so as not to needlessly torment the fathers and sons of the empire's people!"
The King of Hàn laughed and declined, saying:
"I would rather fight with wisdom,
than with brute force."
King Xiàng three times ordered strong warriors to go forth and issue challenges.
Hàn had an expert archer and horseman named Lóufán who would shoot and kill them each time.
Yīng Shào said: Lóufán
is a Hú person.
Lǐ Qí said: Later it became a county,
belonging to Yànmén.
The people of this county are skilled in archery and horsemanship.
Calling a warrior 'Lóufán'
is using the term as a title,
and he was not necessarily from Lóufán.
Master Yán said: Lǐ Qí's explanation is correct.
'Shoot'
is also pronounced 'shè'.
Then Yǔ himself donned armor, took up a halberd, and issued a challenge.
Lóufán wanted to shoot him,
but King Xiàng glared and shouted at him.
Lóufán dared not look him in the eye,
nor could he release his arrow,
so he turned and fled back into the fortress,
not daring to come out again.
The King of Hàn sent someone to discreetly inquire,
'discreetly inquire'
means to inquire subtly.
'Discreet'
is pronounced 'jiàn'.
The King of Hàn was greatly astonished.
Thereupon, King Xiàng personally approached the King of Hàn,
"Jí" meaning
to approach,
to follow.
Xiàng Yǔ wished to challenge the King of Hàn to single combat.
The King of Hàn enumerated Yǔ's crimes, saying:
"Yǔ broke his promise,
making me king in Shǔ and Hàn,
crime one;
falsely killing Qīngzǐ Guànjūn,
crime two;
rescuing Zhào but not returning to report,
instead forcibly leading the allied lords' troops through the pass,
crime three;
burning the Qín palaces,
excavating the First Emperor's tomb,
seizing its treasures for himself,
crime four;
"seizing for himself" means
taking the treasures to make them his private property.
Crime five;
deceitfully massacring two hundred thousand surrendered Qín soldiers at Xīn'ān,
crime six;
enfeoffing his own generals in good lands while expelling the former kings,
crime seven;
driving out the Righteous Emperor,
making Péngchéng his own capital,
seizing the lands of the King of Hán,
annexing and ruling over Liáng and Chǔ,
taking much for himself,
crime eight;
sending someone to secretly murder the Righteous Emperor south of the river,
crime nine;
governing unjustly,
breaking covenants as a leader,
intolerable to all under heaven,
a great traitor devoid of morality,
crime ten.
I lead a righteous army with the allied lords to punish a cruel brigand,
I could have criminals and convicts attack you,
why should I trouble myself to challenge you personally!"
Yǔ was greatly enraged,
and had a crossbowman shoot and hit the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn was wounded in the chest,
but he clutched his foot, saying:
"The scoundrel hit my toe."
The King of Hàn lay ill from his wound,
but Zhāng Liáng strongly urged the King of Hàn to rise and tour the army,
to reassure the troops,
and not let Chǔ exploit the victory.
The King of Hàn went out to inspect the army,
but his injury was severe,
so he galloped into Chénggāo.
3 Hán Xìn had already pacified Línzī,
and then pursued the King of Qí eastward.
King Xiàng sent Lóng Jū to lead troops,
said to be two hundred thousand,
to rescue Qí,
and they joined forces with the King of Qí at Gāomì.
A guest advised Lóng Jū, saying:
"The Hàn troops fight far from home, desperate in battle,
their vanguard is irresistible.
Qí and Chǔ are fighting on their own soil,
their soldiers are easily defeated and scattered.
In Sūnzǐ's 'Nine Terrains',
it says when lords fight on their own land it is 'dispersive ground'.
Cáo Cāo said: The soldiers are attached to their land,
and the routes are short, so they easily scatter.
Yì,
pronounced with the tone of chǐ;
same below.
Order the King of Qí to send his trusted ministers to rally the lost cities;
'trusted ministers' means
ministers he always trusts.
When Chǔ comes to the rescue,
they will surely turn against Hàn.
The Hàn troops are guests two thousand lǐ away in Qí territory,
if all the Qí cities rebel,
their situation will leave them with no food,
and they can be made to surrender without a fight."
Lóng Jū said:
"I have long known Hán Xìn's character,
he is easy to deal with!
He relied on a washerwoman for food,
having no means to support himself;
he suffered humiliation under the crotch,
lacking the courage to face others;
these events are recorded in the first year of the previous scroll.
Moreover, to rescue Qí
and have them surrender without a fight,
what merit would I have!
If we fight and defeat them now,
I can gain half of Qí."
In the eleventh month,
Qí and Chǔ faced Hán across the Wéi River in battle formation.
Xú Guǎng said: The Wéi River flows from Dōngguǎn northeast,
to Dūchāng County in Běihǎi, where it enters the sea.
Suǒyǐn said: The Wéi River flows from Jī County in Lángyá northeast,
to Dūchāng where it enters the sea.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Wéi River passes west of the old city of Gāomì County;
Hán Xìn and Lóng Jū faced each other across the water in formation,
which was at this place.
Wéi,
pronounced wéi.
Chén,
read as zhèn (battle array).
Hán Xìn had previously ordered men to fill over ten thousand sacks with sand,
to block the river's upper flow;
he then led half his army across to attack Lóng Jū,
feigned defeat,
and retreated.
Lóng Jū indeed said joyfully:
"I always knew Xìn was a coward!"
He then pursued Xìn.
Xìn sent men to break open the dam of sandbags,
a great flood came down,
and most of Lóng Jū's army could not cross.
Xìn immediately attacked fiercely and killed Lóng Jū,
the army east of the water scattered and fled,
and the King of Qí, Tián Guǎng, fled.
Xìn then pursued the defeated forces north to Chéngyáng,
and captured the King of Qí, Tián Guǎng.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Chéngyáng,
is Léizé County,
located ninety-one lǐ southeast of Pú Prefecture.
According to my reference to Bān Zhì,
Léizé is northwest of Chéngyáng County in Jìyīn Commandery,
this is Liáng territory;
pursuing north from the Wéi River to Chéngyáng,
this is the territory of the Hàn-era Chéngyáng Kingdom.
The Zhèngyì is mistaken here,
same as in the second year of the previous scroll regarding Tián Héng rising in Chéngyáng.
He advanced to Bóyáng.
Tián Héng, hearing of the King of Qí's death,
proclaimed himself King of Qí,
turned back and attacked Guàn Yīng,
but Yīng defeated Héng's army at Yíngxià.
Tián Héng fled to Liáng,
and submitted to Péng Yuè.
Yīng advanced and attacked the Qí general Tián Xī at Qiānshèng,
Qiānshèng County belonged to Běihǎi Commandery,
Gāozǔ later established it as Qiānshèng Commandery.
Kuòdìzhì: The old city of Qiānshèng,
is located twenty-five lǐ north of Gāoyuàn County in Zī Prefecture.
Shèng,
pronounced shèng.
He killed them all,
and completely pacified the land of Qí.
4 He established Zhāng Ĕr as King of Zhào.
5 The King of Hàn recovered from his illness,
and went west into the pass.
Arriving at Yuèyáng,
he displayed the head of the former King of Sài, Sīmǎ Xīn, in the Yuèyáng market.
Shī Gǔ said: Displaying a head on a wooden pole is called xiāo.
Suǒyǐn said: Xīn cut his own throat on the Sì River,
now displaying it at Yuèyáng,
because it was his former capital,
so it was displayed there as a warning.
He then returned to the army,
which was at Guǎngwǔ.
6 Hán Xìn sent a messenger to tell the King of Hàn:
"Qí is deceitful and fickle,
a state of repeated reversals;
its southern border is near Chǔ.
Shī Gǔ said: Biān,
means near.
The King of Hàn opened the letter,
was greatly angered,
and cursed:
"I am trapped here,
day and night hoping you would come to aid me;
yet you want to make yourself king!"
Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng stepped on the King of Hàn's foot,
and leaning close to his ear, said:
"Hàn is currently in a difficult position,
how can you stop Xìn from making himself king!
It would be better to take this opportunity to establish him,
treat him well,
and let him guard the area for himself;
otherwise,
trouble will arise."
The King of Hàn also realized this,
and so continued cursing:
"A true man who pacifies the lords,
should be a true king,
what need is there for a 'acting' title!"
In spring,
the second month,
he sent Zhāng Liáng bearing the seal to establish Hán Xìn as King of Qí,
and summoned his troops to attack Chǔ.
7 When King Xiàng heard that Lóng Jū had died,
he was greatly frightened,
and sent Wǔ Shè of Xūyí
to go and persuade King Qí, Xìn, saying:
"All under heaven have long suffered bitterly under Qín,
and joined forces to attack Qín.
After Qín was defeated,
achievements were calculated and lands were divided,
territories were apportioned and kings were established,
so that the soldiers might rest.
Now King Hàn has again raised troops and marched east,
encroaching upon others' shares,
seizing others' lands;
having already destroyed the Three Qín,
he leads his troops out of the passes,
gathers the armies of the various lords to attack Chǔ in the east,
his intention is not to stop until he has swallowed the whole world,
his insatiable greed is as extreme as this!
Moreover, King Hàn cannot be relied upon: he was several times within King Xiàng's grasp,
and King Xiàng, taking pity, spared him;
yet once he escaped,
he would immediately break the agreement,
and attack King Xiàng again,
his untrustworthiness is such.
Now, though you yourself consider
King Hàn to be a close friend,
and exert your utmost effort and military strength for him,
you will surely end up being captured by him.
The reason you have been able to survive until now
is because King Xiàng still exists.
In the current affairs of the two kings,
the power lies with you;
if you turn to the right, King Hàn will win,
if you turn to the left, King Xiàng will win.
If King Xiàng perishes today,
then next he will come for you.
You have a past connection with King Xiàng,
why not turn against Hàn and ally with Chǔ,
and divide the world into three to rule as kings!
'Divide into three,'
that is, three parts.
Moreover, is it not thus that a wise man should act?"
Hán Xìn declined, saying:
"When I served King Xiàng,
my office was no higher than Lángzhōng,
my position no more than halberd-bearer;
Lángzhōng,
halberd-bearer, palace guard.
Xìn first served Chǔ as a Lángzhōng,
hence he spoke thus.
My plans were not employed,
so I turned against Chǔ and joined Hàn.
King Hàn bestowed upon me the seal of Supreme General,
gave me command of tens of thousands of troops,
took off his own clothes to clothe me,
pushed aside his own food to feed me,
listened to my words and employed my strategies,
therefore I have been able to reach this point.
When someone deeply trusts and believes in me,
it would be inauspicious for me to betray him;
even unto death I will not change!
I beg you to convey my apologies to King Xiàng."
After Wǔ Shè had left,
Kuǎi Chè knew that the power of the world lay with Hán Xìn.
He then used the art of physiognomy to persuade Hán Xìn, saying:
"I have examined your face,
and it indicates no more than being enfeoffed as a marquis,
and even that is precarious and insecure.
But examining your back,
the nobility it portends is beyond words."
He used subtle words to move Hán Xìn,
implying that turning his back on Hàn would bring great nobility.
Xiàng,
read as xiàng.
"What do you mean?"
Kuǎi Chè said:
"When the world first rose in revolt,
the concern was only about destroying Qín.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Their aim was to destroy Qín,
this was their sole worry.
They caused the people of the world to have their livers and gall spilled on the ground,
fathers and sons exposed their bones in the wilderness,
too many to count.
The men of Chǔ fled to
Péngchéng,
fought and pursued the defeated northward,
riding the tide of victory they swept across like a mat being rolled up,
their might shaking the world.
Yet their troops were trapped between Jīng and Suǒ,
pressed against the western hills and unable to advance,
for three years now.
The King of Hàn led an army of a hundred
thousand men,
held Gǒng and Luò,
relying on the natural barriers of mountains and rivers,
fought several battles a day,
yet gained not an inch of ground,
suffered defeats and routs without relief.
Zhé,
means setback.
Běi,
means to flee.
'Bù jiù' means
unable to save themselves.
Zhé,
read as shé.
The common people were exhausted and full of resentment,
with nowhere to turn or rely on.
In my estimation,
the situation is such that only a sage of the world can surely end the world's calamities.
Now the fates of the two lords
hang upon you.
If you side with Hàn, then Hàn will win;
if you side with Chǔ, then Chǔ will win.
If you truly heed my plan,
nothing would be better than to benefit both and let both survive,
divide the world into three parts,
stand like the legs of a tripod,
so that none would dare move first.
With your sagacity and wisdom,
and your multitude of armed troops,
holding strong Qí,
aligning with Zhào and Yān,
you could march into empty territories and control their rear,
follow the people's desires,
face west and plead for the people's lives.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Qí is in the east,
hence 'face west'.
Stop the fighting between Chǔ and Hàn,
so that soldiers do not die,
hence 'plead for their lives'.
Xiàng,
read as xiàng;
same below.
Who would dare not listen!
Carve up the large and weaken the strong to establish feudal lords.
Once the feudal lords are established,
the world will submit and obey,
and give credit to Qí.
Secure Qí's former territories,
possess the lands of Jiāo and Sì.
Jiāo and Sì
are the names of two rivers.
Then the rulers of the world will come in succession to pay homage to Qí.
Yán Shīgǔ said: 'Shēn gǒng'
is like 'gāo gǒng'.
Cháo,
read as cháo.
'On the contrary, one suffers misfortune;
when the time comes but one does not act,
on the contrary, one suffers disaster.'
I hope you will consider this carefully!"
Hán Xìn said:
"The King of Hàn has treated me with great kindness.
How could I turn toward profit and betray righteousness!"
Kuǎi Shēng said:
"Initially, Chángshān Wáng and Chéng'ān Jūn, when they were commoners,
were sworn friends willing to die for each other.
Later, they quarreled over the matter of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé.
Chángshān Wáng killed Chéng'ān Jūn south of the Chí River,
his head and feet in separate places.
These two men's relationship
was the happiest in the world,
yet they ended up capturing each other.
Why?
Trouble arises from many desires and the human heart being hard to fathom.
Now you wish to act with loyalty and trust in your dealings with the King of Hàn,
but surely it cannot be as firm as the relationship between those two men,
and there are many matters greater than Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé.
Therefore, I believe that you are certainly mistaken
in thinking the King of Hàn will not endanger you!
Great Fū Zhǒng preserved perishing Yuè,
made Gōu Jiàn a hegemon,
achieved merit and fame but himself met death.
When the wild beasts are gone, the hunting dogs are boiled.
In terms of friendship,
yours is not as good as that between Zhāng Ěr and Chéng'ān Jūn.
In terms of loyalty and trust,
yours does not exceed that of Great Fū Zhǒng towards Gōu Jiàn.
These two cases are enough to see clearly.
I hope you will consider this deeply!
Moreover, I have heard, 'He whose courage and strategy shake his lord endangers himself;
he whose merit overshadows the world receives no reward.'
Now you bear the awe that shakes your lord,
hold merit that goes unrewarded.
If you return to Chǔ,
the men of Chǔ will not trust you;
if you return to Hàn,
the men of Hàn will be shaken with fear.
With this, where do you intend to go and find safety?"
Hán Xìn declined, saying:
"Sir, please stop for now.
I will think about it."
Several days later,
Kuǎi Chè again tried to persuade him, saying:
"The ability to listen
is the sign of affairs;
Yán Shīgǔ said: It means being able to listen to good counsel.
Fù,
read as fù.
is the pivot of affairs;
to err in listening and planning and yet remain secure for long is rare!
Xiǎn,
read as xiǎn.
Decisiveness in judgment
Duàn,
read as duàn.
is the bane of affairs.
To scrutinize calculations as fine as a hair,
Háo,
means long hair.
Ten háo make a lí.
even if wisdom truly knows it,
to decide but dare not act
is the calamity of all affairs.
Merit
is hard to achieve but easy to ruin;
opportunity
is hard to obtain but easy to lose.
Opportunity, ah,
opportunity does not come twice!"
Hán Xìn hesitated,
unable to bear betraying Hàn.
Moreover, he thought himself having much merit,
and that Hàn would ultimately not take Qí from him.
So he declined Kuǎi Chè.
'Xiè qù' means
to dismiss him and send him away.
Kuǎi Chè then feigned madness and became a shaman.
8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Qíng Bù was established as King of Huáinán.
9 In the eighth month,
the northern Mò and people of Yān came to offer fierce cavalry to aid Hàn.
Yīng Shào said: Běi Mò
is a state.
Xiāo
means robust.
Zhāng Yàn said: Xiāo
means brave,
like the xiāo in the game of liù bó.
Yán Shīgǔ said: The Mò are in the northeast,
the Sānhán and such
are all of the Mò kind.
Probably both the Mò people and Yān came to aid Hàn.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The classics and commentaries often say the Mò are mostly eastern barbarians, hence the Zhífāng official is in charge of the nine Yí and nine Mò.
Zhèng Xuán's answer to Zhào Shāng says: The nine Mò
are the nine Yí.
Also, the Zhōuguān mentions Mò slaves,
the commentary says they are captives from expeditions against the northeastern barbarians.
Mò,
read the same as mò.
10 The King of Hàn issued an order: For soldiers who unfortunately died,
officials were to provide shrouds and coffins,
and transport them back to their families.
Thus, the hearts of all quarters turned towards him.
11 This year,
Zhou Chāng was appointed as the Imperial Censor from the position of Commandant of the Palace Guards.
According to the Bān Biǎo: The Commandant of the Palace Guards,
was an official position established during the Qin dynasty,
responsible for patrolling and maintaining order in the capital;
in the first year of the Tàichū era of Emperor Wǔ, it was renamed to the Commandant of the Metal Mace.
He was a cousin of Zhou Kē.
12 Xiàng Yǔ himself knew he had little support;
provisions were exhausted,
and Hán Xìn advanced his troops to attack Chǔ,
causing Xiàng Yǔ great concern.
Hàn sent Hóu Gōng to persuade Xiàng Yǔ to request the release of Tàigōng.
Tàigōng and Empress Lǚ had been captured by Chǔ,
as seen in the third year of the previous volume.
They divided the empire in half,
with the Hóng Gōu as the boundary: the area west of the Hóng Gōu was assigned to Hàn,
and the area east to Chǔ.
Wén Yǐng said: The Hóng Gōu was a canal dug from the Yellow River southeast of Yíngyáng,
connecting Sòng, Zhèng, Cài, Cáo, and Wèi,
and converging with the Jǐ, Rǔ, Huái, and Sì rivers in Chǔ territory,
which is the present-day Guāndù River.
Yìng Shào said: Twenty lǐ southeast of Yíngyáng,
it is said to have diverted the Yellow River southeast into the Huái and Sì rivers.
Zhāng Huá said: The city of Dàliáng was located in Jùnyí County.
Northwest of this county,
the Qú River flowed east past the south of this city,
then turned north,
splitting into two channels: one channel flowed southeast,
excavated by Qín Shǐhuáng,

The Hàn system: The emperor's written orders had four types: first, cèshū (imperial decree),
second, zhìshū (imperial ordinance),
third, zhàoshū (imperial edict),
fourth, jièchì (admonitory order).
Cèshū,
are bound bamboo slips,

the shorter ones half that;
written in seal script,

they are also granted a cè,
but written in clerical script,

with two lines,
this being the difference.
Zhìshū,
are the emperor's institutional commands.
Their text reads
"Zhì zhào sāngōng" (By ordinance, we inform the Three Dukes),
all sealed with the imperial seal,
the Shàngshū Lìng's seal double-sealed,

Zhàoshū,
zhào,
means to inform,

Jièchì,

"Yǒu zhào,
chì mǒu guān" (There is an edict, ordering such-and-such official).

Shī Gǔ said: Zhāng's explanation is incorrect.

then Chancellor Xiāo Hé, Grand Commandant Lú Wǎn, as well as Zhāng Liáng, Chén Píng and their ilk were all present,
Líng would not have been able to answer first.
The Xìngpǔ states: Descendants of the Grand Duke of Qí,
who received the fief of Gāo for their sustenance,
thus took it as their surname.
"Your Majesty sends men to attack cities and seize territories,
and then bestows them upon them,
sharing the benefits with all under heaven;
Xiàng Yǔ was not like this,
he harmed those who achieved merit,
and suspected the worthy,
this is why he lost the empire."
The Emperor said:
"You gentlemen know one aspect,
but not the other.
For devising strategies within the command tent,
and determining victory a thousand lǐ away,
I am not equal to Zǐfáng;
for stabilizing the state,
comforting the common people,
supplying provisions,
and keeping the supply routes open,
I am not equal to Xiāo Hé;
for leading a host of a million men,
ensuring victory in every battle,
and capturing every objective attacked,
I am not equal to Hán Xìn.
These three are all outstanding men,
yet I was able to employ them,
this is how I gained the empire.
Xiàng Yǔ had one Fàn Zēng and could not use him,
this is why he was captured by me."
The assembled ministers were convinced.
When Hán Xìn arrived in Chǔ,
he summoned the washerwoman,
and bestowed upon her a thousand pieces of gold.
He summoned the young man who had humiliated him by making him crawl between his legs,
and appointed him as a Commandant of the Center;
the event is recorded in the ninth scroll, first year.
'Piǎo' (漂)
is pronounced 'piào'.
"This is a brave man.
When he was humiliating me,
could I not have killed him?
Killing him would have been without just cause,
therefore I endured it and achieved this."
11 Since Péng Yuè had received his Hán enfeoffment,
Tián Héng, fearing execution,
along with over five hundred of his followers, went out to sea,
and dwelled on an island.
A mountain in the sea is called an island.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: In Dōnghǎi County of Hǎi Prefecture there is an island mountain,
eighty lǐ from the shore.
I note that according to the Běishǐ,
Yáng Yīn, avoiding slander, went east to Tián Héng Island,
thus the island is named after Tián Héng's residence there.
'Dǎo' (島)
is pronounced 'dǎo'.
Many worthy men of Qí attached themselves to him;
now that they are at sea,
if we do not subdue them,
later they may cause trouble.
He therefore sent an envoy to pardon Héng's crime,
and summon him.
Héng declined, saying:
"I boiled Your Majesty's envoy Lì Shēng,
the event is recorded in the previous scroll, fourth year.
I am filled with fear,
and dare not receive the command,
I beg to remain a commoner,
guarding this island in the sea."
The envoy returned and reported,
the Emperor then issued an edict to Commandant of the Palace Guard Lì Shāng, saying:
According to the Bān Biǎo: The Commandant of the Palace Guard,
was an office of the Qín,
in charge of the garrison troops at the palace gates.
"When King of Qí Tián Héng arrives,
if any among his men or horses dare to make a move,
it will lead to the extermination of their clans!"
He then sent another envoy bearing the tally, fully informing him of the edict's instructions to Shāng,
The Zhōulǐ states: The Director of Tallies is in charge of guarding the state tallies,
distinguishing their uses to assist the king's commands.
The commentary says: A tally (jié)
is held while traveling as a credential.
State tallies
are the zhēn guī, yá zhāng, gǔ guī, wǎn guī, and yǎn guī.
Guarding the states and fiefdoms uses jade tallies,
made of jade;
guarding the capital and its outskirts uses horn tallies,
made of horn.
Envoys of states and fiefdoms
use metal tallies;
gates and passes
use tally tokens;
for goods and bribes,
they use seals;
for roads,
they use pennants.
Examining this,
then what was held in ancient times as a credential,
was all called a 'jié'.
Since the Qín era,
there have been seals, tally tokens, and tallies,
then seals were seals,
tally tokens were tally tokens,
tallies were tallies,
divided into three categories.
The Hàn tally,
was the ancient pennant tally.
Zhèng's commentary takes the tally token as the Hàn palace edict tallies,
the seal tally as the Hàn seals and stamps,
and the pennant tally as the tally held by Hàn envoys;
thus we know what the Hàn called a tally,
was likely the ancient pennant tally.
Xián said: The tally,
is used as a credential,
made of bamboo,
with a handle eight chǐ long,
adorned with yak tail hair,
in three layers of tufts.
This was the Hàn system.
"If Tián Héng comes,
at best he will be made a king,
at least he will be made a marquis;
if he does not come,
we will raise troops and punish him."
Tián Héng then traveled with two of his retainers by post carriage to Luòyáng.
Rú Chún said: For four-horse carriages,
those with swift horses were called "zhì chuán" (station carriages),
those with medium-paced horses were called "chí chuán" (galloping carriages),
and those with slower horses were called "chéng chuán" (riding carriages);
one-horse or two-horse carriages were called "yáo chuán" (light carriages).
In urgent matters, one would ride a single "chéng chuán".
Shī Gǔ said: These are probably like today's postal stations,
in ancient times they used carriages,
called "chuán chē" (post carriages);
later they used single horses alone,
called "yì qí" (postal riders).
Hàn law: All those who should ride post carriages or dispatch and establish post stations,
all held a one-foot-five-inch wooden tally,
sealed with the seal of the Yùshǐ Dàfū;
for those riding "chéng chuán",
it was sealed three times,
"cān",
meaning three;
if there was a scheduled meeting,
the two ends were sealed repeatedly,
each end with two seals,
making four seals in total;
for riding "zhì chí chuán",
it was sealed five times,
two seals at each end,
and one in the center;
for "yáo chuán",
with two horses, it was sealed twice;
with one horse, sealed once,
using a horse to pull a light carriage and riding as a post was called "yī fēng yáo chuán".
Shǐ Zhào's so-called reliance on tallies and passes to travel was based on this;
but his selection was not precise,
and his explanation was not detailed,
ultimately not as concise and clear as Yán's explanation.
Chuán,
read as zhàng liàn fān.
Upon reaching Shīxiāng, they halted at the post station.
Yìng Shào said: Shīxiāng,
is west of Yǎnshī city.
Chén Zàn said: According to the post station,
it refers to stationing horses for postal relay.
"When a subject meets the Son of Heaven,
he should bathe and cleanse himself."
Thereupon he stopped and stayed,
saying to his retainers:
"I, Héng, initially faced south as king alongside the King of Hàn;
Shī Gǔ said: Kings refer to themselves as 'gū' (the solitary one),
probably as a gesture of humility.
The Lǎozǐ Dàodé Jīng says: The noble takes the humble as its root,
the high takes the low as its foundation,
therefore marquises and kings call themselves 'gū', 'guǎ', 'bù gǔ'.
Yet I, Héng, am now a fugitive,
serving him facing north,
the shame is already extreme.
Moreover, I boiled that man's elder brother,
and now stand shoulder to shoulder with his younger brother serving the same lord;
even if he, fearing the Son of Heaven's decree, dares not act,
how can I alone not feel ashamed in my heart!
Furthermore, the reason His Majesty wishes to see me,
is merely to see my face once;
now if you cut off my head,
and gallop thirty lǐ,
my features will not yet have decayed,
and it will still be viewable."
Thereupon he cut his own throat,
ordering his retainers to present his head,
and follow the envoy galloping to report it.
The Emperor said:
"Alas!
Rising from common cloth,
three brothers successively became kings,
how could they not be worthy!"
He shed tears for them,
and appointed his two retainers as Dūwèi;
he dispatched two thousand soldiers,
to bury him with royal rites.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Tián Héng's tomb is fifteen lǐ west of Yǎnshī.
The two retainers dug holes beside his mound,
and both cut their own throats,
descending to follow him.
The Emperor heard of this,
and was greatly astonished.
Considering Héng's retainers all worthy,
and the remaining five hundred men still on the island,
he sent an envoy to summon them;
when they arrived,
upon hearing of Tián Héng's death,
they all committed suicide as well.
12 Initially,
a man of Chǔ, Jì Bù, served as a general under Xiàng Jí,
Jì,
is a surname.
Among the Eight Scholars of Zhōu were Jì Suí and Jì Guā;
in Lǔ there was the Jì clan.
After Xiàng Jí was destroyed,
the Emperor offered a thousand catties of gold for Bù's capture;
anyone daring to shelter or hide him,
would be punished with extermination of three clans.
Shě,
means to stop.
Nì,
means to conceal.
He sold himself to Zhū Jiā of Lǔ.
Zhū Jiā knew in his heart it was Jì Bù,
bought him and settled him on a farm;
then personally went to Luòyáng to see Téng Gōng,
and persuaded him, saying:
"What crime has Jì Bù committed!
Subjects each serve their own lord,
it is their duty;
Shī Gǔ said: Zhí,
means constant;
meaning this is the constant way.
Another interpretation: Zhí,
means to be in charge of the matter.
Wéi,
read as yú wèi fān.
Now the Emperor has just gained the empire,
yet seeks one man due to personal enmity,
how this shows a lack of breadth!
Moreover, with Jì Bù's worth,
if the Hàn pursuit is urgent,
he will have no choice but to flee north to the Hú,
or south to Yuè.
To resent a strong man and thereby aid an enemy state,
this is why Wǔ Zǐxū whipped King Píng of Jīng's tomb."
Wǔ Zǐxū,
was the son of Wǔ Shē, a senior official of Chǔ.
King Píng of Chǔ believed slander and killed Wǔ Shē,
Zǐxū fled to Wú,
borrowed Wú's army to defeat Chǔ,
entered Yǐng,
opened King Píng's tomb and whipped his corpse.
Téng Gōng waited for an opportunity,
spoke to the Emperor,
according to Zhū Jiā's intention.
The Emperor then pardoned Bù,
summoned and appointed him as Lángzhōng,
and Zhū Jiā thereafter never saw him again.
Bù's maternal younger brother Dīng Gōng,
also served as a general under Xiàng Yǔ,
pursued and cornered the Emperor west of Péngchéng.
Close combat ensued,
the Emperor in dire straits,
turned and said to Dīng Gōng:
"How can two worthies oppress each other!"
Mèng Kāng said: Dīng Gōng and Lài Yǐ of Péngchéng were pursuing the Emperor,
hence 'two worthies'.
Shī Gǔ said: Mèng's interpretation is wrong.
The two worthies,
refers to Gāozǔ himself and Dīng Gōng,
meaning I and you are both worthy,
how can we oppress and distress each other!
Therefore Dīng Gōng, moved by these words, stopped.
Although he pursued together with Lài Yǐ,
Gāozǔ spoke only to Dīng Gōng.
Xìng Pǔ: The surname Dīng originally came from the Jiāng surname,
Duke Dīng, posthumously titled, was the son of Duke Tài of Qí,
hence taking it as the clan name.
After King Xiàng was destroyed,
Dīng Gōng came for an audience.
The Emperor took Dīng Gōng and paraded him in the army,
saying:
"Dīng Gōng was disloyal as a subject of King Xiàng,
he is the one who caused King Xiàng to lose the empire."
Thereupon he beheaded him,
saying:
"Let future subjects not emulate Dīng Gōng!"
Your subject Guāng says: Since Gāozǔ rose from Fēng and Pèi,
he has ensnared heroes and stalwarts,
recruited fugitives and accepted traitors,
and indeed it has been many.
Yet upon ascending the imperial throne,
Dīng Gōng alone was executed for disloyalty,
why?
For advancing to seize and guarding what is achieved,
the circumstances differ.
During the time when heroes vied for supremacy,
the people had no fixed lord;
accepting those who came,
was certainly appropriate.
But upon becoming honored as Son of Heaven,
within the four seas,
all are his subjects;
if he does not clearly demonstrate ritual and righteousness to them,
causing those who serve as ministers,
each to harbor divided loyalties seeking great profit,
then how can the state long remain secure!
Therefore, judging by great righteousness,
he made all under heaven clearly understand that disloyal ministers have nowhere to hide;
and those who cherish private favors and form personal bonds,
even if they spared his own life,
righteousness still does not permit it.
Executing one man causes ten thousand to fear,
his consideration of affairs was indeed deep and far-reaching!
His descendants enjoyed Heaven's mandate for over four hundred years,
fitting indeed!
13. A man from Qí named Lóu Jìng, who was garrisoning Lǒngxī,
(according to the *Genealogy of Surnames*: The surname Lóu
originated from the descendants of the state of Zhūlóu;
another theory states they are descendants of Lílóu.)
removed the crossbar from his cart,
wore a sheepskin robe,
and through a man from Qí named General Yú, sought an audience with the Emperor.
General Yú wanted to give him new clothes.
Lóu Jìng said:
"If I wear silk,
I will see him wearing silk;
if I wear coarse cloth,
I will see him wearing coarse cloth;
'wear'
means to put on.
'Silk'
refers to fine fabrics.
'Coarse cloth'
refers to garments woven from wool.
Thereupon, General Yú went in and spoke to the Emperor;
the Emperor summoned him for an audience,
and questioned him.
Lóu Jìng said:
"Does Your Majesty establish the capital at Luòyáng,
wishing to rival the prosperity of the Zhōu dynasty?"
The Emperor said:
"Yes."
Lóu Jìng said:
"The way Your Majesty obtained the empire differs from that of the Zhōu.
The ancestors of the Zhōu,
starting from Hòujì who was enfeoffed at Tái,
(according to Bān's *Treatise*,
Tái county belonged to Yòufúfēng.
Master Yán Gǔ said: This is the present-day old city of Wǔgōng.
The *Correct Meaning of the Records of the Grand Historian* states: Twenty-three *lǐ* southwest of Wǔgōng county in Yōngzhōu,
is the old Líchéng.
The *Shuōwén* states: Tái,
was the state enfeoffed to the descendants of the Yán Emperor, surnamed Jiāng,
the maternal family of Qì.
Máo Cháng said: Tái,
was the state of Jiāng Yuán.
Because Yáo believed that Heaven, through Tái, gave birth to Hòujì,
he therefore enfeoffed him at Tái;
pronunciation: tǔ cái fān.
'Lěi'
is the ancient form of the character 'lěi'.
down to Tàiwáng, Wángjì, King Wén, and King Wǔ, when the feudal lords voluntarily submitted to them,
they subsequently destroyed the Yīn and became the Son of Heaven.
When King Chéng ascended the throne,
the Duke of Zhōu served as his minister,
and then built the city of Luòyì,
considering it the center of the empire,
where feudal lords from all directions presented tribute and duties,
as the distances were equal.
With virtue, it was easy to rule as king;
without virtue, it was easy to perish.
Therefore, during the prosperous era of the Zhōu,
the empire was harmonious and well-governed,
and the feudal lords and the Four Barbarians all submitted,
offering their tribute and duties.
When it declined,
no one in the empire came to court,
and the Zhōu could not control them;
not only was their virtue shallow,
but their strategic position was also weak.
Now Your Majesty arose from Fēng and Pèi,
swept through Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified the Three Qín,
fought Xiàng Yǔ between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo,
engaging in seventy major battles,
and forty minor battles;
causing the people of the empire,
their livers and brains to spill on the ground,
fathers and sons to expose their bones in the wilderness,
countless in number,
the sound of weeping not yet ceased,
the wounded not yet recovered;
yet you wish to rival the prosperity of the eras of Kings Chéng and Kāng,
I privately believe this is not comparable.
Moreover, the land of Qín is backed by mountains and girded by rivers,
with four strategic passes forming a stronghold;
should a sudden emergency arise,
a million troops can be assembled instantly.
Relying on the old foundations of Qín,
and utilizing its exceptionally fertile and rich land,
this is what is called the 'Storehouse of Heaven'.
'Storehouse'
means a gathering place;
where all things gather,
is called the Storehouse of Heaven.
Although the area east of the mountains is in chaos,
the old territory of Qín can be completely held and possessed.
When wrestling with a man,
if you do not seize his throat,
and press his back,
you cannot achieve complete victory;
(Zhāng Yàn said: 'Seize'
is the same as 'strangle',
meaning to grip tightly.
'Throat',
pronunciation: gāng,
also pronounced xià láng fān,
means the gullet.)
This is also seizing the throat of the empire and pressing its back."
The Emperor asked his ministers.
His ministers were all men from east of the mountains,
and they contended, saying:
"The Zhōu kings lasted for several hundred years,
while the Qín dynasty perished in the second generation.
Luòyáng has Chénggāo to the east,
and Yáo and Miǎn to the west.
(Master Yán Gǔ said: 'Yáo'
refers to Mount Yáo,
which is the present-day two Yáo mountains east of Shǎnzhōu.
'Miǎn'
is Miǎnchí.)
Facing the Yī and Luò rivers,
(the Huáng Hé is north of Luòyáng city,
hence it is said to be 'behind';
the Yī
and Luò rivers are south of Luòyáng city,
hence it is said to be 'facing'.
'Behind',
pronunciation: pú mèi fān.
'Facing',
read as 'xiàng'.)
The Emperor asked Zhāng Liáng.
Liáng said:
"Although Luòyáng has these strongholds,
its interior is small, not exceeding a few hundred *lǐ*,
the land is poor,
and it is exposed to enemies on all sides;
this is not a land suitable for military operations.
Guānzhōng has Yáo and Hán to the left,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
and a thousand *lǐ* of fertile plains;
(Master Yán Gǔ said: 'Fertile'
means irrigated;
it means the land all has the benefit of irrigation,
hence it is called fertile plains.)
To the north, it has the advantage of the Hú pastures.
(Master Yán Gǔ said: This refers to the areas of Āndìng, Běidì, and Shàngjùn that border the Hú to the north,
where animal husbandry can be practiced.
Places where birds and beasts are raised are called 'pastures',
pronunciation: yú ruǎn fān.)
With only one side facing east to control the feudal lords;
when the feudal lords are pacified,
the Huáng Hé and Wèi River can transport goods from the empire by water and land,
supplying the capital from the west;
(when the Hàn transported grain from east of the passes,
it went from the Huáng Hé into the Wèi River,
and from the Wèi River upstream to deliver it to Cháng'ān.)
Going downstream with the current,
is sufficient for transportation and supply;
(Kāng said: 'Transport',
pronunciation: yú wèi qiē,
is the same as the 'transport' in 'accumulated supplies'.
'Supply',
is the same as the 'supply' in 'transportation of supplies'.
'Supply',
pronunciation: chōng yù fān.)
It is the Storehouse of Heaven.
'Storehouse'
means a place where things gather.
Where the things of Heaven gather,
without relying on human effort,
hence it is called the Storehouse of Heaven.)
The Emperor that very day set out by carriage westward,
and established the capital at Cháng'ān.
He appointed Lóu Jìng as a Gentleman of the Palace,
bestowing upon him the title 'Lord Fèngchūn',
and granted him the surname Liú.
(Master Yán Gǔ said: Whenever 'carriage' is mentioned,
it refers to the Son of Heaven traveling by carriage,
not daring to refer directly to him.
Cháng'ān,
originally was a village name in Qín,
where Gāozǔ established his capital.
'Lord Fèngchūn',
Zhāng Yàn said: 'Chūn'
is the beginning of the year;
now Lóu Jìng initiated this affair at the beginning,
hence he was called Lord Fèngchūn.)
14 Zhāng Liáng had always suffered from frequent illness.
After following the Sovereign into the Guānzhōng region,
he practiced dǎoyǐn (guiding and stretching exercises),
abstained from grains,
shut his door and did not go out,
saying:
"My family served Hán for generations;
when Hán was destroyed,
I did not cherish my wealth in gold,
but sought to avenge Hán against the powerful Qín,
shaking the world.
(These events are recorded in Scroll 7, the twenty-ninth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng.)
I was enfeoffed as a Marquis of Ten Thousand Households;
this is the ultimate achievement for a commoner,
and for Liáng, it is sufficient.
I wish to abandon the affairs of the mortal world
and desire to wander with Chìsōngzǐ."
Master Yán Shígǔ comments: Chìsōngzǐ
is the name of an immortal.
During the time of Shénnóng, he was the Master of Rain.
He ingested "water jade" (a mineral),
instructed Shénnóng,
and could enter fire and burn himself without harm.
He ascended to Mount Kūn,
often staying in the stone chamber of the Queen Mother of the West (Xīwángmǔ),
rising and descending with the wind and rain.
The youngest daughter of Emperor Yán pursued him,
and she too attained immortality and went away with him.
Your subject, Guāng, remarks: That life has death
is as inevitable as night following day;
from ancient times to the present,
there has certainly never been
one who transcended this and existed alone.
With Zǐfáng's (Zhāng Liáng's) clarity of discernment and understanding of principle,
he was fully capable of knowing that the affairs of immortals were empty and deceptive;
yet his desire to wander with Chìsōngzǐ
shows his wisdom.
At the juncture of achievement and fame,
it is difficult for a minister to find his place.
As the High Emperor (Liú Bāng) himself acknowledged,
there were only three outstanding heroes;
Huáiyīn (Hán Xìn) was executed and his clan wiped out,
Xiāo Hé was imprisoned,
was it not because they trod the path of great success and fullness yet did not know when to stop!
Therefore, Zǐfáng took refuge in the concept of immortals,
cast aside the mortal world,
regarded achievement and fame as external things,
set aside glory and profit without a second thought.
This is what is called
"the wise man preserves himself."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"He is both intelligent and wise,
and thus preserves his person."
15 In the sixth month,
on the Rénchén day,
a great amnesty was proclaimed throughout the land.
16 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the King of Yān, Zāng Tú, rebelled;
the Sovereign personally led the army to campaign against him.
17 King Jǐng of Zhào (Zhāng Ěr) and King Wén of Chángshā (Wú Ruì) both passed away.
18 In the ninth month,
Zāng Tú was captured.
On the Rénzǐ day,
the Grand Commandant, the Marquis of Cháng'ān, Lú Wǎn, was established as King of Yān.
The *Biǎo* (Tables) of Bān Gù state: The Grand Commandant
is an office of Qín,
in charge of military affairs.
Under the Hàn system, it forms the Three Dukes together with the Chancellor and the Imperial Secretary.
Yìng Shào says: Wèi (Commandant) means bringing peace from above to below.
According to the *Records of the Grand Historian*, biography of Lú Wǎn,
Cháng'ān
was the former Xiányáng.
The *Zhèngyì* commentary says: Qín's Xiányáng was north of the Wèi River;
Cháng'ān was south of the Wèi River,
the place where Xiāo Hé built the Wèiyāng Palace.
Wǎn was also born on the same day as the Sovereign;
the Sovereign favored and doted on Wǎn,
and none of the other ministers dared to aspire to his status,
therefore he was specially made a king.
An examination of discrepancies notes: The *Records of the Grand Historian* and the *Annals of Gāozǔ* in the *Book of Hàn*
both state here
"sent the Chancellor Kuài to lead troops to pacify the Dài region."
Checking the biography of Fán Kuài: He followed in pacifying Hán Wáng Xìn,
and was then promoted to Left Chancellor;
at this time he was not yet Chancellor,
furthermore, there was no rebellion in the Dài region,
and Kuài's biography also does not record this event;
it is suspected that the annals are in error.
19 Lì Jī, a former general of King Xiàng (Xiàng Yǔ), rebelled;
Lì Jī had surrendered while serving as Magistrate of Chén,
and the Sovereign enfeoffed him as a marquis in Yǐngchuān.
When the Sovereign arrived in Luòyáng,
he summoned him;
Lì Jī, fearing, rebelled.
The *Fēngsú Tōng* states: Lì
is a surname.
The *Xìng Pǔ* states: A Chǔ prince received Lì as his fief,
and later took it as his clan name.
20 In the intercalary ninth month,
construction began on the Chánglè Palace.
Chéng Dàchāng's *Yōng Lù* states: The Chánglè Palace
was originally the Xīnglè Palace of Qín,
with a circumference of twenty *lǐ*,
which Gāozǔ renovated and resided in;
it was located in the eastern corner of Cháng'ān city.
Lè
is pronounced luò.
21 Zhōnglí Mò, a general of King Xiàng,
had always been on good terms with the King of Chǔ, Xìn (Hán Xìn).
After King Xiàng's death,
he fled and took refuge with Xìn.
The King of Hàn (Liú Bāng) bore a grudge against Mò,
and hearing he was in Chǔ,
issued an edict ordering Chǔ to arrest Mò.
When Xìn first went to his kingdom,
he toured the counties and towns,
moving about with armed escorts.
1 In winter,
the tenth month,
someone submitted a letter to the throne accusing the King of Chǔ, Xìn, of rebellion.
The Emperor consulted his various generals,
who all said:
"Send troops quickly,
and bury that scoundrel!"

Common officers were capped at twenty.

then a leather cap,
then a ceremonial cap,

"the three additions become increasingly honorable,
signifying the achievement of adulthood."
For feudal lords, there was a fourth addition of the dark ceremonial cap,

If feudal lords had four additions,

Third Year of the Former [Period]

3 An edict stated:
"Previously, I dispatched the marquises to their fiefdoms,
as recorded in the previous scroll of the previous year.
The Chancellor
is someone I hold in high regard;
In the twelfth month,
Chancellor Bó was dismissed
and sent to his fiefdom.
On the yǐhài day,
Grand Commandant Guàn Yīng was appointed as Chancellor;
the office of Grand Commandant was abolished,
and its duties were incorporated under the Chancellor.
The Hàn dynasty followed the Qín system,
with the Chancellor, Grand Commandant, and Imperial Secretary forming the Three Excellencies.
Now, Zhōu Bó was dismissed from the Chancellorship and sent to his fiefdom,
and Guàn Yīng was appointed Chancellor from the position of Grand Commandant;
consequently, the office of Grand Commandant was abolished.
This reflects the principle that the Three Excellencies need not always be fully staffed,
and also that military authority should not be lightly delegated.

According to the rules for posthumous titles: achieving success through righteousness is called "Jǐng";

spreading righteousness and acting with firmness is called "Jǐng".

He repeatedly disregarded the laws;
arrogant and obstinate,

That year,

The King was talented

Consequently, [the Emperor] began to change the reign period, making the seventeenth year into the first year of a new era,

Hàn law: If three people gathered to drink without reason,
they were fined four taels of gold.
Now an edict granted permission for gatherings to eat and drink.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Pú means to bestow;
it means the king's virtue is bestowed upon the empire, and gathering to eat and drink is called 'pú'.
The *Zhōulǐ*, section on Clan Leaders, mentions: In spring and autumn, sacrifice to 'pú'.
Commentary: 'Pú' refers to
spirits that cause disasters to people.
There is the horse 'pú',
the locust and caterpillar 'pú', and the human ghost 'pú'.
Altars were also established for them like for the rain and flood sacrifices.
Clan elders had no ritual for drinking alcohol,
but on the occasion of the 'pú' sacrifice, they would offer toasts to each other with the people according to age.
*Zhèngyì* says: In ancient times, for the 'pú' sacrifice,
people pooled money to drink,
therefore in later times, allowing the people to gather and drink
was all called 'pú'.
The *Hànshū* records
that whenever there was a celebration,
the people were ordered to hold a great 'pú' feast,
which refers to this.
That commentary says it was on the occasion of the 'pú' sacrifice that they toasted each other according to age with the people,
which is what Zhèng's commentary calls the 'pú' sacrifice and communal drinking.
Pú,
pronounced 'pú'.
"The Zhōu tripod was lost in the Sì River.
Now the Hé River has broken its banks,
connecting with the Sì.

Fényīn County belonged to Hédōng Commandery.

precisely facing Fényīn.

The old Fényīn city, ninety *lǐ* north of the present county, is the location.
The omen has appeared;
if it is not welcomed, it will not arrive."
Thereupon, the Emperor sent an envoy to build a temple at Fényīn,
facing south towards the river,
intending to perform sacrifices to recover the Zhōu tripod.

(Wùyín, 163 BCE)

Yǔ,
is the same as yǔ yú;
the same below.

Now, measuring the farmland, it is not that there is increasingly less

means respect.
"Do not speak of it,

Master Yán Gǔ said: Meaning he intended to privately admonish him.
Seated in his office,

means gathering,

is a wooden document,
two chǐ in length.
and was about to execute Tōng.

"I have heard that: All living things under heaven,

the sovereign employs wicked ministers,
