encroaches upon and reduces the territories of the feudal lords,
and metes out punishments that are truly severe.
Shī Gǔ says: Liáng,
means 'truly,'
'indeed.'
There is a saying:
'Licking the chaff leads to the rice.'
Shī Gǔ says: Shì,
is an ancient character,
pronounced as 'shì.'
Shì means to eat with the tongue,
using a dog as a metaphor.
It means that initially licking the chaff
eventually leads to eating the rice.
Suǒyǐn says: It means that when the chaff is licked clean, one reaches the rice;
it is said that when the land is reduced to nothing, it leads to the destruction of the state.
The well-known feudal lords,
once scrutinized,
will no longer be able to act freely and unrestrainedly.
Shī Gǔ says: Sì,
means 'to indulge.'
Shī Gǔ says: It means that the ailment is within the body,
not manifesting outwardly.
Constantly worried about being suspected,
with no way to clear oneself,
hunching the shoulders and piling the feet,
still fearing not to be released.
Shī Gǔ says: Xié,
means 'to contract,'
meaning to draw them in;
lěi zú,
means 'stacked feet';
both refer to fear.
Shì,
means 'to release,'
'to let go.'
Lěi,
is the same as lěi.
What I have heard about the feudal lords having their lands reduced,
their crimes do not warrant this;
Shī Gǔ says: It means their crimes are not severe enough to warrant the reduction of their lands.
The King said:
"That is true.
What do you plan to do?"
Gāo said:
"The King of Wú considers himself to share the same worries as Your Majesty.
He wishes to follow the times and reason,
sacrificing his life to eliminate calamity for the world.
Does this intention seem acceptable?"
The King of Jiāoxī, startled and alarmed, said:
"How dare I act like this!
Though the sovereign is pressing,
I would rather die,
how can I not serve him!"
Gāo said:
"The Imperial Secretary Cháo Cuò,
confuses and misleads the Son of Heaven.
Shī Gǔ says: Yíng,
means 'to encircle.'
The feudal lords all have thoughts of rebellion,
human affairs have reached an extreme.
A comet has appeared,
locusts have arisen,
this is a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity;
and worry and toil
are what give rise to sages.
Suǒyǐn says: This is what is meant by 'deep worry gives rise to enlightened sages.'
Following behind Your Majesty's carriage from the outside,
roaming the world,
wherever we go, they will surrender,
wherever we point, they will submit,
none will dare to disobey.
If Your Majesty would truly deign to grant a word of consent,
then the King of Wú will lead the King of Chǔ to capture Hángǔ Pass,
guard the granaries of Xíngyáng and Áocāng,
resist the Hàn army,
prepare lodging places,
and await Your Majesty.
Shī Gǔ says: Cì shè,
means places to rest and stay.
Xū,
means 'to wait.'
Zhì,
is pronounced as 'zhí.'
Then the world can be united,
and the two sovereigns can divide it,
would that not be acceptable!"
The King said:
"Excellent!"
Returning,
he reported to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú, still fearing that he might not follow through,
then personally acted as an envoy,
going to Jiāoxī to make the agreement face-to-face.
Some of the ministers of Jiāoxī heard of the king's plot,
and admonished him, saying:
"The lands of the feudal lords do not amount to one-twelfth of Hàn's territory.
To rebel and cause worry for the Empress Dowager,
is not a wise plan.
Wén Yǐng says: This refers to the king's mother, the Empress Dowager.
It is still said to be not easy;
even if the affair succeeds,
the two sovereigns will contend for division,
and troubles will only multiply."
The king did not listen,
and then sent envoys to make agreements with Qí, Zīchuān, Jiāodōng, and Jǐnán,
all of whom agreed.
The King of Qí, Jiāng Lǘ,
the King of Zīchuān, Xián,
the King of Jiāodōng, Xióng Qú,
the King of Jǐnán, Pì Guāng,
were all enfeoffed by Emperor Wén.
Jǐ,
is pronounced as 'zǐ.'
Initially,
King Yuán of Chǔ was fond of books,
and together with Shēn Gōng of Lǔ, Mù Shēng, and Bái Shēng, all studied the Book of Songs under Fú Qiū Bó.
When he became King of Chǔ,
he appointed the three men as Grand Masters of the Palace.
Mù Shēng did not care for wine;
whenever King Yuán hosted a banquet,
he would always set out sweet wine for Mù Shēng.
When his son King Yí and grandson King Wù succeeded to the throne,
King Yuán of Chǔ, Jiāo,
was a younger half-brother of Emperor Gāozǔ.
Zǐ Zhòng and Zǐ Xīn of Chǔ both descended from King Mù,
and the people of Chǔ called them
"the Two Mùs,"
hence the surname Mù existed in Chǔ.
In Qín there were Bái Yǐ Bǐng and Bái Guī,
and in Chǔ there was Lord Bái.
Fú Qiū
is a compound surname.
King Yí,
named Yǐng Kè,
was the son of King Yuán.
Wù,
was the grandson of King Yuán.
Master Yán Gǔ said: Sweet wine,
is a sweet wine,
made with less malt and more rice,
fermented for two nights until ready.
The character "耆" in "not fond of,"
is read as "shì" (to be fond of).
The character "為,"
is pronounced "yú wèi fān";
the same below.
Later, they forgot to set it out.
Mù Shēng withdrew and
said:
"It is time to leave!
The sweet wine is not set out;
the king's intention has slackened.
If I do not leave,
the people of Chǔ will clamp me in the market."
He then claimed illness and took to his bed.
Shēn Gōng and Bái Shēng urged him to rise,
saying:
"Do you not remember the virtue of the former king?
Now that the present king has momentarily neglected a minor courtesy,
why go to such lengths!"
Mù Shēng said:
"The Yì Jīng says: 'To know the subtle signs is divine indeed!
Subtle signs
are the minute beginnings of movement,
the precursors of good and ill fortune.
The gentleman, seeing the subtle signs, acts,
without waiting for the day to end.'
The reason the former king treated the three of us with courtesy
was because the Way was present.
Now that he neglects it,
it means he has forgotten the Way.
How can one long associate
with those who have forgotten the Way?
Is it merely for the sake of trivial courtesy!"
Trivial,
means small.
Associate,
is pronounced "chāng lǚ fān."
For,
is pronounced "yú wèi fān."
Shēn Gōng and Bái Shēng alone remained.
King Wù gradually became dissolute and cruel.
The Grand Tutor Wéi Mèng composed a poem to admonish him,
but he did not listen,
so Wéi Mèng also left,
and resided in Zōu.
The Surname Genealogy says: The surname Wéi descends from Zhuān Xù's descendant Dà Péng Shǐ Wéi.
Then he conspired with Wú.
Shēn Gōng and Bái Shēng admonished Wù,
but Wù made them convict laborers,
clothed them in red garments,
and had them pound grain in the market.
Jìn Zhuó said: Raising the pestle high with the arm,
standing upright to pound.
Master Yán Gǔ said: Using a wooden pestle and pounding by hand,
is what is now called a step mortar.
Clothed them,
is pronounced "yú jì fān."
Mèngzǐ left Qí and resided in Xiū.
Zhào Qí's commentary says: Xiū,
is a place name;
likely the place where Fù was enfeoffed.
Fù,
was the son of King Yuán of Chǔ,
and younger brother of King Yí.
"If my uncle does not join me,
when I rise,
I will first seize my uncle!"
Marquis Xiū was afraid,
and fled with his mother, the Grand Lady, to the capital.
Chén Zàn said: The mother of a marquis is called the Grand Lady.
When the edict stripping Wú of the commanderies of Kuàijī and Yùzhāng arrived,
the King of Wú was the first to raise troops,
killing Hàn officials of the rank of two thousand piculs and below.
Jiāoxī, Jiāodōng, Zīchuān, Jǐnán, Chǔ, and Zhào also all rebelled.
The Chancellor of Chǔ, Zhāng Shàng, and the Grand Tutor, Zhào Yí Wú, admonished King Wù,
but Wù killed Shàng and Yí Wú.
The Chancellor of Zhào, Jiàn Dé, and the Internal History, Wáng Hàn, admonished King Suì,
and Suì burned and killed Jiàn Dé and Hàn.
The King of Qí later regretted it,
broke the agreement, and fortified the city for defense.
The King of Jìběi's city walls were damaged and not yet repaired,
and his Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace seized control,
so the king could not send out troops.
The Kings of Jiāoxī and Jiāodōng acted as leaders,
Master Yán Gǔ said: Qú,
means great.
Shuài,
is pronounced "suǒ lèi fān."
They besieged Línzī.
Línzī,
was the capital of Qí.
They intended to wait for Wú and Chǔ to advance together,
and sent envoys north to the Xiōngnú to join forces.
The King of Wú mobilized all his soldiers,
and issued an order in his state saying:
"I am sixty-two years old,
and will personally lead the army;
my youngest son is fourteen,
and will also march at the head of the soldiers.
All those whose age is the same as mine or above,
and those the same as my youngest son or below,
are all to be conscripted."
In total, over two hundred thousand men.
He sent envoys south to Mǐn and Eastern Yuè,
and Mǐn and Eastern Yuè also sent troops to follow.
The King of Wú raised troops in Guǎnglíng,
Guǎnglíng,
was the capital of Wú.
He then combined with the troops of Chǔ,
and sent envoys with letters to the various lords,
enumerating the crimes of Cháo Cuò,
intending to join forces to execute him.
Wú and Chǔ together attacked Liáng,
and captured Jíbì.
Suǒ Yǐn said: According to the Zuǒzhuàn,
in the second year of Duke Xuān,
Huá Yuán of Sòng fought at Dàjí.
Dù Yù said: It is southeast of Xiāngyì;
likely this is Jíbì.
The Expanded Gazetteer says: The old city of Dàjí
is seventy lǐ southwest of Nínglíng County in Sòng Prefecture.
They advanced victoriously,
with great momentum.
King Xiào of Liáng sent generals to attack them,
but they again defeated two armies of Liáng,
and the soldiers all fled back.
The King of Liáng fortified Suíyáng for defense.
Suíyáng,
was the capital of Liáng.
Suí,
is pronounced "suī."
Initially,
when Emperor Wén was about to pass away,
he cautioned the Crown Prince, saying:
"If there is an emergency,
Zhōu Yàfū is truly capable of leading troops."
When the news of the rebellion of the seven states reached him,
the Emperor appointed the Commandant of the Palace Guard, Zhōu Yàfū, as Grand Commandant,
leading thirty-six generals to attack Wú and Chǔ.
He sent Marquis Qūzhōu, Lì Jì, to attack Zhào.
According to Bān Zhì,
Qūzhōu County belonged to the Principality of Guǎngpíng.
He also recalled Dòu Yīng,
appointing him as Grand General,
and had him station at Xíngyáng to oversee the troops of Qí and Zhào.
According to Bān Zhì,
Xíngyáng County belonged to the Commandery of Hénán.
Oversee,
is pronounced "gǔ xián fān."
Initially,
the thirty ordinances that Cháo Cuò had revised
caused an uproar among the feudal lords.
Cuò’s father heard of this
and came from Yǐngchuān—
Cuò
was a native of Yǐngchuān.
“The Emperor has just ascended the throne,
and you, sir, are in charge of governance and administration,
encroaching upon and diminishing the feudal lords,
alienating the flesh and blood of the imperial clan.
Alienating—
is the same as ‘shū’ (to distance).
Why are you doing this?”
Cuò replied:
“It is indeed so;
if we do not act this way,
the Son of Heaven will not be revered,
and the ancestral temple will not be secure.”
His father said:
“The Liú clan may be secure, but the Cháo clan is in peril—
I am leaving you and returning home!”
Thereupon, he drank poison and died,
saying:
“I cannot bear to see disaster befall me!”
More than ten days later,
the seven states of Wú and Chǔ all rebelled,
using the execution of Cuò as their pretext.
The Emperor discussed military affairs with Cuò,
and Cuò wanted the Emperor to personally lead the troops while he himself remained to guard the capital.
He also said:
“The areas adjacent to Xú and Tóng that Wú has not yet taken
could be given to Wú.”
The two counties of Xú and Tóng both belonged to Línhuái Commandery.
Initially, Cuò proposed reducing the territories of the feudal lords to strengthen Hàn,
but when the seven states rebelled,
he wanted to give the areas adjacent to Xú and Tóng to Wú.
This was a contradiction of his own argument—
how could he avoid death?
“Yǔ”
is read as “yǔ” (to give).
Wherever Cuò sat,
Àng would avoid him;
wherever Àng sat,
Cuò would also avoid him.
The two never spoke together in the same hall.
When Cuò became the Grandee of Censors,
he sent officials to investigate Àng for accepting wealth and goods from the King of Wú,
and Àng was convicted;
but an imperial decree pardoned him and reduced him to a commoner.
When Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
Cuò said to his assistants and secretaries:
According to the official table, the Grandee of Censors had two assistants,
with a rank of one thousand shí;
and fifteen attendant censors.
“Yuán Àng received much gold and money from the King of Wú,
deliberately covering up and concealing
his rebellious intentions;
now he has indeed rebelled.
I wish to request to investigate Àng,
as we should know his schemes.”
The assistants and secretaries said:
“Before the affair erupted,
investigating him could have prevented it;
Rú Chún said: If he had been investigated before the affair erupted,
it could have been prevented.
‘Zhì’
is pronounced ‘zhí.’
What good would investigating him do now?
Moreover, Àng likely had no part in the schemes.”
Cuò hesitated and could not decide.
“Yóu yǔ”
means “yóu yù” (to hesitate).
“Yǔ”
is read in the departing tone.
Àng grew fearful
and went at night to see Dòu Yīng,
explaining to him why Wú had rebelled,
and expressed his wish to go before the Emperor
to give an oral account of the situation.
Yīng entered and reported this,
and the Emperor then summoned Àng.
Àng entered for an audience,
and the Emperor was at that time discussing troop provisions with Cuò.
Master Yán noted: “Tiáo”
means to calculate,
to calculate the provisions for dispatching troops.
“Tiáo”
is pronounced “tiáo.”
“Now that Wú and Chǔ have rebelled,
what is your opinion on the matter?”
Àng replied:
“It is not worth worrying about!”
The Emperor said:
“The King of Wú mines the mountains to mint coins,
boils the sea to make salt,
and lures the brave and talented from across the land.
He launches this undertaking in his old age—
if his plan were not perfectly secure,
would he have acted?
How can you say he is incapable?”
Àng replied:
“Wú does have the profits from copper and salt,
but how could it lure brave and talented men?
If Wú truly had brave and talented men,
they would assist him in righteousness,
and he would not rebel.
Those Wú lured are all unscrupulous youths, fugitives, and counterfeiters.”
Crown Prince Zhāng Huái Xián said: “Mìng”
means name,
referring to those who erase their names from the registers and flee.
Cuò said:
“Àng’s assessment is sound.”
The Emperor said:
“What plan do you propose?”
Àng replied:
“I wish for the attendants to withdraw.”
The Emperor dismissed the attendants,
but only Cuò remained.
Àng said:
“What I have to say
cannot be known by other ministers.”
So the Emperor dismissed Cuò as well.
Cuò hurriedly withdrew to the eastern wing,
deeply resentful.
The Emperor finally asked Àng,
and he replied:
“Wú and Chǔ have exchanged letters,
stating that Emperor Gāo granted fiefs to the imperial princes,
but now the treacherous minister Cháo Cuò has arbitrarily accused the feudal lords,
seizing and diminishing their territories.
For this reason, they rebelled,
intending to march west together to execute Cuò,
restore their former lands, and then cease hostilities.
The only plan now is to behead Cuò,
send envoys to pardon the seven states of Wú and Chǔ,
restore their former lands,
and then the troops can lay down their arms without bloodshed and all hostilities will cease.”
At this, the Emperor remained silent for a long while,
then said:
“But what is truly to be done?
I would not begrudge sacrificing one man to appease the realm.”
Àng said:
“My foolish plan is just this—
I only ask Your Majesty to consider it carefully!”
“Shú”
is the same as “shú” (thorough).
In the sixth year of the Zhōngyuán era,
Fèngcháng was first changed to Tàicháng,
but at this time Àng was still Fèngcháng.
More than ten days later,
the Emperor ordered Chancellor Qīng, Commandant Jiā, and Commandant Ōu
—Chancellor Táo Qīng,
Commandant Jiā
(his surname is lost),
and Commandant Zhāng Ōu—
to say: “He failed to uphold the virtue and trust of the sovereign,
sought to alienate the ministers and common people,
and also wanted to give cities to Wú.
He showed no respect due to a minister,
committing great impiety and unrighteousness.
Cuò deserves to be cut in half at the waist,
and his parents, wife, children, and siblings, regardless of age, should all be publicly executed.”
The decree said:
“Approved.”
Cuò knew nothing of this.
On the rénzǐ day,
the Emperor sent the commandant to summon Cuò,
deceiving him into riding through the market.
Master Yán noted: He was tricked into thinking he was riding to inspect the market.
“Xíng”
is pronounced “xìng.”
The Emperor then sent Yuán Àng and the King of Wú’s nephew, the Director of the Imperial Clan and Marquis of Dé, Tōng, as envoys to Wú.
The son of Emperor Gāo’s elder brother Zhòng, Guǎng, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dé,
and he fathered Tōng.
Dé
was a marquisate
located within the boundaries of Tàishān.
The Gentleman of the Palace Gate, Commandant Dèng Gōng,
submitted a memorial discussing military affairs.
He was granted an audience with the Emperor,
who asked him:
"On the road from the army's location,
(Rú Chún states: The road from which the Wú army came.)
(Chén Zàn states: Dào,
means 'via'.)
Have Wú and Chǔ ceased their activities?"
Dèng Gōng replied:
"Wú has been preparing to rebel for decades;
they are venting their anger over the reduction of their territories,
using the execution of Cháo Cuò as their pretext,
but their true intention is not Cháo Cuò.
Moreover, I fear that the scholars of the realm will now shut their mouths and dare not speak out again."
The Emperor said:
"Why is that?"
Dèng Gōng replied:
"Cháo Cuò was concerned that the feudal lords were growing too powerful and could not be controlled,
so he requested reducing their territories to strengthen the capital,
a benefit for ten thousand generations.
The plan had just begun to be implemented,
yet he suddenly suffered a violent death;
internally, this silences the mouths of loyal ministers,
externally, it avenges the feudal lords.
I privately believe this is not a course Your Majesty should take."
Thereupon, the Emperor sighed deeply and said:
"Your words are good,
I too regret it!"
Yuán Àng and Liú Tōng arrived in Wú,
but the Wú and Chǔ armies had already attacked Liáng's fortifications.
The Superintendent of the Imperial Clan, due to their familial relationship,
entered first for an audience,
to advise the King of Wú,
ordering him to kneel and receive the imperial edict.
The Superintendent of the Imperial Clan was a close relative to Bì,
akin to a father-son relationship.
Knowing he intended to persuade him,
[Bì] laughed and responded:
"I have already become the Eastern Emperor,
whom should I still kneel to!"
He refused to see Yuán Àng,
and detained him within the army camp,
intending to coerce him into becoming a general;
Yuán Àng refused,
so [Bì] had men surround and guard him,
and was about to kill him.
Yuán Àng found an opportunity,
escaped, and fled back to report.
The Grand Commandant, Yàfū, said to the Emperor:
"The Chǔ troops are swift and light,
it is difficult to contend with them head-on.
I propose we abandon Liáng to them,
cut off their supply routes,
then we can control them."
The Emperor approved.
Yàfū rode a six-horse relay carriage,
(Zhāng Yàn states: A relay carriage with six horses.)
(Chéng,
pronounced as shèng.)
(Zhuàn,
pronounced as zhuàn.)
According to my research, the Hàn had relay carriages and fast relay carriages;
when Emperor Wén traveled from Dài to assume the throne,
Zhāng Wǔ and others rode six-horse relay carriages.
Now Yàfū rode a six-horse relay carriage.
The appearance of the six-horse relay carriage in historical records is twice,
indicating it was also different from the regular relay carriage.)
(Yán Shīgǔ states: Huì bīng,
means to assemble a large army.)
Zhào Shè intercepted and advised Yàfū, saying:
"The King of Wú has long been wealthy,
and has been gathering and comforting daring men for a long time.
Knowing that you, General, are about to march,
he will certainly place spies in the narrow passes between Xiáo and Miǎn;
moreover, military affairs value
secrecy and mystery.
Why does the General not proceed from here to the right,
head towards Lántián,
exit through Wǔguān,
and arrive at Luòyáng!
The difference in time would be no more than one or two days.
From Bàshàng, taking the left route towards Xiáo and Miǎn to reach Luòyáng,
the road is convenient and near;
if from Bàshàng, taking the right route towards Lántián, exiting Wǔguān to reach Luòyáng,
the road is circuitous and winding,
hence the difference of one or two days.)
(Zǒu,
pronounced as zòu.)
(Jiàn,
pronounced according to its character.)
Luòyáng has an armory.
When the feudal lords hear of it,
they will think the General descended from the heavens."
The Grand Commandant followed his plan,
and upon reaching Luòyáng,
said joyfully:
"The Seven Kingdoms have rebelled,
I rode relay carriages to reach here,
never expecting to arrive safely.
(Yán Shīgǔ states: Meaning he did not expect to safely reach Luòyáng.)
East of Xíngyáng,
there is nothing to worry about."
(Textual analysis note: Both Shǐjì and Hànshū state:
"The Grand Commandant was pleased to obtain Jù Mèng,
as if obtaining a rival state,
saying: 'Wú and Chǔ are nothing to worry about.'"
In my opinion, Mèng was merely a wandering knight,
what significance could Yàfū obtaining him possibly have!
It is likely his followers wanted to enhance Mèng's reputation,
and fabricated this statement,
which is not credible.)
They indeed discovered Wú's ambush troops.
He then requested Zhào Shè be appointed as Protector of the Army.
The Grand Commandant led his troops northeast towards Chāngyì.
Chāngyì,
was territory of Liáng,
later becoming the seat of Shānyáng Commandery.
(Zǒu,
pronounced as zòu;
same below.)
Liáng repeatedly sent envoys to Marquis Tiáo requesting rescue,
but Marquis Tiáo refused;
they again sent envoys to accuse Marquis Tiáo before the Emperor.
The Emperor sent orders to Marquis Tiáo to rescue Liáng,
but Yàfū did not obey the edict,
firmly holding his position and not emerging;
instead, he sent Marquis Gāogāo and others to lead light cavalry out of the Huái-Sì River mouth.
(Tuídāng, son of King Xìn of Hán, returned from among the Xiōngnú,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis Gāogāo.
The Table of Meritorious Officials: Gāogāo belonged to Yínglíng;
the Treatise on Geography,
states Gāogāo belonged to Héjiān Kingdom.
It seems Tuídāng received his enfeoffment early in Emperor Wén's reign,
while Héjiān Kingdom was established in the third year,
hence the difference between the Treatise and the Table.)
The Sì River flows south into the Huái,
hence it is called the Huái-Sì River mouth.
(Qí,
pronounced as jì.)
They blocked their supply routes.
Liáng sent the Palace Grandee Hán Ānguó and the Chǔ Chancellor Zhāng Shàng's younger brother, Yǔ, as generals;
Yǔ fought fiercely,
Ānguó was cautious and steady,
and they managed to somewhat defeat the Wú troops.
The Wú troops wished to head west,
but Liáng's city was defended,
so they dared not go west;
they then went to Marquis Tiáo's army,
meeting at Xiàyì.
(Xiàyì county belonged to the Kingdom of Liáng.)
Marquis Tiáo held his position firmly and refused to engage in battle;
Wú's provisions were exhausted and the soldiers hungry,
they repeatedly challenged to battle,
but he never emerged.
One night, there was an alarm in Marquis Tiáo's camp,
internal fighting broke out,
the disturbance reached his tent,
but Yàfū lay firmly still and did not rise.
After a short while,
order was restored.
Wú troops charged the southeastern corner of the fortifications,
Yàfū had defenses prepared in the northwest;
soon after, their elite troops indeed charged the northwest,
but could not break in.
Many Wú and Chǔ soldiers died of hunger or deserted,
so they withdrew and left.
In the second month,
Yàfū sent out elite troops in pursuit and attack,
and routed them completely.
The King of Wú, Bì, abandoned his army,
and fled at night with several thousand strong men;
the King of Chǔ, Wù, committed suicide.
When the King of Wú first raised his forces,
the Wú minister Tián Lùbó served as Grand General.
Tián Lùbó said:
"If the army masses together and marches west,
without any other extraordinary route,
it will be difficult to achieve merit.
I wish to take fifty thousand men,
separately follow the Jiāng and Huái rivers upstream,
capture Huáinán and Chángshā,
enter through Wǔguān,
and rendezvous with Your Majesty.
This would also be an extraordinary move."
The Crown Prince of Wú admonished, saying:
"Your Majesty uses rebellion as your name,
such troops are difficult to lend to others,
for others might also rebel against Your Majesty.
What then?

Yán Shīgǔ comments: He suspected Bùyí had stolen it.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Bùyí admitted he had indeed taken it.
Later, the lodger who had returned home came back and returned the gold,
and the Gentleman who had lost the gold was greatly ashamed.
Because of this, Bùyí was praised as a magnanimous man,
and was gradually promoted to Grand Master of the Palace.
Some people slandered Bùyí at court,
Yán Shīgǔ comments: They slandered him during an audience at court.
Bùyí heard about it,
and said:
"I actually have no elder brother."
Yet he never tried to clear himself.
8 The Emperor, residing in the inner palace,
summoned Zhōu Yàfū and bestowed food upon him,
but set out only a large piece of meat,
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Zì,
means a large slice of meat.
Kǒng Yǐngdá says: Cooked meat with bones sliced is called yáo;
pure meat sliced is called zì.
Zì,
is pronounced cè lì fān.
And no chopsticks were provided.
Yàfū felt discontented,
and looked around, asking the attendant in charge of seating to bring chopsticks.
Yīng Shào says: The attendant in charge of seating is the one who manages the seating arrangements.
"Is this not sufficient for you, sir?"
Mèng Kāng says: Setting out meat without chopsticks—does this not indicate dissatisfaction with you, sir?
It shows resentment.
Rú Chún says: It was not that the food utensils were intentionally insufficient for you, sir,
but merely an oversight.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Mèng's explanation is closer to the truth.
The Emperor said, "I bestow food upon you but do not provide chopsticks;
this is my intention.
Is there any insufficiency for you, sir?"
The Emperor said:
"Rise!"
Yàfū then hurriedly withdrew.
The Emperor watched him leave and said:
"This discontented fellow
is not a minister fit for a young ruler."
Not long after,
Yàfū's son purchased five hundred sets of armor and shields from the Office of Imperial Workshops for his father,
intended for burial.
The hired laborers were treated harshly,
and were not paid.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Yōng refers to hired laborers;
kǔ means treating them extremely harshly.
I say: Yàfū's son was ignorant;
he treated the laborers harshly and did not pay them,
causing them to harbor resentment, which brought disaster upon his father.
Although Yàfū's death was due to Emperor Jǐng's lack of kindness,
his son was also deeply culpable.
The laborers, resentful, reported the matter to the authorities,
accusing the son,
and the matter implicated Yàfū.
When the report reached the Emperor,
he handed Yàfū over to the officials.
The officials interrogated Yàfū with written records,
Rú Chún says: They questioned him in detail and recorded his statements.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Interrogation with written records means writing everything down in a ledger and questioning him point by point.
Wū,
is pronounced wū gù fān.
Xià,
is pronounced hù jià fān.
The Emperor scolded him, saying:
"I have no use for you!"
Mèng Kāng says: This means, "I will not listen to your defense;
I intend to kill you."
Rú Chún says: The Emperor feared that the prison officials, fearing Yàfū might return to power,
would not dare to interrogate or humiliate him.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Mèng's interpretation is correct.
Another version says: The Emperor reprimanded the officials,
saying they were incompetent,
"I have no use for you,"
and thus summoned Yàfū to be handed over to the Commandant of Justice.
The Commandant of Justice interrogated him, saying:
"Do you, Marquis, intend to rebel?"
Yàfū replied:
"The items I purchased are burial objects.
How can that be called rebellion?"
The official said:
"Even if you do not intend to rebel on earth,
you must intend to rebel underground!"
The officials pressed him more urgently.
Initially, when the officials arrested Yàfū,
Yàfū wanted to commit suicide,
but his wife stopped him,
so he did not die then.
After being handed over to the Commandant of Justice,
he refused to eat for five days,
and eventually vomited blood and died.
9 In this year,
Āi King of Jìyīn, Liú Bùshí, passed away.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the earth shook three times in one day.
2 In the third month,
the Xiōngnú invaded Yànmén,
and the Grand Administrator Féng Jìng fought them,
dying in battle.
Chariots, cavalry, and skilled infantry were dispatched to garrison Yànmén.
3 In spring,
due to poor harvests,
the consumption of horse grain in the interior commanderies was prohibited;
violators would have it confiscated.
Summer,
fourth month,
an edict was issued:
"Engraved and carved decorations
harm agricultural endeavors;
brocade embroidery and ornamental weaving
damage female labor.
Yìng Shào said: the word 'ornamental weaving'
is now associated with five-colored textiles,
which refers to weavings of varied colors.
'Decorative cords,'
now refers to multicolored sashes and bands.
Minister Zàn said: Xǔ Shèn states: 'ornamental weaving'
refers to red cords.
Shī Gǔ said: Zàn's explanation is correct.
'Different colors,'
means 'joined together';
combining five colors
is now called 'mixed colors,'
not 'ornamental weaving.'
'Joined,'
is pronounced 'zǐ nèi.'
'Band,'
is pronounced 'tā láo.'
When female labor is harmed, it originates from coldness.
When hunger and coldness occur simultaneously, few can refrain from wrongdoing.
The word 'wrongdoing'
has no ancient written form.
The empress personally supervises the mulberry trees,
to offer food for ancestral temples and ceremonial garments,
setting an example for the empire;
she does not accept offerings,
reduces the Imperial Kitchen,
decreases taxes and labor duties,
aiming for the empire to focus on agriculture and sericulture,
storing resources to prepare for disasters.
The strong should not oppress the weak,
and the many should not bully the few;
the elderly should die of natural causes,
and the young and orphaned should be allowed to grow to maturity.
Shī Gǔ said: 'allowed,'
means 'to accomplish.'
'Mature,'
is pronounced 'zhī liǎng.'
The people's food supply is quite sparse,
what is the cause?
Some fraudulently pretend to be officials.
Zhāng Yàn said: they deceive people by pretending to be officials.
Minister Zàn said: it refers to those bending the law to serve.
Shī Gǔ said: both explanations are incorrect,
it simply means pretending to claim the title of an official.
They exploit and rob the people,
oppressing and taking from the masses.
Shī Gǔ said: 'exploit,'
implies actions like fishing and hunting.
Lǐ Qí said: 'taking,'
refers to insects consuming crop roots.
Invasion and exploitation of the population
can be compared to theft and robbers.
Dù Yòu said: 'taking'
means 'to seize.'
The chief officials;
acting wrongly according to the law and as thieves,
this is very absurd!
Lǐ Fěi said: 'acting wrongly by the law,'
means using the law to commit wrongdoing.
Wén Yǐng said: 'with thieves,'
means, although the thieves should be punished,
they instead aid them knowingly,
making them no different from the thieves.
Shī Gǔ said: 'with thieves,'
means joining the thieves as an accomplice.
Failing their official duties, causing disorder,
the Chancellor should report it,
recommending punishment.
Announce to the empire,
to clearly convey Our intent."
Fifth month,
an edict was issued that wealth equivalent to four units earns an official rank.
Fú Qián said: ten thousand coins
equate to one hundred and twenty-seven units.
Yìng Shào said: in ancient times, corrupt officials were loathed,
having sufficient clothing and food brought awareness to honor and disgrace,
and a wealth limit of ten units was required to become an official;
ten units,
equal to one hundred thousand.
Merchants with wealth could not serve as officials,
while honorable men without wealth also could not achieve rank,
thus reducing the required wealth to four units allowed for such rank.
In autumn,
a great drought occurred.
Winter,
tenth month,
both sun and moon were eclipsed,
for five days.
On the last day of the twelfth month,
there was thunder;
the sun appeared purple;
the five planets reversed and aligned at Tài Wēi.
Jìn Astronomical Records: Tài Wēi,
is the court of the Son of Heaven,
seats of the Five Emperors,
and the palaces of the twelve lords.
Outside its borders,
are the Nine Ministers;
between the two stars in the middle of the southern border is called Duān Gate,
to the east is called Left Directorate of Justice,
representing the Minister of Justice;
to the west is called Right Directorate of Justice,
representing the Grand Minister of Justice.
East of the Left Directorate of Justice,
is the Left Side Gate;
west of the Right Directorate of Justice,
is the Right Side Gate.
The Four Stars of the Eastern Border: the first southern star is called the Senior Minister,
its northern side is Dong Tàiyáng Gate;
the second star is called the Next Minister,
its northern side is Zhōnghuá East Gate;
the third star is called the Next General,
its northern side is Dong Tàiyīn Gate;
the fourth star is called the Senior General,
these are known as the Four Assists.
The Four Stars of the Western Border: the first star is called the Senior General,
its northern side is Xī Tàiyáng Gate;
the second star is called the Next General,
its northern side is Zhōnghuá West Gate;
the third star is called the Next Minister,
its northern side is Xī Tàiyīn Gate;
the fourth star is called the Senior Minister,
this is also the Four Assists.
Spring,
first month,
an edict was issued:
"Agriculture,
is the foundation of the empire.
Gold, pearls, and jade,
cannot be eaten when hungry,
nor worn for warmth,
they are used for trade.
Shī Gǔ said: 'trade,'
enables exchange between the haves and have-nots,
balancing worth and esteem.
In occasional years when there are poor harvests,
it is because there are many who pursue minor matters,
and few are dedicated to agriculture.
Let the prefectures and kingdoms strive to encourage farming and sericulture,
increase tree planting,
so that food and clothing can be obtained.
If officials impose corvée labor
Wéi Zhāo said: 'impose on the people,'
it means using the people;
*to obtain labor,*
stealing as thieves.
Even two-thousand-bushel officials
should be punished equally.
On Jiǎyín day,
the Crown Prince had his capping ceremony.
On Jiǎzǐ day,
the Emperor passed away at the Wèi Yáng Palace.
Minister Zàn said: aged forty-eight.
It was the sixteenth year.
Empress Dowager was honored as Grand Empress Dowager,
and the Empress was acknowledged as Empress Dowager.
Second month,
on Guǐyǒu day,
the burial of Emperor Xiào Jǐng took place at Yánglíng.
Minister Zàn said: from the passing to the burial took ten days.
Third month,
the Empress Dowager's brother, Tián Fén, was granted the title Marquis of Wǔ'ān;
Bān Zhìgōng,
noted that Wǔ'ān County belonged to Wèi Prefecture.
Also according to Gōuxù Records,
Fén was titled Wǔ'ān,
and had the fief of Zhù in Qīnghé.
'Fén,'
is pronounced 'fáng late.'
1 Bān Gù commented: Kǒngzǐ said:
"These people,
are those who walked the straight path in the Three Dynasties."
Shī Gǔ said: These are words from the Analects of Confucius.
He said that the people of this time,
were also governed by Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu,
using governance to cultivate simplicity and unity,
therefore able to follow the straight path.
Lamenting that now it is not so.
The troubles of Zhōu and Qín,
where the laws were stringent and severe,
yet deceit could not be overcome.
Shī Gǔ said: They could not be overcome.
Sweeping away complicated harshness,
giving the people rest;
until Xiàowén,
who added respect and frugality;
Xiàojǐng adhered to his works.
Within fifty to sixty years,
they changed customs and habits,
the common people became simple and sincere.
Shī Gǔ said: "Lí,"
means 'multitude.'
"Chún,"
means 'not mixed or impure.'
Hàn spoke of Wén and Jǐng,
how splendid they were!
2 When Hàn arose,
it followed the troubles of Qín,
the undertakings were burdensome, and the resources scarce,
even the Son of Heaven could not afford a uniform chariot team,
having four horses of the same kind,
known as "jūnsì."
Shī Gǔ said: It was drawn by oxen.
During the Hàn era, ox carts were considered cheap,
after Wèi and Jìn,
the nobles started to use ox carts.
Sū Lín said: There were no goods to store.
Gāo Zǔ ordered that merchants could not wear silk or ride in carriages,
increasing taxes to distress and humiliate them.
During the time of Xiàohuì and the Empress Lǚ,
as the realm settled initially,
they relaxed the laws against merchants;
yet, children of the market towns
were still not allowed to hold official positions or become officials.
They assessed the salaries of officials,
measured public expenditures,
levying taxes on the people.
Shī Gǔ said: Only taking what was necessary.
"Liàng,"
pronounced as "liáng."
"Dù,"
pronounced as "dù."
From the Son of Heaven to the nobles with fiefs,
each supported themselves privately,
without drawing on the Son of Heaven
for expenses.
Shī Gǔ said: Each collected their assigned taxes for self-supply,
not included in the state treasury.
"Jīng,"
means 'constant.'
Shī Gǔ said: "Zhōngdūguān,"
refers to the offices in the capital.
Successive with Xiàowén and Xiàojǐng,
being clean, tranquil, respectful, and frugal,
they nourished the world,
within more than seventy years,
the state was without incident,
unless encountering flood or drought,
the people then had enough to eat.
Town and countryside granaries were full,
the treasuries had surplus wealth;
in the capital, the money amounted to tens of thousands,
the strings rotted and could not be counted;
Shī Gǔ said: "Lěi jùwàn,"
means hundreds of millions.
"Xiào,"
means to calculate.
Shī Gǔ said: "Chén,"
means old and long-standing.
So decayed it was unfit to eat.
Amongst the populace, there were horses,
and the paths in the fields became narrow,
Shī Gǔ said: refers to the pathways among fields.
Mèng Kāng said: All rode stallions,
but mares were kept apart for kicking and biting,
thus driven away and not allowed to assemble.
Shī Gǔ said: It implies abundance,
ashamed to ride mares,
not merely because of their kicking and biting.
As officials, they fathered children and grandchildren,
Rú Chún said: At that time, there were no incidents,
officials rarely transferred,
such that they grew old with children and grandchildren without career changes.
"Zhǎng,"
pronounced as two sounds.
Rú Chún said: Refers to the merchants and storage clerks.
First conduct righteousness before
shame prevails.
Shī Gǔ said: Prioritizing righteousness then feeling shame,
opposing each other this way.
"Xíng,"
pronounced as 'xià.'
With widening rifts and the populace becoming wealthy,
extravagance and arrogance overflowed,
some even merging those in powerful cliques,
wielding force at the local level.
Shī Gǔ said: Relying on their wealth to impose power and punishment.
"Duàn,"
pronounced as 'dīng.'
Shī Gǔ said: referring to those who received enfeoffed lands among the clans of the state.
Competing in extravagance,
their residences and carriages exceeding those above them,
without limit.
As wealth accumulates and declines,
change is inevitable;
thereafter,
Xiàowǔ exhausted himself in luxury,
repelling foreign invaders externally,
the realm became desolate,
and the financial strength was depleted!

Xún Yuè said: Taboo on

Jiànyuán's first year
(xīngchǒu, 140 BCE) from ancient times no emperor had a reign name,
this began at this time.

officials said: 'The origin should be named after the heavenly omen,

'three years later'

From this, we say,
that the years prior to Yuán Dǐng,
were posthumously named by the officials;

1 In winter,
the tenth month,
an edict was issued to raise and recommend virtuous, sincere, forthright, and candid gentlemen,
the emperor personally questioned them on the governance methods of ancient and contemporary times,
over a hundred responded.
Guǎngchuān’s Dǒng Zhòngshū replied:
"The Way is,
that which one follows to reach the path of governance,
Shī Gǔ said: 'Yóu,'
means 'following.'
'Shì,'
means 'to go.'
'Zhì,'
meaning to direct officials.
'Yóu,'
was the ancient character for 'yóu.'
It is all encompassing.
Therefore, after the sage kings passed,
their descendants endured long,
in peace and stability for hundreds of years,
this is all due to the efficacy of ritual and music education and transformation.
Every ruler desires security,
yet many suffer from chaotic governance and perilous states;
because they employ the wrong people and follow the wrong way,

The decline of Zhōu's Way during Yōu and Lì,

Until King Xuān,
he aspired the virtue of previous kings,

Confucius said: "Man can enlarge the Way;

This means that a wise and intelligent person can practice the Way;
if one lacks the inner substance,

It is not that Heaven has decreed a fate

losing its proper order.
For a ruler of men,
rectify the mind to rectify the court,

Confucius said: "The phoenix does not come;

It is all over with me!"
The Analects records these words of Confucius.
And he was of lowly status and could not bring them about.

Zhòngní sighed that he had virtue but no position,

One who is rich enough to possess the four seas,

whose conduct is lofty and whose kindness is deep,

Yet if Heaven and Earth do not respond and fine auspices do not arrive,
why is this?
It is all because teaching and transformation are not established and the myriad people are not rectified.
Now the myriad people's pursuit of profit
is like water flowing downward;
if one does not use teaching and transformation as dikes to restrain it,

The ancient kings understood this,

none failed to make teaching and transformation their great task.
They established the Grand Academy to teach in the capital,
set up village and district schools to transform in the towns,
The Record of Learning says: In ancient teaching,

district schools,

They polished the people with righteousness,

When a sage king succeeded a chaotic age,

when teaching and transformation were made clear,
and customs were formed,
his descendants followed them.
Shǐ Gǔ said: Follow,
means to comply;
comply and act accordingly.
Qín destroyed the Way of the former sages,

It caused customs to become shallow and wicked,

Wén Yǐng said: Defy,
means to clash.
Shǐ Gǔ said: A mouth that does not speak loyal and trustworthy words is deceitful;

Resist,
means to oppose.
Defy,
means to offend.
Extreme,
means to sever.
Defy,
means to reject.
Deceitful,
yú yīn fān.
Defy,
read as the character,
also mò kè fān.
When something is extreme, it must be unraveled and restrung,

when governance is practiced but does not work,

Therefore since Hàn obtained the world,

Your servant has heard that when sage kings govern the world,
from here onward,
belongs to the second policy response.
When they are grown, they test their talents in positions,
meaning they grant positions to test their talents.
Shǎo,
shī zhǎo fān.
Zhǎng,
zhī liǎng fān.
They use punishments to deter their evil,

King Wǔ practiced great righteousness,
pacified the cruel and wicked,
and the Duke of Zhōu created ritual and music to adorn it;
reaching the prosperity of Chéng and Kāng,
the prisons were empty for over forty years:

[Liú Xī]
means to oversee;
yǔ,

overseeing and recording prisoners and guarding them.

Master Jiāo answered:
"The Yuèlìng,
a Qín text,
then it is a prison name;

This too is the gradual effect of teaching and transformation and the flow of humaneness and righteousness,
not merely the effect of injuring skin and flesh.
But when it came to Qín, it was not so.
It followed the methods of Shēn and Shāng,
Shēn Bùhài and Shāng Yāng.
It hated the Way of the emperors and kings,
and made greed and wolfishness its custom,
Shǐ Gǔ said: Wolves by nature are all greedy,

Shǐ Gǔ said: Punish,
means to blame.
Therefore all the officials embellished empty words without regard for reality,

and none do not submit,

Master Zēng said: "Revere what you have heard,
then you will be lofty and bright;
practice what you know,
then you will be glorious and great.
Lofty, bright, glorious, and great
do not lie in other things,
but in applying your mind to it."
Shǐ Gǔ said: This is from the book of Master Zēng.
Master Zēng,
is Zēng Shēn.
If you establish sincerity within and carry it out to the full,
then how would you differ from the Three Kings!
To seek worthy men without nurturing scholars in advance is

Therefore, the greatest means of nurturing scholars
is none other than the Imperial Academy;
the Imperial Academy is
the gateway for worthy scholars.
Yǎn Shīgǔ’s note: Guān means
“by way of.”
Now, if we compare the population of a commandery or a kingdom,

Wú,

9 The Xiōngnú came to request a marriage alliance.
The Son of Heaven put the matter to discussion.
Dàxíng Wáng Huī,
a man of Yān,
familiar with barbarian affairs,
argued:
"When Hàn makes marriage alliances with the Xiōngnú,
it usually lasts no more than a few years
before they break the treaty again;
it is better not to agree,
but to raise troops and attack them."
Hán Ānguó said:
"The Xiōngnú migrate like birds taking flight,
difficult to subdue and control.
This means they are swift and mobile,
migrating following water and grass,
like birds taking flight.
They are not to be treated like ordinary people.
Then our men and horses would be exhausted;
the enemy, at full strength, would exploit our weakness.
This is a perilous course.
It is better to make a marriage alliance."
Most of the courtiers discussing the matter sided with Ānguó,
so the Emperor agreed to the marriage alliance.

Zhāng Yī says: The Sūn River originates from Táidēng County,
flows south to Huìwú,
and enters the Ruò River.
Kāng says: Also called the White Sand River.
Lǐ Wénzǐ says: The Sūn River,
originally named the Chánghé River.
They established one Commandant and over ten counties,
subordinate to Shǔ.
The Son of Heaven was greatly pleased.
3 An edict was issued to dispatch ten thousand soldiers to fortify the strategic points at Yànmén.
Yán Shīgǔ says: Strategic points,
are used for defense,
to stop the incursions of the Xiōngnú.
Gòngfù says: Fortifying strategic points means
opening roads to make them level and easy,
to facilitate attacking the Xiōngnú.
Zhì,
is pronounced zhí zhī fān.
4 In autumn,
the seventh month,
a great wind uprooted trees.
5. The witch Chǔ Fú and others taught Empress Chén to perform sacrificial rites and practice malevolent magic,
employing the seductive arts of women;
when the affair was discovered,
the Emperor ordered the Imperial Censor Zhāng Tāng to thoroughly investigate it.
Tāng deeply pursued the accomplices,
and those implicated and executed numbered over three hundred people,
with Chǔ Fú's head displayed in the marketplace.
On the Yǐsì day,
the Empress was presented with the decree,
her imperial seal and ribbons were confiscated,
she was deposed,
and resided in the Chángmén Palace.
The Chángmén Palace,
Rú Chún said: Chángmén is located southeast of Cháng'ān city.
According to the biography of Dōngfāng Shuò: The Grand Princess Dòu presented the Chángmén Garden,
and the Emperor made it into a palace.
She kowtowed to apologize to the Emperor.
The Grand Princess Dòu,
was the mother of Empress Chén.
稽 (kowtow),
pronounced qǐ.
"The Empress's actions were not in accordance with great righteousness,
and she could not avoid being deposed.
You, Princess, should adhere to the proper path to console yourself,
and not listen to baseless rumors that give rise to suspicion and fear.
Although the Empress is deposed,
her provisions will be as per regulations,
and the Chángmén Palace is no different from the upper palace."
6. Initially,
the Emperor once held a banquet at the home of the Grand Princess Dòu,
where the Princess introduced her favored pearl merchant Dǒng Yǎn,
and the Emperor bestowed upon him robes and headgear,
showing him respect without using his personal name,
addressing him as
"Master Wēng,"
and had him serve at the drinking;
from then on, Lord Dǒng became noble and favored,
and no one in the empire was unaware of it.
Examination of discrepancies says: The Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
"After Empress Chén was deposed and resided in the Chángmén Palace,
the Grand Princess Dòu, due to past affection, still remained close.
Later, when a banquet was held at the Princess's home,
the Princess introduced her favored Dǒng Yǎn."
According to the biography of Dōngfāng Shuò:
"Yuán Shū devised a plan for Yǎn,
having the Princess present the Chángmén Garden,
and its name was changed to Chángmén Palace,"
then it is clear that Yǎn's meeting with the Emperor occurred before Empress Chén's deposition.
They raced at the Pínglè Observatory,
the Pínglè Observatory is north of the Wèiyāng Palace,
with a circumference of fifteen lǐ;
during Emperor Gāozǔ's time,
the system was rudimentary.
By Emperor Wǔ's time, it was expanded and renovated.
The Sānfǔ Huángtú says: Within the Shànglín Park there is the Pínglè Observatory.
乐 (lè, music),
pronounced luò.
观 (guān, observatory),
pronounced gǔwán.
They engaged in cockfighting and cùjū.
鞠 (jū, ball),
is a ball,
made of leather.
鞠 (jū),
pronounced jūliù.
Master Yán Gǔ said: 角 (jué, compete),
means to compare.
The Emperor held a banquet for the Grand Princess Dòu in the Xuānshì Hall,
Sū Lín said: The Xuānshì Hall,
is the main hall of the front palace of Wèiyāng Palace.
Rú Chún said: The Xuānshì Hall,
is the hall for promulgating governance and teachings.
乐 (lè, music),
pronounced luò.
为 (wèi, for),
pronounced yúwèi.
At that time,
the Gentleman of the Palace Dōngfāng Shuò stood holding a halberd at the foot of the palace steps,
Master Yán Gǔ said: Holding a halberd and standing at the side of the steps.
"Dǒng Yǎn has three crimes deserving of beheading,
how can he be allowed to enter!"
The Emperor said:
"What do you mean?"
Shuò said:
"Yǎn, as a subject, privately serves the Princess,
that is his first crime.
He corrupts the transformation between men and women,
and disrupts the rites of marriage,
damaging the royal system,
that is his second crime.
Your Majesty is in the prime of youth,
and should be accumulating thoughts on the Six Classics;
Yǎn does not follow the classics and encourage learning,
but instead esteems extravagance and beauty,
Master Yán Gǔ said: 右 (yòu, right),
means to honor.
思 (sī, thought),
pronounced xiànglì.
Exhausting himself in the pleasures of dogs and horses,
indulging to the utmost the desires of the eyes and ears,
this is a great thief of the state,
a great venomous creature for the ruler,
that is his third crime."
The Emperor remained silent and did not respond,
after a long while said:
"I have already set up the banquet,
after drinking I will correct it myself."
Shuò said:
"The Xuānshì Hall,
is the proper place of the former emperor,
and no affairs not in accordance with law and propriety should enter it.
Therefore, the beginning of licentiousness and disorder,
its transformation leads to usurpation.
Thus, Shù Diāo's licentiousness led to Yì Yá causing calamity,
and only after Qìng Fǔ died did the state of Lǔ become secure."
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá,
were both ministers of Duke Huán of Qí.
When Guǎn Zhòng was ill,
Duke Huán asked him:
"What will you teach me?"
Zhòng said:
"I hope you will keep Shù Diāo and Yì Yá at a distance."
The Duke said:
"Yì Yá cooked his own son to please me,
can he still be suspected?"
He replied:
"Human nature is not to not love one's own son,
if he could be cruel to his own son,
what would he not do to you!"
The Duke said:
"Shù Diāo castrated himself to be close to me,
can he still be suspected?"
He replied:
"Human nature is not to not love one's own body,
if he could be cruel to his own body,
what would he not do to you!"
The Duke said:
"Alright."
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
he expelled them all;
but the Duke found food tasteless,
and the palace was not well managed.
After three years,
the Duke said:
"Wasn't Father Zhòng excessive!"
Thereupon he summoned them all back.
The next year,
the Duke fell ill.
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá together started a rebellion,
blocking the gates and building walls so no one could enter.
A woman climbed over the wall to where the Duke was,
the Duke said:
"I want to eat."
The woman said:
"I cannot get anything."
He said again:
"I want to drink."
The woman said:
"I cannot get anything."
The Duke said:
"Why?"
She said:
"Shù Diāo and Yì Yá have rebelled,
so I cannot get anything."
The Duke sighed with emotion:
"If the dead have consciousness,
what face do I have to see Father Zhòng!"
He covered his head with his sleeve and died in the Shòu Palace;
worms flowed out from the door,
and they covered it with a poplar door,
and he was not buried for three months.
Qìng Fǔ,
was the son of Duke Huán of Lǔ by a concubine,
the elder brother of Duke Zhuāng,
and had an affair with Āi Jiāng.
When Duke Zhuāng died,
Qìng Fǔ murdered his son Bān and Duke Mǐn,
wanting to cause chaos but failing,
fled to Jǔ.
The people of Jǔ returned him,
and he hanged himself in Mì,
and only then did Lǔ become stable.
父 (fǔ),
pronounced fǔ.
"Well said!"
An edict was issued to stop it,
and instead a banquet was set up in the Běi Palace,
leading Lord Dǒng to enter through the East Sima Gate;
the Wèiyāng Palace has East and North Towers,
the East Tower is called Cānglóng.
The East Sima Gate,
is the Sima Gate inside the Cānglóng Tower.
更 (gèng, change),
pronounced gōnghéng.
Lord Dǒng's favor from then on declined daily.
After this,
princesses and noble ladies often transgressed ritual regulations.
7. The Emperor appointed Zhāng Tāng as Grand Master of the Palace.
Together with Zhào Yǔ, they jointly established various laws and ordinances,
striving for severe and intricate provisions.
They constrained officials who merely adhered to their duties,
creating the "Law of Knowing and Seeing,"
whereby officials monitored and supervised each other.
From this point onward, the application of laws became increasingly harsh.
Sū Lín said: They constrained and were harsh toward officials who merely adhered to their duties.
Shī Gǔ said: Seeing or knowing that someone has violated the law but failing to report it
is called deliberate connivance.
The Jìn Treatise states: Those who see or know but do not impeach
shall each be held equally guilty;
if failing to impeach was due to negligence,
it shall be punishable by redemption;
if one did not see or did not know,
one shall not be held liable.
"Chuán"
is pronounced as Zhāng Liàn fān.
"Jiān"
is pronounced as Gǔ Xián fān.
8. In the eighth month,
there was a plague of borers.
Borers are insects that eat the hearts [of crops].
9. That year,
officials and commoners who understood the affairs of the contemporary world and were well-versed in the methods of the ancient sages were summoned.
The counties along the way were to provide them with successive provisions,
and they were ordered to travel together with the accounting envoys.
Shī Gǔ said: The "accounting" refers to the envoys presenting the accounting registers;
each commandery and kingdom annually dispatched them to the capital to submit these.
"Together" means
to accompany;
it means ordering the summoned individuals to come together with those presenting the accounts,
with counties along the way supplying their food.
Later generations, through errors and misunderstandings,
based on this phrasing,
mistakenly referred to presenting accounts as "jì xié."
Kàn Yīn, lacking detailed knowledge,
arbitrarily explained it,
saying that during the Qín and Hàn dynasties, the envoys of feudal lords coming to court were called "jì xié."
"Xié"
means sequence.
The Jìn dynasty had a "jì xié register,"
and later changed
"xié"
to
"jiē,"
straying even further from the truth,
leading later scholars into error.
Gōngsūn Hóng from Zīchuān presented a policy response, saying:
"Your servant has heard that in the ancient times of Yáo and Shùn,
they did not value noble ranks and rewards, yet the people were encouraged to do good;
they did not emphasize punishments and penalties, yet the people did not transgress.
This was because they personally led with correctness and treated the people with trust.
In degenerate ages, noble ranks and generous rewards are valued, yet the people are not encouraged;
severe punishments and heavy penalties are imposed, yet wickedness does not cease.
This is because those above are not correct,
and they treat the people without trust.
Generous rewards and heavy punishments
are insufficient to encourage goodness and prohibit wrongdoing;
trustworthiness alone is essential.
Therefore, appointing officials based on their abilities
leads to orderly division of duties;
eliminating useless words
allows affairs to be handled appropriately;
not creating useless objects
reduces taxes and levies;
not encroaching on the people's farming seasons,
not hindering the people's labor power,
then the common people will prosper;
advancing those with virtue,
removing those without virtue,
then the imperial court will be respected;
promoting those with merit,
demoting those without merit,
then ministers will be orderly and deferential;
Lǐ Qí said: This means there is proper sequence.
Shī Gǔ said: "Qūn"
is pronounced as qī xún fān.
Then wickedness and evil will cease;
rewarding the worthy appropriately,
then ministers will be encouraged.
All these eight points
are the foundation of governance.
Therefore, regarding the people:
if they have occupations, they will not contend;
if they receive just treatment, they will not resent;
if they have ritual propriety, they will not be violent;
if they are loved, they will be affectionate toward their superiors.
Shī Gǔ said: When each has their proper occupation,
there will be no contentious hearts;
when each can articulate their principles,
there will be nothing to resent;
guiding them through ritual,
there will be no violence or disrespect;
treating them like children and loving them,
they will know to be affectionate toward their superiors.
Ritual and righteousness
are what the people submit to;
and if rewards and punishments accord with them,
then the people will not violate prohibitions.
Your servant has heard: When the vital energy is the same, there is compliance;
when the sounds harmonize, there is resonance.
Now, if the ruler above cultivates harmonious virtue,
and the common people below live in harmony and unity,
then when hearts are harmonious, vital energy becomes harmonious;
when vital energy is harmonious, forms become harmonious;
when forms are harmonious, sounds become harmonious;
when sounds are harmonious, the harmony of Heaven and Earth responds.
Therefore, yīn and yáng are in harmony,
wind and rain come in season,
sweet dew descends,
the five grains ripen,
the six domestic animals multiply,
auspicious grain flourishes,
vermilion grass grows,
mountains are not barren,
marshes do not dry up.
This is the ultimate state of harmony."
At that time, there were over a hundred respondents.
The Minister of Ceremonies reported that Gōngsūn Hóng's ranking was among the lowest.
When the policy responses were presented,
the Son of Heaven promoted Gōngsūn Hóng's response to first place,
appointed him as Erudite,
and had him await orders at the Golden Horse Gate.
Rú Chún said: During Emperor Wǔ's time,
a horse appraiser named Dōngfāng Jīng created a method for bronze horses and presented it.
A horse statue was erected outside the Lǔ Bān Gate,
and the Lǔ Bān Gate was renamed the Golden Horse Gate.
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states: The Golden Horse Gate
was the office of the eunuchs.
When Emperor Wǔ obtained horses from Dàyuān,
he had them cast in bronze
and erected at the gate of the office,
hence the name.
Yuán Gù from Qí,
over ninety years old,
was also summoned as a Worthy and Good candidate.
Gōngsūn Hóng looked askance at Yuán Gù and served him,
but Yuán Gù said:
"Master Gōngsūn,
you must base your words on orthodox learning,
and not distort your learning to flatter the age!"
Many Confucian scholars envied and slandered Yuán Gù,
so Yuán Gù, due to old age, was dismissed and returned home.
At that time,
the four commanderies of Bā and Shǔ
(the four commanderies are Shǔjùn, Guǎnghànjùn, Qiánwéijùn, and Bājùn)
had garrisons stretching over a thousand *li*, transporting supplies to each other.
After several years,
the roads remained impassable,
and many soldiers died from exhaustion, starvation, or exposure to the heat and dampness;
the southwestern barbarians also rebelled repeatedly.
Troops were dispatched to attack them,
costing hundreds of millions with no success.
The Emperor was troubled by this
and ordered Gōngsūn Hóng to inspect the situation.
Upon returning to report,
he strongly criticized the southwestern barbarian campaign as useless,
but the Emperor did not heed him.
Whenever Gōngsūn Hóng attended court assemblies,
he would present the issues clearly,
allowing the sovereign to make his own choice,
refusing to argue face-to-face or dispute in court.
Thereupon, the Emperor observed that his conduct was cautious and sincere,
his arguments were ample,
he was well-versed in legal statutes and administrative affairs,
and he embellished them with Confucian teachings.
(Yán Shīgǔ comments: It is like adding a pure border to a garment.
"折" is pronounced as *zhé*.
"爭" is read as *zhèng*.
"行" is pronounced as *xìng*.)
Within a year, he was promoted to Left Interior Commandant.
(Sīmǎ Guāng's *Examination of Discrepancies* states: The *Hànshū* "Annals of Emperor Wǔ" says:
"In the fifth month of Yuánguāng's first year,
an edict was issued to examine the worthy and virtuous,
whereupon Dǒng Zhòngshū, Gōngsūn Hóng, and others emerged."
According to Gōngsūn Hóng's biography:
"In Yuánguāng's fifth year,
worthy and virtuous scholars were again summoned,
and the state of Zīchuān recommended Gōngsūn Hóng."
The examination text closely resembles the one from the first year in the "Annals of Emperor Wǔ."
It also says:
"Within a year, he reached the position of Left Interior Commandant."
The "Table of Officials" states:
"In Yuánguāng's fifth year,
Gōngsūn Hóng became Left Interior Commandant."
Thus, it is clear that Gōngsūn Hóng's second recommendation as worthy and virtuous did not occur in Yuánguāng's first year.
Xún Yuè's *Hàn Jì* records under this year:
"Summoned officials and commoners who understood contemporary affairs."
Gé Hóng's *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* also states:
"Gōngsūn Hóng was recommended as worthy and virtuous by scholars of the state in Yuánguāng's fifth year."
If this edict for continued provisions was issued in the eighth month,
then Gōngsūn Hóng could not have already become Left Interior Commandant this year.
Probably this edict was issued this year,
but it is unknown in which month,
so Bān Gù placed it at the end of the year.
The similarity in the examination texts is likely coincidental;
or perhaps this examination was Gōngsūn Hóng's response when first recommended as worthy and virtuous,
and Bān Gù mistakenly attributed it to this year's examination.
This cannot be clarified with certainty,
so we now follow the *Hàn Jì*.)
When Gōngsūn Hóng reported on affairs,
if something was unacceptable,
he did not argue in court.
He often requested a private audience with Jí Àn,
(Yán Shīgǔ comments: Seeking a moment of free time.)
and Gōngsūn Hóng would defer to him.
The Son of Heaven was often pleased,
listened to all his suggestions,
and thus grew increasingly fond and respectful of him.
Gōngsūn Hóng once made an agreement with the high ministers during discussions,
but when before the Emperor,
he would betray that agreement to comply with the Emperor's wishes.
Jí Àn confronted him in court, saying:
"People from Qí are often deceitful and insincere;
initially, you agreed with us on this proposal,
but now you betray it—this is disloyal!"
The Emperor asked Gōngsūn Hóng about it.
Gōngsūn Hóng apologized, saying:
"Those who understand me consider me loyal;
those who do not understand me consider me disloyal."
The Emperor agreed with Gōngsūn Hóng's words.
Whenever the Emperor's favored attendants slandered Gōngsūn Hóng,
the Emperor treated him even more generously.
1. In winter,
commercial carts were first taxed.
(Lǐ Qí states: Began taxing merchants' carts and boats,
ordering them to pay taxes.)
2. The Grand Minister of Agriculture, Zhèng Dāngshí, said:
"Dredge the Wèi River to create a canal,
flowing down to the Huáng Hé.
The canal starts from Cháng'ān,
runs along the southern mountains down to the Huáng Hé for over three hundred *li*.
It can also irrigate over ten thousand *qǐng* of farmland for the people living along the canal."
In spring,
an edict was issued to conscript tens of thousands of laborers to dredge the canal,
according to Zhèng Dāngshí's plan.
It was completed in three years,
and people found it convenient.
3. The Xiōngnú invaded Shànggǔ,
killing and plundering officials and commoners.
Chariot and Cavalry General Wèi Qīng was dispatched from Shànggǔ,
Cavalry General Gōngsūn Áo from Dài,
Light Chariot General Gōngsūn Hè from Yúnzhōng,
and Valiant Cavalry General Lǐ Guǎng from Yànmén,
each with ten thousand cavalry,
to attack the Hú at the border markets.
Wèi Qīng reached Lóngchéng
(Lóngchéng was where the Xiōngnú offered sacrifices to heaven and assembled their various tribes).
Gōngsūn Hè gained nothing;
Gōngsūn Áo was defeated by the Hú,
losing seven thousand cavalry;
Lǐ Guǎng was also defeated by the Hú.
The Hú captured Lǐ Guǎng alive,
placed him between two horses,
tied him in a net and laid him across,
traveling over ten *li*.
Lǐ Guǎng pretended to be dead,
then suddenly leaped up onto a Hú youth's horse,
(Yán Shīgǔ comments: "腾" means to jump.
"上" is pronounced *shàng*.)
whipped the horse southward,
and thus managed to escape and return.
The Hàn court handed Áo and Guǎng over to the officials,
who sentenced them to execution,
but they redeemed themselves and became commoners;
only Wèi Qīng was enfeoffed as a Marquis of the Imperial Domain.
Although Wèi Qīng came from slave origins
(Wèi Qīng was originally a mounted slave in Princess Píngyáng's household),
his talent and strength surpassed others.
He treated scholars and officials with courtesy,
showed kindness to his soldiers,
and the masses were willing to serve under him.
He possessed the qualities of a commander,
so each time he went out, he achieved merit.
The world thus admired the Emperor's ability to recognize talent.
4. In summer,
there was a great drought;
locusts swarmed.
5. In the sixth month,
the Emperor traveled to Yōng.
6. In autumn,
the Xiōngnú repeatedly raided the border,
with Yúyáng suffering the most.
Commandant Hán Ānguó was appointed as General of Skilled Soldiers
and stationed in Yúyáng.
First year of Yuánshuò
(Guǐchǒu, 128 BCE) (Yìng Shào states: "朔" means to revive.
Mèng Kē said:
"The later ones will revive."
"苏" means to rest;
it signifies the great revival and growth of the myriad people and all things.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: "朔" means beginning;
it indicates a renewal of the beginning.
The "rest" in revival does not mean growth;
Yìng's explanation is mistaken.)
1. In winter,
in the eleventh month,
an imperial edict stated:
"We have deeply instructed the officials in charge
to promote incorruptibility and
recommend filial piety,
hoping that this will become a prevailing custom,
continuing the splendid legacy of the former sages.
(Yán Shīgǔ notes: Xiū means
'splendid';
xù means
'legacy': meaning to continue the splendid legacy of the former sages.
Jī,
pronounced jū yī fān.)
There must be loyalty and trustworthiness;
when three people walk together,
among them is my teacher.
(The Analects says: In a village of ten households,
there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I am.
It also says: When three people walk together,
there must be my teacher among them.
Yán Shīgǔ notes: Hé means
'to close';
it refers to the entire commandery,
hence the term hé.)
Yet virtuous gentlemen of accumulated conduct are blocked from reaching the emperor's ears.
(Yán Shīgǔ notes: Jiū means
'to exhaust';
meaning they are obstructed,
unable to have their names reach the Son of Heaven.
Xíng,
pronounced xià mèng fān.)
Obstructing the worthy incurs manifest punishment,
which is the ancient way.
Let it be deliberated what crime
those officials of two thousand piculs who fail to recommend should bear!"
The responsible officials memorialized:
"Failing to recommend the filial,
disobeying the imperial edict,
should be judged as disrespect;
(Zhāng Yàn says: This means they do not diligently seek scholars to serve the state.
Being incompetent,
they should be dismissed.")
(Zhāng Yàn says: Officials of two thousand piculs should lead by personal example to transform those below;
now, personally governing the herds and yet having no worthy men,
is considered incompetence.
Shèng,
pronounced shēng.)
2. In the twelfth month,
Jiāngdū Yì King Liú Fēi passed away.
(Fēi was
a son of Emperor Jǐng;
in the second year of the former era,
he was enfeoffed in Rǔnán;
in the third year,
he was transferred to Jiāngdū.)
3. The imperial son Jù was born,
the son of Lady Wèi.
This was Lì Crown Prince.
(Textual analysis notes: The "Hànshū · Wǔ Wǔ Zǐ Zhuàn" praise states:
"In the spring of the sixth year of Jiànyuán,
Lì Crown Prince was born."
The "Wàiqī Zhuàn" states:
"Empress Wèi,
gave birth to a son, Jù, in the first year of Yuánshuò."
According to the "Méi Gāo Zhuàn":
"Emperor Wǔ was twenty-nine years old when he had an imperial son,"
which matches the "Wàiqī Zhuàn."
Probably the praise mistakenly attributed this to the appearance of the Chīyóu banner,
just as the gathering of the five planets occurred in the final years of Qín Èrshì,
but was mistakenly recorded as the first year of Hàn.)
On the jiǎzǐ day,
Lady Wèi was established as empress,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
4. In autumn,
twenty thousand Xiongnu cavalry invaded Hàn,
killed the governor of Liáoxī,
captured over two thousand people,
and besieged Hán Ānguó's camp;
they also entered Yúyáng and Yànmén,
each killing and capturing over a thousand people.
Ānguó moved further east,
stationing troops in Běipíng;
after several months,
he died of illness.
(Textual analysis notes: Ānguó died the following year,
but it is mentioned here to conclude the matter.)
Lǐ Guǎng was appointed as governor of Yòuběipíng.
The Xiongnu called him
"the Flying General of Hàn,"
avoided him,
and for several years did not dare to enter Yòuběipíng.
5. Chariot and Cavalry General Wèi Qīng led thirty thousand cavalry out of Yànmén,
and General Lǐ Xī marched out of Dài;
Qīng beheaded and captured several thousand enemies.
6. The eastern barbarian chieftain Nányú and others, totaling
two hundred and eighty thousand people, surrendered,
and the Cānghǎi Commandery was established;
(Fú Qián says: The Huìmò were north of Chénhán,
south of Gāolì and Wòjū,
extending east to the great sea.
Yán Shīgǔ notes: Nányú
is the name of the Huì chieftain.
The "Shíhuò Zhì" states: Péng Wú opened a route to connect with Huìmò and Cháoxiān,
and established the Cānghǎi Commandery.
Chén Shòu's "Fūyú Zhuàn": During the Wèi period,
the Fūyú treasury contained jade discs, guǐ scepters, and zǎn ladles,
passed down through generations as treasures.
The elders said they were bestowed by former dynasties,
and the inscription on the seal read
"Seal of the King of Huì."

the people have long been scattered."
See the Analects.
If they are shown what is good and evil,
and regulated with ritual and law,
how could the people know the prohibitions and return to righteousness!
According to the ancient correct law: the Five Hegemons,
were offenders against the Three Kings;
and the Six States,
were offenders against the Five Hegemons;
as for the Four Heroes,
they were offenders against the Six States.
As for figures like Guō Xiě,
with the insignificance of commoners,
usurping the power of life and death,
their crimes already deserved execution.
Observing their gentleness, benevolence, and love for all,
aiding the poor and relieving the distressed,
humility and lack of boastfulness,
they also possessed extraordinary talents.
Alas,
they did not enter the path of virtue,
but recklessly indulged in the baser currents,
leading to their deaths and the extinction of their clans,
which was not unfortunate.
Xún Yuè commented: There are three types of wanderers in the world,
which are thieves of virtue: the first is the wandering knight,
the second is the wandering persuader,
the third is the wandering activist.
Establishing an imposing manner,
wielding authority and power,
forming private connections to build strength in the world—
these are called wandering knights;
embellishing arguments,
devising deceitful schemes,
racing across the world to seize opportunities—
these are called wandering persuaders;
superficially adopting benevolence to suit contemporary tastes,
forming cliques,
establishing false reputations to gain power and profit—
these are called wandering activists.
These three types
are the sources of chaos;
they harm the Way and virtue,
corrupt laws and mislead the world,
and were carefully guarded against by the former kings.
The state has four classes of people,
each attending to their own occupations;
those who do not belong to these four classes
are called treacherous people.
The four classes
are scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
Only then can the kingly Way be achieved.
All these three types of wanderers
arise in times of decline,
especially at the end of the Zhōu and Qín dynasties.
When those above are not enlightened,
those below are not upright,
institutions are not established,
and laws and regulations are lax and abandoned;
when praise and blame determine honor and disgrace,
without verifying the truth;
when likes and dislikes determine benefit and harm,
without considering the reality;
when joy and anger determine rewards and punishments,
without examining the principles.
Superiors and subordinates deceive each other,
and all affairs go awry,
so those who speak calculate gains and losses before uttering words,
and those who select officials gauge closeness and distance before making recommendations.
Good and evil are mistaken by public opinion,
merit and crime are confused by royal law.
Thus, benefit cannot be sought through righteousness,
and harm cannot be avoided through the Way.
Therefore, gentlemen violate ritual,
petty people violate law,
rushing about,
overstepping duties and exceeding bounds,
embellishing appearances and neglecting substance,
competing for temporary gains.
Neglecting the respect due to fathers and elder brothers while honoring the etiquette of guests,
weakening the affection for flesh and blood while deepening the love for friends,
forgetting the path of self-cultivation while seeking the praise of the masses,
cutting into the livelihood of food and clothing to supply the pleasures of feasting,
with bribes filling the courtyards,
and exchanges of gifts filling the roads,
wrapped items are called "bāo,"
padded items are called "jū."
The Shī Jīng commentary: Those who give fruits as gifts use "bāo jū."
Also said: "Bāo jū"
refers to wrapped fish or meat,
using either reeds
or straw.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn commentary states: "Pìn"
means holding jade and silk to inquire after each other.
Private affairs outnumber official duties,
thus customs become corrupt and the right path is ruined.
Therefore, when a sage king rules above,
governing the state and ordering the people,
he rectifies its institutions;
distinguishing good and evil based on merit and crime, not swayed by praise or blame,
listening to their words and holding them accountable for their actions,
examining their reputations and pointing out the reality.
Thus, when reality does not match the reputation, it is called emptiness;
when feelings do not match the appearance, it is called hypocrisy;
when praise or blame loses its truth, it is called slander;
when words and deeds are inconsistent, it is called deceit.
Hypocritical behavior must not be allowed,
slanderous and deceitful words must not be spread,
the guilty must not find luck,
the innocent must not fear unjust punishment,
and personal requests must not be entertained.
"Qǐng"
means to seek.
"Yè"
means to inform.
Eliminate flowery language,
discard empty words,
prohibit false arguments,
eradicate excessive cleverness,
reject the chaos of the hundred schools,
unify with the supreme Way of the sages,
nurture with benevolence and kindness,
adorn with ritual and music,
then customs will be settled and great transformation achieved.

Thereupon, Zhǔfù Yǎn and his clan were exterminated.

Second Year of Yuánfēng

1 Winter,

2 Spring,

At the time, the year was dry,

3 Earlier,
the Yellow River breached at Hùzǐ,

This year,

which naturally have holes,
if the cracks resemble human or object shapes it is auspicious,
if insufficient it is inauspicious.
This method is still practiced in Lǐngnán.
Fàn Chéngdà's Guìhǎi Yúhéng Zhì: Chicken divination,
a southern divination method,
takes a young rooster by its two feet,
burns incense and prays for the divination subject,
then kills the chicken by striking it,
pulls out the two thigh bones,
cleans them,
binds them with thread,
inserts a bamboo splinter at the binding point,
so the two bones are back-to-back at the splinter's end,
holds the bamboo and prays again.
The left bone represents "nóng",
nóng,
meaning "me".
The right bone represents "rén",
rén,
the matter being divined.
Observe the fine pores on the sides of the two bones,
insert short bamboo splinters about an inch long into all of them,
the slant, straightness, deviation, or correctness,
each follows the pore's natural state,
to determine auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
The method has eighteen variations,
generally, straight and correct, or close to the bone, mostly
auspicious;
curved and slanted, or far from the bone, mostly
inauspicious.
There is also chicken egg divination,

writing ink on the shell,
marking the four directions;
after boiling, cut it crosswise,
look at the ink-marked spots,
discern the thickness of the egg white inside the shell to determine the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of "nóng" and "rén".

Jūnsù,

he forged ties of marriage with the Xiongnu,
and advised the Xiongnu to block the passage from Han to Wūsūn."
In this year,
the Court Gentleman Zhèng Jí of Kuàijī and the Commandant Sīmǎ Xǐ,

to accumulate grain.
The convicts had their sentences commuted
and were made to garrison and farm.
Among the various states of the Western Regions,
those who followed water and pasture and shared customs with the Xiōngnú
were called "mobile states";
those who lived in walled cities
were called the "walled-city states."
They defeated them;
the king of Chēshī requested to surrender.
The Xiōngnú dispatched troops to attack Chēshī;
Zhèng Jí and Sīmǎ Xǐ led troops north and encountered them,
and the Xiōngnú dared not advance.
Zhèng Jí and Sīmǎ Xǐ then left one scout and twenty soldiers to guard the king,
while Zhèng Jí and others led the troops back to Qúlí.
Textual Analysis states: The "Treatise on the Western Regions" says
"in the second year of Dìjié";
comparing it with the "Treatise on the Xiōngnú,"
it is known to be in the third year.
He then fled lightly mounted to Wūsūn.
Zhèng Jí immediately welcomed his wife and children,
