The Xiōngnú further made Dōumò, the younger brother of the king of Chēshī, the king of Chēshī,
gathered the remaining people and moved east,
not daring to dwell in the former lands;
and Zhèng Jí for the first time sent three hundred officials and soldiers to farm the lands of Chēshī to populate it.
This sets the stage for the conflict over Chēshī with the Xiōngnú in the second year of Yuánkāng below.
11. Since first ascending the throne,
the Emperor had repeatedly sent envoys to seek his maternal relatives;
due to the long passage of time,
many were similar but not the correct ones.
In this year,
his maternal grandmother Wáng Ǎo was found.
Wén Yǐng said: In Yōuzhōu and Hànzhōng, an old woman is called Ǎo.
Shī Gǔ said: Ǎo
is a term for an elderly woman;
pronunciation: wū lǎo fān.
Wúgù and Wǔ
were both sons of Ǎo.
Within ten days,
the rewards bestowed amounted to tens of thousands.
1. In spring,
the second month,
the maternal grandmother was granted the title of Bópíng Jūn;

Lèchāng,

2. In summer,
the fifth month,
in Shānyáng and Jìyīn, hailstones as large as chicken eggs fell,

3. An edict stated:

4. Wén, grandson of King Huì of Guǎngchuān, was established as King of Guǎngchuān.
In the fourth year of Běnshǐ,
King Qù of Guǎngchuān committed suicide due to crime;
now Wén is re-established,

Shān said:
"Now the Chancellor is in power,
the Emperor trusts him,

Moreover,
many of the Confucian scholars are sons of poor families,
Shī Gǔ said: Jù,
means poor and without propriety.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Being poor and unable to perform rituals is called jù,
pronunciation: qí yǔ fān.
They delight in wild talk and reckless words,
avoiding no taboos,

Shī Gǔ said: Meaning he detested them like enemies.
Each person writes their own responses to affairs,

There was once a memorial accusing our brothers of arrogance and willfulness,

Later memorial writers became more cunning,
all
submitting sealed memorials,

Also, I hear rumors among the people saying 'the Huò family poisoned Empress Xǔ to death,'
Shī Gǔ said: Huān,
means the sound of a crowd;

The matter of poisoning Empress Xǔ is seen in the third year of Běnshǐ in the previous scroll.
Xiǎn, terrified and anxious,

Zhang Shè, who was close to Lǐ Jìng, the maternal uncle of Yún,

To have the Emperor moved,

A man named Zhāng Zhāng from Cháng'ān reported this,

the Capital Military Commander,

Shān and others became even more fearful,

Shī Gǔ said: Zhòng,
means to find difficult.
Jìng,
means to thoroughly investigate the matter.
If it is exposed after a long time,

Shī Gǔ said: Meaning to rebel first.
They all said:
"Where can we avoid it!"
Shī Gǔ said: Meaning there is no place to avoid,

At that time, Lǐ Jìng was implicated for associating with the feudal lords and kings,

An imperial edict was issued:

The Administrator of Shānyáng, Zhāng Chǎng, submitted a sealed memorial stating:

Eventually, the Tián clan usurped Qí,

Prince Jì Yǒu of Lǔ
killed Qìngfǔ,
established Duke Xī,

Subsequently, his family served as chief ministers for generations,

When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn went into exile,

Upon his return to the state,
he became the leader among the feudal lords,

Subsequently, his family served as ministers of Jìn for generations,

by the time of Zhào Yāng,
they, along with the Zhì, Hán, and Wèi clans, partitioned the state of Jìn.
Tián Wán fled from Chén to Qí,
and Duke Huán treated him with courtesy and employed him.
During Duke Huán's hegemony,
Wán contributed to his achievements;
later, Chén Chéngzǐ gained control over the governance of Qí,
and by the time of Tián Hé,
he usurped Qí and took possession of it.
Tracing the patterns of prosperity and decline,
the criticism of hereditary high ministers is most severe.
Previously, the Grand General made major decisions,
stabilized the imperial ancestral temple,
and pacified the realm.
His achievements were also not insignificant.
Now, the Duke of Zhōu only served for seven years.
The Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng for seven years and then returned governance to King Chéng.
From the second year of the Hòuyuán era of Emperor Wǔ to the second year of the Dìjié era,
it is exactly twenty years.
At the peak of his power,
he moved heaven and earth,
and encroached upon the forces of yīn and yáng.
The court ministers should have clearly stated: 'Your Majesty has honored and favored the late Grand General to repay his merits and virtue, which is sufficient.
Recently, the assisting ministers have monopolized governance,
the noble relatives have become too powerful,
and the distinction between ruler and subject is unclear.
We request that the three Huò marquises be dismissed and ordered to return to their residences;
as for General of the Guard Zhāng Ānshì,
he should be granted a cane and allowed to retire,
with occasional inquiries and summons,
serving as the Son of Heaven's teacher with the rank of marquis.'
If Your Majesty had explicitly issued an edict and, out of grace, refused to accept it,
and the ministers had firmly argued based on righteousness until it was granted,
the realm would certainly regard Your Majesty as not forgetting merits and virtue, and the court ministers as understanding propriety.
The Huò family would then have no troubles for generations.
Now, the court hears no straightforward voices.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: This means the court ministers do not advance straightforward words to present the matter.
This is not a wise strategy.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: This means it is a miscalculation.
Human sentiments are not far apart;
judging by your servant's heart,
the Grand Marshal and his branches and affiliates must harbor fear and apprehension.
When close ministers feel endangered,
it is not a sound plan.
Your servant Chǎng wishes to openly raise this issue in the grand court,
but as I am merely guarding a distant commandery,
there is no way to do so.
I only hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully!"
The Emperor thought his plan was excellent,
but did not summon him.
The families of Huò Yǔ, Huò Shān, and others repeatedly experienced strange and ominous occurrences,
causing the entire household to worry and grieve.
Huò Shān said:

Rú Chún comments: During Empress Gāo's time, a decree was established:

Tù (hare),
is pronounced as tǔgù fān.
Wā (frog),
is the ancient character for frog.
They planned to summon the Chancellor, Marquis Píng'ēn, and others below,
and have Fàn Míngyǒu and Dèng Guǎnghàn, under the Empress Dowager's authority, seize and execute them,

The plan was agreed upon,

Then the affair was discovered.
In autumn,
the seventh month,

Huò Xiǎn, Huò Yǔ, Dèng Guǎnghàn, and others were captured;

Yāo (waist),
is interchangeable with the ancient character for waist.
Dozens of families connected to the Huò clan were implicated and executed.
The Grand Coachman Dù Yánnián, because of his past association with the Huò clan,
was also implicated and dismissed from office.
In the eighth month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Empress Huò was deposed
and placed in Zhāotái Palace.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Located within the Shànglín Imperial Park.
Chǔ (to place),

Bǎiguān Biǎo: Palace Attendants, Left and Right Attendants are all additional offices.

handle memorials submitted to the Imperial Secretariat,

Yùn,
is pronounced as yúfěn fān.
Zhāng was enfeoffed as Marquis Bóchéng.
Zhōng,
as Marquis Gāochāng.
Yùn,
as Marquis Píngtōng.
Ānshàng,
as Marquis Dūchéng.
Gāo as Marquis Lèlíng.
The son of Chancellor Chǎng;
Ānshàng,
the younger brother of the Chariot and Horse General Jīn Rìdī;
Gāo,
the son of the brother of Shǐ Liángdì.
Initially,
the Huò family was extravagant,

contempt for superiors.

Being in a position above others,
Shǐ Gǔ notes: 'Above' means
superior.

He then submitted a memorial stating:
"The Huò family is excessively powerful;

The memorial was submitted three times,

According to Hàn regulations: when a submitted memorial is not acted upon,
it is reported as received,
and the matter is dropped.
However, those who reported on the Huò family were all enfeoffed,
so someone submitted a memorial on behalf of Xú Shēng, saying:
"Your servant has heard of a guest who visited a host,
and saw that his stove had a straight chimney,
with firewood piled beside it.
The guest said to the host: 'Change it to a curved chimney,
the chimney,
is the stove's flue.
Change,
pronounced gēng.
Otherwise, there will be a fire disaster!'
The host remained silent and did not respond.
Soon after, the house indeed caught fire,
and the neighbors together came to rescue them,
fortunately managing to extinguish it.
Thereupon, they slaughtered an ox and prepared wine,

Those who were scorched and burned were seated in the places of honor,
Shǐ Gǔ notes: 'Scorched'
refers to those who were burned.
'Seated,'
pronounced xíng.

Someone said to the host: 'If you had listened to the guest's words earlier,

The host then realized his mistake and invited him.
Now, Xú Fú of Màolíng

If Fú's advice had been followed earlier,

Past events are already done,

The Emperor then bestowed upon Fú ten bolts of silk,

When the Emperor first ascended the throne,

in the grand procession,
the Grand General rides alongside.
Ride,
pronounced shèng;
the same below.

Shǐ Gǔ notes: 'Began'
means to start to grow.
Empress Huò was further moved to the Yúnlín Lodge,

Bān Gù's commentary says: Huò Guāng received the trust of an infant ruler,

means to rely on.

Wú,

Concealing his wife's evil schemes,

Drowning in overflowing desires,

Your subject Guāng says: Huò Guāng's assistance to the Hàn house
can be called loyal;

For authority and favor
are the tools of the ruler;
when a subject holds them,
for a long time without returning them,

With Xiàozhāo's wisdom,
at fourteen he knew of Shàngguān Jié's deceit,

Moreover, Xiàoxuān ascended the throne at nineteen,
intelligent and resolute,

not knowing to step aside and withdraw,
placing many
partisans,
filling the court,

Even so,

gave them military authority,

Xiàoxuān also brewed and brought it about.
In the past, Dòu Jiāo rebelled in Chǔ,

Zhēn,
pronounced zhēn.
Although they deserved extermination,

thus causing the family to have no survivors—

The generals advanced eastward to Zī in Chénliú.
Mèng Kāng said: Zī was the former state of Dài,
located in Liáng,
later belonging to Chénliú,
now called Kǎochéng.
The *Customs of Chénliú* records: Zī County,
was the Qín county of Gǔ.
When the Hàn troops rose up,
the region suffered many calamitous years,
so it was renamed Zī County.
When Emperor Zhāng passed through the county on his eastern tour,
he issued an edict: "Chénliú's Zī County,
its name is inauspicious.
Let it be changed to Kǎochéng."
They defeated them,
and beheaded Liú Pán.
Wáng Mǎng was greatly pleased,
and again issued an edict, first enfeoffing the Cavalry Commander Sūn Xián and fifty-four others as marquises,
appointing them in the army.
Subsequently, a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the land.
Thereupon, the elite officers and soldiers attacked and besieged Zhái Yì in Yǔ City.
In the twelfth month,
they inflicted a major defeat.
Zhái Yì and Liú Xìn abandoned their army and fled.
Reaching the border of Gùshǐ,
Yì was captured,
his corpse dismembered in the market of Chén;
Xìn was never caught.
According to the *Treatise on Geography*,
Yǔ, Gùshǐ, and Chén
were all three counties belonging to the Kingdom of Huáiyáng.
Xián said: The old city of Yǔ is southeast of present-day Yōngqiū County in Biàn Prefecture.
Zú,
read as zǐ xù fān.
The first year of Shǐchū
(Wùchén, 8 AD) In the eleventh month of this year,
Wáng Mǎng first changed the era name to Shǐchū.
1 Spring,
an earthquake occurred.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the land.
2 Wáng Yì and others returned to the capital,
and joined forces with Wáng Jí and others to attack Zhào Péng and Huò Hóng in the west.
In the second month,
Péng and others were annihilated,
and the various counties were pacified.
The army returned and regrouped.
Wáng Mǎng then held a banquet at the White Tiger Hall,
rewarding and bestowing gifts upon the generals.
An edict ordered Chén Chóng to assess military achievements,
ranking them from high to low.
Following the Zhōu system of five noble ranks,
he enfeoffed meritorious officials as hóu, bó, zǐ, and nán,
totaling three hundred and ninety-five individuals.
It was said
"All, through fierce anger,
striking east and west,
against Qiāng bandits and Mán robbers,
rebels and traitors,
without turning heel,
were annihilated in timely fashion,
and all under heaven submitted"
— such were the achievements for which they were enfeoffed.
Those who should have been granted the rank of Guānnèihóu
had their title changed to Fùchéng,
numbering several hundred more.
Xiàng Ānshì's *Family Explanations* states: When Wáng Mǎng enfeoffed the various nobles,
he established the Fùchéng rank.
The people of Hàn likely interpreted chéng as yōng (wall).
The ancient character yōng
is the character yōng (wall),
later people added the earth radical to distinguish it.
Those not forming a full state were called Fùchéng,
similar to today calling a subordinate commandery a shǔchéng.
I note that according to the *Royal Regulations*,
those with less than fifty lǐ cannot reach the Son of Heaven directly,
but are attached to the various nobles,
called fùyōng (attached wall).
Zhèng's commentary says: A small walled town is called fùyōng.
Fùyōng means
attaching the affairs of the state to a larger state.
The *Correct Meaning* says: Yōng
means walled town.
It refers to a small state's walled town that cannot communicate independently,
attaching its state affairs to a large state,
hence called fùyōng.
Xiàng's explanation is based on this.
Gēng,
read as gōng héng fān.
Their coffins were burned;
their three clans were exterminated,
punishment extending to offspring,
all thrown into the same pit,
buried together with thorns and the five poisonous plants.
Rú Chún said: The five poisons
are wild kudzu, langdu, and the like.
Zhái Fāngjìn
was originally from Shàngcài in Rǔnán.
They were gathered beside the main roads,
at Púyáng, Wúyán, Yǔ, Huáilǐ, and Zhōuzhì — five locations in total.
Púyáng, Wúyán, and Yǔ
were for the corpses of Yì's faction.
Huáilǐ and Zhōuzhì
were for the corpses of Péng and Hóng's faction.
Zhōuzhì,
pronounced Zhōu Zhì.
Shī Gǔ said: Biǎo (tablet/marker) is used
to clearly indicate.
"Rebel traitors, fish [AS-FBED] jiāng ní (whales and giant salamanders)."
Shī Gǔ said: Fish [AS-FBED] jiāng ní,
are large fish that cause harm;

5. Sīwēi Chén Chóng
Wáng Mǎng established the position of Sīwēi
to oversee and investigate all officials.
He ordered killings;
those who privately reported matters,
were considered his private subordinates.
Huò Xiǎn said: Shàofū, I am fortunate that you reported the matter to me.
To enforce his laws.
Wáng Mǎng was greatly enraged,
severely reprimanding Huò Guāng.
Huò Guāng's mother said:
"Look at yourself, how do you compare to Zhǎngsūn and Zhōngsūn!"
Zhǎngsūn and Zhōngsūn refer to
the courtesy names of Yǔ and Huò.
Huò's death is recorded in the first year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Āi in the previous volume.
Yǔ's death is recorded in the third year of Yuánshǐ of Emperor Píng in the previous volume.
Yán Shīgǔ notes: Zhōng
is read as Zhòng.
Both Kuàng and the others died.
Initially,
Wáng Mǎng built his reputation by serving his mother, caring for his sister-in-law, and raising his brother's son,
as recorded in the first year of Yǒngshǐ of Emperor Chéng in the thirty-first volume.
He again used this to demonstrate public righteousness.
Fú Qián said: Not pardoning Huò Guāng's crime was for public righteousness.
Zhòng Féng said: Wáng Mǎng did not observe mourning for his mother,
also to demonstrate public righteousness.

All the governors and grand administrators in the empire, because previously there had been rebellions like Zhái Yì and Zhào Péng, etc.,
(events seen in the first year of the Jūshè era in the previous scroll),
'shǒu,'
pronounced shì yòu fān;
same below.
and because they cherished loyalty and filial piety,
were enfeoffed, the governors as barons,
and the grand administrators as attached city lords.
He made the Han Gaozu temple the Wénzǔ Temple.
Yán Shīgǔ said: He wished to emulate Shùn receiving the mandate from Wénzǔ.
It was not abolished,
and sacrifices and offerings continued as before.
The various Liú clan members were not to have their exemptions revoked,
each to retain them for life;
the regional governors were to frequently inquire after their well-being,
and not allow them to suffer encroachment or injustice.
4. Wáng Mǎng, because the character for Liú (劉)
consists of '卯, 金, 刀'
(mǎo, jīn, dāo),
decreed that the benefits of the Gāngmǎo (made in the first month on a mǎo day) and the metal knives were not to be used.
Fú Qián said: The Gāngmǎo
is made on a mǎo day in the first month,
worn as a pendant,
three cùn long,
one cùn wide,
square,
sometimes made of jade,
sometimes of gold,
sometimes of peachwood,
attached to a leather belt and worn.
There are still some jade ones existing today,
with an inscription on one side saying:
"First month Gāngmǎo."
The metal knives
refer to the coins cast by Wáng Mǎng.
Jìn Zhuó said: The Gāngmǎo,
one cùn long,
five fēn wide,
square,
has a hole pierced through the center from top to bottom,
strung with colored silk threads,
its bottom like the tasseled end of a hat string.
On its top surface, two lines of text are engraved,
the inscription reading:
"In the first month, the Gāngmǎo is complete and central,
the numinous shū protects the four directions,
blue, red, white, yellow,
the four colors are in place.
The Emperor orders Zhùróng,
to instruct Kuí and Lóng,
all pestilences and fierce fevers,
dare not confront me!"
Another inscription says:
"On the severe day, the Yánmǎo,
the Emperor orders Kuí to transform,
following your firm submission,
transforming this numinous shū,
now upright, now straight,
now angular, now square,
all pestilences and fierce fevers,
dare not confront me!"
Yán Shīgǔ said: Nowadays, jade Gāngmǎo are sometimes found in the earth.
Examining their size and inscription,
Fú's explanation is correct.
Wáng Mǎng, because the character Liú has
'卯' (mǎo) above,
and
'金' (jīn) below,
with
'刀' (dāo) beside,
therefore prohibited the Gāngmǎo and metal knives.
I note: The character Liú originally has
'[AS-FBF9]'
above.
Wáng Mǎng, because
the character '[AS-FBF9]'
resembles
'卯' (mǎo),
therefore said so.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: In ancient script, there is the knife coin,
of two kinds: one is the Qìdāo,
the other is the Cuòdāo.
The Qìdāo was worth five hundred;
the Cuòdāo was worth one thousand.
The Qìdāo had no inlay, while the Cuòdāo was inlaid with gold.
The knife coin is shaped like a coin but with a knife-shaped edge,
hence people still sometimes call coins 'qián dāo' (money knife).
He then made small coins,
six fēn in diameter,
weighing one zhū,
inscribed
"small coin, value one,"
which, together with the previous
"large coin, value fifty,"
formed two denominations,
circulating together.
Wishing to prevent the people from privately minting coins,
he prohibited the possession of copper and charcoal.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
the Marquis of Xúxiāng, Liú Kuài, gathered a faction of several thousand men and raised troops in his fiefdom.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Kuài
was the son of the Prince Gōng of Jiāodōng.
However, the Table of Marquises Who Are Sons of Kings records his name as
"Guì",
with the radical
"fire",
which differs from this.
I suspect the table is mistaken.
The former Prince of Jiāodōng of Hàn,
was at this time the Duke of Fúchóng.
Kuài raised troops to attack Jímò,
Jímò,
was the capital of the Jiāodōng Kingdom.
Yīn,
was the son of the great-great-grandson of Prince Kāng of Jiāodōng, Jì.
He imprisoned himself.
Officials and people resisted Kuài;
Kuài was defeated and fled,
dying at Chángguǎng.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
Chángguǎng County,
belonged to Lángyá Commandery.
His fiefdom was increased to a full ten thousand households,
with a territory of one hundred *li*.
6 Wáng Mǎng said:
"In ancient times, one man had one hundred *mu* of fields,
and was taxed one-tenth,
Mèngzǐ said: The Zhōu people had one hundred *mu* and practiced the 'chè' system.
This refers to the Zhōu system.
Qín destroyed the sage's institutions,
abolishing the well-field system,
see the nineteenth year of King Xiǎn of Zhōu in the second scroll.
Destroyed,
pronunciation 'guài'.
Greed and baseness arose,
the strong possessed fields by the thousands,
while the weak did not even have a place to stand an awl.
Moreover, markets for male and female slaves were established,
placing them in the same pens as oxen and horses,
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Pen,
means to pen them in,
like the pens for oxen and horses.
Arbitrarily deciding their fate,
contradicting the principle that
'Of all creatures produced by Heaven and Earth, man is the most noble.'
The Classic of Filial Piety: Confucius said: Of all creatures produced by Heaven and Earth, man is the most noble.
Decide,
pronunciation 'dīng luàn fān'.
Lightening the land tax,
to one-thirtieth,
there were always corvée duties,
even the disabled had to pay;
while powerful people encroached and oppressed,
dividing fields and forcibly renting them out.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Dividing fields,
means that the poor, having no fields, take the fields of the rich to cultivate,
sharing the harvest with them.
Renting,
also means poor people renting fields from the rich.
Forcibly,
means the rich forcibly seize their taxes,
encroaching and cheating them.
In reality, the tax was fifty percent.
Therefore, the rich had surplus grain even for their dogs and horses,
becoming arrogant and turning to evil;
the poor could not even get their fill of chaff and husks,
becoming destitute and turning to crime;
both fell into guilt,
and punishments were used without cease.
Now I rename all land under heaven as 'Royal Land',
and male and female slaves as 'Private Dependents',
neither may be bought or sold.
Those households with fewer than eight males but possessing more than one well-field's worth of land,
must divide the surplus land among their nine clans, neighbors, and local communities.
Those who previously had no land, and now should receive land,
shall do so according to the regulations.
Anyone who dares to criticize the sage well-field system or create lawless confusion among the masses,
shall be cast out to the four wildernesses,
to ward off mountain demons and goblins,
Yán Shīgǔ comments: *Chī*,
are mountain spirits.
*Mèi*,
are old object spirits.
*Chī*,
pronunciation 'chī'.
*Mèi*,
pronunciation 'mèi'.
Shùn cast out the Four Fiends to the four wildernesses,
to ward off mountain demons and goblins.
7 In autumn,
the Five Majestic Generals Wáng Qí and eleven others were dispatched
The Five Majestic Generals,
were divided into Left, Right, Front, Rear, and Center Commanders,
their clothing, caps, carriages, attire, and harnessed horses each corresponded in color and number to their direction.
General,
pronunciation 'jí liàng fān'.
Commander,
pronunciation 'suǒ lèi fān';
same below.
They carried twenty-five tallies of mandate,
and twelve auspicious responses.
The Five Majestic Generals, bearing the tallies of mandate,
carrying seals and ribbons,
from kings and marquises down to officials whose titles were changed,
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Changed,
means altered.
all were immediately granted the new seals and ribbons of the Xīn dynasty,
and their former Hàn seals and ribbons were collected.
A great amnesty was proclaimed throughout the land.
The Five Majestic Generals rode in Qian-patterned carriages,
Zhèng's commentary says: Astronomical patterns were painted on the carriage.
Zhèng's commentary says: Kūn,
represents the mare.
Six,
is the number of earth.
Their attire and ornaments were very grand.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: The bì bird,
is a type of pheasant,
that is, the *jūnyí*;
nowadays commonly called the mountain chicken,
is incorrect.
Bì,
pronunciation 'biē'.
The generals held tallies,
the commanders held banners.
Those going east reached Xuāntù, Lèlàng, Gāogōulí, and Fúyú;
those going south crossed beyond the borders,
passed through Yìzhōu,
and changed the King of Gōutǐng to a Marquis;
Beyond the borders,
means outside the frontier boundaries.
Yìzhōu,
refers to the Yìzhōu Commandery established by Emperor Wǔ.
During Emperor Zhāo's time,
the Gūzēng and Yèyú barbarians rebelled,
the Marquis of Gōutǐng, Wángbō, attacked the rebels and achieved merit,
and was established as King.
Crossed,
is the same as 'yú'.
Border,
pronunciation 'gōng diào fān'.
Gōutǐng,
pronunciation 'qú tǐng'.
Reaching the Western Regions,
they changed all their kings to marquises;
those going north reached the court of the Xiōngnú,
bestowed a seal upon the Chányú,
altering the inscription on the Hàn seal,
removing the word 'Imperial Seal' and saying
'Seal'.
Seal,
is a tally,
a token of trust,
also a means of reliance,
sealing objects to be transferred in reliance.
The Hàn Official Regulations state: For kings of vassal states,
a gold seal with a camel knob,
inscribed 'Imperial Seal'.
For marquises,
a gold seal with a turtle knob,
inscribed 'Seal'.
For the Imperial Counselor,
a gold seal;
for officials of fully two thousand piculs,
a silver seal,
with a turtle knob,
inscribed 'Seal'.
For officials of one thousand piculs down to four hundred piculs, all had bronze seals,
inscribed 'Seal'.
This was the beginning of Wáng Mǎng using the changing of seals and ribbons to disrupt the Four Barbarians.
Remove,
pronunciation 'qiāng lǚ fān'.
Imperial Seal,
pronunciation 'sī shì fān'.
8 In winter,
there was thunder,
and the paulownia trees bloomed.
9 He appointed Tǒngmù Hóu Chén Chóng as the Director of Fate,
responsible for overseeing all officials from the Grand Dukes downward.
He also appointed Shuōfú Hóu Cuī Fā and others as Generals of the Central City and the Four Passes,
responsible for the twelve city gates and the strategic strongholds of Ràoliù, Yángtóu, Yáomiǎn, and Qiānlǒng.
The General of the Central City
was in charge of the twelve city gates.
The Generals of the Four Passes
were respectively in charge of the four locations: Ràoliù, Yángtóu, Yáomiǎn, and Qiānlǒng.
The "Yellow Map of the Three Adjuncts" states: The first gate on the southern end of the eastern side of Cháng'ān City is called Bàchéng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Rénshòu Gate;
the second gate is called Qīngmíng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Xuāndé Gate;
the first gate on the northern end of the eastern side is called Xuānpíng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Chūnwáng Gate;
the first gate on the eastern end of the southern side is called Fù'àng City Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Gēngqīng Gate; the second gate is called Ān Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Guānglǐ Gate;
the third gate is called Biàn Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Xìnpíng Gate;
the first gate on the southern end of the western side is called Zhāngchéng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Wànqiū Gate;
the second gate is called Zhíchéng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Zhèngdào Gate;
the third gate is called Yōng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Zhāngyí Gate;
the first gate on the eastern end of the northern side is called Luò Gate;
the second gate is called Chúchéng Gate,
which Wáng Mǎng called Jiànzǐ City Gate;
the third gate is called Héng Gate.
Fú Qián said: Ràoliù
is a narrow and perilous road.
Shī Gǔ said: It is called Ràoliù
because it is surrounded on all sides by narrow passes,
its path winding and twisting,
with the waters of the streams and valleys circling and flowing around it;
the location is what is now the Qīpán and Shí'èr Rào in the Shāngzhōu region.
Liù
is pronounced as lì jiù fān.
Yángtóu
is the name of a mountain,
located in Zhǎngzǐ County, Shàngdǎng.
Yáo
refers to Yáo Mountain;
Miǎn
refers to Miǎnchí: both are east of Shǎn County.
Qiān
refers to Qiān County in Fúfēng,
which has the natural barriers of Wú Mountain and the Qiān River.
Lǒng
refers to the Lǒng Dǐ.
Qiān and Lǒng are connected.
Miǎn
is pronounced as mí yǎn fān.
Qiān
is pronounced as kǒu jiān fān.
Dǐ
is pronounced as dīng lǐ fān.
10 He also dispatched fifty Grand Masters of Remonstrance to various commanderies and kingdoms to mint coins.
11 In this year,
Zhēndìng and Chángshān experienced heavy hail.
1 Spring,
second month,
a general amnesty was declared across the land.
2 The seventy-two commanders of the Five Majestic Armies returned to report on their duties.
All Hàn feudal lords who held the rank of Duke submitted their seals and ribbons and became commoners,
with none disobeying the order.
Only the former Guǎngyáng King Jiā, for presenting prophetic texts,
(Guǎngyáng King Jiā
was the great-great-grandson of King Dàn of Yān.)
and Zhōngshān King Chéngdū, for submitting writings praising Wáng Mǎng's virtue,
were enfeoffed as Marquises.
Bān Gù's commentary states: In the past, Zhōu enfeoffed eight hundred states,
with over fifty of the same surname,
thereby fostering kinship and honoring the worthy,
which was crucial to its prosperity and decline,
deepening its roots and solidifying its foundation,
making it unshakable.
Thus, in times of prosperity, Zhōu and Shào assisted in governance,
achieving a state where punishments were set aside;
in times of decline, the Five Hegemons supported its weakness,
sharing in its defense;
all under heaven regarded it as the common sovereign.
Rú Chún said: Even in extreme weakness,
they still jointly regarded it as sovereign.
Shī Gǔ said: This means that even though the feudal lords were powerful,
they dared not overthrow Zhōu.
When its numbers reached their limit and virtue was exhausted,
it was reduced to commoner status,
living out its natural lifespan.
This refers to King Nǎn.
Privately styling himself as emperor,
while his sons and brothers were mere commoners,
internally lacking the support of kin as a fundamental root,
externally without even a foot of land for protective wings;
Chén and Wú raised their white clubs,
Yìng Shào said: White clubs,
are large staves.
Mèngzǐ said: They could be made to fashion clubs to strike against Qín and Chǔ,
this is it.
Shī Gǔ said: Tǐng,
is pronounced as tú dǐng fān.
Therefore it is said,
Zhōu exceeded its allotted span,
Qín did not reach its expected term,
such is the nature of state power.
Yìng Shào said: King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
divining thirty generations,
and seven hundred years;
yet it reached thirty-six generations,
eight hundred and sixty-seven years,
this is what is meant by exceeding its allotted span.
Qín, due to the paucity of posthumous titles,
fearing later generations would follow suit,
called himself the First Emperor,
his son the Second Generation,
intending to continue to the ten-thousandth;
yet it ended with his son,
this is what is meant by not reaching its expected term.
3 The Grand Tutor, Liú Xiù, said:
"In the Zhōu dynasty, there was the office of the Quánfǔ,
which collected unsold goods and supplied what was desired.
Shī Gǔ comments: This means that for goods that could not be sold,
the officials would collect them;
for those who lacked something and desired to obtain it,
the officials would supply it to them.
This was to 'prevent the people from wrongdoing.'"
The Xì Cí of the Yìjīng states: "To manage wealth, rectify words,
and prevent the people from wrongdoing
is called righteousness."
"The Zhōulǐ includes provisions for credit and loans.
Shī Gǔ comments: The duties of the Quánfǔ office in the Zhōulǐ state: For all credit transactions,
for sacrifices, repayment must not exceed ten days;
for funerals, repayment must not exceed three months.
For all loans to individuals,
the officials must assess and approve them,
with interest calculated according to the state's tax rate.
This means that for reasons such as sacrifices or funerals,
if one borrows goods from the government on credit,
repayment must be made within ten days or three months.
For those who borrow goods from the government,
the officials in charge
determine the price before lending,
and interest is paid based on the tax rate of their respective states.
For example, if someone borrows ten thousand coins for land in gardens or orchards,
within one period (a month),
the interest is five hundred coins.
Loan,
pronounced as tǔ dài fān.
Dèng Zhǎn said: The Yuèyǔ,
also known as Yuè Yuányǔ,
transmitted by Xiànwáng of Héjiān,
discusses the affairs of the Five Equalities.
Chén Zàn said: The text states:
'The Son of Heaven takes lands from the feudal lords
to establish the Five Equalities,
so that markets have no dual prices,
the four classes of people are always balanced,
the strong cannot oppress the weak,
the rich cannot exploit the poor,
then the state will have surplus,
and kindness will extend to the common people.'"
"Now, opening credit and loans, implementing the Five Equalities, and establishing various regulations
are meant to equalize the masses
and suppress monopolies."
Subsequently, in Cháng'ān, Luòyáng, Hándān, Línzī, Wǎn, and Chéngdū, offices for the Five Equalities Market Supervision and the Coin Treasury were established.
The Market Supervisor would regularly, in the middle month of each season, determine the high, medium, and low prices of goods,
setting the standard market price for each city.
If people were unable to sell grains, cloth, silk, or cotton goods,
the Equalization Office would inspect the actual goods,
and purchase them at their original cost;
if the price of goods exceeded the standard by one coin,
they would be sold to the people at the standard price;
if the price fell below the standard,
the people were allowed to trade among themselves.
Additionally, if people were in dire need and wished to borrow on credit,
the Coin Treasury would lend to them;
with an interest of three coins per hundred coins per month.
Furthermore, following the Zhōuguān, taxes were levied on the people.
For all uncultivated land that was not productive,
a tax equivalent to that of three men was imposed;
for houses in the city walls where no trees or crops were planted, it was considered barren.
Shī Gǔ comments: Planting trees and crops
refers to cultivating fruit trees and vegetables.
For people who wandered idly without occupation,
a tax of one bolt of cloth per man was imposed;
those unable to pay the cloth tax
were provided clothing and food by the government.
Shī Gǔ comments:
Means dispersed,
pronounced rén yǒng fān.
Clothing,
pronounced yú jì fān.
Food,
read as sì.
Mèng Kāng said: Lián
is another name for tin.
Lǐ Qí said: Lead and tin.
Yìng Shào said: Lián
resembles copper.
Shī Gǔ comments: The explanations of Mèng and Lǐ are both incorrect.
Xǔ Shèn said: Liàn
is a type of copper;
alternatively: it is ore.
Liàn,
pronounced chōu yán fān,
also líng yán fān.
Women engaged in sericulture, weaving, spinning, mending, and sewing,
artisans, physicians, shamans, diviners, ritualists, and other skilled practitioners,
merchants, and traders,
all had to report their occupations to the local authorities.
The government would deduct their capital,
calculate their profit as ten parts,
and take one-tenth as tribute;
those who dared not report or reported falsely
would have all their goods confiscated and serve the government for one year.
The Minister of Ceremonies, Lǔ Kuāng, again petitioned for a state monopoly on alcohol sales,
which Wáng Mǎng approved.
He also prohibited the people from possessing crossbows or armor,
with violators exiled to Xīhǎi.
4 Initially,
after Wáng Mǎng issued the Four Regulations to the Xiōngnú,
the Four Regulations are recorded in the 35th year of Emperor Píng's Yuánshǐ era, second year.
they were no longer allowed to collect leather and cloth taxes from the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú sent envoys to demand the taxes,
and the Protector of the Wūhuán,
i.e., the Colonel Protector of the Wūhuán.
Fàn Yè said: After the Wūhuán were defeated by Mòdú,
they often submitted to the Xiōngnú,
paying annual tributes of cattle, horses, sheep, and leather;
if they failed to deliver on time,
their wives and children would be confiscated.
Emperor Wǔ dispatched Huò Qùbìng to attack and defeat the Xiōngnú's eastern territory,
and subsequently relocated the Wūhuán to the frontiers beyond the five commanderies of Shànggǔ, Yúyáng, Yòuběipíng, Liáoxī, and Liáodōng;
later, the Colonel Protector of the Wūhuán was established,
with a rank of two thousand shí,
holding authority to oversee them.
Shī Gǔ comments: Because taxes were previously collected,
they now demanded them.
They bound them,
hanging them upside down.
The chieftains and their brothers grew angry,
and together they killed the Xiōngnú envoys.
Upon hearing this, the Chányú
dispatched the Left Wise King's troops into Wūhuán territory,
attacking them,
killing many people,
and driving away nearly a thousand women, children, and the weak,
relocating them to the eastern territory.
He then declared to the Wūhuán:
"Bring horses, livestock, leather, and cloth to redeem them!"
The Wūhuán brought wealth and livestock to redeem them,
but the Xiōngnú accepted the goods
and kept the people, refusing to release them.
Shī Gǔ comments: They accepted the wealth and livestock but detained the people, refusing to release them.
When the Five Majestic Generals
Wáng Jùn and five others arrived among the Xiōngnú,
(the six men comprised
one general and five colonels). They explained the situation of receiving the Mandate to replace the Hàn,
and proceeded to exchange the old seal of the Chányú.
The inscription on the old seal read
"Seal of the Xiōngnú Chányú";
Wáng Mǎng changed it to
"Seal of the New Xiōngnú Chányú".
Yán Shīgǔ comments: The term "New"
refers to Wáng Mǎng's own dynastic title.
"Gēng" (change)
is pronounced gēng.
They presented the new seal and its ribbon to the Chányú,
with an imperial order commanding him to hand over the old seal and ribbon.
The Chányú bowed twice and received the edict.
An interpreter stepped forward,
intending to untie and take the old seal ribbon.
(The interpreter
was one who conveyed the language of the Central States to the Xiōngnú).
The Left Gūxīhóu Sū, standing to the side, said to the Chányú:
(Sū
is the name of this Gūxīhóu).
"We have not yet seen the inscription on the new seal,
it would be best to not give it yet."
The Chányú stopped
and was unwilling to hand it over.
He requested the envoys to be seated in the yurt,
and the Chányú intended to come forward to offer a toast.
(To present wine as a toast to the envoys).
"The old seal and ribbon should be handed over in due time."
The Chányú said:
"Agreed."
He again raised his arm to give it to the interpreter,
but Sū again said:
"We have not seen the seal's inscription,
do not give it yet."
The Chányú said:
"How could the seal's inscription be changed!"
He then untied the old seal ribbon and respectfully presented it;
the general and colonels received it and attached the new ribbon,
but did not untie it to look at the seal.
They feasted until night,
and then concluded.
The Right Colonel Chén Ráo said to the other generals and colonels:
"Earlier, the Gūxīhóu was suspicious about the seal inscription,
nearly causing the Chányú not to hand it over.
If we now let him see the seal,
and he finds it has been altered,
he will certainly demand the old seal back.
This is not something that can be refused by mere argument.
Having obtained it only to lose it again,
there would be no greater disgrace to our mission!
It would be better to smash the old seal to cut off the root of trouble."
The generals and colonels hesitated,
with none responding.
Ráo,
a man from Yān,
was resolute and fierce.
Yán Shīgǔ comments: Guǒ (resolute)
means decisive.
Hàn (fierce)
means brave.
Hàn
is pronounced hàn;
also pronounced hǎn.
The next day,
the Chányú indeed sent the Right Gǔdūhóu Dāng to inform the generals and colonels, saying:
"The Hàn Chányú seal said 'Imperial Seal'
and not 'Seal',
and also lacked the character 'Hàn';
only the seals of the various kings and below had 'Hàn',
and said 'Seal'.
(Meaning the inscriptions on the seals of the various kings and below contained
the character "Hàn",
and the lowest part of the text said
"Seal"
Adding 'New',
and saying to remove
the character "Imperial Seal" and replace it with
"Seal"
and also adding
"New"
(is the explanation).
Qù (remove)
is pronounced qù.
This means there is no distinction.
Bié (distinction)
is pronounced bié.
The generals and colonels showed him the old seal,
and said to him:
"The New Dynasty, in accordance with Heaven's will, has established new institutions,
therefore the old seal was destroyed by the generals and colonels themselves.
The Chányú should accept the Mandate of Heaven,
and uphold the institutions of the New Dynasty!"
Dāng returned and reported,
and the Chányú, knowing he had no alternative,
and also having received many gifts,
immediately sent his younger brother, the Right Wise King Yú, to present horses and cattle and follow the generals and colonels to offer thanks,
and also submitted a written request for the old seal.
The generals and colonels returned to
the territory where the Left Líwū King Xián resided,
and seeing many Wūhuán people there,
asked Xián about it;

9 Wáng Mǎng again promulgated the currencies of gold, silver, tortoise shell, and cowries,
somewhat increasing and decreasing their face values,
and abolished the large and small coins,
changing to produce two types, the huòbù and huòquán, to circulate concurrently.
The huòbù,
is two and a half inches long,
one inch wide;
the head is eight fen and a fraction long,
eight fen wide;
its round hole,
has a diameter of two and a half fen;
the foot branches are eight fen long,
with a space between them two fen wide;
its inscription on the right says
"huò,"
on the left says
"bù,"
weighs twenty-five zhū,
and is worth twenty-five huòquán.
The huòquán,
has a diameter of one inch,
weighs five zhū;
the inscription on the right says
"huò,"
on the left says
"quán";
its inscription denotes a value of one.
Kǒng Yǐngdá says: According to the Treatise on Food and Money,
what is now called
"⿱竹卞 coin,"

the edges still bear the characters for huòquán.
The large coin,
is what is now the four-wén coin,
with inscriptions on all four sides.
The shape of the huòbù
is difficult to recognize nowadays;
people still sometimes find them when plowing fields,
in ancient times one piece was equivalent to twenty-five coins.
I note: What was anciently called quánbù,
its storage form was called quán (spring),
its circulation form was called bù (cloth),
taking its name from water springs,
whose flow reaches everywhere;
reaching everywhere is the meaning of bù (to spread).
Wáng Mǎng considered them as two types of currency,
which is not the ancient meaning.
Textual analysis notes: The Treatise on Food and Money
records the change to making huòbù in the first year of Tiānfèng.
Wáng Mǎng's biography records it in the first year of Dìhuáng,
probably because it was the year the large coins were exhausted;
by the first year of Dìhuáng they had completely ceased circulation,
not that they began making huòbù that year.
Fearing that the people would hoard them and not stop using them if abolished,
he ordered the people to temporarily use only the large coins;
after six full years,
they were not allowed to hoard large coins anymore.
Each time the currency was changed,
the people's livelihoods were ruined and they fell heavily into punishment.

Wáng Mǎng appointed Qīn as General Who Pacifies the Outer Regions,

Lǐ Chóng gathered the remaining soldiers,

When Wáng Mǎng fell,
Chóng perished,
and the Western Regions were thus cut off.
1. Summer,
sixth month,
Wáng Mǎng again conferred fiefs of sacred soil upon the various feudal kings
at the Míngtáng;
personally setting up a leveled stone tablet,
he displayed the four-colored soil and jīngmáo grass. (Yán Shīgǔ said: In the Shàngshū's "Yǔ Gòng" chapter,

The Great Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals states: The Son of Heaven's state has the Great Shè altar.
The east is green,
the south is red,
the west is white,
the north is black,
the top is yellow.
Therefore, one to be enfeoffed in the east takes green soil,
one in the south takes red soil,
one in the west takes white soil,
one in the north takes black soil.
Each takes the soil of their direction,
wraps it with white máo grass,

This is how one first receives enfeoffment from the Son of Heaven.
This is called "sovereign soil";
sovereign soil means
establishing a shè altar to honor it.
Jīng
is pronounced jīng.)
Wáng Mǎng was fond of empty words,
admired ancient methods,
and generously bestowed titles and ranks upon people;
but his nature was actually stingy,
so he used the pretext that the geographical divisions were not yet settled,
thus first bestowing only the máo and soil,
to placate those who were pleased with their enfeoffments.
2. Autumn,
eighth month,
Wáng Mǎng personally went to the southern suburbs,

It was made of five-mineral bronze. (Lǐ Qí said: Made from five-colored medicinal minerals and copper.

when he entered, it was by the ruler's side.
3 Wang Mǎng established the offices of Xìhé and Mìngshì,

Salt,
the first;
wine,
the second;
iron,
famous mountains and great marshes,
the fourth;
the Five Equities and credit loans,
the fifth;
iron currency and copper smelting,
the sixth.
All were managed by wealthy merchants,
who traveled by official carriages seeking profit,
crisscrossing the empire;
thus colluding with commanderies and counties in corruption,
they inflated empty ledgers,
causing the treasury stores to be unreal,
and the common people to suffer increasingly.
That year,
Wang Mǎng again issued an edict reaffirming the Six Controls,
establishing regulations and prohibitions for each control,
with the death penalty for violators.
Corrupt people and cunning officials encroached together,
and the masses each lived in insecurity,
and moreover, a general levy was imposed on all those from the Dukes and below who owned slaves,
at a rate of one person
paying three thousand six hundred,
causing the empire to become even more distressed.
The Nàyán Féng Cháng remonstrated about the Six Controls,
and Wang Mǎng became greatly enraged,
dismissing Cháng from office.
Laws and decrees were numerous and harsh,
the people, with a shake of the hand, would violate a prohibition,
unable to farm or tend mulberries,
corvée labor was heavy and intense,
and drought, locusts followed one another,
lawsuits remained unresolved.
Officials used harshness and brutality to establish authority,
exploiting Wang Mǎng's prohibitions,
to encroach upon and exploit the common people,
the wealthy could not
distinguish themselves,
the poor had no means to survive,
so together they rose up to become bandits,
relying on the shelter of mountains and marshes,
officials could not capture them but instead covered up for them,
and the situation spread and grew daily.
Línhuái's Guātián Yí

given name Yí.

Kuài,
pronounced gōng wài fān.

Wang Mǎng sent envoys to pardon the bandits on the spot,

to go to the places where they gathered as bandits and pardon them.
"The bandits dispersed but then reunited.

they all said: 'We are distressed by the numerous and harsh laws and prohibitions,
unable to raise a hand to work with effort,

The people, impoverished,

Wang Mǎng became greatly enraged,

Those who followed his intent saying
"the people are arrogant and cunning and should be executed"

1 Spring,
first month,
the new moon,

when he had an audience,

Jiàn,

"The people of Jīng and Yáng,

all engaged in corrupt profiteering,

Wang Mǎng then investigated all military officials and border officials of rank Dàfū and above who had engaged in corrupt profiteering and increased their wealth since the second year of Shǐ Jiànguó when the Hu barbarians troubled Xià,

To aid the urgent expenses of the border.

Yáng Xióng passed away.
Initially,

Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Xián became the Three Excellencies,
wielding power surpassing the sovereign,

When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
Yáng Xióng, due to his seniority and long service,
was transferred to the position of Grand Master.
Indifferent to power and profit,
Yán Shīgǔ notes: Tián (恬)
means contentment.
He wished to achieve fame in later generations through literary works,
so he composed the Tàixuán to synthesize the ways of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity;
Huán Tán said: Yáng Xióng wrote the Xuánshū,
believing that: Xuán (玄)
is Heaven,
is the Way,
meaning when sages and worthies established laws and undertook affairs,
they all drew upon the Way of Heaven as the fundamental principle,
and accordingly affiliated the myriad categories,
such as royal governance, human affairs, and legal institutions.
Thus, Fúxī called it the Yì,
Lǎozǐ called it the Dào,
Confucius called it the Yuán,
and Yáng Xióng called it the Xuán.
The Xuánjīng consists of three chapters,
recording the ways of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity,
establishing three systems,
with upper, middle, and lower,
like the three grades presented in the Yǔgòng,
three times three equals nine,
thus using nine times nine equals eighty-one,
hence forming eighty-one hexagrams.
Using four as the base number,
numbers ranging from one to four,
repeatedly overlapping and changing,
ultimately covering eighty-one comprehensively,
neither adding nor subtracting,
using thirty-five milfoil stalks for divination.
The Xuánjīng contains over five thousand words,
with twelve chapters of commentary.
Yán Shīgǔ notes: Chuǎn (舛)
means contradictory.
They create strange, far-fetched, analytical, and deceptive arguments to disrupt worldly affairs,

is pronounced zǐ.

is pronounced yú,
náo (撓)
is pronounced náo.
Ultimately, they destroy the great Way and delude the masses,
causing them to drown in what they hear without realizing its fallacy,
so whenever people questioned Yáng Xióng,

He focused his mind inwardly,
not seeking external recognition,

Yán Shīgǔ notes: Without equal.

In the past, Lǎo Dān composed two chapters on emptiness and nothingness,

which were not based on ritual learning,

(Gēngchén, 20)

There were nearly ten groups daily,

pronounced as xī zé fān.
Inquiry,
pronounced as qù jí fān.)
providing supplies and funds,
to avoid execution,
(Yán Shīgǔ said: They all feared the punishment of decapitation.
Provide,
read as supply.
Execution,
pronounced as dīng guǎn fān,
also pronounced as dīng luàn fān.)
The generals, moreover, could not personally lead their officers and soldiers,
and when they fought, they were defeated by the bandits,
the morale of the officials gradually deteriorated,
merely wasting the people's resources.
Previously, fortunately, an amnesty decree was issued,
and the bandits intended to disperse,
but some were instead intercepted and attacked,
fearing to enter the mountains and valleys,
they spread the word among themselves;
therefore, the bandits who had surrendered in the commanderies and counties all became alarmed again,
fearing they would be deceived and exterminated,
and because famine made them easily agitated,
within ten days, their numbers increased by over a hundred thousand,
this is the reason why the bandits became so numerous.
Now, east of Luòyáng,
a shí of rice costs two thousand coins.
I have privately seen the imperial edict intending to dispatch the Grand Tutor and the General of Renewal;
these two are important ministers with claws and teeth,
they bring many followers and large entourages,
depleting supplies along the way,
meaning the army provisions are insufficient.)
We should urgently select Governors and Magistrates and below,
clarify rewards and punishments,
gather those who have left their hometowns;
for small states without city walls,
(Small states,
refers to the various marquisates.)
store up grain supplies,
and unite efforts to firmly defend.
When the bandits come to attack the cities,
they will not be able to capture them;
where they pass, there will be no food,
and they will be unable to gather in force;
in this way,
if we summon them, they will surely surrender,
if we attack them, they will be destroyed.
Now, merely sending out many more generals,
only burdens the commanderies and counties,
and is even worse than the bandits.
We should recall all the envoys traveling by relay carriage
to allow the commanderies and counties to rest;
entrust me, Kuàng, with the two provinces, and the bandits will certainly be pacified."
Wáng Mǎng feared and disliked Tián Kuàng,
(He feared and disliked his ability.
Dislike,
pronounced as wū lù fān.)
He sent an envoy to bestow an imperial edict upon Tián Kuàng.
When the envoy arrived,
he met Tián Kuàng,
and then ordered him to hand over command of his troops,
sending Tián Kuàng west to Cháng'ān,
where he was appointed as Grand Master of the Division of the Capital.
After Tián Kuàng left,
the Qí region subsequently fell.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Nine Temples were completed,
and the spirit tablets were installed.
(Wooden spirit tablets.)
The imperial carriage was drawn by six horses,
adorned with dragon-patterned trappings made of five-colored hair,
with green horns,
three chǐ long.
(Yán Shīgǔ said: These were placed on the horses.
Green,
pronounced as zhì lüè fān.
Long,
pronounced as zhí liàng fān.)
The "Notes on Ancient and Modern Matters" states: The Huágài,
was created by the Yellow Emperor.
When the Yellow Emperor fought Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,
there were often clouds and mist,
with golden branches and jade leaves,
and thus he created the Huágài.
Layers,
pronounced as zhí lóng fān.)
It was carried on a four-wheeled cart;
the pullers all shouted
"Ascend to immortality!"
When Wáng Mǎng went out,
he ordered it to go in front.
The officials secretly said:
"This resembles a funeral carriage,
not an immortal object."
2 In the second month,
Fán Chóng and others killed Jǐng Shàng.
(Jǐng Shàng,
was the one dispatched last year.)
3 East of the Hánguān Pass, people resorted to cannibalism.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
the Grand Tutor Wáng Kuāng and the General of Renewal Lián Dān were sent east to suppress the numerous bandits.
Initially,
after Fán Chóng and others' forces had gradually grown strong,
they made a pact among themselves:
"Those who kill shall die,
those who injure shall compensate for the wound."
Among them, the most honored title was Sānlǎo,
next was Cóngshì,
next was Zúshǐ.
(Yán Shīgǔ said: This means they did not adopt grand titles.
I say that Sānlǎo, Cóngshì, and Zúshǐ were all commandery and county officials.
Fán Chóng and others arose from among the common people,
and these were the only titles they knew.
Later, as their faction grew daily stronger,
and their momentum daily increased,
they attacked Cháng'ān,
and set up Péngzǐ as emperor,
which was not their initial intention of not adopting grand titles.)
Fearing that their followers would be confused with Wáng Mǎng's troops,
they all dyed their eyebrows red to recognize each other,
hence they were called the Red Eyebrows.
Wáng Kuāng and Lián Dān jointly led over a hundred thousand elite soldiers,
but wherever they went, they acted wantonly.
In the eastern regions, a saying arose:
"Better to encounter the Red Eyebrows,
than to encounter the Grand Tutor!
The Grand Tutor is still tolerable,
but the General of Renewal will kill me!"
This ultimately matched Tián Kuàng's words.
5 Wáng Mǎng also sent many Grand Masters and Court Gentlemen to teach the people to boil grass and trees to make cheese,
(Fú Qián said: Boiling tree fruits.
Some say,
like the methods for making medicinal pastes today.
Rú Chún said: Making things like apricot cheese.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Rú Chún's explanation is correct.)
which further added to the burdens and expenses.
6 The Green Forest bandits encountered a pestilence,
with nearly half of them dying,
so they dispersed and withdrew.
Wáng Cháng and Chéng Dān went west into Nánjùn,
calling themselves
the "Xiàjiāng Troops";
Wáng Fèng, Wáng Kuāng, Mǎ Wǔ, and their subordinate leaders Zhū Wěi, Zhāng Áng, etc., went north into Nányáng,
calling themselves
the "Xīnshì Troops";
The Treatise on Commanderies and Principalities states,
Xīnshì County belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Xīnshì County's seat was at Dù City,
belonging to Jìnglíng Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Hàn's Xīnshì County
was northeast of Fùshuǐ County in Yǐng Prefecture.
Wáng Mǎng dispatched the Grand General of the Director of Fate, Kǒng Rén, to oversee Yùzhōu,
and the Grand General of the Chamberlain for Ceremonials, Yán Yóu, and the Grand General of the Chamberlain for the Imperial Clan, Chén Mào, to attack Jīngzhōu.
Wáng Mǎng bestowed the title of Grand General upon the Directors of the Nine Ministers and the Six Ministers.
They traveled by relay carriage to their posts to recruit soldiers.
Yóu said to Mào:
"To send generals without giving them the military tally,
requiring them to request permission before acting,
is like tying up a Hán Lǔ hound and demanding it catch prey."
Yán Shīgǔ said: Xiè means
to tie up.
Hán Lǔ
was the name of a famous dog from the ancient state of Hán.
A black-colored dog was called Lǔ.
Xiè
is pronounced sī liè fān.
7 Locusts came from the east,
flying so thickly they obscured the sky.
8 Tens of thousands of refugees entered the passes,
so [the court] established relief officials to provide them with grain rations.
Envoys were appointed to supervise,
but they colluded with petty officials to steal the provisions.
Yán Shīgǔ said: "To steal the provisions" means
to steal the goods that were supplied.
Previously,
Wáng Mǎng had the Palace Attendant Wáng Yè oversee market purchases in Cháng'ān,
buying goods cheaply from the people;
the people were greatly troubled by this.
Yè was credited with reducing expenses,
and was awarded the noble rank of Fùchéng.
Wáng Mǎng heard there was famine in the city,
and asked Yè about it.
Yè said:
"They are all refugees."
He then bought some millet rice and meat broth being sold in the market,
brought them in to show Wáng Mǎng, saying:
"The residents' food is all like this."
Wáng Mǎng believed him.
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Xīnshì bandit Wáng Kuāng and others attacked Suí;
Lǐ Xián said: Suí County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery;
it is present-day Suízhōu County.
They called themselves
the "Pínglín Troops",
and responded to them.
The Surname Genealogy states: The surname Liào
descends from Bó Liào, son of King Wén of Zhōu.
The Comprehensive Meaning of Customs states: In ancient times there was Liào Shū'ān;
the Zuǒzhuàn writes it as
"Liào",
probably his descendant.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Zhāng River flows south past the old city of Pínglín County in Suí Commandery,
commonly called Jiāngbēi City,
bordering Xīnshì.
Lǐ Xián said: Liào
is pronounced lì diào fān.
Pínglín
is a place name,
located northeast of present-day Suí County in Suízhōu.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
10 Wáng Mǎng issued an edict reproaching Lián Dān, saying:
"The granaries are exhausted,
the treasuries are empty,
it is time for anger,
it is time for battle!
General, you bear the state's heavy responsibility.
If you do not sacrifice your body on the field,
you will have no way to repay this favor and fulfill your duty!"
Dān was alarmed and fearful.
That night,
he summoned his subordinate Féng Yǎn,
and showed him the letter.
Yǎn then advised Dān, saying:
"Zhāng Liáng, whose family served five generations of Hán,
struck the First Emperor of Qín at Bólàng.
The event is recorded in the seventh scroll, the twenty-ninth year of the First Emperor of Qín.
Shuì
is pronounced shuì ruì fān.
Xiàng
is pronounced xī xiàng fān.
He became a trusted minister of Hàn;
Lǐ Xián said: Lián Bāo,
a man of Xiāngwǔ,
served as General of the Rear during Emperor Xuān's reign,
and was Dān's ancestor.
Talented men did not submit.
Now, with the realm in chaos and collapse,
the people cherish the virtue of Hàn,
even more than the people of Zhōu
longed for Duke Shào;
Duke Shào's teachings
were illustrious in the southern states.
The people of Zhōu thought of him,
and composed the ode "Gāntáng".
Shào
is pronounced shào.
Heaven is sure to comply.
Lǐ Xián said: The Odes, Minor Court Hymns states: Though I have no virtue for you,
I sing and dance.
This speaks of the virtue of the Hàn house,
for which people sing and dance.
The Book of Documents says: What the people desire,
Heaven is sure to comply with.
It would be best to garrison and hold a large commandery,
pacify and comfort the officials and soldiers,
hone their integrity,
recruit heroic and outstanding men,
seek loyal and wise counsel,
promote the state's interests,
and eliminate the harm to the myriad people.
Then fortune and emolument will flow on endlessly,
and your achievements will be recorded for eternity;
How can this compare to having your army destroyed on the central plains,
your body fattening the wild grasses,
your merit ruined and name lost,
bringing shame upon your ancestors!"
Dān did not listen.
Yǎn
was the great-grandson of Left General Féng Fèngshì.
In winter,
Suǒlú Huī and others in Wúyán raised troops,
turning their city over to join the bandits.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Suǒlú
is a surname.
Huī
is the given name.
The Annals of Lü Buwei: Qín Gǔlí had a disciple named Suǒlú Cān.
"Turning the city" means
seizing the city to rebel.
Another interpretation says: Fǎn
is pronounced fān,
and in current speech, rebels are still called "fān chéng".
Suǒ
is pronounced xiān gè fān.
I believe the latter interpretation is correct.
Lǐ Xián said: Wúyán County
belonged to Dōngpíng Commandery;
its old city was east of present-day Xūchāng County in Yùn Prefecture.
Over ten thousand heads were taken.
Wáng Mǎng sent a Palace Attendant General bearing the imperial seal and letter to reward Dān and Kuāng,
promoting them to the rank of Duke;
and enfeoffing over ten officials and soldiers who had merit.
A separate division of the Red Eyebrows, Dǒng Xiàn and others with tens of thousands of troops, were in Liáng Commandery.
Wáng Kuāng wanted to advance and attack them;
Lián Dān believed that having just captured a city, the troops were weary,
and they should rest the soldiers and build up their might.
Kuāng did not listen,
leading his troops forward alone,
and Dān followed him.
They joined battle at Chéngchāng.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Chéngchāng
is a place name.
I surmise, based on the Book of Later Hàn,
it was also within the boundaries of Wúyán County.
Kuāng fled;
Dān had an officer take his seal, ribbon, and tally and deliver them to Kuāng,
saying:
"A boy may flee,
but I cannot!"
He then halted,
and died fighting.
Commandants Rǔ Yún, Wáng Lóng, and over twenty others fought separately.
Rǔ
is a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn mentions the Jìn senior official Nǚ Qí.
Lù Démíng said: Nǚ
is pronounced rǔ.
They all said:
"Duke Lián is already dead,
for whom should we live!"
They galloped towards the enemy,
and all died fighting.
The Grand Master of State Āi Zhāng personally requested to pacify the area east of the mountains.
Wáng Mǎng sent Zhāng racing east to join forces with Grand Tutor Kuāng.
He also sent Grand General Yáng Jùn to guard the Áocāng Granary;
Minister over the Masses Wáng Xún led over a hundred thousand troops to garrison Luòyáng,
guarding the Southern Palace;
Grand Minister of War Dǒng Zhōng trained soldiers and practiced archery at the Central Army's Northern Barracks;
It probably should read
"Northern Army's Central Barracks."
11. Initially,
Chángshā Dìng Wáng Liú Fā begot Chōnglíng Jié Hóu Liú Mǎi,
Mǎi begot Dài Hóu Liú Xióngqú,
Xióngqú begot Kǎo Hóu Liú Rén.
Rén, because the southern regions were low and damp,
had his fief transferred to the Báishuǐ Township in Nányáng Commandery,
and moved there with his clan to settle.
(Lǐ) Xián said: Chōnglíng,
was a township name,
originally belonging to Língdào County in Línglíng Commandery,
located north of Tángxīng County in present-day Yǒngzhōu;
during Emperor Yuán's time,
it was moved to Nányáng,
but still called Chōnglíng,
its old city is east of Zǎoyáng County in present-day Suízhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Zǎoyáng,
was the Later Hàn's Càiyáng County;
the Hàn dynasty Chōnglíng old city is east of the present county.
His son Liú Chǎng succeeded to the title;
encountering Wáng Mǎng's usurpation of the throne,
the fiefdom was abolished.
Jié Hóu's youngest son Liú Wài served as Governor of Yùlín Commandery,
(Lǐ) Xián said: Yùlín Commandery,
is present-day Chēnzhōu County.
I note that in the Táng dynasty, Chēnzhōu had no Yùlín County,
but the Táng dynasty's Guì, Liǔ, Yù, Yōng, Xiàng, Yān, Xún, Nán, Yǐn, Lè, Róng, Bīn, and other prefectures,
were all territory of the Hàn dynasty Yùlín Commandery.
(Lǐ) Xián said: Jùlù Commandery,
is present-day Xíngzhōu County.
I note that the Táng dynasty Xíngzhōu originally had Jùlù County,
but the Táng dynasty Xíng and Zhào prefectures were both territory of the Hàn dynasty Jùlù Commandery.
(Lǐ) Xián said: Nándùn County,
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery;
its old city is west of present-day Xiàngchéng County in Chénzhōu.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Nándùn County in Chénzhōu,
was the ancient state of Dùnzǐ;
pressured by Chén,
it moved south,
hence called Nándùn.
Húyáng County,
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Húyáng County,
was the territory of the ancient state of Liǎo.
(Liú) Zhòng,
(Liú) Xiù,
the brothers were orphaned early,
and were raised by their uncle Liú Liáng.
Liú Yǎn was by nature resolute and strong-willed,
passionate and of great integrity,
ever since Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn,
he was constantly indignant,
harboring plans to restore the dynasty,
he did not attend to family livelihood or business,
exhausting his resources and bankrupting himself,
to associate with the heroic talents of the realm.
Liú Xiù had a high nose bridge and a sun-like prominence on his forehead,
(Lǐ) Xián said: Lóng,
means high.
Xǔ Fù said: The tip of the nose is the zhǔn.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Shàngshū Zhōnghóu states: Rì jiǎo,
refers to a bone protrusion in the center of the forehead shaped like the sun.
(Lǐ) Xián said: Planting is called jià,
harvesting is called sè.
He was compared to Gāozǔ's elder brother Zhòng.
(Lǐ) Xián said: Zhòng,
was Héyáng Hóu Liú Xǐ,
who was capable of managing property.
Gāozǔ, toasting the Grand Emperor (his father), said: "Initially, you, Great Father, often said that I could not manage property,
not as capable as Zhòng;
now, the scale of my achievements,
who has more compared to Zhòng?"
Liú Xiù once traveled with Liú Chén to visit the Ráng man Cài Shàogōng,
Shàogōng,
Shàogōng had studied charts and prophecies quite a bit,
and said
"Liú Xiù shall become the Son of Heaven";
someone said:
"Is it the State Preceptor Gōng Liú Xiù?"
Liú Xiù jokingly said:
"How do you know it's not me!"
Everyone present laughed heartily.
Only Chén was secretly pleased in his heart.
The Wǎn man Lǐ Shǒu,
was fond of astrology, calendars, and prophetic texts,
and served as Zōngqīngshī for Wáng Mǎng,
(Lǐ) Xián said: In the fifth year of Emperor Píng,
Wáng Mǎng acted as regent,
and established Zōngshī in commanderies and kingdoms to oversee the imperial clan.
Probably respected at the time,
hence called Zōngqīngshī.
I note that Wáng Mǎng established Zōngshī,
to oversee the Hàn imperial clan.
This Zōngqīngshī,
was established after Wáng Mǎng's usurpation.
"The Liú clan shall rise again,
with the Lǐ clan as assistants."
When the Xīnshì and Pínglín troops arose,
Nányáng became turbulent,
(Lǐ) Tōng's younger cousin Lǐ Yì said to Tōng:
"Now the four quarters are in turmoil and disorder,
the Hàn should be restored.
Among the imperial clan in Nányáng,
only the brothers Liú Bóshēng are broadly benevolent and accommodating to the masses,
we can plan great matters with them."
Yǎn,
styled Bóshēng.
"That is my thought too!"
It happened that Liú Xiù was selling grain in Wǎn,
Tōng sent Yì to go welcome Xiù,
and meet with him,
then fully explained the matter of the prophetic text,
formed an alliance with him,
and settled plans.
Tōng wanted to, on the day of the Autumn Commencement when the local troops and cavalry were assembled for inspection,
seize the Qiánduì Dàfū Zhēn Fù and his subordinate commander Liángqiū Cì,
(Wáng Mǎng changed Nányáng to Qiánduì,
establishing the Dàfū position equivalent to Governor,
and the Shǔzhèng position equivalent to Commandant.)
Yán Shīgǔ said: Duì,
is pronounced suì.
Zhēn,
is pronounced zhī rén fān.
He sent Yì and Xiù back to Chōnglíng to raise troops in response.
Thereupon, Yǎn summoned various local leaders to discuss plans, saying:
"Wáng Mǎng is tyrannical and cruel,
the common people are divided and collapsing;
now drought has persisted for years,
armed conflicts arise everywhere,
this is also Heaven's time to destroy him,
to restore Gāozǔ's enterprise,
and settle the age for ten thousand generations!"
(Meaning to settle the realm and pass it on for ten thousand generations,
this is the time for it.)
Thereupon, he separately dispatched close associates to raise troops in various counties,
Yǎn himself mobilized the young men of Chōnglíng.
The youths from various families were fearful,
all fled and hid,
saying:
"Bóshēng is getting me killed!"
But when they saw Xiù in crimson clothes and a great cap,
(Dǒng Bā's Yúfúzhì states: The great cap,
is worn by military officers.
The Dōngguān Jì states: The Emperor at the time wore crimson clothes and a great cap, the attire of a general.)
"Even a cautious and honest man like him is also doing this!"
Then they gradually calmed themselves.
In total, they gathered seven or eight thousand young men,
organized the followers,
and proclaimed themselves
"The Pillar of Heaven Chief Command."
(Lǐ) Xián said: Zhùtiān,
means like a pillar of heaven.
Dūbù means,
to command all the troops.
Before Lǐ Tōng could act,
the affair was discovered,
he fled;
his father Shǒu and family members, sixty-four people in total, were executed for involvement.
Yǎn sent a clansman, Jiā, to persuade and recruit the Xīnshì and Pínglín troops,
and together with their commanders Wáng Fèng and Chén Mù, attacked Chángjù to the west;
advancing, they slaughtered the Tángzǐxiāng township,
(Lǐ) Xián said: Tú means to kill many.
Tángzǐxiāng had Tángzǐ Mountain,
located southwest of present-day Húyáng County in Tángzhōu.
In the army, the distribution of plundered goods was unequal,
the masses were resentful and angry,
wanting to turn and attack the various Liú;
Liú Xiù collected the goods obtained by his clansmen,
and gave them all to the masses,
whereupon the masses were pleased.
Advancing, they captured Jíyáng,
(Lǐ) Xián said: Zǎoyáng,
is a county name,
belonging to Nányáng Commandery,
located on the north bank of the Jí River,
the ancient state of Xiè;
its old city is northwest of present-day Húyáng County in Tángzhōu.
Jí,
is pronounced jǐ lì fān.
12. Yán Yóu and Chén Mào defeated the Xiàjiāng troops;
Chéng Dān, Wáng Cháng, Zhāng Áng, and others gathered scattered soldiers and entered Lóuxī,
raiding between Zhōng and Lóng,
and their forces revived;
leading their army, they fought the Governor of Jīngzhōu at Shàngtáng,
(Lǐ) Xián said: Shàngtáng,
was a township name,
its old city is northeast of present-day Zǎoyáng County in Suízhōu.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: Shàngtáng was originally the Shàngtáng Township of Càiyáng County,
the state of Táng during the Spring and Autumn period.
13. In the eleventh month,
a comet appeared in the Zhāng constellation.
(Lǐ) Xián said: Zhāng,
is a southern constellation.
The Xù Hànzhì states: Zhāng corresponds to the territory of Zhōu.
The Jìnshū Tiānwénzhì states: The Zhāng constellation has six stars,
located north of the Celestial Temple.
Bó,
is pronounced pú nèi fān.
14 Liú Yǎn intended to attack Wǎn,
arriving at Xiǎocháng'ān Jù,
Xián said: According to the Xù Hàn Shū: Yùyáng County had a Xiǎocháng'ān Jù,
its old city is south of present-day Dèngzhōu Nányáng County.
Dù Yòu said: Nányáng,
was the Hàn Wǎn County;
thirty-seven lǐ south of the county was Xiǎocháng'ān.
At that time, the sky was thick with fog,
and the Hàn army suffered a great defeat.
Liú Xiù fled alone on horseback,
encountered his younger sister Bó Jī,
and they rode together in flight;
proceeding ahead,
he again saw his elder sister Yuán,
and urged her to mount the horse,
but Yuán waved her hand and said:
"Go on,
you cannot save me,
do not let us both perish!"
Just then, the pursuing troops arrived,
and Yuán along with three daughters all died,
Yǎn's younger brother Zhòng and dozens of clan followers also died.
Yǎn again gathered his troops,
and retreated to hold Jíyáng.
Fù and Cì, riding on their victory, left their heavy baggage at Lán Xiāng,
Xián said: Bǐyáng County had a Lán Xiāng.
Heavy,
pronounced zhí yòng fān.
Xián said: According to Lì Dàoyuán's Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: The two lakes of the Zhū River flow and converge,
joining to form the Huáng River;
further south it passes by the Huángchún Jù of Jíyáng County,
and is also called the Huángchún River.
It is located in present-day Tángzhōu Húyáng County.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: The Bǐ River originates from the Dàhú Mountain northeast of Bǐyáng County,
flows south and meets the Lǐ River,
called the Pài River;
in the past, Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ defeated Zhēn Fù and Liángqiū Cì at,
the west of the Bǐ River,
and beheaded them at this river.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Hàn Wǔyáng is north of present-day Tángzhōu Bìyáng County;
there is the Bì River,
south of the county,
where Guāngwǔ defeated Fù and Cì.
They destroyed the rear bridge,
showing no intention to return.
Xīnshì and Pínglín, seeing the Hàn troops repeatedly defeated,
and with Fù and Cì's army arriving in great force,
each wanted to disband and leave,
which greatly troubled Yǎn.
Just then, over five thousand Xiàjiāng troops arrived at Yíqiū,
Xián said: Yíqiū,
is a settlement name,
located in Bǐyáng County.

and killed Wáng Láng's senior general Zhào Hóng.
Kòu Xún returned,
and then led troops south together with Jǐng Dān, the Chief Clerk of Shànggǔ, and Gěng Yǎn.
They joined forces with the Yúyáng army,
and along the way attacked and beheaded Wáng Láng's generals, ministers of the Nine Courts, colonels, and others below them.
In total, they beheaded thirty thousand men,
and pacified twenty-two counties in the commanderies of Zhuōjùn, Zhōngshān, Jùlù, Qīnghé, and Héjiān.
Advancing ahead to Guǎng'ē,
they heard there were many chariots and cavalry in the city.
Jǐng Dān and others marshaled their troops and asked:
"Whose troops are these?"
The reply was:
"It is Grand Marshal Lord Liú."
The generals were delighted,
and immediately advanced to the city walls.
Initially, rumors at the city walls said the troops from the two commanderies had come for Hándān,
and everyone was afraid.
Liú Xiù personally ascended the western city tower, marshaled his troops, and questioned them;
Gěng Yǎn bowed at the foot of the city wall,
and was immediately summoned inside,
where he fully explained the circumstances of raising troops.
Liú Xiù then summoned Jǐng Dān and the others inside,
and said with a laugh:
"The generals of Hándān repeatedly said I was raising troops from Yúyáng and Shànggǔ,
and I casually responded, 'I am raising them too.'
(Xián's note: Wáng Láng's generals repeatedly said they wanted to raise troops from the two commanderies to resist Guāngwǔ,
and Guāngwǔ also casually responded in kind,
much like two armies teasing each other nowadays.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Liáo,
is a word meaning 'tentatively' or 'roughly.')
(Textual analysis note: Yuán Jì records
'the good governor came for me,'
but here we follow Jǐng Dān's biography.
Rhyme explanation: Liáng,
means 'head,'
or 'trustworthy.')
He then appointed Jǐng Dān, Kòu Xún, Gěng Yǎn, Gài Yán, Wú Hàn, and Wáng Liáng all as Lieutenant Generals,
sending them back to lead their own troops,
and promoted Gěng Kuàng and Péng Chǒng to Grand Generals;
he enfeoffed Kuàng, Chǒng, Dān, and Yán all as Marquises.
Wú Hàn's character
was simple and honest, lacking refinement,
and in haste he could not express himself with words.
However, he was steady and profound,
possessing wisdom and strategy.
Dèng Yǔ repeatedly recommended him to Liú Xiù,

Gēngshǐ sent the Minister over the Masses Xiè Gōng to lead six generals to attack Wáng Láng,
but they could not defeat him;

he joined forces with them,
and they besieged Jùlù to the east.
After over a month, they still had not taken it.
Wáng Láng sent a general to attack Xìndū,
and the powerful clan Mǎ Chǒng and others opened the gates to let them in.
Gēngshǐ sent troops to attack and capture Xìndū,
and Liú Xiù sent Lǐ Zhōng back,

Wáng Láng sent his generals Ní Hóng and Liú Fèng to lead tens of thousands of men to relieve Jùlù,
and Liú Xiù engaged them in battle at Nánluán,

Gěng Chún said to Liú Xiù:

Liú Xiù attacked urgently,

on the day Jiǎchén,

Wáng Láng fled at night,

Liú Xiù collected Wáng Láng's documents,
and found several thousand memorials from officials and commoners communicating with Wáng Láng and slandering him;
(Guān,

He gathered the generals and burned them,

The 'Great Tree General,'

He was humble and retiring, not boasting of his achievements.

Whenever they stopped to rest,

The Protector of the Army, Zhū Yòu of Wǎn,

Wéi Shùn was appointed Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ,

Prince Xiāo was residing in the Hándān Palace.
During the day, he was lying down in the Wēnmíng Hall.

Its former foundation is located within present-day Hándān County of Míng Prefecture.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Wēnmíng Hall lies west of the Cóng Terrace.
Gěng Yǎn entered beneath the bed and requested a private audience.
Taking the opportunity, he advised:
"The number of officers and soldiers who have died or been wounded is great.
I request to return to Shànggǔ to increase our troops."
Prince Xiāo said:
"Wáng Láng has already been defeated,
and Héběi is largely pacified.
What need is there to use more troops?"
Gěng Yǎn replied:
"Although Wáng Láng has been defeated,
the warfare under heaven is only just beginning.
Now envoys are coming from the west,
wishing to disband the armies.
This must not be heeded.
Groups like the Tóngmǎ and Chìméi, numbering several tens of bands,
each band comprising several hundred thousand to a million men,
are invincible wherever they go.
Shènggōng is incapable of handling them,
and his defeat is surely not far off."
Prince Xiāo sat up and said:
"You have spoken improperly.
I shall behead you!"
Gěng Yǎn said:
"Your Highness has treated Yǎn with the compassionate affection of a father towards a son,
therefore I dare to bare my loyal heart."
Prince Xiāo said:
"I was jesting with you.
Why do you say these things?"
Gěng Yǎn replied:
"The common people suffered bitterly under Wáng Mǎng,
and again longed for the Liú clan.
Hearing that the Hàn armies had risen,
none were not overjoyed,
as if escaping a tiger's maw to return to a loving mother.
Now Gēngshǐ is the Son of Heaven,
yet his various generals seize command east of the mountains,
and his noble relatives act recklessly within the capital.
They plunder and indulge themselves freely,
causing the masses to beat their breasts in anguish,
and even to long for the days of Wáng Mǎng's court.
From this, I know he is certain to fall.
Your merit and fame are already illustrious.
Waging campaigns with righteousness,
you could pacify all under heaven simply by issuing proclamations.
The empire is of the utmost importance.
You should take it for yourself,
and not let another surname obtain it!"
Prince Xiāo then excused himself on the grounds that Héběi was not yet pacified,

Fù Xián said: The Son of Heaven plows personally to provide the sacrificial grains.

Jì is
