whom Péng Chǒng had dispatched,
as recorded in the second year of Gēngshǐ's reign in the previous scroll,
were all rewarded, but Péng Chǒng alone received nothing additional,
making him increasingly disgruntled and discontented.
He sighed, saying:
"If things are like this,
I should be made a king;
but as it is,
has Your Majesty forgotten me!"
"Ĕr" means
"like this."
At that time, the northern provinces were devastated and scattered,
but Yúyáng was relatively intact.
It had an old iron office,
as recorded in the "Treatise on Geography,"
Yúyáng County in Yúyáng Commandery had an iron office.
It accumulated treasures,
becoming increasingly wealthy and powerful.
The Governor of Yōuzhōu, Zhū Fú,
was young and talented,
and sought to promote virtuous governance.
Xián's commentary: This refers to the traces of moral transformation.
"Shào"
is pronounced as in "shī zhào fān."
He recruited renowned elders in the province
— famous and venerable scholars.
He appointed them all to his staff;
and frequently distributed grain from the commandery granaries to support their wives and children.
Péng Chǒng believed that the empire was not yet pacified,
and military campaigns were just beginning,
so it was inappropriate to appoint too many officials and thereby deplete military supplies.
Xián's commentary: This refers to armor, weapons, and grain reserves.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says: "To ruin military supplies."
Zhū Fú was arrogant, impatient, and self-important,
Xián's commentary: "Jīn" means
to boast;
"duō" means
self-aggrandizement.
Resentment between them grew.
Zhū Fú repeatedly slandered and framed him,
secretly reporting that Péng Chǒng was amassing troops and grain,
with intentions difficult to gauge.
The emperor deliberately leaked this information to Péng Chǒng,
to intimidate and threaten him.
At this point,
an edict was issued summoning Péng Chǒng.
Péng Chǒng submitted a memorial,
requesting to be summoned together with Zhū Fú;
the emperor did not permit it.
Péng Chǒng grew increasingly suspicious;
his wife, who was by nature strong-willed,
could not bear to be suppressed and wronged,
firmly urging him not to accept the summons,
saying:
"The empire is not yet pacified,
and all regions are establishing their own power.
Yúyáng is a large commandery,
with the most elite troops and horses.
Why should we abandon this because someone has accused us!"
Péng Chǒng also consulted with his trusted officials,
who all harbored resentment toward Zhū Fú,
and none advised him to go.
The emperor sent Péng Chǒng's nephew, Zǐhòu Lánqīng, to persuade him;
Péng Chǒng detained Zǐhòu Lánqīng,
then raised troops in rebellion.
He appointed generals and commanders,
personally leading over twenty thousand men,

He also believed that, like Gěng Kuàng, he had rendered great service,
yet both had received little reward.
He repeatedly sent envoys to invite and entice Gěng Kuàng;
Gěng Kuàng did not accept,
and beheaded his envoys.
Yán Cén rebelled again,
besieging Nánzhèng.
Cén's surrender to Jiā is recorded in the second year of Gēngshǐ's reign in the previous scroll.
"Fù"
is pronounced "fú yòu fān";
the same below.
Cén then occupied Hànzhōng,

as recorded in the "Treatise on Geography,"
Wǔdū County
belonged to Wǔdū Commandery.

Gōngsūn Shù sent his general Hóu Dān to capture Nánzhèng;

The battle was unfavorable,

belonging to Wǔdū Commandery,

Xiàbiàn District,

Cén led his troops north,
entered Sǎnguān,
and reached Chéncāng;

There was the Sǎngǔ River,

As recorded in the "Treatise on Geography,"
Chéncāng County belonged to Yòufǔfēng;

He defeated them.
Gōngsūn Shù also sent General Rèn Mǎn from Lángzhōng down to Jiāngzhōu,

Lángzhōng

The Hàn Yìzhōu region included commanderies such as Hànzhōng, Bā, Guǎnghàn, Shǔ, Qiánwéi, Zāngkē, Yuèxī, and Yìzhōu.
On the xīnmǎo day,

In the third month,

Many of Gēngshǐ's great generals in the south had not yet surrendered.
The emperor summoned his generals to discuss military affairs.
Tapping the ground with a wooden tablet, he said:

In the summer,
in the fourth month,

Gēngshǐ's three sons, Qiú, Xīn, and Lǐ, were all made marquises.

19. King Wáng Cháng of Dèng surrendered.
The Emperor met him and was very pleased,

"Now that I have seen the Commandant of Justice,
I have no worries about the south!"
(Gēngshǐ had appointed Wáng Cháng as Commandant of Justice,

Cháng's surrender secured the commandery of Nányáng,
hence the saying 'no worries about the south'.)
(The Former Hàn's Table of Officials states: The Left and Right Attendants
were additional offices,

At this time, it seems to have been a dedicated office.)
(Lǐ Xián's note:) Shānsāng County
belonged to Pèi Commandery;

20. In the fifth month,
on the gēngchén day,
he enfeoffed his clan uncle Liú Xī as King of Sìshuǐ.
21. The Emperor, considering Consort Yīn's noble and gentle nature,
wished to establish her as Empress.
However, Consort Yīn declined because Consort Guō had a son. (In the Western Capital, the harem had fourteen ranks,
but none was called 'Consort'.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ restored the dynasty,
he simplified extravagance into plainness.
The titles for the six palaces
were only Empress and Consort.
Consorts had gold seals with purple ribbons,
and their stipend did not exceed several dozen hú.)
In the sixth month,
on the wùxū day,
he established Consort Guō as Empress,
and made her son Liú Qiáng the Crown Prince;
a general amnesty was declared.
22. On the bǐngwǔ day,
he enfeoffed Liú Zhōng, son of the King of Sìshuǐ, as King of Zīchuān.
Zhōng
was the son of Liú Xī,
and had been close to the Emperor since youth,
hence he was enfeoffed as a king.
23. In autumn,
Jiǎ Fù campaigned south and attacked Zhàolíng and Xīnxī,

(Zhàolíng and Xīnxī were two counties

(Lǐ Xián's note:) The old city of Xīnxī was southwest of present-day Xīnxī County, Yù Prefecture.
Kòu Xún, the Administrator of Yǐngchuān, captured [Jiǎ Fù's officer] and
imprisoned him.
At the time, the dynasty was still newly established,
and military officers who broke the law
were often tolerated.
Kòu Xún, however, executed him in the marketplace.
Jiǎ Fù considered this a humiliation.
Upon returning,
passing through Yǐngchuān,
he said to his attendants:
"I and Kòu Xún are both generals,
yet he has entrapped me.
If I see Kòu Xún now,
I will surely run him through with my sword!"
Kòu Xún learned of his plan
and did not wish to meet him.
His nephew Gǔ Chóng said:
"I, Chóng,
am a general.
I can wear my sword and attend by your side.
Should anything happen suddenly,
I can handle it."
Kòu Xún said:
"Not so.
In the past, Lìn Xiàngrú did not fear the King of Qín yet yielded to Lián Pō,
for the sake of the state."
(This event is recorded in the 36th year of King Nǎn of Zhōu, in the fourth scroll.)
(Wèi is pronounced yú wèi fān.)
He prepared fine wine;
(Shuōwén states: Láo
is wine with both liquid and sediment.)
and had each person's meal portion doubled.

He then feigned illness and returned.
Jiǎ Fù led his troops intending to pursue him,

Kòu Xún sent Gǔ Chóng to report the situation to the Emperor,

When Kòu Xún arrived,

Jiǎ Fù was already present and seated,

The Emperor said:
"The empire is not yet settled,

Today, I shall mediate between you."
(Fēn means 'to mediate'.)
Thereupon, they left together in the same carriage,
became friends, and departed.

the Emperor personally led his generals to campaign against the Wǔxiào bandits.
On the bǐngchén day,
he arrived at Nèihuáng.

He accepted the surrender of fifty thousand of their followers.
(Lǐ Xián's note:) Yìyáng

By the time you return,

Liú Yǒng fled to Yú,

Jiǎo,

Wǎn,

"The flowing water of Lǒngtóu,

Thinking of my labor service,

Crossing Qiān and Lǒng,
there is no silkworm mulberry;

He defeated them;
and pursued and defeated them again between Wūzhī and Jīngyáng.

Defeated,

Zhī,

Fān,

The pits and valleys were all filled,

All those buried in jade coffins,

Yùyí County,

According to the Geographical Treatise,
Yúnyáng County,

Yán Cén was stationed at Dùlíng,
Xián says: A county name,

according to the Geographical Treatise,
Gǔkǒu County,

Liào,
pronounced lì diào fān,

Jiā personally killed Zhàn,
and then went to Yúnyáng to obtain grain.
Jiā's brother-in-law, Xīnyě native Lái Xī,

I have consulted Fàn's History,
and examined the whole matter,
the King of Hànzhōng, Jiā, appointed Lǐ Bǎo, Marquis Zhùgōng of Gēngshǐ, as his Chancellor,
Yù executed him,
it was not another person.
32 In winter,
the eleventh month,
the Court Commandant Cén Péng was appointed General-in-Chief Who Subdues the South.
The Emperor, at a grand assembly, pointed to Wáng Cháng and said to the assembled ministers:
"This man led the various generals of the Xiàjiāng to assist and support the Hàn dynasty,
his heart is like metal and stone,
truly a loyal subject!"
"This man"
means this person.
He appointed Cháng as General of Hàn Loyalty,
and sent him, together with Cén Péng, to lead General-in-Chief of Establishing Righteousness Zhū Hù and six other generals to suppress Dèng Fèng and Dǒng Xīn.
Péng and others first attacked Dǔxiāng,
and Dèng Fèng came to its rescue.
Zhū Hù's army was defeated,
and he was captured by Fèng.
33 Remnants of the Tóngmǎ, Qīngdú, and Yóulái bandits together set up Sūn Dēng as Son of Heaven.
Dēng's general Yuè Xuán killed Dēng,
and surrendered with his over fifty thousand troops.
34 After Dèng Yǔ's subordinate Féng Yīn rebelled,
Dèng Yǔ's prestige and reputation suffered somewhat.
Moreover, he was short on provisions,
and suffered several defeats in battle.
Consequently, those who had pledged allegiance to him increasingly drifted away.
The Chìméi bandits and Yán Cén were wreaking havoc in the Sānfǔ region,
and the powerful local clans in each commandery and county had gathered their own armed followers.
Dèng Yǔ was unable to pacify the situation.
The Emperor therefore dispatched the Lieutenant General Féng Yì to replace Dèng Yǔ and lead the campaign against them.
The imperial carriage escorted him as far as Hénán.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
Hénán County
belonged to Hénán Commandery.
It was the ancient territory of Jiá and Rǔ.
King Wǔ of Zhōu moved the Nine Tripods here,
and the Duke of Zhōu built it up to serve as the capital.
This became the Royal City.
Luòyáng
was where the Duke of Zhōu relocated the people of Yīn,
and this became Chéngzhōu.
The Jìn Dìdào Jì states: Hénán City was forty lǐ from Luò City.
Sòng Bái said: Hénán County
was where King Píng of Zhōu moved his residence.
By the time of King Jìng, the residence was moved to Chéngzhōu.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Hénán County.
Through the Wèi, Jìn, and Later Wèi dynasties,
its administrative seat was consistently located in the northeastern corner of the Tángyuàn City.
"The Sānfǔ region has suffered through the chaos of Wáng Mǎng and Gēngshǐ,
compounded by the villainy of the Chìméi and Yán Cén.

The gardens and temple of four generations from the Chōnglíng Marquis Jié downwards.
Gěng Yǎn calmly spoke to the Emperor,
volunteering to go north and gather the troops from Shànggǔ that had not yet been mobilized,
subdue Péng Chǒng in Yúyáng,
capture Zhāng Fēng in Zhuōjùn,
then pacify Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ,
attack Zhāng Bù from the east,
and thus pacify the Qí region.
The Emperor admired his ambition,
and approved it.
21 In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
the Emperor returned from Chōnglíng.
22 That year,
Lǐ Xiàn declared himself emperor,
established all the officials,
held nine cities,
with a following of over a hundred thousand.
Of the twelve cities in Lújiāng,
Lǐ Xiàn had only obtained nine.
23 The Emperor said to Grand Master of the Palace Lái Xī:
(Genealogy: Lái,
a surname from the Zǐ clan,
a descendant of the Shāng,
who was enfeoffed at Lái,
thus taking it as his surname;
later, to avoid trouble, he removed the radical "邑".
The "Table of Meritorious Officials of Hàn" includes Marquis of Dài Lái Cāng.
Xī,
pronounced Xǔ jí fān.)
"Now the western provinces have not yet submitted,
(Western provinces,
referring to Wěi Xiāo.)
Zǐyáng,
courtesy name of Gōngsūn Shù.
The generals are currently focused on Guāndōng,
and I am thinking about strategies for the western provinces,
but do not know where to begin."
Lái Xī said:
"I once met Wěi Xiāo in Cháng'ān.
When he first rose,
he used the name of Hàn.
(See the first year of Gēngshǐ in scroll thirty-nine.)
If we show him sincere trust,
(Yáng Zǐ said: The words of a sage
are as bright as cinnabar and azurite.)
then Shù will be in a situation where he will bring about his own downfall,
and he is not worth plotting against!"
The Emperor agreed,
and began sending Lái Xī as an envoy to Xiāo.
Xiāo had already rendered service to Hàn,
and had also received an official appointment from Dèng Yǔ,
(see the first year of the previous scroll.)
so Xiāo then submitted a memorial to the court.
The Emperor responded with exceptional courtesy,
addressing him by his courtesy name,
using the rituals of a rival state,
and treated him with great comfort and support.
(Xián said: Wèi,
to pacify.
Jiè,
to recommend.
Meaning to comfort and recommend him.)
1 In the first month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
a great amnesty was issued.
2 In the second month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
the Emperor traveled to Huái;
on the Rénshēn day,
he returned to Luòyáng.
3 Yán Cén again raided Shùnyáng;
(Treatise on Commanderies and States: Shùnyáng County belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
The Shùn River flows southeast into Cài.
Kuòdìzhì: The old city of Shùnyáng
was thirty lǐ west of Rǎng County in Dèng Prefecture,
and was the Xún settlement of Chǔ.)
Cén fled to Hànzhōng;
Gōngsūn Shù appointed Cén as Grand Marshal,
and enfeoffed him as King of Rǔníng.
4 Tián Róng heard that Qín Fēng had been defeated,
and, fearful,
wanted to surrender.
His wife's elder brother Xīn Chén drew a map of the commanderies and states obtained by Péng Chǒng, Zhāng Bù, Dǒng Xiàn, and Gōngsūn Shù to show Róng, saying:
"Luòyáng is as small as the palm of a hand."
(Like a palm,
a metaphor for its narrowness.)
Róng said:
"Even with the strength of the King of Qín,
he was still besieged by Zhēngnán;
I am determined to surrender!"
(Cén Péng was then the Great General Who Conquers the South,
hence Róng spoke thus.)
Xīn Chén led troops along the river, upstream on the Miǎn to Líqiū.
(From Yílíng downstream along the river
to Miǎnkǒu;
from Miǎnkǒu upstream on the Miǎn
one could reach Líqiū.)
He took a shortcut and surrendered first to Cén Péng,
then sent a letter urging Róng:
"You should surrender now,
and not cling to your previous plan!"
Róng suspected that Chén had betrayed him,
heated a tortoise shell for divination,
and the crack indicating surrender split in the middle.
(Zhōulǐ, Chuíshì: For all divination,
use a bright fire to light the torch,
blow on the ember,
and carve the shell to give to the diviner.
Zhèng Xuán said: The torch and ember
use thorny branches and the like.
The crack is
from heating the tortoise shell,
produced by the fire,
its form can be interpreted.)
He joined forces with Qín Fēng;
Cén Péng attacked and defeated them,
and Róng fled back to Yílíng.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Dīngsì day,
the Emperor traveled to Yè;
on the Jǐsì day,
he went to Línpíng.
(Xián said: A county name,
belonging to Jùlù Commandery,
the old city is southeast of present-day Gǔchéng County in Dìng Prefecture.)
The five clans of Gé County jointly expelled the acting magistrate,
occupied the city, and rebelled;
(Xián said: Gé County belonged to Píngyuán Commandery,
the old city is northwest of present-day Dé Prefecture.
The five clans
were likely powerful local families and influential magnates.
Gé,
pronounced gé.
I say the acting magistrate
was the acting magistrate of Gé County,
not the regular official.)
Wú Hàn said:
"What caused Gé to rebel
was the fault of the acting magistrate.
Anyone who dares to rashly advance troops will be beheaded!"
He then issued a proclamation ordering the commandery to arrest the acting magistrate,
and sent someone to apologize;
the five clans in the city were greatly pleased,
and immediately surrendered together.
The generals then admired him,
saying:
"To take a city without fighting
is beyond what the rest of us could achieve!"
6 In the fifth month,
the Emperor went to Yuánshì;
on the Xìnsì day,
he went to Lúnú,
intending to personally campaign against Péng Chǒng.
Fú Zhàn admonished:
"Now Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, and Jì
are the heartland of the Central Plains,
yet bandits run rampant,
and have not yet been transformed.
Yúyáng is a remote and desolate border region.
(Border region means
bordering on foreign tribes.)
Your Majesty abandons what is near to attend to what is far,
discards the easy to seek the difficult;
this truly perplexes me!"
The Emperor then returned.
7 The Emperor dispatched the Grand General for Advising Strategy Zhū Yòu, Grand General for Establishing Might Gěng Yǎn, General for Subduing the Caitiffs Zhài Zūn,
and General of the Swift Cavalry Liú Xǐ to attack Zhāng Fēng in Zhuōjùn.
Zhài Zūn arrived first,
and urgently attacked Fēng;
he captured him.
Initially,
Fēng was fond of occult arts,
and a Dàoshì said that Fēng was destined to become the Son of Heaven.
In the Western Capital, those who practiced occult arts were called Fāngshì,
while in the Eastern Capital they were consequently called Dàoshì.
Hào,
pronounced hū dào fān.
He said
"There is a jade seal within the stone."
Fēng believed him,
and thus rebelled.
After being captured,
and about to be executed,
he still said
"There is a jade seal in the stone at my elbow."
Someone nearby smashed it with a hammer,
and only then did Fēng realize he had been deceived.
He looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"I deserve to die and have no regrets!"
The Emperor ordered Gěng Yǎn to advance and attack Péng Chǒng.
Yǎn, because his father Gěng Kuàng had achieved merits together with Chǒng,
Kuàng and Chǒng both had the merit of aiding the Hàn,
as seen in the events of the second year of Gēngshǐ in the previous scroll, volume thirty-nine.
did not dare to advance alone,
and requested to go to Luòyáng.
The imperial edict replied:
"General, your entire clan serves the state,
your achievements and contributions are especially prominent.
What suspicion or doubt is there,
that you seek to be summoned?"
When Kuàng heard this,
he further sent Yǎn's younger brother Guó to enter the court and serve.
At that time, Zhài Zūn was stationed in Liángxiāng,
and Liú Xǐ was stationed in Yángxiāng.
Xián said: Liángxiāng and Yángxiāng,
were both county names,
and both belonged to Zhuōjùn.
The old city of Yángxiāng,
was located northwest of the old Ān County in Yōuzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Liángxiāng,
during the Yān period was Zhōngdū,
and during the Hàn was Liángxiāng County.
Gěng Kuàng sent his son Shū to launch a surprise attack and defeat the Xiōngnú troops,
killing two kings,
and Chǒng then retreated and fled.
8 In the sixth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Dīnghài day,
the Emperor went to Qiáo.
Examination of discrepancies says: In Yuán Jì,
it says "went to Qiáo in the sixth month,"
but now we follow Fàn Shū.
10 Dǒng Xiàn's general Bēn Xiū surrendered with Lánlíng;
when Xiàn heard this,
he personally besieged it from Tán.
Xián said: Tán County,
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery;
its old city was located northeast of Xiàpī County in Sìzhōu.
Tán,
pronounced tán.
Chǔ,
was Péngchéng.
The Emperor commanded:
"You may directly strike at Tán,
Xián said: Dǎo,
means to attack.
I say dǎo,
means to strike at the weak point;
this is what military strategy calls attacking what the enemy must rescue.
Yán and others, because Bēn Xiū's city was in danger,
thus first rushed to aid it.
Xiàn engaged in battle and feigned defeat and retreat,
and Yán and others thus broke through the siege and entered the city.
The next day,
Xiàn sent out a large force to encircle them;
Yán and others were afraid,
hastily broke out and fled,
and thus went to attack Tán.
The Emperor reproached them, saying:
"Earlier, I wanted you to first attack Tán,
precisely because it would be unexpected!
Now that you have already fled,
the enemy's plan is already set,
how can the siege be lifted?"
When Yán and others reached Tán,
they indeed could not conquer it;
and Dǒng Xiàn then captured Lánlíng,
killing Bēn Xiū.
11 In the eighth month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
the Emperor went to Shòuchūn.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
Shòuchūn County,
belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
Xián said: It is present-day Shòuzhōu County.
In the ninth month,
they besieged Xiàn at Shū.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
Lújiāng Commandery,
administered Shū County.
Xián said: Its old city was west of Lújiāng County in Lúzhōu.
Huì,
pronounced gǔ wài fān.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
when the world was in chaos,
Hóu Bà, the Grand Administrator of Línhuái from Hénán, alone was able to preserve and protect his commandery.
Treatise on Commanderies and States: Línhuái Commandery was 1,400 lǐ east of Luòyáng.
He was appointed Imperial Secretary.
At that time, the court lacked established regulations,
and also had few old ministers.
Bà was well-versed in past precedents,
collected and recorded lost documents,
systematically memorialized the good governance laws and systems of previous generations,
and implemented them.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
12 Wěi Xiāo sent Mǎ Yuán to go and observe Gōngsūn Shù.
Yuán had originally lived in the same village as Shù,
and they were on good terms.
Yuán and Shù were both from Màolíng.
Shuōwén says: Hàn,
means village lane,
pronounced hóu gàn fān.
They should have shaken hands joyfully as in the past;
but Shù grandly arrayed palace guards to escort Yuán in,
and after the ceremonial exchange of bows was completed,
he had him go out to the guesthouse.
He further had Dūbù single-layer robes made for Yuán.
Hé Chéngtiān's Zuǎnwén says: Dū, Zhì, Cuò, Lǚ, Wújí,
were all names of cloth.
Fāngyán says: Chányī,
in the regions of Jiāng, Huái, and Nánchǔ, are called Dié,
while east and west of the passes they are called Chányī.
Wéi,
pronounced yú wèi fān.
He assembled all officials in the ancestral temple,
and set up a position for his old friend.
Shù had Luán banners and Máo cavalry.
The annotation for Luán banners is found in the thirteenth scroll, first year of Emperor Wén.
Máo cavalry,
refers to Máo-tóu cavalry.
When Duke Mù of Qín attacked the great Catalpa tree of Nánshān,
a black ox ran out,
and entered the Fēng River;
later, when the ox emerged from the Fēng River,
he sent cavalry to attack it,
but they could not overcome it;
one cavalryman fell to the ground and got back up,
his hair came loose,
and the ox feared him,
and entered and did not come out: therefore, they established Máo-tóu cavalry to lead the vanguard.
Bending like a qìng stone chime, he entered.
Xián said: Qìngzhé,
means bending the body like the curve of a qìng stone chime,
showing respect.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Qìngzhé means
bending the body like the angled break of a qìng stone chime.
According to the Kǎogōng Jì: The qìng maker makes the qìng,
with an angle of one and a half right angles.
Zhèng says: One must first measure one right angle for the shorter side,
one right angle for the longer side,
and then find the hypotenuse.
Once one and a half right angles touches the hypotenuse,
then that is the angle of the qìng.
Thus, the angled break of the qìng,
its shape must be curved,
and a person leaning on a carriage rail should also be like this.
He wished to confer upon Yuán the position of Marquis and Grand General.
All the guests were happy to stay,
but Yuán enlightened them, saying:
"The world's outcome between victor and vanquished is not yet decided.
Gōngsūn does not spit out his food and run to welcome a man of talent for the state.
The Duke of Zhōu would spit out his food three times during a single meal to attend to the talents of the world.
Instead, he pays excessive attention to superficial formalities,
Xián said: This means like cloth and silk trimming its edges.
How can this man be worthy of long detaining the talents of the world?"
Jī,
means to detain.
He said to Xiāo:
"Zǐyáng
is nothing but a frog at the bottom of a well.
This means his ambition and understanding are narrow and limited,
like a frog in a pit well.
It is better to focus our intentions on the East."
The East,
refers to Luòyáng.
2 The Emperor sent Lái Xī to escort Mǎ Yuán back to Lǒngyòu with the imperial insignia.
Textual analysis notes: The Yuánjì states:
"Yuán and Jùshǔ Hóu Guó Yóuxiān were both sent as envoys.
Yóuxiān arrived at Cháng'ān,
where he was killed by an enemy.
His younger brother served Wéi Xiāo as the Yúnqí General.
Lái Xī, fearing his resentment,
returned to Cháng'ān together with Yuán."
According to the records, the envoy of Xiāo who was killed
was Zhōu Yóu,
and it did not happen at this time.
(Wéi Xiāo) asked (Mǎ Yuán) about affairs in the east,
and (Mǎ Yuán) said:
"When I previously arrived at the imperial court,
the Emperor summoned me for an audience dozens of times.
The Dōngguān Jì states: In total, fourteen audiences.
From evening until dawn,
his talent, intelligence, courage, and strategic insight
are unmatched by any man.
Moreover, he is open-hearted and sincere,
with nothing hidden or concealed.
He is broad-minded and possesses great integrity,
somewhat similar to Emperor Gāo;
his mastery of the classics is extensive and his learning broad,
his handling of government affairs and literary debates
are unparalleled by any in previous generations."
Xiāo said:
"How do you think he compares to Emperor Gāo?"
Yuán replied:
"He is not as good.
Emperor Gāo could adapt to anything, with no fixed 'must' or 'must not';
Xián's note: This is from the Analects, where Confucius speaks of his own conduct.
(The current Emperor's) actions follow rules and measures,
and moreover, he does not enjoy drinking wine."
Xiāo was displeased,
and said:
"According to what you say,
does that mean he is even better?"
3 In the second month,
on the bǐngwǔ day,
a general amnesty was issued.
4 Sū Mào led the Wǔxiào troops to rescue Zhōu Jiàn at Chuíhuì.
Mǎ Wǔ was defeated by Mào and Jiàn,
and fled past Wáng Bà's camp,
shouting loudly for help.
Bà said:
"If the enemy troops emerge in full force,
we will surely both suffer defeat.
We must simply exert our strength!"
He then closed the camp gates and fortified the walls.
The military officers all argued with him,
but Bà said:
"Mào's troops are elite and sharp,
and their numbers are great.
Our officers and soldiers are fearful at heart,
while the Capturing Brigands General and I rely on each other.
Mǎ Wǔ held the title of Capturing Brigands General.
This is the path to defeat.
Now, by closing the camp and holding firm,
showing that we will not aid each other,
the enemy will certainly take advantage of their victory and advance lightly;
the Capturing Brigands General, having no rescue,
will fight with double the effort on his own.
When each man fights to the death,
then one man exerts the strength of two.
When Mào's troops are exhausted,
and we strike at their weakness,
then we can overcome them."
Mào and Jiàn indeed came out in full force to attack Wǔ,
meaning they brought out all their troops to attack.
Dozens of brave warriors in Bà's army cut their hair and requested to fight.
Bà then opened the rear of the camp,
and sent out elite cavalry to attack the enemy's rear.
Mào and Jiàn, attacked from front and rear,
panicked, fell into disorder, and fled in defeat.
Bà and Wǔ each returned to their camps.
Mào and Jiàn regrouped their troops and came to challenge,
but Bà lay firmly still and did not emerge.
Instead, he feasted his soldiers with music and performances;
Mào rained arrows into the camp,
meaning arrows fell like rain.
Shè,
pronounced as yì.
Bà sat calmly without moving.
The military officers all said:
"Mào was defeated the other day,
now he is easy to attack!"
Bà said:
"Not so.
Sū Mào's troops are guest soldiers who have come from afar,
and their food supplies are insufficient.
Therefore, they repeatedly challenge us to battle,
seeking a momentary victory.
Now, by closing the camp and letting our soldiers rest,
this is what is called 'subduing the enemy's troops without fighting.'"
Master Sūn said: To win a hundred battles is not the ultimate skill;
to subdue the enemy's troops without fighting is the ultimate skill.
Bà was likely quoting his words.
(Mào and Jiàn) then led their troops back to camp.
That night,
Zhōu Jiàn's nephew, Sòng, rebelled,
closed the city gates, and resisted them. Jiàn died on the road;
Mào fled to Xiàpī.
According to the Treatise on Geography,
Xiàpī County
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Liú Yū fled to Jiǎo Qiáng.
5 On the yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor traveled to Wèi Commandery.
6 Péng Chǒng's wife repeatedly had nightmares,
and also witnessed many strange and abnormal occurrences;
diviners and those who observed celestial omens all said that armed conflict would arise from within.
Chǒng, because his son Hòu Lánqīng had returned from being a hostage in Hàn,
did not trust him,
(his son Hòu Lánqīng's return
is recorded in the second year of the previous scroll).
Zhì,
pronounced as zhì.
(and thus) had no close kin within (to rely on).
Chǒng was fasting in a side chamber,
Xián's note: A side chamber for informal sitting,
not the main chamber.
Xián's note: The Qín called the common people 'qiánshǒu' (black heads);
calling slaves 'cāngtóu' (blue/green heads)
was to distinguish them from commoners.
(The slaves) together bound him to the bed,
and announced to the officials outside:
"The Great King is observing fasting restrictions,
let all the officials rest."
Falsely claiming Chǒng's orders,
they arrested and bound the male and female servants,
placing them in separate locations.
Then, using Chǒng's name, they summoned his wife.
When the wife entered,
she cried out in alarm:
"The slaves have rebelled!"
A slave then seized her by the head,
and struck her face.
Chǒng urgently called out:
"Hurry and prepare baggage for these generals!"
Thereupon, two slaves took the wife inside to fetch treasures and valuables,
leaving one slave to guard Chǒng.
Chǒng said to the guarding slave:
"You, young man,
I have always loved you.
Now you are only forced and coerced by Zǐ Mì!
Untie my bonds,
and I will give you my daughter Zhū as your wife,
and all the wealth and goods in the household will be given to you."
Ruò,
also means 'you'.
(The slave) looked outside the door,
saw Zǐ Mì listening to their conversation,
and thus did not dare to untie him.
Thereupon, they collected the gold, jade, clothing, and other items,
brought them to where Chǒng was, and packed them.
They saddled six horses,
and made the wife sew two silk bags.
After nightfall,
they untied Chǒng's hands,
and ordered him to write a note instructing the city gate general, saying:
"Now I am sending Zǐ Mì and others to where my son Hòu Lánqīng is,
do not detain them."
After the note was finished,
they beheaded Chǒng and his wife, placed their heads in the bags,
then took the note and galloped out of the city,
and thus went to the capital.
The next morning,
the inner gate did not open.
The officials climbed over the wall and entered,
saw Chǒng's corpse,
and were shocked and terrified.
His Secretary Hán Lì and others together established Chǒng's son Wǔ as king.
The State Preceptor Hán Lì beheaded Wǔ and presented his head to Jì Zūn, surrendering.
The title State Preceptor
was an appointment made by Chǒng,
likely following the system of Wáng Mǎng.
The Emperor enfeoffed Zǐ Mì as the Marquis of Bùyì.
Quán Déyú's discussion states: Bótōng's rebellion,
Bótōng,
is Péng Chǒng's courtesy name.
Both ended in chaos,
their crimes do not shield each other,
each should be brought to justice,
to make clear the king's law;
wáng dù,
means the king's law.
Moreover, they took 'unrighteousness'
as their banner.
And to raise the banner of unrighteousness,
none can be enfeoffed;
if such can be enfeoffed,
then the Han nobility is insufficient to encourage virtue.
The meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals recording Qí Bào as a thief and naming the three rebels,
refers to when Wèi's Minister of Justice Qí Bào, out of personal enmity, killed Mèng Zhí, the elder brother of the Marquis of Wèi,
the Spring and Autumn Annals records him as a thief.
Naming the three rebels,
refers to the twenty-first year of Duke Xiāng,
when Zhū Shùqí fled to our state bringing the territories of Qī and Lǘqiū;
the fifth year of Duke Zhāo,
when Jǔ Móuyí fled bringing Móulóu and Fángzī;
the fourteenth year of Duke Āi,
when Xiǎozhū Shè fled bringing Jūyì.
Jū,
pronounced gōu.
7 The Emperor appointed Guō Jí of Fúfēng as the Grand Administrator of Yùyáng.
Treatise on Commanderies and States: Yùyáng Commandery,
is two thousand lǐ northeast of Luòyáng.
He nurtured the people and trained the troops,
establishing authority and trust,
bandits dispersed,
the Xiōngnú kept their distance;
during his five-year tenure,
the registered households doubled.
8 The Emperor sent the Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments Fán Hóng, bearing the imperial tally, to welcome Gěng Kuàng from Shànggǔ,
Treatise on Commanderies and States: Shànggǔ Commandery,
is two thousand lǐ northeast of Luòyáng.
"The border commanderies are cold and harsh,
not suitable for long-term residence."
Kuàng arrived at the capital,
was granted a mansion,
appointed as a court advisor,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Mùpíng.
Treatise on Geography,
Mùpíng County,
belonged to Dōnglái Commandery;
in the Táng and Sòng dynasties, it belonged to Dēng Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Mùpíng County is named because it lies south of Mù Mountain,
the land is flat,
hence called Mùpíng.
The old city of Hàn Mùpíng,
is located one hundred and thirty lǐ east of present-day Huáng County.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Qǐng,
pronounced cái xìng fān,
also as the usual pronunciation.
Wú Hàn led Gěng Yǎn and Wáng Cháng to attack the Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ bandits in Píngyuán,
Treatise on Commanderies and States: Píngyuán Commandery,
is one thousand three hundred lǐ north of Luòyáng.
They pursued and attacked the remaining factions,
reaching Bóhǎi,
Treatise on Commanderies and States;
Bóhǎi Commandery is one thousand six hundred lǐ north of Luòyáng.
The Emperor then issued an edict ordering Yǎn to advance and attack Zhāng Bù.
9 Páng Méng, General Who Pacifies Enemies,
was humble and compliant in character,
previously written as
"General Who Pacifies the Dí."
He often said:
"One who can be entrusted with a six-chǐ orphan,
or the fate of a hundred-lǐ state,"
are words of Confucius from the Analects.
Lǚ Yǔshū said: Entrusting a six-chǐ orphan,
means assisting a young ruler;
entrusting the fate of a hundred-lǐ state,
means serving as a feudal lord.
He was sent to jointly attack Dǒng Xiàn with Gài Yán.
At that time, the imperial edict was issued only to Yán and not to Méng,
Méng believed Yán had slandered him,
grew suspicious himself,

striking the weak with strength,
within ten days,
Bù's head can be captured."
Thereupon, Yǎn first went out to the Zī River,
Water Classic: The Zī River originates from Yuán Mountain northeast of Làiwú County in Tài Shān,
passing east of Línzī County.
The assault cavalry wanted to charge,
but Yǎn feared blunting their edge,
causing Bù not to dare advance,
so he feigned weakness to boost their morale,
then withdrew to the small city,
deploying troops inside,
having Commandant Liú Xīn and Tài Shān Prefect Chén Jùn separately deploy under the city walls.
Bù, with high morale,
directly attacked Yǎn's camp,
engaging in battle with Liú Xīn and others.
Yǎn ascended the ruined terrace of the king's palace to observe,
Xián said: Línzī,
originally the capital of the Qí state,
meaning within the Qí king's palace there was a ruined terrace.
Then he personally led elite troops to flank and assault Bù's formation under the eastern city walls,
greatly defeating them.
A stray arrow hit Yǎn's thigh,
he cut it off with his sword,
and none around him knew.
By dusk,
the battle ceased;
the next morning, Yǎn again led his troops out.
At this time, the Emperor was in Lǔ,
hearing Yǎn was attacked by Bù,
he personally went to rescue him.
Before arriving,
Chén Jùn said to Yǎn:
"The formidable enemy troops are strong,
we could close the camp and rest the soldiers,
awaiting the Emperor's arrival."
Yǎn said:
"The imperial carriage is about to arrive,
as subjects, we should slaughter cattle and strain wine to await the officials,
how can we instead leave the enemy for our sovereign!"
So he led his troops out for a major battle.
From dawn till dusk,
again he greatly defeated them;
countless were killed or wounded,
ditches and moats were filled.
Yǎn knew Bù was exhausted and about to retreat,
he preemptively set left and right wings in ambush to await them;
the ambush troops on both sides like a bird spreading its wings.
Bù indeed led his troops away,
after dusk,
called the time when people settle.
They pursued to the Jù Mò River,
Xián said: Jù Mò,
is a river name,
also called Jù Yáng River,
now west of Shòuguāng County in Qīngzhōu.
Water Classic Commentary: Jù Yáng River originates from Tài Shān east of Zhūxū County,
Yuán Hóng called it Jù Mò,
Wáng Shàozhī considered it Jù Miè;
north past east of Línqú County,
then north past west of Línqú County,
then northeast past west of Shòuguāng County.
Mò,
pronounced mò.
Corpses lay connected,
capturing over two thousand carts of supplies.
Bù returned to Jù,
brothers each dispersed their troops.
Several days later,
the imperial carriage arrived at Línzī,
personally comforting the army,
gathering ministers for a grand assembly.
The Emperor said to Yǎn:
"In the past, Hán Xìn broke Lìxià to establish a foundation,
event seen in year four of Gāozǔ, volume ten.
These are all Qí's western borders,
achievements are comparable.
Yet Hán Xìn attacked after surrender,
General, you alone uprooted a formidable enemy,
your achievement is even more difficult than Xìn's.
Also,
Tián Héng cooked Lì Shēng,
and when Tián Héng surrendered,
Emperor Gāozǔ ordered the Commandant of the Guards not to pursue vengeance;
event seen in year five of Gāozǔ, volume eleven.
Hēng,
same as pēng.
Event seen in year three above.
I shall order the Grand Minister over the Masses to release his grudge,
again events are especially similar.
General, earlier in Nányáng,
you proposed this grand strategy,
referring to winter of year three when Yǎn followed the Emperor to Chōnglíng,
personally requesting to pacify Qí.
Xián said: Luòluò,
means distant and broad.
The Emperor advanced to Jù.
Gěng Yǎn again pursued Zhāng Bù,
Bù fled to Píngshòu,
Xián said: Píngshòu,
is a county name,
belonging to Běihǎi Commandery;
old city now in Běihǎi County, Qīngzhōu.
Fù,
pronounced fù.
Sū Mà admonished Bù, saying:
"With Nányáng's elite troops,
Yán Cén skilled in battle,
yet Gěng Yǎn drove him away,
event seen in year three above.
Since you called Mà,
could you not wait!"
Bù said:
"Shame, shame,
nothing more to say!"
Xián said: Fù,
means shame.
Saying fù twice,
means extreme shame.
Whoever can kill and surrender,
will be enfeoffed as a marquis.
Bù then beheaded Mà,
going to Gěng Yǎn's army gate, baring his upper body to surrender;
Yǎn sent him to the imperial traveling lodge,
and led troops to occupy the city,
Píngshòu city.
Ordering Bù's soldiers each to gather under banners by commandery,
they still numbered over a hundred thousand,
with over seven thousand carts of supplies,
all were disbanded and sent back to their hometowns.
Zhāng Bù's three younger brothers each imprisoned themselves where they were,
an edict pardoned them all,
enfeoffing Bù as Marquis of Ānqiū,
Geographical Records,
Ānqiū,
a marquisate,
belonging to Lángyé Commandery;
also, Běihǎi Commandery has Ānqiū County.
Sòng Bái said: Mìzhōu has Ānqiū County,
ancient Gēnmóu state city,
Hàn era as Ānqiū;
the county has Qúqiū Pavilion,
where the old Jǔ Qúqiū Duke resided.
Thus Lángyé was not yet pacified,
Commandery and Kingdom Records: Lángyé Commandery,
is fifteen hundred lǐ east of Luòyáng.
As soon as they entered the territory,
bandits all scattered.
Gěng Yǎn again led troops to Chéngyáng,
Geographical Records,
Chéngyáng Kingdom,
capital at Jǔ.
Xián said: Chéngyáng old city,
now south of Línyí County, Yízhōu.
Qí lands were all pacified,
they regrouped and returned to the capital.
Yǎn as a general,
pacified a total of forty-six commanderies,
sacked three hundred cities,
never suffering a setback.
18. The Imperial University was first established.
The imperial carriage returned to the palace,
and the Emperor visited the Imperial University.
Lù Jī's "Luòyáng Jì" states: The Imperial University was located outside the old Kāiyáng Gate of Luòyáng City,
eight lǐ from the palace.
The lecture hall was ten zhàng long
and three zhàng wide.
Rituals and music were cultivated and made clear,
and the cultural artifacts became splendid and worthy of admiration!
19. In the eleventh month,
the Grand Minister over the Masses, Fú Zhàn, was dismissed,
and Hóu Bà was appointed as Grand Minister over the Masses.
Bà, having heard of the reputation of Mǐn Zhòngshū from Tàiyuán, summoned him to office.
After his arrival,
Bà did not discuss governmental affairs with him,
but only subjected him to toil and hardship.
Xián's commentary: This means to make him labor diligently and suffer hardship.
Láo (toil)
is pronounced lì dào fān.
"At first, receiving your gracious command,
I was both joyful and fearful.
Now, having met Your Excellency,
both joy and fear have vanished.
Do you consider Zhòngshū unworthy of consultation?
Then you should not have summoned me.
To summon someone yet not consult them
is to lose a person!"
He then took his leave,
submitted a self-impeachment, and departed.
Xián's commentary: To impeach means to accuse of a crime.
He submitted his own impeachment document and left.
Tóu (submit)
means to present or hand down.
Nowadays, there are expressions like 'tóu cí' (submit a statement) and 'tóu dié' (submit a petition).
Hé (impeach)
is pronounced hù gài fān.
20. Earlier,
Lǐ Xīng and Suí Yù from Wǔyuán,
(Surname genealogy: descendants of the Marquis of Suí.)
Also, a great-grandson of Dù Bó became a senior official of Jìn,
receiving Suí as his fief,
and was called Suí Huì.
Shí Wěi and Mǐn Kān from Dàijùn each raised troops and proclaimed themselves generals.
The Xiōngnú Chányú sent envoys to make peace and form marriage alliances with Xīng and the others,
intending to have Lú Fāng return to Hàn territory to become emperor.
Xīng and the others led troops to the Chányú's court to welcome Fāng.
In the twelfth month,
they entered the frontier together,
establishing their capital at Jiǔyuán County.
Xián's commentary: Jiǔyuán,
a county name,
belonged to Wǔyuán Commandery.
Its old city was located in the present-day Yínchéng County of Shèng Prefecture.
They also appointed governors and magistrates,
and together with Hú
troops, they invaded and harassed the northern border regions.
21. Féng Yì governed Guānzhōng.
After three years of coming and going,
the Shànglín area became like a metropolis.
Xián's commentary: Chéngdū (becoming a metropolis)
means that the number of people submitting and attaching themselves was great.
The "Shǐ Jì" states: In one year, it becomes a town;
in two years, it becomes a metropolis.
Zhì (govern)
is pronounced zhí zhī fān.
"Yì's authority and power are extremely weighty,
the hearts of the common people turn to him,
and he is called the King of Xiányáng."
The Emperor showed the memorial to Yì.
Yì became alarmed and fearful,
and submitted a memorial expressing apology.
An imperial edict replied:
"Between you, General, and the state,
in principle, it is a relationship between ruler and minister,
but in affection, it is like that between father and son.
What grounds for suspicion or doubt,
that you should feel fear!"
22. Wěi Xiāo prided himself and adorned his wisdom,
often comparing himself to King Wén of the West.
Xī Bó (King of the West)
refers to King Wén.
Zhèng Xīng said:
"In ancient times, King Wén possessed two-thirds of the world,
yet he still served the Yīn dynasty.
The "Lúnyǔ" records Confucius's words.
He still withdrew his troops and awaited the proper time.
King Wǔ displayed his army at Mèngjīn,
and eight hundred feudal lords gathered without prior arrangement,
all saying:
'Zhòu can be attacked.'
The King said:
'You do not yet know the Mandate of Heaven.'
He then led the army back.
He still acted as the Lord of Pèi leading his army.
Now, although your virtuous conduct is illustrious,
the world lacks the good fortune of the Zhōu lineage;
although your martial prowess is impressive,
you lack the achievements of Gāozǔ;
yet you wish to undertake what cannot yet be done,
clearly hastening
sù (hasten)
means a hastening that is not hasty,
a clear summons.
Zhāo (clear)
means to make clear.
Xiāo then desisted.
Later, he again widely established official positions to elevate himself.
Zhèng Xīng said:
"Positions such as General of the Household, Grand Master of the Palace, and Commissioner Bearing Credentials
are all instruments of a king,
not what a subject should institute.
They bring no benefit in substance,
but damage your reputation.
This is not the intention of honoring your superiors."
Xiāo found this difficult and stopped.
Xián's commentary: Bìng (find difficult)
means to regard as difficult.
At that time, generals and commanders from Guānzhōng repeatedly submitted memorials discussing the situation for attacking Shǔ.
The Emperor showed these documents to Xiāo,
thereby instructing him to attack Shǔ to test his sincerity.
Xiào (test)
means to verify.
They strongly argued that the Three Adjuncts were weak and vulnerable,
and Liú Wénbó was on the border.
(Lú Fāng called himself Liú Wénbó.)
The Emperor knew that Xiāo wished to maintain a dual stance,
not desiring the unification of the realm.
Thereupon, he gradually reduced the ceremonial honors accorded to him,
rectifying the rituals between ruler and minister.
Previously, the Emperor's letters to Xiāo used the etiquette for a rival state.
Now, he reduced that etiquette.
He frequently sent Xī and Yuán as envoys back and forth,
urging him to come to court,
promising him a high noble rank.
Xiāo repeatedly sent envoys,
deeply maintaining humble words,
saying he had no merit or virtue,
and that he must wait until all regions were pacified,
then he would retire to his village.
The Emperor again sent Lái Xī to persuade Xiāo to send his son to serve at court.
Xiāo heard that Liú Yǒng and Péng Chǒng had both been defeated and destroyed,
so he sent his eldest son, Xún, to accompany Xī to the capital.
The Emperor appointed him as Colonel of the Hú Cavalry,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis Juān Qiāng.
Colonel of the Hú Cavalry
was established by Emperor Wǔ,
with a salary of two thousand shí.
Xián's commentary: Juān (engrave)
means to carve or chisel.
Juān
is pronounced zǐ quán fān.
Zhèng Xīng took the opportunity of Xún's journey to request permission to return and bury his parents.
Xiāo did not permit it,
but instead moved Xīng to a different residence,
increasing his salary and honors.
Xīng went to see him and said:
"Now, because my parents are not yet buried,
I beg to retire.
If you increase my salary and move my residence,
causing me to change my mind and stay,
this would be using my parents as bait.
Xián's commentary: Like fishing bait.
How could you, General, use such a method!
I wish to leave my wife and children behind and return alone to bury them.
What suspicion could you, General, still have then!"
Xiāo then ordered him to go east together with his wife and children.
Mǎ Yuán also brought his family to follow Xún back to Luòyáng.
Because the number of retainers he brought was large and miscellaneous,
he requested to settle and farm in the Shànglín Park.
The Emperor permitted it.
Jiàng (bring)
is pronounced according to its usual reading.
Wáng Yuán, a general under Wěi Xiāo, believed that the outcome of the empire was still uncertain,
and he was unwilling to focus solely on internal affairs.
He advised Wěi Xiāo, saying:
"In the past, when Gēngshǐ established his capital in the west,
all regions responded in support,
and the people of the world looked up with anticipation,
calling it an era of peace.
Yet once it collapsed,
you, General, had almost nowhere to turn.
(This event is recorded in the first year of the previous volume.)
To the north, there is Wén Bó,
and across the rivers, lakes, seas, and Mount Tài,
there are dozens of lords and princes.
Yet you wish to follow the advice of Confucian scholars.
(Xián notes: 'Confucian scholars' refers to Mǎ Yuán persuading Wěi Xiāo to submit to Emperor Guāngwǔ.)
I believe 'Confucian scholars' refers to Zhèng Xīng, Bān Biāo, and others.
With the resources of various states,
there are a thousand war chariots.
(Chéng, pronounced shèng.)
This is following the path of a overturned cart.
Now, Tiānshuǐ is prosperous and wealthy,
with the strongest soldiers and horses.
I, Yuán, request to use a single pellet of clay to seal the Hángǔ Pass for you, Great King, in the east.
This is a once-in-a-millennium opportunity.
If you do not consider this plan,
then at least nurture your soldiers and horses,
hold strategic positions and defend yourself,
prolong the situation,
and wait for changes across the land.
Even if you fail to achieve kingship,
the worst outcome would still allow you to become a hegemon.
(As stated in the previous text by Xú Lè.)
A fish cannot leave the depths;
a divine dragon that loses its power
is no different from an earthworm!"
(Lǎozǐ said: "A fish cannot leave the spring."
Tuō means to lose;
losing the spring means drying up.
Shènzǐ said: "The soaring snake travels through the mist,
the flying dragon rides the clouds.
When the clouds disperse and the mist clears,
they are no different from earthworms,
because they have lost what they relied on.")
Although Wěi Xiāo sent his son as a hostage,
he still relied on his strategic advantages,
seeking to control the region independently.
Shēntú Gāng admonished him, saying:
"I have heard that those whom people follow are supported by Heaven,
and those whom people abandon are forsaken by Heaven.
Our court is truly blessed by Heaven,
not by human effort.
(Xián notes: 'Our court' refers to Emperor Guāngwǔ.)
To entrust the state and pledge loyalty,
wishing to share fortune and misfortune with you, General—
even among commoners,
there is a trust that lasts a lifetime without breaking promises,
let alone for one who commands ten thousand chariots!
Now, what fear or benefit
makes you hesitate for so long?
(Xián notes: This means, what is there to fear in following Hàn, and what benefit is there in attaching to Shǔ, that you remain undecided for so long?)
Above, you betray loyalty and filial piety;
below, you bring shame upon the present age.
Before events occur, predictions are often empty;
once they occur, it is too late to act.
Thus, loyal advice and earnest admonitions
are rarely heeded.
I sincerely hope you will reconsider the words of this foolish old man!"
Wěi Xiāo did not accept his advice,
and as a result, wandering scholars and elders gradually left him.
23 At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
the various commanderies of Jiāozhǐ closed their borders and defended themselves.
(Xián notes: Jiāozhǐ Commandery is present-day Jiāozhōu County, bordering the sea to the south.
Yǔdìzhì states: The barbarians there have splayed big toes; when both feet are placed together, they cross.
Yìng Shào said: 'They began opening the north and then extended to the south, establishing a foundation for their descendants.')
I note: In the sixth year of Yuándǐng under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Jiāozhǐ Province was established,
with its seat at Guǎngxìn.
At that time, the north had already been opened,
and they extended to the south, establishing a foundation for their descendants.
The seven commanderies refer to Nánhǎi, Cāngwú, Yùlín, Hépǔ, Jiāozhǐ, Jiǔzhēn, and Rìnán,
all belonging to Jiāozhōu.
I note that Táng's Jiāozhōu and Fēngzhōu were both within the territory of Hàn's Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
so one cannot simply refer to Táng's single Jiāozhǐ County.)
He wrote to Ràng,
detailing the state's authority and virtue.
He also sent the Deputy General Qū Chōng to issue proclamations south of the Yangtze River,
disseminating imperial decrees.

As a result, Ràng, along with Jiāngxià's Grand Administrator Hóu Dēng, Wǔlíng's Grand Administrator Wáng Táng, Chángshā's Chancellor Hán Fú, Guìyáng's Grand Administrator Zhāng Lóng, Línglíng's Grand Administrator Tián Xī, Cāngwú's Grand Administrator Dù Mù, and Jiāozhǐ's Grand Administrator Xī Guāng, among others, sent envoys one after another to offer tribute.
(Jùn Guó Zhì: Jiāngxià Commandery is 1,500 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Wǔlíng Commandery is 2,100 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Chángshā Commandery is 2,800 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Guìyáng Commandery is 3,900 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Línglíng Commandery is 3,300 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Cāngwú Commandery is 6,410 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Jiāozhǐ Commandery is 11,000 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Xià is pronounced yǎ.
Shǒu is pronounced shì yòu;
the same below.
Xī is a surname;
Guāng is a given name.)
Xī Guāng was from Hànzhōng
and served in Jiāozhǐ,
teaching the barbarians rituals and righteousness.
The Emperor also appointed Rèn Yán from Wǎn as the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn.
(Jùn Guó Zhì: Jiǔzhēn Commandery is 11,580 lǐ south of Luòyáng.
Fù is pronounced fú yòu.
Rèn is pronounced rén.)
Thus, the influence of Huáxià culture south of the Língnán Mountains began with these two administrators.
24 In this year,
an edict summoned recluses such as Zhōu Dǎng from Tàiyuán and Yán Guāng from Kuàijī to the capital.
When Zhōu Dǎng entered for an audience,
he prostrated himself but did not pay homage.
(Generally, those attending court audiences must bow and kowtow, announcing their names.)
(Jiàn is pronounced xián biàn.)
The Erudite Fàn Shēng submitted a memorial, saying:
"I observe that Zhōu Dǎng from Tàiyuán, Wáng Liáng from Dōnghǎi, and Wáng Chéng from Shānyáng, among others,
having received great favor,
were invited three times by envoys
before they consented to board the carriage.
Yet when they appeared before the imperial court,
Zhōu Dǎng did not humble himself according to ritual,
prostrating without paying homage,
acting arrogantly and defiantly,
and departing together at the same time.
Zhōu Dǎng and the others are incapable of expounding righteousness through literature
or dying for their sovereign through martial prowess.
They fish for empty fame,
hoping to attain the position of the Three Excellencies.
I am willing to sit with them beneath the Yúntái
(Xù Hàn Zhì states: Yúntái was built by the Zhōu dynasty, where books, records, rare treasures, and curiosities were stored.)
If my words are untrue,
I will accept the charge of falsehood.
Yet they dare to privately seek empty fame,
boasting to the Emperor and seeking high positions—
all of this is grossly disrespectful!"
After the memorial was submitted,
an edict stated:
"Since ancient times, enlightened kings and sage rulers
have inevitably encountered those who would not submit.
Bóyí and Shūqí refused to eat the grain of Zhōu,
and Zhōu Dǎng of Tàiyuán refuses to accept my salary.
Each has his own principles.
Bestow upon him forty bolts of silk
and dismiss him."
The Emperor had studied with Yán Guāng in his youth.
After ascending the throne,
he sought him out based on his appearance.
(Xián notes: This means searching for him based on his physical features.)
After repeated summons, Yán Guāng finally came.
He was appointed as Grand Master of Remonstrance,
but he refused to accept the position.
He left
to farm and fish in the Fùchūn Mountains.
(Dìlǐ Zhì: Fùchūn County belonged to Kuàijī Commandery.
Xián notes: Present-day Fùyáng County in Hángzhōu was originally Hàn's Fùchūn County.
To avoid the taboo of the personal name of Jìn's Emperor Jiǎnwén's mother, Empress Dowager Zhèng,
it was renamed Fùyáng.)
Wáng Liáng later served as the Grand Administrator of Pèi Commandery and the Director of the Grand Minister over the Masses.
While in office, he was respectful and frugal,
using cloth bedding and earthenware,
and his wife and children did not enter the official residence.
Later, he returned home due to illness.
After one year, he was summoned again;
upon reaching Xíngyáng,
his illness became severe,
and he was unable to continue the journey.
It is said that due to his severe illness, he lingered on the road,
unable to proceed.
"Rèn"
is pronounced as "rén."
His friend refused to see him,
saying:
"Without loyal advice or extraordinary strategies, yet you attained high positions.
How tirelessly you have scurried back and forth, undaunted by the trouble!"
Yáng Xióng's *Fāngyán* states: "Xièxiè"
means restless;
in Qín and Jìn, it is called "xièxiè."
Guō Jǐngchún said: It describes the appearance of going back and forth.
Liáng felt ashamed,
and thereafter, despite repeated summons, he did not respond,
eventually dying at home.
During the reign of Emperor Yuán,
the King of Shāchē, Yán, once served as an attendant prince in the capital,
and admired and delighted in the Central Kingdom.
During the chaos of Wáng Mǎng's rebellion,
the Xiōngnú encroached upon the Western Regions,
but only Yán refused to submit;
he often instructed his sons:
"You must serve the Hàn family generation after generation,
and must not betray them!"
After Yán's death,
his son Kāng succeeded him.
Kāng led neighboring states to resist the Xiōngnú.
"Neighboring states"
means adjacent countries.
During the chaos of Wāng Mǎng's rebellion,
the Western Regions attacked and annihilated the Protector General,
and his officials, soldiers, wives, and children were all unable to return.
He inquired about the situation in the Central Kingdom.
Dòu Róng then, acting on imperial authority, established Kāng as the Hàn Shāchē Jiàngōng Huáidé King and Grand Commandant of the Western Regions,
and fifty-five states all submitted to him.

Later Student Tiāntāi Hú Sānshěng
Emperor Shìzǔ, the Middle Part of the Reign of Emperor Guāngwǔ
Sixth Year of Jiànwǔ
(Gēngyín, 30)
1 Spring,
First Month,
Bǐngchén,
Chōnglíng Township was made Zhānglíng County,
with perpetual exemption from corvée labor,
comparable to Fēng and Pèi.
2 Wú Hàn and others captured Qú,
beheading Dǒng Xiàn and Páng Méng.
The regions of Jiāng, Huái, and Shāndōng were all pacified.
According to Fàn's Annals,
that year, Mǎ Chéng and others captured Shū,
capturing Lǐ Xiàn;
Wú Hàn and others captured Qú,
beheading Dǒng Xiàn and Páng Méng.
It seems that capturing Lǐ Xiàn pacified Jiāng and Huái,
and beheading Dǒng Xiàn and Páng Méng
pacified Shāndōng.
Before capturing Qú,
the capture of Shū was omitted.
A banquet was held with rewards.
The Emperor, weary from prolonged military campaigns,
since Wěi Xiāo had sent his son to serve in the capital,
and Gōngsūn Shù was entrenched in a distant border region,
said to his generals:
"For now, let us set aside these two individuals."
He thus allowed the generals to rest in Luòyáng,
stationed troops in Hénèi,
and repeatedly sent messages to Lǒng and Shǔ,
explaining the consequences of fortune and misfortune.
*Shuōwén* states: "Téng"
means to transmit.
"Shuò"
is pronounced as "suǒ jiǎo fān."
Gōngsūn Shù repeatedly sent messages to the Central Kingdom,
proclaiming his own mandate,
hoping to confuse the masses.
The Emperor wrote to Shù:
"The prognosticatory texts speak of a Gōngsūn,
referring to Emperor Xuān.
Emperor Xuān had
the prophecy 'Gōngsūn Bìngyǐ.'
His name was exalted;
are you, sir, his embodiment?
Moreover, you take the lines on your palm as an auspicious sign."
Shù carved the lines on his palm as
"Gōngsūn Emperor,"
claiming his palm lines were extraordinary.
"Fù"
is pronounced as "fú yòu fān."
Wáng Mǎng proclaimed his own mandate,
