breath.
If we now pacify these two commanderies,
then Shù's schemes and strategies will be exhausted.
We should increase the selection of troops and horses,
and accumulate supplies and provisions.
Now Xīzhōu has recently been broken,
the soldiers and people are weary and hungry.
If we recruit them with wealth and grain,
then their masses can be gathered.
I know the state has many expenditures,
and resources are insufficient,
but this is a matter of necessity!"
The Emperor agreed.
Thereupon, an edict ordered the accumulation of sixty thousand hú of grain at Qiān.
In autumn, the eighth month,
Lái Xī led Féng Yì and four other generals to campaign against Wěi Chún in Tiānshuǐ.
7. Piàojì General Dù Mào fought Jiǎ Lǎn at Fánshí.
Xián said: Fánzhì County
belonged to Yànmén Commandery,
present-day Fánzhì County in Dài Prefecture.
Zhì:
pronunciation zhǐ.
I note: Although Táng Dynasty Dài Prefecture's Fánzhì retains the Hàn county name,
it is not the ancient Fánzhì.
8. Since the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign, the various Qiāng tribes had entered and settled within the frontier,
and many counties under Jīnchéng were occupied by them.
Wěi Xiāo could not subdue them,
so he appeased and accepted them,
mobilizing their masses to resist the Hàn.
Sītú Yuàn Bān Biāo submitted a statement:
According to the Continued Hàn Records: The Sītú had thirty-one yuàn and shǔ officials.
Yuàn were ranked equivalent to three hundred shí,
shǔ equivalent to two hundred shí.
"Now all the provinces of Liáng Prefecture have surrendered Qiāng.
The Qiāng and Hú wear their hair loose and fasten their garments on the left,
and live intermingled with Hàn people.
Their customs are already different,
and languages are not mutually intelligible.
They are repeatedly encroached upon and plundered by petty officials and cunning individuals,
driven to poverty, resentment, and hopelessness,
hence they rebel.
The raids and disturbances by the Mán and Yí barbarians
are all due to this.
According to the old system,
the Yìzhōu province established a Cavalry Commandant for the Mán and Yí.
When Emperor Wǔ opened up the Southwestern Yí,
he established one Commandant.
The Liángzhōu province established a Protector of the Qiāng Colonel.
Both held credentials and led and protected [the tribes].
Yìng Shào said: According to Hàn officialdom,
the Protector of the Wūhuán Colonel and the Protector of the Qiāng Colonel
were ranked equivalent to two thousand shí,
and held credentials.
They had one Chief Clerk,
and two Majors,
all ranked six hundred shí.
Xiào:
pronunciation hù jiào fān.
They made annual inspection tours,
inquiring about hardships and grievances.
They also frequently dispatched interpreters as envoys,
to communicate and guide, reporting on activities,
making the Qiāng and Yí tribes outside the frontier serve as the eyes and ears of the officials,
so that the provinces and commanderies could thereby be alerted and prepared.
Now we should restore the old system,
to clarify authority and defenses."
The Emperor followed this.
He appointed Niú Hán as Protector of the Qiāng Colonel.
9. Bandits killed Noble Lady Yīn's mother, Lady Dèng, and her younger brother, Xīn.
The Emperor was deeply grieved.
He enfeoffed the Noble Lady's younger brother, Jiù, as Marquis of Xuān'ēn.
The Emperor posthumously enfeoffed the Noble Lady's father, Lù, as Marquis of Xuān'ēn,
with Jiù succeeding to the marquisate.
According to the old system of the Later Hàn,
only the Empress's father was enfeoffed as a marquis.
The Noble Lady had not been formally established in the central palace, yet her father was posthumously enfeoffed;
this was not according to the old system.
When he wished to enfeoff him,
he placed the seal and ribbon before him.
Xìng firmly declined, saying:
"I have not achieved the merit of being first to ascend and break the enemy formation,
yet several members of my family
have all received noble titles and lands.
This would cause disappointment throughout the land;
I truly do not wish for this!"
The Emperor praised him,
and did not force his will.
The Noble Lady asked him the reason,
and Xìng said:
"The families of imperial in-laws suffer from not knowing modesty and restraint.
When marrying off daughters, they desire to match them with marquises and kings;
when taking wives, they covet princesses.
My foolish heart is truly uneasy about this.
Wealth and honor have limits;
one should know contentment.
Boasting and extravagance only invite more ridicule from observers and listeners."
The Noble Lady was moved by his words,
and deeply humbled and restrained herself.
To draw water with a vessel bowing down is called yì;
those who are humble and modest are also described as yì.
10. The Emperor recalled Kòu Xún,
and appointed Yúyáng Grand Administrator Guō Jí as Yǐngchuān Grand Administrator.
Jí recruited and accepted the surrender of mountain bandits Zhào Hóng and Shào Wú, among several hundred others,
and sent them all back to become attached farmers;
"attached farmers" means
being registered in the agricultural population.
Shào:
read as Shào.
Xián said: This refers to [the act of] releasing surrendered bandits.
Hé:
pronunciation hù gài fān.
Later, Hóng and Wú's partisans, hearing of Jí's prestige and trustworthiness,
came from as far as Jiāngnán,
or from Yōu and Jì,
arriving without prior arrangement to surrender,
in an endless stream.
11 The king of Shāchē, Kāng, died.
His younger brother Xián succeeded him.
He attacked and killed the kings of Jūmí and Xīyè.
Jūmí
was the Wūmí of the Former Hàn.
The Táng called it Níngmí.
The state of Xīyè
was 14,400 lǐ from Luòyáng.
Wáng,
read as Yúkuàng.
1 Spring,
first month,
Wú Hàn again led the four generals including the General Who Captures Foes, Wáng Bà, with 60,000 men out of Gāoliǔ to attack Jiǎ Lǎn.
Several thousand Xiongnu cavalry came to their rescue.
They fought successive battles below Píngchéng.
Píngchéng County
belonged to Yànmén Commandery.
2 Xiàyáng Marquis Féng Yì and others
The Biography of Féng Yì says: Féng Yì was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yánghxià.
Xián said: Xià
is pronounced Jiǎ.
At the end of the Biography of Mǎ Wǔ, the official positions and names of the twenty-eight generals are listed,
saying: Marquis of Xiàyáng, Féng Yì.
Yángjiǎ County belonged to Huáiyáng Commandery.
Xiàyáng County belonged to Zuǒ Féngyì.
It is unknown which is correct.
The "xià" in Xiàyáng
is pronounced hù yǎ.
All were beheaded.
Wěi Chún had not yet surrendered.
The various generals wanted to temporarily return and rest the troops.
Yì firmly held his ground and did not move.
Together they attacked Luòmén.
Jì County in Tiānshuǐ had the settlement of Luòmén,
and there was Luòmén Mountain.
Xián said: It is located southeast of present-day Lǒngxī County in Wèi Prefecture.
In summer,
Yì died in the army.
3 Autumn,
eighth month,
Jǐhài,
the Emperor went to Cháng'ān.
4 Initially,
Wěi Xiāo's general Gāo Jùn from Āndìng held troops and occupied Gāopíng Dìyī.
When the Emperor went up to Lǒng,
he sent Mǎ Yuán to summon Jùn to surrender.
When Wú Hàn and the other armies retreated,
Jùn fled back to his old camp.
He again assisted Xiāo in resisting at Lǒngdǐ.
For a year it could not be taken.
The Emperor personally led a campaign against him.
Kòu Xún admonished, saying:
"Cháng'ān is centrally located in terms of road distances.
Xián said: From Luòyáng to Gāopíng,
Cháng'ān is the midpoint.
Āndìng and Lǒngxī will certainly harbor fear and trepidation;
by remaining calmly in one place,
one can control the four quarters.
Now the soldiers and horses are weary,
and we are about to traverse dangerous terrain;
this is not secure for the imperial carriage.
The events of the previous year in Yǐngchuān
can serve as the utmost warning."
The Emperor did not heed him,
advanced
and went to Qiān.
Jùn still did not surrender.
The Emperor sent Kòu Xún to go and make him surrender.
Xún, bearing the imperial seal document, arrived at Dìyī.
Jùn sent his military advisor Huángfǔ Wén out to meet him.
His speech and demeanor were not submissive.
Xún was angry
and was about to execute him.
The various generals admonished, saying:
"Gāo Jùn has ten thousand elite troops,
mostly strong crossbowmen,
blocking the Lǒng road to the west.
For years we could not take it.
Now we wish to make him surrender, yet instead kill his envoy;
is this not unacceptable?"
Xún did not respond,
then beheaded him.
He sent his deputy back to report to Jùn, saying:
"The military advisor was disrespectful;
he has already been executed!
If you wish to surrender,
surrender quickly;
if not,
hold firm!"
Jùn was terrified
and that very day opened the city gates and surrendered.
The various generals all congratulated him,
and then said:
"May we ask, by killing his envoy you made his city surrender;
why is that?"
Xún said:
"Huángfǔ Wén
was Jùn's trusted confidant,
the one from whom he sought plans.
Now he came
with speech and intent unyielding;
he certainly had no intention to surrender.
Sparing him would allow Wén to achieve his plan;
killing him destroys his courage.
This means that with Wén dead, Jùn lost his courage.
The various generals all said:
"This is beyond our reach!"
5 Winter,
tenth month,
Lái Xī and the various generals attacked and took Luòmén.
Zhōu Zōng, Xíng Xún, Xún Yǔ, Zhào Huī, and others led Wěi Chún to surrender.
Wáng Yuán fled to Shǔ.
The various members of the Wěi clan were relocated to the area east of the capital.
Wěi Chún surrendered, and his clan was relocated
because they were a powerful clan of Xīzhōu,
and it was feared they might later again be able to cause trouble.
When they reached Wǔwēi,
they were captured
and executed.
6 The Xiānlíng Qiāng and various tribes raided Jīnchéng and Lǒngxī.
Lái Xī led Gài Yán and others to advance and attack them,
greatly defeating them,
beheading and capturing several thousand.
Thereupon, granaries were opened to relieve famine and want.
Lǒngyòu was then pacified,
and Liáng Prefecture became accessible.
The various commanderies of Liáng Prefecture, to reach the capital,
all had to cross Lǒng.
With Lǒngyòu pacified,
the road to Liáng Prefecture was open.
7 Gēngyín,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
1 Spring,
third month,
Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor went to Nányáng.
Textual analysis says: The Annals of the Emperor:
"Jǐyǒu,
went to Nányáng;
Gēngwǔ,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace."
Above it has
"second month Jǐmǎo."
The Annals of Yuán:
"Third month Jǐyǒu,
went to Nányáng."
Using the perpetual calendar to examine it,
the second month began on Rénshēn,
Jǐmǎo was the eighth day.
Jǐyǒu and Gēngwǔ
are both in the third month.
Probably in the Annals of the Emperor,
above "Jǐyǒu"
the characters
"third month"
are missing.
Now follow the Annals of Yuán.
Gēngwǔ,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
2 Cén Péng was stationed at Jīnxiāng,
repeatedly attacking Tián Róng and others,
but could not defeat them.
The Emperor sent Wú Hàn to lead the three generals including the General Who Punishes Foes, Liú Lóng,
mobilizing the troops of Jīng Prefecture totaling over 60,000 men and 5,000 cavalry,
to join Péng at Jīngmén.
Péng outfitted several thousand
warships.
Wú Hàn considered that the oarsmen from the various commanderies consumed much grain,
and wanted to dismiss them.
Oarsmen
are those who handle oars to move boats.
Péng considered that they could not be sent away,
and sent a memorial reporting the situation.
The Emperor replied to Péng, saying:
"The Grand Marshal is accustomed to using infantry and cavalry;
he does not understand naval warfare.
Matters at Jīngmén
are entirely to be decided by you, the Duke Who Conquers the South."
Péng was the Great General Who Conquers the South,
hence he was called the Duke Who Conquers the South.
In the intercalary month,
Cén Péng ordered the army to recruit volunteers to attack the pontoon bridge,
promising the highest reward to the first to ascend.
Thereupon, the Assistant General Lǔ Qí responded to the recruitment and advanced.
At that time, the east wind was fiercely strong,
and Lǔ Qí's boat went upstream against the current,
heading straight for the pontoon bridge.
There were reverse grappling hooks on the bridge's clustered pillars.
These reverse grappling hooks,
once they hooked onto an enemy boat,
prevented it from retreating,
and also resisted it from advancing.
Qí and others took advantage of the situation and fought desperately,
then hurled torches to burn it.
The wind fanned the flames,
and the bridge towers collapsed and burned.
Cén Péng led his entire army to advance with the wind,
unstoppable wherever they went.
The Shǔ troops fell into great chaos,
with several thousand drowning.
Rén Mǎn was beheaded,
Chéng Fàn was captured alive,
and Tián Róng fled to defend Jiāngzhōu.
Péng recommended Liú Lóng to be the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn;
he first had Lóng act as Grand Administrator of Nánjùn and then submitted the recommendation.
"Shàng" [to recommend]
is pronounced according to the contemporary reading.
The Huáyáng Guózhì states: When Bā and Chǔ attacked each other,
the Jiāngguān was established.
It was originally at Chìjiǎchéng,
but later moved to the southern bank of Jiāngzhōu,
facing Báidìchéng.
The old city is located south of Yúfù County in Kuízhōu today,
which is the ancient Hànguān.
Dù Yòu said: Bāshān County
is the ancient Hànguān.
If so, then it is a different place.
The common people along the way all offered oxen and wine to welcome and reward them.
Péng again declined and did not accept;
the common people were greatly pleased,
and competed to open their city gates and surrender.
An edict appointed Péng as Acting Governor of Yìzhōu,
and for each commandery he captured, he was to act as its Grand Administrator.
If Péng left the region,
he was to transfer the title of Grand Administrator to the Rear General.
The Rear General
was the one leading troops to follow behind Péng and advance.
Péng arrived at Jiāngzhōu,
and because its walls were strong and provisions plentiful,
making it difficult to capture quickly,
he left Féng Jùn to guard it;
he himself led troops to take advantage of the victory and head straight for Diànjiāng,
attacking and capturing Píngqū.
Xián said: Diànjiāng,
a county name,
belonged to Bā Commandery,
which is today's Zhōngzhōu County.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn: Zhōngzhōu Diànjiāng County was originally the territory of Línjiāng County in the Later Hàn,
and later, during the Wèi, Emperor Gōng divided Línjiāng to establish Diànjiāng County.
Shíjìng County in Hézhōu
was originally Hàn's Diànjiāng County.
Generally, all counties under Hézhōu's jurisdiction
were the territory of Hàn's Diànjiāng.
"Diàn"
is pronounced "tuó xié fān."
Píngqū,
its location is missing.
Wú Hàn stayed at Yílíng,
preparing boats with exposed oars to follow and advance.
The Ěryǎ says: "Jí is called ráo."
"Lù ráo"
means the oars are exposed outside,
while people are inside the boat.
"Ráo"
is pronounced "ráo."
3 In summer,
the Xiānliáng Qiāng invaded Líntáo.
Líntáo County
belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery.
"Líng"
is pronounced "lián."
"Táo"
is pronounced "tāo."
The Jùn Guó Zhì states: Lǒngxī Commandery
was 2,220 lǐ west of Luòyáng.
They were greatly defeated.
4 Gōngsūn Shù appointed Wáng Yuán as a general,
and sent him with the Army Commander Huán Ān to defend Héchí.
The Xìng Pǔ states: Huán,
a surname,
descended from the Huánliè Yǐn of Chǔ;
also, there was a worthy man named Huán Yuān in Chǔ.
Héchí County
belonged to Wǔdū Commandery.
Lái Xī and Gài Yán, among others, attacked Yuán and Ān,
greatly defeating them,
and then captured Xiàbiàn.
They took advantage of the victory to advance.
The people of Shǔ were greatly frightened,
and sent an assassin to stab Xī.
He was not yet dead,
not yet dead,
meaning not yet expired.
"Cì" [to stab]
is pronounced "qī yì fān."
Yán went to see Xī,
and prostrated himself in grief,
unable to look up.
Xī rebuked Yán, saying:
"How dare you, Hǔyá, act like this!
Yán was the Hǔyá Grand General,
hence he was addressed as Hǔyá.
I have no way to repay the state,
so I called Jùqīng,
wishing to entrust military affairs to you."
Gài Yán's
courtesy name was Jùqīng.
"Zhǔ" [to entrust]
is pronounced "zhī yù fān."
"Although the blade is in my body,
can you not command the troops and behead me!"
Yán wiped his tears and forced himself to rise,
accepting the instructions.
Xī personally wrote a memorial, saying:
"Your subject was stabbed after the hour of Réndìng at night,
when the sun had set and all was quiet.
Hence, the first watch of the night is called Réndìng.
I was struck in a vital spot.
By whom,
meaning it is not known by whom.
I deeply regret that I have not been worthy in performing my duties,
bringing shame upon the court.
Governing a state is fundamentally about obtaining worthy men.
The Grand Palace Grandee Duàn Xiāng,
upright and steadfast, can be entrusted with responsibilities.
Xián said: "Gǔgěng"
means upright and honest.
The Shuōwén states: "Gěng,"
fish bone;
a bone stuck in the throat while eating is called "gěng."
Also, my brothers are unworthy,
and I fear they will eventually be punished.
I beg Your Majesty to take pity,
and frequently instruct and supervise them."
He threw down the brush, pulled out the blade, and died.
Generally, for those who are stabbed by others,
the blade remains in the body and is not yet seen;
pulling out the blade causes the breath to cease.
The Emperor was greatly shocked,
read the letter, and wiped away tears;
he appointed the General Who Spreads Martial Might, Mǎ Chéng, to act as General of the Household and replace him.
Xī's coffin was returned to Luòyáng,
and the Emperor, in plain white mourning clothes, came to pay his respects,
and attended the funeral.
5 King of Zhào, Liáng, followed the Emperor to see off Xī's coffin and return.
Entering the Xiàchéng Gate,
Luòyáng had twelve city gates,
with the Xià Gate located in the Hài position.
He shouted at Hán to turn the carriage around;
he also interrogated and reprimanded the gate captain.
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: The Colonel of the City Gates was in charge of Luòyáng's twelve city gates,
with one gate captain for each gate.
"Hán"
is pronounced "hù gān fān."
The Colonel-Director of Retainers, Bào Yǒng, impeached him,
stating, "Liáng showed no respect as a feudal lord,
committing a grave act of disrespect."
Liáng was noble, a relative, and held high status,
yet Yǒng impeached him,
and the court was awed into solemnity.
Yǒng recruited Bào Huī of Fúfēng as the Capital Official Clerk.
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: The Colonel-Director of Retainers had twelve Clerks,
and the Capital Official Clerk
was in charge of investigating and impeaching officials who broke the law.
Cài Zhì's Hàn Yí states: The Capital Official was in charge of Luòyáng court assemblies,
and was the same as the assistants of the Three Excellencies.
He did not avoid the powerful.
The Emperor often said:
"The noble relatives should restrain themselves and avoid the two Bàos."
Bào Yǒng traveled from Yǒngxíng County to Bàlíng.
The Inspector of the Capital Region
was in charge of the three Hé regions, the three Fǔ regions, and Hóngnóng.
Bàlíng County
belonged to Jīngzhào.
Traveling,
read as xià mèng fān.
He dismounted and bowed,
wept to express his utmost grief, and then departed.
He went west to Fúfēng,
where he sacrificed an ox at Xún Jiàn's grave.
The incident of Xún Jiàn protecting Bào Yǒng is recorded in the thirty-sixth year of the Gēngshǐ era.
Sacrificed,
read as shí zhǎng fān.
The Emperor was displeased,
and asked the high ministers:
"What do you think of
an envoy acting like this?"
Emperor Wǔ established thirteen Regional Inspectors,
all of whom were regional envoys.
The Inspector of the Capital Region was now acting within his jurisdiction,
hence it was said he was acting as an envoy.
Envoy,
read as shū lì fān.
"Benevolence
is the root of conduct,
and loyalty
is the master of righteousness.
Benevolence does not abandon the old,
loyalty does not forget the ruler.
This is the highest form of conduct."
The Emperor's displeasure then subsided.
6 The Emperor personally led the campaign against Gōngsūn Shù.
In autumn, the seventh month,
he encamped at Cháng'ān.
7 Gōngsūn Shù sent his generals Yán Cén, Lǚ Wěi, Wáng Yuán, and Gōngsūn Huī with all their troops to resist at Guànghàn and Zīzhōng.
Guànghàn County
belonged to Guànghàn Commandery.
Xián said: Zīzhōng,
a county name,
belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery.
Its location is in present-day Zīyáng County, Zī Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: The various counties of Zī Prefecture
were all part of the Hàn-era Zīzhōng territory.
Pánshí County,
the seat of Zī Prefecture,
is the site of the old Hàn Zīzhōng city.
Xián said: This is Huángshí Tān.
The Commentary on the Water Classic says: The Jiāng River flows east from Fúlíng for a hundred lǐ and reaches Huángshí.
It is in present-day Fúlíng County, Fú Prefecture.
Dù Yòu said: It is now called Héngshí Tān.
Cén Péng advanced from the Fú River to Píngqū,
to resist Yán Cén.
He then divided his forces, sending some to float down the river to return to Jiāngzhōu,
and others to sail up the Dū River.
Xián said: The Dū River
is the Chéngdū River.
Sòng Bái said: The Pí River,
also called the Dū River,
also called the Chéngdū River.
He inflicted a major defeat on them.
Then, marching day and night, covering over two thousand lǐ at double speed,
he directly captured Wǔyáng.
Xián said: Wǔyáng County,
belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery.
Its old city is east of present-day Lóngshān County, Lóng Prefecture.
He also said: The old city is in present-day Méi Prefecture.
Liú Xù said: Táng-era Rénshòu County, Líng Prefecture,
was the territory of Hàn-era Wǔyáng County.
Some say: Present-day Méishān and Péngshān counties, Méi Prefecture,
were originally the territory of Hàn-era Wǔyáng County.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Hàn-era Wǔyáng County
is east of Suíshān County, Jiā Prefecture.
He then sent a light cavalry to attack Guǎngdū,
Xián said: Guǎngdū,
a county name,
belonged to Shǔ Commandery.
Its old city is southeast of present-day Chéngdū County, Yì Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: According to Shǔ records,
Guǎngdū County was established in the second year of Yuánshuò of the Hàn.
In the first year of Rénshòu of the Suí,
to avoid the taboo of Emperor Yáng's name,
it was changed to Shuāngliú.
In the third year of Lóngshuò of the Táng,
Shuāngliú County was divided,
and Guǎngdū County was re-established twelve lǐ south of the old county.
Wherever they arrived, the enemy scattered and fled.
Initially,
Shù heard that the Hàn army was at Píngqū,
so he sent a large force to oppose it.
By the time Péng reached Wǔyáng,
he had circled behind Yán Cén's army.
Shǔ was shaken with terror.
Shù was greatly alarmed.
Striking the ground with his staff, he said:
"What kind of god is this!"
Yán Cén massed his troops at Yuánshuǐ.
The Imperial Annals record it as
"Shěnshuǐ".
Here it is written as
"Yuán",
following the error in Zāng Gōng's biography.
Xián said: The Commentary on the Water Classic says: The Shěn River originates from Guànghàn County
and flows into the Fú River.
Some versions write it as
"Chénshuǐ"
or
"Yuánshuǐ",
but both are incorrect.
According to my research, present-day Tōngquán County, Tóngchuān Prefecture, has the Shěn River to its north.
Supplies did not arrive,
and those who had surrendered all wanted to disperse and rebel in the commanderies and counties.
They again gathered for protection,
watching to see the outcome.
Gōng wanted to withdraw,
but feared they would
rebel.
Just then, the Emperor sent a Court Gentleman with troops to Cén Péng,
who had seven hundred horses.
Gōng falsely appropriated them by imperial decree to strengthen himself.
Advancing day and night,
he displayed many banners and flags,
climbed hills and raised a clamor,
with infantry on the right and cavalry on the left,
pulling boats along,
their shouts shaking the mountains and valleys.
Cén had not expected the Hàn army to arrive so suddenly.
Climbing a hill to look,
he was greatly shocked and terrified.
Gōng then launched an attack,
inflicting a major defeat.
Over ten thousand were beheaded or drowned,
and the water was muddied by it.
Yán Cén fled to Chéngdū.
His troops all surrendered,
and all his horses, troops, and treasures were captured.
From then on, he pursued the defeated northward.
Xián said: People prefer yang and dislike yin.
The north is a dark, yin region,
so those defeated in battle are all called 'north'.
The Records of the Grand Historian, Treatise on Music says: 'North'
means defeat.

yíng,

Lǐ Xián's note: Stiff-necked,

"Piào",

the Left Wing King Liú Yān was transferred to become King of Zhōngshān.
4 In the fifth month,
there was a great flood.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the dīngyǒu day,
the Emperor traveled to Lǔ;
in winter,
in the eleventh month,
on the dīngyǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
6 Jiāo Dōng's Gāng Marquis Jiǎ Fù passed away.
The rules for posthumous titles state: One who can remedy past faults is called 'Gāng' (Firm).
Here, Jiǎ Fù was simply given this title because of his firm and resolute character.
Textual analysis notes: His biography places this in the thirty-first year.
Here we follow Yuán Jì.
He never suffered defeat,
and repeatedly broke through enemy encirclements with various generals to resolve crises,
receiving twelve wounds on his body.
The Emperor, because Jiǎ Fù dared to penetrate deep [into enemy lines],
rarely ordered him on distant campaigns,
yet admired his brave spirit,
and often kept him by his side,
meaning the Emperor often had Jiǎ Fù accompany him.
Whenever the generals discussed merits and achievements,
Jiǎ Fù never spoke.
The Emperor would always say:
"The merits of Sir Jiǎ,
I know them myself."
1 In summer,
in the fifth month,
there was a great flood.
2 On the last day of the month, guǐyǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 Locusts [appeared].
4 The Yuán of Jīngzhào, Dìwǔ Lún,
Lún's ancestors
were from the various Tián clans of Qí,
who were relocated to Chánglíng;
as many of the various Tián clans were relocated to the imperial tombs,
they thus took their order of relocation as their surname.
Yuàn (掾),
is pronounced yú juàn fān.
He was fair, upright, incorruptible, and principled,
and the market had no deceit or injustice.
Whenever he read an imperial edict,
he would often sigh and say:
"This is a sage ruler;
one meeting would decide it."
His peers laughed at him, saying:
"You cannot even persuade a general to accept you,"
Xián's commentary: 'General' refers to the provincial general.
Shuō (说),
is pronounced shū ruì fān.
Jiàng (将),
is pronounced jí liàng fān.
Lún said:
"I have not yet met one who understands me;
it is because our ways differ."
Later, he was recommended as Xiàolián,
and appointed as the Medical Artisan Chief of the Prince of Huáiyáng.
The Treatise on Officials states: Among the officials of a princely state, there is a Director of Rites and Music,
in charge of musicians;
a Chief of Guards,
in charge of guards;
a Chief of Medical Artisans,
in charge of medicine;
a Chief of the Eternal Lane,
in charge of palace maids;
a Chief of Sacrifices,
in charge of sacrificial rites;
all are ranked at four hundred shí.
Zhǎng (长),
is pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
the Prince of Huáiyáng came to court,
and Lún, following his official retinue, was able to have an audience.
The Emperor asked him about government affairs,
and Lún responded accordingly;
the Emperor was greatly pleased.
The next day,
he specially summoned Lún again,
and spoke with him until evening.
The Emperor said to Lún:
"I have heard that when you were an official,
you caned your father-in-law,
and would not even eat a meal with your elder cousin;
is there any truth to this?"
He replied:
"Your servant has been married three times,
and none of my wives had a father.
In my youth, I suffered famine and turmoil,
and truly did not dare to casually accept meals from others.
People, because I am foolish and ignorant,
thus created such talk."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
He appointed Lún as the Chief of Fúyí,
Xián's commentary: Fúyí County
belonged to Línglíng Commandery;
its old city is northeast of present-day Wǔgāng County in Shào Prefecture.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Fūyí County is west of Shàolíng.
He was subsequently appointed as the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī;
his governance was pure and benevolent,
and the people loved him.
In this year,
the construction of the Bright Hall, Spirit Terrace, and Piyong Academy began.
Xian's commentary: According to the Han Official Rituals, the Bright Hall was located about two li from the Pingcheng Gate.
When the Son of Heaven went out through the Pingcheng Gate,
he would first pass by the Bright Hall
before proceeding to the suburban sacrifices.
It also states: The Piyong Academy
was three hundred paces from the Bright Hall.
When the imperial carriage arrived at the Piyong Academy,
it entered through the north gate.
In the third and ninth months,
the village archery ceremonies were all held within it.
The Piyong Academy
was surrounded by water on the outside,
to regulate the view for observers.
The Han Palaces and Towers Record states: The Spirit Terrace
was three zhang high,
with twelve gates.
Yáng Xuànzhī's Record of Luòyáng states: Directly south of the Píngchāng Gate,
east of the main road was the Bright Hall,
and west of the main road was the Spirit Terrace.
Initially,
the Emperor ascended the throne based on the Red Talisman prophecy,
see the 40th scroll, first year of the Jiànwǔ era.
He often used it to resolve doubts and suspicions.
The Court Gentleman-in-Attendance, Huán Tán, submitted a memorial admonishing:
"Generally, people tend to overlook what is before their eyes and value unusual tales.
Examining the records and accounts of the former kings,
all were fundamentally based on benevolence, righteousness, and the correct Way,
and did not contain strange or fantastical matters.
Matters such as the Way of Heaven and human nature and destiny
are difficult even for sages to speak of.
From Zǐgòng downward,
none were able to hear of them.
The Analects: Zǐgòng said: 'The Master's discourses about man's nature, and the way of Heaven,
cannot be heard.'
How could they comprehend it!
Now, all those clever, petty-talented individuals skilled in techniques and calculations,
augmenting charts and texts,
falsely claiming prognostications and records—
'Jì'
refers to methods and techniques,
such as those of medical practitioners.
'Shù'
refers to numerology and divination.
The Bright Hall officials Yì Hé and the historians and diviners.
'Charts and texts'
refers to things like prophecies, apocrypha, and portentous mandates.
'Jì'
is pronounced qí, with the qǐ tone.
They mislead the ruler;
how can they not be suppressed and kept at a distance!
Your subject Tán humbly hears that Your Majesty has thoroughly refuted the alchemists' techniques for producing gold and silver,
which is most wise;
'Huáng bái'
refers to using elixirs to transform into gold and silver.
'Fāngshì'
are men possessing esoteric arts.
How mistaken this is!
Although such matters may occasionally coincide,
it is akin to the occasional hits of divination or the matching of pairs.
Xián's commentary: Meaning occasional accuracy.
I urge Your Majesty to
reject these petty, biased theories,
and expound the orthodox meaning of the Five Classics."
The memorial was submitted,
and the Emperor was displeased.
Later, when discussing the location for the Spirit Terrace,
the Emperor said to Huán Tán:
"I wish to decide it using the prophecies.
What do you think?"
Huán Tán remained silent.
After a long while, he said:
"Your subject does not read the prophecies."
The Emperor asked him why,
and Huán Tán again exhaustively argued that the prophecies were not canonical.
The Emperor became furious and said:
"Huán Tán defies the sages and has no respect for law!
Take him down,
and execute him!"
Huán Tán kowtowed until his head bled.
After a long while,
he was finally spared.
He was sent out to serve as Assistant Administrator of the Liù'ān Commandery.
Xián's commentary: The old city of Liù'ān Commandery
was located south of present-day Ānfēng County, Shòu Prefecture.
According to my reference to the Treatise on Commanderies and States,
in the 16th year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the Kingdom of Liù'ān was abolished,
and its counties were placed under Lújiāng Commandery.
Huán Tán being sent out as a commandery assistant
certainly did not occur in this year.
The Comprehensive Mirror, due to the Spirit Terrace matter,
records it all together here.
Fàn Yè's commentary states: Huán Tán was exiled for not being skilled with the prophecies;
Zhèng Xīng barely escaped by using humble words;
Jiǎ Kuí was able to accommodate and embellish the texts,
and consequently became the most honored and prominent;
Zhèng Xīng's affair is seen in the 42nd scroll, seventh year.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng,
Jiǎ Kuí submitted a statement saying: The Zuǒ Commentary accords with the charts and prophecies,
clarifying that the Liú clan are descendants of Yáo.
The Emperor praised him,
and he was successively promoted to Palace Attendant,
concurrently holding the post of Commandant of Cavalry,
and was greatly trusted and employed.
'Fù'
is read as 'attach'.
How lamentable!
Kuí
was from Fúfēng.
14. The Southern Chányú Bǐ died.
His younger brother, the Left Virtuous King Mò, succeeded him,
becoming the Qiūfúyóudī Chányú.
The Emperor sent an envoy bearing the imperial seal and edict to confer the seal and ribbons,
and bestowed robes, caps, and silks.
Thereafter, this became the customary practice.
1. Spring,
first month,
on Xīnwèi day,
the Northern Suburban Altar was first established,
to sacrifice to the Earth Spirit.
2. Second month,
on Wùxū day,
the Emperor passed away in the front hall of the Southern Palace,
at the age of sixty-two.
The Emperor held court every morning,
and only retired when the sun began to decline.
The sun declining means past midday.
'Cháo' (court)
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
He would discuss and lecture on the principles of the classics,
and only sleep at midnight.
Xián's commentary: 'Fēn'
means half.
Taking an opportunity to admonish him, they said:
"Your Majesty possesses the wisdom of Yǔ and Tāng,
yet lacks the life-nourishing blessings of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ.
We hope you will cherish and nurture your vital spirit,
and leisurely enjoy peace."
The Emperor said:
"I find joy in this myself,
and do not feel weary!"
'Lè' (joy)
is pronounced luò.
After the empire was stabilized,
he retired the meritorious generals and advanced civil officials,
was clear and cautious in governance,
personally controlled the reins of power,
measured the times and assessed capabilities,
and undertook no misguided actions.
Therefore, he was able to restore the former glory,
and personally brought about great peace.
The Grand Commandant Zhào Xǐ presided over the funeral arrangements.
At that time, following the turmoil of Wáng Mǎng's rebellion,
the old rituals no longer existed.
The Crown Prince and the various kings mingled and sat together on the same mat.
Officials from the feudal states entered and exited the palace precincts.
'Palace precincts'
refers to the palace forbidden areas.
Zhào Xǐ assumed a stern expression,
placed his sword across the palace steps,
and escorted the various kings down to clarify the distinction between noble and humble.
He memorialized to send court ushers to lead and guard the officials, having them reside separately in other counties.
He ordered all the kings to proceed to their lodges.
Each king's state maintained a lodge in Luòyáng.
He rectified the rituals and ceremonies,
and strictly enforced the gate guards.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn said: At each gate of the Hàn palaces, one Commandant was assigned to guard the gate,
with a rank comparable to 1,000 shi,
all called Commandants of the Palace Gates.
3. The Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne,
and honored the Empress as Empress Dowager.
3. Dōnghǎi Gōngwáng Liú Qiáng fell ill.
The Emperor dispatched envoys and imperial physicians via the postal relay system to attend to his illness,
with a continuous stream of messengers.
"Yì" refers to
relay horses for transmission.
The Zuǒzhuàn calls them "chéng rì,"
meaning riding relay horses.
In the Western Hàn, they were called "zhì zhuàn" and "chí zhuàn."
"Luò yì" means
an unbroken flow of traffic.
On the Wùyín day,
Qiáng passed away.
On his deathbed,
he submitted a memorial expressing gratitude for imperial grace,
stating:
"I, having met an untimely fate,
leave my orphaned and weak descendants to be a source of worry for the Empress Dowager and Your Majesty."
This means that he, having died prematurely,
would cause his descendants to bring worry to those above.
"Yāo"
is pronounced yāo.
"Fù"
is pronounced fù;
the same below.
My son Zhèng,
a petty man,
"Xī" meaning
son;
Zhèng is his name.
He is certainly not one who can preserve and benefit from it.
I wish to return the Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Now that the realm has newly suffered a great sorrow,
referring to Emperor Guāngwǔ's demise.
I have repeatedly presented imperial meals.
I, Qiáng, am frail and feeble,
and words cannot fully express my thoughts.
I wish to also convey my gratitude to all the kings.
I never imagined I would never see you all again!"
The Emperor, upon reading the letter, was deeply grieved and mournful.
He accompanied the Empress Dowager to the Jīnmén Pavilion to express mourning.
Xián's commentary states: Jīnmén
is the westernmost gate on the southern wall of Luòyáng,
also called Jīnyáng Gate.
Each gate had a pavilion.
Lǐ Yóu's inscription
mentions Jīnmén's position.
The Treatise on Officials states: The Minister of Works is in charge of water and earth affairs;
for major funerals,
he oversees the officers and troops for the burial mound construction.
Now he is sent to oversee the funeral of a feudal king,
an exceptional ritual.
An edict ordered King Yīng of Chǔ, King Xǔ of Zhào, King Xīng of Běihǎi, and relatives in the capital to all attend the funeral.
The Emperor, reflecting on Qiáng's profound adherence to humility and frugality,
"wéi" meaning
to think,
issued a special edict:
"The items sent for the funeral
must be frugal and simple.
Clothing sufficient to cover the body,
a thatched carriage and earthenware vessels,
items reduced from the standard regulations,
to manifest the king's outstanding and uniquely steadfast will."
The Superintendent of the Palace Buildings remained to construct the tomb and temple.
In the Qín dynasty, it was called the Junior Minister of the Palace Buildings;
Emperor Jǐng changed it to Superintendent of the Palace Buildings.
He was in charge of construction work for ancestral temples, the main palace hall, palaces, and tomb gardens,
and also planting trees like tóng and zǐ,
lining the sides of the roads.
4. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Mǎ Wǔ and others attacked the Shāodāng Qiāng,
inflicting a major defeat upon them.
The remnants all surrendered or dispersed.
5. Shānyáng King Liú Jīng privately received a person skilled in astrology,
and conspired with him,
hoping for upheaval in the realm.
The Emperor, hearing of this,
transferred Jīng's title to King of Guǎnglíng,
and sent him to his fief.
The Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms states,
Guǎnglíng
is 1,640 lǐ east of Luòyáng.
6. Liáodōng Grand Administrator Jì Róng sent Piān Hé to attack Chìshān.
The surname Piān
descended from Gāoxīn.
The Jíjiùpiān includes the surnames Piān, Lǚ, and Hé.
The Account of the Wūhuán states: Chìshān
is several thousand lǐ northwest of Liáodōng.
The Account of the Xiānbēi states: Piān Hé attacked the Wūhuán leader Qīn
[Xīn]
of Chìshān in Yùyáng. It seems Xīn Zhìbēn was of the Chìshān tribe and lived outside the Yùyáng frontier.
He inflicted a major defeat upon them,
beheading their chieftain.
The regions beyond the frontier were awed and terrified.
From Wǔwēi in the west
to Xuāntú in the east,
the Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms states: Wǔwēi Commandery
is 3,500 lǐ west of Luòyáng.
Xuāntú Commandery
is 4,000 lǐ northeast of Luòyáng.
"Tú"
is pronounced tú.
The wilds were free of turmoil,
so all border garrison troops were withdrawn.
7. King Cāng of Dōngpíng believed that over thirty years since the restoration,
the four quarters were without concerns,
and it was appropriate to cultivate rites and music.
He thus deliberated with the high ministers to establish the ceremonial caps, chariots, and attire regulations for the southern and northern suburban sacrifices.
In the second year of Emperor Guāngwǔ's Jiànwǔ reign,
the southern suburban altar was established.
In the first year of the Zhōngyuán reign period,
the northern suburban altar was established four lǐ north of Luòyáng.
Now their caps, chariots, and attire regulations were determined.
The Hàn Official Ceremonial states: The northern suburban altar is at the northwest corner of the city,
about one lǐ from the city walls.
It was submitted to the Emperor.
The Record states: Singing,
valued for its human voice by those above.
The Son of Heaven's ceremonial dance uses eight rows of eight dancers each,
sixty-four persons in total,
as eight times eight equals sixty-four.
"Yì"
is pronounced yì,
meaning dance rows.
"Shàng"
is pronounced shàng.
8. Hǎozhì Mǐn Hóu Gěng Yǎn passed away.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
the Emperor visited the Imperial Academy,
where for the first time the ceremony of honoring the elderly was performed;
Lǐ Gōng was appointed as the Sānlǎo,
and Huán Róng as the Wǔgēng.
The Sānlǎo wore a robe of fine Dūzhù cloth,
a Jìnxián cap,
and held a jade staff;
the Wǔgēng was similarly attired,
but without a staff.
The imperial carriage arrived at the ceremonial hall of the Imperial Academy,
and the Emperor took his seat in the eastern wing.
Messengers were dispatched with comfortable carriages to welcome the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng from the lecture hall of the Imperial University.
The Emperor greeted them at the gate screen,
and they exchanged courtesies.
The Emperor proceeded along the eastern steps,
while the Sānlǎo ascended by the guest steps.
Upon reaching the steps,
the Emperor bowed in accordance with ritual.
The Sānlǎo ascended,
facing east.
The Three Excellencies set out a small table,
and the Nine Ministers straightened his shoes.
The Emperor personally bared his arm and cut the sacrificial animal,
then, holding the sauce, he served the food.
"Served"
means to present food.
"Sauce,"
being the primary flavoring for food,
was thus held while serving.
A prayer against choking was recited beforehand,
and a prayer against choking was recited afterward.
The Wǔgēng faced south,
and the Three Excellencies presented offerings;
the ritual was similarly conducted.
Xián's commentary states: Sòng Jūn said: The Sānlǎo
is an elderly person knowledgeable in the affairs of heaven, earth, and humanity;
the Wǔgēng,
is an elderly person knowledgeable in the cyclical changes of the Five Phases.
Zhèng Kāngchéng said: The Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng
are both elderly individuals who have retired after long service;
the Emperor treats them as fathers and elder brothers,
demonstrating filial piety and fraternal duty to the world.
They are named "Three" and "Five"
to symbolize the Three Luminaries and the Five Planets,
which illuminate the world.
Dū cloth
is a type of cloth.
The Jìnxián cap,
is the ancient black cloth cap,
the attire of scholars and Confucians,
seven inches high in front,
three inches high in back,
and eight inches long.
The ceremonial hall
is dedicated to the former sages and former teachers.
The eastern steps,
are the host's steps;
the guest steps,
are the western steps.
Xián's commentary states: Sauce,
is a type of paste;
rinsing,
is to cleanse the mouth,
used to purify the mouth.
Lù Démíng said: Using wine is called rinsing,
using water is called cleansing.
The Yīnyì Yǐn states: After eating, one rinses the mouth,
pronounced "yìn."
Elderly people often choke while eating,
so attendants are placed before and after to pray,
ensuring they do not choke.
Dū
refers to fine cloth.
The Jìnxián cap,
is the ancient black cloth cap.
The jade staff,
is seven feet long,
with a dove bird ornament at the end.
The dove,
being a bird that does not choke,
symbolizes the wish for the elderly not to choke.
Gēng
is pronounced "gōng héng fān."
Huán Róng and his disciples were led into the hall,
and the Emperor personally lectured below.
Xián's commentary states: "Lecturing below"
means speaking from a lower position to explain.
Officials and scholars gathered around the bridge gate to watch and listen,
numbering perhaps tens of thousands.
The Hàn Guān Yí states: Outside the four gates of the Imperial Academy,
there is water
to regulate the spectators.
Outside the gates, there are bridges,
and spectators stand beyond the water,
hence "around the bridge gate."
"Around"
means to encircle.
The Kǎoyì states: The imperial annals record the edict,
mentioning Lǐ Gōng above but only enfeoffing Róng below,
seemingly omitting
"Gōng"
in the text.
Huán Róng's biography and Yuán Jì
record the edict mentioning only Huán Róng,
not Lǐ Gōng.
This remains uncertain.
Wine was bestowed upon all the Sānlǎo in the realm,
one dàn per person,
and forty catties of meat.
Since becoming Crown Prince,
the Emperor had studied the Shàngshū under Huán Róng.
Upon ascending the throne,
he continued to honor Róng with the rites due a teacher.
Once, he visited the Office of the Imperial Clan,
had Róng sit facing east,
set out a small table and staff,
and assembled hundreds of officials and Róng's disciples.
"Disciples"
refers to those who studied under him.
"Holding their studies"
means holding their texts.
"Raising questions"
means posing difficult inquiries.
"Question"
is pronounced "nǎi dàn fān."
"The Grand Tutor is here."
After the assembly concluded,
all the provisions from the imperial kitchen were bestowed upon Huán Róng's household.
Whenever Róng fell ill,
the Emperor would send messengers to inquire after his health,
with officials and physicians constantly traveling back and forth on the roads.
When his condition became critical,
Róng submitted a memorial thanking the Emperor for his grace,
and offered to return his titles and lands.
The Emperor visited his home to inquire about his well-being,
dismounting his carriage upon entering the street,
and proceeding forward holding his text.
He comforted Róng, shedding tears,
and bestowed upon him a bed mat, curtains, a sword, clothing, and bedding,
lingering for a long time before departing.
Thereafter, when nobles, generals, and officials came to inquire about his illness,
none dared to ride their carriages to his gate;
instead, they all bowed at the foot of his bed.
When Róng passed away,
the Emperor personally changed into mourning attire to attend the funeral and escort the procession,
and bestowed a burial mound at the southern slope of Shǒuyáng Mountain.
Xián's commentary states: Shǒuyáng Mountain
is located northwest of present-day Yǎnshī County.
Huán Yù offered to yield the title to his elder brother's son, Huán Fàn;
the Emperor did not permit it,
so Yù accepted the enfeoffment
but gave all the rental income to him.
The Emperor appointed Huán Yù as Palace Attendant.
The Emperor, regarding Zhōngshān King Liú Yān,
the youngest son of Empress Dowager Guō,
whom the Empress Dowager particularly loved,
had thus kept him alone in the capital.
At this time, he finally went to his fief along with the other kings,
and was bestowed with Tiger Guard and official cavalry.
Xián's commentary states: The Hàn Guān Yí states: Zōu cavalry
is the term for official cavalry in royal households.
According to Yān's biography,
he was bestowed with a hundred Hu cavalry from the Northern Army,
skilled in warfare and archery.
Zōu
is pronounced "cè yóu fān."
He alone was permitted to travel to and from the capital.
The Emperor treated the Yīn and Guō families with equal courtesy,
ensuring fairness in all matters,
and they frequently received rewards,
both enjoying deep favor and grace.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Emperor traveled to Cháng'ān.
In the eleventh month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
he dispatched envoys to offer sacrifices with a medium-grade sacrifice to Xiāo Hé and Huò Guāng.
When the Emperor passed by,
he paid respects at their tombs.
He then proceeded to Hédōng;
on the Guǐmǎo day,
he returned to the palace.
5 In the twelfth month,
the Protector of the Qiang, Dòu Lín, was charged with deception and corruption,
and was imprisoned and died.
At that time, the Qiang leader Diān Wú rebelled,
and Diān Àn came to surrender.
Dòu Lín reported to the emperor that Diān Àn should be made a great chief.
Later, Diān Wú also surrendered,
and Dòu Lín again reported that he should be made the first chief.
The emperor was puzzled that one tribe had two great chiefs,
and questioned Dòu Lín.
After thorough investigation,
the truth was discovered.
The emperor was furious and dismissed Dòu Lín from his post.
The Inspector of Liáng Province further reported Dòu Lín's corruption charges,
and he was subsequently imprisoned and died.
下 (xià),
is pronounced with the tone xiá.
He was the son of Dòu Róng's cousin.
At that time, the Dòu family had one duke, two marquises, three princesses, and four officials with a salary of two thousand shí, all prominent at the same time.
Xián's commentary says: The one duke refers to the Grand Minister of Works.
The two marquises refer to Ānfēng and Xiǎnqīn.
The four officials with a salary of two thousand shí refer to the Commandant of the Guards, the Colonel of the City Gates, the Protector of the Qiang, and the General of the Household.
According to Dòu Róng's biography,
Dòu Róng's son, Dòu Mù, married Princess Nèihuáng.
Dòu Mù's son, Dòu Xūn, married Princess Bǐyáng, the daughter of Liú Qiáng, the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
Dòu Yǒu's son, Dòu Gù, married Princess Wēnyáng, the daughter of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
Their official residences and mansions lined the capital,
and among relatives and meritorious officials, none could compare.
After Dòu Lín was executed,
the emperor repeatedly issued edicts sternly reprimanding Dòu Róng.
Dòu Róng, terrified, begged to retire due to old age.
An edict ordered him to return home and recuperate from illness.
6 That year,
the ritual of welcoming the seasonal energies at the five suburban altars was first performed.
The Continued Book of Hàn says: The markers for welcoming the energies at the five suburban altars,
each marker in the four directions corresponds to its position,
the central marker is in the wèi direction,
and the altars are all three chǐ high.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
spring is welcomed at the eastern suburban altar,
offering sacrifices to the Green Emperor and Gōumáng,
with carriages and robes all in green,
singing the "Qīngyáng" song,
and performing the "Yúnqiào" dance with eight rows of dancers.
On the day of the Beginning of Summer,
summer is welcomed at the southern suburban altar,
offering sacrifices to the Red Emperor and Zhùróng,
with carriages and robes all in red,
singing the "Zhūmíng" song,
and dancing as in the welcoming of spring.
Eighteen days before the Beginning of Autumn,
the Yellow Spirit is welcomed at the central marker,
offering sacrifices to the Yellow Emperor and Hòutǔ,

singing the "Zhūmíng" song,

On the day of the Beginning of Autumn,
autumn is welcomed at the western suburban altar,

with carriages and robes all in white,
singing the "Báicáng" song,
and performing the "Yùmìng" dance with eight rows of dancers.
On the day of the Beginning of Winter,
winter is welcomed at the northern suburban altar,
offering sacrifices to the Black Emperor and Xuánmíng,
with carriages and robes all in black,
singing the "Xuánmíng" song,
and dancing as in the welcoming of autumn.

The Empress

During Emperor Guāngwǔ's time,

She was able to serve Empress Yīn respectfully,

Her conduct was proper and complete,

When the emperor ascended the throne,

Since the Empress had no sons of her own,

The Empress then devoted herself to raising him,
laboring and worrying more than if he were her own.
The Crown Prince was also naturally filial and sincere,
and the mother and son were loving and affectionate,
without the slightest discord from beginning to end.

Jiàn means

When the officials proposed establishing the Empress of the Chángqiū Palace,
the Empress's palace is called the Chángqiū Palace.
the Empress Dowager said:

She often wore coarse silk,

When officials presented matters that were difficult to decide,

the Empress would analyze the reasoning,

in the fourth month,

According to the "Treatise on Commanderies and States": Emperor Gāo established Qiānshèng Commandery with Xīpíngchāng,

In the second year of the Wǔfèng era of Emperor Xuān,

Xián states: The old city of Guǎngpíng County,

Shèng,

According to the "Treatise on Astronomy" of the Jìn dynasty,
the eight stars of Dàlíng are north of Wèi,

The Milky Way runs southwest,

6 The Emperor extensively constructed the Northern Palace.
At that time, there was a drought.
The Imperial Secretary Deputy Zhōnglí Yì from Kuàijī
went to the palace gate, removed his official cap, and submitted a memorial stating:
"In the past, when Chéng Tāng encountered a drought,
he reproached himself with six matters, saying: 'Is it because governance is not restrained?
Or because the people are made to suffer?
Or because palace construction
"construction"
in Fàn's History is written as
"flourishing."
[Chapter note: The twelve-line edition correctly has
"flourishing";
the eleven-line edition is the same.
Or because the influence of women is excessive?
Or because bribery is practiced?
Or because slanderers prosper?'"
The "Records of Emperors and Kings" states: Chéng Tāng suffered a great drought for seven years,
he fasted and purified himself,
cut his hair and nails,
offered himself as a sacrifice,
and prayed at the Shè altar of Sānglín,
reproaching himself with six matters.
The people lost their farming season;
since ancient times, it has not been that palace buildings were considered too small and narrow,
but rather the worry has been that the people are not peaceful and secure.
Construction should be halted for now,
to respond to the will of Heaven."
The Emperor issued an edict in response, stating:
"Tāng cited six matters,
placing the blame on one person.
You may wear your cap and shoes,

"Issuing an edict" means
writing the edict on bamboo slips.
He reduced non-urgent expenditures.
The Emperor issued an edict apologizing to the dukes, ministers, and all officials,

Zhōnglí Yì recommended Liú Píng, the Chief of Quánjiāo.
Quánjiāo County

While in Quánjiāo,

When the Inspector and Grand Administrator conducted their tours of inspection,

People felt they were in their proper place,

The Emperor had a narrow and suspicious nature,

Xián states: Yǐn means
private.

what people's ears and eyes cannot perceive.

Hào,
is pronounced hū dào fān.
Even high-ranking officials such as Imperial Secretaries and below were sometimes dragged and pulled.
He once became angry with the Gentleman-of-the-Palace Yào Sōng over some matter.

is the surname;

Sōng then said:
"'The Son of Heaven is dignified and solemn,

This is from the text of the "Qū Lǐ" chapter of the Book of Rites.
Zhèng states: Both describe the appearance of demeanor and bearing.
Xián states: Mùmù means
beautiful.
Huánghuáng means
splendid.
Yet you personally rise to strike a gentleman."
The Emperor then pardoned him.
At this time, everyone in the court was terrified,
vying to be strict and severe to avoid blame and punishment.
Only Zhōnglí Yì dared to remonstrate and argue,
repeatedly sealing and returning imperial edicts.
When subordinates made errors,
he would always rescue and exonerate them.
Coinciding with successive unusual phenomena,

"Your Majesty reveres and fears ghosts and spirits,

The hundred officials lack mutual affection,
and officials and people lack harmonious feelings.
The Ěryǎ states: Yōngyōng means
harmony.
This has led to heavenly disasters.
The common people can be won over by virtue,
but are difficult to subdue by force.
The poem 'Lù Míng' necessarily speaks of feasting and music because
'Lù Míng'
is a poem from the Minor Odes of the Shījīng, feasting with ministers.
The poem says: 'The deer call out yōuyōu,

Lè,

Only then does the weather become harmonious.

) The Emperor was greatly angered,

1 In spring,

To memorialize [shàng],

(To fool [chī],

1 In spring,
the first month,
on the guǐmǎo day,
the Empress Dowager, née Yīn, passed away.
In the second month,
on the gēngshēn day,
Empress Guāngliè was buried.
(The various empresses of the Western Capital all received posthumous titles following the emperor's,
only Empress Wèi Sī and Empress Xǔ Gōng'āi, who did not die of natural causes, received separately conferred posthumous titles.
Following the emperor's title and adding another character
began with Empress Yīn.
Fàn Yè said: In the Hàn period, empresses all took their titles from the emperor's posthumous name.
Emperor Míng began the use of the title Guāngliè,
thereafter all were matched with a virtue character,
regardless of wisdom, folly, excellence, or inferiority,

Li Xián said: According to the rules of naming: Holding to virtue and following one's task is called 'Liè'. )
2 The Northern Xiōngnú were still strong,
and frequently raided the borders.
They sent envoys requesting to establish border markets;
the Emperor, hoping that communication
would cause them to cease raiding,
agreed.
3 Zōng Jūn, Chancellor of Dōnghǎi, was appointed Imperial Secretary.
Earlier,
Zōng Jūn was Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng.
(Jiǔjiāng Commandery
was 1,500 lǐ southeast of Luòyáng.)
He dismissed all Assistants and Clerks,
and confined the Inspectorial Officials within their offices.
(The subordinate counties were peaceful.
The commandery had five divisions of Inspectorial Officials,
who supervised the subordinate counties.
Confining them within their offices
was because he feared they would make surveillance their achievement,
encroaching upon and harassing the subordinate counties,
which would precisely create many incidents.)
Jiǔjiāng had long suffered from frequent tiger attacks,
and often recruited people to set up traps and pits.
(Li Xián said: A trap [jiǎn]
is a mechanism for catching animals.
A pit [jǐng],
means digging a hole to trap them.)
Zōng Jūn issued a notice to the subordinate counties stating:
"The presence of fierce beasts in the Jiāng and Huái regions
is like the presence of chickens and pigs in the northern lands.
Now that they harm the people,
the fault lies with cruel officials.
To labor strenuously setting up nets for capture
(To set up [zhāng],
means to arrange.
Arranging mechanical traps to await birds and beasts is called 'zhāng'.
As in Péi Yán's *Inscription on the Orangutan* which says
'The slave wants to trap me'
is an example.)
The task is to expel the wicked and greedy,
and consider promoting the loyal and good.
You may remove all traps and pits,
and abolish the quota system."
After that, there were no more tiger troubles.
The Emperor heard of Zōng Jūn's reputation,
and therefore entrusted him with a pivotal position.
Zōng Jūn said to others:
"The state favors legalistic clerks and incorrupt officials,
believing they are sufficient to stop wickedness.
However, clerks are practiced in deception and fraud,
and an incorrupt official's purity benefits only himself,
it does not help the people's exile and wandering, nor the harm caused by bandits.
I, Jūn, wished to kowtow and argue this,
but the times were not yet ready for change.
After a long time, they will suffer from it themselves,
then it will be possible to speak!"
Before he could speak,
he happened to be promoted to Colonel of the Capital.
Later, the Emperor heard his words,
and thought well of him in retrospect.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the jǐmǎo day,

rank one thousand piculs.)
Zhòng did not yield.
The Chányú had him surrounded and guarded,
confining him without giving him water or fire;
Zhòng drew his sword and swore an oath,
swearing to die
rather than yield to the Chányú.
(The Chányú) then sent another envoy,

Initially,
the Grand Minister of Agriculture Gěng Guó submitted a memorial stating:
"It would be appropriate to establish a General Who Crosses the Liao River, stationed at Wǔyuán,
to prevent the Southern Xiōngnú from fleeing."
The court did not follow this advice.
When the Southern Xiōngnú Xūbǔ Gǔdūhóu and others learned that Hàn was exchanging envoys with the Northern Barbarians,
they harbored resentment within,
and intended to rebel.
The Xiōngnú had ministers of different surnames,
the Left and Right Gǔdūhóu.
Among the different surnames were also the Hūyǎn, Xūbǔ, Lìlín, and Lán clans,

They were ordered to send troops to welcome them.
When Zhèng Zhòng went beyond the frontier,
he suspected something was amiss;
he kept watch,
and indeed captured an envoy from Xūbǔ.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"It would be appropriate to establish a greater general,

Thus, the Crossing the Liao River Camp was first established,
with the General of the Gentlemen of the Household Wú Táng acting as General Who Crosses the Liao River,
leading the troops of the Líyáng Tiger's Teeth Camp to station at Mànbó in Wǔyuán.
The Hàn Official Ceremonial states: Emperor Guāngwǔ used the troops of Yōu and Jì to conquer and pacify the realm,
therefore he established a camp at Líyáng,
with a Receptionist overseeing it,
with a thousand cavalry soldiers.
Xián states: Emperor Zhāo appointed Fàn Míngyǒu as General Who Crosses the Liao River,
and it was reestablished at this time.
Mànbó County
is located within the boundaries of Yínchéng County in Shèng Prefecture today.

The King of Chǔ, Liú Yīng, presented yellow silk and white fine silk to the Chancellor of the Principality, saying:
Emperor Chéng of Hàn abolished the position of Internal Historian in the principalities,
ordering the Chancellor to govern the people,
with duties like those of a Grand Administrator,
and a salary of two thousand shi.
Wán
is what is called juàn today.
Master Yán Gǔ states: Wán
is plain silk;
jiān,
is a type of silk fabric.
Xiàng,
is pronounced xiàng.
"Entrusted as a supporting vassal,
my faults and transgressions have accumulated,
yet I joyfully receive the great grace,
and present silk fabrics,
to redeem my transgressions."
The Chancellor of the Principality reported this to the throne,
and an imperial edict replied:
"The King of Chǔ recites the subtle words of Huáng-Lǎo,
esteems the benevolence and compassion of the Buddha,
purifies himself in fasting for three months,
and makes vows with the spirits.
What suspicion or doubt could there be,
that he should have regret or remorse!
Let the redemption be returned,
to assist in the sumptuous feasts for the upāsakas and śramaṇas."
Initially,
the Emperor heard that in the Western Regions there was a deity,
whose name was Buddha,
and thus sent an envoy to Tiānzhú to seek his teachings,
obtaining his scriptures and bringing back śramaṇas.
These scriptures generally take emptiness and non-being as their foundation,
valuing compassion and non-killing;
they believe that when a person dies,
the spirit does not perish,
but follows and receives a new form;
the good and evil deeds performed during life
all receive retribution,
therefore they value cultivating the spirit,
ultimately to become a Buddha.
They are skilled at using grand and magnificent words,
to persuade and guide the ignorant common people.
Those proficient in this teaching
are called śramaṇas.

Fán Chóu's younger brother, Fán Wéi,
sought a daughter of King Yīng of Chǔ as a wife for his son, Fán Shǎng.
Chóu heard of this and stopped him, saying:
"During the Jiànwǔ era,
our family enjoyed great honor and favor,
with one clan producing five marquises.
This refers to Fán Hóng being enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángluó,
his younger brother Fán Dān as Marquis of Shèyáng,
his nephew Fán Xún as Marquis of Xuánxiāng,
his clansman Fán Zhōng as Marquis of Gēngfù,
and Fán Hóng also being enfeoffed as Marquis of Shòuzhāng.
Our daughters could marry kings,
and our sons could marry princesses;
Xián commented: Hóng held the position of Tèjìn.
If we seek such connections,
it will bring disaster,
so we should not do it.
Moreover, you have only one son;
how can you abandon him to Chǔ!"
Wéi did not listen.
When the Chǔ incident came to light,
Chóu had already passed away.
The Emperor, recalling Chóu's caution and integrity,
spared all his sons from punishment.
Yīng Yīn listed renowned scholars throughout the empire,
and the emperor obtained his register,
which included the name of Yǐn Xīng, the Grand Administrator of Wújùn.
Wújùn was located three thousand two hundred lǐ east of Luòyáng.
The officials could not endure the torture,
and more than half of them died;
only the Attendant Clerk Lù Xù, the Registrar Liáng Hóng, and the Merit Officer Sì Xūn,
suffered all five tortures.
(Attendant Clerk:
in the commandery, he oversees and records all matters.
Merit Officer:
in charge of selecting and recording merits.
Five tortures:
the four limbs and the body all suffer severe torment;
some say
whipping, caning, burning, branding, and strangulation are the five tortures.)
In the end, they did not change their statements.
Lù Xù’s mother came from Wú to Luòyáng,
prepared food, and sent it to Xù.
Although Xù was under interrogation,
his expression and tone never changed,
yet when facing the food, he wept uncontrollably in sorrow.
The judicial officer inquired about the reason,
and Xù said:
“My mother has come, but I cannot see her,
hence my sorrow.”
The officer asked:
“How did you know?”
Xù replied:
“When my mother cuts meat, it is always square,
and she cuts scallions to the length of one cùn,
so I knew.”
The officer reported the situation,
and the emperor then pardoned Yǐn Xīng and others,
but confined them for life.
Yán Zhōng and Wáng Píng implicated in their confessions Gěng Jiàn, Marquis of Suìxiāng; Zāng Xìn, Marquis of Lǎnglíng; Dèng Lǐ, Marquis of Huòzé; and Liú Jiàn, Marquis of Qǔchéng.
Gěng Chún’s younger brother Sù
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Suìxiāng,
and Jiàn likely succeeded to the title.
Zāng Xìn, Marquis of Lǎnglíng,
was the son of Zāng Gōng.
Dèng Lǐ and Liú Jiàn have no records to verify.
Huòzé
was a marquisate,
belonging to Hédōng Commandery.
Qǔchéng
was a marquisate,
belonging to Dōnglái Commandery;
Xián said: The old city is northwest of Yè County in present-day Láizhōu.
Shīgǔ said: Huò
is pronounced wū guó fān.
At that time,
the emperor was extremely angry,
and the officials were all terrified.
All those implicated
were indiscriminately accused,
with no one daring to show leniency based on circumstances.
The Attendant Censor Hán Làng was pained by the injustice.
(Textual variant note: Fàn’s history writes
“Hán”;
Lù Guīméng’s separation poem says:
“Chū hán lǎng yǒng páihuái lì.”
Yuán’s annals write
“Jiǎn.”
According to records, there is now the surname Jiǎn,
pronounced jiàn,
matching Yuán’s annals.
Now follow this.
I note that the surname register includes the surname Hán,
believed to be descendants of the Xià feudal lord Hòu Hán.
It also says: descendants of Hán Hóu, son of King Wǔ of Zhōu.) He separately questioned Zhōng and Píng.
(Xián said: Wùsè
means appearance.)
(Xián said: Cuò’è
means hastily.
Cuò
is pronounced qī gù fān.
È
is pronounced wǔ gù fān.)
He then submitted a report:
“Jiàn and others are not guilty;
they were falsely accused solely by Zhōng and Píng.
I suspect that many innocent people in the empire
are similarly treated.”
The emperor said:
“If so,
why did Zhōng and Píng implicate them?”
He replied:
“Zhōng and Píng knew their crimes were heinous,
(Hàn law included great impiety and heinous crimes.)
and hoped to clear themselves.”
The emperor said:
“If so,
why did you not report earlier?”
He replied:
“I feared others in the empire might expose their crimes.”
The emperor angrily said:
“Officials are duplicitous!”
and ordered him taken down and beaten.
(Beaten
is pronounced zhǐ ruǐ fān.)
Làng said:
“I wish to speak one word before dying.”
The emperor said:
“Who collaborated on the memorial?”
He replied:
“I alone wrote it.”
The emperor said:
“Why did you not consult the Three Offices?”
(The Three Offices
are the offices of the Grand Commandant, Minister over the Masses, and Minister of Works.)
“I knew I would certainly face clan extermination,
and did not dare to implicate others.”
The emperor said:
“Why clan extermination?”
He replied:
“I have investigated the case for a year,
unable to fully uncover the crimes,
yet instead plead for the accused’s innocence,
so I know I deserve clan extermination.
However, the reason I speak
is truly hoping Your Majesty will awaken.
I see those handling interrogations
all say that major crimes of evil
(Gù
means matter,
also prisoner.
Yāo
is pronounced yú jiāo fān.)
are better charged than cleared,
meaning it is better to assign guilt
than to exonerate.
Thus, interrogating one implicates ten,
interrogating ten implicates a hundred.
Moreover, at court assemblies,
when Your Majesty asks about successes and failures,
all kneel and say: ‘By old regulations,
major crimes bring disaster to nine clans;
by Your Majesty’s great grace,
punishment stops at the individual—
how fortunate for the empire!’
(Cái
is the same as cái.)
Though they say nothing, they look up at the ceiling and sigh secretly,
all knowing many are wronged,
yet none dare contradict Your Majesty.
What I state now,
I will die without regret!”
The emperor’s anger subsided,
and he ordered Làng released.
Two days later,
the emperor personally
went to the Luòyáng prison to review the prisoners.
(Shīgǔ said: Review them,
to know if their cases involve injustice or delay.
Present-day lǜ qiú
originally derived from the departing tone of lù,
pronounced lì jù fān;
but recent custom misunderstands its meaning,
distorting the text,
making it the lǜ of thought,
losing its origin.)
At the time, there was a drought,
and then heavy rain fell.
Empress Mǎ also, due to the many abuses in the Chǔ case,
took the opportunity to speak to the emperor.
The emperor, moved and awakened,
rose at night and paced restlessly.
(Pánghuáng
is explained as pacing,
Zhuāngzǐ’s commentary: like soaring.
I say pánghuáng
means a state of unease.)
Yuán Ān, Magistrate of Rénchéng in Rǔnán, was appointed Grand Administrator of Chǔ Commandery.
(Rénchéng County
belonged to Dōngpíng Principality.
Rén
is pronounced rén.)
He first went to handle the case of King Yīng of Chǔ,
sorting out those without clear evidence,
and listing them for release.
The Assistant, Clerks, and Officers all kowtowed in protest,
believing
“colluding with rebels
carries the same penalty by law—
this cannot be done.”
Ān said:
“If there is any discrepancy,
I as Grand Administrator will bear the responsibility,
and it will not extend to you.”
He then separately submitted detailed memorials.
The emperor, awakened,
immediately approved,
and over four hundred households were released.
3. In summer,
in the fifth month,
the son of the former Prince of Guǎnglíng, Jīng, Yuánshòu, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎnglíng,
with an estate of six counties.
This was to deepen the affection between brothers,
and to remember the descendants of meritorious officials.
4. The construction of the Shòu Líng (Longevity Mausoleum) began for the first time.
The regulations stated:
"It should only allow water to flow through;
no mound is to be raised.
After ten thousand years have passed,
sweep the ground and offer sacrifices,
using only a ladle of water and dried provisions.
After one hundred days,
only seasonal offerings shall be set.
A few officials and soldiers shall be stationed there
to provide cleaning and sweeping services.
Anyone who dares to undertake any construction
shall be dealt with according to the law for disrespecting the ancestral temple."
The previous text states:
Those who disrespect the ancestral temple
shall be executed in the marketplace.
1. In spring,
in the second month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
the Emperor traveled east on an inspection tour.
On the Guǐhài day,
he plowed the fields in Xiàpī.
Xiàpī County
originally belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery;
in this year,
Línhúai Commandery was made the Kingdom of Xiàpī,
and Xiàpī County was placed under it,
located 1,400 lǐ east of Luòyáng.
He reached Lǔ,
visited the residence of Confucius,
and personally ascended the lecture hall.
The residence of Confucius
is in Quèlǐ.
The lecture hall
is the hall for teaching.
Prince Gòng of Lǔ ascended Confucius's hall
and heard the sounds of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments;
this is the same place.
He also visited Dōngpíng and Dàliáng.
Jùnyí County
was originally Dàliáng.
In the fourth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
he returned to the palace.
2. The Emperor's son Gōng was enfeoffed as Prince of Jùlù,
Dǎng as Prince of Lèchéng.
The Kingdom of Lèchéng
was originally Xìndū Commandery;
the Emperor changed its name.
It is located 2,000 lǐ north of Luòyáng.
Chàng was enfeoffed as Prince of Rǔnán,
Bǐng as Prince of Chángshān,
and Cháng as Prince of Jìyīn.
The Emperor personally determined the size of their fiefs,
decreeing that they should be only half the size of those of Chǔ and Huáiyáng.
Empress Mǎ said:
"Only a few counties for your sons—
isn't this too frugal according to the regulations?"
The Emperor replied:
"How can my sons be equal to the sons of the previous Emperor?
An annual allowance of twenty million cash is sufficient!"
3. On the Yǐsì day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
4. The Attendant Gentleman Gěng Bǐng repeatedly submitted memorials requesting an attack on the Xiōngnú.
According to the Treatise on Officials: The Attendant Gentleman
holds a rank equivalent to one thousand shí,
serves as the head of the Gentlemen's Office,
and oversees the gentlemen.
In ancient times, military training was emphasized;
there was a supervisor of archery to oversee and record it,
hence the title 'Attendant.'
'Shuò'
is pronounced 'suǒ jiǎo fān.'
According to the *Erya*: Among a father's brothers,
the elder is called 'shìfù,'
and the younger is called 'shūfù.'
The Emperor then sent Bǐng and Gù, along with the Grand Coachman Jì Róng, the Leader of the Gentlemen of the Household of the Rapid as Tigers Mǎ Liào,
and the Marquis of Xiàbó Liú Zhāng.
Zhāng
was the grandson of Prince Yǎn of Qí.
Gěng Bǐng said:
"In the past, the Xiōngnú allied with the bow-wielding tribes
and combined with the left-lapel-wearing groups,
so they could not be controlled.
After Emperor Wǔ of Hàn obtained the four commanderies of Héxī, as well as Jūyán and Shuòfāng,
Jūyán
was established as a county by Emperor Wǔ,
belonging to Zhāngyè Commandery.
Xián said: The old city is north of Zhāngyè County in Gān Prefecture.
The Qiāng and Hú were separated;
only the Western Regions remained,
but they soon submitted again;
thus, Hūhányé Chányú requested to serve and guard the frontier,
and the situation became easy to exploit.
Now we have the Southern Chányú,
and the situation is similar;
however, the Western Regions have not yet submitted,
and the northern barbarians have not yet shown any signs of conflict.
In my humble opinion, we should first attack Báishān.
According to the *Old Affairs of Xīhé*: Báishān has snow in both winter and summer,
hence the name Báishān (White Mountain).
The Xiōngnú call it Tiānshān (Heavenly Mountain).
When passing by it,
everyone dismounts and bows,
and it is within a hundred lǐ of Púlèi Sea.
Xián said: Yīwú is the area of Yīwúlú,
originally belonging to the Xiōngnú.
Later, the land was taken and the Yìhé Commandant was established,
for the purpose of garrison farming.
This is the old city of Yīwú in Nàzhí County of Yī Prefecture.
He also said: The old city of Yīwú
is north of Jìnchāng County in Guā Prefecture.
We should send envoys to the various states of Wūsūn to cut off their right arm.
In Yīwú, there is also a southern Hūyǎn tribe of the Xiōngnú.
If we defeat this,
we will also break their left horn.
Only then can the Xiōngnú be attacked."
The Emperor approved his words.
Some advisors argued that
"if troops are sent to Báishān now,
the Xiōngnú will certainly combine their forces to assist,
so we should also divide their eastern forces to disperse their troops."
The Emperor followed this advice.
In the twelfth month,
Bǐng was appointed as Commandant of the Capital Cavalry,
and Gù as Commandant of the Imperial Chariots.
The Commandant of Cavalry Qín Péng was made Bǐng's deputy.
These three commandants were all established by Emperor Wǔ.
The Commandant of the Imperial Chariots is in charge of the imperial carriage,
and the Commandant of the Capital Cavalry is in charge of the Emperor's secondary horses.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Fù'
means secondary;
another interpretation is: close,

All were assigned assistants and marshals,
and they were sent to garrison Liáng Prefecture.
Bǐng
is the son of Guó;
Zhōng

Liào

1. In spring,
in the second month,

Gāoquè,

the water emerges from the southwest,

According to my reference to the "Treatise on the Southwestern Barbarians",

Guō,

The Cavalry Commandant Lái Miáo and the Protector of Wūhuán Colonel Wén Mù led 11,000 cavalry from the Tàiyuán, Yànmén, Dàijùn, Shànggǔ, Yúyáng, Yòuběipíng, and Dìngxiāng commanderies, along with Wūhuán and Xiānbēi troops, to march out from the Píngchéng Pass,

Dòu Gù and Gěng Zhōng reached Tiānshān,

Lái Miáo and Wén Mù reached the shore of the Xiōng Hé Shuǐ,

They gained nothing.
Jì Yǒng and the Southern Xiōngnú's Zuǒxiánwáng Xìn did not get along,

imprisoned,

if you fully record all the items obtained,
if,
meaning you,

Shàng,
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
Strive to the death in advancing forward,
