After his death,
his son Féng submitted a memorial,
detailing his last words.
The Emperor highly esteemed Yǒng,
and was about to reappoint him,
upon hearing this,
he was greatly shocked,
and sighed for a long time.
Whenever the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi came to the capital to offer congratulations,
they would often pass by Yǒng's tomb to pay respects,
weeping and crying out to heaven;
the officials and people of Liáodōng erected a shrine for him,
offering sacrifices in all four seasons.
Yǒng,
had previously been the Governor of Liáodōng,
his prestige and trustworthiness were renowned among the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi.
Hào,
is pronounced hù dāo fān.
Wéi,
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
He was posthumously granted the additional rank of Tèjìn.
Emperor Ming therefore sent the Acting Major Bān Chāo, together with the Attendant Official Guō Xún, on a joint mission to the Western Regions.
The Treatise on the Hundred Officials states: In the Great General's camp there are five divisions;
each division has one Colonel;
one Army Major;
and also an Army Acting Major,
who serves as deputy.
"Shǐ" (to send)
is pronounced "shǐ" (to send).
The same below.
The King of Shànshàn, Guǎng, received Chāo with complete ritual courtesy and respect,
but later suddenly became distant and negligent.
Chāo said to his subordinates:
"Do you sense that Guǎng's courtesy and intentions have grown thin?"
His subordinates said:
"The Hu people cannot maintain constancy for long;
there is no other reason."
Chāo said:
"This must be because envoys from the northern barbarians have arrived,
and he is wavering, uncertain which side to follow.
A perceptive person sees what has not yet sprouted,
let alone when it is already evident!"
He then summoned the Hu attendant,
and tricked him, saying:
"The Xiongnu envoys have been here for several days;
where are they now?"
The Hu attendant, frightened, said:
"They arrived three days ago;
they are thirty *li* from here."
Chāo then confined the Hu attendant,
The Hu attendant
was sent by Shànshàn to serve Chāo.
"Shǐ" (envoy)
is pronounced "shǐ" (envoy).
He drank with them,
and when the wine was flowing freely,
he provoked and angered them, saying:
"You gentlemen and I are all in this remote land.
Now the barbarian envoys have arrived only a few days ago,
and King Guǎng's courtesy and respect are already abandoned.
If Shànshàn were to seize us and send us to the Xiongnu,
our bones would forever become food for jackals and wolves.
What shall we do about this?"
The subordinates all said:
"Now we are in a place of peril and destruction;
life and death we follow the Major!"
Chāo said:
"If you do not enter the tiger's lair,
you cannot catch the tiger's cub.
The plan for now
is solely to take advantage of the night to attack the barbarians with fire,
so that they do not know how many we are.
They will certainly be greatly shocked and terrified,
and we can annihilate them completely.
Destroying these barbarians,
then Shànshàn will be utterly terrified,
and our achievement will be accomplished and our task established."
The men said:
"We should discuss this with the Attendant Official."
Chāo angrily said:
"Good fortune or disaster will be decided today.
The Attendant Official is a petty civil official;
hearing this, he will certainly be afraid and the plan will leak out.
We would die for nothing,
and that is not the way of brave men."
The men said:
"Good!"
At the beginning of the night,
Chāo then led his officers and soldiers rushing to the barbarian camp.
"Beginning of the night"
means the first watch of the night.
Chāo ordered ten men to take drums and hide behind the barbarians' quarters,
agreeing:
"When you see the fire blaze,
you must all beat the drums and shout loudly.
The rest of you all take up weapons and crossbows,
and lie in ambush on both sides of the gate."
Chāo then set fire with the wind;
drums and shouts rose from front and back,
the barbarian crowd was startled and thrown into chaos,
Chāo personally fought and killed three men,
his officers and soldiers beheaded their envoy and over thirty of his attendants,
and the remaining crowd of about a hundred men were all burned to death.
The next day he returned,
and reported to Guō Xún.
Xún was greatly startled;
then his expression changed,
his mind wanting to share in Chāo's merit but unable to conceal it outwardly,
hence his expression changed.
Raising his hand, he said:
"Although I, the subordinate official, did not go,
how could Bān Chāo have the heart to claim it all for himself!"
"Attendant Official"
means subordinate official.
"Yuàn" (subordinate official)
is pronounced "yú juàn".
Chāo then summoned the King of Shànshàn, Guǎng,
and showed him the heads of the barbarian envoys.
The entire state was shocked and terrified.
Chāo informed him of the Han's might and virtue,
saying, "From now on,
do not again have dealings with the northern barbarians."
Guǎng kowtowed,
saying, "I wish to belong to Han,
with no divided heart."
He then offered his son as a hostage.
Returning, he reported to Dòu Gù.
Gù was greatly pleased,
and fully reported Chāo's achievements and merits,

The Emperor said:
"An official like Bān Chāo,

Now appoint Chāo as Army Major,

Gù again sent Chāo on a mission to Yútián,

Chāo wished only to lead the original thirty-six men who followed him,

"The state of Yútián is large and distant.
Now leading several hundred men
would not add to our strength;
if there is any unforeseen event,

At that time, the King of Yútián, Guǎngdé, was domineering and powerful on the southern route.
Xián said: "Xióng zhāng" (domineering and powerful)
means flourishing and vigorous.
"Zhāng"
is pronounced "zhú liàng".
I say that "zhāng"
means a self-aggrandizing attitude.
After Chāo arrived in Yútián,
Guǎngdé's courtesy and intentions were very distant.
Moreover, their custom was to believe in shamans.
A shaman said:
"The god is angry.
Why do you wish to turn towards Han?
The Han envoy has a *guā* horse;
quickly seek to take it and sacrifice it to me!"
Xián said: The *Continued Han* and Huá Qiáo's *History* both write
"guī".
*Shuōwén* says: A horse of light black color,
pronounced "jīng mèi".
I say that "guā"
is pronounced "guā";

read with its original pronunciation.
He sent the State Minister Sīláibǐ to Chāo to request the horse.
Chāo secretly knew the situation,
replied agreeing to it,

After a while,
the shaman arrived.
Chāo immediately beheaded him;
seized Sīláibǐ,
and flogged him several hundred times.
He sent the shaman's head to Guǎngdé,
and thereupon reprimanded him.
Guǎngdé had long heard that Chāo in Shànshàn had exterminated the barbarian envoys,
and was greatly terrified.
He immediately killed the Xiongnu envoy and surrendered.
Chāo heavily rewarded the king and those below him,
and thereupon pacified and settled them.
Thereupon, the various states all sent their sons to serve as attendants,
and the Western Regions, having been cut off from Han for sixty-five years,
were at this time reconnected.
In the third year of the Tiānfèng era of Wáng Mǎng,
Yānqí attacked and killed Wáng Jùn,
and the Western Regions were then cut off.
Up to this point, it was fifty-eight years;
here it says cut off from Han for sixty-five years,
probably counting from the first year of the Shǐjiànguó era,
meaning that when Mǎng usurped the throne, the Western Regions were then cut off from Han.
"Fù" (again)
is pronounced "fú yòu".
"Zǎi" (year)
is pronounced "zǐ hǎi".
He was the son of Biāo.
2. The King of Huáiyáng, Yán,
was by nature arrogant and extravagant,
and treated his subordinates harshly and severely.
Someone submitted a memorial accusing
"Yán, together with his concubine's brother Xiè Yǎn and his sister's husband Hán Guāng, recruited cunning and crafty men,
created prognosticatory texts and charts,
and performed sacrificial rituals with curses."
The matter was handed down for investigation.
In the fifth month,

"The state's financial resources are insufficient,

Boiling salt and the equal transportation system

Xián comments: Emperor Wǔ established the equal transportation system,
meaning the taxes and levies collected by the commanderies and prefectures, along with the costs of hiring transportation,
were all taken by the government,
which then purchased goods produced locally,
and the government itself transported them to the capital,
calling it equal transportation.
Zhū Huī said:
"The equal transportation system
is no different from merchant trade,
and if the profits from salt go to the government,
the common people will be impoverished and resentful.
This is truly not something a wise ruler should implement."
The emperor, in anger, severely reprimanded the Imperial Secretaries,

After three days,
an edict was issued pardoning and releasing them,

"The state is pleased to hear dissenting opinions,

Why did you imprison yourselves!"
Zhū Huī then claimed to be critically ill,
and refused to sign any further deliberations.
The Imperial Secretary Director and below were terrified,

"Now we are about to face reprimand,
meaning reprimand is imminent.
'Terrified'
is pronounced as 'pǔbù'.
The consequences will not be minor!"
Zhū Huī said:
"I am eighty years old,

I should repay with my life.
If I know something is wrong

I would betray the duty of a minister!
Now, with my ears and eyes closed to all,

He then fell silent and said no more.
The Imperial Secretaries did not know what to do,
so they jointly submitted an impeachment against Zhū Huī.
The emperor's anger subsided,

A few days later,

Xián comments: 'On-duty court gentleman'

he rose to express gratitude;

He was also given one hundred bolts of cloth
and ten sets of clothing.

to attract Qiāng tribes who wished to submit.
7 The King of Shūlè, Zhōng, borrowed troops from the King of Kāngjū,
returned and occupied Sǔnzhōng.
(Regarding Zhōng's rebellion, see the first year of the previous volume.)
Xián said: Sǔnzhōng
is not clearly known;
the Dōngguān Jì records it as
"Dùnzhōng,"
while the Xù Hànshū and Huá Qiáo's book both record it as
"Sǔnzhōng."
Some versions also have
"Zhēn,"
and it is unknown which is correct.
I note that in the "Treatise on the Western Regions,"
in the third year of the Jiànníng era of Emperor Líng,
the Governor of Liángzhōu, Mèng Tuó,
sent troops to attack Shūlè,
assaulting the city of Zhēnzhōng.
"Zhēnzhōng"
is correct.
Bān Chāo, aware of his treachery, pretended to agree to his terms.
Zhōng came to Bān Chāo with a light cavalry escort,
where Bān Chāo beheaded him,
then attacked and defeated his followers,
thus opening the southern route.
8 The Dowager Empress Xǔ of Chǔ passed away.
When King Yīng of Chǔ was exiled,
Dowager Empress Xǔ remained in the Chǔ palace.
She was posthumously granted the title and posthumous name of Marquis Lì of Chǔ.
(According to the rules for posthumous names: "Lì" means killing the innocent.)
9 The Emperor appointed Guō Gōng of Yǐngchuān as Commandant of Justice.
In adjudicating cases and determining punishments,
he often showed compassion and leniency,
compiling forty-one articles where severe penalties could be reduced to lighter ones,
which he submitted in a memorial,
and all were implemented.
10 The Erudite Cáo Bāo of Lǔguó submitted a memorial,
arguing that
"a literary system should be established,
to compile and complete the Hàn rituals."
The Minister of Ceremonies, Cháo Kān,
(The surname Cháo
derives from the Yǒucháo clan;
in the Spring and Autumn period, there was Cháo Niúchén.)
said, "A grand ritual code for the dynasty
is not something Cáo Bāo can establish,"
meaning it was beyond Cáo Bāo's capability to establish.
The Emperor knew that the Confucian scholars were rigid and constrained,
and difficult to collaborate with on new initiatives.
(Xián said: "Jūluán" means constrained.)
(It means being restrained.)
Believing it timely to establish the rituals,
he appointed Cáo Bāo as Palace Attendant.
Bān Gù, the Sima of Xuánwǔ, believed that
"we should broadly gather Confucian scholars
to jointly discuss the merits and flaws."
(According to the "Treatise on Officials": The Sima of Xuánwǔ
is in charge of the Xuánwǔ Gate of the Southern Palace,
with a rank equivalent to one thousand shí.)
"As the proverb says: 'If you build a house by the roadside,
it will not be completed in three years.'
Those who gather to discuss rituals
are known for contentious debates,"
(meaning gathering to discuss rituals.)
(It means gathering to discuss rituals.)
(Xián said: "Jùsòng" means arguing without reaching a conclusion.)
(It means arguing without reaching a conclusion.)
and the writing cannot proceed.
In ancient times, when Yáo created the Dàzhāng,
one Kuí was sufficient."
(Yáo's music was called Dàzhāng.
The record says: Dàzhāng
means to make illustrious.
Xián said: Kuí
was Yáo's music official.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states: Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius: 'The Music Director,
Kuí, one is enough.'
Huáng Kǎn said: 'Zhāng' means
to illuminate.
The people rejoiced that Yáo's virtue was greatly illuminated,
hence the music was named Dàzhāng.")
First year of Zhānghé
(Dīnghài, 87 AD) (The era name was changed in July this year.)
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Emperor summoned Cáo Bāo
and gave him
the twelve chapters of Shūsūntōng's Hàn Rituals,
(Shūsūntōng established the Hàn rituals;
see the sixth and seventh years of Emperor Gāozǔ in scroll ten.
His work was stored together with laws and decrees by judicial officials.)
saying, "This system is scattered and incomplete,
often not conforming to the classics.
Now it should be corrected according to the rituals,
so that it can be implemented."
2 The Protector of the Qiāng, Fù Yù, wanted to attack the Shāodāng Qiāng.
As they had recently surrendered,
he did not wish to send troops,
so he recruited people to incite conflict among the various Qiāng and Hú tribes;
(meaning to sow discord among the Qiāng tribes,
making them fight among themselves.)
Consequently, they rebelled again and fled beyond the frontier,
seeking refuge with Míwú.
Fù Yù requested the mobilization of tens of thousands of troops from various commanderies to jointly attack the Qiāng.
Before the forces could assemble,
in the third month,
Fù Yù advanced alone with his army.
When Míwú heard of this,
he moved his encampment away.
(Lú means
a dome tent;
luò means
a dwelling.)
At night,
they reached Sāndōu Valley.
(Sāndōu Valley
is south of Jiànwēi.)
Míwú launched a surprise attack,
inflicting a major defeat,
killing Fù Yù and 880 officers and soldiers.
By the time troops from the various commanderies arrived,
the Qiāng had already withdrawn.
An edict appointed the Governor of Lǒngxī, Zhāng Yū, as Protector,
leading ten thousand troops to garrison Línqiāng.
3 In summer,
the sixth month,
on the Wùchén day,
the Minister over the Masses, Huán Yú, was dismissed.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Minister of Works, Yuán Ān, was appointed Minister over the Masses,
and the Minister of the Imperial Household, Rén Kuí, was appointed Minister of Works.
(Kuí
was the son of Rén Guāng.)
4 The King of Qí, Huǎng, and his younger brother, the Marquis of Lì, Gāng,
(According to Bān's treatise,
Lì County
belonged to Qí Commandery.)
(Huǎng
was the great-grandson of Qí Wǔwáng Yǎn,
and the son of King Shāng Shí.)
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
an edict demoted Huǎng's noble rank to Marquis of Wúhú.
(Xián said: Wúhú
is a county name,
belonging to Dānyáng Commandery.
Its old city is southeast of present-day Dāngtú County in Yízhōu.)
The seal and ribbon of the Grand Consort were confiscated.
5 On the Rénzǐ day,
the King of Huáiyáng, Qīng Bǐng, passed away.
(Bǐng
was a son of Emperor Míng.)
6 The Xiānbēi invaded the Left Region,
(the Left Region of the Xiōngnú.)
inflicting a major defeat,
beheading the Chányú Yōuliú and returning.
7 The Qiāng chieftain Míwú again, along with various tribes, raided the Jīnchéng frontier.
(Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
Zhǒng,
read as zhāng yǒng fān;
same below.)
Zhāng Yū sent his Assistant, Sīmǎ Fáng of Hénèi,
(According to the "Treatise on Officials": The General of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household for All Purposes
had two Assistants;
the Protector of the Qiāng likely also had two.)
Míwú's troops were defeated and fled,
and through an interpreter, he expressed a desire to surrender,
which Zhāng Yū accepted.
Míwú led his people to Línqiāng,
where Zhāng Yū arranged a grand assembly with troops.
(An interpreter
communicates in foreign languages,
acting as an envoy;
hence called an interpreter-envoy.
"Shè bīng" means
to deploy troops.)
(Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
Xiáng,
read as hù jiāng fān.)
Ambushed troops killed over 800 of his chieftains and leaders,
beheaded Míwú, and used his head to sacrifice at Fù Yù's tomb.
They then released troops to attack the remaining followers,
killing and capturing several thousand people.
Míwú's son, Mítáng,
reconciled with the various tribes,
intermarried and exchanged hostages,
and occupied the Great and Little Yù Valleys to rebel.
(According to the Shuǐjīng: The Yellow River passes south of Xīhǎi Commandery,
then east through Yǔnchuān and past the north of the Great Yù Valley and Little Yù Valley.
The two Yù lands are fertile and beautiful,
and the Qiāng relied on them for defense.)
Zhāng Yū was unable to control them.
8 On the Rénxū day,
an edict was issued: because auspicious omens continued to gather,
the era name was changed to Zhānghé.
Zhāng means
bright,
signifying that harmonious qi brings forth auspiciousness.
In the capital and the four directions, auspicious signs repeatedly appeared,
amounting to several hundred thousand in total.
Those who discussed affairs all considered this beautiful.
However, Hé Chǎng, a clerk under the Grand Commandant from Pínglíng, alone despised them.
He said to Sòng Yóu and Yuán Ān:
"Auspicious responses arrive in accordance with virtue,
while disasters and anomalies arise from governance.
Now, strange birds soar over the palace halls,
and bizarre grasses grow in the courtyard.
This cannot go unexamined!"
Yóu and Ān were afraid and did not dare to reply.
9 In the eighth month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor toured south.
On the Wùzǐ day,
he visited Liáng;
on the Yǐwèi day, the last day of the month,
he visited Pèi.
These were the two kingdoms of Liáng and Pèi.
10 There was a solar eclipse.
11 In the ninth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
the Emperor visited Péngchéng.
On the Xīnhài day,
he visited Shòuchūn;
Shòuchūn County belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
The demotion of Yán is seen in the first year of the Jiànchū era in the previous scroll.
On the Jǐwèi day,
he visited Rǔyīn.
Rǔyīn County,
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.
Xián said: present-day Yǐngzhōu County.
In the tenth month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
he returned to the palace.
12 The Northern Xiōngnú were in great turmoil.
Qūlánchǔ and others, fifty-eight tribes comprising 280,000 people, surrendered at Yúnzhōng, Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, and Běidì.
13 Cáo Bāo, following the old standards,
and incorporating texts from the Five Classics and prognosticatory records,
compiled and arranged the systems for capping, marriage, auspicious, inauspicious, and funeral ceremonies from the Son of Heaven down to commoners.
Compiling and arranging the systems,
he detailed their entire process.
Chèn,
read as Chǔ Zèn.
Zhuàn,
read as Chú Miǎn.
Guàn,
read as Gǔ Wán.
He submitted it.
The Emperor, because opinions among the multitude were difficult to unify,
merely accepted it,
and did not again order the relevant officials to deliberate and report.
Deliberating and reporting means
assessing whether it is feasible or not and then reporting.
Fù,
read as Fú Yòu.
14 That year,
Bān Chāo mobilized troops from the various states of Yútián, totaling twenty-five thousand men, to attack Shāchē.
In the first year of the Yuánhé era,
Chāo had attacked Shāchē but not conquered it, hence this action.
Tián,
read as Tú Xián.
Shā,
read as Sù Hé.
Chāo summoned his generals, colonels, and the King of Yútián to deliberate, saying:
"Now our troops are few and cannot match the enemy.
The best plan is for each to disperse and leave.
Yútián will go east from here,
and the Chief Clerk will also return west from here."
Bān Chāo was then the Chief Clerk Commanding Troops,
likely returning west to Shūlè.
Xū means
to wait for.
The sound of drums at night,
refers to the sound of night-watch drums.
The Zhōulǐ states: armies have night drums.
The commentary says: Qì,
is the drum for night watch and guard.
The Sīmǎ Fǎ states: four beats of the drum at dusk is the great qì,
three beats at midnight is the morning watch,
five beats at dawn is the call to depart at sunrise,
these are the so-called three qì.
This then means waiting for the midnight drum sound.
Qì,
read as Qiān Lì.
Xù,
read as Xiū Jù,
Liú Xiūwǔ's reading.
Let the captives return,
meaning they are about to disperse and leave.
They were greatly pleased,
and personally led ten thousand cavalry to intercept Chāo at the western border.
The King of Wēnsù led eight thousand cavalry to intercept Yútián at the eastern border.
Chāo, knowing the two enemies had already set out,
secretly summoned the various units to marshal their troops,
and raced to the Shāchē camp.
The Hú were greatly shocked and thrown into chaos,
fled,
and over five thousand were pursued and beheaded.
Shāchē then surrendered,
and Qiūcí and others each retreated and dispersed.
From then on, his might shook the Western Regions.
1 In spring,
the first month,
King Kāng of Jǐnán, King Yán of Fùlíng, and King Yān of Zhōngshān came to court.
The Emperor was by nature lenient and benevolent,
deeply devoted to his kin.
Therefore, his uncles, the two kings of Jǐnán and Zhōngshān,
frequently came to court many times,
receiving special favor and宠爱.
Along with his various brothers, they all remained in the capital,
not being sent to their fiefdoms.
According to Hàn regulations,
after the court assembly rituals for the various feudal kings were completed,
each should go to his fiefdom,
and not remain in the capital.
Exceeding the regulations,
the granaries and treasuries were depleted.
Hé Chǎng submitted a memorandum to Sòng Yóu, saying:
"In recent years, floods and droughts
have caused the people to have no harvest;
in Liángzhōu along the border,
households suffer from calamitous harm."
Xián said: At that time, the Western Qiāng invaded the border, causing harm.
Bǐ,
read as Pí Zhì.
Bèi,
read as Pí Yì.
Both public and private resources are exhausted;
this is truly the time to reduce feasts and curtail expenditures.
The state's grace covers and supports all,
meaning grace equal to heaven and earth.
Fù,
read as Fū Jiù.
Yet I only hear of the Là festival gifts,
from officials of the rank of Láng and above,
down to the Three Excellencies, nobles, and marquises,
to the point of emptying the treasury stores,
depleting the state's resources. Considering the public expenditures,
all come from the people's labor.
An enlightened ruler's bestowal of rewards
should have grades and regulations;
loyal ministers receiving awards
should also have limits.
Xián said: According to Hàn official regulations: For the Là festival,
the Grand General and the Three Excellencies are each granted two hundred thousand coins,
two hundred catties of beef,
and two hundred hú of non-glutinous rice;
Special Advance Marquises one hundred and fifty thousand,
Ministers one hundred thousand,
Colonels fifty thousand,
Imperial Secretaries thirty thousand,
Palace Attendants, Generals, and Grand Masters each twenty thousand,
officials of one thousand and six hundred shí each seven thousand,
the Tiger Guard and Feather Forest Guards, two men
share three thousand,
to be used for sacrifices at the gate.
The Shū Yǔgòng says: Yǔ was granted the dark jade tablet.
Xián said: The Shàngshū says: Duke Shào went out to fetch silk,
and entered to grant it to Duke Zhōu.
The responsibility is deep and the burden great.
Above, one should rectify the guiding principles;
below, one should aid and pacify the common people.
How can one merely be emptily compliant without transgression!
Kōng [empty]
should be Kōng [sincere].
Kōngkōng [sincere and earnest],
describes a respectful and earnest manner.
Return the gifts received,
and accordingly state gains and losses,
memorialize that the kings and marquises should go to their fiefdoms,
remove the prohibitions on parks and preserves,
reduce wasteful expenditures,
relieve and pity the poor and orphaned.
Then the grace and favor will flow downward smoothly,
and the common people will be joyful and content."
Yóu could not adopt this.
Examination of discrepancies: In Hé Chǎng's biography,
this matter is placed after Emperor Sùzōng's death,
saying
"the Dòu clan monopolized governance,
the imperial relatives were extravagant,
rewards and gifts exceeded regulations,
Chǎng submitted a memorandum saying such and such."
Yuán Jì places it in the third year of Yuánhé.
According to Chǎng's record:
"Since you, illustrious sir, took office,
two full years have passed,"
and also mentions the Là festival gifts.
It is known to be at this time.
1. In spring,
Mítáng desired to return to his former territory.
Dèng Xùn dispatched six thousand men from Huángzhōng,
ordering Chief Clerk Rèn Shàng to lead them.
They sewed leather to make boats,
placed them on rafts to cross the river,
launched a surprise attack on Mítáng,
and inflicted a major defeat upon him,
beheading over eighteen hundred men in total,
capturing two thousand people alive,
and seizing over thirty thousand head of horses, cattle, and sheep,
nearly annihilating his entire tribe.
Xián's note: "One tribe"
refers to Mítáng.
Zhǒng (tribe),
is pronounced zhāng yǒng fān.
Textual analysis notes: The "Chronicles of the Western Qiāng" states:
"In the first year of the Yǒngyuán era,
Zhāng Yū was dismissed from his post,
and Xùn was appointed in his place as Commandant."
The "Biography of Dèng Xùn" states:
"In the second year of the Zhānghé era,
Yū lured the Qiāng into a trap and executed them.
The Qiāng plotted revenge,
and the high ministers recommended Xùn to replace Yū.
He attacked and defeated them.
That spring,
Mítáng again wished to submit to Xùn,
but was again defeated."
According to Xùn's biography,
the text below states
"the second year of Yǒngyuán,"
therefore, "that spring"
refers to the spring of the first year of Yǒngyuán.
We now follow Xùn's biography.
The various attached tribes and smaller clans all rebelled against him.
"Attached tribes"
refers to Qiāng tribes that were attached to Mítáng.
They kowtowed and submitted, offering their lives.
"Offering their lives"
means they came of their own accord and requested death.
Shuài (to lead),
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
Thereupon, Xùn pacified and received those who submitted,
and his prestige and trustworthiness spread widely.
He then disbanded the garrison troops,
ordering each to return to their commanderies.
Because the Qiāng had rebelled,
troops had been levied from various commanderies and stationed on the frontier.
Now that the Qiāng were defeated,
he disbanded them and ordered each to return to their commandery.
He only allocated them for garrison farming and repairing fortifications.
2. Dòu Xiàn was about to campaign against the Xiōngnú.
The Three Dukes and Nine Ministers went to the court hall to submit memorials remonstrating,
believing that:
"The Xiōngnú have not violated the border fortifications,
yet without cause we toil the army on a distant expedition,
depleting the state's resources,
seeking achievement ten thousand *li* away—
this is not a strategy for the altars of state."
Memorials were submitted repeatedly,
but they were consistently ignored.
Sòng Yóu grew fearful,
and consequently did not dare to add his signature to the deliberations again.
The various ministers gradually withdrew and desisted.
Only Yuán Ān and Rén Kuí held firm to righteousness without wavering.
They even removed their caps in the court hall to firmly dispute,
submitting memorials nearly ten times in total.
Everyone considered them to be in peril and feared for them,
but Ān and Kuí maintained a stern countenance, composed as ever.
Palace Censor-in-Chief Lǔ Gōng submitted a memorial stating:
"The state has recently suffered a great mourning; Your Majesty is still in the mourning hut.
The common people are desolate.
For three seasons they have not heard the sounds of imperial guards clearing the way.
Xián's note: The three seasons
are summer, autumn, and winter.
The Son of Heaven, when going out, has guards 'warn' (*jǐng*); when entering, they 'stop traffic' (*bì*).
Shěn Yuē states: The Hàn system says: Going out is called *jǐng*,
entering is called *bì*,
but nowadays both terms are used together.
The historian-official believes *jǐng* means
to be on guard and alert;
*bì* means
to halt travel.
Nowadays, those accompanying the imperial carriage when it goes out
all take precautions and remain alert to prepare for emergencies;
when coming in from outside,
those who might interfere with the imperial carriage
are stopped by the *bì*.
Emperor Hé ascended the throne in the second month of the second year of the Zhānghé era.
The following spring, discussion arose about attacking the Xiōngnú.
The Emperor was in the mourning hut and did not emerge,
hence for three seasons the sounds of *jǐng* and *bì* were not heard.
It is as if they sought something but could not obtain it.
The *Book of Rites* records
that Yán Dīng was good at observing mourning.
When a death first occurred,
he was anxious as if seeking something he could not find.
This expresses the sentiment of the people's longing and remembrance.
To disturb and mobilize the world to serve military affairs against the barbarians
is truly not the way to bestow grace upon the Central States,
to reform the calendar and rectify the seasons,
proceeding from the inner to the outer.
The myriad people
are born of Heaven.
Heaven loves what it has born,
just as parents love their children.
If even one creature does not find its proper place,
then the celestial *qì* becomes disordered and erroneous because of it.
How much more so for humans!
Therefore, those who love the people will certainly receive Heaven's recompense.
Now, the Róng and Dí
are aberrant *qì* from the four directions,
no different from birds and beasts.
If they intermingle and dwell within the Central States,
they will disrupt and confuse the celestial *qì*,
defiling and shaming good people.
Therefore, the system of the sage kings
was merely to bridle and tether them without severing ties.
The character dictionary says: *Jī*
means a horse's bridle.
The *Cāngjié Piān* says: *Mí*
means an ox's halter.
They are now far hidden west of the Hé River at Shǐhóu,
several thousand *li* from the frontier.
Yet you wish to take advantage of their emptiness and exhaustion,
and profit from their weakness.
This is not where righteousness arises.
Now, conscription has just begun,
yet the Grand Minister of Agriculture's allocations are insufficient.
Those above and below press upon each other.
The distress among the common people
is already extreme.
All officials and the common people say it cannot be done.
How can Your Majesty,
for the sake of one man's plan,
abandon the lives of ten thousand people,
and not heed their words?
Look above to observe the heart of Heaven,
look below to examine the will of the people—
that is sufficient to know the success or failure of an affair.
I fear the Central States will cease to be the Central States;
how could it be merely about the Xiōngnú alone!"
The Imperial Secretary Hán Léng, the Cavalry Commandant Zhū Huī, and Court Gentleman for Consultation Yuè Huī of Jīngzhào,
all submitted memorials remonstrating.
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
Furthermore, an edict ordered envoers to build mansions for Xiàn's brothers Dǔ and Jǐng,
imposing corvée labor on the common people.
Palace Censor-in-Chief Hé Chàng submitted a memorial stating:
"Your servant has heard that the Xiōngnú have been rebellious and wicked for a long time.
The siege of Píngchéng,
the event is seen in scroll eleven, the seventh year of Emperor Gāo.
The event is seen in scroll twelve, the third year of Emperor Huì.
It is for this that subjects and sons would sacrifice their lives and certainly die.
Yet Emperor Gāozǔ and Empress Lü bore their anger and swallowed their rage,
letting it pass without executing them.
Now the Xiōngnú have committed no crime of rebellion,
and the Hàn court has no shameful disgrace to feel ashamed of.
Yet in the flourishing spring, when eastern work begins—
Xián's note: The year begins in the east,
people first begin plowing,
hence it is called 'eastern work.'
The common people harbor resentment and hatred,
all feeling displeasure.
Moreover, you indiscriminately have Commandant of the Guards Dǔ and Commandant of Attendant Chariots Jǐng repair and build their mansions,
blocking streets and cutting off neighborhoods.
Dǔ and Jǐng are close, favored ministers;
they should serve as models for all officials.
Now the multitudes of the army are on the march,
the court is anxious to the point of parched lips,
the common people are distressed and suffering,
and the state treasury has nothing to use—
meaning no financial resources.
Yet you extravagantly adorn playthings and curios.
Hào (curio),
is pronounced hū dào fān.
You should temporarily halt the artisans,
focus your concern on the northern frontier,
and sympathize with the people's hardship."
The memorial was submitted,
but went unheeded.
Dòu Xiàn once sent a disciple to deliver a letter to the Imperial Secretary Deputy Yè, Zhì Shòu,
making some requests and entrustments.
Shòu immediately sent him to the imperial prison,
and submitted memorials repeatedly,
stating that Xiàn was arrogant and unrestrained,
citing Wáng Mǎng as a warning to the state;
also, during court assemblies,
he criticized and mocked Xiàn and others regarding the campaign against the Xiōngnú and the construction of mansions,
with stern tones and solemn expression,
the wording and intent were very earnest.
Xiàn was furious,
framing Shòu with charges of purchasing public land and slander,
handing him over to the officials,
who sentenced him to death.
Hé Chǎng submitted a memorial saying:
"Shòu is a confidential close minister,
whose duty is to correct and rescue.
If he harbors silence and does not speak,
his crime deserves death.
Now Shòu opposed the majority to uphold righteous counsel in order to stabilize the ancestral temple,
how could that be for private gain!
The reason I risk death to offer blind words,
the Analects says: Serving a gentleman, there are three faults,
speaking without observing the countenance is called blindness.
A loyal minister exhausts his integrity,
taking death as his destination;
although I do not know Shòu well,
I surmise he would accept it willingly.
Truly, I do not wish the sage court to carry out executions for slander,
thereby harming the harmonious transformation,
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Shūjīng Kǎolíngyào says: Tolerant and all-encompassing,
is called harmony.
Leaving behind endless criticism.
I, Chǎng, erroneously involved in confidential matters,
speaking what is inappropriate,
the charges are clear,
I should fill the prison,
preceding Shòu in falling dead,
ten thousand deaths would be more than enough."
The memorial was submitted,
Shòu's sentence was reduced from death,
and he was exiled to Hépǔ.
Before departing,
he committed suicide.
Shòu was
the son of Zhì Yùn.
Zhì Yùn served Emperor Guāngwǔ.
Yùn,
pronunciation: yú fěn fān.
In the summer, sixth month,
Dòu Xiàn and Gěng Bǐng set out from Shuòfāng Jīlù Sài,
Xián said: Now north of Shuòfāng Yǔhún County.
Yányīn's Shísānzhōuzhì says: Yǔhún County has a great road,
leading northwest out of Jīlù Sài.

Clerk,

"dī",

"jiān".

"dī"
"jiān"

Palace,

I note that according to the Geographical Records and the Records of Commanderies and States,

Yīng Shào said: The Yì River originates from Gù'ān in Zhuō Commandery;

At this time, the State of Zhào only had the territories of the Táng-era Xíng and Míng prefectures.
How could it have had a subordinate county as far north as the Yì River?

From this, it can be seen that

Chéng,

Shàng,

Subordinate (yuàn),

All places not reached by previous generations,

favorable winds,

Therefore, the one posing the challenge must clarify his master's teaching as the basis.
The one answering the challenge must also strive to establish the great meaning to elaborate his master's teaching.

Zhāng,

Sī,

Your subject Guāng remarks: The noble person of antiquity
served when the state was well-ordered,
and went into seclusion when the state was not.
Seclusion was not what the noble person desired.
When no one understood him and his Way could not be practiced,
when he had to dwell together with the wicked and corrupt,
and harm was about to befall him,
therefore he hid deeply to avoid it.
When a king raises up recluses,
and promotes those from obscurity,
(The Analects say: Raise up recluses,
and the people of the world will turn their hearts to you.
The Canon of Yáo says: Clearly promote those from obscurity.)
it is not to pander to the eyes and ears of the common world.
Therefore, if one possesses virtue and the Way sufficient to honor the ruler,
wisdom and ability sufficient to protect the people,
wearing coarse cloth yet concealing jade within,
hiding deeply and not putting oneself on the market—
(The sage wears coarse cloth yet conceals jade;
jade
is the ultimate treasure.
Wearing coarse cloth yet concealing it
metaphorically means precious beauty is not outwardly displayed.
A good merchant hides his goods deeply as if he had nothing;
a merchant with fine goods
hides them deeply as if he possessed nothing,
not selling unless he gets a good price.
These are both metaphors for scholars who embrace the Way and harbor talent.
'Pī' is pronounced pī.)
The ruler humbles himself
to seek them out,
restrains himself to follow them,
and only then can benefits and grace extend to the four quarters,
and achievements and merit reach above and below.
For he values their Way, not the person;
he seeks the substance, not the name.

The bronze instruments used by the official astronomers in the observation towers today

tracks the movements of the sun and moon,

Wáng Fān said: The form of heaven and earth

with heaven enveloping the earth on the outside,
just as the shell wraps around the yolk.
It revolves endlessly,
its shape perfectly spherical,
hence it is called the celestial sphere (Húntiān).
The circumference of heaven is 365 degrees and 145/589 parts of a degree,
with half exposed above the earth,
and half hidden below.
Its two ends are called the South Pole and the North Pole.
The North Pole rises 36 degrees above the earth,
and the South Pole sinks 36 degrees below the earth.
The distance between the two poles is slightly more than 182.5 degrees.
Around the North Pole,
within a diameter of 72 degrees,
the stars are always visible and never hidden,
which is called the upper circle.
Around the South Pole,
within 75 degrees,
the stars are always hidden and never seen,
which is called the lower circle.
The celestial equator encircles heaven's middle,
and is slightly more than 91 degrees away from each pole.
The ecliptic
is the path of the sun,
half of which lies outside the celestial equator,
and half inside.
It intersects with the celestial equator in the east at approximately 5 degrees in Jiǎo,
and in the west at approximately 14 degrees in Kuí.
The point where it is farthest outside the celestial equator
is 24 degrees away from the equator,
which is at 21 degrees in Dǒu.
The point where it is farthest inside the celestial equator
is also 24 degrees away,
which is at 25 degrees in Jǐng.
When the sun reaches its southernmost point,
it is at 21 degrees in Dǒu,
which is slightly more than 115 degrees from the pole.
The sun is at its southernmost,
farthest from the pole,
so the shadows are longest.
At 21 degrees in Dǒu on the ecliptic,
the sun rises at Chén and sets at Shēn,
so the sun also rises at Chén and sets at Shēn.
The sun travels slightly more than 146 degrees above the earth during the day,
so the days are short;
it travels slightly less than 219 degrees below the earth at night,
so the nights are long.
After the southern solstice,
the sun gradually moves closer to the pole,
so the shadows gradually shorten.
The sun travels slightly more degrees above the earth during the day,
so the days gradually lengthen;
it travels slightly fewer degrees below the earth at night,
so the nights gradually shorten.
The sun's position moves slightly northward,
so the sun rises and sets slightly farther north.
Until the summer solstice,
when the sun is at 25 degrees in Jǐng,
which is slightly more than 67 degrees from the pole.
The sun is at its northernmost, closest to the pole,
so the shadows are shortest.
At 25 degrees in Jǐng on the ecliptic,
the sun rises at Yín and sets at Xū,
so the sun also rises at Yín and sets at Xū.
The sun travels slightly less than 219 degrees above the earth during the day,
so the days are long;
it travels slightly more than 146 degrees below the earth at night,
so the nights are short.
After the summer solstice,
the sun gradually moves farther from the pole,
so the shadows gradually lengthen.
The sun travels slightly fewer degrees above the earth during the day,
so the days gradually shorten;
it travels slightly more degrees below the earth at night,
so the nights gradually lengthen.
The sun's position moves slightly southward,
so the sun rises and sets slightly farther south,
until it returns to the southern solstice and the cycle begins anew.
From 21 degrees in Dǒu
to 25 degrees in Jǐng,
the north-south distance is 48 degrees.
At the spring equinox, the sun is at approximately 14 degrees in Kuí,
and at the autumn equinox, it is at approximately 5 degrees in Jiǎo.
These are the intersection points of the ecliptic and the celestial equator,
both slightly more than 91 degrees from the pole.
They lie midway between 21 degrees in Dǒu and 25 degrees in Jǐng,
so the shadows are of intermediate length between the two solstices.
At 14 degrees in Kuí and 5 degrees in Jiǎo,
the sun rises at Mǎo and sets at Yǒu,
so the sun also rises at Mǎo and sets at Yǒu.
The sun travels above the earth during the day
and below the earth at night,
both slightly more than 180.5 degrees,
so the duration of daylight,
measured by the water clock, is 50 marks,
and the duration of darkness is also 50 marks,
making day and night equal.
Now, the division of day and night in heaven is based on the sun's rising and setting,
while for humans, it is based on dusk and dawn as the limits.
Dawn occurs two and a half marks before sunrise,
and dusk occurs two and a half marks before sunset,
so five marks are subtracted from the night and added to the day.
Therefore, during spring and autumn, the water clock
shows 55 marks for daylight.

and takes his position.
The ceremony concludes.
Since the Hàn dynasty, only Wèi Qīng, due to his merits, was appointed Grand General in the army;
it has never been heard of someone being appointed at his residence,
let alone such an exceptional honor being bestowed upon an empress's father!
He was humble, respectful, and fond of scholars,
recruiting Jù Lǎn from Hànyáng—
Jù
is the surname;
Lǎn,
the given name—
and appointing Lǐ Gù as an Assistant to the Imperial Clerk and Yáng Lún as a Chief Clerk.
Li Gu, considering that Shang was mild and self-restrained, unable to carry out any reforms,
submitted a memorial to Shang, saying:
"For several years now,
calamities and anomalies have frequently appeared.
Confucius said: 'The wise see changes and reflect on their form;
the foolish witness anomalies and conceal their names.'
In the biography of Li Gu in the Book of the Later Han,
'form'
is written as
'punishment.'
These two phrases likely originate from apocryphal texts.
They should be revered and feared.
The commentary says: Reverence means
respect.
It is said that Heaven has no partiality,
but only rewards the good,
and thus should be respected and feared.
When the Way is practiced and loyalty is established,
Your Excellency follows the lofty example of Bóchéng.
Zhuangzi said: Bóchéng Zǐgāo
was a feudal lord during the reigns of Táng and Yú;
when Yǔ came to power,
he left and plowed in the wilderness.
How can he be compared with those ordinary relatives by marriage who are obsessed with glory and covet high positions!"
Shang was unable to adopt his advice.
6 In autumn,
on the intercalary eighth month,
on the first day, Dīnghài,
there was a solar eclipse.
7 In winter,
in the tenth month,
the Wūhuán raided Yúnzhōng.
General Dùliáo Gěng Yè pursued and attacked them,
but was unsuccessful.
In the eleventh month,
the Wūhuán besieged Yè at Lánchí City;
according to the Continued Records of the Han: Shānán County in Yúnzhōng Commandery had Lánchí City.
The Wūhuán then withdrew.
8 In the twelfth month,
on Bǐng
yín,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
First Year of Yǒnghé
(Bǐngzǐ, 136)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on Jǐsì,
the era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
2 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on Dīnghài,
the Chéngfú Palace caught fire.
3 In the eleventh month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Grand Commandant Páng Cān was dismissed.
4 In the twelfth month,
the barbarians of Xiànglín rebelled.
Xiànglín County
belonged to Rìnán Commandery.
From the Jìn and Sòng dynasties onward, it became the kingdom of Línyì.
5 On Yǐsì,
the former Minister of Works Wáng Gōng was appointed Grand Commandant.
Gōng detested the eunuchs' monopoly of power,
and submitted a memorial strongly criticizing their conduct.
The various eunuchs and their associates falsely accused Gōng of crimes;
the emperor ordered Gōng to quickly prove his innocence.
Li Gu submitted a memorial to Liáng Shāng, saying:
"Lord Wáng, with his steadfast and upright character,
has been unjustly slandered by flatterers and sycophants.
When people heard of this,
none did not sigh in sorrow and tremble in fear.
The Three Excellencies hold positions of great respect,
and there is no principle that they should go to court to plead their innocence.
During the reign of Emperor Āi,
when Chancellor Wáng Jiā was summoned to the Court of the Commandant of Justice,
his secretary said:
'Generals and chancellors do not go to court to state their grievances;
this has become a precedent followed by one after another.
Your Excellency should take your own life.'
He then took his own life,
so according to the old regulations, unless there was a major crime,
they would not be subjected to severe interrogation.
The commentary says: Cases involving high ministers are serious,
hence called 'severe interrogation.'
During the reign of Emperor Chéng,
when Chancellor Xuē Xuān and the Imperial Counselor Zhái Fāngjìn were accused of crimes,
the emperor ordered five officials of the two-thousand-dan rank to jointly interrogate them.
The commentary on pronunciation and meaning says: Cases involving high ministers are serious,
so five officials of the two-thousand-dan rank jointly interrogated them.
If this happens, the court will gain a reputation for harming the worthy,
and loyal ministers will lose the integrity to rescue and protect them!
As the saying goes: 'When a good man is in distress,
one is so anxious that one forgets to eat.'
This means one should rescue him quickly.
Shāng then spoke to the emperor about it,
and the matter was resolved.
6 That year,
the Commandant of the Capital Liáng Jì was appointed Governor of Hénán.
Jì had a fondness for alcohol,
indulged in unrestrained wandering and self-indulgence,
and in office often acted violently and unlawfully.
Lǚ Fàng, the Magistrate of Luòyáng, who was close to his father Shāng, reported this to Shāng,
and Shāng reprimanded Jì for it.
Jì sent someone to assassinate Fàng on the road,
but fearing that Shāng would find out,
he shifted suspicion to Fàng's enemies,
and requested that Fàng's younger brother, Lǚ Yǔ, be appointed Magistrate of Luòyáng,
to have him capture them;
the commentary says: to comfort Fàng's family,
and to silence them.
I believe this interpretation is incorrect.
Jì requested from Shāng
to appoint Fàng's younger brother as magistrate,
claiming that he would urgently capture the criminals,
but secretly had Yǔ exterminate his elder brother's clan, relatives, and guests to satisfy his own resentment.
7 The Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng submitted a memorial,
stating that the barbarians had submitted,
meaning they came one after another to submit.
He proposed increasing their taxes and tributes,
and those discussing the matter all considered it acceptable.
The Imperial Secretary Yú Xǔ said:
"Since ancient times, sage kings
did not treat those of different customs as subjects.
According to the old regulations of the previous emperors,
the amount of tribute and taxes
has been established for a long time;
since the rise of the Hàn,
the various barbarians of Wǔlíng
were required to pay one bolt of cloth per adult per year,
and two zhang per child,
which is called 'cóng cloth.'
If this is increased now, they will certainly resent and rebel.
Calculating the gains,
they will not compensate for the losses,
and there will surely be regret later."
The emperor did not listen.
The barbarians of Lǐzhōng and Hànzhōng each disputed that the increased tribute cloth was not according to the old agreement,
and they killed the local officials,
and the entire tribe rebelled.
1 In spring,
twenty thousand Wǔlíng barbarians besieged Chōng City,
and eight thousand raided Yídào.
The commentary says: Chōng County,
belonged to Wǔlíng Commandery,
its old city was located northeast of Chóngyì County in Lǐ Prefecture.
Chōng
is pronounced chōng.
Yídào
belonged to Nán Commandery.
2 In the second month,
the Commandant of the Dependent State of Guǎnghàn defeated the White Horse Qiāng.
Emperor Ān changed the Commandant of the Northern Division of Shǔ Commandery to the Commandant of the Dependent State of Guǎnghàn,
separately administering the three circuits of Yīnpíng, Diànshī, and Gāngshī,
belonging to Yì Province.
3 The emperor sent the Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng, Lǐ Jìn, to attack the rebellious barbarians,
and he defeated and pacified them.
Jìn then selected good officials,
to comfort and pacify the barbarians,
and the commandery became peaceful.
4 In the third month,
the Minister of Works Wáng Zhuó passed away.
On Dīngchǒu,
the Minister of the Imperial Household Guō Qián was appointed Minister of Works.
Textual analysis says: The Yuánshū writes
"Gān,"
but here we follow the Book of the Later Han.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on Bǐngshēn,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
6 In the fifth month,
on Guǐchǒu,
the Lady of Shānyáng, Sòng É, was accused of fabricating false accusations and deceit,
her seal and ribbon were confiscated,
and she was sent back to her hometown.
The nine marquises Huáng Lóng, Yáng Tuó, Mèng Shū, Lǐ Jiàn, Zhāng Xián, Shǐ Fàn, Wáng Dào, Lǐ Yuán, and Lǐ Gāng were accused of exchanging bribes with Sòng É,
seeking high positions and increased fiefs,
and they were all sent back to their fiefs,
with their land taxes reduced by one-fourth.
Textual analysis says: The biography of Sūn Chéng states:
"Lóng and others falsely accused Cáo Téng and Mèng Bēn,"
but according to the biography of Liáng Shāng,
those who falsely accused Téng and Bēn were Zhāng Kuí and others,
not Lóng and others.
7 The Xiànglín barbarians, such as Ōu Lián,
attacked the county offices,
and killed the chief officials.
The Inspector of Jiāozhǐ, Fán Yǎn, dispatched over ten thousand troops from Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn to rescue them;
the soldiers feared the distant campaign,
and in autumn,
in the seventh month,
the troops of the two commanderies rebelled,
and attacked their headquarters.
Although the headquarters defeated the rebels,
the barbarians' momentum grew stronger.
8 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
the Emperor traveled to Cháng'ān.
Tián Ruò of Fúfēng recommended Fǎ Zhēn of the same commandery, who was well-versed in both inner and outer studies.
Scholars of the Eastern Capital considered the seven apocrypha as inner studies,
and the six classics as outer studies.
It would be appropriate to appoint him to a high ministerial position.
Xián said: The Máo Shī states: "When the duties of the high minister are deficient."
This refers to the Three Dukes.
He was summoned four times in succession,
but ultimately did not yield.
His friend Guō Zhèng praised him, saying:
"Fǎ Zhēn's name may be heard,
but his person is difficult to see.
He flees from fame, yet fame follows him;
he avoids fame, yet fame pursues him.
Truly, he can be called a teacher for a hundred generations!"
Zhēn was
the son of Xióng.
Fǎ Xióng appears in the forty-ninth scroll, in the fourth year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Ān.
9 On the Dīngmǎo day,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
10 Grand Commandant Wáng Gōng, because the eunuch Zhāng Fǎng and others monopolized state power,
wished to memorialize for their execution.
A relative advised him by citing the example of Yáng Zhèn's actions.
Yáng Zhèn's affair is recorded in the fiftieth scroll, in the third year of the Yánguāng era of Emperor Ān.
11 In the twelfth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the Emperor returned from Cháng'ān.
1 In spring,
in the second month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the capital, as well as Jīnchéng and Lǒngxī, experienced earthquakes,
and mountains collapsed in these two commanderies.
2 In summer,
in the intercalary fourth month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
3 In the fifth month,
Yáng Zhēn, the assistant of Wú Commandery, rebelled
and attacked the commandery headquarters;
the Grand Administrator Wáng Héng defeated and beheaded him.
4 Attendant Censor Jiǎ Chāng, together with the provincial and commandery forces, campaigned against Ōu Lián,
but was unsuccessful.
He was besieged by them;
after more than a year,
troops and provisions were not replenished.
The Emperor summoned the dukes, ministers, officials, and the staff of the Four Offices
(the Grand General's office had twenty-nine staff members,
the Grand Commandant's office twenty-four,
the Minister over the Masses' office thirty-one,
and the Minister of Works' office twenty-nine)
to discuss sending a senior general
and dispatching forty thousand troops from Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù to reinforce them.
Lǐ Gù objected, saying:
"If Jīng and Yáng were peaceful,
dispatching troops would be feasible.
But now bandits in these two provinces are entrenched and not dispersed.
(The two provinces refer to Jīng and Yáng.)
Chángshā and Guìyáng have been repeatedly conscripted;
if they are disturbed again,
further troubles will surely arise.
This is the first reason it is inadvisable.
Moreover,
the people of Yǎn and Yù, suddenly conscripted,
would have to travel ten thousand lǐ afar,
with no certainty of return.
With urgent imperial decrees pressing them,
rebellion and desertion would inevitably occur.
This is the second reason it is inadvisable.
The southern regions have warm, humid climates,
plus miasmic air,
causing deaths of four or five out of ten.
This is the third reason it is inadvisable.
Traveling ten thousand lǐ afar,
soldiers would be exhausted,
and by the time they reached south of the mountains,
they would no longer be fit for combat.
This is the fourth reason it is inadvisable.
An army marches thirty lǐ per day as the standard,
and it is over nine thousand lǐ to Rìnán,
taking three hundred days to arrive.
Calculating five shēng of grain per person,
(Xián said: The ancient shēng was small,
hence five shēng.)
(Lǐn means to supply.)
not including the provisions for officers and pack animals,
just carrying armor themselves,
the expense would be this great.
This is the fifth reason it is inadvisable.
Wherever the army is stationed,
deaths would certainly be numerous.
If they are insufficient to resist the enemy,
further conscription would be necessary.
This would be like cutting out the heart to mend the limbs.
This is the sixth reason it is inadvisable.
Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán are a thousand lǐ apart.
Conscripting their officials and people is already unbearable,
let alone forcing soldiers from four provinces to endure the hardships of ten thousand lǐ!
This is the seventh reason it is inadvisable.
Previously, the Central Courtyard General Yīn Jiù campaigned against rebellious Qiāng in Yìzhōu.
A Yìzhōu proverb said: 'When the enemy comes, it's tolerable;
when Yīn comes, he kills us.'
Later, Yīn Jiù was recalled,
and his troops were handed over to Inspector Zhāng Qiáo.
Qiáo, relying on his officers,
annihilated the bandits within a month.
(This affair is recorded in the forty-ninth scroll, the second year of the Yuánchū era of Emperor Ān,
up to the fiftieth scroll, the fifth year.)
This is proof that provincial and commandery officials can be entrusted.
We should instead select courageous, strategic, benevolent, and capable individuals fit to be generals
to serve as Inspectors and Grand Administrators,
and have them all stationed in Jiāozhǐ.
Currently, Rìnán has few troops and no grain.
(Meaning a lone army amidst rebellious barbarians,
also lacking provisions.)
They cannot fight,
so all officials and people should be relocated,
moving north to rely on Jiāozhǐ.
After peace is restored,
they can be ordered to return to their homeland.
Also, recruit barbarians to fight among themselves,
transporting gold and silk to fund them.
Those who can sow discord and deliver enemy leaders' heads
should be promised rewards of enfeeffment and land grants.
Former Yìzhōu Inspector Zhù Liáng of Chángshā,
by nature brave and decisive,
and also Zhāng Qiáo of Nányáng,
who previously achieved merit in defeating bandits in Yìzhōu,
are both suitable for appointment.
In the past, Emperor Tàizōng appointed Wèi Shǎng as Grand Administrator of Yúnzhōng on the spot.
(Wèi Shǎng appears in the fourteenth scroll, the fourteenth year of Emperor Wén;
the on-the-spot appointment is not recorded.)
(Shǒu is read as shòu;
same below.)
The former Hànshū records: Gǒng Shě,
a man of Chǔ,
was first summoned as Remonstrance Grandee,
but resigned due to illness;
summoned again as Erudite,
he again resigned due to illness.
Shortly after,
Emperor Āi sent an envoy to Chǔ to appoint Shě as Grand Administrator of Tàishān.
He assumed office on the way."
The Four Offices all followed Lǐ Gù's proposal.
Immediately, Zhù Liáng was appointed Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn,
and Zhāng Qiáo as Inspector of Jiāozhǐ.
When Qiáo arrived,
he openly showed comfort and persuasion,
and all surrendered and dispersed.
When Liáng reached Jiǔzhēn,
he entered the bandits' territory in a single carriage,
devised strategies,
and appealed with authority and credibility.
Tens of thousands surrendered
and all built government offices for Liáng.
Thus, peace was restored beyond the mountains.
5 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Minister over the Masses Huáng Shǎng was dismissed.
In the ninth month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
Liú Shòu of Chángshā, Commandant of the Palace Gentlemen, was appointed Minister over the Masses.
6 On the Bǐngxū day,
an order was issued for the Grand General and the Three Dukes to recommend two individuals each who are resolute, brave, fierce,
and capable of planning and serving as generals,
and for the Specially Advanced, Ministers, and Commandants to recommend one each.
Initially,
the Imperial Secretary Líng Zuǒ Xióng recommended the Inspector of Jì Province, Zhōu Jǔ, to be an Imperial Secretary;
later, Xióng became the Colonel Director of the Retainers,
and Jǔ recommended the former Inspector of Jì Province, Féng Zhí, for a military command.
Zhí had once been convicted for accepting bribes,
is an ancient character interchangeable with 贓.)
Xióng impeached Jǔ for recommending an unsuitable person.
pronounced hài,
also pronounced hé.)
"The imperial edict instructed me to select martial and fierce men,
not to select men of pure and lofty character."
Jǔ said:
"The imperial edict instructed you to select martial and fierce men,
not to select corrupt men!"
Xióng said:
"By recommending you,
I have brought trouble upon myself."
Jǔ said:
"In the past, Zhào Xuānzǐ appointed Hán Jué as Marshal;
Jué executed Xuānzǐ's charioteer according to military law.
Xuānzǐ said to the assembled ministers: 'You may congratulate me!
I selected Jué, and he fulfills his duties.'
(When Qín and Jìn fought at Héqū,
Zhào Xuānzǐ commanded the central army,
and Hán Jué was the Marshal.
Xuānzǐ sent his own chariot to disrupt the ranks,
and Hán Jué executed his charioteer.
The multitude said:
'Hán Jué will surely not survive,
his master promoted him in the morning, and by evening he executed his master's charioteer.'
Xuānzǐ said to the assembled ministers:
'You may congratulate me!
I recommended Jué, and he fulfills his duties,
now I know I can avoid blame!')
pronounced rén.)
I dare not flatter you, lest I bring shame upon you;
I did not realize your intention differed from that of Xuānzǐ."
Xióng was pleased,
and apologized, saying:
"I once served Féng Zhí's father,
and was also on good terms with Zhí;
now Xuānguāng has impeached me for this,
it is my fault!"
(Zhōu Jǔ,
styled Xuānguāng.)
Hearing of his fault and submitting to it,
the world esteemed Zuǒ Xióng all the more for this.
How do those who conceal their faults compare!
At this time,
the eunuchs vied in selling favors and influence,
using their power to trade for gratitude,
thereby selling themselves.
(In the Spring and Autumn period, Zǐ Liáng, son of Duke Mù of Zhèng,
later took Liáng as his surname.)
(Xián said: modest and retiring, yet dignified and substantial.)
(I say that being retiring and substantial means
not competing for advancement with one's peers,
nor contending in frivolity and shallowness.)
Liáng Hé alone made no recommendations.
The Emperor asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"I was born in the thatched huts,
and grew up in the palace;
I have neither the wisdom to know men,
nor have I ever associated with the scholar class.
In the past, Wèi Yāng gained an audience through Jǐng Jiān,
and those with discernment knew he would not come to a good end.
(The event is recorded in the second year of King Xiǎn of Zhōu's reign.)
It is not an honor but a disgrace,
meaning it is not enough to be considered an honor,
but rather a disgrace.)
(考異曰: The Biography of the Eunuchs says:
'In the Yángjiā era,
an edict called for recommending martial and fierce men,
and Liáng Hé alone made no recommendations.')
(I believe this edict mistakenly records Yǒnghé as Yángjiā.)
The Emperor therefore rewarded him.
7 In winter,
tenth month,
Nàlí of the Shāodāng Qiāng and over three thousand cavalry raided Jīnchéng,
Commandant Mǎ Xián attacked and defeated them.
8 Twelfth month,
on the first day, Wùxū,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 The Grand General Liáng Shāng, because the Minor Eunuch Nányáng Cáo Jié and others wielded power within the palace,
sent his sons Jì and Bùyí to befriend them;
but the eunuchs, jealous of his favor,
instead sought to entrap him.
The Regular Palace Attendants Zhāng Kuí, Qú Zhèng, Yáng Dìng, and others
(Qú,
is a surname.
In Wèi, there was the Grand Master Qú Bóyù.)
together slandered Shāng and the Regular Palace Attendants Cáo Téng and Mèng Bēn,
saying
"they intend to summon the various princes,
plot to depose and enthrone,
we request that Shāng and others be arrested and tried for their crimes."
The Emperor said:
"The Grand General and his sons,
are my kin,
Téng and Bēn,
are my favorites,
they certainly would not do such a thing,
it is only that you all are jealous of them."
is the same as 妬.)
Fearing and feeling pressured,
meaning since their words were not heeded,
they feared disaster would befall them.)
They forged an edict and arrested and bound Téng and Bēn within the palace.
The Emperor heard of this,
was greatly angered,
and ordered the eunuch Lǐ Xī to urgently summon Téng and Bēn and release them;
he arrested Kuí and the others and imprisoned them.
1 In spring,
first month,
on Gēngchén,
Kuí and others were executed;
the matter implicated the Governor of Hóngnóng, Zhāng Fèng, and the Chancellor of Ānpíng, Yáng Hào,
who were both sentenced to death;
the confessions implicated others,
extending to ministers in office.
Shāng, fearing many would be wrongfully implicated,
then submitted a memorial saying:
"According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
merit lies with the commander-in-chief,
and punishment stops with the chief culprit.
(The Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals: Jìn's Xì Kè led troops and defeated the Qí army at Ān;
when the army returned,
Fàn Wénzǐ entered last,
and said:
'The army has achieved merit,
the people of the state are happy to welcome them;
if I enter first,
I will surely attract attention,
this would be to take the commander's fame for myself,
therefore I dare not.')
(The Yú army and the Jìn army destroyed Xiàyáng,
the Gōngyáng Commentary says: Yú,
is a small state,
why is it placed above the great states?
To make Yú the chief culprit.)
pronounced shuài.)
The innocent are many,
death-row prisoners long detained,
trivial matters become major,
(Xián said: meaning if detained for long,
then minor matters are dragged in to become major.)
to govern peacefully and accomplish transformation.)
This should be concluded early,
to stop the trouble of arrests."
(Meaning in the first month of spring,
one should bestow rewards and favors,
following the heart of Heaven and Earth in nurturing life,
to welcome harmonious energy,
it is not fitting to let legal cases branch out and spread.)
(Xián said: 逮,
means 'to reach';
those implicated in the confessions,
are then pursued and arrested.)
Punishment should stop with the guilty parties.
In the second month,
the Emperor appointed Liáng Shāng's youngest son, the Tiger Guard Commandant Liáng Bùyí, as Commandant of Infantry.
Liáng Shāng submitted a memorial declining the appointment, stating:
"Bùyí is but a child,
yet he is presumptuously placed in a position meant for adults.
In the past, Yàn Píngzhòng declined the fief of Bèidiàn to secure
his wealth.
*Zuǒzhuàn*: When Qí punished Qìng Fēng,
it offered Yànzi the fief of Bèidiàn,
comprising sixty border towns;
he did not accept it.
Zǐ Wěi said:
'Wealth
is what all men desire,
why do you not accept it?'
He replied:
'The Qìng clan's cities were sufficient to satisfy their desires,
and thus they perished.
My cities are not sufficient to satisfy my desires;
if I add Bèidiàn to them,
then they would become sufficient,
and my ruin would not be far off!
My refusal of Bèidiàn
is not because I dislike wealth,
but because I fear losing wealth.'"
Bèi,
is pronounced *pú duì*.
Diàn,
is pronounced *duō jiàn*,
or also as the common reading.
Gōngyí Xiū served as Chancellor of Lǔ;
a guest presented fish to the Chancellor,
but the Chancellor did not accept it.
The guest said:
'I have heard you are fond of fish,
so I present you with fish,
why do you not accept it?'
The Chancellor said:
'It is precisely because I am fond of fish
that I do not accept it.
Now, as Chancellor, I can supply myself with fish;
if I accept fish and am dismissed from office,
who will supply me with fish again!
Therefore, I do not accept it.'
I too wish to firmly secure fortune and emolument in this sagely age!"
The Emperor then appointed Bùyí as Palace Attendant and Commandant of Chariots and Cavalry.
Liáng Shāng's act of declining
demonstrates the power of mastering the Classics and Commentaries.
2 In the third month,
on Yǐhài,
an earthquake occurred in the capital.
3 The Qiāng chieftains Nàlí and others rebelled again;
in summer,
the fourth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
Protector of the Qiāng, Mǎ Xián, attacked and beheaded them,
capturing over twelve hundred heads and prisoners.
4 On Wùwǔ,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
5 In the fifth month,
on Wùchén,
Liú Ān, son of the late Jìběi Huì King Liú Shòu, was enfeoffed as King of Jìběi.
Last year, the King of Jìběi, Liú Duō, passed away,
leaving no heir;
now Ān was appointed to continue the line.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* biographies record
"Ānguó";
this follows the Imperial Annals.
Jì,
is pronounced *zǐ lǐ*.
6 In autumn,
the eighth month,
there was a drought in Tàiyuán.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on Wùshēn,
an earthquake occurred in the capital.
2 The Southern Xiōngnú chieftains Wúsī and Chēniǔ, among others, rebelled,
raiding Xīhé;
they enticed the Right Worthy King to join forces and besiege Měijí,
killing the senior officials of Shuòfāng and Dàijùn.
In summer,
the fifth month,
General Who Crosses the Liao, Mǎ Xù, and the Palace Attendant Commandant Liáng Bìng, among others,

"Clothing,"

This impoverishes families with daughters;
now the women in the rear palace,

The Emperor casually asked his attendant, Ài Yán of Chénliú:

"In the past, Zhū Yún broke the palace railing in court remonstrance;

Kǒng Yǐngdá said:
"Yǐ"
and

"using one great sacrificial ox for the seasonal sacrifices in spring and autumn,"

Yǐ and yǐ have the same meaning,
