so the multitude's slanders and secret harms
are certainly fitting!"
The emperor then summoned Guī back,
appointed him as a Counsellor,
and his achievements were deemed worthy of enfeoffment.
However, the Regular Palace Attendants Xú Huáng and Zuǒ Guàn wanted to seek bribes from him,
and repeatedly sent their clients to inquire about the details of his merits,
but Guī ultimately did not respond.
Huáng and the others grew angry,
and framed him using a previous incident.
(The previous incident
refers to the matter of false accusations and slander.)
His subordinates wanted to collect funds to offer as apology gifts,
but Guī swore an oath and would not listen,
and so, on the grounds that remnant bandits had not been completely eradicated,
he was imprisoned in the Court of the Imperial Secretariat,
sentenced, and sent to the Left Labor Battalion.
Various high officials and over three hundred Imperial University students, including Zhāng Fèng, went to the palace gates to plead his case.
A general amnesty was then issued,
and he returned home.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the Wùwǔ day, the Minister over the Masses, Chóng Hào, passed away.
2 In the third month,
on the Wùxū day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
3 The Commandant of the Guards, Xǔ Xǔ of Yǐngchuān, was appointed as Minister over the Masses.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
a fire broke out at the eastern office of the Kānglíng Mausoleum.
5 In the fifth month,
the Xiānbēi invaded the Dependent State of Liáodōng.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
a fire broke out in the funerary park and temple of the Pínglíng Mausoleum.
(Pínglíng
is Emperor Zhāo's mausoleum.)
7 The bandits Lǐ Yán and others from Guìyáng invaded the commandery borders,
and the Wǔlíng Man tribes rebelled again;
the Grand Administrator Chén Jǔ
suppressed and pacified them.
The eunuchs had long detested Féng Gǔn.
In the eighth month,
Gǔn was held responsible for the army's return
and the resurgence of bandits,
and was dismissed from office.
8 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
the emperor went on an inspection hunt at Guǎngchéng,
and then proceeded to the Hángǔ Pass and the Shànglín Park.
The Minister of the Imperial Household, Chén Fān, submitted a memorial admonishing:
"In times of peace and stability,
hunting excursions should be moderate,
how much more so now when we face the threefold emptiness crisis!
The fields and countryside are empty,
the court and government are empty,
the granaries and treasuries are empty.
Moreover, armed conflicts have not ceased,
and the four quarters are scattered and dispersed.
This is a time for Your Majesty to be anxious and careworn,
sitting up and awaiting the dawn.
(Careworn
means having a worried expression on one's face.
To be above ministers and people
and have nothing to show for one's face.)
How can one indulge in the spectacle of carriages and horses!
Furthermore, last autumn there was much rain,
and the people have just begun planting wheat.
Now, missing the season to encourage planting,
and ordering them to perform the labor of driving game and clearing roads,
is not in accordance with the intentions of a wise and sagely ruler who shows compassion for the people."
The memorial was submitted,
but was not accepted.
9 In the eleventh month,
the Minister of Works, Liú Chǒng, was dismissed.
In the twelfth month,
the Commandant of the Guards, Zhōu Jǐng, was appointed as Minister of Works.
Jǐng
was the grandson of Zhōu Róng.
At that time, the eunuchs' power was at its peak.
Jǐng and the Grand Commandant Yáng Bǐng submitted a statement:
"The official positions, both inside and outside the court,
are largely filled by unsuitable individuals.
According to old statutes,
the sons and younger brothers of palace attendants
should not hold positions of authority;
yet now their branches and clients,
(Branches
refers to the clansmen and relatives of the palace attendants.)
(Shǔ,
means official residences.)
occupy and control the posts of governors and magistrates;
both superiors and inferiors are resentful and troubled,
and the four quarters are filled with sorrow and suffering.
We should follow the old regulations,
dismiss the greedy and cruel,
and block disasters and slander.

We request that orders be issued to the Colonel Director of the Retainers, the officials of the two thousand picul rank, the Colonel of the City Gates, the Colonels of the Five Barracks, and the Leader of the Northern Army,
each to thoroughly investigate their own departments;
(The Colonel Director of the Retainers oversees the Three Adjuncts, the Three Rivers, and Hóngnóng.
Officials of the two thousand picul rank
are the various ministers,
each leading their subordinates.
The Colonel of the City Gates oversees the twelve City Gate Majors and Gate Captains.
The Colonels of the Five Barracks
are: the Chariot and Horse Colonel, the Rapid as Tigers Colonel,
the Infantry Colonel, the Ever-flowing Waters Colonel, and the Archery and Sound Colonel,
each having their own Majors and subordinate officials.
The Leader of the Northern Army
is in charge of supervising the Five Barracks.
Xià,
is pronounced xiá.)
They should each report the situation to the Three Ducal Offices,
and if the investigation reveals omissions,
they should submit further reports."
(This means each official thoroughly investigates their own department,
and reports those who should be dismissed to the Ducal Offices.
They should further investigate any omissions and submit additional reports,
so that no one deserving punishment escapes.)
(Shàng,
is pronounced shǎng.)
Thereupon, Bǐng itemized and impeached over fifty people, including the Regional Inspector of Qīng Province, Yáng Liàng, and various Governors and Grand Administrators.
Some died, some were dismissed,
and the whole empire was filled with awe.
10 An edict was issued summoning Huángfǔ Guī to serve as General Who Subdues the Liáo.
Earlier,
Zhāng Huàn had been implicated as a former subordinate of Liáng Jì,
dismissed from office and barred from holding office.
Among all his old friends and associates,
none dared to speak on his behalf;
only Guī recommended him,
submitting memorials seven times in succession.
As a result, Huàn was appointed as Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi.
When Guī became General Who Subdues the Liáo,
a few months after arriving at the camp,
he submitted a memorial recommending Huàn,
saying he "possesses both talent and strategy in abundance,
and should rightfully hold the position of commander-in-chief."
(Commander-in-chief
refers to the General Who Subdues the Liáo.)
"If it is still considered that this foolish minister should fill the position
of handling affairs,
I am willing to beg for a sinecure,
to serve as Huàn's deputy."
The court complied.
Huàn replaced Guī as General Who Subdues the Liáo,
and Guī was appointed as Palace Attendant Who Pacifies the Xiōngnú.
11 Officials and commoners from the western provinces guarding the palace gates to plead the injustice suffered by the former Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, Duàn Jiǒng, were very numerous;
at that time, the various tribes of Qiāng, such as Diānnà and others, grew even more powerful,
and Liáng Province was nearly lost.
(Diān,
is pronounced diān.
Zhǒng,
is pronounced zhǒng.
Jī,
is pronounced jī.)
Guō Tài was inherently wise in understanding people,
fond of encouraging and instructing scholars,
and traveled extensively through the commanderies and kingdoms.
Máo Róng,
over forty years old,
was plowing in the fields
when he and his companions took shelter from the rain under a tree.
Everyone else sat cross-legged facing each other,
Xián’s note: Yí,
means level.
Shuōwén states: Jù,
means to squat.
The Analects says: Yuán Rǎng sat levelly and waited.
This means he sat levelly and arrogantly.
Wēizuò,
means to sit upright with the front of the robe straightened.
Guō Tài then requested to lodge there for the night.
The next morning,
Máo Róng killed a chicken to prepare a meal,
and Guō Tài thought it was prepared for him;
but Máo Róng gave half to his mother,
set aside the other half,
and ate only vegetables with his guest.
Xián’s note: Cǎo,
means coarse.
Fàn,
pronounced fù yuǎn fān.
“You are virtuous indeed, far beyond others!
Having said ‘virtuous indeed,’
and also ‘far beyond,’
means his virtue far surpasses that of ordinary people.
The provision of the three sacrificial animals,
refers to the means of supporting one’s parents.
The Classic of Filial Piety says: Daily provide the nourishment of the three sacrificial animals.
Bīnlǚ,
means guests.
You are my friend.”
He stood up,
bowed to him,
urged him to pursue learning,
and he eventually became a man of great virtue.
Mèng Mǐn from Jùlù,
was staying in Tàiyuán,
when he dropped a pottery steamer he was carrying,
and walked away without looking back.
Guō Tài saw this and asked him why,
to which he replied:
“The steamer is already broken,
what good is there in looking at it!”
Guō Tài considered him decisive,
spoke with him,
recognized his moral character,
and thus urged him to travel and study,
after which he became renowned in his time.
Shēntú Pán from Chénliú,
came from a poor family,
and worked as a lacquerer;
Yǔ Chéng from Yānlíng,
in his youth served at the county court as a gate guard;
Yānlíng County,
belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Shī Gǔ’s note: Yān,
pronounced yǎn.
Lù Dé Míng’s note: Yān,
pronounced yè wǎn fān,
also yú jiàn fān.
Xián’s note: Ménshì,
means gate guard.
Shào,
pronounced shī zhào fān.
Later, both became famous scholars.
Others came from backgrounds such as butchers, wine sellers, or soldiers,
and many achieved fame through Guō Tài’s encouragement and recommendation.
A youth from Chén Kingdom, Wèi Zhāo, requested of Guō Tài:
“A teacher of the classics is easy to find,
but a teacher of virtue is hard to come by.
A teacher of the classics,
refers to a specialist who teaches with established methods.
A teacher of virtue,
refers to one who cultivates himself and sets an example for society.
Yì,
pronounced yǐ chì fān.
I wish to serve and perform menial tasks.”
Guō Tài agreed.
Once, when Guō Tài was unwell,
meaning his body was not in proper condition,
it was said he was unwell,
indicating a slight illness.
Wèi Zhāo prepared porridge,
and presented it to Guō Tài,
who scolded him:
“When making porridge for an elder,
you did not pay proper attention,
making it inedible!”
And threw the bowl to the ground.
Wèi Zhāo made porridge again and presented it,
and Guō Tài scolded him once more.
This happened three times,
yet Wèi Zhāo’s expression remained unchanged.
Guō Tài then said:
“At first, I only saw your face,
but from now on,
I know your heart!”
He then befriended and treated him well.
Zuǒ Yuán from Chénliú,
was a student in the commandery school,
but was expelled for breaking the law.
Guō Tài met him on the road,
and prepared wine and food to comfort him.
He said:
“In the past, Yán Zhuōjù,
was a great bandit from Liángfǔ,
and Duàngān Mù,
was a great broker in the state of Jìn,
yet they eventually became loyal ministers of Qí
and a renowned worthy of Wèi;
The Annals of Lü Buwei states: Yán Zhuōjù,
was a great bandit from Liángfǔ,
who studied under Confucius.
The Zuǒzhuàn records,
when Jìn attacked Qí,
they fought at Líqiū,
and the Qí army was defeated,
with Zhì Bó personally capturing Yán Gēng.
Dù Yù’s commentary states: Líqiū,
is a low-lying area.
Yán Gēng,
is the Qí minister Yán Zhuōjù.
It also says: When Jìn’s Xún Yáo attacked Zhèng,
Zhèng sought aid from Qí.
As the Qí army was about to set out,
Chén Chéngzǐ prepared a carriage and two horses,
and attached five towns,
summoning Yán Zhuōjù’s son, Jìn, and said:
“In the battle at Xí,
your father died.
Now, the ruler grants you these towns,
ride in the carriage to court,
and do not waste his previous efforts.”
The Annals of Lü Buwei states: Duàngān Mù was a broker in the state of Jìn.
Shuōwén states: Zǎng,
means to meet,
referring to bringing together two parties for trade,
like a market broker today.
The Xīnxù states: When Duke Wén of Wèi passed by Duàngān Mù’s lane, he bowed to his gate,
and the people chanted:
“Our lord loves righteousness,
hence he honors Duàngān Mù;
our lord loves loyalty,
hence he esteems Duàngān Mù.”
When Qín wanted to attack Wèi,
Simá Táng advised:
“Duàngān Mù is a worthy,
and Wèi honors him,
which is known throughout the world.
Would it not be wrong to attack them!”
Zǎng,
pronounced zǐ lǎng fān.
Zú,
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
The Analects says: Qú Bóyù sent a messenger to Confucius,
and Confucius asked him:
“What is your master doing?”
He replied:
“My master wishes to reduce his faults but has not yet succeeded.”
It also says:
“Yán Huí loved learning,
and did not repeat his mistakes.”
Qú,
pronounced qiú yú fān.
Yuàn,
pronounced yú juàn fān.
Do not harbor resentment,
but reflect on yourself!”
Zuǒ Yuán accepted his words and left.
Some criticized Guō Tài for not cutting ties with wicked people,
to which Guō Tài said:
“If a man is not benevolent,
and you despise him too much,
it will lead to disorder.”
Xián’s note: These are Confucius’s words from the Analects.
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary states: For an unrighteous person,
one should influence him through moral transformation.
If you despise him too much,
it will only cause him to create disorder.
Zuǒ Yuán later wanted to take revenge on the students.
On that day,
Guō Tài was at the school,
and Zuǒ Yuán felt ashamed for betraying his earlier words,
so he gave up and left.
Later, when the matter came to light,
everyone expressed admiration and respect.
Someone asked Fàn Pāng:
"What kind of man is Guō Línzōng?"
Pāng replied:
"In seclusion, he does not abandon his kin;
Xián said: He is like Jiè Tuī.
Xián said: He is like Liǔxià Huì.
Lords cannot make him a friend,
I know nothing else about him."
Tài was once recommended for the 'Yǒudào' selection,
but did not take office.
The matter of recommending 'Yǒudào'
began in the first year of the Jiànguāng era of Emperor Ān, in the fiftieth scroll.
He considered that since the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
there had been no one his equal.
He once urged him to take office.
Hàn Yuán,
refers to the beginning of the Hàn dynasty.
Pǐ,
means companion,
equal,
match.
"I observe the celestial phenomena at night,
and examine human affairs by day.
What Heaven intends to destroy,
cannot be supported.
I shall simply pass my years in leisurely ease."
Yet he still moved about in the capital,
teaching and guiding without cease.
Xú Zhì wrote to admonish him, saying:
"When a great tree is about to fall,
it cannot be held by a single rope.
Why do you rush about without finding a place of peace!"
Xián said: Diān,
means to fall,
wéi,
means to tie,
metaphorically meaning the times are declining,
and cannot be saved by one person alone.
Yǐn Tūn said: Xīxī,
means hurried and anxious.
Chǔ,
is pronounced Chāng Lǚ fān.
"I respectfully accept these words,
and take them as my guide."
Huáng Yǔn of Jìyīn,
was renowned for his outstanding talent.
Tài, upon seeing him, said:
"Your high talent surpasses others,
sufficient to achieve greatness.
Past forty years of age,
your fame is established.
However, at this point,
you must deeply restrain and uphold yourself.
Otherwise,
you will lose it!"
Later, the Minister over the Masses Yuán Wěi sought a marriage match for his niece.
Upon seeing Yǔn,
he sighed and said:
"To have a son-in-law like this,
is enough."
Yǔn, hearing this, divorced and sent away his wife.
Yǔn's wife was from the Xiàhóu clan.
Yǔn divorced his wife,
wishing to become Yuán's son-in-law.
Thereupon, in front of the crowd, she rolled up her sleeves and enumerated fifteen hidden faults of Yǔn before leaving.
Because of this, Yǔn was ruined in his time.
Initially,
Yǔn and Jìn Wénjīng of Hànzhōng both relied on their talent and wisdom,
making their names known far and wide,
but declined summons to office.
They claimed to be treating illness in the capital,
not receiving guests.
High officials and nobles sent their disciples morning and evening to inquire after their health,
and minor officials crowded at their gates,
yet still could not get an audience;
those recommended for appointment by the Three Excellencies
would often be consulted about them,
and according to their praise or criticism,
decisions on appointments were made.
Fú Róng said to Lǐ Yīng:
"These two men have no reputation for virtuous conduct,
yet set themselves up as heroes.
They have caused high officials to inquire after their health,
and royal ministers to sit at their gates.
I fear their petty ways undermine righteousness,
and empty praise contradicts reality.
They should be specially investigated."
Yīng agreed.
From then on, the reputation and standing of the two men gradually declined,
and their followers and visitors gradually decreased.
Within ten days,
ashamed and sighing, they fled.
Later, both were dismissed from office due to crimes.
Qiú Xiāng of Chénliú,
was of the highest conduct, pure and silent.
The surname genealogy: The surname Qiú
descends from the Sòng grandee Qiú Mù.
Xíng,
is pronounced xià mèng fān;
same below.
At forty years of age,
he became the chief of Pú Village.
Pú Village,
belonged to Kǎochéng County in Chénliú Commandery.
He lived alone with his mother.
His mother came to Xiāng to accuse Yuán of being unfilial.
Xiāng, startled, said:
"I recently passed by Yuán's house.
The courtyard and dwelling were tidy and orderly.
Xián said: Luò,
means dwelling,
nowadays people call a courtyard 'luò'.
This is not a wicked man.
It must be that teaching and transformation have not yet reached him.
You, mother, have guarded your widowhood and raised an orphan,
toiling into old age.
How can you, in a moment of anger,
abandon years of diligence!
Moreover, you, mother, are raising another's orphaned child.
If you cannot bring him to success,
and if the dead have consciousness,
after a hundred years,
how will you face the deceased!"
The mother wept and rose.
Xiāng then personally went to Yuán's home,
expounding to him the principles of human relations and filial conduct,
illustrating with words of fortune and misfortune.
Yuán was moved to understanding,
and in the end became a filial son.
The magistrate of Kǎochéng, Wáng Huàn of Hénèi, appointed Xiāng as his Registrar.
Kǎochéng County,
belonged to Chénliú Commandery;
formerly Zī County,
Emperor Zhāng disliked its name,
and changed it to Kǎochéng.
"I heard that in Pú Village,
you transformed Chén Yuán without punishment.
Could it be that you lack the ambition of a hawk or sparrowhawk?"
Yīng zhān,
refers to birds that take fierce attack as their duty.
The Zuǒzhuàn says: When seeing those without propriety, punish them,
like hawks and sparrowhawks pursuing small birds.
Shǎo,
is pronounced shī zhǎo fān.
"I consider that hawks and sparrowhawks are not equal to phoenixes,
therefore I do not act like them."
Huàn said:
"A forest of thorny trees is no place for phoenixes to gather,
and a district of a hundred *li* is not the path for a great worthy."
Xián said: At that time, Huàn was a county magistrate,
hence he referred to himself as governing a hundred *li*.
He sent him to enter the Imperial University.
Guō Tài and Fú Róng, bearing their name cards, called upon him.
Writing one's name to request an audience is called a 'cì';
between the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it was called a 'yè'.
The next morning,
Tài rose,
descended from his bed and bowed to him, saying:
"You, sir,
are Tài's teacher,
not Tài's friend."
After Xiāng completed his studies, he returned to his hometown.
Even when at leisure at home,
Xián said: Yàn,
means peaceful.
Master Zhū said: Yànjū,
means times of leisure without affairs.
His wife and children served him as a stern father;
if his wife or children made a mistake,
he would remove his cap and blame himself.
His wife and children would apologize in the courtyard, reflecting on their faults.
Only after Xiāng put on his cap,
would his wife and children dare to enter the hall.
To the end, no change in his expressions of joy or anger was seen.
He did not respond to summons for office,
and died at home.
2 In the third month,
on the Guǐhài day,
a meteorite fell at Hù.
Hù County,
belonged to Fúfēng.
Hù,
is pronounced hù.
3 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
hail fell in the capital.
4 The Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Dù Shàng, recruited various Mán and Yí tribes to attack the bandits in Ài County,
and inflicted a major defeat upon them.
Tens of thousands surrendered.
The long-standing bandits of Guìyáng, Bǔ Yáng and Pān Hóng, fled deep into the mountains.
"Long-standing bandits"
refers to those who have been bandits for a long time.
(Dù Shàng) destroyed three of their camps,
capturing much treasure.
The followers of Yáng and Hóng were still numerous,
and Shàng wished to attack them,
but his soldiers had grown arrogant and wealthy,
and had no will to fight.
Shàng calculated that if he delayed, they would not fight,
but if he pressed them, they would certainly flee.
He therefore declared:
"Bǔ Yáng and Pān Hóng have been bandits for ten years,
skilled in both attack and defense.
Our troops are now few,
and it is not easy to advance.
We must wait until all the forces dispatched by the various commanderies have arrived,
then combine our strength to attack them."
He then issued an order to the army, allowing them freely to go hunting.
"Issued an order" means
having given the order, he reiterated it.
"Shēn"
means to repeat.
All, great and small, went out.
Shàng then secretly sent a trusted retainer to stealthily set fire to their camp,
and all their accumulated treasures were destroyed.
When the hunters returned,
there was none who did not weep.
Shàng personally comforted and consoled each man,
deeply blaming and reproaching himself,
taking the blame for the fire upon himself.
"Láo"
is pronounced lì dào fān.
"The wealth and treasures of Bǔ Yáng and others are enough to enrich several generations.
If only you gentlemen would combine your efforts,
what was lost is but a trifle,
hardly worth troubling over!"
The men all became indignant and eager.
Shàng ordered them to feed their horses and eat a hearty meal.
The next morning,
they went straight to the bandit camp.
Yáng, Hóng, and the others, confident in their remote and secure position,
had made no further preparations.
The officers and soldiers, riding the crest of their sharp morale,
subsequently defeated and pacified them.
Shàng had been leading troops for three years.
In the fifth year of Yánxī,
Shàng became Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and by now it had been three years.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yòuxiāng.
5 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Rényín day,
the Emperor made a southern tour;
on the Gēngshēn day,
he visited Zhānglíng;
on the Wùchén day,
he visited Yúnmèng,
overlooking the Hàn River,
then returned,
and visited Xīnyě.
At that time, the carriages and cavalry of the high ministers and noble relatives numbered in the tens of thousands,
and the exactions, expenses, and corvée labor
were beyond measure.
Hùjià Cóngshì Hú Téng of Guìyáng submitted a memorial stating:
"Hùjià Cóngshì"
likely refers to someone dispatched by the Inspector of Jīngzhōu to protect the imperial carriage.
"The Son of Heaven has no 'outside',"
The Gōngyáng Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals says: The King has no 'outside'.
meaning it is the capital.
I request that the Inspector of Jīngzhōu be treated as equivalent to the Colonel-Director of Retainers,
and that I myself be treated as equivalent to a Dūguān Cóngshì."
The Emperor agreed.
From then on, order was strictly maintained,
and none dared to arbitrarily interfere with the commanderies and counties.
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu could investigate and recommend officials within his own jurisdiction but could not investigate the ministers accompanying the imperial carriage.
If treated as equivalent to the Colonel-Director of Retainers,
then he could investigate and expose their misconduct,
hence the strict order.
Those close to the Emperor all engaged in illicit profiteering,
and many imperial edicts appointed people as Gentlemen of the Palace.
The Grand Commandant, Yáng Bǐng, submitted a memorial stating:
"The accumulated stars of Tàiwēi,
are named the positions of the Gentlemen.
Xián's note: The Treatise on Astronomy in the Records of the Grand Historian states: Behind the seats of the Five Emperors in the Tàiwēi Palace,
a cluster of twenty-five stars flourishes,
called the positions of the Gentlemen.
"Jī"
means to gather.
(Those appointed) go out to shepherd the people.
You should sever the bonds of unbearable favor,
to cut off the path of those seeking their desires."
Thereupon, the edicts for appointments ceased.
6 The Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, Duàn Jiǒng, attacked the Dāngjiān Qiāng,
and defeated them.
7 In the twelfth month,
on the Xīnchǒu day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
8 The Regular Palace Attendants, the Marquis of Rǔyáng, Táng Héng, and the Marquis of Wǔyuán, Xú Huáng, both died.
Rǔyáng County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.
Wǔyuán County
belonged to the Principality of Péngchéng.
9. Earlier,
the Palace Attendant Kòu Róng,
a great-grandson of Kòu Xún,
was by nature aloof and fastidious,
having few associates,
and for this reason was resented by those in power and favor.
Kòu Róng's cousin's son married the emperor's younger sister, Princess Yìyáng,
and the emperor also took his grand-niece into the rear palace.
Those around the emperor grew even more jealous of him,
and together they framed him with a crime,
resulting in him and his clan being dismissed and sent back to their home commandery.
The Kòu clan were originally from Chāngpíng in Shànggǔ.
The pressure on him grew increasingly severe.
Kòu Róng, fearing he would not escape,
went to the palace gate to plead his case.
Before he arrived,

a fire broke out at the Shuòpíng Office in the Southern Palace.
This was the Shuòpíng Commandant's office.
*Treatise on Officials*: The Shuòpíng Commandant
was in charge of the northern gate of the Northern Palace.
15 Duàn Jiǒng attacked and defeated the Western Qiāng,
advancing and pursuing relentlessly,
maneuvering through mountains and valleys,
from spring to autumn,
fighting daily without cease,
until the enemy was defeated and scattered.
In total, over twenty-three thousand heads were taken,
tens of thousands of captives were seized,
and over ten thousand settlements surrendered.
Jiǒng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
16 Autumn,
seventh month,
Tàizhōng Dàfū Chén Fán was appointed as Grand Commandant.
Fán yielded the position to Tàicháng Hú Guǎng, Court Counselor Wáng Chàng, and the pardoned convict Lǐ Yīng,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Chàng was the son of Gōng;
Wáng Gōng served Emperor Ān as a duke.
He detested the many imperial relatives and powerful clans,
and upon taking office,
he vigorously enforced authority and severity.
When prominent families committed offenses,
he sometimes ordered officials to tear down houses and cut down trees,
and to fill in wells and level stoves,
thereby destroying their family fortunes.
"Figures such as Wén Wēng, Shào Fù, and Zhuó Mào
all governed with gentleness and benevolence,
and their reputations spread to later generations.
Tearing down houses and cutting down trees,
though intended as stern measures to punish evil,
are unlikely to be remembered favorably in the long run.
Nà was an ancient capital,
a state within the domain of marquises and earls.
According to the ancient system of the Son of Heaven,
a square area of a thousand li was designated as the royal domain;
beyond that, an additional five hundred li constituted the domain of the marquises.
Emperor Guāngwǔ rose from Nányáng,
which later became known as the Southern Capital.
Furthermore, Luòyáng was located within the domain of marquises and earls,
hence this statement.
Three empresses were born in Xīnyě.
The commentator Xián said: The four ancestral temples above Emperor Nándùn are located in Zhānglíng.
Empress Guāngliè, Empress Yīn of Emperor Hé, and Empress Dèng were all from Xīnyě.
Meritorious officials, generals, and ministers
flourished across generations.
I believe that being overly diligent in applying punishments
is not as effective as practicing benevolence;
eagerly pursuing evildoers
(eagerly,
meaning diligently)
is not the way to govern. Shùn appointed Gāo Yáo,
and those who were not benevolent stayed away.
This is a saying of Zǐxià recorded in the Analects.
Yáo is pronounced yáo.
It does not lie in the use of punishments."
Chàng deeply accepted his advice,
and instead promoted lenient governance,
leading to the widespread implementation of moral education.
17 In the eighth month,
on the day Wùchén,
it was first ordered that commanderies and states with farmland collect a tax per mu.
The commentator Xián said: Ten coins per mu.
According to my research in the Biographies of Eunuchs: Zhāng Ràng and others advised Emperor Líng to collect taxes on all farmland in the empire,
at ten coins per mu,
but that was not an event of this time.
The Han land tax was one-thirtieth of the harvest,
while collecting money based on the mu area began at this time.
18 In the ninth month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
an earthquake struck the capital.
19 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Minister of Works Zhōu Jǐng was dismissed;
Tàicháng Liú Mào was appointed Minister of Works.
Mào was the son of Kǎi.
Liú Kǎi was esteemed in his time for yielding his marquisate,
and rose to the rank of duke.
20 Court Gentleman Dòu Wǔ,
a great-great-grandson of Róng,
had a daughter who was a Noble Lady.
Palace Maid Tián Shèng was favored by the emperor,
who intended to make her empress.
Colonel-Director of Retainers Yìng Fèng submitted a memorial stating:
"The position of empress is of great importance,
as it determines the rise and fall of the state.
The Hàn dynasty established Fēiyàn as empress,
leading to the extinction of the imperial line.
This event is recorded in the thirty-third scroll, in the first year of the Jiànpíng era of Emperor Āi.
The 'Guān Jū' ode celebrates obtaining a virtuous lady to match the gentleman.
The Han Poetry Outer Commentary states: There are five types of women one should not marry: the eldest daughter of a widowed mother,
because she does not accept authority;
a family with hereditary illness,
because it is forsaken by heaven;
a family with criminals,
because it is forsaken by people;
a woman from a disorderly family,
because her nature is not upright;
a woman from a rebellious family,
because it violates human relations.
Yuǎn is pronounced yuàn.
The Dòu clan is of good family,
and the opposition was very firm."
The emperor had no choice,
and on the day Xīnsì,
he established Noble Lady Dòu as empress.
He appointed Wǔ as Special Counselor and Colonel of the City Gates,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Huáilǐ.
21 In the eleventh month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
a fire broke out in the Northern Bureau of the Yellow Gates.
22 Chén Fān repeatedly spoke of the injustice suffered by Lǐ Yīng, Féng Gǔn, and Liú Yòu,
requesting that they be pardoned and forgiven,
promoted in rank and appointed to office.
He spoke of this repeatedly,
with sincere words and earnest pleas,
even to the point of shedding tears;
but the emperor did not listen.
Yìng Fèng submitted a memorial stating:
"Loyal and worthy civil and military officials
are the heart and backbone of the state.
I have observed that convicts serving at the Left Bureau such as Féng Gǔn, Liú Yòu, Lǐ Yīng, and others,
who punished and exposed treacherous ministers,
applying the law to them;
Xián said: Sì means
to display.
Yet they have unjustly suffered slanderous accusations,
causing loyal ministers to share the blame with arch-villains.
From spring until winter,
they have not received pardon or forgiveness.
Observers and listeners far and near
sigh over this.
The essence of establishing governance
is to record merits and forget faults.
Therefore, Emperor Wǔ pardoned
Ān Guó from among the convicts.
Xián said: During Emperor Jǐng's time,
Hán Ānguó was a Grand Master of Liáng.
He committed an offense and was punished;
later, when the post of Internal History of Liáng became vacant,
he was appointed from among the convicts to a salary of two thousand shi.
This text says Emperor Wǔ,
which is an error.
The event is recorded in the twenty-seventh scroll, in the first year of Emperor Xuān's Gānlù era.
He equaled the achievements of Jí Fǔ.
The Odes say: Illustrious and sincere was Fāng Shū, who campaigned against the Xiǎnyǔn,
and the Mán and Jīng submitted to his might.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: Fāng Shū first campaigned against the Xiǎnyǔn together with Jí Fǔ.
Now he specifically campaigns against the Mán and Jīng,
causing them all to submit to the might of King Xuān.
Gǔn, because he achieved merit in campaigning against the Wǔlíng and Chángshā barbarians during Emperor Shùn's time,
is thus compared to Jí Fǔ.
He possessed the integrity of not spitting out the hard nor swallowing the soft.
Xián said: This refers to Yòu impeaching Liáng Jì's younger brother Miǎn,
and also serving as Colonel Director of Retainers,
whom the powerful and influential feared.
The Odes say: The soft he does not swallow,
the hard he does not spit out.
Shù,
is pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
He left behind affection in Dùliáo.
Yīng served as Grand Administrator of Yùyáng,
and as Colonel Protecting the Wūhuán,
both in the Yōu region.
The General Who Crosses Liao,
then stationed in the Bìng region,
these are the places where he displayed his might and left behind affection.
The royal armies are not yet roused.
I beg to pardon Yīng and the others,
to prepare for unforeseen events."
After the memorial was submitted,
they were all exempted from punishment.
After a long time,
Lǐ Yīng was again appointed Colonel Director of Retainers.
At that time, the younger brother of the Minor Huangmen Zhāng Ràng, named Shuò, was Magistrate of Yěwáng.
He was greedy, cruel, and without principle.
Fearing Yīng's stern authority,
he fled back to the capital.
Yěwáng County belonged to Hénèi Commandery,
and Hénèi Commandery belonged to the Sī region.
Fearing that Yīng would investigate and impeach him for his crimes,
he therefore fled back to the capital.
He joined wooden pillars to form a hollow space,
which was sufficient to conceal a person.
Joined pillars
refers to two pillars aligned,
where two rooms meet.
Yīng led clerks and soldiers to break open the pillars and capture Shuò,
delivering him to the Luòyáng prison.
After the confession was taken,
he immediately killed him.
Ràng complained of injustice to the emperor.
The emperor summoned Yīng,
questioning him about the meaning of executing without first requesting permission.
He replied:
"In the past, when Zhòngní was Minister of Crime of Lǔ,
after seven days he executed Shàozhèng Mǎo.
Now, I have been in office for over ten days.
I privately feared that delay would be a fault,
and did not expect to incur the crime of excessive haste.
I am truly aware of my offense and responsibility.
Death will come before I can turn my heels.
I only beg to be allowed five more days,
to eliminate the arch-villain,
and then to retreat to face the cauldron and boiling oil.
This is my initial wish."
The emperor had nothing more to say.
Turning to Ràng, he said:
"This is your brother's crime.
What fault has the Colonel Director of Retainers?"
He then sent Yīng out.
From then on, all the Huangmen and Regular Attendants bowed respectfully and held their breath,
not daring to leave the palace compound even during rest periods.
The emperor, finding this strange, asked the reason.
They all kowtowed and wept, saying:
"We fear Colonel Director Lǐ."
At that time, the court administration grew increasingly chaotic,
laws and discipline deteriorated and collapsed.
But Yīng alone upheld moral judgment,
elevating himself through his reputation.
Scholars who received his acceptance and接待
were said to have ascended the dragon's gate.
Xián said: This uses fish as a metaphor.
Lóngmén,
is the mouth where the river water descends,
located in present-day Lóngmén County, Jiàng Prefecture.
The Xīn Family's Records of Sān Qín states: Héjīn,
also called Lóngmén,
where the water is treacherous and impassable.
Fish and turtles and the like cannot ascend it.
Several thousand large fish from rivers and seas
gather close below Lóngmén.
They cannot ascend.
Those that ascend become dragons.
Bèi,
is pronounced pí yì fān.
23 The Chancellor of Dōnghǎi, Liú Kuān, was summoned to be Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
Kuān
was the son of Qí.
Liú Qí served Emperor Shùn
as Minister over the Masses.
Qí,
is pronounced qiū yí fān.
Xián said: He was the Chancellor of Liú Zhēn, great-grandson of King Dōnghǎi, Liú Qiáng.
According to Kuān's biography: In this year, he was summoned from being Chancellor of Dōnghǎi to be Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
then promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
governing three commanderies in succession.
Even in haste,
he never spoke harshly or showed a hurried expression.
When clerks or commoners committed offenses,
he only used cattail whips to punish them.
In ancient times, whips were made of raw leather.
He never inflicted severe pain.
Whenever he saw elderly folk,
he comforted them with words about farming and villages.
When he saw youths,
he encouraged them with teachings on filial piety and fraternal duty.
People were all pleased and transformed by him.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day, Xīnmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
An edict ordered the dukes, ministers, commanderies, and kingdoms to recommend men of utmost filial piety.
The recommendation by Tàicháng Zhào Diǎn was Xún Shuàng, who responded in a policy examination, saying:
"In ancient times, the sages established what is central between Heaven and Earth and called it ritual.
Among the many rituals,
the marriage ceremony is foremost.
The male nature is pure and capable of bestowing,
the female body is compliant and capable of transformation.
Using ritual to harmonize with music,
regulates and diffuses their vital energy,
(Xún Shuàng's words directly pointed to the Emperor having many inner favorites.)
The Zuǒzhuàn states: The Marquis of Jìn was ill,
Physician Hé examined him,
and said:
'The illness cannot be treated!
This is called an illness like gǔ,
not caused by ghosts nor by food,

The Duke said:
'Should women not be approached?'
He replied:
'Regulate it.
The music of the former kings
was used to regulate all affairs.
Heaven has six qi,
excess becomes disaster,

Bestow,
read as shì zhì.
To achieve the blessings of longevity.
By the end of the Three Dynasties,
there was licentiousness without regulation,
yang was exhausted above,
yin was blocked below,
therefore the warning of the Duke of Zhōu said:
(This is from the phrase in the Shàngshū's "Wú Yì".)
'The sparrow's foot,

How can such a person,
pursuing desires, lose his body?'
Truly lamentable.
(Xián's note: Shì,
means to follow,
meaning the folly of losing one's life,

Lose,
read as xī làng.
Attendant officials and serving envoys are again outside,
needlessly taxing innocent people,
to provide for useless women,
the common people are impoverished and distressed outside,

therefore disturbing harmonious qi,
disasters and anomalies frequently arrive.
Your subject foolishly believes that all those women who have not yet been favored,
should all be sent out to form marriages,
this would truly be a great blessing for the state."
An edict appointed him as a Lángzhōng.
2. In Sīlì and Yùzhōu there was famine,
the dead were four or five out of ten,
to the extent that there were households wiped out.
Household,
refers to those registered with the authorities.
Wiped-out households,
means no old, no weak,
all died of famine,
leaving no survivors.
3. An edict summoned Zhāng Huàn to be Dàsīnóng,
and again appointed Huángfǔ Guī to replace him as Dùliáo General.
Guī himself felt he had held high positions consecutively,
and wished to retire and withdraw,
several times pleading illness,
but it was not heeded.
It happened that a friend's funeral arrived,
Guī crossed the boundary to meet it,
and thus ordered a client to secretly inform Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ Hú Fāng,
saying Guī had presumptuously left the military camp far away,
and should urgently be impeached.
Fāng said:
"Wēimíng wishes to avoid the path of officialdom,
(The Dùliáo General was stationed at the Xīhé boundary,
under the jurisdiction of the Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Huángfǔ Guī,
courtesy name Wēimíng.
Xián's note: It means he wishes to return home,
avoiding the path of official service.)
I should cherish talent for the court,
how can I carry out this man's scheme!"
Thus he made no inquiry.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
in Jìyīn, Dōngjùn, Jìběi, and Píngyuán, the Yellow River water cleared.
5. Sītú Xǔ Xǔ was dismissed;
in the fifth month,
Tàicháng Hú Guǎng was made Sītú.
6. On Gēngwǔ day,
the Emperor personally sacrificed to Lǎozǐ at the Zhuólóng Palace,
using patterned woolen felt to decorate the altar,
pure gold-inlaid vessels,
setting up a canopied seat,
using suburban sacrifice to Heaven music.
(The historian says this was improper ritual.)
Seat,
read as cú wò.
7. The Xiānbēi, hearing that Zhāng Huàn had left,
gathered and incited the Southern Xiōngnú and Wūhuán to rebel together.
In the sixth month,
the Southern Xiōngnú, Wūhuán, and Xiānbēi entered the frontier passes by several routes,
raiding and plundering the nine border commanderies.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Xiānbēi again entered the passes,
luring and inciting the Eastern Qiāng to join them in swearing oaths.
With the Shěndí of Shàngjùn, the Xiānlíng tribes of Āndìng,
together they raided Wǔwēi and Zhāngyè,
the border regions greatly suffering their poison.
An edict again appointed Zhāng Huàn as Protector of the Xiōngnú General of the Household,
with the rank of the Nine Ministers.
(Protector of the Xiōngnú General of the Household,
rank equivalent to 2,000 dàn.
The Nine Ministers,
rank 2,000 dàn fully.
This refers to the camps of the Dùliáo General and the Protector Wūhuán Colonel.)
8. Initially,
when the Emperor was Marquis of Líwú,
he studied under Zhōu Fú of Gānlíng,
and upon ascending the throne,
promoted Fú to Shàngshū.
At that time, his fellow commandery man, Hénán Yǐn Fáng Zhí, was famous at court,
and the villagers made a rhyme about them:
"The world's compass and square,
Fáng Bówǔ;
through the teacher obtaining the seal,
Zhōu Zhòngjìn."
(Fáng Zhí,
courtesy name Bówǔ.
Zhōu Fú,
courtesy name Zhòngjìn.)
They mocked and speculated about each other,
and thus each gathered followers and disciples,
gradually forming deep rifts.
From this, Gānlíng had northern and southern factions,
and the discussion of factions began from this.
The Rǔnán Tàishǒu Zōng Zī appointed Fàn Pāng as Gōngcáo,

having them praise the good and correct wrongs,
to bring order to the commandery offices.
(Office,
refers to the commandery office.
The residences of dukes, ministers, governors, and grand administrators are all called offices.
Office,
read as zhí yáo.)
They hated evil like an enemy.
Fàn Pāng's nephew Lǐ Sòng,
originally without conduct,
the Regular Attendant Táng Héng
recommended him to Zī,
Zī employed him as an official;
Pāng suppressed it and did not summon him.
Zī redirected his anger,
beating the clerk Zhū Líng,
(Bǎiguānzhì: Under the commandery offices and the various bureaus each have clerks,
in charge of documents.)

today I would rather be beaten to death,

Zī then stopped.
Among the people of the commandery, those of middle rank and below,
none did not resent him.
Thereupon, the two commanderies made a rhyme:
"The Rǔnán Tàishǒu is Fàn Mèngbó,
the Nányáng Zōng Zī just draws 'approved';

is Fàn Pāng's courtesy name.
'Approved',

Drawing 'approved',

the Hóngnóng Chéng Jīn only sits and whistles."
(Gōngxiào,
is Cén Zhì's courtesy name.
Whistle,
means to chant,
meaning he just sits and chants,

There were over thirty thousand students at the Imperial Academy,
with Guō Tài and Jiǎ Biāo from Yǐngchuān as their leaders.
They praised and esteemed each other with Lǐ Yīng, Chén Fān, and Wáng Chàng.

"The model for the world,
is Lǐ Yuánlǐ;
fearless against the strong and oppressive,

the outstanding talent of the world;

Lǐ Yīng,
styled Yuánlǐ,
Chén Fān,
styled Zhòngjǔ,
Wáng Chàng,
styled Shūmào.
They competed in evaluating and criticizing others,
and from the highest ministers down,
none did not fear their censure,
hurrying to their doors.
"Hurrying to their doors" means
not even bothering to put on one's shoes properly.
In Wǎn, there was a wealthy merchant named Zhāng Fàn,
who was related to the imperial harem,

He frequently bribed the palace eunuchs,
and thus obtained a prominent position,
wielding his power arbitrarily.
Cén Zhì and the officer in charge of banditry, Zhāng Mù,
the officer in charge of banditry,
handled matters related to thieves and bandits.
Later, when an amnesty was declared,

The minor eunuch Zhào Jīn from Jìnyáng,

The Grand Administrator of Tàiyuán, Liú Zhì from Píngyuán,

The Grand Administrator of Shānyáng, Zhái Chāo,

When Lǎn's mother died and he returned home,

Jiǎn submitted a memorial accusing Lǎn of crimes,
but Lǎn intercepted and blocked it,

Yuàn Kāng's biography also states:

Lǎn deeply resented him for this,

According to Hóu Lǎn's biography:

Chén Fān's biography states:

Xú Huáng's nephew, Xuān, served as magistrate of Xiàpī,
and was exceptionally cruel and tyrannical.
He once sought the daughter of the former Grand Administrator of Rǔnán, Lǐ Gǎo, but failed to obtain her,

abducted his daughter,

arrested Xuān's family members,

His subordinates and clerks strongly protested,

"Xú Xuān is a traitor to the state.
If I kill him today,

I can die with my eyes closed!"
He then tried Xuān for his crimes and had him executed in the marketplace,
exposing his corpse.
Thereupon, the eunuchs complained to the emperor of injustice,
and the emperor was furious.
Chāo and Fú were both punished with head-shaving and the cangue,

Grand Commandant Chén Fān and Minister of Works Liú Mào jointly remonstrated,
requesting the crimes of Chéng Jīn, Liú Zhì, Zhái Chāo, and Huáng Fú;
A textual note states: In the biography of Chén Fān, Minister over the Masses Liú Jǔ is also mentioned,

not Liú Jǔ.
The responsible officials impeached them,

"Now, bandits and rebels are abroad—
an ailment of the limbs;

Heaven inspired the sage's intent,

The minor eunuch Zhào Jīn and the great villain Zhāng Fàn

currying favor with those around you.
Former Tàiyuán Prefect Liú Zhì and Nányáng Prefect Chéng Jīn
investigated and executed them.
Although it is said that after a pardon they should not have been killed,

it lay in removing evil—
what cause for anger

(Shuōwén states: Juānjuān means
indignant anger.
Juān is pronounced
as yuān.)

passed through Hángǔ Pass,
and then hunted at the Guǎngchéng Park.
In the twelfth month,
he returned,
and visited the Imperial Academy.
13 Huán Diǎn served as Palace Censor,
and the eunuchs feared him.
Diǎn often rode a piebald horse,
and the capital had a saying about him:
"Walk on and stop,
make way for the piebald horse censor!"
A piebald horse
is mixed blue and white in color.
He was the grandson of Yān.
In the early years of Emperor Shùn's Yǒngjiàn era,
Yān served as Grand Tutor.
Yān
was the grandson of Róng.
1 In spring,
the third month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared.
2 In summer,
there was a great drought.
3 The Empress's mother was granted the title of Wǔyáng Jūn.
4 In autumn,
the Jīnchéng River overflowed for over twenty lǐ.
5 The mountain banks in Wǔyuán collapsed.
A note on discrepancies: The Basic Annals states:
"It was a year of great abundance."
However, considering the great drought this summer,
even if there was a harvest in autumn,
it could not be called a year of great abundance.
Therefore, this is not adopted here.
6 Initially,
Zhāng Jué from Jùlù served the teachings of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ,
and taught sorcery,
calling it
"the Way of Great Peace."
He chanted spells and used talisman water to cure illnesses,
ordering the sick to kneel and confess their sins.
Sometimes the sick recovered,
and the masses revered and believed in him.
Jué sent his disciples to travel in all directions,
deceiving and enticing people in turn.
Over more than ten years,
his followers numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
People from the eight provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, Jì, Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù
all responded without exception.
Some abandoned or sold their property,
moving and rushing to join him,
filling the roads.
Those who died of illness before arriving also numbered in the tens of thousands.
The commanderies and counties did not understand the situation,
but instead said that Jué was teaching goodness and transforming people,
and was beloved by the masses.
Grand Commandant Yáng Cì, who was then Minister over the Masses,
(Cì became Minister over the Masses
in the fifth year of the Xīpíng era.)
said: "Jué deceives and dazzles the people,
and even after being pardoned, he shows no remorse,
gradually spreading further.
If we now order the commanderies and counties to arrest and suppress him,
I fear it will cause even greater disturbance
and hasten the disaster.
We should urgently instruct the Regional Inspectors and Administrators of Two Thousand Dàn
to distinguish the displaced people,
and escort them back to their home commanderies,
to weaken his faction,
and then execute their chieftains.
This could be achieved without much effort."
However, Cì was removed from his position,
and the matter was left unresolved in the palace.
Xián said: This means the proposed matter was left in the palace,
and not implemented.
According to my investigation, Cì was dismissed in the sixth year of Xīpíng.
Shuài,
read as suǒ lèi.
Yuàn,
read as yú juàn.
Fù,
read as fú yòu.
"Jué and his followers' conspiracy grows more serious.
Rumors from all directions
say that Jué and others have secretly entered the capital,
to spy on court affairs.
With the cries of birds and the hearts of beasts,
they secretly call out together.
The commanderies and counties avoid mentioning this,
unwilling to hear of it.
They only pass the word among themselves,
but no one is willing to put it in official documents.
An explicit edict should be issued,
heavily rewarding the capture of Jué and others,
with land and titles as rewards.
Those who dare to evade or conceal
shall be punished as accomplices."
The Emperor paid no attention to this,
and instead ordered Táo to systematically compile the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Táo was knowledgeable about the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and wrote commentaries on it,

Jué then established thirty-six "Fāng";
"Fāng"
is like a general,
with large Fāng having over ten thousand people,
and small Fāng having six to seven thousand.
A note on discrepancies: Yuán Jì writes
"Fāng" as "Fáng,"

They spread the false prophecy:
"The Blue Heaven is already dead,
the Yellow Heaven shall rise,
in the year of Jiǎzǐ,

They wrote with white earth on the gates of government offices in the capital
(the gates of government offices,
meaning the gates of various official buildings in the capital)

"Jiǎzǐ"
characters.
The leader of a large Fāng, Mǎ Yuányì, first gathered tens of thousands from Jīng and Yáng,
planning to launch the uprising in Yè.
Yuányì frequently traveled to the capital,
using the Palace Attendants Fēng Xū and Xú Fèng as internal agents,
agreeing to rise both inside and outside on the fifth day of the third month.
The first year of Zhōngpíng
(Jiǎzǐ, 184 AD) (The era name was changed in the twelfth month of this year.)
1. In spring,
Ji’nan native Táng Zhōu, a disciple of Jiǎo, submitted a written report denouncing him.
Consequently, Mǎ Yuányì was apprehended,
and torn apart by chariots in Luòyáng.
Textual analysis notes: Yuán Jì states:
"On the day Yǐmǎo in the fifth month,
Mǎ Yuányì and others plotted rebellion in the capital,
and were executed."
We now follow Fàn Shū.
Over a thousand people were executed;
orders were issued to Jìzhōu to pursue and capture Jiǎo and others.
Jiǎo and his followers, realizing their plot was exposed,
urgently dispatched orders day and night to all quarters,
and they rose up simultaneously.
All wore yellow turbans as their identifying mark,
hence people of the time called them
"the Yellow Turban Bandits."
In the second month,
Jiǎo proclaimed himself the "General of Heaven,"
his younger brother Bǎo proclaimed himself the "General of Earth,"
and Bǎo's younger brother Liáng proclaimed himself the "General of Man."
Textual analysis notes: Sīmǎ Biāo's Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū states:
"Jiǎo's younger brother Liáng,
Liáng's younger brother Bǎo."
Yuán Jì states
"Jiǎo's younger brothers Liáng and Bǎo."
We now follow Fàn Shū.
They plundered and seized towns and settlements,
the provinces and commanderies lost their foothold,
and many senior officials fled;
within a month,
the whole realm responded in support,
and the capital was shaken.
The people of Ānpíng and Gānlíng each seized their respective kings and submitted to the bandits.
In the third month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Hé Jìn, the Governor of Hénán, was appointed Grand General,

Shèn County,
belonging to Rǔnán Commandery.

Hángǔ Pass,

Guǎngchéng,

Huányuán Pass,

Mèngjīn,

Xiǎopíngjīn,

The Emperor summoned his close ministers for a council.
Tàishǒu of Běidì, Huángfǔ Sōng, believed that the prohibition against the partisans should be lifted,
and that more funds from the Central Treasury and horses from the Western Garden Stables should be distributed to reward the troops.
The Central Treasury Prefect,
was subordinate to the Privy Treasurer,
and held by eunuchs.
The Central Treasury funds,
were what the Hàn called 'forbidden money.'
The Western Garden Stables horses,
were the Lùjì Stables horses.
Cáng (藏),
is pronounced cáng, with the tone of cáng làng.
He was the nephew of Guī.
The Emperor asked for advice from the Regular Palace Attendant Lǚ Qiáng,
who replied:
"The prohibition against the partisans has long festered,
and people's sentiments are filled with resentment and anger.
If they are not pardoned and forgiven,
they may easily join forces with Zhāng Jiǎo in conspiracy,
causing the rebellion to grow larger,
and it will be too late for regrets.
I now request that first, those among your attendants who are corrupt and venal be executed,
then grant a general amnesty to the partisans,
and assess the capabilities of the Regional Inspectors and the two-thousand-picul officials.
Then, the bandits will surely be pacified."
The Emperor, alarmed, complied.
On the day Rénzǐ,
a general amnesty was granted to the partisans throughout the realm,
and those who had been exiled were allowed to return;
referring to the wives and children of partisans who had been exiled to the borderlands.
Elite troops from across the realm were mobilized,
and the Northern General of the Household Lú Zhí was dispatched to suppress Zhāng Jiǎo.
The Hàn had three bureaus of Generals of the Household,
the Five Offices and the Left and Right Bureaus.
There was also the General of the Household to the Xiōngnú.
The Northern General of the Household was created at this time,
likely to suppress the Yellow Turbans in Héběi.
At this time, the Regular Palace Attendants Zhào Zhōng, Zhāng Ràng, Xià Yùn, Guō Shèng, Duàn Guī, Sòng Diǎn, and others were all enfeoffed as marquises, enjoying noble status and favor.
The Emperor often said:
"Attendant Zhāng is my father,
Attendant Zhào is my mother."
Consequently, the eunuchs had nothing to fear or dread,
and they all built mansions and residences,
imitating the imperial palaces.
The Emperor once wished to ascend the watchtower at Yǒng'ān Palace.
According to the Xù Hàn Zhì: Yǒng'ān Palace was northeast of the Northern Palace,
and within the palace was a watchtower.
Luòyáng Gōngdiàn Míng states: Yǒng'ān Palace,
had a circumference of six hundred and ninety-eight zhàng,
and its former foundation lies within the old city of Luòyáng.
The eunuch attendant Shàng Dàn admonished him, saying:
Xián states: Shàng is the surname;
Dàn is the given name.

In the Later Hàn, there were Shàng Shì and Shàng Zǐpíng.
"The Son of Heaven should not ascend to high places;
if he ascends to high places, the common people will become dispersed and scattered."
From then on, the Emperor did not dare to ascend towers or pavilions again.
Observing that Emperor Líng, due to Shàng Dàn's words, did not dare to ascend towers or pavilions again,
truly fearing the common people would become dispersed and scattered,
can one say he lacked a heart that cared for the people?
If he had trusted the words of the noble men as he trusted Shàng Dàn's words,

Xián states: The Chūnqiū Qiántán Bā states: The Son of Heaven should not have high towers and pavilions;

He likely used this to deceive the Emperor.
Fù (復),
is pronounced fù, with the tone of fú yòu;
the same below.
The Emperor reproached the various Regular Attendants, saying:
"You all constantly said the partisans wished to act unlawfully,
and had them all imprisoned and restricted,
with some even being executed.
Now the partisans are instead being employed by the state,
yet you all are actually in league with Zhāng Jiǎo.
Is this not worthy of execution?"
They all kowtowed and said:
"This was all done by Wáng Fǔ and Hóu Lǎn!"
Thereupon, all the Regular Attendants sought to resign,
and each recalled their clansmen and sons or younger brothers serving in the provinces and commanderies.
Zhào Zhōng, Xià Yùn, and others then jointly slandered Lǚ Qiáng,
saying he conspired with the partisans to discuss court affairs,
and frequently read the biography of Huò Guāng.
Meaning he intended to plot a deposition.
Shù (數),
is pronounced shuò, with the tone of suǒ jiǎo.
The Emperor sent a Yellow-Gate Attendant bearing arms to summon Qiáng.
Qiáng, hearing the Emperor's summons,

"If I die,

A true man wishes to exhaust his loyalty for the state;

Thereupon, he committed suicide.
Zhōng and Yùn further slandered him, saying:
"When Qiáng was summoned,

Xián states: "Screened himself off"
means he committed suicide.
Píng (屏),
is pronounced píng, with the tone of bì yǐng.
Consequently, his clansmen were arrested,

The Palace Attendant Xiàng Xǔ from Hénèi submitted a memorial on advantageous policies,

Zhāng Ràng falsely accused Xiàng Xǔ of being of one mind with Zhāng Jué,

He was arrested and sent to the Northern Prison of the Yellow Gates,

The Gentleman of the Interior Zhāng Jūn from Zhōngshān submitted a memorial stating:
"I humbly consider that the reason Zhāng Jué was able to raise troops and create rebellion,
and why the myriad people gladly followed him,

is that the root cause lies entirely in the fact that the Ten Regular Attendants have placed many of their fathers, brothers, sons, nephews, marriage relatives, and guests in charge of provinces and commanderies,
monopolizing wealth and profit,
encroaching upon and plundering the common people.
The grievances of the common people
had nowhere to be told,
so they plotted unlawful actions,
gathering to become bandits and rebels.
The Ten Regular Attendants should be beheaded,
and their heads hung in the southern suburbs,
to apologize to the common people.
According to the Biographies of the Eunuchs,
at that time, Zhāng Ràng, Zhào Zhōng, Xià Yùn, Guō Shèng, Sūn Zhāng, Bì Lán, Lì Sōng, Duàn Guī, Gāo Wàng, Zhāng Gōng, Hán Kuī, and Sòng Diǎn—twelve individuals—
all served as Palace Attendants.
Speaking of the 'Ten Regular Attendants'
is using a round number.
'Xiàn'
is read as 'xuán'.
The Textual Examination of Discrepancies states: In the Biographies of the Eunuchs in Fan Ye's Book of the Later Han, twelve names of Regular Attendants are listed above,
yet below it says 'Ten Regular Attendants'.
The details are unclear.
Then the great rebels would disappear of themselves, without the need for armies."
The emperor showed Zhāng Jūn's memorial to the various Regular Attendants.
They all removed their caps, went barefoot, and kowtowed,
begging to be sent to the imperial prison in Luòyáng,
and offering to contribute their family wealth to aid military expenses.
An edict was issued,
ordering them all to resume wearing their caps and shoes and attend to their duties as before.
The emperor angrily said of Zhāng Jūn:
"This is truly a madman!
Among the Ten Regular Attendants, surely there must be at least one good person, no?"
The Censor, following the emperor's intent,
then falsely accused Zhāng Jūn of studying the Way of the Yellow Turbans.
He was arrested and tortured,
and died in prison.

Zhāng Mànchéng of the Nányáng Yellow Turbans attacked and killed the Grand Administrator Chǔ Gòng.

Cì's reply was blunt and straightforward,

In summer,
the fourth month,

Dèng Shèng from Hóngnóng, the Grand Coachman, was appointed as Grand Commandant.

Xián states: Its old city is southwest of present-day Cháoyì County in Tóng Prefecture.
'Shàng'

belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.

'Bài'

7 Bō Cái besieged Huángfǔ Sōng at Chángshè.
Sōng's troops were few,
and the entire army was fearful.
The rebels camped among grass and reeds.
A strong wind arose.
Sōng ordered his soldiers to all tie torches and mount the city walls.
He sent elite troops to slip out beyond the encirclement,
set fires and shout loudly.
Those on the city walls raised torches in response.
Sōng led troops charging out from within the city with great clamor,
rushing to attack the rebel formation.
The rebels were startled,
and fled in disorder.
At that time, the Cavalry Commandant Cáo Cāo from the state of Pèi arrived with troops.
In the fifth month,
Sōng, Cáo, and Zhū Jùn combined their armies,
engaged the rebels again in battle,
and routed them completely,
beheading tens of thousands.
Sōng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
Cáo Cāo's father, Cáo Sōng,
was the adopted son of the Palace Attendant Cáo Téng.
His exact birth origins cannot be ascertained.
Some say he was a son of the Xiàhóu clan.
A man from Wú wrote the Biography of Cáo Mán and Guō Bān's Tales of Generations,
both stating that Sōng
was a son of the Xiàhóu clan,
the younger uncle of Xiàhóu Dūn.
Thus, Cáo Cāo and Dūn were paternal cousins.
Cáo Cāo was resourceful and calculating,
chivalrous yet unrestrained and unconventional.
He did not attend to proper conduct or livelihood.
People of the time did not find him remarkable.
Only Grand Commandant Qiáo Xuán and Hé Yóng from Nányáng thought him exceptional.
Xuán said to Cáo:
"The world is about to fall into chaos.
Without talent that commands an age,
it cannot be saved.
He who can bring it peace—
is it not you, sir?"
Yóng, upon meeting Cáo,
sighed and said:
"The Hàn house is about to perish.
He who will bring peace to the world
must be this man."
Xuán said to Cáo:
"You, sir, lack reputation.
You should befriend Xǔ Zǐjiāng."
Zǐjiāng
was Xùn's nephew, Xǔ Shào.
Xǔ Shào,
styled Zǐjiāng.
Xǔ Xùn served as a Duke;
see the third and fourth years of the Xīpíng reign period in the previous scroll.
'Cóng'
is pronounced 'cóng'.
He was widely discerning in judging people,
and together with his elder cousin Xǔ Jìng, enjoyed high repute.
They liked to critically discuss local personages together.
Each month they would renew their grading and comments,
hence the custom of the 'First of the Month Evaluation' in Rǔnán.
The later establishment of the Central Evaluators in provinces and commanderies originated from this.
'Hào'
is pronounced 'hào'.
'Gēng'
is pronounced 'gēng'.
Hearing of this in the prefectural offices,
none failed to amend their conduct and cultivate their behavior.
Cáo Cāo went to visit Shào and asked him,

"What kind of man am I?"
Shào despised his character
and did not reply.
Cáo then pressured him.
Shào said:
"You, sir,
are a capable minister in times of order,

This means his talent was peerless in his generation.
When the world is well-governed, he would fully employ his abilities in service of the age;

The account of Cáo Cāo begins here.
When Zhū Jùn was attacking the Yellow Turbans,

Army Supervisor and Marshal—

"Your servant has heard that the calamities of the world do not arise from external causes,

Now Zhāng Jué arose in Zhào and Wèi,

What your servant fears

Even if Zhāng Jué were to be beheaded and exterminated,

It will only grow deeper.

The king said:

Loyal ministers will again face execution like at Dùyóu!

'Yóu'
is pronounced yóu.
If you swiftly execute the slanderers and flatterers,
