belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Xīhuá County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.
Xián said: The old city of Xīhuá
is west of modern Xiàngchéng County in Chénzhōu;
also said
to be northwest of modern Yīnshuǐ County.
The remaining bandits surrendered or dispersed,
and the three commanderies were completely pacified.
Sōng then reported the situation to the throne,
attributing the merit to Jùn,
whereupon Jùn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīxiāng,
and promoted to General Who Pacifies Bandits.
This official was established to pacify the remaining Yellow Turban bandits.
Jùn was ordered to attack Nányáng.
The General of the North, Lú Zhí, fought consecutive battles and defeated Zhāng Jué,
beheading and capturing over ten thousand men.
Jué and others fled and defended Guǎngzōng.
Guǎngzōng County
belonged to Jùlù Commandery.
Xián said: It is modern Zōngchéng County in Bèizhōu.
They constructed cloud ladders,
and were on the verge of capturing it.
'On the verge'
means nearly.
'Moat'
is pronounced qī yàn fān.
Someone advised Zhí to send bribes to Fēng,
but Zhí refused.
Fēng returned
and reported to the Emperor:
"The bandits at Guǎngzōng are easy to defeat,
but General Lú fortifies his camp and rests his troops,
waiting for Heaven to punish them."
The Emperor was enraged,
had Zhí arrested and transported in a cage cart,
reducing his death sentence by one degree;
he sent the General of the East, Dǒng Zhuó from Lǒngxī, to replace him.
Lú Zhí was first General of the North,
and Zhuó was General of the East.
The Four Generals began from this.
11. In Bājùn, Zhāng Xiū used sorcery to treat people's illnesses.
His methods were roughly the same as those of Zhāng Jué.
He ordered the families of the sick to contribute five dǒu of rice,
and was called
the "Five Dǒu Rice Master."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Xiū gathered a crowd and rebelled,
plundering commanderies and counties;
people at the time called them
"Rice Bandits."
Examination of discrepancies says: Fàn Yè's "Annals of Emperor Líng" mentions this Zhāng Xiū.
Chén Shòu's "Wèi Zhì: Biography of Zhāng Lǔ" mentions
"Liú Yān's Marshal Zhāng Xiū,"
Liú Ài's "Diǎn Lüè" mentions
"Zhāng Xiū of Hànzhōng,"
Péi Sōngzhī believed that
"Zhāng Xiū"
should be
"Zhāng Héng,"
and that if it was not an error in the "Diǎn Lüè,"
then it was a mistake in transcription.
According to the biography of Lǔ:
"His grandfather Líng,
and father Héng,
both practiced the Way of the Five Dǒu of Rice.
After Héng died,
Lǔ continued it."
Liú Yān's Marshal Zhāng Xiū and Lǔ together attacked Hànzhōng,
and Lǔ ambushed and killed Xiū,
so he was not his father.
Here, we follow Fàn Yè's account.
12. In the eighth month,
Huángfǔ Sōng fought the Yellow Turbans at Cāngtíng.
Cāngtíng
is within the boundaries of Fàn County in Dōngjùn.
Dǒng Zhuó attacked Zhāng Jué without success,
and was punished for his failure.
On the yǐsì day,
an edict ordered Sōng to attack Jué.
13. In the ninth month,
Ānpíng King Xù was found guilty of misconduct,
and executed.
In the first year of the Yánguāng era of Emperor Ān,
the state of Lèchéng was renamed Ānpíng,
and King Xiào Dé was enfeoffed to continue the line.
Xù
was Dé's son.
Earlier,
Xù had been captured by the Yellow Turbans,
and his countrymen ransomed him to secure his return.
The court deliberated on restoring his state.
Court Gentleman for Consultation Lǐ Xiè said:
"Xù was unfit to guard the fiefdom,
bringing disgrace to the sacred court.
His state should not be restored."
The court did not heed this.
Xiè was convicted of slandering the imperial clan,
and sentenced to labor service in the Left Workshop;
before a year had passed,
the king was executed,
and Xiè was reinstated as Court Gentleman for Consultation.
In the capital, people said of him:
"The father refused to establish an emperor,"
referring to Lǐ Gù's refusal to establish Emperors Zhì and Huán.
14. In winter,
the tenth month,
Huángfǔ Sōng fought Zhāng Jué's younger brother Liáng at Guǎngzōng.
Liáng's troops were elite and brave,
and Sōng could not overcome them.
The next day,
he closed the camp to rest his soldiers and observe the enemy's movements.
Seeing that the bandits had grown somewhat lax,
he secretly mobilized his troops at night.
At cockcrow,
he charged their battle formation.
The battle lasted until late afternoon,
when he routed them completely,
beheading Liáng,
and taking thirty thousand heads.
About fifty thousand people drowned in the river.
Jué had already died of illness earlier.
His coffin was opened and his corpse mutilated,
and his head was sent to the capital.
In the eleventh month,
Sōng again attacked Jué's younger brother Bǎo at Xiàqūyáng,
and beheaded him.
Xiàqūyáng County
belonged to Jùlù Commandery.
Because Chángshān had a Shàngqūyáng,
this one was called Xià.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
Sōng was immediately appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Left,
concurrently Governor of Jìzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Huáilǐ.
Sōng was kind and caring toward his soldiers.
Whenever the army halted on the march,
he would wait until the tents and camp were fully set up
before retiring to his quarters.
Only after all his soldiers had eaten
would he taste his own meal.
Ěr
means "like this."
15. The Xiānlíng Qiāng in Běidì, along with bandits from Fúhǎn and Héguān, rebelled.
Héguān and Fúhǎn were both counties
belonging to Lǒngxī Commandery.
Líng
is pronounced lián.
Fú
is pronounced fū.
Běigōng
took his residence as his surname.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" mentions the Wèi grandee Běigōng Wénzǐ.
Mèngzǐ mentions Běigōng Yǒu.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì of Jīnchéng had long been famous in the western provinces.
The bandits lured and coerced them,
putting them in charge of military affairs.
They killed the Grand Administrator of Jīnchéng, Chén Yì,
and attacked and burned commanderies and provinces.
Earlier,
the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi relied on powerful connections,
and indulged in greed and tyranny.
The Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi
is not named in the historical records.
Inspector Liáng Hú feared him,
and wanted to kill Zhèng Hé to avoid being implicated.
He consulted with the Chief Clerk of Hànyáng, Gài Xūn of Dūnhuáng.
According to the "Continued Hàn Records": A commandery grand administrator had one assistant;
in commanderies on the frontier,
the assistant was called Chief Clerk.
Dūn
is pronounced tú mén fān.
Gài
is pronounced tú gài fān.
Some advised Xūn to use this opportunity to take revenge,
but Xūn said:
"To plot against and kill a good person
is not loyalty;
to take advantage of another's peril
is not benevolence."
He then advised Hú:
"To keep a hawk or falcon tethered and fed,
is to desire its fierceness.
The commentator says: Xiè means to tie.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says: Zhì means to seize.
It refers to its ability to subdue and capture other birds.
Sǔn
is pronounced sǒng yǐn fān.
Shí
is read as sì.
What use would it be otherwise!"
Hú then desisted.
Zhèng Hé went to Xūn to apologize,
but Xūn refused to see him,
saying:
"I advised Inspector Liáng for his sake,
not for Sū Zhèng Hé."
He remained as resentful toward him as before.
Later, Inspector Zuǒ Chāng embezzled tens of thousands of hu of army grain.
Gài Xūn admonished him.
Zuǒ Chāng was angry,
and sent Gài Xūn, along with his assistants Xīn Zēng and Kǒng Cháng, to station separately at Āyáng to resist the rebels.
Āyáng County
belonged to Hànyáng Commandery.
Gài Xūn repeatedly achieved military merits.
When Běigōng Bóyù attacked Jīnchéng,
Gài Xūn urged Zuǒ Chāng to rescue it,
but Zuǒ Chāng did not comply.
After Chén Yì died,
Biān Zhāng and others advanced and besieged Zuǒ Chāng at Jì.
Zuǒ Chāng summoned Gài Xūn and others to save him.
Xīn Zēng and others hesitated and were unwilling to go.
Gài Xūn angrily said:
"In the past, Zhuāng Jiǎ arrived late,
and Ráng Jū raised his sword.
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Qí,
Yān and Jìn invaded Qí.
Duke Jǐng appointed Marshal Ráng Jū as general
to defend against them,
and ordered his favored minister Zhuāng Jiǎ to supervise the army.
Ráng Jū set a meeting time with him for dawn.
Zhuāng Jiǎ, being arrogant and privileged,
did not arrive until evening.
Ráng Jū summoned the Army Judge and asked:
'According to military law,
what is the punishment for being late after the appointed time?'
He replied:
'Should be beheaded.'
Thereupon, he beheaded Zhuāng Jiǎ and displayed his head to the three armies."
Xīn Zēng and the others, frightened, obeyed him.
Gài Xūn arrived at Jì,
and reproached Biān Zhāng and the others for their crime of rebellion.
They all said:
"If Inspector Zuǒ had earlier followed your advice,
and brought troops against us,
perhaps we could have reformed ourselves.
Now our crime is already grave,
and we cannot surrender."
They then lifted the siege and left.
Rebel Qiāng besieged Commandant Xià Yù at the Pasturage Office.
The former Book of Hàn, in the biography of Yǐn Wēngguī, mentions convicts being sent to manage the Pasturage Office.
The commentary on pronunciation and meaning says: In Yòufúfēng,
where animal husbandry was located,
there were officials like the Park Master,
hence it was called the Pasturage Office.
is pronounced xù.
At Húpán,
during the Jìn period,
Fú Shēng of Qín buried Yáo Yìzhòng at Húpán.
The Records of the Sixteen Kingdoms says: It was in Jì County of Tiānshuǐ.
Gài Xūn's remaining troops numbered less than a hundred men.
He himself suffered three wounds,
but sat firmly unmoving,
pointing to a wooden marker and saying:
"Bury my corpse here!"
The Qiāng chieftain Diānwú of the Gōujiù tribe used his troops to shield the crowd, saying:
(Lǐ Xián's note: Gōujiù
is a separate branch of the Qiāng.
is pronounced gōu.
is pronounced zhǒng.
is pronounced diān.)
"Chief Clerk Gài is a worthy man.
If you kill him, you will betray Heaven."
Gài Xūn looked up and cursed:
"You rebel traitors bound for death!
What do you know?
Hurry up and kill me!"
The crowd looked at each other in shock.
Diānwú dismounted and gave his horse to Gài Xūn.
Gài Xūn refused to mount it,
and was subsequently captured by the Qiāng.
The Qiāng admired his righteousness and courage,
and did not dare harm him,
sending him back to Hànyáng.
Later, Inspector Yáng Yōng recommended Gài Xūn to serve as Administrator of Hànyáng.
16 The remaining forces of Zhāng Mànchéng again appointed Zhào Hóng as their leader.
Their numbers flourished once more,
reaching over a hundred thousand,
and they occupied Wǎn City.
Zhū Jùn, together with Jīngzhōu Inspector Xú Qiú and others, combined forces and besieged them.
From the sixth month to the eighth month, they could not capture it.
The responsible officials petitioned to recall Zhū Jùn.
Minister of Works Zhāng Wēn submitted a memorial saying:
"In the past, Qín employed Bái Qǐ,
and Yān employed Yuè Yì.
Both took years and seasons
before they could overcome the enemy.
The Records of the Grand Historian states: Bái Qǐ served King Zhāoxiāng of Qín as Dàliángzào.
He attacked Wèi
and defeated it.
Five years later,
he attacked Zhào,
capturing Guāngláng City.
Seven years later,
he attacked Chǔ,
capturing Yān, Dèng, and five other cities.
The following year,
he captured Yǐng,
burned Yílíng,
and then advanced east to Jìnglíng.
Yuè Yì served King Zhāoxiāng of Yān,
serving as Supreme General.
He attacked Qí,
entered Línzī,
and campaigned through Qí for five years,
capturing over seventy cities.
Now the army is directed south,
and the strategy is already set.
Changing generals in the midst of a campaign
is something military strategists caution against.
We should grant him time,
and hold him responsible for achieving success."
The Emperor then desisted.
Zhū Jùn attacked Zhào Hóng
and beheaded him.
The rebel leader Hán Zhōng again occupied Wǎn and resisted Zhū Jùn.
Zhū Jùn beat the drums and attacked its southwest,
and the rebels all rushed there.
Zhū Jùn personally led elite troops to strike its northeast,
scaling the walls and entering.
Hán Zhōng then retreated to defend the small inner city,
and in panic begged to surrender.
All the generals wanted to accept,
but Zhū Jùn said:
"In warfare, there are situations that appear the same but whose circumstances differ.
In the past, during the time between Qín and Xiàng Yǔ,
the people had no fixed ruler,
so rewards were given to those who submitted to encourage others to come over.
Now the realm is unified,
and only the Yellow Turbans have created rebellion.
Accepting surrender does not encourage good,
while attacking them is sufficient to punish evil.
If we accept them now,
it will further open the way for rebellious intentions.
When it benefits them, the rebels will advance and fight;
when they are hard-pressed, they will beg to surrender.
Sparing the enemy and nurturing the rebels
is not a good plan!"
Thereupon he attacked urgently,
but in successive battles could not overcome them.
Zhū Jùn climbed an earthen mound to observe,
turned and said to his Major Zhāng Chāo:
"I understand now.
The rebels now have a solid outer encirclement,
and their inner camp is pressed urgently.
Their plea for surrender is not accepted,
and they wish to break out but cannot.
This is why they fight to the death.
Ten thousand men united as one heart are still irresistible,
let alone a hundred thousand!
It would be better to lift the siege,
concentrate our troops and enter the city.
When Hán Zhōng sees the siege lifted,
he will certainly come out on his own.
Once he comes out, their resolve will scatter,
and that is the way to defeat them."
Soon after lifting the siege,
Hán Zhōng indeed came out to fight.
Zhū Jùn took the opportunity to attack,
greatly defeating him,
and beheading over ten thousand.
Nányáng Administrator Qín Xié killed Hán Zhōng.
The remaining forces again honored Sūn Xià as their leader,
and returned to occupy Wǎn.
Zhū Jùn attacked them urgently.
Major Sūn Jiān led his troops in scaling the walls first.
On the guǐsì day,
they captured Wǎn City.
Sūn Xià fled.
Zhū Jùn pursued him to Jīng Mountain in Xī'è.
Xī'è County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Lǐ Xián's note: The old city was south of Xiàngchéng County in Dèng Prefecture;
Jīng Mountain is south of it.
They beheaded over ten thousand.
Thereupon, the Yellow Turbans were broken and scattered.
In the other commanderies and prefectures, those executed
numbered several thousand per commandery.
17 In the twelfth month,
on the jǐsì day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed for the realm,
and the era name was changed.
18. The Inspector of Yùzhōu, Wáng Yǔn of Tàiyuán, defeated the Yellow Turbans and
obtained letters from Zhāng Ràng's guests
communicating with the Yellow Turbans.
He submitted them to the throne.
The Emperor angrily reprimanded Ràng;
Ràng kowtowed and pleaded for forgiveness,
and in the end he could not be punished.
Ràng therefore used an affair to incriminate Yǔn,
who was then arrested and imprisoned.
Xián said: "Chuán" means
to arrest.
Chuán is pronounced
zhū liàn fān.
Xià is pronounced
xiá jià fān.
He was later reinstated as Inspector;
within ten days,
he was again arrested on another charge.
Yáng Cì did not wish him to suffer further humiliation and torture.
Xián said: Gèng means
to undergo.
Chǔ means
bitter pain.
Gèng is pronounced
gōng héng fān.
"Because of the affair with Zhāng Ràng,
you have been summoned twice in one month.
The malice is difficult to measure.
I hope you will consider deeply!"
Xián said: "Deep consideration"
means to have him kill himself.
Together they wept and offered him poison.
Yǔn sternly said:
"I am a subject of the sovereign.
Having offended the sovereign,
I should suffer capital punishment to apologize to the world.
How could I take poison to seek death!"
The former book, the Biography of Wáng Jiā, says: "What does it mean to die by chewing poison?"
Rǔ should be
jǔ.
He went out to the prison cart.
After arriving,
the Grand General Jìn, together with Yáng Cì and Yuán Kuí, jointly submitted a memorial pleading for him.
He was granted a reduction from the death penalty.
Examination of discrepancies: Yǔn's biography says
"Grand Commandant Yuán Kuí, Minister over the Masses Yáng Cì."
Checking, Kuí and Cì were not holding these offices at the time.
This is probably an error.
1. Spring,
first month,
a great epidemic occurred.
2. Second month,
Jǐyǒu day,
the Yúntái Hall in the Southern Palace caught fire.
Gēngxū day,
the Lèchéng Gate caught fire.
According to the Continued Hàn Records: This was probably the gate of the Lèchéng Hall.
"Chéng"
should be
"chéng".
The Treatise on the Five Elements writes it as
"Lèchéng Gate".
Liú Zhāo said: It is the central gate of the Southern Palace.
The Regular Attendants Zhāng Ràng and Zhào Zhōng advised the Emperor to collect a tax on all land under heaven,
ten coins per mǔ,
to repair the palace buildings
and cast bronze figures.
The Administrator of Lè'ān, Lù Kāng, submitted a memorial admonishing:
"In the past, Duke Xuān of Lǔ taxed the mǔ, and locust disasters arose of themselves.
The Gōngyáng Commentary says: What was the initial tax on the mǔ?
It was to tax according to the mǔ.
Hé Xiū's annotation says: Duke Xuān had no kindness or trustworthiness among the people,
and the people were unwilling to exert their full effort on the public fields.
He initiated the practice of walking over and inspecting the mǔ,
taxing the good grain.
Yuán means
locust larvae.
The Commentary says: In winter,
yuán were born.
Why does it say yuán were born?
It was because he altered the ancient and changed the constant.
The annotation says: Shàng means
the Duke above.
It means Duke Xuān changed the old system of public fields and taxed the mǔ.
Yuán is pronounced
yú zhuān fān.
The Zuǒ Commentary: Jìsūn wished to use a land tax,

Zhòngní privately said to Rǎn Yǒu: If Jìsūn wishes to implement the law,
then the statutes of the Duke of Zhōu exist;

To discard the sage's admonition

The favored eunuchs slandered Kāng for citing perished states to analogize the sagely and enlightened,
a great disrespect,

The Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk Liú Dài submitted a statement explaining and interpreting,
and he was spared and allowed to return to his fields and village.
Kāng was
the grandson of Lù Xù.
Lù Xù's
affair is seen in the 45th scroll, the 14th year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng.
Further, an edict was issued to requisition timber and patterned stone from the commanderies and prefectures,
to be delivered to the capital.
The Yellow Gate Regular Attendants often ordered the rejection of those not meeting standards,
then forced a reduction and bought them cheaply,
obtaining them for only one-tenth of their original price.
They then resold them,
and the eunuchs
again did not immediately accept them.
The timber thus piled up and rotted,
and the palace buildings remained unfinished for years.
The Inspectors and Administrators further increased private levies,
causing the common people to wail and sigh.
Also, they ordered the grooms of the Western Garden to separately supervise and hasten,
intimidating the commanderies and prefectures,
and receiving many bribes.
For the promotions and appointments of Inspectors, officials of two thousand picul rank, Màocái, and Xiàolián,
all were demanded to contribute money for the army and palace repair,

On his way to Méngjīn,

When the memorial was presented,

3. Zhū Jùn was appointed as General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Right.

bandits arose everywhere.
Zhāng Niújiǎo of Bólíng, Chǔ Fēiyàn of Chángshān, and Huáng Lóng, Zuǒ Xiào, Yú Dīgēn, Zhāng Báiqí, Liú Shí, Zuō Zī Wénbā,
Pínghàn Dàjì, Sīlì Yuánchéng, Léi Gōng, Fúyún, Báiquè, Yáng Fèng, Yú Dú, Wǔlù, Lǐ Dàmù, Báirào, Suī Gù, Kǔ Qiú, and others,

Cóng,

6 Běigōng Bóyù and others invaded the Three Adjuncts.
An edict ordered General of Chariots and Cavalry on the Left Huángfǔ Sōng to garrison Cháng'ān to attack them.

Fēn also summoned Huá Xīn of Píngyuán and Táoqiū Hóng to jointly finalize the plan.
Hóng intended to go,
but Xīn stopped him, saying:
"Deposing and installing rulers is a major affair,
difficult even for Yǐ Yǐn and Huò Guāng.
Fēn is by nature careless and lacks military prowess,
this will certainly not succeed."
Hóng then desisted.
At that time, a red glow appeared in the northern sky at midnight,
stretching east to west across the heavens.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"There is a conspiracy in the north,
it is not advisable to travel north."
The Emperor then halted.
He ordered Fēn to disband his troops,
and soon summoned him to court.
Fēn, in fear,
removed his official seal and fled.
Reaching Píngyuán,
he committed suicide.
12 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Mǎ Rìmī, Colonel of Archers Who Shoot by Sound, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Rìmī
was a clansman of Mǎ Róng.
13 In the eighth month,
the Eight Colonels of the Western Garden were first established.
Junior Attendant Jiǎn Shuò was appointed Colonel of the Upper Army,
(Surname Compendium: Jiǎn
is a surname.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn, there was a Qín Grand Master Jiǎn Shū.)
Colonel of Garrison Cavalry Bào Hóng was appointed Colonel of the Lower Army,
Court Counselor Cáo Cāo was appointed Colonel Who Manages the Army,
Zhào Róng was appointed Colonel Who Aids the Army on the Left,
Féng Fāng was appointed Colonel Who Aids the Army on the Right,
Grand Master of Remonstrance Xià Móu was appointed Colonel of the Left Army,
Chúnyú Qióng was appointed Colonel of the Right Army;
all were under the command of Jiǎn Shuò.
Examination of discrepancies: In Fàn Yè's Book of Hòu Hàn, the Account of Yuán Shào
states "Shào was Colonel of the Assistant Army";
the Account of Hé Jìn
states "Chúnyú Qióng was Colonel of the Assistant Army."
Here we follow Yuè Zī's Records of the Duke of Shānyáng.
The Emperor paid attention to military affairs;
Shuò was robust and had military strategy,
the Emperor personally trusted him,
so that even the Grand General was placed under his command.
14 In the ninth month,
Minister over the Masses Xǔ Xiàng was dismissed;
Minister of Works Dīng Gōng was appointed Minister over the Masses,
and Court Architect Liú Hóng of Nányáng was appointed Minister of Works.
15 Commandant of the Guards, Marquis of Tiáo, Dǒng Zhòng, was appointed General of Agile Cavalry.
Zhòng
was the nephew of the Grand Empress Dowager of Yuèlìng.
16 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Yellow Turbans in Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu rose again,
plundering commanderies and counties.
17 Observers of celestial phenomena believed that the capital would experience major military conflict,
with bloodshed in the two palaces.
The Emperor, wishing to avert this,
extensively mobilized troops from all directions,
and conducted a military review below the Pínglè Tower.
(Commentary on the Waterways Classic: The Gǔ River flows southeast from Báimǎ Temple past the Pínglè Tower,
located outside the Upper West Gate.
Lè,
pronounced lè.
Guān,
pronounced guàn.)
Above, a twelve-layer canopy was erected,
the canopy being ten zhàng high;
northeast of the platform, a smaller platform was built,
with a nine-layer canopy erected upon it,
nine zhàng high.
Tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry were arrayed,
forming encampments into battle formations.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
the Emperor personally came to the army,
stationing himself beneath the large canopy,
while Grand General Jìn stationed himself beneath the small canopy.
The Emperor personally donned armor and barded his horse,
proclaiming himself
"The Supreme General,"
rode around the formation three times and returned,
then handed over command to Jìn.
The Emperor asked Colonel Who Subdues Caitiffs Gài Xūn:
"With my military review like this,
what do you think?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that the ancient kings displayed virtue, not military might.
(The Guóyǔ records the words of Zhài Gōng Móufù.)
This is insufficient to demonstrate resolute courage.
(The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: To display resolute courage in warfare is called martial.
Killing the enemy is resolute,
achieving resoluteness is courage.) The Emperor said:
"Well said!
I regret meeting you so late,
the other ministers never spoke like this."
Xūn said to Yuán Shào:
"The Emperor is very intelligent,
but is merely obscured by those around him."
He plotted with Shào to jointly eliminate the favored minions.
Jiǎn Shuò, fearing this,
had Xūn appointed as Governor of the Capital Province.
18 In the eleventh month,
Wáng Guó besieged Chéncāng.
An edict reappointed Huángfǔ Sōng as General of the Left,
to supervise Former General Dǒng Zhuó,
combining forces of forty thousand men to resist him.
Initially,
Emperor Líng summoned Dǒng Zhuó to serve as Shǎofǔ (Minister of Stewards).
According to Dǒng Zhuó's biography,
in the sixth year of Zhōngpíng, he was summoned to be Shǎofǔ.
This was likely in that same year.
"The volunteer troops from Huángzhōng and the Qín and Hú soldiers under my command
all came to me and said: 'Our military pay has not been fully issued,
our rations and rewards have been cut off,
and our wives and children are starving and freezing.'
They clung to my carriage,
preventing me from leaving.
The Qiāng and Hú have vicious hearts and dog-like dispositions.
Xián's note says: This means the Qiāng and Hú have malicious hearts,
and their temperament is like that of dogs.
The Fāngyán states: 'Biē' means
wicked.
Guō Pú notes: 'Biē fū' means
hot-tempered.
'Biē' is pronounced
fāng liè fān.
'Fū' is pronounced
fāng yú fān.
I then complied and comforted them,
and if there were any further changes or unusual developments, I would report again."
Xián's note says: If they develop further rebellious intentions,
it should be reported to the emperor again.
Hóng's Lì Shì states: In the second year of Jiànníng under Emperor Líng of Hàn,
Shǐ Chén, the Chancellor of Lǔ, in his memorial after sacrificing at the Confucius Temple, wrote
"'if there are any changes or unusual developments, I will report them,'"
and in the second year of Guānghé,
Fán Yì, in his memorial after reducing the poll tax for the people of Huáxià, wrote
"'if there are any changes or unusual developments, I will report again.'"
This was likely a common concluding phrase in memorials of that time.
It means that if any future matters exceed this,
or differ from this,
they will be reported again.
'Fù' is pronounced
fú yòu fān.
'Shàng' is pronounced
shí zhǎng fān.
When the emperor fell seriously ill,
an edict appointed Dǒng Zhuó as Governor of Bīngzhōu,
ordering him to place his troops under Huángfǔ Sōng's command.
Dǒng Zhuó again submitted a memorial stating:
"I have mistakenly received the emperor's grace,
commanding troops for ten years.
The soldiers, both high and low,
have grown accustomed to me over a long time,
cherish the kindness I have shown in nurturing them,
and are willing to risk their lives for me in a moment.
I beg to lead them to the northern provinces,
to serve on the frontier."
Sōng's nephew Lì advised Sōng:
"The command of the empire's military forces
lies with you, sir, and Dǒng Zhuó.
Now that enmity has arisen between you,
it is inevitable that one of you will not survive.
Dǒng Zhuó received an edict ordering him to hand over his troops, yet he submitted a memorial making his own request—
this is defiance of orders.
He estimates that the capital's government is in chaos,
hence he dares to hesitate and not advance—
this harbors treachery.
Both of these
are crimes that the law does not pardon.
Moreover, he is cruel and ruthless, without affection for anyone,
and his officers and soldiers are not attached to him.
You, sir, are now the commander-in-chief,
(Sōng was the commander when he campaigned against Wáng Guó,
hence he is called commander-in-chief.)
To act would demonstrate loyalty and righteousness to the emperor above,
and eliminate a vicious threat below—
there is no reason it would not succeed."
Sōng said:
"Although defying orders is a crime,
unauthorized execution also carries responsibility.
Dǒng Zhuó's refusal to relinquish his troops is defiance of orders;
if Sōng were to hastily attack Dǒng Zhuó, that would be unauthorized execution.
Let the imperial court decide."
He then submitted a memorial to inform the emperor.
The emperor reprimanded Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó also did not obey the edict,
instead stationing his troops in Hédōng to observe how the situation would change.
Hé Jìn summoned Dǒng Zhuó, ordering him to lead troops to the capital.
Kǎo Yì states: Hé Jìn's biography says:
"He summoned Dǒng Zhuó to station troops in the Shanglin Garden within the Pass."
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó was already stationed in Hédōng.
If he were to station troops in Shanglin,
that would be further west,
and not a way to pressure the Empress Dowager.
We now follow Dǒng Zhuó's biography.
"Dǒng Zhuó is strong-willed, ruthless, and lacking in righteousness,
his ambitions are insatiable.
If we entrust him with court affairs,
and give him great responsibilities,
he will indulge his vicious desires,
inevitably endangering the imperial court.
You, illustrious sir, with the weight of your kinship and virtue,
holding the authority of a regent,
should firmly decide on your own,
punish and eliminate the guilty—
it is truly inappropriate to rely on Dǒng Zhuó for support!
Moreover, if matters are delayed, changes will arise;
the lesson from history is not far away—
referring to the incident of Dòu Wǔ,
which can serve as a historical lesson.
The Imperial Secretary Lú Zhí also said it was inappropriate to summon Dǒng Zhuó,
but Hé Jìn did not listen to any of them.
Tài then abandoned his official post and left,
saying to Xún Yōu:
"Lord Hé is not easy to assist."
Hé Jìn's subordinate official Wáng Kuāng,
and the Commandant of Cavalry Bào Xìn,
were both from Tàishān.
Hé Jìn sent them back to their hometown to recruit troops;
he also summoned the Governor of Dōngjùn, Qiáo Mào, to station troops at Chénggāo,
and ordered the Commandant of Martial Ferocity, Dīng Yuán, to lead several thousand men to raid Hénèi,
burning Mèngjīn,
the flames illuminating the city.
Xián's note says: 'Martial Ferocity'
means having martial skills and being brave and fierce.
It is an auspicious title,
hence used to name the office.
Dǒng Zhuó, upon hearing the summons,
immediately set out,
and also submitted a memorial stating:
"The Regular Palace Attendants Zhāng Ràng and others,
relying on favor and enjoying imperial grace,
have corrupted and thrown the empire into chaos.
I have heard that to stop water from boiling by stirring it is
not as good as removing the firewood;
lancing an abscess, though painful,
is better than letting it fester internally.
This means that if a boil accumulates and festers,
breaking it open, though painful,
is better than letting it internally consume the flesh,
gradually spreading and growing larger.
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn says: Why did Jìn's Zhào Yǎng take the armor from Jìnyáng to drive out Xún Yín and Shì Jí Shè?
Because they were wicked men at the ruler's side.
This act of driving out wicked men at the ruler's side—
why is it described as rebellion?
Because it was done without the ruler's command.
Xián's note says: Those who sound the bells and drums
are proclaiming their crimes.
The Empress Dowager still did not consent.
Hé Miáo said to Hé Jìn:
"We started together from Nányáng,
both relying on the palace to rise from poverty and low status to wealth and honor.
This means Empress Hé gained her position through the eunuchs,
and the Hé brothers thereby attained wealth and honor.
It was not easy either.
Spilled water cannot be gathered back;
you should think deeply about this.
Water spilled on the ground
cannot be gathered back—
meaning once things happen, they cannot be undone.
When Dǒng Zhuó reached Miǎnchí,
Hé Jìn grew hesitant again,
and sent the Grand Master of Remonstrance, Chóng Shào, to proclaim an edict ordering him to stop.
Dǒng Zhuó did not accept the edict,
and proceeded forward to Hénán;
Hénán,
the royal city of the Zhōu,
was not far from Luòyáng.
'Chóng' is pronounced
chōng.
He then tried to persuade him to turn his army back.
Dǒng Zhuó suspected a plot,
and ordered his soldiers to threaten Shào with weapons.
Shào grew angry,
invoked the imperial edict and shouted at them;
the soldiers all stepped back,
and he then went forward to confront and reprimand Dǒng Zhuó;
Dǒng Zhuó was left speechless,
and then turned his army back to Xīyáng Pavilion.
Xián's note says: Xīyáng Pavilion was west of Hénán City.
He was the grandson of Hào.
Yuán Shào, fearing Hé Jìn might change his mind,
thus threatened him, saying:
"The scheme has already been formed,
the situation has been revealed.
What is the General waiting for, that he does not make an early decision?
If matters are delayed, changes will arise,
and we will become another Dòu family!"
Hé Jìn thereupon appointed Yuán Shào as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
granted him the imperial tally,
with authority to act on his own initiative and to execute decisions.
The Colonel-Director of Retainers of Hàn originally held the tally.
By the time of Emperor Yuán,
when Zhūgé Fēng served as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
the tally was first removed.
Now granting Shào the tally
was to increase his authority.
"Decisions" (duàn)
is pronounced dùan.
Shào dispatched skilled military officers from Luòyáng to secretly observe the eunuchs,
and urged Dǒng Zhuó and others to send urgent memorials by post,
intending to advance troops to Pínglèguān.
The Empress Dowager then became frightened,
and dismissed all the Regular Palace Attendants and Junior Yellow Gates, sending them back to their village homes,
keeping only those personally close to Hé Jìn to guard the palace precincts.
All the Regular Attendants and Junior Yellow Gates went to Hé Jìn to apologize for their offenses,
submitting to whatever arrangements he would make.
Hé Jìn said to them:
"The unrest in the empire
is precisely due to you gentlemen.
Now Dǒng Zhuó is about to arrive.
Why don't you gentlemen each return to your fiefs early!"
Yuán Shào advised Hé Jìn to settle the matter right then,
advising Jìn to kill them all at this time.
Hé Jìn refused.
Shào also wrote letters to the various provinces and commanderies,
falsely declaring Hé Jìn's intentions,
ordering them to arrest and investigate the relatives of the palace eunuchs.
Hé Jìn's plot had been developing for many days,
and was somewhat leaked.
The palace eunuchs, fearful, considered a change of plans.
Zhāng Ràng's daughter-in-law
was the younger sister of the Empress Dowager.
Ràng bowed his head to his daughter-in-law, saying:
"This old minister has committed offenses,
and should return with you, my new daughter-in-law, to our private home.
But having received favor for generations,
(Xián's note: Wéi means
to think upon.)
my feelings are full of attachment.
I wish to once more enter for duty,
to be able to briefly gaze upon Her Majesty the Empress Dowager's countenance,
and then retire to the ditches and gullies.
I would die without regret!"
The daughter-in-law spoke to the Lady of Wǔyáng,
who informed the Empress Dowager.
An edict was then issued ordering all the Regular Attendants to return to duty.
In the eighth month,
on the day Wùchén,
Hé Jìn entered the Chánglè Palace,
informed the Empress Dowager,
and requested the execution of all the Regular Attendants.
The Regular Attendants Zhāng Ràng and Duàn Guī said to each other:
"The Grand General claims illness,
did not attend the mourning,
did not attend the burial.
Now he suddenly enters the palace precincts.
What is his intention?
Is the affair of the Dòu family about to happen again?"
They sent someone to eavesdrop secretly,
and heard all his words.
They then led several dozen of their partisans, armed, and secretly entered through a side gate,
hiding beneath the doors of the palace hall.
When Hé Jìn came out,
they falsely summoned him with an edict from the Empress Dowager.
He entered and sat in the palace chamber.
Ràng and the others questioned Hé Jìn, saying:
"The chaos in the empire
is not solely our fault.
The late Emperor was once displeased with the Empress Dowager,
nearly leading to success or failure.
The affair is seen in the fourth year of Guānghé in the previous scroll.
"Nearly" (jī)
is pronounced jī.
Each of us contributed ten million in family wealth as gifts,
to please His Majesty's mind,
wishing only to entrust ourselves to your household.
Now you wish to exterminate our kind.
Is this not too extreme!"
Thereupon, the Director of the Imperial Workshop, Qú Mù, drew his sword and beheaded Hé Jìn in front of the Jiādé Hall.
According to the Treatise on Officials,
the Imperial Workshop had a Prefect and a Deputy, but no Director.
During the reigns of Emperors Huán and Líng,
the heads of all the offices were entirely eunuchs.
The Director of the Imperial Workshop must also have been established at that time.
Qú
is a surname.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: The Son of Heaven sent the Steward Qú Bó Jiǔ to pay a visit.
Also, Wèi had Qú Kǒng who drove the chariot.
They appointed the former Grand Commandant Fán Líng as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
and the Minister of Lesser Treasury Xǔ Xiàng as Governor of Hénán.
The Imperial Secretary received the edict board,
was suspicious of it,
and said:
"We request the Grand General to come out and discuss together."
A Palace Attendant threw Hé Jìn's head to the Imperial Secretary, saying:
"Hé Jìn plotted rebellion,
and has already been executed!"
Hé Jìn's subordinate commanders Wú Kuāng and Zhāng Zhāng were outside.
Hearing that Hé Jìn had been killed,
they wished to lead troops into the palace,
but the palace gates were closed.
The General of the Household Rapid as Tigers Yuán Shù, together with Kuāng, hacked at and attacked them.
Palace Attendants held weapons and guarded the gates.
As dusk fell,
Shù then set fire to the Qīngsuǒ Gate of the Southern Palace.
Wèi Guàn said: Qīngsuǒ
refers to the green carvings by the gate.
Another says: Inside the Son of Heaven's gate there are double lattice frames,
painted green inside, called suǒ.
The Textual Analysis states: The biography of Hé Jìn writes
"Jiǔlóng Gate".
Now we follow the Yuán Jì.
Ràng and the others went in and informed the Empress Dowager,
saying the Grand General's troops had rebelled,
burning the palace,
and attacking the gate of the Imperial Secretariat.
The gate of the Imperial Secretariat
is the gate of the Imperial Secretariat.
They fled to the Northern Palace via the elevated passageway.
"To lead" (jiāng)
is pronounced according to its usual reading,
meaning to lead,
to take along.
They looked up and counted Duàn Guī;
Guī became afraid,
and released the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager threw herself against the gate,
and thus
escaped.
Yuán Shào and his uncle Yuán Wěi forged an edict summoning Fán Líng and Xǔ Xiàng,
and beheaded them.
Shào and Hé Miáo led troops and camped below the Zhūquè Gate Tower,
captured Zhào Zhōng and others,
and beheaded them.
Wú Kuāng and others had long resented Miáo for not being of one mind with Hé Jìn,
and also suspected he was in secret communication with the eunuchs.
They then ordered the army, saying:
"The one who killed the Grand General is
the Chariot and Horse General.
At that time Miáo was General of Chariots and Cavalry.
They all shed tears, saying:
"We are willing to fight to the death!"
Kuāng then led troops and, together with Dǒng Zhuó's younger brother, the Commandant of Imperial Carriages Dǒng Mín, attacked and killed Miáo,
abandoning his corpse in the gardens.
Shào then closed the gates of the Northern Palace,
marshaled troops, and arrested all the eunuchs,
killing them all regardless of age,
over two thousand in total.
Some were beardless and died by mistake.
"Beard" (xū)
is the ancient character for "beard" (xū).
Some climbed onto the roof of the Duānmén gatehouse,
to attack within the palace precincts.
The main south gate of the palace is called Duānmén,
which is the forbidden palace area.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī and others, hard-pressed,
then led the Emperor and the Prince of Chénliú, along with several dozen others, on foot out of the Gǔ Gate.
The Gǔ Gate,
located in the zǐ position,
is the due north gate of Luò City.
They reached Xiǎopíng Ford.
Xián's note: Xiǎopíng Ford is northwest of present-day Gǒng County.
Dù Yòu said: Northwest of Gǒng County is the old city of Xiǎopíng County.
Further north is a ford,
called Xiǎopíng Ford.
None of the high ministers were able to follow.
Only the Imperial Secretary Lú Zhí and the Central Section Officer of Hénán, Mǐn Gòng, reached the riverbank at night.
Hàn Official Ceremonial: Each commandery established five Sectional Inspecting Secretaries to oversee the subordinate counties.
The Governor of Hénán established four Sectional Inspecting Secretaries,
with a Central Section Officer.
"Officer" (yuàn)
is pronounced yùan.
Mǐn Gòng said:
"If you do not die quickly now,
I will kill you!"
He then personally struck and killed several with his sword.
Ràng and the others were terrified,
clasped their hands and bowed repeatedly,
kowtowed to the Emperor and took their leave, saying:
"We ministers die.
May Your Majesty take care of yourself!"
They then threw themselves into the river and died.
5. Dǒng Zhuó, because the forces east of the mountains were strong,
wanted to move the capital to avoid them.
The high ministers all disapproved but none dared speak out,
fearing his tyranny.
An envoy was sent to summon and appoint Jùn,
but Jùn declined
and refused to accept the post.
He then said:
"If the state moves west,
it will surely disappoint the hopes of the realm.
'Disappoint' means
to betray.
I do not see how this can be done."
The envoy said:
"You are summoned to receive an appointment, yet you refuse it.
You are not asked about the relocation, yet you state your opinion on it.
Why is this?"
Jùn replied:
"The position of deputy chancellor
is not one I can bear.
Moving the capital is an unwise plan,
yet it is a matter of urgency.
To decline what I cannot bear,
and to speak on what is urgent,
is what is proper for a minister."
Consequently, he was not made deputy.
Dǒng Zhuó convened a grand assembly of high ministers to deliberate,
saying:
"Emperor Gāozǔ established his capital in Guānzhōng,
for eleven generations.
Emperor Guāngwǔ's palace was in Luòyáng,
and now it has also been eleven generations.
According to the Stone Chamber Prophecy,
besides the apocryphal texts of the time,
there was also the Stone Chamber Prophecy,
likely augmented by people of that era,
similar to works like the *Confucius's Sealed Room Records*.
This is to accord with the will of Heaven and men."
All the officials remained silent.
Minister over the Masses Yáng Biāo said:
"Moving the capital and altering institutions
are major affairs of the realm.
Thus, when Pángēng moved to Bó,
the people of Yīn all complained.
The preface to the *Book of Documents* states: Pángēng moved five times,
intending to govern from Bó,
and the people of Yīn lamented and complained.
Therefore, when Emperor Guāngwǔ changed the capital to Luòyì,
many years had already passed,
and the common people were content and happy.
Now, without cause, to abandon the ancestral temples
and forsake the imperial tombs,
I fear it will alarm the populace,
and surely lead to turmoil like a boiling pot.
Xián's note: Like the boiling of congee.
The *Book of Songs* says: Like boiling, like bubbling soup.
Such deceitful and heterodox writings
— how can they be trusted and relied upon!"
Zhuó said:
"Guānzhōng is fertile and rich,
which is why Qín was able to annex the six states.
Moreover, Lǒngyòu produces its own timber,
and at Dùlíng there are the pottery kilns of Emperor Wǔ,
so by combining efforts to construct,
it can be accomplished in a single morning.
What need is there to discuss with the common people!
If any hesitate or retreat,
I will drive them forward with my great army,
and can make them reach the vast sea."
Xián's note: This means they would not dare avoid dangers and hardships.
"To stir the realm is extremely easy,
but to pacify it is very difficult.
I hope Your Excellency will consider this!"
Zhuó changed countenance and said:
"Do you, sir, wish to thwart the state's plans!"
Grand Commandant Huáng Wǎn said:
"This is a major affair of the state.
Minister Yáng's words —
should they not be given thought?"
Zhuó did not reply.
Minister of Works Xún Shuàng, seeing Zhuó's resolve was firm,
feared he would harm Biāo and others,
and so said calmly:
"Would the chancellor delight in this!
The troops east of the mountains have risen,
and cannot be quelled in a single day.
Therefore, we must relocate to plan for it.
This is the strategic position of Qín and Hàn."
Meaning that Qín and Hàn had their capitals in Guānzhōng,
relying on the natural barriers of mountains and rivers to control the realm.
Wǎn withdrew,
and again submitted a dissenting opinion.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Zhuó, citing disasters and anomalies, petitioned to dismiss Wǎn, Biāo, and others.
He appointed Commandant of the Palace Gentlemen Zhào Qiān as Grand Commandant,
and Minister Coachman Wáng Yǔn as Minister over the Masses.
Colonel of the City Gates Wǔ Qióng and Colonel of the Supervising Army Zhōu Bì firmly advised against moving the capital.
Zhuó became greatly enraged and said:
"When I first entered the court,
you two gentlemen urged me to employ worthy men,
so I followed your advice.
Yet once these men took office,
they raised troops to plot against me.
This means you two gentlemen betrayed me.
How have I wronged you!"
On the day Gēngchén,
he arrested Qióng and Bì,
and executed them.
Yáng Biāo and Huáng Wǎn, in fear,
went to Zhuó to apologize.
Zhuó also regretted killing Qióng and Bì,
and so again petitioned to appoint Biāo and Wǎn as Palace Attendants.
6. Zhuó summoned the Governor of the Capital Province, Gài Xūn, to be a Court Gentleman for Consultation.
At that time, General of the Left Huángfǔ Sōng commanded thirty thousand troops stationed in Fúfēng.
Pān Yuè's *Records of Guānzhōng* states: The three metropolitan regions formerly administered from within Cháng'ān city,
with senior officials in each county governing the people.
After Emperor Guāngwǔ moved the capital east,
Fúfēng's administration moved to Huáilǐ,
and Féngyì's administration moved to Gāolíng.
It happened that Zhuó also summoned Sōng to be Colonel of the City Gates.
Sōng's Chief Clerk Liáng Yǎn advised Sōng, saying:
"Dǒng Zhuó has plundered the capital region,
deposing and installing rulers at will.
Now he summons you, General.

鼻息,

When the nasal breath is exhaled, it is warm;

Medical texts say: Blood constitutes the vessels,
and *qì* constitutes the breath.
The terms for vessels and breath are thus distinguished.
Breathing in and out
is the bellows of *qì*;
its movement and response
are the waves of blood.
Its pathway is measured in body inches,
totaling sixteen *zhàng* and two *chǐ*.
With one exhalation, the vessels move twice;
with one inhalation, the vessels move twice;
with one complete breath cycle, the vessels move five times;
intercalated with a deep breath, then six times.
One movement equals one *cùn*,

ten breath cycles, six *chǐ*;
one hundred breath cycles, six *zhàng*;
two hundred breath cycles, twelve *zhàng*;
seventy breath cycles, four *zhàng* and two *chǐ*.
Calculating two hundred and seventy breath cycles,
as the water clock drips for two marks, the sixteen *zhàng* and two *chǐ* are completed,
circulating once through the entire body;
within one hundred marks, there are fifty circulations.
Therefore it is said: the vessels travel through the yang twenty-five times and through the yin twenty-five times.
Breath cycles are determined by inhalation and exhalation,
totaling thirteen thousand five hundred cycles in one day.
Since the advance and retreat of breathing is slower than the vessels,
it takes one full day and night to complete the travel through the sixteen *zhàng* and two *chǐ* of the channels and network vessels,

converging greatly at the Wind Mansion.
The vessels belong to yin,
and yin travels swiftly,
like the Grand Yin (the moon) completing one circuit of the heavens in one month.
Breath belongs to yang,
and yang travels slowly,
like the Grand Yang (the sun) completing one circuit of the heavens in one year.
Thus it corresponds to the constant measures of heaven.

So the two went,
but actually summoned troops and returned.
Jué gathered troops along the way,
and by the time they reached Cháng'ān,
they already had over a hundred thousand men.
Together with Dǒng Zhuó's former troops Fán Chóu, Lǐ Méng, and others, they surrounded the city of Cháng'ān.
The city walls were steep and could not be attacked,
so they besieged it for eight days.
Textual analysis says: In the Records of the Three Kingdoms of Wèi, it says ten days,
but here we follow Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Han.
Xián's note: Sōu troops are Shǔ troops;
in the Hàn dynasty, Shǔ was called Sōu.
On Wùwǔ,
they led Jué's troops into the city,
and released the soldiers to plunder.
Lǚ Bù fought them within the city,
but could not prevail.
He led several hundred cavalry, with Dǒng Zhuó's head tied to his horse's saddle, and fled,
halting his horse outside the Qīngsuǒ Gate.
Wèi Guàn said: Qīngsuǒ,
refers to the green carvings beside the door.
Another says: Inside the Son of Heaven's gate, there are double lattice frames,
painted green inside, called suǒ.
Wáng Yǔn said:
"If by the grace of the state altars,
the state above is secured,
that is my wish;
if it is not achieved,
then I will dedicate myself to death.
The court is young,
'The court,'
refers to the Son of Heaven.
To flee from difficulty and seek survival,
I cannot bear it.
Strive to thank the various lords of Guāndōng,
and diligently keep the state in mind!"
Tàicháng Chóng Fú said:
"As a great minister of the state,
if I cannot suppress violence and resist humiliation,
allowing blades to point towards the palace,
where else can I go!"
So he fought and died.
Lí Jué and Guō Sì stationed troops at the southern palace side gate,
killing Grand Coachman Lǔ Kuí,
Grand Herald Zhōu Huàn,
Commandant of the Capital Gates Cuī Liè, and Commandant of the Rapid-as-Tigers Cavalry Wáng Qí.
Over ten thousand officials and commoners died,
their bodies scattered and filling the roads.
Wáng Yǔn helped the Emperor ascend the Xuānpíng Gate to avoid the soldiers.
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states: The gate at the northern end of the eastern wall of Cháng'ān city was named Xuānpíng Gate.
Ascend,
shí zhǎng fān.
The Emperor said to Jué and others:
"You gentlemen have unleashed your soldiers to run rampant,
what do you intend to do?"
Jué and others replied:
"Dǒng Zhuó was loyal to Your Majesty,
yet was killed without cause by Lǚ Bù.
We, your subjects, are avenging Zhuó,
and dare not commit rebellion.
We request that once this matter is concluded, we present ourselves at the Court of the Commandant of Justice to receive punishment."
Jué and others surrounded the gate tower,
jointly petitioning for Minister Over the Masses Wáng Yǔn to come out,
asking
"What crime did the Grand Tutor commit?"
Yǔn, cornered and desperate,
then descended to meet them.
On the Jǐwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the land,
appointing Lǐ Jué as General Who Spreads Martial Might,
and Guō Sì as General Who Spreads Ferocity.
The General Who Spreads Martial Might first appeared at the beginning of the Jiànwǔ era,
with Mǎ Chéng holding the title.
The General Who Spreads Ferocity likely began at this time.
Jué and others arrested the Colonel-Director of Retainers Huáng Wǎn,
and killed
him.
Earlier,
Wáng Yǔn had appointed Sòng Yì of the same commandery as Administrator of the Left of the Capital,
and Wáng Hóng as Administrator of the Right of the Capital.
Yǔn was
from Tàiyuán.
Fearing trouble from these two commanderies,
he first summoned Yì and Hóng.
Hóng sent a messenger to tell Yì:
"Guō Sì and Lǐ Jué, because we two are outside [the capital],
have not yet endangered Lord Wáng.
Endanger,
means to kill.
Tomorrow our entire clans will be exterminated;
what plan should we adopt?"
Yì said:
"Although fortune and calamity are difficult to gauge,
the Emperor's command
is something we cannot avoid!"
Hóng said:
"The righteous troops east of the pass are seething,
wishing to execute Dǒng Zhuó.
Now Zhuó is already dead,
his faction is easy to control.
If we raise troops together to attack Jué and the others,
coordinating with the regions east of the mountains,
this would be a plan to turn calamity into fortune."
Yì did not agree.
Hóng could not act independently,
so they both accepted the summons.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Jué arrested Yǔn along with Yì and Hóng,
and executed them all;
Yǔn's wife and children all died.
Hóng, facing death, cursed:
"Sòng Yì is a petty pedant,
not worth discussing great plans with!"
Xián's commentary states: Shù,
means base and inferior like a servant boy.
No one dared to collect the bodies,
but a former subordinate, the Magistrate of Pínglíng, Zhào Jiǎn of Jīngzhào, abandoned his office to collect and bury them.
Initially,
Yǔn monopolized the credit for campaigning against Zhuó.
Shìsūn Ruì yielded the merit and did not accept a marquisate,
therefore he was able to escape disaster.
Your subject Guāng remarks: The Yìjīng states
"The gentleman who toils with humility will have good fortune in the end."
The Xìcí of the Yìjīng says: To toil yet not boast,
to have merit yet not claim virtue,
is the height of generosity.
This speaks of one who subordinates himself despite his merit.
Virtue speaks of abundance,
ritual speaks of reverence.
Humility
is using utmost reverence to preserve one's position.
Chéng Yí's annotation states: To have toil and yet be able to be humble,
and further require a gentleman to practice it,
having good fortune in the end means auspiciousness.
Delighting in superiority and enjoying victory
is the common sentiment of people.
To be able to be humble in ordinary times
is already rare indeed,
let alone when one has merit and toil worthy of respect!
Even if one knows the goodness of humility,
and strives to practice it,
if a conceited, self-important heart is not forgotten,
then one cannot be constant and enduring.
To desire good fortune in the end is unattainable.
Only the gentleman treads the path of humility and compliance with ease,
therefore enduring without change,
which is what is called having good fortune in the end and being auspicious.
Thereby preserving his person,
can he not be called wise!
9 Jué and the others appointed Jiǎ Xǔ as Administrator of the Left of the Capital,
wishing to enfeoff him as a marquis.
Xǔ said:
"This was a plan to save my life,
what merit is there in it!"
He firmly declined and did not accept.
They also appointed him as Imperial Secretary Deputy.
Xǔ said:
"The Imperial Secretary Deputy
is the leader among officials,
what the world looks up to.
My name carries no usual weight,
it is not something to make people submit."
They then appointed him as Imperial Secretary.
10 Lǚ Bù fled from Wǔguān Pass to Nányáng,
where Yuán Shù treated him with great generosity.
Bù, relying on his having rendered service to the Yuán family,
considered killing Dǒng Zhuó as avenging the Yuán family.
Shù grew wary of him.
Bù felt insecure,
and left to join Zhāng Yáng in Hénèi.
Lǐ Jué and others urgently sought Bù with a reward.
Bù fled again and returned to Yuán Shào.
11 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
former General of the Front Zhào Qiān was appointed Minister Over the Masses.
12 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Grand Commandant Mǎ Mìdī was appointed Grand Tutor,
in charge of the Imperial Secretariat;
in the eighth month,
General of Chariots and Cavalry Huángfǔ Sōng was appointed Grand Commandant.
13 An edict ordered Grand Tutor Mǎ Mìdī and Grand Coachman Zhào Qí, bearing the imperial staff, to pacify and soothe the regions east of the pass.
14 In the ninth month,
Lǐ Jué was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, concurrently Colonel-Director of Retainers, and given the imperial staff;
Guō Sì as General of the Rear,
Fán Chóu as General of the Right,
and Zhāng Jì as General of Agile Cavalry,
all were enfeoffed as marquises.
Jué, Sì, and Chóu managed the court administration.
Guǎn,
is the same as guǎn (to manage).
15 Minister Over the Masses Zhào Qiān was dismissed.
16 On the Jiǎshēn day,
Minister of Works Chúnyú Jiā was appointed Minister Over the Masses,
Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Yáng Biāo was appointed Minister of Works,
in charge of the Imperial Secretariat.
17 Earlier,
when Dǒng Zhuó entered the pass,
he persuaded Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng to join him in plotting against the regions east of the mountains.
Suì and Téng led their multitudes to Cháng'ān.
It happened that Zhuó died.
Lǐ Jué and others appointed Suì as General Who Guards the West,
sending him back to Jīnchéng;
Téng as General Who Conquers the West,
sending him to station at Méi.
The Treatise on Officials of the Jìnshū states: The Four Conquering Generals originated in the Hàn dynasty,
the Four Guarding Generals facilitated pacifying distant regions.
18 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Liú Biǎo, sent an envoy to present tribute.
Biǎo was appointed General Who Guards the South and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéngwǔ.
Chéngwǔ County,
belonged to Shānyáng Commandery in the Former Hàn,
and to Jìyīn Commandery in the Later Hàn.
19 In the twelfth month,
Grand Commandant Huángfǔ Sōng was dismissed.
Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Zhōu Zhōng was appointed Grand Commandant,
participating in charge of the Imperial Secretariat.
20 Cáo Cāo pursued the Yellow Turbans to Jìběi,
and they all surrendered.
He obtained over three hundred thousand soldiers,
and over a million men and women,
selecting the most elite among them,
calling them the Qīngzhōu Troops.
Those who surrendered were the Yellow Turbans of Qīngzhōu,
hence they were called the Qīngzhōu Troops.
5 In the third month,
Yuán Shào was at Bóluò Ford.
According to the *Xù Hàn Zhì*,
west of Jīng County in Ānpíng State there was a ford on the Zhāng River,
named Bóluò Ford.
In Yǐngtáo County of Jùlù Commandery, there was a Bóluò Post Station.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states,
the Zhāng River passes west of the old city of Jùlù County,
where there is an old ford,
called Bóluò Ford.
Together with tens of thousands of men from the Black Mountain bandits such as Yú Dú, they jointly captured Yè City,
killing its Grand Administrator.
Shào then returned and stationed his troops at Chìqiū.
Chìqiū County,
belonged to Jùlù Commandery.
Xián states: The old city is southeast of present-day Chéng'ān County in Xiàng Prefecture.
The *Shísānzhōu Zhì* says: The land is saline and alkaline,
hence the name Chìqiū (Saline Hill).
6 In summer,
Cáo Cāo led his army back to Dìngtáo.
7 Wáng Lǎng, the Administrative Clerk of Xú Province from Dōnghǎi, and Zhào Yù, the Assistant Officer from Lángyá, advised Inspector Táo Qiān, saying:
"To seek the support of the feudal lords, nothing is better than diligently serving the king,"
words of the Jìn minister Hú Yǎn from the *Zuǒzhuàn*.
Shuì,
pronounced shuì, with the ruì tone.
"We should send an envoy to present tribute."
Qiān then sent Yù to present a memorial to Cháng'ān.
An edict appointed Qiān as Governor of Xú Province,
additionally conferring the title of General Who Pacifies the East,
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Lìyáng.
Lìyáng County belonged to Dānyáng Commandery.
Lǎng was appointed Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
At that time,
the common people of Xú were prosperous and numerous,
ancient speech often referred to provinces as "fāng,"
hence the eight regional chiefs of the eight provinces were called "fāngbó."
The *Shū* says
"Only this Táng of Táo,
possessed this Jìfāng,"
the *Shī* says
"Xúfāng does not submit to court"
are examples.
Many displaced people returned there.
However, Qiān trusted and employed slanderous and wicked men,
alienated loyal and upright ones,
penal administration was not well-governed,
thus Xú Province gradually fell into disorder.
Xǔ Shào took refuge in Guǎnglíng,
Qiān treated him with great courtesy and generosity,
Shào told his followers:
"Táo Gōngzǔ outwardly admires reputation,
but inwardly is not truly sincere,
Táo Qiān,
styled Gōngzǔ.
His situation will inevitably decline."
He then left.
Later, Qiān indeed arrested various resident scholars,
and people then admired Shào's foresight.
8 In the sixth month,
in Fúfēng, there was heavy hail.
9 Huà Mountain collapsed and split.
10 Grand Commandant Zhōu Zhōng was dismissed,
and Grand Coachman Zhū Jùn was appointed Grand Commandant,
overseeing the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
11 Quē Xuān of Xiàpī gathered several thousand followers,
Xián states: The *Fēngsútōng* says: Quē,
is a surname,
descended from the child of Quēdǎng;
among the School of Diplomats, there was a Master Quē who wrote books.
Táo Qiān attacked and killed him.
*Kǎoyì* states: The biography of Qiān in Fàn's history writes
"Yán Xuān."
Here we follow the *Wèi Zhì*'s Annals of Emperor Wu and the biography of Qiān.
The Annals of Emperor Wu of Wei further states:
"Qiān and Xuān jointly raised troops,
captured Huà and Fèi in Tàishān,
and plundered Rénchéng."
Qiān's biography also says:
"Qiān initially allied with him,
but later killed him,
and absorbed his followers."
Considering that Qiān held Xú Province,
claiming righteousness in diligently serving the king,
why would he need Xuān's several thousand followers to ally with him!
Probably a separate general under Qiān joined Xuān in jointly attacking Cáo Sōng,
hence Cáo Cāo used this as Qiān's crime to attack him.
12 Heavy rain,
lasting over twenty days and nights,
flooded and destroyed people's homes.
13 Yuán Shào led his army into Cháogē Lùcháng Mountain,
Cháogē County,
belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
Xián states: The old city of Cháogē is west of present-day Wèi County.
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* says: Cháogē has Lùcháng Mountain.
They besieged and attacked for five days,
broke through,
and beheaded Dú and over ten thousand of his men.
Shào then followed the mountains northward,
attacked various bandits such as Zuǒzī Zhàngbā,
and beheaded them all.
He also attacked Liú Shí, Qīngniújiǎo, Huánglóng Zuǒxiào, Guō Dàxián, Lǐ Dàmù, Yú Dīgēn, and others,
again beheading tens of thousands,
and slaughtered their encampments and fortifications.
He then fought against the Black Mountain bandit Zhāng Yàn, along with the Four Garrisons of the Tuge and the Wūhuán of Yànmén, in Chángshān.
Yàn had tens of thousands of elite troops,
and several thousand cavalry horses.
Shào and Lǚ Bù jointly attacked Yàn,
fighting continuously for over ten days,
although Yàn's troops suffered many casualties,
Shào's army was also exhausted,
so both sides withdrew.
Lǚ Bù's officers and soldiers were often violent and tyrannical,
which troubled Shào,
so Bù requested to return to Luòyáng.
Shào, acting under imperial authority, appointed Bù as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
and sent strong men to escort Bù,
but secretly plotted against him.
Bù had someone play the zheng within his tent,
the *Shuōwén* states: Zheng,
is a musical instrument,
with strings plucked on a bamboo body.
It has thirteen strings,
created by Méng Tián.
Another theory: The people of Qín were lacking in righteousness,
a father and son fought over a se and split it,
hence it got its name.
According to this, the zheng's construction is similar to the se,
the se has twenty-five strings while the zheng has thirteen,
hence the explanation.
The *Fēngsútōng*: Zheng,
is a Qín instrument,
with five strings and a body like a zhù.
The zheng,
has a round top symbolizing heaven,
a flat bottom symbolizing earth,
hollow in the middle representing the six directions,
with twelve string pillars representing the twelve months,
thus it is an instrument of benevolence and wisdom.
Nowadays in Bīng and Liáng provinces, the zheng's shape resembles a se,
it is unknown who changed it.
The *Shìmíng*: Zheng,
has strings set high,
producing a "zheng zheng" sound,
pronounced zhēng.
The escorts arose at night,
and hacked at the tent and bedding, destroying them.
The next morning,
when Shào heard that Bù was still alive,
he was afraid,
and closed the city gates to defend himself.
Bù led his army back to Zhāng Yáng.
14 The former Grand Commandant Cáo Sōng was taking refuge in Lángyá,
his son Cáo Cāo ordered the Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Yìng Shào, to welcome him.
Sōng had over a hundred carts of baggage,
a separate general of Táo Qiān was guarding Yīnpíng,
Yīnpíng County,
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Xián states: The old city is southwest of present-day Chéng County in Yí Prefecture.
They ambushed Sōng between Huà and Fèi,
killing him.
According to the *Qián Hàn Zhì*,
both Huà and Fèi counties belonged to Tàishān Commandery.
The *Xù Hàn Zhì*
lists Fèi County in Tàishān,
but not Huà County,
probably it was merged or abolished.
The *Shuǐjīng*: The Shí River flows south past the east of Huà County,
then further south past the east of Fèi County,
entering the Yí River.
Xián states: The old city of Fèi County,
is northeast of Fèi County.
Fèi,
pronounced bì.
Cāo led troops to attack Qiān,
captured over ten cities,
reached Péngchéng,
fought a major battle,
Qiān's troops were defeated,
and he fled to defend Tán.
Tán County,
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery,
the seat of the Inspector of Xú Province.
Initially,
when the capital and Luòyáng suffered the turmoil of Dǒng Zhuó,
the people fled eastward,
many relying on Xú territory,
encountering Cāo's arrival,
he buried alive hundreds of thousands of men and women in the Sì River,
so that the water ceased to flow.
Cáo Cāo attacked Tán but could not capture it,
so he left,
attacking and taking Qǔlǜ, Suīlíng, and Xiàqiū,
all three counties belonging to the Xiàpī Kingdom.
Dù Yòu said: North of Xiàpī County in Sìzhōu is the old city of Hàn Wǔyuán,
and further north is the old city of Tán County.
The old city of Suīlíng is southeast of Xiàpī.
Xiàqiū,
where Yáo enfeoffed Yǔ as the Earl of Xià,
had its capital here,
and in Hàn times it was Xiàqiū County.
Shī Gǔ said: Qǔ
is pronounced qū,
also pronounced qiū.
Lǜ
is pronounced lú.
Suī
is pronounced suī.
Xià
is pronounced with the reading hù yǎ fān.
Even chickens and dogs were exhausted,
and the ruined settlements had no more passersby.
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnchǒu day,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
16 A comet appeared in Tiānshì.
17 Minister of Works Yáng Biāo was dismissed.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Grand Minister of Ceremonies Zhào Wēn was appointed Minister of Works,
overseeing the Department of State Affairs.
18 Liú Yú and Gōngsūn Zàn had long been at odds,
and Zàn repeatedly attacked Yuán Shào.
Yú tried to stop him,
but to no avail,
so he gradually reduced his provisions and allowances.
Zàn was angered,
frequently disobeyed orders,
and again encroached upon the people.
Yú could not control him,
so he sent a courier to submit a memorial detailing Zàn's violent plundering crimes.
Zàn also reported that Yú had failed to provide adequate grain supplies.
The two memorials raced back and forth,
each denouncing the other,
and the court merely vacillated.
Vacillating means
that when A's memorial arrived, they sided with A and opposed B,
and when B's memorial arrived, they sided with B and opposed A,
with no clear right or wrong.
Jì County,
belonging to Guǎngyáng Kingdom,
was the seat of the Governor of Yōuzhōu.
Jì
is pronounced jì.
Zàn then feigned illness and did not respond;
Yú feared he would eventually rebel,
so he led his own troops, totaling one hundred thousand, to attack him.
At the time, Zàn's troops were scattered outside,
and in haste he dug at the eastern wall intending to flee.
Cù
is the same as cù.
Yú's troops were inexperienced in battle,
and he also cared for the people's homes,
ordering them not to be burned,
and instructing his soldiers:
"Do not harm others,
only kill Bóguī."
Gōngsūn Zàn,
styled Bóguī.
Zàn then selected several hundred elite soldiers,
took advantage of the wind to set fires,
and charged straight through them,
causing Yú's forces to collapse.
Yú and his officials fled north to Jūyōng,
Jūyōng County,
belonging to Shànggǔ Commandery.
Hú Qiáo said: From the northwest of Yōuzhōu, one enters Jūyōng Pass.
Sòng Qí said: Fifty lǐ southeast of Huáiróng County in Táng Guīzhōu is Jūyōng Fortress,
connecting east to Lúlóng and Jiéshí,
and west to Tàiháng and Chángshān,
truly a strategic stronghold of the realm.
After three days,
the city fell,
and Zàn captured Yú along with his wife and children and brought them back to Jì,
still allowing him to handle the administrative documents of the province.
Just then, an edict sent the envoy Duàn Xùn to increase Yú's fief,
overseeing the affairs of six provinces;
appointing Zàn as General of the Vanguard,
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Yì.
Yì County,
in Former Hàn belonged to Zhuō Commandery,
and was abolished in Later Hàn.
He forced Xùn to execute Yú and his wife and children in the Jì market.
Former Chángshān Chancellor Sūn Jǐn, Attendants Zhāng Yì, and Zhāng Zàn, among others, gathered around Yú,
cursing Zàn vehemently,
and then died together.
Zàn sent Yú's head to the capital,
but Yú's former subordinate Wěi Dūn intercepted it on the road,
and returned it for burial.
Xián said: Wěi
is the surname;
Dūn
is the given name.
I note that in ancient times there was a Wěi Shēng.
The people of the northern provinces, both newcomers and old residents, all deeply mourned.
Newcomers
were those who had migrated to Yōuzhōu from other provinces;
old residents
were those long registered in Yōuzhōu.
Earlier,
Yú wanted to send an envoy to submit a memorial to Cháng'ān,
but found it difficult to choose a person,
and everyone said:
"Tián Chóu of Yòuběipíng,
twenty-two years old,
though young,
possesses extraordinary talent."
Yú then prepared the ceremony,
and invited him to serve as an attendant.
Carriages and horses were readied for the journey,
but Chóu said:
"Now the roads are blocked,
and bandits and enemies roam freely.
To travel officially as an envoy
would draw attention.
I wish to travel privately,
hoping only to reach the destination."
Yú agreed.
Chóu then selected twenty horsemen from his household retainers,
together went up to the Western Pass,
exited the frontier,
skirted the northern mountains,
headed straight for Shuòfāng,
and followed back roads to Cháng'ān to deliver the message.
An edict appointed Chóu as Cavalry Commandant.
Chóu felt that as the Son of Heaven was in exile and unsettled,
he could not bear the honor and glory,
and firmly declined.
Upon receiving the reply,
he galloped back,
but by the time he arrived,
Yú was already dead.
Chóu paid respects at Yú's tomb,
presented and read the memorial,
the memorial,
which should, according to the following text, be the memorial reply.
Gōngsūn Zàn was angered,
sought and captured Chóu,
and said to him:
"Why did you not deliver the memorial reply to me?"
Chóu replied:
"The Hàn house is in decline,
and people harbor disloyal thoughts,
only Lord Liú remained faithful.
What the memorial reply said
was not favorable to you, General,
and I feared you would not be pleased to hear it,
so I did not present it.
Moreover, General, you have already destroyed an innocent lord,
and now oppose a righteous minister.
I fear the gentlemen of Yān and Zhào will all leap into the Eastern Sea to their deaths,
and none will follow you, General."
Zàn then released him.
When Lü Bù left Yuán Shào to join Zhāng Yáng,
(this event is recorded in the previous volume of the previous year.)
at their parting,
they clasped hands and swore an oath together;
Shào heard of this,
and greatly resented Miǎo, fearing that Cáo would ultimately kill him on Shào's behalf,
and felt uneasy in his heart.
The former Governor of Jiǔjiāng, Biān Ràng of Chénliú, had once criticized and mocked Cáo,
Cáo heard of it and killed him,
along with his wife and children.
Ràng had always been renowned for his talent,
and because of this, the scholar-officials of Yǎnzhōu were all terrified.
Chén Gōng was by nature upright, resolute, and fervent,
and inwardly he also harbored suspicions,
so he conspired with the Attendant Officer Xǔ Fàn, Wáng Kǎi, and Miǎo's younger brother Chāo to rebel against Cáo.
Gōng persuaded Miǎo, saying:
"Now the empire is divided and in chaos,
heroes and champions are rising together,
with your forces spanning a thousand *li*,
holding a land contested on all sides,
if you grasp your sword and survey the scene,
you are fully capable of becoming a leader among men,
yet instead you are controlled by others,
is that not shameful!
Now the provincial army is campaigning eastward,
(referring to Cáo's troops attacking Xúzhōu.)
Lü Bù is a mighty warrior,
skilled in battle and unmatched,
if we temporarily welcome him,
and jointly govern Yǎnzhōu,
observe the situation of the empire,
and await changes in the times,
this would also be an opportunity to maneuver freely."
Miǎo agreed with him.
At that time, Cáo had ordered Gōng to lead troops and remain stationed in Dōngjùn,

"Act so pointlessly"
means to behave like this.
"Benevolence and righteousness are not fixed constants;
those who tread their path are gentlemen,
those who turn their backs are petty men.
Today, I would rather die on the same day as Zāng Hóng
than live on the same day as you, General!"
Subsequently, he too was killed.
None among those present failed to sigh in lament,
whispering to each other:
"How can two righteous martyrs be killed in a single day!"
15 After Gōngsūn Zàn killed Liú Yú,
(events seen in the fourth year of the Chūpíng era in the previous scroll).
his ambition and spirit grew even more vigorous.
Relying on his talent and strength,
he showed no compassion for the common people,
recording faults while forgetting virtues,
and avenging even the slightest grievance.
Among the refined scholars and gentlemen,
those whose reputations surpassed his
he would invariably harm through legal means.
Those with outstanding talent

Someone asked him the reason,
and Zàn said:
"These gentlemen all consider it their due right to be noble,

Therefore, those he favored and loved

Wherever they went, they encroached and tyrannized,

Liú Yú's attendant from Yúyáng, Xiānyú Fǔ, and others,

is a branch of the Zǐ surname.

considering that Yánguó's Yán Róu had always been known for kindness and trustworthiness,

is pronounced Yúxián.

Thereupon, the commanderies of Dàijùn, Guǎngyáng, Shànggǔ, and Yòuběipíng each killed the chief officials appointed by Zàn,
and again joined forces with Xiānyú Fǔ and Liú Hé's troops.
Zàn's army suffered repeated defeats.
Previously, there had been a children's rhyme:

Continued Hàn Records states: It belonged to Héjiān.

same below.

He used iron for the gates,

He distanced himself from guests,

His strategists and fierce generals

From then on,

Someone asked him the reason.
Zàn said:

(events seen in the fifth year of the Língdì Zhōngpíng era in scroll fifty-nine).

Observing this,

According to military strategy,

is the character for lǔ,
