Xiàoxiàn Emperor Dīng
First Year of Jiàn'ān
(Bǐngzǐ, 196)
1 Spring,
first month,
Guǐyǒu day,
a great amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
2 Dǒng Chéng and Zhāng Yáng wanted to return the Son of Heaven to Luòyáng,
but Yáng Fèng and Lǐ Lè did not wish to,
causing the various generals to become increasingly suspicious and divided.
Second month,
Hán Xiān attacked Dǒng Chéng,
and Chéng fled to Yěwáng.
(Yěwáng
was where Zhāng Yáng was stationed.)
Xiān
is pronounced xīliánfān.
Hú Cái and Yáng Fèng went to Wùxiāng.
(Commandery and State Records: Southwest of Gōushì County in Hénán was the Wù settlement.)
The Emperor sent someone to persuade them to stop.
3 The Huángjīn rebels Hé Yí and others from Rǔnán and Yǐngchuān, with their followers, submitted to Yuán Shù,
but Cáo Cāo defeated them.
4 Zhāng Yáng sent Dǒng Chéng ahead to repair the Luòyáng palace.
The Grand Coachman Zhào Qí persuaded Liú Biǎo on behalf of Chéng,
causing him to send troops to Luòyáng
to assist in repairing the palace buildings.
Military supplies and provisions
were sent continuously.
Summer,
fifth month,
Bǐngyín day,
the Emperor sent an envoy to the camps of Yáng Fèng, Lǐ Lè, and Hán Xiān,
requesting to be escorted to Luòyáng,
and Fèng and others complied with the edict.
Sixth month, Yǐwèi day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Wénxǐ.
5. Yuán Shù attacked Liú Bèi to contend for Xúzhōu.
Bèi sent his Military Marshal Zhāng Fēi to guard Xiàpī,
while he personally led troops to resist Shù at Xūyí and Huáiyīn.
(Commentary from the Treatise on Commanderies and States: Xūyí and Huáiyīn were two counties belonging to the Principality of Xiàpī.)
(Note on pronunciation: Xūyí is pronounced xū yí.)
The battles had mixed outcomes.
The Chancellor of Xiàpī, Cáo Bào,
a former general under Táo Qiān,
had a falling out with Zhāng Fēi.
Fēi killed him,
causing turmoil within the city.
Yuán Shù sent a letter to Lǚ Bù,
urging him to attack Xiàpī,
promising to supply him with military provisions.
Bù was greatly pleased,
and led his army eastward by both land and water.
(Bù had fled to Bèi the previous year,
and was likely stationed west of Xiàpī.)
Zhāng Fēi was defeated and fled.
Bù captured Bèi's wife, children, and the families of his officers and officials.
When Bèi heard this,
he turned his army back.
By the time he reached Xiàpī,
his troops had disintegrated.
Bèi gathered his remaining soldiers and went east to capture Guǎnglíng,
fought Yuán Shù,
and was defeated again.
He then stationed his troops at Hǎixī.
(According to the Treatise of the Former Hàn,
Hǎixī County
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery;
according to the Treatise of the Later Hàn,
it belonged to Guǎnglíng Commandery.)
(Textual analysis note: The biography of Liú Bèi in the Records of Shǔ states here,
"Yáng Fèng and Hán Xiān invaded the area between Xú and Yáng,
Bèi intercepted and attacked them,
and beheaded them all."
However, Xiān and Fèng later joined Lǚ Bù in defeating Yuán Shù,
so they were not dead at this time;
therefore, the biography of Bèi is mistaken.)
(Bèi's) officers and soldiers resorted to cannibalism.
His Assistant Clerk Mí Zhú of Dōnghǎi used his family wealth to aid the army.
Bèi requested to surrender to Bù.
Bù was also resentful that Yuán Shù's grain shipments were not arriving as promised,
so he summoned Bèi,
reinstated him as Governor of Yùzhōu,
and joined forces with him to attack Shù,
stationing him at Xiǎopèi.
(Commentary by Lǐ Xián: Gāozǔ (Liú Bāng) was originally a man of Péi County in Sìshuǐ Commandery.
After gaining the empire,
he changed Sìshuǐ to Péi Commandery.
Xiǎopèi refers to Péi County.)
(Sòng Bái said: The Treatise on Commanderies and States states: It was the ancient state of Bīyáng.
In Hàn times it was Péi County.
The seat of Péi Commandery was at Xiàngchéng,
so Péi County was called Xiǎopèi.)
(Textual analysis note: Bèi's biography states:
"He sent Guān Yǔ to guard Xiàpī."
This occurred after Bù's defeat;
therefore, Bèi's biography is mistaken.)
Bù's general, Hǎo Méng from Hénèi, attacked Bù at night.
Bù, bare-headed and with his clothes disheveled,
fled to the camp of his Commander Gāo Shùn.
("Bare-headed"
means not wearing a cap, exposing the hair knot.)
(People in Jiāngdōng still refer to exposing the hair knot as "bare-headed.")
Méng was defeated and fled.
By dawn,
Méng's subordinate Cáo Xìng attacked and killed Méng.
6. On the gēngzǐ day,
Yáng Fèng and Hán Xiān escorted the Emperor eastward back (to Luòyáng).
Zhāng Yáng supplied provisions along the road.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Luòyáng,
and the Emperor stayed at the former residence of the Palace Attendant Zhào Zhōng.
On the dīngchǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared.
In the eighth month,
on the xīnchǒu day,
the Emperor visited the Yáng'ān Hall in the Southern Palace.
Zhāng Yáng considered this his own achievement,
hence he named the hall "Yáng'ān."
Yáng said to the various generals:
"The Son of Heaven should be shared with all under heaven.
The court has its own high ministers and senior officials.
I, Yáng, should go out to defend against external threats."
He then returned to Yěwáng.
Yáng Fèng also went out to station his troops at Liáng.
(Commentary from the Treatise on Commanderies and States: Liáng County
belonged to the Governor of Hénán,
and was the state of Liáng in the Spring and Autumn period.)
On the guǐmǎo day,
(the court) appointed General of Pacifying the State Zhāng Yáng as Grand Marshal,
Yáng Fèng as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and Hán Xiān as Grand General and concurrently Colonel-Director of Retainers,
all were granted the symbols of authority (the tally and battle-axe).
At this time,
the palace buildings were completely burned down.
The hundred officials made their way through brambles and thorns,
sheltering among broken walls.
The various provinces and commanderies each held strong military forces,
and no tribute or supplies were sent to the court.
The officials were hungry and destitute.
Officials of the rank of Secretary Gentleman and below had to go out themselves to gather wild grain.
(Commentary from the Treatise of the Later Hàn: There were thirty-six Secretaries' Gentlemen,
with a salary of four hundred shi.)
(The original note states: Each bureau had six men,
responsible for drafting documents.)
(Cài Zhì's Hàn Ceremonial states: A Secretary Gentleman, upon first being selected from the Three Bureaus to take the examination at the Secretariat,
is initially called a Probationary Secretary Gentleman,
after a full year is called a Secretary Gentleman,
and after three years is called a Gentleman Attendant.)
(Lǐ Xián's note: The character for "wild grain" is pronounced lǚ.)
(The Pi Cāng dictionary says: "Lǚ" means self-sown/growing wild.)
(The character variant used here is equivalent to "lǚ".)
Some were killed by soldiers.

"The one who will replace Hàn is 'Dāngtúgāo'",

(Lǐ Xián's note:
"Dāngtúgāo"
refers to
Wèi.

He heard that Sūn Jiān had obtained the Imperial Seal,

His Registrar, Yán Xiàng, came forward and said:
"In the past, Zhōu, from Hòujì down to King Wén,

(Our situation) is not as flourishing as that of Zhōu;

Shù fell silent.
Shù invited the Recluse Scholar Zhāng Fàn;

Shù said to Chéng:

Chéng replied:
"It depends on virtue, not on strength.
Using virtue to align with the desires of all under heaven,

But if one merely presumes to usurp and emulate,

Who can then raise him up!"
Shù was displeased.
Sūn Cè heard of this and
wrote to Yuán Shù, saying:
"When King Tāng of Shāng attacked King Jié of Xià, he declared, 'The Xià have many crimes,'

Xià,
read as hù yǎ.

Even with sagely virtue,
if the times were not marked by the fault of losing the Way,

Now, the sovereign has not brought evil upon the world;

Moreover, Dǒng Zhuó was greedy, licentious, arrogant, and oppressive,

Yet even he had not gone so far,

How much more so for those who imitate his wrongdoings and exceed them!
The Zuǒzhuàn says: 'To imitate wrongdoing,

If one possesses long-cultivated virtue,
sù,
meaning early.
all will turn their hearts to him.
Your Lordship's family has served as ministers for five generations.

Jīng begot Yáng,
Yáng begot Féng,
Féng begot Shù,
totaling five generations.
Bèi,
read as pí yì.
The abundance of glory and favor you have received

You should demonstrate loyalty and uphold integrity

Then, the praise due to Dàn and Shì
is what all under heaven expect of you.
Many people of the time are misled by prophecies and apocryphal texts,
recklessly citing irrelevant writings,
merely to please their lords as a virtue,
without considering plans for success or failure.
This is something cautioned against in both ancient and modern times.
Should you not consider it thoroughly!
Shú,
interchangeable with shú (thorough).
The Qiánshū records: Zhāng Liáng said: 'Loyal words offend the ear,
but benefit conduct.'
Xián notes: Bó,
means mixed,
differing opinions;
meaning that holding dissenting views leads to hatred and resentment.
Bó,
read as běi jiǎo.
I dare not decline."
Yuán Shù initially believed that with the masses of Huáinán under his control,
he assumed Sūn Cè would surely align with him.
But upon receiving this letter,
he grew distressed, despondent, and fell ill.
Since he did not accept the advice,
Sūn Cè then severed ties with him.
8 Cáo Cāo was in Xǔ.

"Shāndōng is not yet pacified;

Xún Yù said:

Wéi,
read as yú wèi.
Méng,
means to brave,
referring to living in exile among the wild grasses,

Now, the imperial carriage has turned its wheels back.

is the horizontal wood at the back of a carriage.

If we take this opportunity

upholding utmost impartiality to win over the world,

supporting grand righteousness to attract heroes,

Cáo Cāo then sent General of the Household for Rapid as Tigers Cáo Hóng to lead troops westward to welcome the emperor.

Here, we follow the biography.
Court Gentleman for Consultation Dǒng Zhāo,

Now, the General has rescued the Son of Heaven from hardship,

Your supporting merit
surpasses all in this age, without equal.
How splendid it is!
Currently, numerous villains disrupt Xià.

means to disturb.
Xià,
refers to Huáxià.
Xià,
read as hù yǎ.

here it likely refers to death
and life,

Qì,

pronounced as cuó.

Hán Xiān, proud of his achievements, acted arbitrarily and willfully.
Dǒng Chéng was troubled by this,

On the Xīnhài day,
Cáo Cāo was appointed as Colonel-Director of Retainers and placed in charge of the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.

Yuán Hóng’s Annals states: He executed Shuò, as well as the Court Counselor Hóu Qí and the Palace Attendant Hú Chóng.

Hóng’s Annals states: He enfeoffed General of the Guards Dǒng Chéng, General Who Supports the State Fú Wán, Palace Attendant Dīng □, and Zhǒng Fǔ.
He posthumously honored Colonel of the Rapid as Tigers Jǔ Jùn as the Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng,
to honor those who died for their principles.
Jǔ Jùn died,
as recorded in the second year of the Xīngpíng era in the previous volume.
Jǔ,
pronounced Zǐyú.
Cáo Cāo invited Dǒng Zhāo to sit beside him
and asked:
“Now that I have come here,
what strategy should I employ?”
Zhāo replied:
“You, General, raised righteous troops to eliminate violence and chaos,
entered the court to serve the Son of Heaven,
and supported the royal house.
This is the achievement of the Five Hegemons.
The various generals below,
each with different intentions,
may not necessarily submit.
To remain here to assist and support
would be inconvenient given the circumstances.
The only option is to move the imperial carriage to Xǔ.
However, the court has been wandering and displaced,
and has only recently returned to the old capital.
People near and far are eagerly watching,
hoping for peace and stability.
To move the carriage again now
may not satisfy the hearts of the masses.

Moreover, Huàn serving General Liú in the past,
is like serving you today,
if one day I leave here,
and again insult you,
would that be acceptable?"
Bù felt ashamed and stopped.
16 Zhāng Jì led troops from Guānzhōng into Jīngzhōu territory,
attacked Rǎng city,
Rǎng county,
belonged to Nányáng commandery.
Jīngzhōu officials all congratulated,
Liú Biǎo said:
"Jì came in distress,
the host showed no courtesy,
meaning no courtesy of welcoming and lodging.
This is not the governor's intent,
the governor receives condolences,
not congratulations."
Sent someone to accept his troops;
the troops heard this and were pleased,
all turned their hearts to him.
Jì's nephew Jiànzhōng General Xiù took over leading his troops,
stationed at Wǎn.
Initially,
after the Emperor left Cháng'ān,
General of Manifested Might Jiǎ Xǔ returned his official seal and ribbons,
and went to rely on Duàn Wēi at Huàyīn.
Xǔ had long been well-known,
and was highly regarded by Wēi's army.
Wēi treated him with great respect and provided for him generously.
Xǔ secretly planned to join Zhāng Xiù.
Someone said:
"Wēi treats you so well,
why are you leaving?"
Xǔ said:
"Wēi is by nature suspicious,
and harbors jealousy toward me.
Although his treatment is generous,
it cannot be relied upon for long,
and I will eventually be plotted against.
Since I am highly regarded by Wēi's army,
I will inevitably be envied by Wēi.
If I stay long, Wēi will fear that I will seize his army,
and will certainly plot to kill me.
Moreover, he hopes that I will secure strong external support for him,
so he will surely treat my wife and children well.
Xiù lacks a chief strategist,
and also wishes to have me: thus, both my family and myself will be preserved."
Xǔ then went,
and Xiù treated him with the respect due to a father or grandfather.
Wēi indeed treated his family well.
Xǔ persuaded Xiù to ally with Liú Biǎo,
and Xiù agreed.
Xǔ went to see Biǎo,
and Biǎo treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
Xǔ said:
"Biǎo
has the talent to be one of the Three Excellencies in peaceful times,
but he fails to recognize changing circumstances,
is overly suspicious and indecisive,
and is incapable of great achievements!"
Liú Biǎo loved the people and nurtured scholars,
maintaining his position with ease and self-preservation.
Within his territory, there was no unrest.
Scholars from Guānxī, Yǎn, and Yù who came to join him numbered in the thousands.
Biǎo then established schools,
where classical studies were taught and elucidated.
He ordered the former Master of Ceremonial Music, Dù Kuí from Hénán, to compose ceremonial music.
Cài Yōng said: Han music has four categories: first, the Tàiyǔ Music,
used for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, and imperial tombs;
second, the Zhōusòng Ceremonial Music,
used for the Imperial Academy, banquets, archery ceremonies, and sacrifices to the six deities and the gods of soil and grain;
third, the Huángmén Drum and Wind Music,
used by the Son of Heaven to entertain his ministers;
fourth, the Short Flute and Cymbal Songs,
which are military music.
Biǎo wanted to have it performed in his court.
Kuí said:
"Now, General, your title is not that of the Son of Heaven.
To have ceremonial music performed in your court—
is that not inappropriate?"
Biǎo then stopped.
Mí Héng from Píngyuán
was talented and eloquent from a young age,
but he was arrogant and prone to anger.
Kǒng Róng recommended him to Cáo Cāo.
Héng insulted and humiliated Cāo,
so Cāo summoned Héng to serve as a drum officer,
intentionally provoking Héng's insults.
Cāo said to Róng:
"That brat Mí Héng—
if I kill him,
it would be like killing a sparrow or a rat!
However, this man has long had a false reputation,
and people near and far would say that I cannot tolerate him."
So he sent him to Liú Biǎo.
Biǎo received him with courtesy and treated him as an honored guest.
Héng praised Biǎo effusively,
but enjoyed mocking and belittling those around him.
As a result, those around him seized the opportunity to slander him, saying:
"Héng says that your benevolence, General,
surpasses even that of King Wén of Zhōu,
but he believes you are indecisive,
and that you will ultimately fail—
surely because of this."
These words actually pointed out Biǎo's weakness,
but they were not what Héng had said.
Biǎo became angry because of this,
and knowing that Huáng Zǔ, the Governor of Jiāngxià, was hot-tempered,
he sent Héng to him.
Zǔ also treated him well.
Later, Héng publicly humiliated Zǔ,
and Zǔ killed him.
Cāo was angry with Héng but sent him to Biǎo,
still thinking that Biǎo was tolerant, gentle, and fond of scholars,
to see whether he could tolerate him or not.
Biǎo was angry with Héng but sent him to Zǔ,
knowing that Zǔ was hot-tempered
and would certainly not tolerate Héng.
This was simply to put him in a deadly situation.
Both men employed schemes and tactics,
but Biǎo's were shallow.
In the spring,
the first month,
Cáo Cāo attacked Zhāng Xiù,
stationing his army at the Yù River.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Yù River originates from Gōnglí Mountain in Lúshì County, Hóngnóng,
flows east past the south of Wǎn County,
where Cāo's army was defeated.
Yù
is pronounced "yù."
Cāo took Zhāng Jì's wife as his concubine,
and Xiù resented this.
Cāo also gave gold to Xiù's valiant general Hú Chē'ér,
and Xiù, hearing of this, grew suspicious and fearful.
He launched a surprise attack on Cāo's army,
killing Cāo's eldest son, Áng.
Cāo was hit by a stray arrow,
fled in defeat,
and Commandant Diǎn Wéi fought fiercely against Xiù.
Those around him were almost all dead or wounded,
and Wéi suffered dozens of wounds.
Xiù's soldiers advanced to seize him,
but Wéi grabbed two men and killed them,
glaring and cursing loudly before he died.
Cāo gathered his scattered troops,
and retreated to Wǔyīn.
Wǔyīn County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Cāo attacked and defeated them,
and Xiù fled back to Ráng,
once again allying with Liú Biǎo.
At this time,
the various armies were in great disorder,
but Commandant for Pacifying the Caitiffs Yú Jìn from Tàishān alone rallied his troops and returned in good order.
On the way, he encountered Qīngzhōu troops plundering the people,
and Jìn enumerated their crimes and attacked them.
The Qīngzhōu troops fled
and went to report to Cāo.
After Jìn arrived,
he first established his camp and fortifications,
and did not immediately go to see Cāo.
Someone said to Jìn:
"The Qīngzhōu troops have already accused you.
You should hurry to see the Duke and explain yourself."
Jìn said:
"Now the enemy is behind us,
and they could catch up at any time.
If we do not prepare first,
how can we face the enemy?
Moreover, the Duke is wise,
so how could slander succeed?"
He slowly dug trenches and secured the camp,
and only then went to see Cāo,
explaining the situation in detail.
Cāo was pleased,
and said to Jìn:
"During the disaster at the Yù River,
I was in a desperate situation.
Yet you, General, maintained order amidst chaos,
punished the violent and fortified your camp."
Punishing the violent
refers to attacking the plunderers.
Fortifying the camp
refers to digging trenches and securing the camp first.
Even among ancient famous generals,
who could surpass you?"
Thereupon, he recorded Jìn's merits from before and after,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yìshòu Village.
Cāo led his army back to Xǔ.
2. Yuán Shào sent a letter to Cáo Cāo,
its wording arrogant and disrespectful.
Cáo Cāo said to Xún Yù and Guō Jiā:
"Now I intend to campaign against the unjust, yet my strength is no match for his.
What should be done?"
They replied:
"That Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ were mismatched,
is something you, my lord, know well.
The Han Founder relied solely on wisdom to overcome Xiàng Yǔ.
Therefore, although Yǔ was strong,
he was ultimately captured.
Now, Shào has ten points of defeat,
and you, my lord, have ten points of victory.
Although Shào is strong,
he can accomplish nothing.
Shào is entangled in elaborate rites and excessive ceremony;
you, my lord, embody and follow what is natural.
This is victory in the Way.
Shào acts in rebellion,
while you, my lord, uphold what is proper to lead the realm.
This means upholding the Son of Heaven to lead the realm,
which is proper in principle.
Since the reigns of Emperors Huán and Líng,
governance has erred on the side of laxity.
Shào uses laxity to remedy laxity,
therefore he cannot consolidate control.
'Consolidate'
means to bring order.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: 'The record of the campaign against Qín
shows consolidation.'
Dù Yù's commentary states: 'Able to consolidate and order himself.'
Both superiors and inferiors know the regulations.
This is victory in governance.
Shào is outwardly lenient but inwardly suspicious,
employing men yet doubting them.
Those he appoints are only his relatives and their sons.
You, my lord, are outwardly simple and easy-going but inwardly perceptive and discerning.
You employ men without suspicion,
appointing solely based on suitability of talent,
without distinction between those close or distant.
This is victory in judgment.
Shào has many plans but little decisiveness,
failing by acting too late.
You, my lord, implement a strategy as soon as you obtain it,
adapting to change inexhaustibly.
This is victory in planning.
Shào engages in lofty debates and ceremonial courtesies to garner reputation.
Scholars fond of empty talk and outward show mostly flock to him.
You, my lord, treat others with utmost sincerity,
not engaging in empty praise.
Scholars who are loyal, upright, far-sighted, and substantial all wish to serve you.
This is victory in virtue.
When Shào sees people suffering from hunger and cold,
he pities and thinks of them,
his concern showing on his face.
But for what he does not see,
his consideration may not reach.
You, my lord, regarding minor matters before your eyes,
sometimes overlook them.
But when it comes to major affairs,
connecting with the whole realm,
the grace you bestow
always exceeds expectations.
Even for what you do not see,
your consideration leaves nothing unaddressed.
This is victory in benevolence.
Among Shào's high officials, they contend for power,
and slanderous words cause confusion and disorder.
You, my lord, guide your subordinates with the Way.
Insidious slander does not prevail.
This is victory in clarity.
The *Analects* say: 'Where insidious slander does not prevail,
one may be called clear-sighted indeed.'
This means slanderers are like water that seeps in gradually.
What you, my lord, affirm, you promote according to ritual;
what you do not affirm, you correct according to law.
This is victory in culture.
Shào is fond of creating false displays of strength,
not understanding the essentials of warfare.
Xúnzǐ debated warfare with Línwǔ Jūn before King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
The king said:
'May I ask about the essentials of warfare?'
You, my lord, employ troops like a spirit,
your soldiers rely on you,
and your enemies fear you.
This is victory in military affairs."
Cáo Cāo laughed and said:
"If it is as you gentlemen say,
what virtue do I possess to bear it!"
Guō Jiā added:
"Shào is currently attacking Gōngsūn Zàn in the north.
We can take advantage of his distant campaign
to capture Lǚ Bù in the east.
If Shào becomes an invader
and Bù provides him support,
this would be a grave harm."
Xún Yù said:
"If we do not first capture Lǚ Bù,
it will not be easy to plan for Héběi."
While Yuán Shào attacked Gōngsūn Zàn,
Cáo Cāo seized the opportunity to capture Lǚ Bù in the east.
When Cáo Cāo attacked Liú Bèi,
Yuán Shào could not raid Xǔ.
This is the reason for his defeat.
'Easy'
is pronounced with the *yì* tone.
"However,
what troubles me
is also the fear that Shào might invade and harass Guānzhōng,
causing chaos with the Qiāng and Hú in the west,
and enticing Shǔ-Hàn in the south.
Then I alone, with Yǎn and Yù, would be opposing five-sixths of the realm.
What should a general do?"
Xún Yù said:
"The commanders and generals in Guānzhōng number in the tens,
none able to unite with the others.
Only Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng are the strongest.
Seeing the strife east of the mountains,
they will certainly each gather their masses to protect themselves.
If we now soothe them with kindness and virtue,
and send envoys to form alliances,
although we cannot achieve lasting peace,
by the time you, my lord, have pacified the lands east of the mountains, it will suffice
to keep them from moving.
The rebellion and submission of Suì
and Téng
ultimately turned out as Xún Yù predicted.
'By'
is pronounced *bì mèi*.
If we entrust western affairs to them,
you, my lord, will have no worries."
Cáo Cāo then memorialized to appoint Zhōng Yáo as Palace Attendant acting as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
bearing the imperial staff to oversee the various armies in Guānzhōng,
specially empowered to act without being bound by regulations and systems.
When Yáo reached Cháng'ān,
he sent letters to Téng, Suì, and others.
'Sent'
means to dispatch.
Téng and Suì each sent a son to serve at court.
3. Yuán Shù proclaimed himself emperor at Shòuchūn,
calling himself the Zhòngjiā,
appointing the Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng as the Governor of Huáinán,
establishing the Three Excellencies, Nine Ministers, and all officials,
and performing the suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
The Chancellor of Pèi, Chén Guī,
was a disciple of Chén Qiú.
In his youth, he associated with Shù.
Shù sent a letter summoning Guī,
and also took his son hostage,
determined to force Guī to come.
Guī replied in a letter:
"General Cáo is reviving the classical laws and punishments,
and is about to quell the wicked and evil.
I believed you should join forces wholeheartedly,
to support and assist the Hàn imperial house.
Yet you secretly plot treason,
personally courting disaster.
To want me to scheme for private gain and flatteringly attach myself to you—
I would rather die than do so."
Shù wanted to appoint the former Governor of Yǎn, Jīn Shàng, as Grand Commandant.
Shàng refused and fled.
Shù killed him.
Jīn Shàng fled to Shù; see the third year of the Chūpíng era in scroll 60.
4. In the third month,
an edict ordered the Minister of Works, Kǒng Róng, bearing the imperial staff, to confer upon Yuán Shào the title of Grand General,
concurrently overseeing the four provinces of Jì, Qīng, Yōu, and Bìng.
5. In summer,
the fifth month,
locusts appeared.
6. Yuán Shù sent an envoy, Hán Yìn, to inform Lǚ Bù of his claiming the imperial title,
and to request to fetch Bù's daughter in marriage.
Bù sent his daughter to follow him.
Chén Guī feared that if Xú and Yáng formed an alliance,
troubles would be endless.
Shù governed Yángzhōu,
Bù governed Xúzhōu.
'Alliance'
is pronounced *zǐ róng*.
'Troubles'
is pronounced *nǎi dàn*.
"Duke Cáo has welcomed and supports the Son of Heaven,
assisting in state governance.
You, General, should cooperate with him in planning and strategy,
to jointly preserve the grand design.
Now, by forming a marriage alliance with Yuán Shù,
you are bound to incur the name of unrighteousness,
and will face a danger as precarious as a pile of eggs!"
Bù also resented that Shù had not treated him well initially.
See the third year of the Chūpíng era in scroll 60.
So he pursued and recalled [his daughter], severing the marriage alliance,
put Hán Yìn in cangues and sent him away,
and displayed his head at the market in Xǔ.
Chén Guī wanted to send his son Chén Dēng to meet Cáo Cāo,
but Lǚ Bù firmly refused.
At that time, an imperial edict appointed Lǚ Bù as General of the Left,
and Cáo Cāo also sent a personal letter to Lǚ Bù,
expressing deep consolation and acceptance.
Lǚ Bù was greatly pleased,
and immediately dispatched Chén Dēng to present a memorial expressing gratitude for the imperial favor,
along with a reply to Cáo Cāo’s letter.
When Chén Dēng met Cáo Cāo,
he took the opportunity to describe Lǚ Bù as brave but lacking in strategy,
fickle in his allegiances,
and advised that he should be dealt with early.
Cáo Cāo said:
“Lǚ Bù is a wolf cub with wild ambitions,
truly difficult to keep under control for long.
No one but you can fully uncover his true intentions.”
He immediately increased Chén Guī’s salary to the level of Zhōng Èrqiān Shí.
Under the Hàn system: the Chancellor of a Kingdom received a salary of Èrqiān Shí.
Increasing it to Zhōng Èrqiān Shí
meant his rank was equivalent to that of the Nine Ministers.
At their parting,
Cáo Cāo grasped Chén Dēng’s hand and said:
“Affairs in the eastern region
I now entrust to you.”
He ordered him to secretly gather troops to serve as an internal force.
Earlier,
Lǚ Bù had asked Chén Dēng to request the position of Governor of Xúzhōu for him but failed to obtain it.
When Chén Dēng returned,
Lǚ Bù was furious,
drew his halberd and struck a table, saying:
“Your father advised me to ally with Cáo Cāo
and break off the marriage alliance with Yuán Shù;
now what I sought was not obtained,
yet you and your father have both gained prominence and high rank—
I have simply been betrayed by you!”
Chén Dēng showed no change in expression,
and calmly replied to him:
“When I met Lord Cáo, I said: ‘Raising you, General, is like raising a tiger;
you must feed it until it is full,
for if it is not full, it will bite people.’
Lord Cáo said: ‘It is not as you say.
It is more like raising a hawk:
when hungry, it can be used;
when full, it flies away.’
Those were his words.”
Lǚ Bù’s anger then subsided.
Yuán Shù sent his generals Zhāng Xūn, Qiáo Ruí, and others to join forces with Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng,
leading tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry toward Xiàpī,
attacking Lǚ Bù from seven directions.
Lǚ Bù at the time had only three thousand troops
and four hundred horses,
and feared he could not withstand them.
He said to Chén Guī:
“Now that Yuán Shù’s army has arrived,
it is because of you—
what should be done?”
Chén Guī said:
“Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng with Yuán Shù
are merely a hastily assembled force;
their plans are not settled in advance,
and they cannot maintain cohesion.
My son Chén Dēng assessed them
as being like tethered chickens—
they cannot roost together.”
The Zhànguó Cè records: King Huì of Qín said:
“The feudal lords cannot be united,
just as tethered chickens cannot all roost together.”
Lǚ Bù followed Chén Guī’s strategy,
and wrote to Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng, saying:
“You two generals personally rescued the imperial carriage,
and I personally killed Dǒng Zhuó;
we have both achieved merit and fame.
How can you now join Yuán Shù in becoming rebels?
It would be better for us to join forces and defeat Yuán Shù,
removing a scourge for the state.”
He also promised to give them all of Yuán Shù’s military supplies.
Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng were greatly pleased,
and immediately changed their plans to follow Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù advanced his army,
and when they were a hundred paces from Zhāng Xūn’s camp,
Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng’s troops simultaneously shouted,
and together charged into Zhāng Xūn’s camp.
Zhāng Xūn and others scattered and fled,
Lǚ Bù’s troops pursued and attacked,
beheading ten of their generals,
and nearly all were killed, wounded, or drowned.
Lǚ Bù then joined forces with Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng and marched toward Shòuchūn,
advancing by both land and water.
When they reached Zhōnglí,
Zhōnglí County,
belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery,
and was over two hundred lǐ from Shòuchūn.
They then crossed back north of the Huái River,
leaving a letter to insult Yuán Shù.
Yuán Shù personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry to display his troops along the Huái River,
but Lǚ Bù’s cavalry all laughed derisively at them from the north bank of the river and then withdrew.
The bandit leader of Tàishān, Zāng Bà, attacked the Chancellor of Lángyé, Xiāo Jiàn, at Jǔ.
In the Former Hàn, Jǔ County
belonged to Chéngyáng Kingdom,
and in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Lángyé Kingdom.
Shuài (leader)
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
Zāng Bà obtained Xiāo Jiàn’s supplies and wealth,
and promised to give a portion to Lǚ Bù but had not yet delivered it.
Lǚ Bù went personally to demand it.
His commander Gāo Shùn advised him:
“General, your prestige and reputation are widely known,
feared far and near.
What could you possibly seek and not obtain?
Yet you go personally to demand bribes!
If by any chance you fail,
would it not damage your reputation?”
Lǚ Bù did not listen.
When he arrived at Jǔ,
Zāng Bà and others could not guess his intentions,
and firmly defended themselves against him,
so Lǚ Bù returned empty-handed.
Gāo Shùn was a man of integrity and dignity,
spoke little,
and commanded over seven hundred soldiers.
His orders were strict and orderly,
and he was victorious in every battle,
earning the name
“Camp of the Broken Formation.”
Later, Lǚ Bù grew distant from Gāo Shùn,
and because Wèi Xù was a close relative both inside and outside the family,
he took Gāo Shùn’s troops and gave them to Wèi Xù.
But when it came to battle,
he would again order Gāo Shùn to command,
and Gāo Shùn never showed any resentment.
Lǚ Bù distanced himself from Gāo Shùn and favored Wèi Xù,
yet later it was Wèi Xù who captured Gāo Shùn and contributed to Lǚ Bù’s defeat.
Jiàng (to command)
is pronounced jí liàng fān.
Lǚ Bù’s actions were unpredictable,
and Gāo Shùn often admonished him:
“General, in your actions,
you refuse to think carefully,
and whenever there is a gain or loss,
you immediately say it was a mistake.
But how many mistakes can one make?”
Lǚ Bù knew he was loyal but could not follow his advice.
7 Cáo Cāo sent the Court Counselor Wáng Pǔ
with an imperial edict appointing Sūn Cè as Cavalry Commandant,
and to inherit the title of Marquis of Wúchéng.
Sūn Cè’s father, Sūn Jiān,
had been enfeoffed as Marquis of Wúchéng for his merits in suppressing bandits.
Wúchéng County,
belonged to Wú Commandery,
is present-day Ānjí Prefecture and County.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn:
“In the summer of the second year of Jiàn’ān,
Wáng Pǔ presented the Wùchén Edict to bestow upon Sūn Cè.”
It is not known in which month this occurred.
He was ordered to join Lǚ Bù and the Administrator of Wú Commandery, Chén Yǔ, in jointly attacking Yuán Shù.
Sūn Cè wanted a general’s title to enhance his own prestige,
so Wáng Pǔ, acting on imperial authority, provisionally appointed Sūn Cè as General Who Illuminates the Hàn.
The title General Who Illuminates the Hàn
was also temporarily established with this designation,
meaning he understood right and wrong,
and knew to honor the Hàn court.
The title “Aiding the Hàn” is similar.
Sūn Cè prepared his troops,
Yán (prepared)
means to equip.
Qiántáng County,
in the Former Hàn belonged to Kuàijī Commandery,
but in the Later Hàn it was abolished,
and its territory should have belonged to Wú Commandery.
The Qiántáng Jì states: In the past, the Commandery Councilor Huá Xìn proposed building this embankment to guard against the sea.
He recruited anyone who could deliver one hú of earth,
offering one thousand coins,
and within ten days to a month,
people came in crowds.
Before the embankment was completed, he stopped paying,
so those carrying earth and stones
all abandoned their loads and left.
The embankment was thus completed,
hence the name Qiántáng (Money Embankment).
Chén Yǔ secretly contacted Zǔ Láng, Yán Báihǔ, and others,
to serve as internal allies.
Sūn Cè discovered this,
and sent his generals Lǚ Fàn and Xú Yì to attack Chén Yǔ at Hǎixī.
Chén Yǔ was defeated,
and fled alone on horseback to Yuán Shào.
8. Initially,
Chén Wáng Liú Chǒng was courageous
and skilled at crossbow shooting.
Liú Chǒng
was the great-grandson of Liú Xiàn, the Chén Jìng Wáng, son of Emperor Míng.
Liú Chǒng trained troops to defend himself,
and the people of his state feared him,
not daring to rebel or desert.
The Chancellor of the state, Luò Jùn of Kuàijī, had long been authoritative and benevolent.
At that time, the kings and marquises no longer received land rents and stipends,
and were repeatedly plundered,
some going days without food,
dying in ditches and gullies.
Yet Chén alone remained wealthy and strong,
and many people from neighboring commanderies sought refuge there,
gathering a following of over a hundred thousand.
When the provincial and commandery troops rose up,
Liú Chǒng led his followers to garrison Yángxià.
Xián said: Yángxià County
belonged to the Huáiyáng Kingdom.
Xià,
pronounced gōng yǎ fān.
Yuán Shù requested grain from Chén,
but Luò Jùn refused him.
Yuán Shù was furious,
and sent an assassin to deceitfully kill Luò Jùn and Liú Chǒng.
Chén was thus destroyed.
9. In autumn,
the ninth month,
the Minister of Works Cáo Cāo campaigned east against Yuán Shù.
When Yuán Shù heard Cáo Cāo was coming,
he abandoned his army and fled,
leaving his general Qiáo Ruí and others at Qíyáng to resist Cáo Cāo.
Xián said: The Qí River originates from the northern mountains of Qíchūn County in Jiāngxià.
The Commentary on the Water Classic says: This is Mount Qí.
It flows southwest past Mount Qí,
and then south opposite Qíyáng,
emptying into the Great River,
also called the Qíyáng Estuary.
According to my examination of the Records of the Three Kingdoms,
at that time Yuán Shù was invading Chén,
and Cáo Cāo campaigned east against him.
Yuán Shù left Ruí and others to resist Cáo Cāo.

tenth month,
