Jìn Tiānwén Zhì: In the south, Dōngjǐng consists of eight stars,
the southern gate of heaven,
through which the ecliptic passes,
the watchtower of heaven,
in charge of water balance affairs,
from which laws derive their fairness.
Bó,
Púnèi fān.
3 Gāo Gàn surrendered with Bīngzhōu,
and Cāo reappointed Gàn as Governor of Bīngzhōu.
This sets the stage for Gàn's later rebellion.
Jiàng,
Hùjiāng fān.
Fù,
Fúyòu fān.
4 When Cáo Cāo besieged Yè,
Yuán Tán again betrayed him,
seizing Gānlíng, Ānpíng, Bóhǎi, and Héjiān.
He attacked Yuán Shàng in Zhōngshān.
Shàng was defeated,
fled to Gù'ān,
Gù'ān County,
belonged to Zhuō Commandery.
Xián says: The old city was south of Yì County in modern Yìzhōu.
Tán gathered all his troops,
and returned to garrison at Lóngcòu.
Cāo wrote to Tán,
reproaching him for breaking the agreement,
severed the marriage alliance,
sent the daughter back,
then advanced to attack.
After Yuán Shàng was defeated and fled,
Cāo then began to attack Tán.
Cāo's army reached his gate,
Tán abandoned Píngyuán,
fled to defend Nánpí,
stationed by the Qīnghé River.
Shuǐjīng: The Qīnghé River passes west of Nánpí County.
He pacified the various counties.
5 Cáo Cāo recommended Gōngsūn Dù as General of Martial Might,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngníng Village.
Dù said:
"I am king of Liáodōng,
what need have I for Yǒngníng!"
He stored the seal and ribbon in the armory.
The armory of Liáodōng Commandery.
When Dù died,
his son Kāng succeeded him,
and enfeoffed his brother Gōng with the title Marquis of Yǒngníng Village.
Cáo Cāo, because Qiān Zhāo had once served the Yuán family in commanding the Wūhuán,
Qiān,
surname;
Zhāo,
given name.
Yuán Shào had previously recruited Zhāo as a military supervisor,
concurrently commanding Wūhuán shock cavalry.
Sent him to pacify and console the Wūhuán.
At that time, King Qiào had five thousand cavalry ready to aid Yuán Tán,
also,
Gōngsūn Kāng sent an envoy Hán Zhōng to confer on King Qiào the seal and ribbon of Chányú.
King Qiào convened a great assembly of tribal chiefs,
Wūhuán tribes,
each had their own chieftains.
Qiào,
Qīxiào fān.
Shǐ,
Shūlì fān.
Zhǎng,
Zhīliǎng fān.
King Qiào asked Zhāo:
"Previously, Lord Yuán said he received the Son of Heaven's command,
to appoint me as Chányú;
now Lord Cáo says he will again report to the Son of Heaven,
to appoint me as true Chányú;
Liáodōng also brings the seal and ribbon.
In this situation,
who is legitimate?"
Zhāo replied:
"Previously, Lord Yuán, acting under imperial authority,
could make appointments;
but later he erred against the Son of Heaven's command,
wéi,
means different,
means to betray.
Cuò,
means perverse.
So it must be reported to the Son of Heaven,
to newly appoint a true Chányú;
Liáodōng is a mere commandery,
how can it presumptuously claim to make appointments!"
Zhōng said:
"Our Liáodōng is east of the vast sea,
with over a million troops,
and also has the service of Fúyú and Huìmò.
In the current situation,
the strong are right.
How can Cáo Cāo alone decide this!"
Zhāo rebuked Zhōng:
"Lord Cáo is sincere, respectful, wise, and discerning.
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary on the Shàngshū says: Yǔn,
means trustworthy.
He attacks rebels and pacifies the submissive,
bringing peace to all within the Four Seas.
Your ruler and ministers are stubborn and deceitful,
now relying on remote and dangerous terrain,
defy the royal command,
presumptuously make appointments,
insult and play with the sacred vessels;
authority and blessings,
are the sacred vessels of the emperor.
How dare you slight and slander the great man!"
Great man,
refers to Lord Cáo.
Yì,
Yǐchì fān.
He drew his sword intending to kill him.
King Qiào was frightened,
rushed barefoot to embrace Zhāo,
to plead for Zhōng's rescue,
those around turned pale.
Zhāo then returned to his seat,
and explained to King Qiào and others the outcomes of success and failure,
the consequences of fortune and disaster;
all left their mats and knelt prostrate,
respectfully receiving his instructions,
chì,
means to admonish.
Wèi,
Yúwèi fān.
And dismissed the cavalry they had prepared.
6 The Grand Administrator of Dānyáng, Guī Lǎn, and the Commandery Assistant, Dài Yún, killed the Grand Administrator Sūn Yì.
General Sūn Hé was stationed at Jīngchéng.
He rushed to Wǎnlíng.
Jīngchéng
was the former Dāntú County of Wú Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
Sūn Quán moved his residence there from Wú,
naming it Jīngchéng,
also called Jīngkǒu.
I believe this
"Jīng"
takes its meaning from the *Erya*
"A mound of exceptional height is called a *jīng*."
Wǎnlíng
was the seat of Dānyáng Commandery.
Guī Lǎn and Dài Yún
were partisans of Shèng Xiàn.
Guī,
pronounced *jù wéi fān*;
it is a surname.
Shùn dwelled at Guīruì,
and his descendants later took it as their clan name.
Yún,
pronounced *yún*.
They sent someone to welcome the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Liú Fù.
Fù
was an appointee of Cáo Cāo.
They offered Dānyáng to him in response.
Lìyáng was separated from Dānyáng by the river.
They had Fù come and station troops there,
to serve as a supporting force.
Lǎn entered and took up residence in the military headquarters,
intending to force himself upon Yì's wife, Lady Xú.
Lady Xú deceived him, saying:
"I beg for a delay until the last day of the month.
The end of the month is called *huì*,
the exhaustion of *yīn*.
*Dài*,
pronounced *dàng hài fān*.
After that, I will comply with your command."
Lǎn agreed.
Lady Xú secretly sent a trusted person to speak with Yì's close former generals, Sūn Gāo and Fù Yīng, to join together in plotting against Lǎn.
Gāo and Yīng tearfully agreed.
They secretly summoned over twenty of those who had served and been supported by Yì to swear an oath and conspire together.
*Shì yǎng*
refers to those who served by Yì's side
and received generous support.
They set up a sacrifice.
Lady Xú wept mournfully, expressing her full grief.
When finished,
she removed her mourning garments,
perfumed herself, bathed,
and spoke and laughed joyfully.
Everyone, great and small, felt sorrowful.
*Qī*,
means sorrow,
pain.
*Chuàng*,
means grief,
pronounced *chū liàng fān*.
Lǎn secretly observed her,
and had no further suspicions.
Lady Xú called Gāo and Yīng to hide inside the door,
then sent someone to summon Lǎn to enter.
Lady Xú came out the door and bowed to Lǎn.
Just as she finished one bow,
Lady Xú cried out loudly:
"You two gentlemen may rise!"
Gāo and Yīng both rushed out,
together killed Lǎn,
and the others immediately went outside and killed Yún.
Lady Xú then returned to wearing mourning garments of *cuī dié*.
She put on the *cuī dié* again.
*Cuī*,
pronounced *cāng huí fān*.
The entire army was shocked and terrified.
Sūn Quán heard of the disorder,
and returned from Jiāoqiū.
Jiāoqiū
was in Yùzhāng.
He exterminated the entire clans of Lǎn and Yún's remaining partisans,
promoted Gāo and Yīng to be Yámén,
Yámén
means generals.
Hé's son, Sūn Sháo,
was seventeen years old.
He gathered Hé's remaining troops and stationed them at Jīngchéng.
Quán led his army back to Wú.
At night, he reached Jīngchéng and set up camp below it,
testing an attack to startle them.
The soldiers all ascended the walls,
circulated orders to prepare the alert,
their shouts shaking the earth,
and shot arrows at the outsiders.
Quán sent someone to explain the situation,
and they stopped.
The next day, he met Sháo,
appointed him Chéngliè Xiàowèi,
and put him in command of Hé's troops.
The history states that Sūn Quán was able to employ men to protect Jiāngdōng.
*Shè*,
pronounced *ér yì fān*.
1 Spring,
first month,
Cáo Cāo attacked Nánpí.
Yuán Tán went out to battle,
and many of his soldiers died.
Cāo considered easing the attack,
but the Court Counselor Cáo Chún said:
"Now our army hangs deep in enemy territory.
Chún
was Rén's younger brother.
*Xuán*,
read as *xuán*.
If we advance and cannot conquer,
retreat will surely lose our prestige."
So he personally took up the drumsticks to lead the attackers,
and thus conquered it.
Tán fled,
and they pursued and beheaded him.
Lǐ Fú, calling himself the Registrar of Jìzhōu,
sought an audience with Cāo, saying:
"Now in the city, the strong bully the weak,
and people's hearts are disturbed and chaotic.
I believe it appropriate to order someone who has recently surrendered and is recognized and trusted by those inside to proclaim your clear instructions."
Cāo immediately sent Fú to enter the city,
to instruct the officials and people,
telling each to peacefully continue their former occupations,
and not to encroach upon one another.
Only then did the city become calm.
Lǐ Fú
was a man of minor talent,
using his talent to seek recognition,
not one who harbored talent awaiting employment.
Guō Tú and Shěn Pèi each had their own factions,
inciting conflict between Tán and Shàng,
causing them to take up arms,
thereby paving the way for the Cáo clan's expulsion.
After Tán and Shàng were defeated,
both men were also executed.
The retribution of fortune and misfortune was not inaccurate.
Yuán Tán had sent Wáng Xiū to transport grain from Lè'ān.
Hearing of Tán's crisis,
he led the troops under his command to rush to his aid.
Upon reaching Gāomì,
he heard of Tán's death.
Dismounting, he wailed, saying:
"Without my lord, to whom shall I return!"
He then went to Cáo Cāo,
begging to collect and bury Tán's corpse.
Cāo agreed,
and further sent Xiū back to Lè'ān
to oversee military provisions.
All the cities under Tán's jurisdiction submitted,
except for the Grand Administrator of Lè'ān, Guǎn Tǒng, who would not yield.
Cāo ordered Xiū to take Tǒng's head.
He sent him back to transport grain,
and to take Tǒng's head while there.
He untied his bonds,
and sent him to see Cāo.
Cāo was pleased and pardoned him,
appointing Xiū as an Assistant in the Office of the Minister of Works.
Guō Jiā advised Cáo Cáo to extensively recruit renowned scholars from Qīng, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng provinces to serve as his subordinate officials,
in order to win the hearts and allegiance of the people.
Cáo Cáo followed this advice.
During the Battle of Guāndù,
Yuán Shào had Chén Lín draft a proclamation,
enumerating Cáo Cáo's crimes and evils,
extending the accusations to his family background,
and vilifying him to the extreme.
After the Yuán clan's defeat,
Chén Lín submitted to Cáo Cáo.
Cáo Cáo said:
"When you, sir, previously drafted that document for Běnchū (Yuán Shào),
you could have confined the accusations to my person alone;
why did you have to extend them to my father and grandfather?"
According to the Wénxuǎn,
Lín drafted the proclamation for Shào to Yùzhōu.
Since the capital was at Xǔ,
and Xǔ belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery,
which was under the jurisdiction of Yùzhōu,
the Wénxuǎn specifically mentions the proclamation being addressed to Yùzhōu.
Lín's proclamation roughly stated:
"Cáo's grandfather, Téng,
together with Zuǒ Guàn and Xú Huáng, acted as monstrous villains,
insatiably greedy and tyrannical,
corrupting morals and harming people.
His father, Sōng,
was a beggar raised by others,
who purchased office through bribery,
and stole the position of a high minister.
Cáo himself is the vile leftover of treacherous eunuchs,
cunning, sharp, and given to violence,
delighting in chaos and calamity."
It further enumerated his crimes of persecuting the worthy and virtuous,
monopolizing court authority,
and desecrating tombs and graves.
The text is too lengthy to be fully recorded here.
Cáo Cáo released him,
and appointed him, together with Ruǎn Yǔ from Chénliú, to manage the Records Office.
The ducal offices of the Hàn had a Records Office Clerk,
responsible for handling memorials, reports, and official correspondence.
Previously, Wáng Sōng of Yúyáng occupied Zhuō Commandery.
Liú Fàng, a native of the commandery, persuaded Sōng to surrender the territory to Cáo Cáo.
Cáo Cáo appointed Fàng to participate in military affairs of the Minister of Works.
This was the beginning of Liú Fàng's later involvement in Wèi's confidential matters, which contributed to the disorder in Wèi.
Yuán Xī was attacked by his generals Jiāo Chù and Zhāng Nán,
and fled together with Yuán Shàng to the Wūhuán of Liáoxī.
The Wūhuán of Liáoxī
had a chieftain named Tàdùn.
Chù and Nán compelled the Grand Administrators and county chiefs of various commanderies,
to turn against the Yuán clan and submit to Cáo,
arrayed tens of thousands of troops,
sacrificed a white horse to swear an oath,
and proclaimed:
"Anyone who dares to disobey shall be executed!"
None dared to look up,
and each in turn smeared their lips with blood.
The Assistant Inspector Hán Héng from Dài Commandery said:
"I have received great kindness from Lord Yuán and his sons.
Now that they are defeated and destroyed,
my wisdom is insufficient to save them,
and my courage insufficient to die for them—
I am deficient in righteousness.
As for turning north to submit to the Cáo clan,
that is something I cannot do."
Everyone present turned pale for Héng.
Chù said:
"When undertaking great endeavors,
one must establish great righteousness.
The success or failure of an affair
does not depend on one man alone.
We can fulfill Héng's resolve,
to encourage loyalty to one's lord."
They then spared him.
Chù and others subsequently surrendered to Cáo Cáo,
and all were enfeoffed as marquises.
2 In summer,
the fourth month,
the Black Mountain bandit leader Zhāng Yàn led over a hundred thousand of his followers to surrender.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānguó Village.
3 Zhào Dú and Huò Nú of Gù'ān killed the Governor of Yōu Province and the Grand Administrator of Zhuō Commandery.
The Wūhuán of the three commanderies attacked Xiānyú Fǔ at Guǎngpíng.
The Wūhuán of the three commanderies
were Tàdùn of Liáoxī, Sū Púyán of Liáodōng, and Wū Yán of Yòuběipíng.
Guǎngpíng County
belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
Fú Qián said: Guǎng
is pronounced gǒng.
Shī Gǔ said: pronounced jiǔ yǒng fān,
also pronounced kuàng.
In the eighth month,
Cáo Cáo campaigned against Dú and others,
and executed them;
he then crossed the Lù River to rescue Guǎngpíng,
and the Wūhuán fled beyond the frontier.
4 In winter,
the tenth month,
Gāo Gàn, hearing that Cáo Cáo was campaigning against the Wūhuán,
again rebelled with Bìng Province,
captured the Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng,
and raised troops to guard the Húguān Pass.
Xián said: Lù Province's Shàngdǎng County has the Húshān Pass,
where a barrier was established due to its strategic location.
According to the treatises of the two Hàn histories,
Húguān County
belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery.
Zhāng Shèng from Hénèi,
with over ten thousand followers,
ravaged the area between Xiáo and Miǎn,
and Zhāng Yǎn from Hóngnóng raised troops in response.
The Grand Administrator of Hédōng, Wáng Yì, was summoned to court.
The commandery official Wèi Gù and General of the Household Zhōnglángjiàng Fàn Xiān and others went to the Colonel-Director of Retainers Zhōng Yáo,
requesting that Yì be retained.
Yáo did not permit it.
Gù and others outwardly used the request to retain Yì as a pretext,
but inwardly were actually in secret communication with Gāo Gàn.
Cáo Cáo said to Xún Yù:
"The generals west of the pass,
submit outwardly but are disloyal within.
Zhāng Shèng ravages Xiáo and Miǎn,
communicating with Liú Biǎo in the south.
Gù and others, taking advantage of this,
will cause profound harm.
Presently, Hédōng
is a crucial location in the realm.
Gāo Gàn occupies Bìng Province,
Mǎ Téng, Hán Suì and others occupy Guānzhōng.
Their comings and goings and communications
all pass through Hédōng,
hence it is called a crucial location."
Yù said:
"The Grand Administrator of Xīpíng, Dù Jī from Jīngzhào,
(Xīpíng Commandery was established by dividing Jīnchéng during the late Hàn.)
has wisdom sufficient to respond to changing circumstances."
Cáo Cáo then appointed Jī as Grand Administrator of Hédōng.
Zhōng Yáo urged Wáng Yì to hand over the tally,
(the commandery tally.)
and Yì went directly from Héběi County to Xǔ to submit himself.
Héběi County
belonged to Hédōng Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Shǎnzhōu's Pínglù County
was originally the territory of Dàyáng County in the Hàn,
renamed Héběi County in the Later Hàn.
Wèi Gù and others sent several thousand troops to block the Shǎn Ford.
(Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Yellow River flows east past the north of Shǎn County.
North of the river facing Máo City,
it is called the Máo Ford,
also called the Shǎn Ford.
Shǎn
is pronounced shì rǎn fān.)
For several months, Jī could not cross.
Cáo Cáo sent Xiàhóu Dūn to campaign against Gù and others.
Before he arrived,
Jī said:
"Hédōng has thirty thousand households,
not all of whom wish to rebel.
Now, with troops pressing urgently,
those who wish to do good have no leader,
and will surely fear and obey Gù.
If Gù and others consolidate their power,
and a campaign against them fails,
the trouble will not cease;
if the campaign succeeds,
it will mean devastating the people of an entire commandery.
Moreover, Gù and others have not yet openly defied the royal command;
outwardly, they use the request to retain the former administrator as their name.
They will certainly not harm the new administrator.
I will go directly with a single carriage,
taking them by surprise.
Gù is a man of many schemes but indecisive,
he will surely pretend to accept me.
If I can remain in the commandery for one month,
and devise plans to tie them down,
it will be sufficient."
He then took a covert route and crossed at the Dòu Ford.
(Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Yellow River flows east past the old city north of Hú County,
further east it joins the Bǎigǔ Stream,
and further east, right, it joins the Mén Stream.
Here the Yellow River has the name Dòu Ford.
Dòu
is pronounced dòu.)
Fàn Xiān wanted to kill Dù Jī to intimidate the masses,
and also to observe Dù Jī’s stance,
so he executed over thirty people below the rank of Registrar at the gate,
yet Dù Jī remained composed as usual.
Thereupon, Wéi Gù said:
“Killing him would bring no benefit,
only a bad reputation;
moreover, we control him.”
Thus they submitted to him.
Dù Jī said to Wéi Gù and Fàn Xiān:
“Wèi and Fàn,
are the pillars of Hédōng,
I rely on your accomplishments.
However, the relationship between ruler and minister is defined,
success and failure are shared,
major matters should be discussed together.”
He appointed Wéi Gù as Military Governor,
acting as Assistant Administrator,
and concurrently as Personnel Officer;
having already appointed him as Military Governor,
he also ordered him to act as Commandery Assistant,
and concurrently as Personnel Officer.
The Military Governor controlled the troops,
the Assistant served as deputy to the Grand Administrator,
overseeing all commandery affairs,
the Personnel Officer managed appointments and merits,
thus outwardly granting him full authority over the commandery.
All were supervised by Fàn Xiān.
Wéi Gù and others were pleased,
and though they outwardly served Dù Jī,
they did not take him seriously.
Wéi Gù wanted to raise a large army,
which troubled Dù Jī,
so he persuaded Wéi Gù, saying:
“Now if we raise a large army,
the people’s sentiments will surely be disturbed,
it would be better to gradually recruit soldiers with funds.”
Wéi Gù agreed,
and followed this advice,
but very few soldiers were recruited.
Recruiting soldiers with funds,
meant the commandery’s resources were insufficient to sustain it,
hence very few soldiers were obtained.
“People care for their families,
the various generals and officials,
can be sent in turns to rest,
and summoned easily in times of urgency.”
Wéi Gù and others feared going against popular sentiment,
and again followed his advice.
Thus, the good people remained outside,
secretly supporting him;
the troublemakers were dispersed,
each returning to their homes.
At that time, Bái Qí attacked Dōngyuán,
Bái Qí,
refers to the followers of Zhāng Bái Qí who gathered as bandits.
Yuán County,
belonged to Hédōng Commandery,
the character “Dōng”
is redundant.
According to the Continued Hàn Records,
Yuán County,
notes: the mountain lies to the east,
shaped like a wall.
It seems the name Dōngyuán already existed at this time.
Qí,
pronounced as qí jì fān.
Huòzé County,
belonged to Hédōng Commandery.
Xián said: present-day Zézhōu County.
Shī Gǔ said: Huò,
pronounced as wū hào fān.
Then he went out,
leading only a few dozen cavalry,
and rushed to fortify and defend it,
many officials and people from the city came to assist Dù Jī,
Jǔ chéng,
means raising the cities of subordinate counties.
He gathered over four thousand people.
Wéi Gù and others, together with Gāo Gàn and Zhāng Shèng, jointly attacked Dù Jī,
but failed to capture him,
plundered various counties,
and gained nothing.
Cáo Cāo sent Court Counselor Zhāng Jì to campaign westward against the various generals in Guānzhōng such as Mǎ Téng,
who all led troops to join in attacking Zhāng Shèng and others,
defeated them,
beheaded Wéi Gù, Yǎn, and others,
and pardoned the remaining followers.
Thereupon, Dù Jī governed Hédōng,
focusing on leniency and benevolence.
When people had disputes,
Dù Jī would explain the principles to them,
and send them back to reflect carefully,
the elders would then reprimand each other,
and no one dared to bring lawsuits;
he encouraged farming and sericulture,
supervised animal husbandry,
and every household among the people became prosperous;
then he established schools,
promoted filial piety and fraternal duty,
organized military affairs,
and trained for defense,
and Hédōng thus became peaceful.
Dù Jī served in Hédōng for sixteen years,
often ranking first in the realm.
This laid the foundation for Cáo Cāo to use Hédōng’s resources to pacify Guānzhōng.
Dù Jī’s son was Dù Shù,
and Dù Shù’s son was Dù Yù.
His governance of Hédōng,
judging by his strategies,
was certainly not the work of an ordinary talent.
I privately believe that the Dù family served in Wèi and Jìn,
enjoying prosperity for generations,
and must have had family records,
which historians relied on for their accounts,
likely exaggerating their achievements.
Cáo Cāo appointed Liáng Xí from Chénjùn, who held the position of Biébù Sīmǎ, to serve as the Governor of Bìngzhōu.
At that time, in the aftermath of chaos and turmoil,
the Hú and Dí tribes were powerful and aggressive,
officials and commoners fled and defected to their tribes,
and the Southern Xiōngnú tribes were all within the borders of Bìngzhōu.
Each caused harm through raids.
Referring to the powerful local magnates who gathered followers to protect themselves,
Liáng Xí lured, persuaded, and recruited them,
treating all the magnates with courtesy and summoning them,
gradually recommending and promoting them,
sending them to the military headquarters;
after the magnates were fully recruited,
he next mobilized the able-bodied men to serve as volunteer followers;
meaning they voluntarily joined the army.
Cóng,
pronounced as cái yòng fān.
He ordered the various generals to separately request them to serve as brave and strong soldiers.
After the officials and soldiers had departed,
he gradually relocated their families,
sending them to Yè in succession,
totaling tens of thousands of people;
those who did not comply with orders,
he raised troops to attack,
beheading thousands,
and those who surrendered and submitted numbered in the tens of thousands.
The Chányú became respectful and obedient,
and the renowned kings kowtowed in submission,
renowned kings,
referring to the various tribal kings of the Xiōngnú.
Xiáng,
pronounced as hù jiāng fān.
Jī,
pronounced as qǐ.
They were treated the same as registered households.
Biān,
means to connect in sequence;
registered in the civilian census,
hence called biānhù.
The common people spread across the fields,
diligently encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
orders were carried out and prohibitions were enforced.
When ordered, they acted;
when prohibited, they stopped.
It was believed that based on what he had heard and known,
no governor had been like Liáng Xí.

Liáng Xí then recommended and introduced renowned scholars who had taken refuge within the borders of the province, such as Cháng Lín, Yáng Jùn, Wáng Xiàng, Xún Wěi from Hénèi, and Wáng Líng from Tàiyuán, among others,
Cáo Cāo appointed them all as county magistrates,
and they later all achieved fame in the world.
Initially,
Zhòngcháng Tǒng from Shānyáng traveled to Bìngzhōu for study,
visited Gāo Gàn,
Zhòngcháng,
a compound surname.
Guò,
pronounced as gōng hé fān.
He inquired about worldly affairs.
Zhòngcháng Tǒng said to Gāo Gàn:
"You have great ambitions but lack great talent,
you appreciate scholars but cannot choose the right people,
this is what you should deeply guard against."
Gāo Gàn was highly self-important,
believing himself to be highly talented.
Zhòngcháng Tǒng then left him.
After Gāo Gàn died,
Xún Yù recommended Zhòngcháng Tǒng to serve as a Shàngshū Láng.
According to the Bǎiguān Zhì: there were thirty-six Shàngshū Shìláng,
with a salary of four hundred shí;
each department had six,
responsible for drafting documents.
Cài Zhì's Hàn Yí states: Shàngshū Láng,
initially came from the three offices to the imperial court for examination,
upon first entering the court,
they were called Shǒu Shàngshū Lángzhōng;
after one year,
they were called Shàngshū Láng;
after three years,
they were called Shìláng.
Kǒng Ānguó said: Chāng,
means appropriate.
Appropriate and reasonable words.
Briefly stated:
"Those heroes who are destined by heaven's mandate,
initially have no claim to the world,
having no claim to the world,
thus wars and conflicts arise competitively.
Those who compete with wisdom are all exhausted,
those who compete with strength are all defeated,
jiǎo,
means to compete,
to contend.
When their power is insufficient to contend further,
they then begin to bow their heads and submit,
accepting my reins and bridle.
Xián explains: Xián,
means bridle.
Xiè,
means halter.
Xiè,
pronounced as xī liè fān.
Once the ambitions of the heroes are extinguished,
and the will of the scholars and commoners is settled,
nobility resides in constant families,
and supreme authority rests with one person.
At this time,
even if a person of the lowest intelligence occupies the position,
they can still make kindness akin to heaven and earth,
and authority match ghosts and deities,
even thousands like Zhōu and Kǒng could no longer contend with their sagacity,
and millions like Bēn and Yù could no longer exert their bravery.
Those foolish rulers among later descendants,
seeing that no one in the world dares to oppose them,
believe themselves to be as unshakable as heaven and earth,
then indulge their personal desires,
give free rein to their evil cravings,
the ruler and ministers openly engage in debauchery,
Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Xiè Yě said:
"When the lords and ministers openly engage in debauchery,
the people have no model to follow."
Dù Yù said: Xuān,
means to display.
They neglect and abandon governmental affairs,
disregard and forget about people and matters.
Those they trust and favor,
are all flattering and sycophantic people;
those they ennoble and richly reward,
are all the families of consorts and concubines.
This leads to boiling the fat of the world,
hacking at the marrow of the living people,
resentment and hatred become unbearable,
disasters and chaos arise together,
the central plains are thrown into turmoil,
the four barbarian tribes invade and rebel,
the state collapses and disintegrates,
lost in a single morning,
those who were once my nurturing descendants,
now all become my blood-drinking enemies.
As for those who, even when fortune shifts and power is lost,
still do not realize,
is it not because wealth and honor breed inhumanity,
and indulgence leads to foolish maladies!
Survival and destruction alternate because of this,
order and chaos cycle repeatedly from this,
Zuǒ Zhuàn: beauty and ugliness inevitably cycle,
such is the way of heaven.
3 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi, Zhāng Měng, killed the Governor of Yōngzhōu, Hándān Shāng;
in the first year of Xīngpíng,
the four western counties of Liángzhōu were separated to establish Yōngzhōu.
Yōng,
pronounced as yú yòng fān.
Zhāng Měng,
was the son of Zhāng Huàn.
4 In the eighth month,
Cáo Cāo went east to attack the sea bandit Guǎn Chéng,
reaching Chúnyú,
Chúnyú County,
belonged to the State of Běihǎi.
Xián said: the old city was located northeast of present-day Ānqiū County, Mìzhōu.
Guǎn Chéng fled to the sea islands.
5 Chāng Xī rebelled again,
Cáo Cāo sent Yú Jìn to attack and behead him.
6 In this year,
the son of the late Prince of Lángyé, Róng, named Xī, was established as the Prince of Lángyé.
The eight states of Qí, Běihǎi, Fùlíng, Xiàpī, Chángshān, Gānlíng, Jìyīn, and Píngyuán were all abolished.
Róng
was the great-great-grandson of Liú Jīng, the Filial Prince of Lángyé and son of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
When Róng died,
his state was extinguished,
but now his son was re-established.
Qí
was the state of the descendants of Liú Yǎn, the Martial Prince and elder brother of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
Běihǎi
was the state of the descendants of Liú Xìng, the Tranquil Prince and youngest son of Yǎn.
Fùlíng
was the state of the descendants of Liú Yán, the Substantial Prince and son of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
Xiàpī
was the state of the descendants of Liú Yǎn, the Benevolent Prince and son of Emperor Míng.
Chángshān
was the state of the descendants of Liú Bǐng, the Inclined Prince and son of Emperor Míng.
Gānlíng
was the state of the descendants of Liú Qìng, the Filial Prince of Qīnghé and son of Emperor Zhāng.
Jìyīn
was the state of Liú Cháng, the Mourning Prince and son of Emperor Míng, who died without an heir,
and the state had been abolished long ago;
according to Fàn's history,
it should be Jìběi,
the state of the descendants of Liú Shòu, the Benevolent Prince and son of Emperor Zhāng,
which was also abolished in this year.
Píngyuán
was first enfeoffed to Liú Shèng, the Cherished Prince and son of Emperor Hé,
who died without an heir,
so Liú Yì, son of Prince Kāi of Héjiān, was made his successor;
Yì was later demoted to Marquis of Lǐwú,
and his son Zhì was established as Emperor Huán,
who then made his elder brother Shuò the Prince of Píngyuán,
to continue Yì's line,
but by now this state was also abolished.
All eight states were abolished,
yet Xī alone was established to continue Lángyé
because Róng had earlier sent his younger brother Miǎo to Cháng'ān to present tribute,
while Cáo Cāo was in Dōngjùn at the time,
and Miǎo greatly praised Róng's loyalty.
Cáo Cāo was thus grateful to Róng,
so he established an heir for Róng.
The abolition of the eight states
was a gradual weakening of the Hàn imperial clan.
Jì,
read as zǐlǐ.
7 The Wūhuán took advantage of the turmoil in the realm,
seizing over a hundred thousand households of Hàn people.
Yuán Shào established all their chieftains as Chányú,
and gave them girls from his own family as his daughters,
marrying them off.
Tàdùn of the Liáoxī Wūhuán was especially powerful,
and was favored by Shào,
so Shàng and his brothers turned to him,
frequently raiding across the border,
hoping to help Shàng recover his former territory.
Cáo Cāo was about to attack them,
so he dug the Pínglǔ Canal and Quánzhōu Canal to facilitate transport.
Cáo's annals state: The canal was dug
from the Hūtuó River into the Gū River,
named the Pínglǔ Canal;
also from the mouth of the Jū River,
digging into the Lù River,
named the Quánzhōu Canal,
to connect to the sea.
Gū,
pronounced gū.
Jū,
pronounced jù.
Xián states: The Hūtuó River
originally flowed south of Ráoyáng,
but Cáo Cāo, using the old channel of the Ráo River,
diverted it north to flow into the new ditch water,
so it now flows north of Ráoyáng County.
Shuōwén states: The Gū River
originates from Shòufū Mountain in Suīrén County, Yànmén Commandery,
flowing northeast into the sea.
Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Jū River
originates from the western mountains of Wúzhōng County in Yòuběipíng,
flowing northwest,
passing through Pínggǔ County and then southeast,
then flowing south into the Lù River,
and east to join the mouth of the Quánzhōu Canal,
which was dug by Cáo Cāo.
The canal flows east to the south of Lè'ān Pavilion in Hǎiyáng County, where it merges with the Rú River,
and enters the sea.
Quánzhōu and Pínggǔ counties
both belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
Xián states: The old city of Quánzhōu
was south of Yōngnú County in Yōuzhōu.
Hǎiyáng County
belonged to Liáoxī Commandery.
Suī,
read as xiāngwéi.
8 Sūn Quán attacked the mountain bandits at the Má and Bǎo strongholds,
and pacified them.
Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Jiāng River passes east of Lùkǒu,
and to the left is the mouth of Má Tún,
directly south of Púqí Isle,
with water entering north for over a hundred lǐ,
where Wú had stationed troops.
1 Spring,
second month,
Cáo Cāo returned to Yè from Chúnyú.
Dīngyǒu day,
Cáo memorialized to enfeoff over twenty great meritorious officials,
all as marquises;
he also submitted a report on the merits of Marquis of Wànsuìtíng, Xún Yù,
Jiǔyù Zhì states: Zhèngzhōu has Wànsuìtíng,
which was Yù's fief.
Yù's fief was increased by a thousand households.
Cáo also wanted to appoint him as one of the Three Excellencies,
but Yù sent Xún Yǒu to repeatedly decline on his behalf,
over ten times,
so it was stopped.
2 Cáo Cāo was about to attack the Wūhuán.
His generals all said:
"Yuán Shàng is but a fugitive,
and the barbarians are greedy and lack loyalty,
how could they be used by Shàng?
If we now campaign deep into their territory,
Liú Bèi will surely persuade Liú Biǎo to attack Xǔ,
and if anything changes,
it will be too late for regrets."
Guō Jiā said:
"Although Your Lordship's might shakes the realm,
the barbarians rely on their distance,
and will certainly not prepare defenses.
Taking advantage of their lack of preparation,
suddenly attacking them,
striking them,
they can be destroyed.
Moreover, Yuán Shào had favor among the people and barbarians,
and Shàng and his brothers still live.
The people of the four provinces
only submit out of fear,
and have not yet received your grace.
If we abandon them to campaign south,
Shàng will use the resources of the Wūhuán,
summoning those ministers loyal to the death to their lord,
meaning those who wish to die for their lord,
but have been stranded and unable to act.
Both people and barbarians will respond,
stirring Tàdùn's ambitions,
and forming covetous plans,
I fear Qīng and Jì will no longer be yours.
Biǎo is merely a sitting talker,
knowing his own talent is insufficient to control Bèi.
If he gives Bèi heavy responsibilities, he fears he cannot control him;
if he gives him light responsibilities, Bèi will not be of use.
Even if we empty the state for a distant campaign,
Your Lordship need not worry."
Cáo Cāo followed his advice.
When they reached Yì,
Yì County,
belonged to Zhuō Commandery in the Former Hàn,
and was abolished in the Later Hàn.
Sòng Bái states: The old city of Hàn Yì County
is fifteen lǐ southeast of Guīyì County in Zhuō Prefecture,
which is the old city of Dàyì.
"Speed is crucial in warfare.
Now we attack from a thousand lǐ away,
with much baggage,
it is hard to seize advantage.
Moreover, if they hear of it,
they will certainly prepare;
it is better to leave the baggage behind,
and send light troops by forced march,
catching them by surprise."
Initially,
Yuán Shào repeatedly sent envoys to summon Tián Chóu from Wúzhōng,
but Chóu defended Wúzhōng,
as seen in the fourth year of the Chūyuán era in scroll sixty.
The character "shuò"
is pronounced with the falling-rising tone.
The envoys were sent to pacify and govern the region,
but Chóu refused them all.
After Cáo Cāo pacified Jìzhōu,
Xíng Yóng from Héjiān said to Chóu:
"Since the Yellow Turban uprising began,
over twenty years have passed,
the realm has been in turmoil,
and the people have been displaced.
Now I hear that Lord Cáo's laws and decrees are strict.
The people are weary of chaos,
and when chaos reaches its peak, order returns.
I ask to lead by example."
He then packed his belongings and returned to his hometown.
Chóu remarked:
"Xíng Yóng
is one of Heaven's people who perceives things first."
Yī Yǐn said: I am
one of Heaven's people who perceives things first.
This is someone who takes responsibility for the Way.
As for Xíng Yóng's foresight,
it was merely recognizing the signs.
Chóu resented the Wūhuán for killing many of the prominent figures from his commandery,
referring to the distinguished scholars of the commandery.
Cáo sent an envoy to recruit Chóu,
and Chóu ordered his followers to quickly prepare for the journey.
His disciples said:
"In the past, Lord Yuán admired you,
sending invitations five times with ritual and command,
yet you upheld your principles and did not yield;
now Lord Cáo's envoy has come only once, and you act as if you fear missing the opportunity.
Why is that?"
Chóu smiled and said:
"This is not something you can understand."
He then followed the envoy to the army,
where he was appointed as the magistrate of Tiáo County.
Tiáo County
belonged to Xìndū in the Former Hàn
and to Bóhǎi in the Later Hàn.
Master Yán noted: Tiáo
is pronounced "tiáo."
At that time, it was summer with heavy rains,
and the coastal areas were low-lying,
muddy and impassable.
The enemy also blocked and guarded the narrow paths,
"xī" meaning
a path;
"xī yào" refers to
crucial points along the paths.
"Nìng"
is pronounced with the falling tone.
Cáo was troubled by this
and asked Tián Chóu about it.
Chóu said:
"This route
often has water in autumn and summer,
shallow enough to block carts and horses,
yet too deep for boats to navigate,
making it difficult for a long time.
The old Běipíng Commandery seat was at Pínggāng,
and the road passed through Lúlóng,
reaching Liǔchéng.
In the Former Hàn, the Right Běipíng Commandery seat was at Pínggāng County,
but in the Later Hàn, Pínggāng County was abolished,
and the seat was moved to Tǔyín County.
"Yín"
is pronounced "yín."
Xián noted: The old city of Tǔyín
is southwest of present-day Píngzhōu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: From Wúzhōng eastward, exiting the Lúlóng Pass,
then crossing east over Qīngxíng to Fánchéng is about two hundred li.
From Fánchéng heading northeast,
toward Pínggāng,
is about one hundred eighty li,
and toward Huánglóng is five hundred li.
Thus, Tián Chóu led his army out of Lúlóng Pass,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys,
for over five hundred li,
passing through Báitán,
traversing Pínggāng,
ascending Báiláng Mountain,
and overlooking Liǔchéng.
The road had collapsed and been cut off,
for nearly two hundred years,
yet there were still faint paths that could be followed.
Now the enemy expects the main army to come from Wúzhōng,
and if we cannot advance and retreat,
they will relax and be unprepared.
If we quietly turn the army around,
cross the treacherous Báitán from the Lúlóng Pass,
and emerge in an empty area,
the route is short and convenient,
allowing us to strike them unprepared.
Tàdùn can be captured without a battle."
Cáo said:
"Excellent!"
He then led the army back,
erecting large wooden markers by the roadside near the water, inscribed:
"Currently, it is summer and hot,
the roads are impassable.
We will wait until autumn or winter
to advance the army again."
The enemy scouts saw this
and truly believed the main army had left.
Cáo ordered Chóu to lead his men as guides,
ascending Xúwú Mountain.
The Correct Meaning of the Records of the Grand Historian states: Xúwú Mountain
is northwest of Xúwú County in Right Běipíng.
Xúwú Mountain
is where Tián Chóu gathered and defended his people.
For over five hundred li,
they passed through Báitán,
traversed Pínggāng,
and entered the territory of the Xiānbēi.
Báitán County
belonged to Right Běipíng Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: The old city of Báitán
is within the boundaries of Yànlè County in Tánzhōu.
At this time, the Xiānbēi territory was already within the boundaries of Right Běipíng Commandery,
likely the ancestors of Mùróng Huī.
"Qiàn"
is pronounced with the falling-rising tone.
When they were less than two hundred li away,
the enemy became aware of them.
Yuán Shàng, Yuán Xī, along with Tàdùn, the Chányú of Liáoxī Lóu Bān,
Lóu Bān,
son of Qiū Lìjū,
and the Chányú of Right Běipíng, named Wū Yán.
Néngchén Dǐzhī,
perhaps another name for Wū Yán!
In the eighth month,
Cáo ascended Báiláng Mountain.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Báiláng Mountain
is west of Shíchéng County in Right Běipíng.
The Account of the Wūhuán states: They fought at Fánchéng,
so Báiláng Mountain is likely in Fánchéng.
The enemy forces were very numerous.
Cáo's supply wagons were behind,
"chē zhòng" meaning
the supply wagons.
"Zhòng"
is pronounced with the falling tone.
Those around him were all afraid.
Cáo climbed to a high point,
saw the enemy formation was disorganized,
and then unleashed his troops to attack,
with Zhāng Liáo as the vanguard.
The enemy forces collapsed completely,
and Tàdùn and other renowned chieftains were beheaded.
Over two hundred thousand Hú and Hàn people surrendered.
The Chányú of Liáodōng, Sù Púwán,
Sù Púwán,
also known as Sū Púyán,
with slight variations in pronunciation.
still had several thousand cavalry.
Some urged Cáo to attack them,
but Cáo said:
"I have already ordered Gōngsūn Kāng to behead and send the heads of Shàng and Xī.
There is no need to trouble the troops."
In the ninth month,
Cáo led his army back from Liǔchéng.
Gōngsūn Kāng wanted to capture Shàng and Xī to claim merit,
so he first placed elite soldiers in hiding,
then invited Shàng and Xī to enter.
Before they could sit down,
Kāng shouted, and the hidden soldiers captured them.
He then beheaded Shàng and Xī,
and sent their heads along with Sù Púwán's head.
Some generals asked Cáo:
"You returned, and Kāng beheaded Shàng and Xī.
Why?"
Cáo said:
"They have always feared Shàng and Xī.
If I pressured them, they would unite forces;
if I eased off, they would plot against each other.
That is the natural course of things."
Cáo displayed Shàng's head,
ordering the three armies:
"Anyone who dares to mourn him will be executed!"
Only Qiān Zhāo set up a memorial and wept in sorrow.
Qiān Zhāo had previously served the Yuán family,
hence he mourned them.
He was recommended as a Màocái.
3. Initially, Gān Níng of Bājùn, leading eight hundred retainers and followers, submitted to Liú Biǎo.
(Gān Níng's flight to Jīngzhōu and service there is recorded in the 61st scroll, under the first year of the Xīngpíng era.)
(Liú Biǎo) was not versed in military affairs.
Gān Níng, observing the situation under Biǎo, concluded it would ultimately achieve nothing.
Fearing that one day the multitude would scatter,
and he would suffer calamity along with them,
he thought, "If they are gathered but not used, calamity is sure to arrive."
Huáng Zǔ was at Xiàkǒu.
(Yìng Shào said: The Miǎn River, branching off from Jiāngxià to reach Huáróng in Nánjùn, becomes the Xià River,
passing through Jiāngxiàjùn and entering the Yangtze.
Thus, the place where the Xià River enters the Yangtze is called Xiàkǒu.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said: Xiàkǒu is also called Miǎnkǒu, or sometimes Lǔkǒu.
The "Commentary on the Waterways Classic" says: The Miǎn River flows south to the north of Shāyí County in Jiāngxià,
then enters the Yangtze from the south.
Therefore, it is called Xiàkǒu from the Xià River;
called Miǎnkǒu from the Miǎn River;
called Lǔkǒu from Lǔ Mountain;
but it is actually one place.
Its location was north of the river.
After Sūn Quán established the Xiàkǒu Commandant,
stationed south of the river, it became the seat of present-day Èzhōu.
Thus, Hé Shàngzhī said: Xiàkǒu is in the middle of the Jīng River,
directly opposite Miǎnkǒu.
The commentary by Lǐ Xián also states that the Xiàkǒu garrison was in present-day Èzhōu.
Consequently, it was conventionally accepted that Èzhōu was Xiàkǒu,
and the Xiàkǒu north of the river faded into obscurity.)
So (Gān Níng) stayed,
attaching himself to Zǔ for three years,
but Zǔ treated him as an ordinary person.
When Sūn Quán attacked Zǔ,
Zǔ's army was defeated and fled.
Quán's Commandant Líng Cāo led troops in urgent pursuit.
(The "Surname Genealogy" states: A collateral descendant of Wèi Kāngshū served as the "Língrén" for the Zhōu, and his descendants took this as their surname.)
(Gān Níng), leading troops at the rear,
shot and killed Cāo,
enabling Zǔ to escape.
After the battle ended,
(Zǔ) returned to camp,
but treated Níng as before, without special regard.
Zǔ's Commander Sū Fēi repeatedly recommended Níng,
but Zǔ did not employ him.
Níng wished to leave,
but feared he might not escape harm.
Fēi then informed Zǔ,
appointing Níng as the Chief of Zhū County.
(Zhū County belonged to Jiāngxiàjùn.
The "Records of Geographical Administration" states: Chǔ destroyed Zhū and moved its ruler here.
Lǐ Xián said: The old city of Zhū was east of present-day Jìnglíng County in Fùzhōu.
Fēi likely opened a path for him to flee to Wú.)
(Chief: pronounced zhǎng.)
(Sòng Bái said: Huángzhōu was the Hàn dynasty's Zhū County.)
(The "Examination of Discrepancies" states: In the "Chronicles of Wú," the biography of Sūn Quán records campaigns against Huáng Zǔ in both the eighth and twelfth years of the Jiàn'ān era.
The biography of Líng Tǒng states that when his father Cāo died, Tǒng was fifteen and took over his father's troops.
Later, he attacked Má Bǎo's camp and stabbed Chén Qín to death.
According to the biographies of Zhōu Yú and Sūn Yú, they attacked Má Bǎo's camp in the eleventh year.
Thus, Cāo's death seems to have been in the eighth year.
However, Níng fled to Quán five years later, which seems rather late.
As there is no specific year or month to rely on now, it is mentioned retrospectively.)
Quán treated him with exceptional courtesy,
equal to that of his veteran ministers.
Gān Níng presented a strategy to Quán, saying:
"Now the Hàn dynasty's fortune declines daily,
and Cáo Cāo will ultimately become a usurping thief.
The lands of southern Jīngzhōu,
with their advantageous mountains and rivers,
are truly the western strategic position for our state."
(Meaning it lies to the west of Wú, occupying the strategic upper reaches.)
"Liú Biǎo's foresight is not far-reaching,
and his sons are inferior."
(Meaning they are even weaker than Biǎo.)
"Your Majesty should plan for this early,
and not lag behind Cáo Cāo."
(Meaning if you do not first plan against Liú Biǎo, you will surely be outmaneuvered by Cáo Cāo.)
(Lag behind: hòu, pronounced hòu.)
"It would be appropriate to first capture Huáng Zǔ.
Zǔ is now extremely aged and muddled,
both wealth and grain are lacking,
his close associates are greedy and unrestrained,
officials and soldiers resentful in heart,
boats and war equipment
are neglected and unrepaired."
(Neglected: dùn, meaning ruined.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says: 'armor and weapons are not dùn.'
Dùn is pronounced dùn.)
"The army lacks regulations and organization.
If Your Majesty advances now,
his defeat is certain.
Once Zǔ's army is broken,
we can advance westward with drums beating,
seize the Chǔ Pass."
(The Chǔ Pass is the Hàn Pass.
When Shǔ attacked Chǔ, Chǔ built the Hàn Pass to resist them, hence it is called the Chǔ Pass.)
"Then we can gradually plan for Bā and Shǔ."
Quán deeply accepted his advice.
Zhāng Zhāo, who was present at the time, objected, saying:
"Now in Wú, affairs are precarious.
If the army truly marches,
I fear it will certainly lead to disorder."
Níng said to Zhāo:
"The state has entrusted you with a responsibility like that of Xiāo Hé.
You reside here guarding (the capital) yet worry about disorder—how can you aspire to emulate the ancients!"
(His words certainly had their appropriateness; Zhāng Zhāo could not refute them with forceful rhetoric.)
(Guard: shǒu, pronounced shǒu.)
(Sūn Quán said:) "Xìngbà"
(Gān Níng, courtesy name Xìngbà.)
(Entrust: shǔ, pronounced shǔ.)
"This matter is like this wine—I have decided to entrust it to you.
You should only strive to devise strategies,
ensuring we must defeat Zǔ.
Then your achievement—
why be concerned about Chief Clerk Zhāng's words!"
(Zhāng Zhāo was Quán's Chief Clerk.)
Quán's words here both encouraged Gān Níng's spirit and preserved Zhāng Zhāo's dignity.
If there were no stayers, who would guard the altars of state?
If there were no goers, who would defend the pastures and borders?
(Chief: zhǎng, pronounced zhǎng.)

this would be the foundation for an imperial enterprise.
Now Liú Biǎo has recently died,
his two sons are not in harmony,
and the various generals in the army

Some are said to support Liú Qí,
others support Liú Cóng.
Liú Bèi is at odds with Cáo Cāo,

'divided and at odds'

Liú Bèi and Zhōu Yú advanced by water and land simultaneously,

At that time, Cáo's army was also plagued by famine and disease,

(The title Héngyě Dàjiāngjūn was first bestowed by Emperor Guāngwǔ upon Wáng Cháng.

He went,

The Yìzhōu general Xí Sù surrendered with his entire army.

Xí,

“Sù is courageous and capable,

Líng Tǒng,

Examination of discrepancies says: In the Wèi Zhì, Wǔ Jì,

He did not succeed.

Jiǎng Gàn,

the same below.

following the precedent of Xiāo Hé.
2 When Cáo Cāo was on his western campaign,
the people of Héjiān, Tián Yín and Sū Bó, rebelled,
inciting Yōuzhōu and Jìzhōu.
The General of the Five Offices, Cáo Pī, wanted to lead a campaign against them himself,
but the Merit Official Cháng Lín said:
According to Cháng Lín's biography,
he was then Merit Official to the General of the Five Offices.
"The officials and people of the north,
are content with peace and weary of turmoil,
having long submitted to transformation,
with many upholding goodness;
Yín and Bó are like dogs and sheep gathering together,
unable to cause harm.
Now the main army is far away,
with strong enemies abroad,
the General is the pillar of the realm,
meaning he remained in Yè.
Even if victorious, it would not be glorious."
So he sent General Jiǎ Xìn to suppress them,
and they were promptly defeated and eliminated.
The remaining rebels, over a thousand, requested to surrender.
The advisors all said:
"The Duke has an old rule,
those who surrender only after being besieged are not pardoned."
Chéng Yù said:
"That was during times of turmoil,
a temporary expedient.
Now the realm is largely pacified,
they should not be executed;
even if executing them,
it should first be reported."
The advisors all said:
"In military matters, one may act on authority without requesting permission."
Chéng Yù said:
"Acting on authority is for urgent situations.
It refers to emergencies.
Now these rebels are under Jiǎ Xìn's control,
so this old minister does not wish the General to proceed."
Cáo Pī said:
"Well said."
He immediately reported to Cáo Cāo,
and Cáo Cāo indeed did not execute them.
Later, hearing of Chéng Yù's counsel,
he was greatly pleased,
and said:
"You are not only wise in military strategy,
but also adept at handling relations between father and son."
This praised Cáo Pī for not arbitrarily killing.
Chǔ,
pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
According to precedent: reports on defeating rebels,
multiplied numbers by ten;
but Guó Yuān reported heads taken,
all according to the actual count,
Guó Yuān was then in charge of留守 affairs.
Shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
Guó Yuān said:
"When campaigning against external foes,
inflating the numbers killed or captured
is to magnify military achievements,
and impress the people.
Héjiān is within our borders,
Yín and others rebelled,
though victorious and meritorious,
I privately feel ashamed."
Cáo Cāo was greatly pleased.
3 In summer,
fifth month,
on the guǐwèi day,
Commandant of the Guards Mǎ Téng was executed,
and his clan exterminated.
Mǎ Téng went to Yè; see the thirteenth year of the previous volume.
4 In the sixth month,
on the gēngyín day, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
5 In autumn,
seventh month,
there was a plague of locusts.
6 The remaining forces of Mǎ Chāo and others were stationed in Lántián,
and Xiàhóu Yuān attacked and pacified them.
The bandit Liáng Xīng from Fū County
Fū County,
belonged to Zuǒ Féngyì in the Former Hàn,
and was abolished in the Later Hàn.
Shī Gǔ said: Fū,
is pronounced fū.
The various counties were terrified,
and all sought refuge in the commandery seat.
Some advisors suggested moving to a more defensible location.
Zuǒ Féngyì Zhèng Hún said:
"Xīng and his followers are defeated and scattered,
hiding in the mountains and valleys.
Although some follow him,
they are mostly coerced.
Now we should widely open the path to surrender,
proclaim our authority and credibility,
but if we fortify ourselves and defend,
this shows weakness."
He then gathered officials and people,
repaired the city walls,
and prepared defenses.
He recruited people to pursue the bandits,
allowing them to keep
seventy percent of the captured property and women.
The people were greatly pleased,
and all were willing to capture bandits;
bandits who had lost their wives and children all returned,
seeking to surrender.
Zhèng Hún demanded they return other captured women,
and only then allowed them to surrender.
Thus, they turned to plundering each other,
and their factions disintegrated.
He also sent trusted officials and civilians to spread throughout the mountains and valleys to persuade them,
and those who came out surrendered one after another;
he then ordered the county magistrates to return to their posts,
to pacify and settle the people.
Liáng Xīng and others became fearful,
gathering their remaining followers at Fū City.
Cáo Cāo sent Xiàhóu Yuān to assist Zhèng Hún in attacking them,
and they beheaded Liáng Xīng,
pacifying the remaining followers.
Zhèng Hún
was the younger brother of Zhèng Tài.
Zhèng Tài,
was employed by Dǒng Zhuó but plotted against him.
7 In the ninth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
the emperor's son Xī was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìyīn,
Yì as the Prince of Shānyáng,
Miǎo as the Prince of Jìběi,
and Dūn as the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
At that time, Xǔ Jìng was in Shǔ,
and upon hearing about the enfeoffment of the princes,
said:
"If you wish to close something,
you must first open it;
if you wish to take something away,
you must first give it.
This must refer to Mèngdé."
Jì,
is pronounced zǐlǐ.
8 Earlier,
Zhāng Hóng, considering Mòlíng's advantageous terrain,
advised Sūn Quán to make it his capital;
when Liú Bèi passed through Mòlíng to the east,
he also advised Quán to reside there.
Quán then built Shítóu City,
moved his capital to Mòlíng,
and renamed Mòlíng as Jiànyè.
Mòlíng,
belonged to Dānyáng Commandery,
originally called Jīnlíng,
renamed by Qín Shǐhuáng;
Sūn Quán renamed it Jiànyè;
later, to avoid the taboo of Jìn Mǐndì's name,
it was renamed Jiànkāng.
Shítóu City,
was located two lǐ west of present-day Jiànkāng.
According to the Jīnlíng Zhì: Shítóu City was nine lǐ from Táichéng,
and to the south, it joined the Qínhuái River.
Zhāng Shùnmín said: Shítóu City,
is a naturally formed city wall,
resembling a city,
located on Fùzhōu Mountain north of Qīngliáng Temple.
Those traveling by river from the north
follow Shítóu City,
and turn into the Qínhuái River.
Lù Yóu said: From Lóngwān, looking at Shítóu Mountain,
it is not very high,
but it stands steeply in the river,
winding like a wall.
Qīngliáng Temple is about a lǐ from Shítóu,
and to the west, one can see Xuānhuà Crossing and the mountains of Lìyáng.
Sòng Bái said: After Jìn conquered Wú,
it was divided into two towns,
with the area south of the Huái River called Mòlíng,
and north called Jiànyè.
According to the Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn: Zhāng Hóng said to Quán:
"Mòlíng,
was established by King Wǔ of Chǔ,
and named Jīnlíng;
its terrain consists of ridges connecting to Shítóu.
In the past, when Qín Shǐhuáng toured east,
he passed through this county,
and those who observed the aura said,
the topography of Jīnlíng
had the aura of an imperial capital,
so he ordered the ridges to be dug through,
and renamed it Mòlíng.
Now the site remains intact,
making it suitable for a capital."
The Xiàndì Chūnqiū also records Quán saying:
"Mòlíng has a small river over a hundred lǐ long,
which can accommodate large ships.
I am currently organizing a navy,
and should move to occupy it."
According to the Jìn Shū, Xī Lóng's biography,
when Xī Lóng was the Governor of Yángzhōu,
he garrisoned Mòlíng.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng issued an order to attack Zhào Wáng Lún,
Xī Lóng withheld the order and did not act.
At that time, Wáng Suì garrisoned Shítóu,
and many of Xī Lóng's troops went west to join Suì.
Xī Lóng sent an official to Niúzhǔ to stop them,
but failed.
The officers and soldiers supported Suì and attacked and killed Xī Lóng.
Thus, Shítóu was west of Niúzhǔ.
Examining this matter in detail,
the troops from Mòlíng intended to join Suì,
wanting to go west from Niúzhǔ to support the king;
Shítóu was actually east of Niúzhǔ.
9 Lǚ Méng heard that Cáo Cāo intended to send troops east,
and advised Sūn Quán to build a fortress at the mouth of the Rúxū River.
The generals all said:
"We go ashore to attack the enemy,
wash our feet, and board the ships.
What use is a fortress?"
Lǚ Méng said:
"In war, there are advantages and disadvantages,
and no one wins every battle.
If we encounter the enemy unexpectedly,
and their infantry and cavalry press close,
we may not have time to reach the water.
How could we board the ships then?"
Quán said:
"Well said!"
They then built the Rúxū Fortress.
In the tenth year, winter,
the tenth month,
Cáo Cāo marched east to attack Sūn Quán.
Dǒng Zhāo spoke to Cáo Cāo, saying:
"Since ancient times,
when ministers have restored order to the world,
none have achieved the merit of today;
and even those who achieved such merit
have never long remained in the position of a minister.
Now, Your Excellency is ashamed of any deficiency in virtue,
and delights in preserving your reputation and integrity;
yet, occupying the position of a high minister,
you cause people to suspect you of great ambitions.
This is truly something that must be deeply considered."
He then deliberated with the various marquises and generals,
proposing that the Chancellor should be advanced to the rank of Duke of a State,
with the Nine Bestowals and full regalia,
to manifest his extraordinary achievements.
Xián said: The Rites, Hán Wén Jiā states: The Nine Bestowals are:
first, chariots and horses;
second, robes and garments;
third, musical instruments;
fourth, vermilion gates;
fifth, inner palace steps;
sixth, one hundred tiger warriors;
seventh, axes and yue-axes;
eighth, bows and arrows;
ninth, black millet wine and aromatic herbs.
These are called the Nine Bestowals.
'Bestowal'
means to grant;
the Nine Bestowals all correspond to one's virtue.

The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: [The king] divided with the Duke of Lǔ the grand carriage, the grand banner, the jade of the Xià Hòu clan, Fēngfù's powerful bow, the masters of prayer and ancestral rites, the diviners and historians, the complete regalia and canonical writings.
"Cáo Gōng originally raised righteous troops to support the court and pacify the state,
holding to the sincerity of loyalty and steadfastness,
maintaining the substance of humility and deference.
A gentleman loves others with virtue."
The Record, Tángōng:
Zēngzǐ said: "A gentleman loves others with virtue;
a petty person loves others with indulgence."
Cáo Cāo was displeased by this.
When he attacked Sūn Quán,
he submitted a memorial requesting that Xún Yù encourage the army at Qiáo,
and thereupon detained Xún Yù,
appointing him as Palace Attendant, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Credential Bearer, and Consultant in the Chancellor's Military Affairs.
'Thereupon'
means acting on his own authority.
Xún Yù, due to illness, remained at Shòuchūn,
drank poison, and died.
Xún Yù's biography states: Cáo Cāo sent him food;
upon opening it,
it was an empty vessel.
Thereupon he drank poison and died.
An examination of discrepancies says: Chén Shòu's biography of Xún Yù in the Records states:
"He died of grief."
Fàn Yè's biography of Xún Yù in the Book of the Later Hàn states:
"Cáo Cāo sent him food;
upon opening it,
it was an empty vessel.
Thereupon he drank poison and died."
Sūn Shèng's Wèi Shì Chūnqiū also says the same.
Considering Xún Yù's death,
Cáo Cāo concealed the execution.
Chén Shòu says he died of grief,
likely leaving the matter in doubt.
If we do not now correctly state that he drank poison,
I fear that rulers in later generations
might think that concealed executions can be carried out.
He was fond of recommending worthy men and advancing scholars,
therefore people of the time all lamented his death.
Your subject Guāng says: Confucius's words on benevolence are weighty.
From disciples of high standing like Zǐlù, Rǎn Qiú, and Gōngxī Chì,
to worthy ministers of the feudal lords like Lìngyǐn Zǐwén and Chén Wénzǐ,
none were sufficient to be deemed so,
yet he uniquely praised Guǎn Zhòng's benevolence.
Was it not because he assisted Duke Huán of Qí,
greatly benefiting the common people?
The Analects: Mèng Wǔbó asked:
"Is Zǐlù benevolent?"
The Master said:
"I do not know."
He asked again.
The Master said:
"Yóu,
in a state of a thousand war chariots,
could be entrusted with its military administration,
but I do not know about his benevolence."
"What about Qiú?"
He said:
"Qiú,
in a town of a thousand households or a noble house with a hundred chariots,
could be made its steward,
but I do not know about his benevolence."
"What about Chì?"
He said:
"Chì,
girded with his sash and standing in court,
could be entrusted to converse with guests,
but I do not know about his benevolence."
Zǐzhāng asked:
"Lìngyǐn Zǐwén
thrice took office as Prime Minister
without a look of pleasure;
thrice was dismissed
without a look of resentment.
He invariably reported the affairs of the former administration
to the incoming Prime Minister.
What would you say of him?"
The Master said:
"He was loyal."
"Was he benevolent?"
The Master said:
"I do not know.
How could he be deemed benevolent?"
"When Cuīzǐ assassinated the ruler of Qí,
Chén Wénzǐ, who possessed ten teams of horses,
abandoned them and left the state.
Arriving at another state,
he said, 'They are like our high official Cuīzǐ,' and left it.
He went to yet another state,
and again said, 'They are like our high official Cuīzǐ,' and left it.
What would you say of him?"
The Master said:
"He was pure."
"Was he benevolent?"
The Master said:
"I do not know.
How could he be deemed benevolent?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Was Guǎn Zhòng not benevolent?
Duke Huán killed Prince Jiǔ,
yet Guǎn Zhòng did not die for him,
and moreover became his minister."
The Master said:
"Guǎn Zhòng served as minister to Duke Huán,
made him leader of the feudal lords,
and united and corrected the whole realm.
Down to the present day, the people enjoy his gifts.
But for Guǎn Zhòng,
we should now be wearing our hair unbound and folding our robes to the left!
Must he have been like some ordinary man or woman,
sticking to his small fidelity,
and strangling himself in a ditch without anyone knowing?"
Zǐlù said:
"When Duke Huán killed Prince Jiǔ,
Shào Hū died for him,
but Guǎn Zhòng did not.
May I say he was not benevolent?"
The Master said:
"Duke Huán nine times assembled the feudal lords
without resorting to war chariots,
and this was all due to Guǎn Zhòng!
Such was his benevolence!
Such was his benevolence!"
Guǎn Zhòng was not ashamed to serve as his minister;
his intention was likely that, without Duke Huán, the people could not have been saved.
At the end of the Hàn, there was great disorder,
the people were in dire distress,
and unless one possessed talent surpassing the age, one could not save them.
If so, then whom could Xún Yù have served if not Cáo Cāo?
In the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
though the Zhōu house had declined,
it was not like the beginning of the Jiàn'ān era.
At the beginning of Jiàn'ān,
the whole realm was in turmoil and collapse;
not an inch of land nor a single person
truly belonged to the Hàn.
Xún Yù assisted Cáo Cāo in reviving it:
he recommended the worthy and employed the capable,
trained soldiers and sharpened weapons,
decided on strategies and devised plans,
and in his campaigns was victorious on all sides.
Thus he was able to turn weakness into strength,
transform chaos into order,
and gain possession of eight-tenths of the realm.
How could his merit be inferior to that of Guǎn Zhòng?
Guǎn Zhòng did not die for Prince Jiǔ, yet Xún Yù died for the Hàn house.
His benevolence indeed surpasses that of Guǎn Zhòng!
Yet Dù Mù believed that
"When Xún Yù advised Cáo Cāo to seize Yǎnzhōu, he compared him to Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ;
at Guāndù, he urged him not to retreat to Xǔ, comparing the situation to the conflict between Chǔ and Hàn;
but once the task was accomplished and merits achieved,
he sought fame in the Hàn court.
This is like teaching a thief to dig through walls and open chests, yet refusing to share the loot—
how can one not be considered a thief?"
I believe that Confucius said,
"When refinement prevails over substance, it becomes mere ornamentation,"
as seen in the Analects.
There must be a reason for such embellishment.
Thus, comparing Cáo Cāo to Gāozǔ, Guāngwǔ, Chǔ, and Hàn
is merely the historian's embellishment;
how could all of it have been spoken by Xún Yù himself?
To criticize Xún Yù based on this
is unjust.
Moreover, if Cáo Cāo had become emperor,
then Xún Yù would have been a founding minister,
rewarded like Xiāo Hé;
why would Xún Yù seek fame through martyrdom instead of benefiting from this?
Is this in line with human nature?
11 In the twelfth month,
a comet appeared near the Five Feudal Lords.
The Astronomical Records of the Jìn dynasty state: The Five Feudal Lords are five stars
located north of the Eastern Well constellation.
Also, in the southern part of the Supreme Enclosure,
northeast of the Left Lawmaker star is a star called the Usher;
northeast of the Usher are three stars called the Three Dukes;
north of the Three Dukes are three stars called the Nine Ministers;
west of the Nine Ministers are five stars called the Inner Five Feudal Lords,
who serve the Son of Heaven closely
and do not govern feudal states.
Comet,
pronounced pú nèi fān.
12 Liú Bèi was at Jiāméng,
when Páng Tǒng advised him, saying:
"Now, secretly select elite troops,
march day and night,
and directly attack Chéngdū.
Liú Zhāng is neither martial
nor prepared,
so when our army suddenly arrives,
we can secure victory in one move—
this is the superior plan.
Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi,
Zhāng's renowned generals,
each command strong troops
and guard the pass—
that is, the Báishuǐ Pass.
They have been ordered to send you back to Jīngzhōu.
Send them a message,
saying that Jīngzhōu is in crisis
and you must return to rescue it,
and also prepare your baggage,
pretending to depart.
These two, admiring your reputation
and pleased by your departure,
will surely ride lightly to meet you.
Seize them then,
take their troops,
and advance toward Chéngdū—
this is the middle plan.
Retreat to Báidì,
Báidì,
which is the city of Yúfù County in Bādōng.
Gōngsūn Shù occupied Chéngdū,
proclaimed himself the White Emperor,
and renamed Yúfù as Báidì City.
Then slowly plan your next move—
this is the inferior plan.
If you hesitate and do not act,
you will face great peril,
and it will not last long."
Bèi approved the middle plan.
When Cáo Cāo attacked Sūn Quán,
Quán called for Bèi to rescue him.
Bèi wrote to Zhāng, saying:
"The Sūn clan and I are as close as lips and teeth,
and Guān Yǔ's troops are weak.
If I do not go to rescue them now,
Cáo Cāo will surely take Jīngzhōu,
then invade our borders—
the borders,
meaning the borders of Yìzhōu.
Lǔ is a mere defensive bandit,
not worth worrying about."
He then requested ten thousand additional troops and supplies,
but Zhāng only granted four thousand troops,
and the rest were given half.
Bèi thus incited his troops, saying:
"I am fighting a powerful enemy for Yìzhōu,
and the army is weary,
yet wealth is hoarded and rewards withheld.
How can we make the officers fight to the death?"
Zhāng Sōng wrote to Bèi and Fǎ Zhèng, saying:
"Now, great matters are about to be accomplished;
how can you abandon this and leave?"
Sōng's elder brother, Sù, the governor of Guǎnghàn,
fearing disaster would befall him,
exposed the plot.
Thus, Zhāng arrested and executed Sōng,
and ordered the border garrison commanders to cease all communication with Bèi.
Bèi was furious,
summoned Zhāng's Báishuǐ army commanders Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi,
accused them of disrespect,
and executed them—
blaming them for lacking the etiquette of host and guest.
He took their troops,
advanced, and occupied Fúchéng.
This was the implementation of Páng Tǒng's middle plan.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Cáo Cāo advanced his army to Rúxū Pass,
claiming four hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
and attacked and destroyed Sūn Quán's Jiāngxī camp.
The Great River flows northeast,
so from Lìyáng to Rúxū Pass is called Jiāngxī,
while Jiànyè is called Jiāngdōng.
Quán led seventy thousand troops to resist him,
and they faced off for over a month.
Cáo saw his ships, weapons, and troops in orderly formation,
and sighed, saying:
"To have a son, one should have one like Sūn Zhòngmóu;
Sūn Quán,
styled Zhòngmóu.
The rest are but pigs and dogs!"
Quán sent a letter to Cáo,
saying:
"Spring floods are rising;
you should leave quickly."
On a separate note, he added:
"As long as you live,
I cannot rest easy."
Cáo told his generals:
"Sūn Quán does not deceive me."
He then withdrew his army and returned.
2 On the Gēngyín day,
an edict was issued to merge the fourteen provinces
back into the nine provinces.
The fourteen provinces were:
Sī, Yù, Jì, Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, Jīng, Yáng, Yì, Liáng, Yōng, Bìng, Yōu, and Jiāo.
To restore the nine provinces:
the Hédōng, Hénèi, Féngyì, and Fúfēng regions of Sīzhōu, along with Yōu and Bìng provinces, were merged into Jìzhōu;
the territories under Liángzhōu
were entirely incorporated into Yōngzhōu,
and the Jīngzhào region of Sīzhōu was added to it;
the Hóngnóng and Hénán regions of Sīzhōu were merged into Yùzhōu;
Jiāozhōu was incorporated into Jīngzhōu,
thus abolishing Sī, Liáng, Yōu, and Bìng provinces and restoring the nine provinces of the Yu Gong.
This was Cáo Cāo, as the governor of Jìzhōu,
seeking to expand his control to dominate the realm.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
Cáo Cāo arrived at Yè.
4. Initially,
when Cáo Cāo was in Qiáo,
he feared that the commanderies and counties along the river would be plundered by Sūn Quán,
and wanted to relocate the people inland.
He asked Jiǎng Jì, the Assistant Inspector of Yángzhōu,
saying:
"In the past, when I faced Yuán Běnchū (Yuán Shào) at Guāndù,
I relocated the people of Yān and Báimǎ,
and the people did not flee,
nor did the bandits dare to raid.
The event is recorded in the 63rd scroll, in the fifth year of the Jiàn'ān era.
Yān County and Báimǎ County
both belonged to Dōng Commandery.
Yān
was the state of Nányān during the Spring and Autumn period.
Xián (Lǐ Xián) said: The old city of Yān is present-day Zuòchéng County in Huá Prefecture.
Raid (chāo),
pronounced as in Chǔjiāo fān.
Yān,
pronounced Yúxián fān.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"At that time, our troops were weak and the bandits were strong;
if we had not relocated them, we would certainly have lost them.
Since defeating Yuán Shào,
your prestige has shaken the world,
and the people have no other intentions.
People are attached to their native land,
and truly do not wish to relocate;
I fear they will certainly become unsettled."
Cáo Cāo did not listen.
Soon afterward, the people panicked and spread rumors among themselves,
and from Lújiāng, Jiǔjiāng, Qíchūn, and Guǎnglíng,
over a hundred thousand households all crossed the river eastward.
Qíchūn County
originally belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery.
Shěn Yuē said: Wú established Qíchūn Commandery.
This is recorded according to the Wúzhì.
Qí,
pronounced Qí.
South of Héféi,
only Wǎnchéng remained.
Wǎn County
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery.
Xián (Lǐ Xián) said: Present-day Huáiníng County in Shū Prefecture.
Shīgǔ (Yán Shīgǔ) said: Wǎn,
pronounced Húguǎn fān.
Cáo Cāo met them and
laughed heartily, saying:
"I originally only wanted them to avoid the bandits,
but instead I drove them all away!"
He appointed Jì as the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
Dānyáng Commandery had already been taken by Sūn Quán,
so Jì could not take up his post.
5. In the fifth month,
on Bǐngshēn,
Cáo Cāo was enfeoffed as Duke of Wèi with ten commanderies of Jìzhōu.
At that time, the ten commanderies of Jìzhōu—Hédōng, Hénèi, Wèi, Zhàoguó, Zhōngshān, Chángshān, Jùlù, Ānpíng, Gānlíng, and Píngyuán—were made the state of Wèi.
He was also granted the Nine Bestowments: one grand carriage and one war chariot each;
two teams of black stallions;
ceremonial robes with embroidered dragons and caps;
with red ceremonial shoes to match;
Máo Cháng said: Red shoes (chìxì)
are the grand shoes of a ruler;
explaining xì,
they are double-layered shoes.
Zhèng Xuán said: Shoes with double soles are called xì.
Zhèng Zhòng said: There are three grades of xì,
with red xì being the highest,
worn with ceremonial robes and caps.
A dance of six rows;
according to the Zhōulǐ: The arrangement of musical instruments,
for the king, it is a full set on all four sides;
for feudal lords, it is on three sides.
Zhèng Zhòng said: A full set means
instruments are hung on all four sides;
a three-sided set means
one side is omitted.
Xuán,
read as "hung."
The number of dancers in rows,
for the Son of Heaven, it is eight;
for feudal lords, it is six.
Dù Yù said: Eight rows
means eight times eight, sixty-four people;
six rows
means six times six, thirty-six people.
Fú Qiān said: For the Son of Heaven, it is eight by eight;
for feudal lords, it is six by eight;
for ministers, it is four by eight;
for officers, it is two by eight.
Fù Lóng of Sòng said: When the Earl of Zhèng presented Duke Dào of Jìn with female musicians in two groups of eight,
Jìn gave one group of eight to Wèi Jiàng.
This is evidence that music is performed in rows of eight.
Yì,
pronounced yì.
Steps were built for ascending;
three hundred tiger warriors;
one battle-axe and one ceremonial axe each;
one vermilion bow,
one hundred vermilion arrows;
ten black bows,
one thousand black arrows;
black (lú) is the same as lú,
meaning black in color.
A jade tablet and a jade ladle to match.
6. Heavy rain fell.
7. Zhèng Dù, an Attendant Officer of Yìzhōu from Guànghàn, heard that Liú Bèi had raised troops,
and said to Liú Zhāng:
"The General of the Left (Liú Bèi) has led his army on a distant campaign to attack us,
with fewer than ten thousand troops,
his soldiers are not yet loyal to him,
his army lacks supplies,
and relies on wild grains for sustenance.
The best plan is to drive all the people of Bāxī and Zǐtóng west of the Fú River inland,
Zǐtóng County
belonged to Guànghàn Commandery,
established in the first year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
named for the county's reliance on the Zǐ Forest and proximity to the Tóng River;
in the twenty-second year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Liú Bèi separately established Zǐtóng Commandery.
According to Bān Zhì,
Zǐtóng has the Wǔfù Mountain,
from which the Tuó River flows,
south into the Fú River.
Yìng Shào said: The Fú River flows from Guànghàn,
south into the Hàn River.
The Shuǐjīng says: The Fú River flows from the northwest of Fú County in Guànghàn,
east to Guànghàn, where it merges with the Zǐtóng River,
then flows southwest,
and then south into Diànjiāng.
The annotation says: The Fú River flows from beyond the border of Gāngdī Circuit in the Guànghàn Dependent State;
the Zǐtóng River is the Wǔfù River,
both flow into Diànjiāng,
which is the so-called inner river.
Burn everything,
build high ramparts and deep ditches,
and wait calmly.
When they arrive,
if they request battle,
do not allow it.
After a long time without supplies,
within a hundred days at most,
they will certainly retreat on their own.
When they retreat, attack them,
and they will surely be captured."
Liú Bèi heard of this and disliked it,
so he asked Fǎ Zhèng about it.
Zhèng said:
"Liú Zhāng will never use it,
so there is no need to worry."
Liú Zhāng indeed said to his subordinates:
"I have heard of resisting the enemy to protect the people,
but I have never heard of disturbing the people to avoid the enemy."
He did not adopt Dù's plan.
Liú Zhāng sent his generals Liú Guī, Lěng Bāo, Zhāng Rèn, Dèng Xián, Wú Yì, and others to resist Liú Bèi,
but they were all defeated,
and retreated to defend Fú;
Yì went to the army and surrendered.
Liú Zhāng again sent the Protector of the Army, Lǐ Yán of Nányáng, and Fèi Guān of Jiāngxià to supervise the armies at Fú,
but Yán and Guān also led their troops to surrender to Liú Bèi.
Liú Bèi's army grew stronger,
and he dispatched his generals to pacify the subordinate counties.
Liú Guī, Zhāng Rèn, and Liú Zhāng's son Liú Xún retreated to defend Luòchéng.
Luò County
belonged to Guànghàn Commandery,
from which the Luò River flows;
in the Táng dynasty, it was the seat of Hàn Prefecture.
Rèn led his troops out to battle at Yàn Bridge,
Yàn River,
south of Luò County,
where there was once a golden wild goose,
hence the name Yàn Bridge.
Rèn died.
8. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wèi began to establish its altars of soil and grain and ancestral temples.
9. Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, took three daughters as Noble Ladies.
From this point onward,
Cáo Cāo is not referred to by his surname but prefixed with his state.
Cáo Cāo's three daughters:
the eldest, Xiàn,
the second, Jié,
the third, Huá;
Jié was later established as empress.
Hán Suì was at Xiǎnqīn.
Xiǎnqīn County belonged to Hànyáng Commandery.
The "Treatise on Geography" in the Book of Hàn does not record it,
likely because it was established by Emperor Guāngwǔ,
to enfeoff Dòu Yǒu.
Lǐ Xián states: The old city of Xiǎnqīn
was located east of Chéngjǐ County in Qín Prefecture in modern times.
Suì fled.
Xiàhóu Yuān pursued him to Lüèyáng City,
about thirty-some *lǐ* from Suì.
The various generals wanted to attack him,
but some argued they should attack the Dí of Xīngguó.
The *Wèi Lüè* states: During the Jiàn'ān era,
the Dí king of Xīngguó, Ā Guì,
and the Dí king of Bǎiqǐng, Qiān Wàn,
each had tribes of over ten thousand households,
and followed Mǎ Chāo in rebellion.
After Chāo was defeated,
Ā Guì was attacked and destroyed by Xiàhóu Yuān,
and Qiān Wàn fled south into Shǔ.
"Suì's troops are elite,
and Xīngguó's city is strong.
An attack could not be quickly successful.
It would be better to strike the various Qiāng at Chánglí.
The *Commentary on the Water Classic* states: Wǎtíng River
flows south past Chéngjǐ County in Lǒngxī,
then east through the Chánglí Plain,
where it is called the Chánglí River;
the Qiāng tribes such as Shāodāng resided there.
The character 卒
is read as 猝 (suddenly).
They would certainly return to save their homes.
If Suì abandons the Qiāng and defends alone, he will be isolated."
This means if Suì abandons the Qiāng and does not rescue them,
but instead keeps his troops to defend himself alone,
then his situation will be isolated.
He can certainly be captured."
Yuān then left a supervising general to guard the supply train,
and personally led light troops to Chánglí,
attacking and burning the Qiāng settlements.
Suì indeed came to rescue Chánglí.
The various generals, seeing Suì's numerous troops,
wanted to construct a fortified camp with trenches before engaging in battle.
Yuān said:
"We have fought our way across a thousand *lǐ*.
If we now build camps and trenches again,
then the officers and men will be exhausted,
and cannot be used again.
Although the enemy is numerous,
they are easy to deal with."
He then sounded the drums,
and greatly defeated Suì's army.
He then advanced and besieged Xīngguó.
The Dí king Qiān Wàn fled to Mǎ Chāo,
and the remaining masses all surrendered.
He then turned to attack Gāopíng and the Túgè tribes,
and defeated them all.
2 In the third month,
an edict commanded that Duke Cáo Cāo of Wèi's rank be above that of the various feudal kings,
and changed his insignia to a gold seal, crimson ribbon, and *yuǎnyóu* crown.
Under the Hàn system: feudal kings had a gold seal, crimson ribbon, and *yuǎnyóu* crown.
