Dǒng Bā states: The *yuǎnyóu* crown
is made like the *tōngtiān* crown,
nine *cun* high,
upright, with the top slightly slanted,
then straight down forming an iron scroll beam,
with an extended tube placed horizontally in front,
and no mountain-shaped ornament.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month,
it rained.
4 Earlier,
Duke Cáo Cāo of Wèi sent the Lújiāng Grand Administrator Zhū Guāng to garrison Wǎn,
and extensively opened up paddy fields.
Lǚ Méng said to Sūn Quán:
"The fields of Wǎn are fertile.
If there is one harvest,
their population will certainly increase;
'harvest'
means when the rice ripens and is gathered.
Having grain means they can increase their population.
The character 孰
is interchangeable with the ancient character 熟 (ripe).
In the intercalary month,
Quán personally attacked Wǎn City.
The various generals wanted to build earthen mounds,
adding to the siege equipment.
Lǚ Méng said:
"Constructing siege equipment and earthen mounds
will certainly take many days to complete;
by then the city's defenses will have been repaired,
and external relief will certainly arrive,
making it impossible to capture.
Moreover, we took advantage of the floodwaters to enter.
If we linger for days,
the water will certainly begin to recede,
and the return route will be difficult.
I privately consider this dangerous.
Now observing this city,
it is not very strong.
With the sharp morale of the three armies,
attacking simultaneously from all sides,
it can be captured in no time;
and returning with the water,
is the way to complete victory."
Quán followed this.
Méng recommended Gān Níng as the commander for scaling the city.
Níng held a rope in hand,
and climbed the city wall himself,
taking the lead for the soldiers;
Méng followed with elite troops,
personally holding the drumsticks to beat the drum,
and the soldiers all leapt forward eagerly.
They attacked at dawn,
and by breakfast time had broken through,
capturing Zhū Guāng and several tens of thousands of men and women.
Soon after, Zhāng Liáo arrived at Jiāshí.
Jiāshí is located forty-seven *lǐ* north of Tóngchéng County in Ānqìng Prefecture in modern times,
now called Xīxiá Mountain.
They then withdrew.
Quán appointed Lǚ Méng as Grand Administrator of Lújiāng,
and he returned to garrison Xúnyáng.
5 Zhūgě Liàng left Guān Yǔ to guard Jīng Province,
and together with Zhāng Fēi and Zhào Yún led troops upstream to capture Bādōng.
Qiáo Zhōu's *Bā Jì* states: In the sixth year of Chūpíng,
Zhào Wěi divided Bā Commandery, taking Ānhàn and below to form Yǒngníng Commandery.
In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān,
Liú Zhāng made Yǒngníng into Bādōng Commandery.
This was the area of Kuí and Kāi Prefectures in the Táng.
They defeated the Bā Commandery Grand Administrator Yán Yán,
capturing him alive.
Fēi berated Yán, saying:
"Now that our great army has arrived,
why do you not surrender,
but dare to resist and fight!"
Yán said:
"You people are without principle,
invading and seizing our province.
In our province, there are only beheaded generals,
no surrendering generals!"
Fēi was enraged,
and ordered his attendants to drag him away and behead him.
Yán's expression and demeanor did not change,
and he said:
"To behead is to behead,
why the anger!"
Fēy, impressed by his courage, released him,
and treated him as a guest.
He separately dispatched Zhào Yún to follow the Outer River to pacify Jiāngyáng and Qiánwéi.
Jiāngyáng County,
originally belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery.
Liú Zhāng separately established Jiāngyáng Commandery;
in the Táng it was Lú Prefecture.
Qiánwéi Commandery,
in the Táng was the area of Zī, Jiǎn, Jiā, and Méi.
Modern Yú Prefecture was also part of the Hàn-era Bā Commandery,
situated at the confluence of two rivers.
The right one is the Fú Inner River,
the left one is the Shǔ Outer River.
From Yú upstream to Hé Prefecture and Mián Prefecture,
is called the Inner River;
from Yú upstream to Róng and Lú and to Shǔ,
is called the Outer River.
The character 犍
is pronounced *jiān*.
Qiáo Zhōu's *Bā Jì*: In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān,
Liú Zhāng divided Bā Commandery, taking Diànjiāng and above to form Bāxī.
Déyáng County belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery,
the area of Suí Prefecture in the Táng.
Liú Bèi besieged Luò City for almost a year.
Páng Tǒng was hit by a stray arrow,
and died.
Fǎ Zhèng sent a letter to Liú Zhāng,
explaining the situation of strength and weakness,
and said:
"Since the Left General raised troops,
his original intention remains sincere,
and he truly has no ill will.
It was because people of the time thought Zhāng relied on Bèi for support,
yet Bèi turned and attacked Zhāng,
criticizing Bèi for being ungrateful.
...to preserve your honorable family."
"Honorable family"
means Zhāng's family.
Luò City fell,
and Bèi advanced to besiege Chéngdū.
Zhūgě Liàng, Zhāng Fēi, and Zhào Yún led troops to join him.
Mǎ Chāo knew that Zhāng Lǔ was not worthy of planning affairs with,
and also Zhāng Lǔ’s generals such as Yáng Áng repeatedly harmed his abilities,
so Chāo inwardly harbored resentment.
Liú Bèi sent the Supervisor of Jiànníng, Lǐ Huī, to persuade him.
The Records of Shu: In the third year of the Jiànxīng era of the Later Sovereign,
the Yìzhōu Commandery was renamed Jiànníng Commandery.
At this time, Huī was likely the Supervisor of Yìzhōu Commandery;
the historian used the later name of the commandery when recording it.
Persuade,
read as shuì;
same below.
He secretly wrote a letter requesting to surrender to Liú Bèi.
Liú Bèi sent someone to stop Mǎ Chāo,
but secretly supplied him with troops.
When Chāo arrived,
he was ordered to lead his army to camp north of the city,
causing shock and terror within the city.
Liú Bèi besieged the city for several tens of days,
then sent the Attendant Officer of Zhūolù, Jiǎn Yōng, to persuade Liú Zhāng.
Jiǎn,
is a surname.
In the state of Lǔ, there was a senior official named Jiǎn Shū.
The Records of Shu states: Jiǎn Yōng’s surname was originally Gěng,
but later the pronunciation became corrupted to Jiǎn.
The grain and silk supplies were sufficient for one year,
and both officials and people were willing to fight to the death.
Liú Zhāng said:
“My father and I have been in this province for over twenty years.
In the fifth year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng,
Liú Yān governed Yìzhōu,
up to now, twenty-seven years.
The common people have been fighting for three years,
with their flesh and blood staining the fields and wilderness—
all because of me, Zhāng.
How can my heart be at ease!”
He then opened the city gates,
and rode out in the same carriage with Jiǎn Yōng to surrender,
with all those below weeping.
Liú Bèi relocated Liú Zhāng to Gōng’ān,
returned all his wealth and possessions,
and allowed him to wear the seal and ribbon of the General Who Inspires Awe.
Duke Cáo had previously conferred upon Zhāng the title of General Who Inspires Awe,
so he still wore that seal and ribbon.
Liú Bèi entered Chéngdū,
set out wine,
and feasted the soldiers.
He took the gold and silver from the city of Shǔ,
distributed it among the generals and soldiers,
and returned the grain and silk.
All gold and silver, whether public or private, in the city
was taken and distributed among the generals and soldiers;
as for the grain and silk,
it was returned to its respective owners.
He appointed the General of the Central Army, Zhūgě Liàng, as General of the Army,
and the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu
(this Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu is not the Yìzhōu Commandery established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The Yìzhōu Commandery established by Emperor Wǔ
was in the southern region under Liú Shǔ.
It seems Liú Zhāng established the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu alongside the Grand Administrator of Shǔ Commandery, both governing within the walls of Chéngdū.)
and concurrently assigned him to manage the affairs of the Left General’s office.
Managing the office affairs means
overseeing all matters of the military office.
The Records of Officials of Jìn: The Four Píng
were established during times of chaos.
This refers to the four generals: Píngdōng, Píngxī, Píngnán, and Píngběi.
The Adjutant General, Huáng Zhōng of Nányáng, was appointed as General Who Subdues the Caitiffs;
the Attendant Officer, Mí Zhú, was appointed as General Who Pacifies Hàn;
the office of the Grand General of Hàn had Attendant Officers,
whose duty was to participate in planning and deliberation.
Sūn Qián of Běihǎi was appointed as General Who Upholds Loyalty;
General Who Pacifies Hàn, General Who Manifests Virtue, and General Who Upholds Loyalty
were all military titles established by Liú Bèi.
Xǔ Jìng of Rǔnán was appointed as Chief Clerk of the Left General;
Páng Xī as Marshal;
Lǐ Yán as Grand Administrator of Qiánwéi;
Fèi Guān as Grand Administrator of Bā Commandery;
Yī Jí of Shānyáng as Attendant Officer;
Liú Bā of Línglíng as Chief of the Western Bureau;
Péng Yàng of Guǎnghàn as Chief Clerk of Yìzhōu.
Earlier,
Dǒng Hé, while serving in the commandery,
was honest, frugal, fair, and upright,
loved and trusted by the people and barbarians alike,
and was praised in Shǔ as an exemplary official.
Therefore, Liú Bèi promoted and employed him.
When Liú Bèi fled from Xīnyě to the south of the river,
(events recorded in the 65th scroll, year 13),
Liú Bā alone went north to serve Duke Cáo of Wèi.
Cáo appointed him as an assistant,
and sent him to recruit Chángshā, Línglíng, and Guìyáng.
It happened that Liú Bèi had taken these three commanderies,
so Bā’s mission failed,
and he intended to return to the capital via Jiāozhōu.
At that time, Zhūgě Liàng was in Línzhēng.
Shěn Yuē said: Wú established Héngyáng Commandery,
and Línzhēng County belonged to it.
It seems it was established by Wú.
Commentary on the Water Classic: The Zhēng River originates from Yějiāng Mountain on the border of Shàolíng County, west of Chóng’ān County in Héngyáng,
flows northeast past the north of Línzhēng County,
and empties east into the Xiāng River,
called the Zhēng Estuary.
Bā did not comply,
and Liú Bèi deeply resented this.
Bā then entered Shǔ from Jiāozhǐ to rely on Liú Zhāng.
When Liú Zhāng welcomed Liú Bèi,
Bā advised:
“Bèi
is a heroic man,
and his entry will surely bring harm.”
After Bèi entered,
Bā again advised:
“If you send Bèi to attack Zhāng Lǔ,
it is like releasing a tiger into the mountains and forests.”
Liú Zhāng did not listen,
so Bā shut his door and claimed illness.
When Liú Bèi attacked Chéngdū,
he ordered the army:
“Anyone who harms Bā
will be executed along with his three clans.”
When he obtained Bā,
he was very pleased.
At this time, all the commanderies and counties of Yìzhōu looked to the situation and submitted,
only Huáng Quán closed the city gates and held firm,
waiting until Liú Zhāng surrendered and submitted,
before he surrendered.
Thus, Dǒng Hé, Huáng Quán, Lǐ Yán, and others,
who were originally appointed by Liú Zhāng;
(Zhāng appointed Hé as Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu,
Quán as Chief Clerk of his office,
Yán as Protector of the Army);
who were relatives by marriage of Liú Zhāng;
(Zhāng’s elder brother Mào married the younger sister of Wú Yì,
and Zhāng’s mother was of the Fèi clan);
who were rejected by Liú Zhāng;
(Yàng served in Yìzhōu only as a minor clerk,
and someone slandered him to Zhāng,
so he was shaved, shackled, and made a convict);
and who were long-standing objects of jealousy and hatred;
Liú Bèi placed them all in prominent positions,
fully utilizing their talents and abilities.
As a result, all ambitious individuals
strove to encourage one another,
and the people of Yìzhōu
were thus greatly harmonious.
Earlier,
Liú Zhāng had appointed Xǔ Jìng as Grand Administrator of Shǔ Commandery.
When Chéngdū was about to fall,
Jìng planned to climb over the city wall to surrender to Liú Bèi.
Bèi therefore looked down on Jìng
and did not employ him.
Fǎ Zhèng said:
“In the world, there are those who gain empty fame without real substance—
Xǔ Jìng is such a person.
Xǔ Jìng and his younger brother Shào both had high reputations;
the monthly character assessments in Rǔnán
were conducted by these two.
The address ‘Lord’
began in the Eastern Capital.
Changing ‘Illustrious Lord’ to ‘Lord’
is to honor and serve him as master.
It is not possible to explain to every household,
meaning one cannot go door to door explaining it.
Explain,
read as shuō.
But it is necessary to employ him to comfort the hopes of those near and far.”
Liú Bèi then treated him with courtesy and employed him.
During the siege of Chéngdū,
Liú Bèi made an agreement with his troops:
“If the matter is settled,
all items in the government storehouses,
I will have no share in them.”
When Chéngdū was captured,
the troops all laid down their weapons and rushed to the storehouses,
competing to seize treasures.
Military supplies became insufficient,
and Liú Bèi was very worried.
Liú Bā said:
“This is easy.
We only need to cast coins worth a hundred,
coins worth a hundred,
meaning one coin is worth a hundred.
Dù Yòu said: Shǔ cast coins worth a hundred,
inscribed with
‘worth a hundred.’
There were also those stamped as five zhū,
with size and weight matching,
both with a diameter of seven fēn,
and weight of four zhū.
Order officials to conduct government markets.”
Liú Bèi followed this advice.
Within a few months,
the government storehouses were fully replenished.
At that time, some advisors proposed distributing the famous fields and residences of Chéngdū among the various generals.
Zhào Yún said:
"Huò Qùbìng, because the Xiōngnú were not yet destroyed,
considered having a home useless.
(See Volume 19, the fourth year of Yuánshòu under Emperor Wǔ.)
One should not seek comfort now.
We must wait until the whole land is pacified,
and each returns to his mulberry and catalpa,
(pacified,
meaning all is settled.
Mulberry and catalpa,
refer to those planted by one's ancestors in their hometown.
The Book of Songs says: 'For the mulberry and the catalpa,
one must be reverent and respectful.')
Only then is it appropriate.
The people of Yìzhōu
have just suffered the ravages of war,
their fields and homes should all be returned,
allowing them to live in peace and resume their livelihoods,
after which they can be levied and conscripted,
winning their joyful hearts;
it is not proper to seize them
to favor those we love."
Liú Bèi followed this advice.
When Liú Bèi attacked Liú Zhāng,
he left the General of the Household Huò Jùn of Nánjùn to guard Jiāméng City.
Zhāng Lǔ sent Yáng Áng to entice Huò Jùn, requesting to jointly guard the city.
Huò Jùn said:
"You may take my head,
but you cannot have the city!"
Yáng Áng then withdrew.
Later, Liú Zhāng's generals Fú Jìn, Xiàng Cún, and others led over ten thousand men up the Làngshuǐ River,
(Fú,
a surname;
Jìn,
a given name.
Led,
read as 'shuài'.)
The Làngshuǐ is the Xīhànshuǐ,
which is what the Tribute of Yǔ refers to as
"From Bōzhǒng, the Yàng is guided,
flowing east to become the Hàn."
(The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Yàngshuǐ emerges from Bōzhǒng Mountain in Dīdào County, Lǒngxī,
called the Xīhànshuǐ;
it flows southeast to the west of Báishuǐ County in Guǎnghàn,
then southeast to Jiāméng County,
then southeast past Làngzhōng County in Bājùn, where it meets the Làngshuǐ.
The Làngshuǐ emerges from Làngyáng County and flows east,
passes south of that county,
then turns east to join the Hànshuǐ.
When Liú Zhāng attacked Huò Jùn at Jiāméng in the past,
he came up this river.
Further southeast, it enters the Jiāngjīn County of Hànzhōu and flows southeast into the Jiāng.
According to my research, this river
is now called the Jiālíng Jiāng.)
For nearly a year.
Huò Jùn had only a few hundred soldiers in the city,
but watching for their moments of laxity,
he selected elite troops to sally out and attack,
greatly defeating them,
and beheaded Cún.
After Liú Bèi had secured Shǔ,
he divided Guǎnghàn to establish Zǐtóng Commandery,
(the area of Táng's Zǐzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Miánzhōu's Bāxī County,
originally the Hàn dynasty's Fú County,
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
The Records of Huáyáng states: In the second year of Yuánchū of Hàn,
Guǎnghàn moved its seat from Shéngxiāng to Fú,
later to Luò;
Liú Bèi established Zǐtóng Commandery,
placing the county under it.
Suí changed it to Bāxī County.
Táng's Zǐzhōu seat was at Qī,
and it was renamed Zǐtóng Commandery during the Tiānbǎo era.)
Fǎ Zhèng externally governed the capital region,
(Liú Bèi made Chéngdū his capital,
taking Shǔ Commandery as the capital region.)
For a single meal's kindness or the grudge of a sidelong glance,
he would invariably seek revenge,
personally killing several who had slandered or harmed him.
Someone said to Zhūgě Liàng:
"Fǎ Zhèng is too overbearing,
General, you should inform our lord,
to curb his abuse of power."
Liàng said:
"When our lord was in Gōng'ān,
he feared Cáo Cāo's strength to the north,
dreaded Sūn Quán's pressure from the east,
and nearby, feared that Lady Sūn might cause trouble close at hand.
(See the fourteenth year in the previous volume.)
Now he soars freely,
no longer constrained.
(Referring to welcoming Liú Bèi into Yìzhōu.
Constrained,
read as 'fù yòu fān'.)
How can we not allow him to act somewhat as he wishes!"
(Fǎ Zhèng,
styled Xiàozhí.
Somewhat,
read as 'shī zhǎo fān'.)
Zhūgě Liàng assisted Liú Bèi in governing Shǔ,
rather emphasizing strictness and severity,
so many people complained and sighed.
Fǎ Zhèng said to Liàng:
"In the past, when Gāozǔ entered the passes,
he simplified the laws to three articles,
and the people of Qín knew his virtue.
(See Volume 9, the first year of Emperor Gāo.)
Now you have crossed over and occupy a single province,
having just taken possession of this state,
and have not yet bestowed kindness and安抚;
moreover, considering the principle of guest and host,
you ought to lower yourself,
and I hope you will relax punishments and loosen restrictions to comfort their hopes."
(Considering Liàng and others had just arrived as guests,
the people of Yìzhōu were the hosts.)
"You know one aspect,
but not the other.
Qín, due to its lack of virtue,
governed harshly and the people resented it,
so a single commoner's great shout
caused the empire to crumble;
Gāozǔ followed this,
and could achieve great success.
(Great,
meaning large.)
Since Liú Yān's time,
(Yān,
Zhāng's father.)
laws and regulations were lax and permissive,
with mutual flattery,
virtuous governance was not implemented,
and威严 punishments were not stern.
The gentry of Shǔ
monopolized power and acted willfully,
the way of ruler and minister
gradually declined.
Honoring them with positions,
when positions reach the extreme, they become cheap;
indulging them with favors,
when favors are exhausted, they become disrespectful.
The reason for reaching such decay
truly lies in this.
I now use laws to impose威严,
when laws are enforced, they know恩惠;
I restrict them with ranks,
when ranks are bestowed, they know honor.
Honor and恩惠 applied together,
superiors and inferiors having proper measure,
the essentials of governance,
are manifested herein."
Confucius said: When governance is lenient, supplement it with severity;
Kǒngmíng understood this.
Govern,
read as 'zhí lì fān'.
Liú Bèi appointed Jiǎng Wǎn of Línglíng as Magistrate of Guǎngdū.
Once, while on an excursion,
Liú Bèi suddenly arrived at Guǎngdū,
and saw that Jiǎng Wǎn had left many affairs unmanaged,
and at the time he was also deeply intoxicated.
Liú Bèi was greatly angered,
and was about to punish him with execution.
Zhūgě Liàng pleaded:
"Jiǎng Wǎn is a vessel of state,
not merely a talent for a hundred-li district.
His governance takes安抚 the people as fundamental,
not prioritizing superficial embellishment;
I hope our lord will reconsider and examine him."
Liú Bèi deeply respected Liàng,
so he did not impose punishment,
hastily only dismissing him from office.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, attacked Sūn Quán,
leaving his youngest son, the Marquis of Línzī, Cáo Zhí, to guard Yè.
Cáo Cāo selected high-quality officials for his sons' staff,
appointing Xíng Yǒng as Cáo Zhí's Household Steward;
Yǒng maintained restraint through ritual,
never yielding or bending,
and thus they did not get along.
The Retainer Liú Zhēn was skilled in literary composition,
and Cáo Zhí was fond of him.
(Hàn system: A marquis established one Household Steward and one Retainer each,
to serve the marquis
and manage household affairs.
Zhēn,
pronounced zhēn.)
"My lord, you gather the spring blossoms of the retainer,
forgetting the autumn fruits of the household steward,
bringing criticism upon yourself from above,
the offense is not small,
and I truly fear it."
7. The Wei Minister of Works Xún Yōu passed away.
Yōu was profound and discreet, possessing wisdom and caution.
Wisdom to assess affairs,
caution to protect his person.
He often planned strategies within the command tent,
and neither contemporaries nor his own disciples knew what he said.
Cáo Cāo once remarked,
"When Xún Wénruò recommends goodness,
he does not cease until it is advanced;
when Xún Gōngdá removes evil,
he does not stop until it is gone."
He also said:
"The judgments on men by the two Xún Ministers,
grow more trustworthy with time,
I shall not forget them to the end of my days."
Xún Yù was the Hàn Minister of Works,
Xún Yōu was the Wèi Minister of Works.
8. Earlier,
Sòng Jiàn of Fūhǎn, taking advantage of the chaos in Liángzhōu,
proclaimed himself the Héshǒu Píng Hàn King.
Fūhǎn County,
belonged to Jīnchéng Commandery under the Former Hàn,
and to Lǒngxī Commandery under the Later Hàn.
Fū,
is pronounced fū.
The source of the Cìzhī River is west of Héguān in Jīnchéng.
Jiàn, considering himself to reside at the upper reaches of the river,
thus adopted this title.
He established a full bureaucracy,
which lasted over thirty years.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, sent Xiàhóu Yuān from Xīngguó to attack Jiàn.
He besieged Fūhǎn,
captured it,
and beheaded Jiàn.
Yuān separately dispatched Zhāng Hé and others to cross the Huáng River,
and enter Xiǎo Huángzhōng.
The Huáng River's source is northwest of the Yánchí Salt Lake in Xīhǎi,
flowing east to Yǔnyú County in Jīnchéng before entering the [Yellow] River.
The land on both banks of the Huáng River,
is generally called Huángzhōng.
There is also a Huángzhōng city,
located between Xīpíng and Zhāngyè,
in the territory of the Xiǎo Yuèzhī,
hence it is called Xiǎo Huángzhōng.
The region west of Lǒng was pacified.
9. Since the Emperor moved the capital to Xǔ,
he merely maintained his position,
and all his personal attendants and guards were invariably men of the Cáo family.
The Court Gentleman for Consultation, Zhào Yàn, often presented strategies on current affairs to the Emperor,
and the Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, detested him and had him killed.
Later, Cáo Cāo entered the palace on some business,
and the Emperor, unable to bear his fear,
consequently said:
"If you, Sir, can assist me,
then do so generously;
if not,
I beg you to mercifully release me."
Cáo Cāo turned pale,
According to old protocol: when one of the Three Excellencies leads troops,
and attends court,
the Tiger Guard are ordered to hold blades and flank him.
Because he leads troops,
they fear he might instigate a change,
hence they guard against it.
Cháo (court),
is pronounced zhí yáo fān,
the same below.
Xiàn (attend),
is pronounced xián biàn fān.
Cáo Cāo looked at his attendants,
sweating profusely;
thereafter he no longer attended court audiences.
Dǒng Chéng's daughter was a Noble Lady.
After Cáo Cāo executed Chéng,
he demanded the Noble Lady be killed.
The Emperor, because the Noble Lady was pregnant,
repeatedly pleaded for her,
but to no avail.
Empress Fú henceforth harbored fear,
and wrote a letter to her father, Fú Wán,
describing Cáo Cāo's cruel and oppressive conduct.
One who harms others is called cruel.
Oppressive,
means he oppresses his superior.
Wán did not dare reveal it.
At this time,
the matter was exposed.
The execution of Dǒng Chéng is recorded in the sixty-third scroll, fifth year.
In the eleventh month,
[Cáo Cāo] sent the Imperial Counselor Xī Lǜ, bearing the imperial credentials, to retrieve the Empress's seal and ribbons,
with the Minister of Works Huà Xīn as his deputy.
Leading troops into the palace,
they arrested the Empress.
The Empress shut the door,
and hid within a wall.
Huà Xīn broke down the door and tore open the wall,
then dragged the Empress out.
Huà Zǐyú had a fine reputation at the time,
and together with Bǐng Yuán and Guǎn Níng were hailed as the Three Dragons,
with Xīn as the dragon's head,
Yuán as the dragon's belly,
and Níng as the dragon's tail.
Yet Xīn acted thus;
Bǐng Yuán was also ensnared by the official titles Cáo Cāo offered;
only Guǎn Níng maintained his lofty principles.
Alas!
The contemporary ranking of head and tail,
was likely based on fame and position.
Huài (break),
is pronounced guài.
He led Lǜ to a seat,
while the Empress, with disheveled hair, barefoot, weeping as she walked,
passed by and bid farewell, saying:
"Can you not save me?"
The Emperor said:
"I myself do not know when my life will end!"
Turning to Lǜ, he said:
"Lord Xī,
Hàn Imperial Counselor,
one of the Three Excellencies,
hence he addressed him thus.
They then took the Empress down to the Bàoshì prison,
where she died in confinement;
the two imperial sons she bore,
were all poisoned to death,
and over a hundred of her brothers and clan members were killed.
10. In the twelfth month,
the Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, reached Mèngjīn.
11. Cáo Cāo appointed the Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat Gāo Róu as the Law Section Clerk.
The Law Section,
did not exist in the Hàn central government offices,
it was likely established by Cáo Cāo.
Yuàn (clerk),
is pronounced yú juàn fān.
[The law] extended punishment to the wives and children [of deserters].
It means to investigate thoroughly and pursue to the end.
Cáo Cāo wished to further increase the severity of the punishment,
to also include parents and brothers.
Róu memorialized:
"That soldiers desert the army
is indeed detestable.
Jí (detest),
means to loathe.
The Book of Documents says: Do not be angry with the obstinate.
In my humble opinion, it would be appropriate to pardon their wives and children,
firstly to entice them to return.
As per the existing statute,
their hope is already severed;
if we hastily increase the punishment again,
I fear that from now on, soldiers in the army,
seeing one person desert,
and execution extending to themselves,
will also follow and flee,
and we will not be able to kill them all.
Such severe punishment is not the way to stop desertion,
but rather to increase it!"
Cáo Cāo said:
"Well said!"
And immediately stopped the killings.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
the Noble Lady Cáo was established as Empress;
she was the daughter of the Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo.
2. In the third month,
the Duke of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, personally led troops to attack Zhāng Lǔ.
He planned to enter from Wǔdū into the Dī territory.
Wǔdū,
was originally the land inhabited by the White Horse Dī,
Emperor Wǔ opened it and made it a commandery.
He sent Zhāng Hé and Zhū Líng, etc., who attacked and defeated them.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Cáo Cāo marched from Chéncāng through Sànguān Pass to Héchí.
Chéncāng County,
belonged to Right Fúfēng,
in Táng times, Qízhōu,
present-day Bǎojī County.
The Great Sàn Pass
is southwest of it.
Héchí County,
belonged to Wǔdū Commandery.
According to my investigation, the Great Sàn Pass is in present-day Liángquán County, Fèngzhōu.
The Dī, relying on their perilous terrain, refused to submit.
In the fifth month,
[Cáo Cāo] attacked and massacred them.
Commanders from Xīpíng and Jīnchéng, such as Qū Yǎn and Jiǎng Shí, jointly beheaded Hán Suì and sent his head.
At the end of the Hàn, Jīnchéng was divided to create Xīpíng Commandery.
3 Initially,
when Liú Bèi was in Jīngzhōu,
Zhōu Yú, Gān Nìng, and others repeatedly urged Sūn Quán to seize Shǔ.
Quán sent an envoy to tell Bèi:
"Liú Zhāng lacks military prowess,
and cannot defend himself.
If Cáo Cāo were to obtain Shǔ,
then Jīngzhōu would be in danger.
Now I wish to first attack and capture Zhāng,
then take Zhāng Lǔ,
unifying the southern lands.
Even if there were ten Cáos,
there would be nothing to worry about."
Bèi replied:
"Yìzhōu has a wealthy populace and treacherous terrain.
Although Liú Zhāng is weak,
he is sufficient to defend himself.
Now, to deploy troops in Shǔ and Hàn,
transporting supplies over ten thousand lǐ,
hoping to achieve victory in every battle and capture,
with no setbacks in any undertaking,
this is difficult even for Sūn and Wú.
Sūn and Wú,
refers to Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ.
I mean that their strength would be exhausted,
with no further capacity for long-term plans.
Now Cáo controls two-thirds of the realm,
and intends to water his horses at the Cāng Sea,
and review his troops at Wú Kuài.
Wú Kuài,
refers to Wú territory as a major metropolis.
Kuài,
is read with its usual pronunciation.
Another interpretation,
Wú, Kuài,
refers to the lands of the two commanderies Wú and Kuàijī.
Kuài,
is pronounced gōng wài fān.
Yet our alliance, without cause, attacks each other,
providing Cáo with the pivot.
The pivot,
is what allows a door to move.
This means Cáo wishes to shake Wú and Shǔ but lacks the pivot;
if we attack each other,
we are lending him the movable pivot.
This is not a long-term strategy.
Moreover, Bèi and Zhāng are both members of the imperial clan,
hoping to rely on the dynasty's prestige to restore the Hàn court.
Now if Zhāng has offended you,
Bèi alone is filled with dread,
and dares not hear of it.
I beg you to show leniency."
Quán did not listen,
and sent Sūn Yú to lead the navy to station at Xiàkǒu.
Bèi would not allow the army to pass,
and told Yú:
"If you wish to take Shǔ,
I shall let down my hair and enter the mountains,
so as not to break faith with the world."
Meaning, if a clan member is attacked and he cannot save him,
he would have no face to stand in the world.
Let down,
pí yì fān.
Zhāng Fēi garrisoned Zǐguī.
Zǐguī County,
belonged to Nánjùn,
Táng's Guīzhōu.
Nánjùn,
originally administered Jiānglíng.
When Wú obtained Jīngzhōu,
they established Nánjùn south of the river;
after Jìn pacified Wú,
they made Jiānglíng Nánjùn,
and made the Nánjùn south of the river Nánpíngjùn.
The one Liàng occupied was likely the Nánjùn south of the river.
Quán had no choice but to recall Yú.
When Bèi later attacked Liú Zhāng in the west,
Quán said:
"That cunning rogue,
how dare he deceive me like this!"
Bèi left Guān Yǔ to guard Jiānglíng,
while Lǔ Sù shared a border with Yǔ;
Yǔ often harbored suspicions and disloyalty,
but Sù consistently appeased him with friendship.
When Bèi had obtained Yìzhōu,
Quán ordered Zhōng Sīmǎ Zhūgé Jǐn to request from Bèi the various commanderies of Jīngzhōu.
At that time, Quán appointed various generals with the title Biébù Sīmǎ;
thus Zhōng Sīmǎ likely refers to Zhōngjūn Sīmǎ.
Jǐn was promoted from Chángshǐ to Zhōng Sīmǎ,
indicating his position and responsibility were not light.
Jǐn,
qú lìn fān.
Bèi said:
"I am currently planning to take Liángzhōu.
Once Liángzhōu is pacified,
I will then give all of Jīngzhōu to you."
Quán said:
"This is borrowing without returning,
merely using empty words to拖延 time."
Meaning to拖延 time.
Mencius said: Long borrowing without returning,
how can one know it is not actually possession?
Guān Yǔ drove them all out.
Quán was furious,
and sent Lǚ Méng to command twenty thousand troops to seize the three commanderies.
Méng sent letters to Chángshā and Guìyáng,
and both surrendered upon hearing of his approach.
Only the Tàishǒu of Línglíng, Hǎo Pǔ, defended the city and refused to surrender.
When Liú Bèi heard of this,
he personally came from Shǔ to Gōng'ān,
and sent Guān Yǔ to contest the three commanderies.
Sūn Quán advanced and stationed at Lùkǒu,
to command the various armies;
he sent Lǔ Sù with ten thousand men to garrison Yìyáng to block Yǔ.
Yìyáng County belonged to Chángshā Commandery.
Yìng Shào said: It lies north of the Yì River.
Yúdìzhì states: Present-day Ānhuà County in Tánzhōu,
was originally Hàn's Yìyáng County.
Dù Yòu said: Yìyáng County in Tánzhōu,
the Hàn-era old city is east of the present county.
Sòng Bái said: The old city of Yìyáng is eighty lǐ east of present-day Yìyáng County,
and its walls were built by Lǔ Sù.
Quán sent a letter ordering Méng to abandon Línglíng and quickly return to assist Sù.
Méng received the letter,
kept it secret,
and that night,
summoned his generals to give them strategy.
At dawn,
as they were about to attack Línglíng,
he turned to Hǎo Pǔ's old friend from Nányáng, Dèng Xuánzhī, and said:
"Hǎo Zǐtài has heard of loyal and righteous deeds in the world,
and also wishes to perform them,
but does not understand the times.
Hǎo Pǔ,
styled Zǐtài.
Hǎo,
hū gè fān.
Guān Yǔ is in Nánjùn,
and His Majesty is personally confronting him.
He is currently hanging upside down,
struggling to save his own life,
how could he have any spare strength to manage this place!
Now, having calculated our strength and considered our plans to attack here,
the city will certainly fall within a day.
After the city falls,
you will die.
What good will that do,
and causing your hundred-year-old mother with white hair to suffer execution,
is that not tragic!
I reckon this man has not received outside news,
this man,
refers to Hǎo Pǔ.
hence he has come to this.
You may see him,
and explain the calamities and blessings."
Xuánzhī saw Pǔ,
and fully conveyed Méng's meaning;
Pǔ, frightened, came out and surrendered.
Méng welcomed him,
took his hand and went down to the boat together.
After speaking,
he took out the letter and showed it to him,
then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Pǔ saw the letter,
and learned that Bèi was in Gōng'ān and Yǔ was in Yìyáng,
and was so ashamed and regretful he wished to sink into the ground.
Méng left Sūn Hé behind,
entrusting him with subsequent matters.
Kǎoyì says: According to this, Sūn Hé was already dead;
perhaps it was someone else with the same name.
Lǔ Sù wished to meet with Guān Yǔ for talks.
The various generals suspected there might be a change (in the situation) and feared it,
discussing that he should not go.
Sù said:
"Regarding today's matter,
it is appropriate to mutually open and enlighten (each other).
Liú Bèi has betrayed the state,
right and wrong are not yet decided,
how dare Yǔ further desire to violate orders!"
He then invited Yǔ to meet,
each stationing their troops and horses a hundred paces away,
with only the various generals meeting together with single swords.
Sù thereupon reproached and enumerated Yǔ's faults for not returning the three commanderies.
Yǔ said:
"During the battle of Wūlín,
the Left General (Liú Bèi) was personally in the ranks,
exerting all strength to defeat the enemy,
that is to say, the Battle of Chìbì.
Xíng,
hù gāng fān.
(We) do not have a single clod of earth,
and yet you, sir, come wanting to collect land, is that it!"
Sù said:
"Not so.
Initially, (I) met with Yùzhōu (Liú Bèi) at Chángbǎn,
events all seen in the sixty-fifth scroll, thirteenth year.
His plans were exhausted, his thoughts at an extreme,
his will and situation crushed and weak,
he planned to flee far away,
meaning he intended to seek refuge with Wú Jù.
Our sovereign, taking pity on Yùzhōu having no place for himself,
not begrudging the strength of land, soldiers, and people,
enabled him to have shelter and support to relieve his distress;
yet Yùzhōu privately and solely concealed his true feelings,
transgressing virtue and ruining good relations.
Sīdú,
means privately for his own sole benefit.
Duò,
read as huī.
Hǎo,
hū dào fān;
below same.
Meaning, having obtained Yìzhōu,
he had something to rely on.
This is something even an ordinary man could not bear to do,
let alone a lord who leads and governs people!"
Yǔ had nothing to reply.
At that time, (they) heard that Duke Cáo Cāo of Wèi was about to attack Hànzhōng.
Kǎo yì yuē: The Bèi biography says
"Duke Cáo pacified Hànzhōng",
the Sūn Quán biography says
"entered Hànzhōng",
according to, Cáo entered Hànzhōng in the seventh month,
Bèi should not have heard of it immediately,
and in the eighth month Quán had already attacked Héféi,
probably (Bèi) heard that Duke Cáo's troops were beginning to head towards Hànzhōng,
and then led his troops back.
(Bèi) sent an envoy to seek peace with Quán.
Quán ordered Zhūgé Jǐn to deliver the reply,
renewing the alliance and good relations.
Thereupon they divided Jīngzhōu,
using the Xiāng River as the boundary: Chángshā, Jiāngxià, Guìyáng and east belonging to Quán,
Nánjùn, Línglíng, Wǔlíng and west belonging to Bèi.
Bān zhì,
the Xiāng River originates from Yánghǎi Mountain in Línglíng,
reaches Líng and enters the (Yangtze) River,
passes through two commanderies,
flowing for two thousand five hundred thirty lǐ.
Wú and Shǔ dividing Jīngzhōu,
Chángshā, Guìyáng, Línglíng, Wǔlíng used the Xiāng River as the boundary;
Nánjùn, Jiāngxià each followed their own commandery boundaries.
Xià,
hù yǎ fān.
(Zhūgé Jǐn) with his brother Liàng only met at public gatherings,
retiring without private meetings.
4 Autumn,
seventh month,
Duke Cáo Cāo of Wèi reached Yángpíng.
Shuǐjīng zhù: The Jìn River rises among the Dī in Wǔdū,
flows south past the east of Zhāng Lǔ's city.
The city relies on the Xiáo Ridge,
circumference five lǐ;
east facing a steep valley,
profoundly deep a hundred xún;
west and north two sides,
connected peaks and adjoining cliffs,
none could fathom their extremity;
from the south is a winding path,
ascending for over two lǐ.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng called the mountain Báimǎ Sāi,
east facing Báimǎ City,
also named Yángpíng Pass.
The Jìn River flows south into the Miǎn,
called the Jìn estuary.
Some say: Yángpíng Pass,
is today's Bǎiláo Pass in Xīngyuán.
Dù Yòu said: Yángpíng Pass,
is northwest of Bāochéng County in Hànzhōng.
His (Zhāng Lǔ's) younger brother Wèi would not submit,
leading a multitude of tens of thousands to guard the pass firmly,
building a wall across the mountain for over ten lǐ.
Initially,
Cáo, relying on the words of Liángzhōu officials and surrendered men from Wǔdū,
said
"Zhāng Lǔ is easy to attack,
the north and south mountains at Yángpíng city are far apart,
it cannot be defended",
and believed it to be so.
When he went to personally inspect it,
it was not as he had heard,
and he sighed, saying:
"Others' deliberations and estimations,
seldom match one's wishes."
Attacking the various camps on Yángpíng Mountain,
the mountain was steep and difficult to climb,
since they could not capture it in time,
the soldiers wounded and injured were many,
army provisions were nearly exhausted,
Cáo's will was discouraged,
and he wanted to withdraw the army, cut off the mountain and return.
He sent Grand General Xiàhóu Dūn and General Xǔ Chǔ to call the troops on the mountain back.
It happened that the vanguard army became confused at night,
mistakenly entering Zhāng Wèi's separate camp,
the camp was greatly alarmed and scattered in retreat.
Palace Attendant Xīn Pí, Registrar Liú Yè and others were behind the troops,
spoke to Dūn and Chǔ,
saying
"the official troops have already seized the enemy's key camp,
the enemy has already scattered and fled",
but they still did not believe it.
Dūn went forward to see for himself,
then returned to report to Cáo,
(who) advanced troops to attack Wèi,
Wèi and others fled at night.
Kǎo yì yuē: The Wǔdì jì says:
"The Duke reached Yángpíng,
Zhāng Lǔ sent his younger brother Wèi and others to hold the pass,
attacked but could not capture it,
then led (the troops) back.
The enemy's defensive preparations dissolved,
the Duke then secretly sent Xiè and others to take advantage of the dangerous terrain and attack at night,
greatly defeating them."
The Liú Yè biography says:
"Tàizǔ wanted to return,
ordered Yè to supervise the rear various armies.
Yè assessed that Lǔ could be defeated,
galloped to report to Tàizǔ,
(saying) it was better to press the attack,
then advanced the troops,
and Lǔ then fled."
Guō Bān's Shìyǔ:
"Lǔ sent a Wǔguān Yuàn to surrender,
his younger brother Wèi resisted the royal army and they could not advance.
Lǔ fled to Bāzhōng.
Army provisions were exhausted,
Tàizǔ was about to return.
Western Section Head Guō Chén said: 'Lǔ has already surrendered,
the envoy left behind has not yet returned,
although Wèi is not in agreement,
his isolated followers can be attacked.
An army deep in enemy territory, if it advances it will surely conquer,
if it retreats it will surely not escape.'
Tàizǔ doubted it.
At night there were several thousand wild deer,
that charged and broke Wèi's camp,
the army was greatly alarmed,
Gāo Zuò and others mistakenly encountered Wèi's troops,
Wèi thought the main army was attacking him,
then surrendered.'"
Wèi Míngchén Zòu contains Yáng Jì's memorial saying:
"Emperor Wǔ campaigned against Zhāng Lǔ,
with a host of a hundred thousand,
personally went to inspect.
Zhāng Wèi's defense,
can be considered insignificant.
The terrain was dangerous and easy to defend,
even with elite troops and fierce generals,
their power could not be exerted.
Confronting the troops for three days,
(he) wanted to withdraw the army and return.
Heaven blessed Great Wèi,
Lǔ's defense collapsed by itself,
and thereby he pacified it."
Also contains Dǒng Zhāo's memorial.
Its
"relying on Liángzhōu"
and below,
are all from Zhāo's memorial account,
and must be factual.
Now follow it.
When Zhāng Lǔ heard that Yángpíng had fallen,
he intended to surrender.
Yán Pǔ said:
"If we surrender now under pressure,
our contribution will certainly be considered insignificant.
It would be better to rely on Dù Hù and join Pú Hú.
Dù Hù
was the Marquis of Cóng.
Pú Hú
was the King of the Seven Clans of the Bā tribes.
I note that the leaders of the Bǎn Dùn Man tribes had seven clans: Luó, Pú, Dū, È, Dù, Xī, and Gōng.
They did not pay land taxes or levies,
hence they were called the Kings of the Seven Clans.
The other households paid an annual tribute tax,
forty coins per person,
hence there was the Marquis of Cóng.
Sūn Shèng said: Pú
is pronounced fú;
Hù,
is pronounced hù."
Afterward, they pledged their allegiance,
(the character) zhì
is read according to its usual pronunciation.
Then they fled into the southern mountains and entered Bāzhōng.
The present-day Xīngyuán Prefecture
was the ancient territory of Hànzhōng.
South of Xīngyuán is the Dàháng Road,
which leads to Bāzhōu.
The road is treacherous and steep,
taking three days to reach the mountaintop.
The highest point is called
"Gūyún and Liǎngjiǎo,
a hand's breadth from heaven."
Gūyún and Liǎngjiǎo
are the names of two mountains;
they are located in the northern boundary of Dàngqú County, Hàn Bā Commandery, present-day Bāzhōu.
Of the three Bā territories,
this lies in the middle,
hence called Zhōngbā.
In the northern region of Bā is the Mǐcāng Mountain,
overlooking Xīngyuán below,
truly a strategic thoroughfare.
Zhāng Lǔ said:
"I originally intended to submit to the state,
but my intention was not conveyed.
Now I flee to avoid the sharp edge of the enemy,
not with any malicious intent.
The treasures and storehouses
belong to the state."
So he sealed and stored them away before leaving.
When Cáo Cāo entered Nánzhèng,
Nánzhèng County
was the seat of Hànzhōng Commandery.
Also, because Zhāng Lǔ originally had good intentions,
Cáo sent someone to console and instruct him.
The Chancellor's Registrar, Sīmǎ Yì, said to Cáo Cāo:
"Liú Bèi captured Liú Zhāng through deceit and force,
and the people of Shǔ are not yet attached to him.
Yet he contends for Jiānglíng from afar;
this opportunity must not be missed.
Now that we have conquered Hànzhōng,
Yìzhōu is shaken.
If we advance our troops and press upon it,
it will surely collapse.
Even a sage cannot oppose the times,
nor can he miss the opportune moment."
Cáo Cāo said:
"People suffer from insatiability;
having obtained Lǒng,
they again look toward Shǔ!"
Emperor Guāngwǔ's edict to Cén Péng and others said:
"People suffer from not knowing contentment;
having obtained Lǒng,
they again look toward Shǔ."
"Liú Bèi
is an outstanding man,
capable but slow;
he has held Shǔ for only a short time,
and the people of Shǔ do not yet rely on him.
Now that we have broken Hànzhōng,
the people of Shǔ are terrified,
and their situation will collapse of itself.
With Your Excellency's divine intelligence,
pressing upon them in their collapse,
nothing will be unconquerable.
If we delay even slightly,
Zhūgě Liàng, who excels in governing the state, serves as chancellor,
and Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, whose bravery is unmatched in the army, serve as generals.
Once the people of Shǔ are settled,
and they hold the strategic passes and strongholds,
then they will be unassailable.
If we do not take them now,
they will surely be a future worry."
Cáo Cāo did not follow this advice.
After seven days,
a surrendered man from Shǔ reported
"In Shǔ, there are dozens of alarms daily,
and even though the defending generals execute people, they cannot pacify the situation."
Examination of discrepancies: The biography of Liú Yè says
"even though Liú Bèi executed them."
According to Liú Bèi's biography:
"Liú Bèi was at Gōng'ān,
and upon hearing that Lord Cáo had pacified Hànzhōng,
he returned."
Thus,
Liú Bèi was still at Gōng'ān at that time.
"Can we still attack now?"
Liú Yè said:
"Now they have somewhat stabilized,
and cannot be attacked."
How could they be considered somewhat stabilized within seven days?
Liú Yè probably observed that Liú Bèi's defense of Shǔ was unassailable,
hence he spoke thus in response to Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo appointed Xiàhóu Yuān as General Protector of the Capital,
General Protector of the Capital,
established as a title for a commander who oversees all generals;
Emperor Guāngwǔ first appointed Jiǎ Fù to this position.
He appointed the Chancellor's Chief Clerk, Dù Xí, as Commandant of the Capital Guards,
leaving him to oversee affairs in Hànzhōng.
Dù Xí pacified and guided the people,
and over eighty thousand households willingly moved to Luòyáng and Yè.
5 In the eighth month,
Sūn Quán led a host of one hundred thousand to besiege Héféi.
At that time, Zhāng Liáo, Lǐ Diǎn, and Yuè Jìn commanded over seven thousand men stationed at Héféi.
When Lord Cáo of Wèi was campaigning against Zhāng Lǔ,
he left instructions with the Army Protector at Héféi, Xuē Tì,
writing on the edge of the sealed document:
"When the enemy arrives,
then open it."
When Sūn Quán arrived,
they opened the instructions,
which said:
"If Sūn Quán arrives,
Generals Zhāng and Lǐ shall go out to battle,
General Yuè shall defend,
and the Army Protector shall not engage in battle."
Cáo Cāo considered Zhāng Liáo and Lǐ Diǎn brave and sharp,
so he ordered them to fight;
Yuè Jìn was steady and cautious,
so he ordered him to defend;
Xuē Tì was a civil official,
so he ordered him not to engage in battle.
They were doubtful.
Zhāng Liáo said:
"Our lord is campaigning far away;
by the time rescue arrives,
the enemy will surely have defeated us.
Therefore, the instructions mean to strike them before they fully assemble,
break their formidable momentum,
to calm our troops' hearts,
and only then can we hold."
Yuè Jìn and the others did not respond.
Zhāng Liáo angrily said:
"The key to success or failure
lies in this one battle.
If you gentlemen are doubtful,
I, Liáo, will decide alone."
He intended to go out and fight alone.
Lǐ Diǎn said resolutely:
"This is a matter of state importance.
It depends on what your plan is;
how can I let personal grievances make me forget public duty!
I request to follow you out."
Thereupon, Zhāng Liáo recruited daring volunteers that night,
obtaining eight hundred men,
and slaughtered cattle to feast them.
The next morning,
Zhāng Liáo donned armor and grasped a halberd,
leading the charge to break the enemy formation,
killing several dozen men,
beheading two great generals,
and shouting his own name,
he charged through the ramparts right up to Sūn Quán's command banner.
Sūn Quán was greatly alarmed,
not knowing what to do.
He ran and climbed a high mound,
defending himself with a long halberd.
Zhāng Liáo shouted for Sūn Quán to come down and fight,
but Sūn Quán dared not move.
Seeing that Zhāng Liáo commanded few troops,
he then surrounded Zhāng Liáo with multiple layers of troops.
Zhāng Liáo fiercely attacked and broke open the encirclement,
leading several dozen of his followers out.
The remaining troops cried out:
"General, are you abandoning us?"
Zhāng Liáo turned back
and broke through the encirclement again,
rescuing the remaining troops.
Sūn Quán's men and horses were all thrown into disarray,
and none dared to stand against him.
From morning until noon,
the men of Wú lost their fighting spirit.
Then they returned to repair their defenses,
and the troops' hearts were thus calmed.
Sūn Quán defended Héféi for over ten days,
but the city could not be taken,
so he withdrew his army and returned.
As the troops were all on the march,
Sūn Quán and his generals were north of Xiāoyáo Jīn.
*Shuǐ Jīng Zhù*: East of Héféi lies Xiāoyáo Jīn,
where there was originally a bridge over the water.
Suddenly, enemy infantry and cavalry arrived in force.
Gān Níng and Lǚ Méng fought fiercely to hold off the enemy,
while Líng Tǒng led his close guards to escort Sūn Quán out of the encirclement.
He then returned to fight against Zhāng Liáo,
but all his attendants were killed,
and he himself was wounded.
Estimating that Sūn Quán had already escaped,
he then withdrew.
Sūn Quán rode a fine horse onto the bridge at the ford,
but the southern section of the bridge had been dismantled,
leaving a gap of over ten feet without planks.
His close attendant, Supervisor Gǔ Lì, was behind his horse.
"Close attendant supervisor"
is an official title.
"Gǔ"
is the surname;
"Lì"
is the given name.
*Jiāng Biǎo Zhuàn* states: Gǔ Lì
was originally an attendant serving the ruler,
and due to his caution and integrity, he was appointed as close attendant supervisor.
He tugged
at the horse's bridle,
enabling them to leap across the gap.
Hè Qí led three thousand men to meet Sūn Quán south of the ford,
and thus Sūn Quán was able to escape.
Sūn Quán boarded a large ship to feast and drink,
but Hè Qí left his seat, weeping, and said:
"Your Majesty, as the sovereign,
should always act with caution.
What happened today
nearly led to disaster and defeat.
Your subjects were terrified,
as if heaven and earth had vanished.
I hope you will take this as a lifelong warning!"
Sūn Quán stepped forward, wiped away his tears, and said:
"I am deeply ashamed."
Sūn Quán expressed shame and apologized to Hè Qí.
"I will not merely inscribe it on my sash."
*Analects*: Zǐ Zhāng asked Confucius,
and inscribed Confucius's words on his sash.
Hence, he used this to reply to Hè Qí.
6 In the ninth month,
the leaders of the Bā and Cóng tribes, Pǔ Hú, Dù Huò, and Rén Yuē,
each led their followers to submit.
Consequently, Bā Commandery was divided,
with Pǔ Hú appointed as Administrator of Bādōng,
Dù Huò as Administrator of Bāxī,
and Rén Yuē as Administrator of Bā Commandery,
all enfeoffed as marquises.
Later, all three were defeated by Liú Bèi.
7 In winter,
the tenth month,
titular marquises were first established to reward military achievements.
*Wèi Shū* states: Eighteen ranks of titular nobility were established,
with Guānzhōng Hóu as the seventeenth rank,
both granted gold seals and purple ribbons.
Additionally, Guān Nèiwài Hóu was established as the sixteenth rank,
granted copper seals with turtle-shaped knobs and black ribbons.
None of these received tax revenues.
Péi Sōngzhī states: The current practice of nominal enfeoffment
likely began from this.
8 In the eleventh month,
Zhāng Lǔ led his family to surrender.
Duke of Wèi Cáo Cáo welcomed him and appointed him as General Who Guards the South,
treating him with the courtesy due a guest,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Làngzhōng.
Xián states: Làngzhōng County
belonged to Bā Commandery,
now Lóng Prefecture.
According to my research, Lóng Prefecture was later renamed Làng Prefecture to avoid the taboo of Táng Emperor Xuánzōng.
Dù Yòu states: Làngzhōng
is present-day Làng Prefecture city.
"Làng"
is pronounced làng.
Zhāng Lǔ's five sons and Yán Pǔ, among others, were all enfeoffed as marquises.
Xí Zàochǐ commented: Yán Pǔ advised Zhāng Lǔ not to claim the title of king,
as recorded in the sixty-fourth volume, sixth year of Jiàn'ān.
In the future,
who would not think of submitting?
Block the source, and the flow will stop on its own—
is this not what it means?
If one does not understand this but instead values achievements gained through scorched-earth tactics,
this references the story of Xú Fú's scorched head and burned forehead from the former history,
recorded in the twenty-fifth volume, fourth year of Dìjié of Hàn Emperor Xuān.
Then the people would benefit from having chaos,
and customs would compete in killing and conquest,
relying on military force and strength,
and weapons of war would never be sheathed.
Duke Cáo's enfeoffment here
can be said to understand the essence of rewards and punishments.
9 Chéng Yín, Hóu Xuǎn, and Páng Dé all surrendered with Zhāng Lǔ.
Chéng Yín and Hóu Xuǎn
were commanders from Guānzhōng;
Páng Dé
was a general under Mǎ Chāo: after defeats at Wèinán and Jìchéng,
they all fled to Zhāng Lǔ.
"Dé"
is the ancient character for "virtue."
Dé was appointed as General Who Upholds Righteousness.
10 When Zhāng Lǔ fled to Bāzhōng,
Huáng Quán said to Liú Bèi:
"If we lose Hànzhōng,
then the Three Bā regions will be weakened,
and this would be like cutting off Shǔ's arms and legs."
The Three Bā regions
are Bādōng, Bāxī, and Bā Commandery.
He led the generals to welcome Zhāng Lǔ;
but Zhāng Lǔ had already surrendered,
so Quán attacked Pǔ Hú, Dù Huò, and Rén Yuē,
defeating them.
Duke of Wèi Cáo Cáo sent Zhāng Hé to command various armies to pacify the Three Bā regions,
intending to relocate their people to Hànzhōng,
and advanced his army to Dàngqú.
Dàngqú County
originally belonged to Bā Commandery,
but at that time, it was part of Bāxī Commandery.
Xián states: The old city of Dàngqú
is northeast of present-day Liújiāng County in Qú Prefecture.
Dù Yòu states: It is commonly known as Chēqí City.
Sòng Bái states: Dàngqú City
was expanded by Hàn General of Chariots and Cavalry Féng Gǔn,
and is commonly called Chēqí City.
Shī Gǔ states: "Dàng"
is pronounced tú làng fān.
After over fifty days,
Zhāng Fēi launched a surprise attack on Hé,
inflicting a major defeat.
Hé fled back to Nánzhèng,
and Liú Bèi also returned to Chéngdū.
Cáo Cāo relocated over five thousand soldiers who had previously served under Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo,
appointing Píngnán General Yīn Shǔ and others to oversee and command them.
The title Píngnán General
was established by the Cáo family.
The character "nán"
is pronounced nà.
Cáo Cāo ordered Yǎn to dispatch twelve hundred soldiers to assist in the defense of Hànzhōng,
with Yīn Shǔ overseeing their transfer.
The soldiers were unhappy about the deployment.
Yǎn escorted them to the mouth of the Xiégǔ Pass,
then turned back.
Before he reached camp,
Yīn Shǔ's troops mutinied.
Yǎn had with him an escort of one hundred and fifty infantry and cavalry,
all of whom were relatives or associates of the mutineers.
Upon hearing the news,
they were each alarmed,
donned armor and took up weapons,
and could no longer remain calm.
Yǎn calmly explained to them the consequences of success and failure,
offering sincere consolation and encouragement.
They all declared fervently:
"We will follow the Protector-General in life and death,
and dare not have second thoughts!"
Proceeding to the various camps,
he summoned and identified over eight hundred conspirators involved in the rebellion,
who were scattered across the countryside.
Yǎn issued an order: only the chief instigators and leaders were to be punished,
the rest were not to be questioned;
those arrested and sent by the commanderies and counties were all to be released and sent away,
and consequently they all returned and surrendered together.
Yǎn secretly reported:
"It would be appropriate to send a general to the main camp,
the main camp,
meaning Cáo Cāo's camp.
The character "jiàng"
is read in its usual pronunciation,
meaning to send.
Duke Wèi Cáo Cāo dispatched General Liú Zhù with two thousand men to go,
and it was necessary to wait until they arrived before sending them off.
Soon the matter was exposed,
and the various camps were greatly alarmed,
making it impossible to pacify them with words.
It was not possible to use words to persuade them to settle down.
"We should select and retain one thousand of the more temperate new soldiers,
to garrison Guānzhōng,
and send all the rest east."
Send them east to Cáo Cāo's camp.
Immediately selected and differentiated them.
The person in charge,
is the one in charge of military registers.
The character "chāi"
is pronounced chū jiē,
meaning to choose,
also pronounced chū jiā,
meaning to differentiate them by grade.
The character "bié"
is pronounced bǐ liè,
meaning to divide,
to differentiate.
They were of one mind with Yǎn,
and those who were to leave also did not dare to act.
Yǎn sent them all on their way in a single day,
and had the retained one thousand men dispersed to encircle and intercept them.
Dispersed among those departing,
deployed in a line to intercept them.
The eastern troops,
were the troops led by Liú Zhù.
Together with the relocated one thousand men,
he ordered them to proceed east together.
In total, over twenty thousand people were safely delivered.
1 In spring,
the second month,
Duke Wèi Cáo Cāo returned to Yè.
2 In summer,
the fifth month,
Duke Wèi Cáo Cāo was promoted to the rank of King.
Initially,
Commandant of the Central Army Cuī Yǎn recommended Jùlù's Yáng Xùn to Cáo Cāo,
Commandant of the Central Army,
was an office of the Qín,
the Hàn continued it,
until Emperor Wǔ changed it to Commandant of the Capital.
Now Cáo Cāo re-established the Commandant of the Central Army,
which in practice was the duty of the Hàn Commandant of the Capital.
When Cáo Cāo was promoted in rank,
Yáng Xùn issued a memorial praising his merits and virtues.
Some ridiculed Yáng Xùn as an opportunist and hypocrite,
saying Cuī Yǎn had made a poor recommendation.
Cuī Yǎn obtained the draft of the memorial from Yáng Xùn to read it,
and wrote to Yáng Xùn:
"Having read the memorial, the matter is fine,
but the times,
the times!
Change is bound to come."
At the time, Cuī Yǎn's original intent,
was to satirize the critics for being fond of fault-finding without seeking reason.
At the time, there was someone who had long been at odds with Cuī Yǎn,
who reported
"Cuī Yǎn is arrogant toward the world and full of resentment and slander,
his intent is disrespectful,"
taking
"change is bound to come"
as evidence of disrespectful intent.
Cuī Yǎn was arrested and imprisoned,
shaved and made a convict laborer.
The person who previously reported Cuī Yǎn again reported:
"Cuī Yǎn, as a convict,
faced guests with a bristling beard and a direct stare,
bristling beard,
means curly beard;
direct stare means,
his eyes did not look elsewhere.
The character "fù"
is pronounced fú yòu,
same below.
Consequently, Cuī Yǎn was ordered to commit suicide.
The Imperial Secretary Deputy Máo Jiè grieved that Cuī Yǎn was innocent,
and was displeased in his heart.
Someone again reported that Máo Jiè was resentful and slanderous,
Cáo Cāo arrested Máo Jiè and imprisoned him,
Palace Attendants Huán Jiē and Hé Qià both pleaded his case and argued reason,
but Cáo Cāo would not listen.
Huán Jiē requested to investigate the facts of the matter.
The King said:
"The informant reported,
Máo Jiè not only slandered me,
but also harbored resentment on behalf of Cuī Yǎn.
This severs the grace and duty between ruler and subject,
recklessly showing resentment and lament for a dead friend,
dead friend,
means he turned his back on public duty to die for a personal connection.
The character "wèi"
is pronounced yú wèi.
Hé Qià said:
"If what the informant says is true,
Máo Jiè's offense is grave indeed,
not tolerated by heaven and earth.
I dare not twist reason for Máo Jiè to pervert the great moral principles,
Mencius said: internally, the relationship between father and son,
externally, the relationship between ruler and subject,
are the great moral principles of man.
He is upright, loyal, and public-spirited,
and is feared by the multitude,
he should not be like this.
However, human nature is hard to guarantee,
it is essential to investigate,
and verify the facts from both sides.
Now, Your Majesty's grace is such that you cannot bear to bring him to justice,
but this further obscures the distinction between right and wrong."
Cáo Cāo said:
"The reason for not investigating
is to protect both Máo Jiè and the informant."
Hé Qià replied:
"If Máo Jiè truly has words slandering his lord,
he should be executed and exposed in the marketplace or court;
The Analects: Zǐfú Jǐng Bó said: My strength is still sufficient to have him executed and exposed in the marketplace or court.
Yīng Shào said: Officials of rank Dàfū and above are exposed at court,
Shì and below are exposed in the marketplace.
The character "cháo"
is pronounced zhí yáo.
The informant falsely accused a high minister, misleading Your Majesty's judgment,
if this is not investigated and verified,
I privately feel uneasy."
Cáo Cāo ultimately did not pursue a thorough investigation,
Máo Jiè was dismissed and removed from office,
and died at home.
In the third month,
Cáo Cāo led his army back,
leaving behind General Fúbō Xiàhóu Dūn, Commander-in-Chief Cáo Rén, Zhāng Liáo, and others with twenty-six armies stationed at Jūcháo.
The Jìn Shū states: In the early years of Emperor Guāngwǔ’s Jiànwǔ era,
during campaigns in all directions,
the position of Military Supervisor Censor was first established;
once matters were concluded,
it was abolished.
During the Jiàn’ān era,
when Wèi Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) served as Chancellor,
he first dispatched a Grand General to oversee them.
In the twenty-first year,
Xiàhóu Dūn was ordered to command twenty-six armies, which is this instance.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: During the reign of Emperor Shùn of Hàn,
Censor-in-Chief Féng Shè was sent to suppress bandits in Jiǔjiāng,
overseeing military affairs in Yáng and Xú provinces.
Hé and Xú’s Sòng Shū records it as originating with Wèi Wǔ,
while Wáng Guī’s Zhíyí states it began with Emperor Guāngwǔ;
both are incorrect.
Cáo Cāo sent a reply to restore friendly relations,
vowing to renew the marriage alliance.
Sūn Quán left behind General Pínglǔ Zhōu Tài to oversee Rúxū;
the title General Pínglǔ,
was likely created by the Sūn clan.
Because Zhōu Tài was of humble origin,
others were not convinced.
“Humble origin”
means his background was lowly.
At a grand and joyous feast,
Sūn Quán ordered Zhōu Tài to remove his clothes,
then pointed with his own hand to Zhōu Tài’s scars,
asking how each was acquired.
Zhōu Tài recounted each former battle site in response.
After finishing,
he was told to dress again;
Sūn Quán grasped his arm and said tearfully:
“Yòupíng,
Zhōu Tài,
styled Yòupíng.
You fight like a bear or tiger,
sparing no regard for your own life,
having received dozens of wounds,
your skin carved like a painting.
How could I not treat you with the kindness of flesh and bone,
and entrust you with the weight of military command!”
The biography of Zhōu Tài states: When Sūn Quán was staying at Xuānchéng,
he neglected to maintain defenses.
Mountain bandits suddenly arrived,
and as Sūn Quán first mounted his horse,
the bandits’ blades were already crossing.
Zhōu Tài threw himself in front to protect Sūn Quán,
receiving twelve wounds.
That day,
without Zhōu Tài,
Sūn Quán would have been in grave danger.
He also followed in campaigns against Huáng Zǔ,
resisted Lord Cáo,
attacked Cáo Rén,
all with merit,
hence he was entrusted.
When halting the carriage,
he had Zhōu Tài lead troops along the road as escort,
with drums and horns sounding as they marched out;
Yuè Zuǎn said: According to the Sīmǎ Fǎ: Among military music,
drums and flutes are foremost,
making those who hear them valiant and harmonious;
delicate strings and high-pitched bamboo should not be used,
for fear that mournful sounds would move people,
causing soldiers to think of home.
Táng Shào said: The music of drums and pipes
is used for military display.
In ancient times, after Huángdì achieved merit at Zhuōlù,
it was used for alerts and guards.
Liú Xù said: Drums and pipes,
originally the music of armies,
were played on horseback.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
music of the northern tribes
was all placed under the Drums and Pipes Office.
I note that according to Hàn regulations,
a general commanding ten thousand men was provided with drums and pipes.
“Chuī”
is pronounced chāng ruì.
2 In summer,
the fourth month,
an edict allowed King of Wèi Cáo Cāo to use the banners of the Son of Heaven,
and to have his movements announced with “clear the way.”
3 In the sixth month,
Wèi appointed Army Advisor Huà Xīn as Grandee Secretary.
4 In winter,
the tenth month,
King of Wèi Cáo Cāo was ordered to wear a crown with twelve tassels,
ride in a golden-root carriage,
drawn by six horses,
with five seasonal auxiliary carriages.
Dǒng Bā’s Treatise on Carriages and Dress states: The golden-root carriage;
its wheels all have red patterns and double rims,
two hubs and two linchpins.
Gold leaf entwined dragons,
form the carriage’s side rails,
with patterned tigers crouching on the yoke.
Dragon heads hold the yoke,
with auspicious sun tubes on left and right,
and phoenixes standing on the crossbar.
The shaft is painted with patterns,
feather canopy with flowery ornaments.
It bears a large banner with twelve streamers,
painted with sun, moon, and ascending dragons.
Drawn by six horses,
with ivory bits and engraved forehead ornaments,
gold forehead plaques and square throat guards,
pheasant tail plumes inserted,
red tassels and horse trappings,
red felt and fine fur,
with twelve gold ornaments.
The left banner,
made of yak tail,
is on the left yoke horse’s yoke,
as large as a dou measure.
This is the virtue carriage.
The five seasonal carriages,
both stationary and standing, are all like it,
each according to the color of its direction.
For white horses,
their manes and tails are dyed red to make crimson manes.
The one ridden by the sovereign is drawn by six;
the rest are all drawn by four.
Those following behind are auxiliary carriages.
The Jìn Shū records: The five seasonal stationary and standing carriages,
also bear banners with twelve streamers,
each according to the carriage’s color.
Standing carriages have their banners upright,
while stationary carriages have them slanted.
“Wén”
is pronounced wáng fàn.
“Xì”
is pronounced xǔ yǐ,
meaning an iron aperture.
“Wén”
is a horse head ornament.
5 Wèi appointed Wǔguān Zhōngláng Jiàng Cáo Pī as Crown Prince.
Initially,
King Cáo Cāo of Wèi married Lady Dīng,
who bore no sons.
His concubine, Lady Liú,
gave birth to a son named Áng.
Lady Biàn bore four sons:
Pī, Zhāng, Zhí, and Xióng.
The king had Lady Dīng raise Áng as her own.
Áng died at Ráng;
the event is recorded in the sixty-second volume, second year of the Jiàn'ān era.
Cáo Cāo, enraged, expelled her [Lady Dīng]
and made Lady Biàn his principal wife.
Zhí was by nature quick-witted and versatile,
talented and eloquent,
and Cáo Cāo favored him.
Cáo Cāo wished to marry his daughter to Dīng Yí,
but Pī objected because Yí had a squinting eye,
meaning
one eye was small.
Yí thus resented Pī
and, together with his younger brother, the Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate Yì—
according to the "Treatise on Officials of the Jìn": The Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate
was an office established in the Qín dynasty,
continued by the Hàn and thereafter,
responsible, along with the Palace Attendant, for various matters at the palace gates,
with no fixed number of positions;
by the Jìn dynasty,
four positions were established.
Yì,
pronounced Yìzhí,
also pronounced Yángzhì.
—repeatedly praised the talent of the Marquis of Línzī, Cáo Zhí,
urging Cáo Cāo to establish him as heir.
Xiū
was the son of Biāo.
Cáo Cāo secretly sought opinions from outside officials via sealed letters,
and the Imperial Secretary Cuī Yǎn replied with an unsealed memorial:
"Unsealed memorial"
means not sealed.
"According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the eldest son should be established [as heir].
The Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals states: Establish the eldest son of the principal wife, not based on virtue;
establish the son based on status, not age.
Zhǎng
is pronounced zhǎng.
He [Pī] should inherit the legitimate line,
and I, Yǎn, will uphold this with my life."
Zhí
was the son-in-law of Cuī Yǎn's elder brother.
The Deputy Imperial Secretary Máo Jiè said:
"Recently, Yuán Shào failed to distinguish between the principal wife's son and concubines' sons,
leading to the ruin of his clan and state.
Matters of deposing and establishing heirs are of great importance,
and should not be discussed lightly."
The Eastern Section Clerk Xíng Yóng said:
"Replacing the legitimate heir with a concubine's son
is a warning from past generations.
I hope Your Highness will consider this deeply."
Pī sent someone to ask the Grand Master of Palace Counsel Jiǎ Xǔ about strategies to secure his position.
Xǔ said:
"I hope the General will enhance his virtue and magnanimity,
diligently devote himself to the duties of a scholar,
be assiduous day and night,
and not violate the way of a son.
That is all."
Pī followed this advice,
deeply cultivating himself.
Another day,
Cáo Cāo dismissed others and asked Xǔ,
but Xǔ remained silent and did not reply.
Cáo Cāo said:
"I am speaking with you,
yet you do not answer.
Why?"
Xǔ said:
"I was lost in thought,
so I did not reply immediately."
Cáo Cāo said:
"What were you thinking about?"
Xǔ said:
"I was thinking of Yuán Běnchū [Yuán Shào] and Liú Jǐngshēng [Liú Biǎo], and their sons."
The affairs of Yuán Shào and his sons are recorded in the sixty-fourth volume, sixth and seventh years;
the affairs of Liú Biǎo and his sons are recorded in the sixty-fifth volume, thirteenth year.
Once, when Cáo Cāo was about to go on a campaign,
both Pī and Zhí saw him off by the roadside.
Zhí praised his father's merits and virtues,
speaking eloquently and with literary flair,
attracting the attention of all around,
and Cáo Cāo was pleased.
Pī felt disheartened and lost,
but Wú Zhì of Jìyīn whispered in his ear:
"When the King is about to depart,
you should shed tears."
When bidding farewell,
Pī wept and bowed,
moving Cáo Cāo and those around him to tears.
Thus, everyone felt that while Zhí was eloquent, he lacked sincerity.
Zhí acted willfully,
without restraint or refinement,
while the General of the Five Sense Organs [Cáo Pī] employed tactics,
feigning emotions and presenting himself well,
so that the palace attendants all spoke in his favor.
Thus, he was eventually designated as Crown Prince.
The senior palace attendants congratulated Lady Biàn, saying:
The Hàn imperial harem had senior attendants.
"The General has been made Crown Prince;
Pī was General of the Five Sense Organs,
hence they referred to him as General.
You, Madam, should empty the treasury to reward everyone."
Lady Biàn said:
"The King chose Pī as heir
because he is the eldest.
I am merely fortunate to avoid the blame of failing to educate him properly.
Why should I give lavish rewards?"
The senior attendants returned
and reported her words to Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo was pleased
and said:
"Not showing anger in one's expression,
not losing restraint in joy—
this is truly the most difficult."
The Crown Prince embraced the Court Gentleman for Consultation Xīn Pí by the neck and said:
"Do you know how happy I am, Lord Xīn?"
Pí told his daughter Xiànyīng,
who sighed and said:
"The Crown Prince
is the one who will succeed the ruler in presiding over the ancestral temple and the state.
To succeed the ruler,
one must not lack sorrow;
to preside over the state,
one must not lack caution.
He should feel sorrow
and caution,
yet instead he feels joy.
How can this last long?
Will Wèi not flourish?"
The wisdom and insight of women
can surpass that of men.
Some time later,
the Marquis of Línzī, Cáo Zhí, rode in a carriage along the Imperial Way
and exited through the Sima Gate.
According to Hàn Ordinance B: Riding a carriage or horse on the Imperial Way
results in confiscation of the carriage, horse, and equipment for repeat offenders.
Also, the Palace Guard Ordinance states: All who pass through the Sima Gate must dismount.
Thus, the Sima Gate could still be entered and exited.
Under Wèi regulations,
the Sima Gate was only opened when the imperial carriage passed.
The Director of the Imperial Carriages was sentenced to death.
As a result, restrictions on the feudal lords were tightened,
and Zhí's favor declined daily.
Zhí's wife wore embroidered robes,
and when Cáo Cāo saw this from a tower,
he deemed it a violation of regulations
and ordered her to return home and commit suicide.
To charge Zhí's wife with violating regulations
indicates that wearing brocade and embroidery was prohibited at the time.
Yì
is pronounced yì.
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
the Wūhuán of Dàijùn and Shànggǔ, led by Wúchén Dǐ and others, rebelled.
Previously,
the King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, had summoned Péi Qián, the Grand Administrator of Dàijùn, to serve as the Chancellor’s Legal Officer.
Cáo Cāo praised Péi Qián for his effective governance of Dàijùn.
Péi Qián said:
"Although I have been lenient towards the common people,
I have been strict towards the various Hú tribes.
Now, my successor will certainly think that my governance was overly harsh and will therefore adopt a more lenient and benevolent approach.
Those tribes have always been arrogant and unrestrained;
excessive leniency will inevitably lead to laxity.
Once they become lax,
it will be necessary to restrain them with laws.
'Restrain' means
to control
and to regulate.
Judging by the circumstances,
Dàijùn is bound to rebel again."
Later, the Marquis of Wèilù governed the Gāochē,
and though he lived in a different era from Péi Qián, his approach was the same.
'Fù'
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
Several tens of days later,
news of the rebellion by the three Chányús indeed arrived.
Cáo Cāo appointed his son, the Marquis of Yānlíng, Cáo Zhāng, to act as the General of the Valiant Cavalry.
Yānlíng County
belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
The General of the Valiant Cavalry
was first established during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
and was bestowed upon Lǐ Guǎng.
Lù Démíng said: Yān
is pronounced yè wǎn fān,
and also yú jiàn fān.
The Hànshū writes it as
"Yǎn."
Shǐ Gǔ said: pronounced yǎn.
Cáo Zhāng was skilled in archery and charioteering from a young age,
and his physical strength surpassed that of ordinary men.
Cáo Cāo admonished Cáo Zhāng, saying:
"At home, we are father and son;
in official matters, we are ruler and subject.
In all actions, the laws of the king must be followed.
You must be cautious of this!"
5 Liú Bèi stationed his troops at Yángpíng Pass,
and Xiàhóu Yuān, Zhāng Hé, Xú Huǎng, and others confronted him.
Liú Bèi sent his general Chén Shì and others to cut off the Mǎmíng Gallery Road.
Mǎmíng Pavilion
was located in present-day Zhāohuà County, Lìzhōu.
Zhāng Hé was stationed at Guǎngshí,
which
should have been located between Bā and Hàn.
Urgent dispatches were sent to mobilize troops from Yìzhōu.
Zhūgě Liàng consulted Yáng Hóng, an Attendant Officer from Qiánwéi, about this.
Yáng Hóng said:
"Hànzhōng
is the throat of Yìzhōu,
a matter of survival or destruction.
If we lose Hànzhōng,
then Shǔ will be lost.
This is a calamity for our very household;
why hesitate to send troops?"
At that time, Fǎ Zhèng was accompanying Liú Bèi on his northern campaign,
so Zhūgě Liàng petitioned to have Yáng Hóng act as the Grand Administrator of Shǔ Commandery.
All affairs were handled efficiently,
and he was subsequently confirmed in the position.
Thus, he was made to replace Fǎ Zhèng.
Initially,
Lǐ Yán, the Grand Administrator of Qiánwéi, had recruited Yáng Hóng as his Merit Officer.
Before Lǐ Yán had even left Qiánwéi, Yáng Hóng had already become the Grand Administrator of Shǔ Commandery.
Yáng Hóng recommended Hé Zhī, a Document Clerk under his administration, for his talent and resourcefulness.
According to Hàn regulations: the commandery offices and various bureaus each had document clerks
responsible for handling documents.
The stele from the second year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn, recording Fán Yì's restoration of the Huáxià people's poll tax, includes a memorial submitted to the Imperial Secretariat.
It begins with the year, month, and day,
stating: "Your subject Yì, Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng, bows his head and confesses a capital offense in submitting this to the Imperial Secretariat."
It ends with: "Your subject Yì, in fear and trepidation, bows his head repeatedly, confesses a capital offense, and submits this to the Imperial Secretariat."
Following this are the names of the Assistant Yōu,
the Attendant Huái,
and the Document Clerk Móu.
By this time, Hé Zhī had already become the Grand Administrator of Guànghàn.
Therefore, all in the western region admired Zhūgě Liàng for his ability to fully utilize the talents of the people of his time.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, personally led an army to attack Liú Bèi.
In the ninth month,
he arrived at Cháng'ān.
6 Cáo Zhāng attacked the Wūhuán of Dàijùn,
personally engaging in combat.
His armor was struck by several arrows,
yet his fighting spirit grew even fiercer.
Pursuing the defeated enemy northward,
he reached north of Sānggān.
Sānggān County
belonged to Dàijùn.
Sòng Bái said: Present-day Yúnzhōu is 150 lǐ east of the Sānggān supervisory headquarters.
Mèng Kāng said: Gān
is pronounced gān.
Those beheaded or captured numbered in the thousands.
At that time, the Xiānbēi chieftain Kēbǐnéng
originally belonged to a minor Xiānbēi tribe,
but due to his bravery, strength, and lack of greed,
and his fair and impartial administration of justice,
the masses elected him as chieftain.
Seeing Cáo Zhāng fighting fiercely
and crushing all opposition,
he submitted and pledged allegiance.
Thus, the northern region was completely pacified.
7 The officials and people of Nányáng suffered under the burden of corvée labor.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
the defending general of Wǎn, Hóu Yīn, rebelled.
The Grand Administrator of Nányáng, Dōnglǐ Gǔn
(Zhèng Zǐchǎn resided at Dōnglǐ,
and his collateral descendants took this as their surname).
Hóu Yīn sent cavalry to pursue him,
with arrows flying back and forth.
Yú used his own body to shield Gǔn,
receiving seven wounds and dying.
Hóu Yīn's cavalry captured Gǔn and brought him back.
At that time, General Who Conquers the South, Cáo Rén, was stationed at Fán to guard Jīngzhōu.
The King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, ordered Cáo Rén to return and suppress Hóu Yīn.
Merit Officer Zōng Zǐqīng advised Hóu Yīn, saying:
"Your Excellency has followed the will of the people
and undertaken a great endeavor,
and all near and far look to you with admiration.
However, capturing the commandery's general
is an act of rebellion that brings no benefit.
Why not release him?"
Hóu Yīn agreed.
Zǐqīng then scaled the city wall at night, joined the Grand Administrator, gathered the remaining people, and besieged Hóu Yīn.
Just then, Cáo Rén's army arrived,
and they attacked together.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Cáo Rén massacred Wǎn,
beheaded Hóu Yīn,
and once again stationed his troops at Fán.
2. Initially, although Xiàhóu Yuān had won several battles,
the King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, often admonished him, saying:
"A general should have moments of caution and weakness;
one cannot rely solely on bravery.
A general should take bravery as the foundation,
but execute it with wisdom and strategy.
If one only knows to rely on bravery,
they are merely a match for a single ordinary man."
