When Yuān and Liú Bèi had been confronting each other for over a year,
Bèi crossed the Miǎn River southward from Yángpíng,
advanced gradually along the mountains,
and encamped at Dìngjūn Mountain.
The Huáyáng Guózhì states: In Hànzhōng, Miǎnyáng County has Dìngjūn Mountain,
which faces the Miǎn River to the north.
According to the biography of Fǎ Zhèng: "They made camps at Dìngjūn and Xīngshì,"
so Dìngjūn Mountain is precisely at Xīngshì.
Now note: Xīngshì Mountain is located twenty lǐ northwest of Xīngdào County in Yáng Prefecture,
far from Miǎnyáng in terms of distance.
One should follow the Huáyáng Guózhì.
Examination of discrepancies says: The biography of Bèi states:
"They made camp at the strategic location of Dìngjūn Mountain,"
while the biography of Fǎ Zhèng says
"Dìngjūn and Xīngshì."
Now we follow the biography of Huáng Zhōng.
Fǎ Zhèng said:
"Now is the time to attack."
Bèi sent General Tǎo Lǔ, Huáng Zhōng, to take the high ground, beat drums, and launch a clamorous attack.
Yuān's army was greatly defeated,
and Yuān was beheaded.
Examination of discrepancies says: The biography of Yuān states:
"Bèi set fire to the surrounding deer antlers at night.
Yuān sent Zhāng Hé to guard the eastern perimeter,
while he personally led light troops to guard the southern perimeter.
Bèi provoked Hé to battle,
and Hé's army fared poorly.
Yuān divided half his troops to assist Hé,
was ambushed by Bèi,
and died in battle."
The biography of Zhāng Hé states:
"Bèi set fire to the main perimeter at Zǒumǎ Valley.
Yuān went to fight the fire,
encountered Bèi on another path,
engaged in battle,
and they fought hand-to-hand with short weapons.
Yuān then perished."
Now we follow the biographies of Liú Bèi, Huáng Zhōng, and Fǎ Zhèng.
Yóng was appointed to oversee Yìzhōu,
a command given by Cáo Cāo.
After Yuān's army was defeated,
Yóng also died.
Yóng,
pronounced Yú Róng.
They retreated from Guǎngshí back to Yángpíng.
The army was in turmoil,
not knowing what to do.
The supervising general, Dù Xí—
initially, when Cáo Cāo returned east,
he left Xí to oversee military affairs in Hànzhōng.
Shuài,
pronounced Suǒ Lèi.
Issued orders to the various armies, saying:
"General Zhāng is a renowned general of the state,
feared by Liú Bèi.
Today, in this critical situation,
only General Zhāng can bring stability."
Thus, as a temporary measure, they pushed Hé to take command of the army.
Hé went out,
marshaled the troops, and inspected the formations.
All the generals accepted Hé's command,
and the morale of the troops stabilized.
The next day,
Bèi intended to cross the Hàn River to attack.
The generals, considering they were outnumbered,
wanted to rely on the river to form a defensive formation.
Guō Huái said:
"This would show weakness and would not be enough to defeat the enemy;
it is not a good plan.
It would be better to form a formation away from the river,
lure them in,
and attack when they are halfway across.
Then Bèi can be defeated."
Once the formation was set,
Bèi grew suspicious
and did not cross.
Huái then firmly held his ground,
showing no intention of retreating.
He reported the situation to the King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo approved of this,
sent an envoy to grant Hé the authority of the tally,
and reappointed Huái as a Simǎ.
3. In the second month,
on the last day of the month, Rénzǐ,
there was a solar eclipse.
4. In the third month,
the King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, marched out from Cháng'ān through Xiégǔ Valley,
with his army blocking strategic points to approach Hànzhōng.
The Xiégǔ Valley road was treacherous,
and Cáo Cāo feared being intercepted by Bèi,
so he first had his army block the vital locations
before advancing to Hànzhōng.
Some say: Zhēyào is a place name.
"Even if Lord Cáo comes,
he can do nothing.
I will certainly hold the Hàn River region."
So he gathered his troops to defend the strategic points,
and ultimately did not engage in battle.
Cáo Cāo transported grain from the northern mountains.
Huáng Zhōng led troops intending to seize it,
but he did not return by the appointed time.
General Yì Jūn, Zhào Yún, led several dozen cavalry out of camp to investigate.
The title Yì Jūn Jiāngjūn was created by Bèi.
Yún suddenly encountered the enemy,
charged forward to break through their formation,
and fought while retreating.
The Wèi troops scattered and then regrouped,
pursuing him to the camp's edge.
Yún entered the camp,
then had the gates opened wide,
lowered the flags, and silenced the drums.
The Wèi troops suspected Yún had an ambush
and withdrew.
Yún then thundered the drums, shaking the heavens,
and only used strong crossbows to shoot at the Wèi troops from behind.
The Wèi troops were terrified,
trampled each other in chaos,
and many fell into the Hàn River and drowned.
Bèi came personally the next morning,
arrived at Yún's camp,
and looked at the previous day's battlefield,
saying:
"Zǐlóng is all courage!"
Meaning he was bold,
able to resist Cáo Cāo's large army with a lone force.
Cáo Cāo and Bèi held their positions for several months,
and many Wèi soldiers deserted.
Deserted, meaning they fled.
In the fifth month,
Cáo Cāo led all his troops out of Hànzhōng and returned to Cháng'ān.
Liú Bèi thus gained control of Hànzhōng.
Cáo Cāo feared that Liú Bèi would take the Dí tribes of Wǔdū in the north to threaten Guānzhōng.
Wǔdū was originally the land of the White Horse Dí.
Jì said:
"We can persuade them to move north to seek grain and avoid the bandits.
Those who go first will be richly rewarded,
so the earlier ones will know the benefits,
and the later ones will surely follow."
Cáo Cāo agreed,
sent Jì to Wǔdū,
and relocated over fifty thousand households of Dí tribes to settle in the areas of Fúfēng and Tiānshuǐ.
Cáo Cāo had essentially abandoned Wǔdū and no longer held it.
The various Dí tribes scattered and settled in Qínchuān,
and the rebellion of the Fú clan against Huá began from this.
5. Yán Jùn of Wǔwēi, Hé Luán of Zhāngyè, Huáng Huá of Jiǔquán, and Qū Yǎn of Xīpíng,
each occupied their respective commanderies,
proclaimed themselves generals,
and attacked each other.
Jùn sent an envoy to deliver his mother and son to the King of Wèi, Cáo Cāo, as hostages to seek assistance.
Cáo Cāo asked Zhāng Jì,
and Jì said:
"Jùn and the others outwardly borrow the state's authority,
but inwardly they are arrogant and rebellious.
Once their plans are set and their power sufficient,
they will later rebel.
Now, as we are focused on pacifying Shǔ,
it is best to let both sides exist and fight each other,
like Biàn Zhuāngzǐ stabbing the tigers,
sitting back to reap the benefits of their exhaustion."
The Zhànguó Cè says: Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was about to stab a tiger,
when a young servant stopped him, saying:
"Two tigers are currently eating an ox.
The ox is tasty, so they will surely fight.
Then the larger one will be injured,
and the smaller one will die.
Stab the injured one,
and with one move, you will gain both."
Zhuāngzǐ agreed,
and indeed captured two tigers.
Stab,
pronounced Qī Yì.
"Excellent!"
Over a year later,
Luán killed Jùn,
and Wáng Mì of Wǔwēi then killed Luán.
6 Liú Bèi sent Mèng Dá, the Administrator of Yídū from Fúfēng, to attack Fánglíng from the north starting from Zǐguī,
killing Kuài Qí, the Administrator of Fánglíng.
(Zhāng Bó's Wú Lù states: Liú Bèi established Yídū Commandery by dividing Nánjùn Commandery,
administering the three counties of Yí Dào, Hěn Shān, and Yílíng.)
Fánglíng County,
originally belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery.
This commandery was likely established by Liú Biǎo,
who appointed Kuài Qí to defend it;
otherwise, Qí established it himself.
Kuài,
(pronounced with the characters) kǔ guài fān.
To command Dá's army,
Liú Fēng,
originally the son of the Lóu Marquis of the Kòu family,
was the nephew of the Liú family of Chángshā.
When Bèi arrived in Jīngzhōu,
as he had no heir,
he adopted him as his son.
Shēn Dān, the Administrator of Shàngyōng, surrendered his commandery.
Shàngyōng County,
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery.
(Xián states: The old city is west of present-day Qīngshuǐ County in Fáng Prefecture.)
(Wèi Lüè states: Shēn Dān was initially between Xīchéng and Shàngyōng,
gathering several thousand households,
and communicated with Zhāng Lǔ;
he also sent envoys to Cáo Gōng,
who granted him the title of General,
and appointed him as Commandant of Shàngyōng.)
Surrendered,
(pronounced with the character) hù jiāng fān.
He was appointed Administrator of Shàngyōng,
and his younger brother Shēn Yí was appointed General of Establishing Trust and Administrator of Xīchéng.
Xīchéng County,
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery,
Bèi also divided it into a commandery and appointed Yí;
in the Táng dynasty, it became Jīn Prefecture.
7 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Liú Bèi proclaimed himself King of Hànzhōng,
setting up an altar at Miǎnyáng.
Miǎnyáng County,
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery.
Officials accompanied him in their positions,
after reading the memorial,
he then bowed and received the seal and ribbon,
and donned the king's crown.
He then sent a memorial via post,
returning the seals and ribbons of the Left General and Marquis of Yíchéng Tíng that had been previously conferred upon him.
(The Left General and Marquis of Yíchéng Tíng,
were both titles conferred by Cáo Cāo.)
Presented,
(pronounced with the character) shí zhǎng fān.
He promoted Yìyáng's Wèi Yán, a General of the Yámén, to General Who Pacifies Distant Lands.
(Yámén and Zhènyuǎn,
were both military titles created by Liú Bèi.)
To guard Hànchuān.
(Emperor Wén of Wèi established Yìyáng Commandery by dividing Nányáng Commandery,
and also established Yìyáng County under it;
this occurred after Yán entered Shǔ,
recorded retrospectively by the historian.)
General Who Pacifies Distant Lands,
was likely created by Bèi.
(Sòng Bái states: Yìyáng,
in the Táng dynasty was Shēn Prefecture,
in the Sòng dynasty was Xìnyáng Army.)
He appointed Xǔ Jìng as Grand Tutor,
Fǎ Zhèng as Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
Guān Yǔ as Front General,

Mópō is in Jiá County, Yǐngchuān,
about fifteen lǐ in length and width.
In the first year of Qīnglóng of Wèi,
a dragon appeared at the pond,
so it was renamed Lóngpō.
Guān Yǔ had a camp at Wéitóu,
and another camp at Sìzhǒng,
Huǎng then announced he would attack the Wéitóu camp but secretly attacked Sìzhǒng.
As it was about to collapse,
Yǔ personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry to engage in battle;
above "personally led"
there is
"Yǔ"
to clarify the meaning.
They retreated and fled.
Yǔ's siege trenches had ten layers of deer antlers,
Huǎng pursued Yǔ,
and together entered the siege lines,
breaking them,
Fù Fāng and Hú Xiū both died,
Yǔ then lifted the siege and retreated,
but his boats still occupied the Miǎn River,
isolating Xiāngyáng and cutting off communication.
Lǚ Méng arrived at Xúnyáng,
concealing all his elite troops [AS-87F7] within,
he had men in plain clothes row the oars,
dressed as merchants,
traveling day and night.
The sentry posts Guān Yǔ had placed along the river
were all captured and bound,
which is why Guān Yǔ did not hear of it.
Even though the sentries were captured and bound,
had Mí and Fù not harbored thoughts of betrayal,
Guān Yǔ could still have been informed.
When Guān Yǔ led his army out,
Fāng and Rén did not fully supply the military provisions,
and Guān Yǔ said,
"When I return,
I will deal with them."
Fāng and Rén were both afraid.
Thereupon, Méng ordered the former Cavalry Commandant Yú Fān
to write a letter persuading Rén,
laying out the prospects of success and failure.
Upon receiving the letter, Rén immediately surrendered.
Fān said to Méng:
"This is deceptive warfare,
meaning Méng employed deceptive tactics in his military operations.
Deceptive,
ancient pronunciation: jué.
Leave troops to guard the city."
Then he took Rén to Nánjùn.
Took,
pronounced as usual.
Méng showed Rén to them,
and Fāng then opened the gates and came out to surrender.
Méng entered Jiānglíng,
released Yú Jìn from imprisonment,
and obtained the families of Guān Yǔ and his officers and soldiers.
He comforted them all,
and issued an order to the army:
"Do not disturb the households of the people,
nor make any demands."
A soldier under Méng's command,
who was from the same commandery as Méng,
took a bamboo hat from a civilian household to cover official armor;
although the armor was public property,
Méng still considered it a violation of military orders.
He could not disregard the law because of their shared hometown ties,
so he shed tears and executed him.
Thereupon, the army was shaken with fear,
and lost items were not picked up on the roads.
Méng sent his close associates morning and evening to care for the elderly,
asking about their needs,
providing medicine and doctors to the sick,
and giving clothing and food to the hungry and cold.
The treasures stored in Guān Yǔ's residence
were all sealed and kept until Sūn Quán arrived.
When Guān Yǔ heard that Nánjùn had fallen,
he immediately fled southward.
Cáo Rén gathered his generals for discussion,
and all said:
"Now, taking advantage of Guān Yǔ's peril and fear,
we can pursue and capture him."
Zhào Yǎn said:
"Sūn Quán took advantage of the difficulty of Guān Yǔ's continuous warfare,
took advantage,
should be 'jiǎo',
meaning to seize an opportunity.
Difficulty,
pronunciation: nàn.
Referring to continuous warfare with Cáo Rén.
Considering Guān Yǔ's return to rescue,
fearing we would exploit their mutual exhaustion,
therefore he spoke submissively to seek effectiveness,
seek effectiveness,
meaning to seek to prove oneself.
Some say: to speak humbly in order to achieve success.
Now Guān Yǔ is already isolated and fleeing,
meaning Guān Yǔ has lost his foundation,
and is isolated and fleeing.
If we pursue deeply into the north,
Sūn Quán will then shift his vigilance to that side,
and will create trouble for us.
Vigilance,
means to estimate,
to guard against;
meaning to estimate that Guān Yǔ can no longer cause harm,
then shift his vigilance against Guān Yǔ to guard against Cáo Cāo,
and will certainly become a problem for Cáo Cāo.
Rén then lifted the state of alert.
Zhào Yǎn's strategy,
this is what the strategists of the Warring States period called the strategy of benefiting both sides and preserving both.
Lifted the alert,
meaning to withdraw the troops on alert,
and no longer pursue Guān Yǔ.
Later, Lù Xùn defeated Liú Bèi in the gorge,
gathered his troops and returned,
and did not pursue Bèi further,
his strategy also came from this.
Fearing that the generals would pursue him,
indeed quickly ordered Rén as Yǎn had strategized.
Guān Yǔ repeatedly sent messengers to communicate with Lǚ Méng,
and Méng always treated his messengers generously,
allowing them to roam the city,
delivering greetings to every household,
sometimes writing personal letters to show sincerity.
When Guān Yǔ's men returned,
they privately inquired and discussed,
inquire,
means to ask.
They saw that they were treated better than usual,
so Guān Yǔ's officers and soldiers lost their will to fight.
The reason Lǚ Méng captured Guān Yǔ
was simply to win over his men.
Harm,
pronunciation: yàng.
When Sūn Quán arrived at Jiānglíng,
all the officials and officers of Jīngzhōu submitted and pledged allegiance;
only the Administrative Assistant of Wǔlíng, Pān Jùn, claimed illness and did not appear.
Quán sent people with a bed to his home to carry him,
Jùn lay face down on the bed mat and did not rise,
tears streaming down his face,
sobbing uncontrollably with grief.
Quán called him by his courtesy name and spoke to him,
Pān Jùn's courtesy name was Chéngmíng.
He had his close associates wipe his face with a towel.
Jùn rose,
stepped down to the ground and bowed in gratitude,
and was immediately appointed as Administrative Assistant.
All military affairs of Jīngzhōu
were consulted with him.
Hǎo Pǔ, Mí Fāng, and Fù Shìrén in Wú,
were not heard of for anything notable,
but the way Pān Jùn presented himself
was on par with Lù Xùn and Zhūgě Jǐn.
Those with discernment should observe people from this perspective.
He plotted to attach Wǔlíng to the King of Hànzhōng, Liú Bèi.
According to the Hàn system,
the Regional Governor and Inspector oversaw the commanderies,
and each commandery had an Administrative Assistant.
Zhòu,
is the same as Zhòu.
Entice,
pronunciation: yòu.
Quán did not listen;
he specially summoned and asked Jùn,
Jùn replied:
"With five thousand troops,
it is enough to capture Zhòu."
Quán said:
"Why do you underestimate him?"
Jùn said:
"Zhòu is from an old family of Nányáng,
the Fán clan of Nányáng,
were maternal relatives of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
hence called an old family.
But in reality, he has no talent or strategy.
The reason I know this is,
Zhòu once prepared a feast for people of the province,
but by noon,
food was still not available,
and he himself got up more than ten times,
this is also like observing a dwarf's one act to judge his skill."
Dwarf,
an entertainer,
who uses humor and laughter to gain favor.
Observing one act,
is enough to judge his skill.
He then sent Jùn with five thousand men,
and indeed, he beheaded and pacified him.
Quán appointed Lǚ Méng as the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn,
enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Chánlíng,
awarded him one hundred million cash,
and five hundred catties of gold;
he appointed Lù Xùn as the concurrent Grand Administrator of Yídū.
The Wú Lù states: The Shǔ Emperor Zhāoliè established Yídū Commandery at Xīlíng.
That is Yílíng;
in the Táng dynasty, it was the Yílíng Commandery of Xiázhōu.
In the eleventh month,
Fán Yǒu, the Administrator of Yídū appointed by the King of Hànzhōng Liú Bèi, abandoned his commandery and fled.
The various city officials and the chieftains of the Man and Yí tribes all surrendered to Lù Xùn.
Lù Xùn requested gold, silver, and bronze seals to provisionally confer upon those newly submitting.
He attacked the Shǔ generals Zhān Yàn and others.
Zhān,
is a surname;
during the Zhōu dynasty there was Zhān Fù,
and in Chǔ there was Zhān Yǐn.
He defeated and subdued them all,
and in total, those killed, captured, recruited, and accepted numbered in the tens of thousands.
Sūn Quán appointed Lù Xùn as Right Protector of the Army and General Who Guards the West,
advanced his fief to Marquis of Lóu,
stationed him at Yílíng,
and had him guard the Xiákǒu.
Lóu County,
during the Former Hàn belonged to the Kuàijī Commandery,
during the Later Hàn belonged to the Wú Commandery.
Fàn Chéngdà's *Wújùnzhì* states: Lóu County,
is now called Kūnshān County.
Three *lǐ* to the northeast is a village,
named Lóu County,
which was likely the seat of the ancient Lóu County.
Xiákǒu,
is the mouth of the Xīlíng Gorge.
The *Yídūjì* says: From the Huángniú Rapids eastward into the Xīlíng region,
to Xiákǒu is about one hundred *lǐ*.
The mountains and rivers wind and twist,
with high mountains and layered peaks on both banks.
Unless it is midday or midnight,
one cannot see the sun or moon.
Guān Yǔ, knowing he was isolated and desperate,
then went west to defend Màichéng.
The *Jīngzhōujì* says: Southeast of Dāngyáng County in Nánjùn Commandery is Màichéng.
Guān Yǔ feigned surrender,
set up banners and flags with straw dummies on the city walls,
and then fled.
His troops all dispersed,
leaving him with only a dozen or so cavalry.
Sūn Quán had previously sent Zhū Rán and Pān Zhāng to cut off his escape routes.
In the twelfth month,
Pān Zhāng's Major Mǎ Zhōng captured Guān Yǔ and his son Guān Píng at Zhāngxiāng.
The *Shuǐjīngzhù* states: The Zhāng River originates from the Jīng Mountains east of Línjū County,
flows south past the Zhāngxiāng south of Línjū County,
where Pān Zhāng captured Guān Yǔ.
The Zhāng River then flows south past Dāngyáng County,
and further south past the east of Màichéng.
Thus, Jīngzhōu was pacified.
Earlier,
the Lieutenant General Quán Cóng of Wú Commandery
Quán,
is the surname;
Cóng,
is the given name.
Sūn Quán, fearing the plan would leak,
kept it to himself and did not reply;
but after Guān Yǔ had been captured,
Sūn Quán held a banquet at Gōng'ān,
turned to Quán Cóng and said:
"You previously presented this plan,
and although I did not reply to you,
today's victory,
is also partly your achievement."
Thereupon, he enfeoffed Quán Cóng as Marquis of Yánghuátíng.
Sūn Quán also appointed Liú Zhāng as Governor of Yìzhōu,
stationed at Zǐguī.
Not long after,
Liú Zhāng died.
When Liú Bèi entered Yìzhōu,
he moved Liú Zhāng to Gōng'ān,
and now he was obtained by Sūn Quán.
Jǐ,
is pronounced jū qǐ fān.
Lǚ Méng, before he could receive his enfeoffment, fell ill.
Sūn Quán had him brought and placed in a residence next to his own,
and tried every possible means to treat and care for him.
Whenever acupuncture was applied,
Sūn Quán would feel distressed for him.
Wishing to see his complexion often,
yet fearing to disturb him,
he often peered at him through holes in the wall.
If he saw that he could eat a little,
he would happily look at his attendants;
otherwise, he would sigh and groan,
unable to sleep at night.
When Lǚ Méng's illness showed signs of improvement,
Sūn Quán issued a decree of amnesty,
and all the officials came to congratulate him.
But soon after,
he ultimately died,
at the age of forty-two.
Sūn Quán was extremely grieved,
and established three hundred households to guard his tomb.
Later, Sūn Quán, discussing Zhōu Yú, Lǔ Sù, and Lǚ Méng with Lù Xùn, said:
"Gōngjǐn was heroic and fierce,
with courage and strategy surpassing others.
He thus defeated Mèngdé,
and opened up and expanded Jīngzhōu.
He stands far above, with few peers.
Zǐjìng, through Gōngjǐn's introduction, came to me.
When I feasted and conversed with him,
he immediately spoke of the grand strategy for the imperial enterprise.
This was one delight.
The event is recorded in the sixty-third scroll, fifth year.
When Cáo Cáo boasted that he was leading several hundred thousand troops by both water and land,
'boasting' means,
to exaggerate and speak grandly.
and I consulted my advisors on what to do,
no one was suitable to answer first;
'no one was suitable to answer first,'
means no one was fit to answer first.
Shì,
is pronounced dí.
Qín Sōng,
styled Wénbiǎo.
Zǐjìng immediately refuted them, saying it was not feasible.
Bó,
means to differ;
to raise a dissenting opinion to correct the errors of the majority view.
Bó,
is pronounced běi jiǎo fān.
I entrusted him with the troops,
and he went forth and attacked them.
This was the second delight.
The event is recorded in the sixty-fifth scroll, thirteenth year.
The event is recorded in the sixty-sixth scroll, fifteenth year.
These are not enough to detract from his two strengths.
The Duke of Zhōu did not demand perfection from any one person,
the *Analects* records the words of the Duke of Zhōu to the Duke of Lǔ.
I have often compared him to Dèng Yǔ.
Dèng Yǔ proposed strategies to initiate Emperor Guāngwǔ's restoration enterprise,
but later he could not pacify the Chìméi,
hence I compared Sù to him.
Lǚ Méng,
styled Zǐmíng.
Shào,
is pronounced shì zhào fān.
Jù,
means difficult.
Yì,
is pronounced yǐ chì fān.
When he grew up,
his learning broadened and improved,
his planning and strategy became ingenious and profound.
He can be ranked next to Gōngjǐn,
only his eloquence and brilliance in discussion were not equal.
In planning to capture Guān Yǔ,
he surpassed Zǐjìng.
Zǐjìng replied to my letter saying:
'When an emperor arises,
there are always those who clear the way.
Yǔ is not worth worrying about.'
Meaning Guān Yǔ's strength
was merely sufficient to be the one clearing the way for Wú.
He was just making grandiose statements outwardly,
and I also excused him,
not strictly blaming him.
However, in managing the army and encampments,
he never failed to enforce orders and prohibitions.
Within his jurisdiction, there were no derelictions of duty,
meaning within his jurisdiction,
no one neglected their duties to incur blame.
His methods were also excellent."
Sūn Quán and Yú Jìn were riding horses side by side.
Yú Fān shouted at Yú Jìn:
"You are a surrendered captive,
how dare you ride abreast with my lord!"
He raised his whip as if to strike Yú Jìn.
Kàng,
means to raise.
When Sūn Quán declared himself a vassal,
King of Wèi Cáo Cāo recalled Zhāng Liáo and other armies to rescue Fán.
Before they arrived, the siege was lifted.
Xú Huǎng led his troops back to Mópō.
Cáo Cāo welcomed Huǎng from seven *lǐ* away,
and held a grand banquet.
The King raised his cup to Huǎng and said:
"The preservation of Fán and Xiāngyáng,
is the achievement of you, General."
He also richly rewarded Huán Jiē,
appointing him as a Secretary.
Cáo Cāo was concerned about the remaining people of Jīngzhōu and those engaged in military agriculture in Hànchuān.
This Hànchuān,
refers to the area around Xiāng and Fán, up and down,
the lands on the left and right of the Hàn River.
Sīmǎ Yì said:
"Jīngchǔ is fragile and easily agitated.
Guān Yǔ has just been defeated.
Those who committed evil deeds
are hiding and watching.
If we relocate the good people,
it will hurt their feelings,
and will cause those who leave not to dare return."
Cáo Cāo said:
"That is correct."
16. Emperor Cáo of Wèi appointed Sūn Quán as General of Agile Cavalry,
granted him the imperial tally,
appointed him Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Nánchāng.
Nánchāng County
belonged to Yùzhāng Commandery.
Piào
is pronounced piào.
He also sent Zhū Guāng and others back,
as Zhū Guāng had been captured by Quán,
see the nineteenth year of the previous scroll.
They spoke of the Mandate of Heaven.
Cáo showed Quán’s letter to his subordinates, saying:
“Does this lad want to perch me atop a stove fire!”
Palace Attendant Chén Qún and others all said:
“The fortune of Hàn has already ended,
and not just today.
Your Highness’s merit and virtue are lofty,
and Qún and others look to you with hope.
Zhù
means to look to with hope.
This is the response of Heaven and men,
with different voices speaking in unison.
Your Highness should ascend to the great throne;
what further doubt is there!”
Cáo said:
“If the Mandate of Heaven lies with me,
I shall be King Wén of Zhōu.”
King Wén possessed two-thirds of the realm,
yet served Yīn.
Your subject Guāng remarks: Education and transformation
are urgent tasks of the state,
yet vulgar officials neglect them;
customs and mores
are great matters of the realm,
yet mediocre rulers ignore them.
Only the wise and discerning gentleman,
with deep insight and long-term consideration,
then knows how great their benefit is and how far-reaching their achievement.
Emperor Guāngwǔ encountered the decline of Hàn,
with heroes in turmoil,
yet he rose vigorously from commoner status,
revived and restored the former legacy,
campaigned in all directions,
with not a day to spare,
yet was able to esteem and promote classical learning,
receive and extend courtesy to Confucian scholars,
establish and expand schools,
cultivate and clarify rites and music.
Once military achievements were accomplished,
civil virtue also became pervasive.
Succeeded by Emperors Xiàomíng and Xiàozhāng,
they followed and pursued the former aspirations.
Yù
means to follow,
to comply.
Yù
is pronounced yù.
They studied the classics and inquired about the Way.
From the dukes, ministers, and high officials down to the officials of commanderies and counties,
all selected and employed those who were clear in the classics and cultivated in conduct.
Even the Tiger Guard and imperial guards all studied the Classic of Filial Piety,
and children of the Xiōngnú also attended the Imperial University.
Thus, education was established above,
and customs formed below.
Those loyal, honest, and pure-cultivated gentlemen
were not only esteemed by the gentry,
jìnshēn,
meaning those who inserted the tablet and wore the sash,
the dukes, ministers, and high officials at court.
The foolish, base, and corrupt persons
were not only not tolerated by the court,
but were also rejected by their villages.
Since the Three Dynasties perished,
the beauty of customs and transformation
had never been as flourishing as in the Eastern Hàn.
After Emperor Hé and onward,
noble relatives monopolized power,
favorites wielded authority,
rewards and punishments lacked standards,
bribery was openly practiced,
the worthy and foolish were jumbled together,
right and wrong were overturned,
it could be called chaotic.
Yet it still did not reach the point of perishing,
because above there were dukes, ministers, and high officials like Yuán Ān, Yáng Zhèn, Lǐ Gù, Dù Qiáo, Chén Fān, Lǐ Yīng and their like, who remonstrated at court,
using public righteousness to support its peril,
and below there were commoner scholars like Fú Róng, Guō Tài, Fàn Pāng, Xǔ Shào and their kind,
who established private discussions to rescue its failures.
Private discussions means
that they could not participate in court deliberations,
but privately established discussions below,
to rectify the errors of court deliberations.
Some even braved the axe and halberd,
falling dead in front,
yet loyalty and righteousness stirred fervently,
rising successively behind,
following one after another to execution,
regarding death as returning home.
Was it only the worth of these few men?
It was also the legacy of transformation left by Emperors Guāngwǔ, Míng, and Zhāng.
At that time,
if a wise ruler had arisen and revived it,
then the fortune of the Hàn house might still have been immeasurable.
Unfortunately, inheriting the remnants of decline and decay,
further compounded by the folly and cruelty of Emperors Huán and Líng,
who nurtured treacherous and wicked men,
Kǒng Ānguó said: Huí
means wicked.
Chóng
is pronounced chóng.
They exterminated loyal and good men,
worse than enemies;
accumulating the indignation of many scholars,
storing the anger of the realm.
Then Hé Jìn summoned foreign troops,
Dǒng Zhuó seized the opportunity,
Yuán Shào and his followers thus created calamity,
causing the imperial carriage to wander in exile,
the ancestral temples to become ruins,
the royal house to be overthrown,
the common people to suffer bitterly,
the great mandate to fall and cease,
beyond recovery.
Yet those in the provinces and commanderies who held troops and controlled territories,
though they devoured each other,
still never failed to use honoring Hàn as their pretext.
With the violent and fierce nature of Cáo Cāo of Wèi,
added to his great merit for the realm,
he long harbored the heart of no ruler,
yet until his death he dared not depose Hàn and establish himself,
was it that his ambition did not desire it?
He still feared reputation and righteousness and restrained himself.
From this we see,
how can education and transformation be neglected,
how can customs and mores be ignored!

Zhōngyuán First Year
(Bǐngchén, 56) Hóng's Lì Shì says: In Chéngdū there is a Han dynasty stele for the "Zūn Jiàn Gé" built by the Shǔjùn Prefect Hé Jūn,
at the end of which it says
"Jianwu Zhōngyuán Second Year, sixth month".
According to Fàn's historical work's Basic Annals,
Jianwu lasted only thirty-one years,
the following year was changed to Zhōngyuán,
and it is directly recorded as Zhōngyuán First Year.
Looking at this inscription,
it shows that although Zhōngyuán was separately designated,
it was still prefixed with Jianwu,
like the Wén and Jǐng eras having Zhōngyuán and Hòuyuán designations.
Also, the Treatise on Sacrifices records the edict granting amnesty after the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
explicitly stating
"changed Jianwu thirty-second year to Jianwu Zhōngyuán First Year".
The Treatise on the Eastern Barbarians, section on the Wōguó,
"In Jianwu Zhōngyuán second year,
they came to present tribute,"
provides very clear evidence.
Sòng Jǔgōng's Jìyuán Tōngpǔ says:
"Both the Basic Annals and the Treatise come from Fàn's history,
there must have been errors in transmission and copying,
scholars lacking careful scrutiny,
arbitrarily deleted it.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng had both Dàtóng and Dàtōng eras containing the character 'zhōng'
this also followed this precedent.
Sīmǎ Gōng, when composing the Comprehensive Mirror,
did not adopt this theory."
I note, examining the Kǎoyì,
Wēn Gōng was not rejecting Sòng's theory,
but following Yuán's and Fàn's histories using Zhōngyuán
for the sake of simplicity.
